interpretation: The header image shows the full recipe at once, including hierarchy through opacity: the most important card is the least transparent. Malewicz calls the example “purposefully over the top”.
borrow: Signal hierarchy with opacity: make the front card nearly opaque and let the cards behind it be more transparent.
Put large type behind the glass so that the blur is visible even over a simple gradient.

rights.statement: Text and images © Michał Malewicz / Hype4. Link and quotation only.

references.title: “Ist diese Typografie noch zu retten?”, TM special issue
references.titleBreak: “Ist diese Typografie noch zu retten?”,|TM special issue
references.lede: The December 1976 special issue of Typografische Monatsblätter on Weingart’s work from 1969 to 1976, with banded bilingual text on the cover and dense film collages inside.
references.summary: Cover with bilingual lines on grey and white bands, struck through by rules; inside, a black-and-white collage of halftones, maps, stars, and crosses. Wolfgang Weingart, 1976.

source.label: Letterform Archive: Legacies of Swiss Style, Part 2—Wolfgang Weingart

evidence.note: Inspected Letterform Archive’s photograph of the cover and one interior spread of the Archive’s copy (3000 × 1304) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example. It shows the style’s film collage and the banded, struck-through text at the scale of a whole issue.

context: Letterform Archive says the issue was produced under Weingart’s supervision and marks the end of his early years on the TM editorial board. It shows seven years of his work in collages of image and text, with “spaced-out letterforms, misaligned images, thick black text boxes, and a broken grid”. [Letterform Archive](https://letterformarchive.org/news/from-the-collection-legacies-of-swiss-style-part-2-wolfgang-weingart/).

The compositions were made by layering photographic films, not on a computer. [Letterform Archive](https://letterformarchive.org/news/from-the-collection-legacies-of-swiss-style-part-2-wolfgang-weingart/).
The cover asks “Is This Typography Worth Supporting, Or Do We Live On The Moon?” and calls the issue “a special selection from the works of Weingart, from 1969–1976”.
observed: The cover is light grey with a masthead of thick and thin rules that divides the three journal names into cells.
The heading is bold grotesque. The subtitle lines are white on black bars that change length from line to line.
Body text alternates bold German lines and regular English lines. Each line sits on a grey or white band, and some lines are struck through by horizontal rules.
Four-digit numbers (0001, 0094) mark the lines in the left margin in two weights.

The interior spread is a black-and-white collage: halftone portraits, fragments of a New York street map with zip codes on diagonal bands, stars, Swiss crosses, diagonal stripes, a grid of numbered cells, and a small arrow-shaped caption box.
interpretation: The cover turns reading order into structure: bands, strikes, and line numbers show the alternation of two languages. The collage shows how far the style goes when type is only one layer among many.
borrow: Put alternate lines of a bilingual text on bands of two different tints.
Number lines in the margin in a small bold grotesque.
Use a map fragment on a diagonal band as a texture layer behind photographs.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Photograph by Letterform Archive. Weingart died in 2021, so the design is in copyright.

references.title: “Neumorphism and CSS”
references.lede: A March 2020 CSS-Tricks article that turned the style into CSS and set it against Material Design.
references.summary: Adrian Bece’s CSS-Tricks article: paired box-shadows, a comparison table with Material Design, and accessibility cautions.

evidence.note: Text read from the live page on 2026-09-28; the date is from its `article:published_time` metadata. Figures and demos were not inspected.

styles.note: A widely cited developer text that defines the style by its two shadows, one light and one dark, and by elements that share the background color.

context: The article says the style “got its name in a UX Collective post from December 2019” ([Malewicz](ref:malewicz-neumorphism-article-2019)) and that “Adam Giebl created an online generator for it” (neumorphism.io).

Its comparison table: in Material Design “elements have a single or multiple dark shadows around them”; in neumorphism “elements have two shadows: one light and one dark”. Background colors “must be the same (or very similar) as the background color of the parent element”, and “rounded edges are a defining quality”.

It allows an “optional subtle border to improve contrast”, and credits [Alexander Plyuto](ref:plyuto-skeuomorph-mobile-banking-2019) with having “championed and evolved neomorphic designs on his Dribbble account”.
interpretation: Evidence that by March 2020 the style had moved from Dribbble concepts into web practice, with CSS `box-shadow` pairs as its standard implementation.

rights.statement: © CSS-Tricks / the author. Link and quotation only.

references.title: “Neumorphism in user interfaces”
references.lede: The December 2019 essay that named the style and gave its two-shadow recipe.
references.summary: Michał Malewicz’s essay that named neumorphism, compared it to the Material card, and raised its contrast problem.
references.made: 2019 (first published on UX Collective in December 2019)

evidence.note: Full text read on the live Hype4 Academy page on 2026-09-28. The original UX Collective URL (`uxdesign.cc/neumorphism-in-user-interfaces-b47cef3bf3a6`) returned HTTP 403 to scripts, and the Wayback lookup failed with HTTP 503, so the first-publication date rests on [CSS-Tricks](ref:css-tricks-neumorphism-and-css-2020) (“a UX Collective post from December 2019”). The article’s figures were not inspected.

styles.note: The text that named the style and set out its rules: same material as the background, one light and one dark shadow, and a tinted background that is neither white nor black.

context: Malewicz writes: “This ‘New skeuomorphism’ has been called by Jason Kelley Neuomorphism in the comments. I decided to skip the ‘o’ and the name Neuomorphism came alive.”

On the origin: “The entire hype started with one Dribbble shot that quickly went viral. This shot by Dribbble user alexplyuto gained over 3000 likes and pushed the trend forward” ([Plyuto](ref:plyuto-skeuomorph-mobile-banking-2019)).

On the card: “Neumorphic card however pretends to extrude from the background. It’s a raised shape made from the exact same material as the background.” And: “This effect is pretty easy to achieve by playing with two shadows, one at negative values while the other at positive. But for it to work our background cannot be fully black or fully white.”
On accessibility: “when they’re both the same color there’s no contrast to measure”, so “keep all the important elements on it with high enough contrast”.
interpretation: The founding text of the style. Its three rules (same-color surface, paired opposite shadows, tinted background) are the basis of this catalogue’s rubric, and its contrast warning anticipates the reasons for the decline of the style.

rights.statement: Text and images © Michał Malewicz / Hype4. Link and quotation only.

references.title: “Pony” Wisteria lamp, Tiffany Studios
references.lede: Clara Wolcott Driscoll’s leaded-glass lamp for Tiffany Studios: a shade of hanging wisteria blossoms on a bronze base cast as a gnarled trunk and roots.
references.summary: Blue and lavender leaded-glass blossoms over a bronze tree trunk. Clara Driscoll for Tiffany Studios, c. 1902–10.

source.label: Cleveland Museum of Art: “Pony” Wisteria Lamp, 2018.261

creator.name: Clara Wolcott Driscoll, for Tiffany Studios

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 2018.261 (2598 × 3400 px print file). Read the object record through the museum’s open-access API.

styles.note: The American branch of Art Nouveau: a plant is the whole form, the base grows into the shade, and coloured glass is set in dark lead lines like a key line.

context: The Cleveland Museum of Art records the lamp as leaded glass and bronze, 43.2 cm high and 26.7 cm in diameter, c. 1902–10, designed by Clara Wolcott Driscoll (1861–1944), Tiffany’s chief lamp designer, for Tiffany Studios, New York. [CMA 2018.261](https://clevelandart.org/art/2018.261).

The museum’s text calls Louis Comfort Tiffany’s lamps his contribution to “this new art movement, termed the Art Nouveau”, says that the base rises up to form the branches of the vine, and states that the Wisteria lamp won a grand prize for Tiffany Studios at the 1902 international exposition in Turin. [CMA 2018.261](https://clevelandart.org/art/2018.261).
observed: The shade is a dome of hundreds of small pieces of glass, each outlined by a dark bronze-coloured lead line.
Blossom clusters in pale lavender, white, and mid-blue hang down from the rim in uneven, pointed drops, so the lower edge of the shade is irregular instead of a straight line.
Green leaves sit near the crown of the shade. An open bronze filigree of branches covers the top.
The base is a green-brown bronze trunk with bark texture. It spreads at the foot into a flat, rooted disc.
The museum photograph shows the lamp against a dark gray ground with light falling from above.
interpretation: The lamp shows the Art Nouveau idea that ornament and structure are one: the stem holds the shade, and the shade is the flowering plant.
The palette is cooler than the posters of Paris: blue and lavender over moss-green bronze. The dark lead lines play the same part as the outline in a lithograph.
borrow: Let a decorative edge follow the motif, for example a hanging fringe of blossom shapes instead of a straight bottom border.
Outline every coloured shape with the same dark line, so a dense pattern stays readable.

images.alt: Table lamp on a dark gray ground: a round shade of small blue, lavender, and white glass pieces shaped like hanging wisteria blossoms, with green leaves at the top, on a green bronze base shaped like a tree trunk with roots.
images.caption: Clara Wolcott Driscoll for Tiffany Studios, “Pony” Wisteria lamp, c. 1902–10. [Cleveland Museum of Art 2018.261](https://clevelandart.org/art/2018.261), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art marks the object and its image CC0 (`share_license_status: CC0`). The lamp is an American work made and sold before 1929, so it is in the public domain in the United States, its country of origin.

references.title: “Souper” paper dress
references.lede: A promotional paper dress from Campbell’s Soup, printed with rows of soup-can labels after Andy Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup Cans.
references.summary: A shift dress printed with a grid of red and white Campbell’s labels. Campbell’s Soup, USA, 1967.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, T.66-2016 (1200 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Pop art’s packaging grid returned to commerce: the soup label repeated in rows as a textile print. Partial fit: it has no dots or comic devices.

context: The V&A describes a short sleeveless dress of bonded-fibre “paper”, made in the USA in 1967 and produced to promote Campbell’s vegetable soup, after Andy Warhol’s soup cans of 1962. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1330466/).
The V&A notes that paper dresses were a brief sensation from 1966 to 1968, and that many were free gifts that promoted consumer products. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1330466/).
The painting series it follows is [Campbell’s Soup Cans](ref:warhol-campbells-soup-cans-1962).
observed: The dress is printed with four rows of soup-can labels in a regular grid; the labels are cut off at the side seams.
Each label has a red top half with the white script “Campbell’s” and a white bottom half with “SOUP” in black slab-serif capitals.
A gold medallion sits on the line between red and white; a row of small gold fleurs-de-lis runs along the bottom of each label.
Thin black vertical lines separate the labels.
Two gold stripes run along the hem. The neckline and armholes are bound in black.
interpretation: The dress closes the loop between packaging and Pop: a painter’s grid of labels becomes a product’s own promotion.
Repetition of one unit in a strict grid is a Pop layout device as important as the comic panel.
borrow: Repeat one product unit in a strict grid of cells separated by thin black rules.
Crop the grid at the edges of the container so that it reads as an endless pattern.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The label design is a Campbell’s trademark, and the print follows Andy Warhol’s work; rights are unverified.

references.title: *NSYNC website, 2000
references.lede: The boy band’s Flash intro of August 2000: a wavy blue panel with a wide slanted logo, its mirror reflection, glowing blue orbs, and a member portrait in a halo.
references.summary: Wavy blue panel, wide slanted NSYNC logo with a mirror reflection, glossy blue orb corners, and a portrait in a glowing ring.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The main panel is Flash content, which rendered in the capture. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Clear: glossy orbs, a floor reflection, wide slanted techno lettering, a glowing halo, a blob-edged panel, and speed lines with a star. The page draws its graphics with images, so the CSS fingerprint measures flat, square, unshadowed boxes (see the style page). Judge it by the rubric.

observed: The page background is flat teal-blue. A large panel of brighter blue with soft, wavy edges and rounded corners fills the center.
Four glossy dark-blue orbs with white highlights sit at the panel corners like rivets.
The logo is a big italic “N” with “SYNC” in wide, slanted, outlined capitals; a mirror image of the logo appears below, as on a glossy floor.
A member’s photo sits in a circle with a violet glow and a white lens-flare highlight; his name “CHRIS” is in light-blue italic capitals.
A purple star and horizontal speed lines sit behind the portrait. A red star with speed lines marks the “skip…” link.
Below the panel, a glossy black oval button reads “Get *NSYNC”, next to a plain email form and a Shockwave badge.
interpretation: This intro gathers many Y2K web devices in one frame: orb buttons, a mirror reflection, glow halos, lens flare, wide slanted type, and speed lines.
The pixel palette is almost all saturated blue (chromatic share 0.97). The CSS measurement sees only the plain HTML around the Flash.
borrow: Put a mirror reflection of a wide logo under it on a glossy panel.
Use glossy orbs with one white highlight as corner rivets or buttons.
Circle a portrait with a soft colored glow instead of a border.

images.alt: Archived *NSYNC intro: on teal-blue, a wavy bright-blue panel with glossy blue orbs at its corners, the NSYNC logo in wide slanted capitals with a mirror reflection, a member portrait in a glowing violet ring with a star and speed lines, and a skip link.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20000815052750/http://www.nsync.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to *NSYNC (Jive Records). Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: 100 jaar De Stijl placeholder page
references.lede: A one-screen holding page for the 2017 centenary whose logo spells “100 JAAR DE STIJL” in square-built letters in red, yellow, blue, gray, and black.
references.summary: Rectilinear square-built logo lettering in primaries and black on an otherwise plain white page.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 23 November 2021 and inspected. A 2017 copy was requested; the archive returned the 2021 capture.

references.notice: This is an archived copy. The page says the site was still in development, and it links to an official national website elsewhere.

styles.note: Borderline: the logo follows van Doesburg’s rectilinear alphabet and the primary palette, but the rest of the page is a plain centered holding page.

observed: The page is white with centered small text: “deze site is in ontwikkeling” and the dates “1917 - 2017”.
The logo spells “100 JAAR” and “DE STIJL” in letters built from square strokes and right angles; the numerals are red, yellow, and blue, the other letters gray and black.
Below are an e-mail link, three black social icons, and a footer between two thin gray rules that credits Manschot Grafimedia, Zeist.
interpretation: The logo is the only part in the style, and it is an image, so the measurement sees only the centered Gill Sans text (1 hue, no borders).
borrow: Build a wordmark from square strokes on a grid, and color only a few letters with the primaries.

images.alt: Mostly white web page with a centered logo reading 100 JAAR DE STIJL in square-built letters, the numerals in red, yellow, and blue and the other letters in gray and black, above an e-mail link and social icons.
images.caption: Archived copy of [100jaardestijl.nl](https://web.archive.org/web/20211123002619/http://100jaardestijl.nl/), 23 November 2021.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: 100% ElectroniCON flyer
references.lede: The announcement flyer for the first vaporwave festival: a line-up in black grotesque type on a soft green-to-blue-to-violet radial gradient.
references.summary: Festival line-up in black on a hazy green, blue, and violet radial gradient. Brooklyn, 2019.

evidence.note: The only copy found is the 700 × 700 flyer image on the [DoNYC listing](https://donyc.com/events/2019/8/31/100-electronicon-elsewhere-takeover-w-george-clanton-saint-pepsi-and-many-more), below the size needed to observe it. The description below comes from that small copy and should be checked against a larger one.

styles.note: Partial fit. The scene’s own festival flyer uses only the soft airbrushed gradient; it has no statues, grid, OS chrome, or fullwidth type. Evidence that the scene itself had moved past the meme imagery by 2019.

context: Wikipedia: George Clanton “organized the first-ever vaporwave festival, 100% ElectroniCON, in New York City” in 2019, where Saint Pepsi, Vaperror, Nmesh, 18 Carat Affair, and Clanton performed. [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave).

The FADER reports 22 artists and more than 1,300 fans at Elsewhere, Brooklyn, a cardboard Keanu Reeves in a 100% Electronica T-shirt at the entrance, and “decorations inspired by memes.” [The FADER, September 4, 2019](https://www.thefader.com/2019/09/04/vaporwave-festival-100-electronicon-scene-report).
interpretation: In the small copy, a hazy radial gradient from lime green to blue to violet sits behind curved black line-up text and a small wave-and-cube logo. It suggests that the gradient is the most durable part of the look.

rights.statement: Copyrighted promotional material. No image is stored here.

references.title: 1905: The Road to October
references.lede: Valentina Kulagina’s anniversary poster sends a giant red worker striding diagonally across the sheet over a photomontage of the 1905 street massacres.
references.summary: A red constructed figure strides on the diagonal over black-and-white photomontage; red block capitals at the foot. Valentina Kulagina, 1929.

evidence.note: Viewed the V&A image of its copy, E.1274-1989 (1117 × 1600 px through the museum’s IIIF service), in a scratch folder. No image is stored.

styles.note: A late constructivist photomontage poster by one of the style’s women designers: red and black, a steep diagonal, photographs cut into flat shapes, and block capitals.

context: The V&A describes the poster as half-tone letterpress and colour lithograph, 1025 × 794 mm, published in the USSR in 1929. It commemorates Bloody Sunday in January 1905, and the toppled crown with the head of Nicholas II points forward to the October Revolution of 1917. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O76004/).
The V&A notes that Kulagina “often used photomontage in her work”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O76004/).
observed: A giant figure built from flat red planes strides from upper left to lower right. Four more figures repeat his stance behind him in steep recession.
“1905 ГОД” is set in white capitals on a red band that is tilted on the diagonal at the upper left.
A strip of black-and-white photographs of crowds and street fighting runs diagonally below the figure. Three smaller figures fire rifles from a white block toward the lower right.
A white outline of a toppled crown frames a small photograph of a head at the lower right.
“ПУТЬ К ОКТЯБРЮ” runs across the foot in red square block capitals on a black band.
The palette is red, black, gray, and the paper; the red figure is modeled with tonal shading.
interpretation: The poster shows how the style carried the red diagonal of [Lissitzky’s wedge](ref:lissitzky-beat-the-whites-red-wedge-poster) into figurative agitation by 1929: the figure is still built from planes, but it is a person, which points toward the later Socialist Realist poster.
The square block letters at the foot are drawn, not typeset, and are the kind of lettering that Latin-alphabet imitations of the style copy.
borrow: Run one dominant shape and one strip of photographs on the same diagonal so that they reinforce each other.
Close the page with a full-width black band that carries the main line in red block capitals.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Kulagina died in 1987, so the design is protected in Russia until at least 2057. The V&A image is shown under the museum’s own terms.

references.title: 6 Days of Sound, Fillmore at Winterland
references.lede: Bonnie MacLean’s Fillmore poster for the 1967 New Year shows: a hooded woman holding a peace-sign ornament between stacked blocks of bold, colored lettering.
references.summary: Bonnie MacLean, 1967. Pink and orange slab lettering on black bands around a blue and violet figure.

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object E.427-2004 (IIIF, 1081 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The image is not stored.

styles.note: Clear on color and density: saturated blue ground, violet, pink, and orange, with lettering in every free space. Partial fit on type: the letters are bold slab-serif capitals that stay legible.

context: The V&A catalogues it as psychedelic poster #99 by Bonnie MacLean, colour offset lithograph, 53.5 × 35.6 cm: a woman with blue and purple hair and robe holding mistletoe and a CND sign, with text in red and pink above and below. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O108960/).

MacLean (1939–2020) took over the Fillmore posters after Wes Wilson left and made more than thirty, most in 1967. Wikipedia notes her Art Nouveau manner and the influence of Gothic stained glass and pointed arches. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonnie_MacLean).
observed: The ground is a saturated mid blue that covers the whole sheet.
A woman with a pale face and long blue and violet hair and robe fills the middle. She holds mistletoe in one hand and lifts a white-rimmed oval with an orange-red peace sign on green in the other.
Band names and dates stack in black bands at top and bottom: 6 DAYS OF SOUND, THE DOORS, CHUCK BERRY, BIG BROTHER AND THE HOLDING CO., QUICKSILVER MESSENGER SERVICE.
The letters are wide, bold slab-serif capitals, alternating between pink and orange-red line by line. The lines are justified to fill the width.
A large red numeral 6 runs down the left side of the top block.
interpretation: Pink and orange on black, next to blue and violet, give the vibrating effect without the melting letterforms. The poster shows a legible branch of the style that suits screens better than Wilson’s lettering.
The figure and the peace sign form the central medallion; the text blocks are the dense frame.
borrow: Alternate two warm colors line by line in a stacked, justified title block.
Set the text blocks on dark bands so saturated letters stay readable on a saturated ground.
Use a single emblem, such as the peace sign here, as the central medallion.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. Bonnie MacLean died in 2020.

references.title: About Two Squares
references.lede: El Lissitzky’s “suprematist tale in six constructions” is a picture book whose characters are a red square and a black square.
references.summary: A cover with a black numeral 2 and a red square inside a thin frame, the title words tilted beside it. El Lissitzky, Berlin, 1922.
references.made: Conceived 1920 in Vitebsk; published 1922 in Berlin

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the cover and the first spread of a copy sold at [Swann Galleries, sale 2568, lot 244](https://catalogue.swanngalleries.com/Lots/auction-lot/EL-LISSITZKY-%281890-1941%29--PRO-DVA-KVADRATA-Book-inscribed-by?saleno=2568&lotNo=244&refNo=771260), through its Commons copies ([cover](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:About_Two_Squares_01.jpg), 1200 × 1503 px; [spread](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:About_Two_Squares_02.jpg), 1200 × 752 px). A pencil note on the endpaper of this copy appears to read “zdenek rossmann geschenkt von jan tschichold 1932” (given to Zdeněk Rossmann by Jan Tschichold).

styles.note: Partial fit: a Suprematist tale from the UNOVIS circle that became a model for constructivist book design. It has the red and black, the elementary shapes, and the rotated type, but it is calm and sparse rather than agitational.

context: The full title is *Pro dva kvadrata. Suprematicheskii skaz v 6-ti postroikakh* (About Two Squares: A Suprematist Tale of Two Squares in Six Constructions). [MoMA](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/11113) (title only; the page was not read).

Lissitzky conceived the book in 1920 at UNOVIS in Vitebsk. The Scythian press published it in Berlin in 1922, and it was printed by letterpress in Leipzig, including the slanted text and the illustrations. [ibiblio](https://www.ibiblio.org/eldritch/el/pro.html).
observed: The cover is cream paper with a thin black square frame.
Inside the frame, a large black sans-serif numeral “2” stands to the left and a flat red square to its lower right.
The word “ПРО” (about) is set small in black spaced capitals and slightly tilted, to the left of the numeral.
Lissitzky’s name is set small on a steep diagonal below the frame.

In the first spread, the right page is solid black. A large white letter Р leans to the right, and the rest of the word “РЕБЯТКАМ” (to the children) curves around its bowl in black letters on white. Two small white labels read “ВСЕМ” (to all), one of them tilted.
interpretation: The book shows the source of the style’s red square, black square, and rotated labels: the Suprematist vocabulary of Malevich, turned by Lissitzky into a narrative sequence.
Most of the page is empty paper. The measurement finds one hue and 9% chromatic area, the same as the [Red Wedge poster](ref:lissitzky-beat-the-whites-red-wedge-poster).
borrow: Pair one large numeral or letter with one red square inside a thin frame for a cover or a section opener.
Build a heading around a single oversized letter and let the rest of the word follow its curve.

images.alt: Book cover on cream paper: inside a thin black square frame, a large black numeral 2 and a flat red square, with the small word ПРО to the left and Lissitzky’s name set on a diagonal below.
images.caption: El Lissitzky, *About Two Squares*, Berlin 1922, cover. Copy sold at Swann Galleries (sale 2568, lot 244), image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:About_Two_Squares_01.jpg).

rights.statement: Commons marks the image {{PD-old-70-expired}}. Lissitzky died in 1941, so the book is in the public domain in Germany and Russia, and it was published in 1922, so it is in the public domain in the United States. The image is a flat reproduction of a printed page.

references.title: Agora Road’s Macintosh Cafe portal
references.lede: The Neocities portal of a forum for vaporwave and the old internet, built as a Windows 95 desktop inside a Mac OS window.
references.summary: Windows 95 Control Panel and dialog inside a lavender Mac-style window, over a dim bedroom photograph.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: a community site for the genre that uses its signature device, bevelled Windows 95 windows, in a lavender palette with a pixel-art figure. Its window chrome is real CSS, so it passes the shadow and radius metrics.
Partial fit: a pixel-font menu bar, pixel icons, and a dithered pixel figure, inside a vaporwave collage.

observed: A lavender menu bar with a pixel font runs across the top, with a clock at the right and pixel icons down the right edge.
A central window with a pinstriped title bar reading “Agora Road’s Macintosh Cafe” frames a teal Windows 95 desktop with Start button, taskbar, and desktop icons.
Inside, a Control Panel window and an “ANTI GLOWY CHARM” dialog with a yellow warning icon and YES and NO buttons overlap a dithered pixel-art figure holding a glowing pyramid with an eye.
Below, a bold pixel-font welcome line, a short paragraph, outlined tag chips (vaporwave, nostalgia, art, macintosh, y2k), and square buttons.
The page background is a dim, blue-tinted photograph of a bedroom.
interpretation: The measurement finds hard, unblurred shadows on 29% of boxes with a 1.4 px median offset and zero radius: the two-step Windows bevel, drawn in CSS. It finds almost no gradient or pattern, because the backdrop is a photograph.
borrow: Nest one period operating system inside another for the frame: it signals irony without any statue or sunset.

images.alt: Agora Road portal: a lavender Mac-style window containing a teal Windows 95 desktop with a Control Panel window, a warning dialog, and a pixel-art figure, above a welcome line and square buttons, on a dim bedroom photograph.
images.caption: First viewport of [agoraroad.neocities.org](https://agoraroad.neocities.org/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Airbnb illustration guidelines, “Your Face Here” (Jennifer Hom)
references.lede: Airbnb’s head of illustration explains its 2018 illustration redesign, which kept flat, lightweight figures but rejected the rainbow-colored skin of the tech style.
references.summary: A Big Tech illustration system of the same years that chose realistic skin tones and body types over rainbow figures. Documented, 2018.

source.label: Airbnb Design (Medium): Jennifer Hom, “Your Face Here”, 18 December 2018

evidence.note: Read the article text through a Wayback Machine copy; medium.com returned HTTP 403 to scripts. The article images did not load in that copy, so no illustration was inspected.

styles.note: Partial fit, and a counterpoint: a flat, minimal Big Tech illustration system from the style’s peak years, whose author explicitly rejected the “rainbow-colored figures” that define the style.

context: Hom joined Airbnb in October 2017 to redesign its illustration style. She lists four principles: “grounded, scalable, lightweight, and diverse”, and says the style is “fairly minimal and lightweight” with “intentional white space”. [Airbnb Design](https://medium.com/airbnb-design/your-face-here-9aa1d4970d6c).

She describes a common solution in tech illustration as “a metaphor for diversity through rainbow-colored figures … colored in red, blue, yellow, orange, purple, and green. Put simply, they’re not real.” She tried this in early drafts and rejected it. [Airbnb Design](https://medium.com/airbnb-design/your-face-here-9aa1d4970d6c).

She also rejects “cartoon people outlined in blue or grey”, and asks for reference photos for every person drawn and for different races, ages, abilities, and body types. [Airbnb Design](https://medium.com/airbnb-design/your-face-here-9aa1d4970d6c).
interpretation: The article is a contemporary insider’s description of the style’s central device, non-natural skin, as a way to avoid questions of race. It helps separate the style from other flat tech illustration of the same years.
borrow: When figures must represent real users, use a real range of skin tones and body types; keep the flat fills and white space.
next: Inspect the article’s illustrations in a browser and upgrade the evidence level if they show figures.

rights.statement: © Airbnb. No image is stored.

references.title: Airtable website, 2018
references.lede: Airtable’s 2018 home page: five blue- and pink-skinned figures with long bending limbs climb, lift, and pass shapes to each other beside the heading “Create, your way”.
references.summary: Blue-skinned, gangly figures stacking and passing blocks and plants beside a plain heading. 2018.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. No cookie box covers the page. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: figures with blue skin, small heads, and long, curving arms and legs lift and pass oversized shapes in bright flat colors on white. A light grain and a few doodled lines on the clothes are the only departures.

references.notice: The live Airtable site has changed since this 2018 capture.
observed: The heading “Create, your way” is set in a dark grey sans-serif of regular weight, with grey body text, a grey email field, and a blue “Get started” button with small rounded corners.
On the right, five figures form a human tower: one sits on a yellow circle and draws a line with a pen, one kneels on another’s back with a laptop, one lunges to lift a figure above.
Skin is blue on all figures; hair is black; clothes are coral pink, yellow, and blue, some with small white doodles or dots.
Pink and pale blue blocks, yellow circles, a blue triangle, and teal potted plants are stacked around them.
The fills are flat with a light speckled grain; there are no outlines. A pale lilac curve starts the next section, where a purple app window appears.
interpretation: It shows the style’s core metaphor of teamwork: many bendy figures assembling simple shapes into a structure, which also stands for the product’s building blocks.
borrow: Show collaboration as figures physically stacking or passing simple geometric blocks.

images.alt: Airtable home page, 2018: the heading “Create, your way” and an email sign-up on the left; on the right, five blue-skinned, long-limbed figures in pink, yellow, and blue clothes climb on each other and pass blocks, circles, and potted plants.
images.caption: First viewport of [Airtable](https://web.archive.org/web/20181126004018/https://airtable.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Alegria illustration system for Facebook (Buck)
references.lede: The illustration and animation system that Buck designed for Facebook from 2017: flat figures built from circles and tubes, with long limbs and blue, violet, or pink skin.
references.summary: Buck’s flat, geometric figures for Facebook, with oversized limbs and non-natural skin. The core example of the style.
references.made: Commissioned 2017; Buck gives an end date of 8 February 2020 in its project data

evidence.note: Inspected three images from Buck’s project page at 1400 px wide: the cover image of the printed style guide (`alegria_thumbnail.png`), a hero illustration of figures carrying a thumbs-up, and a spread titled “Figure Construction”. None is stored.

styles.note: The reference work of the style: Buck’s own page describes “flat, minimal, geometric shapes” and figures with “oversized limbs and non-representational skin colors”.

context: Buck describes the project as “a new style guide, illustration and animation system for the entire Facebook ecosystem” and says Facebook engaged it in 2017. “Alegria is Spanish for ‘joy’.” [Buck](https://buck.co/work/facebook-alegria).

Buck credits Xoana Herrera as design lead, Amelia Giller and Janice Ahn as senior art directors, and ten core illustrators. The library also covers transport, plants, animals, buildings, and hands. [Buck](https://buck.co/work/facebook-alegria).

AIGA Eye on Design (21 August 2019) treats Alegria as the model for the tech illustration style and quotes Herrera on “ethnically non-specific” characters. [AIGA Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/dont-worry-these-gangley-armed-cartoons-are-here-to-protect-you-from-big-tech/).
observed: In the hero illustration, six figures in flat fills carry a large blue thumbs-up. Arms and legs are long tubes that bend in smooth curves; one figure rides a unicycle.
Skin is violet, pink, pale blue, green, and yellow. Hair and some trousers are near-black navy.
Heads are small in relation to the bodies, and faces have only dots and short lines.
Some limbs carry a fine speckled grain in one tone, and a few details use thin colored lines.
A style-guide spread titled “Figure Construction” says the figures are “11 1/2 heads tall”, that “limbs are composed of cylindrical shapes”, and that men’s arms reach the knee.
Other guide pages show a woman with blue skin holding up a cup, a dog and fruit built from circles, and a rule on how to crop tall figures at the frame edge.
interpretation: The construction rules (heads as circles, limbs as cylinders, 11½ heads tall) explain why the style spread so fast: any illustrator can follow them and the results match.
The grain on some limbs shows that the original system allowed a little texture. Many later imitations removed it and kept only flat fills.
borrow: Build figures to a fixed head count (about 11 heads tall) with cylinder limbs, so a team of illustrators produces matching people.
Give each scene one oversized object that the figures lift or carry together.

rights.statement: © Facebook (Meta) and Buck. No image is stored; see the project page.

references.title: Alfieri & Lacroix advertising page
references.lede: Franco Grignani’s 1959 advertising page for the Milan printer Alfieri & Lacroix: white stripes that twist and swell across a black page, above a small striped figure.
references.summary: Bending white stripes on black and a striped head in blue and yellow, with small sans-serif text. Franco Grignani, 1959.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design: Franco Grignani (2019)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the AIGA Eye on Design reproduction (1689 × 2400 px), credited to the AIAP archive, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Grignani’s optical graphics before the term op art existed: distorted stripes fill a black page. Partial fit: a photographed figure and two colours are counter-traits.

context: AIGA Eye on Design captions the page “Franco Grignani, Pagina pubblicitaria Alfieri & Lacroix, 1959, offset print, 27.5 x 21 cm, AIAP archive”, and says that from 1952 Grignani had a 30-year partnership with the printer Alfieri & Lacroix, which gave him full creative freedom. [AIGA Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/the-hypnotic-mind-bending-work-of-italian-designer-franco-grignani/).
Wikipedia’s Op art article names Grignani as the graphic designer of the movement (cited in the [style record](style:op-art)).
observed: A black page is crossed from top left to bottom centre by a broad path of white stripes.
At the top the stripes are narrow and close together, and the path bends like a tube; lower down they become wide, flat bars that twist and taper.
At the bottom right a small photographed head and shoulders is striped in blue, white, and yellow.
Small white sans-serif text reads “tavola offerta dall’Alfieri & Lacroix” at upper right, with a dictionary-style definition of “Correlazione” at the lower left.
interpretation: The stripe path is an op device: parallel bands that change width and direction make a flat page look like a bent surface.
The figure and the colour belong to Grignani’s advertising practice, not to the black and white core of the style.
borrow: Let one band of parallel stripes cross the whole page and change width along its path.
Set small plain type in white on the solid black areas the pattern leaves free.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Grignani died in 1999, and the reproduction is credited to the AIAP archive.

references.title: Alphabet in “Stijl letters”
references.lede: Van Doesburg’s capital alphabet of about 1919, built only from thick horizontal and vertical strokes on a square module.
references.summary: Capitals A to Z from thick right-angled strokes, with no curves or diagonals. Theo van Doesburg, about 1919.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Theo van Doesburg, Alphabet

references.made: About 1919 (Commons, after the Hoek catalogue; the 1968 exhibition dated the photograph 1918–1919)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image (3774 × 579 px, viewed at 1920 px), scanned from Joost Baljeu, *Theo van Doesburg* (1974), pp. 108–109. The object is a photograph of the alphabet, 3.5 × 17 cm, in the Centraal Museum Utrecht on loan from the Dutch State (RCE inventory AB5936).

styles.note: The rubric’s rectilinear capitals at their source: every letter is made from horizontal and vertical strokes only.

context: Commons describes the object as “Alfabet in ‘Stijlletters’”, a photograph made in Leiden, inherited by Nelly van Doesburg in 1931 and given to the Dutch State by Wies van Moorsel in 1981. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Typeface_Theo_van_Doesburg.jpg).
The Foundry’s digital typeface [Architype Van Doesburg](https://www.thefoundrytypes.com/fonts/architype-van-doesburg/) revives the alphabet.
observed: Twenty-six capitals, A to M in the top row and N to Z in the bottom row, in solid black on white.
Every stroke is horizontal or vertical and of the same thickness; there are no curves or diagonals.
Letters that normally need diagonals, such as K, M, N, V, W, X, Y, and Z, are rebuilt from right-angled steps.
Counters are small rectangles; the letters are nearly square and set with narrow gaps.
Faint text from the facing book page shows through at the right.
interpretation: The alphabet applies the painting rule to type: no curves and no diagonals. Legibility suffers for letters such as K, X, and Z, which is the known cost of the approach.
The same letterforms appear in van Doesburg’s [poster design for La Section d’Or](ref:van-doesburg-section-dor-poster-design-1920).
borrow: Build display capitals from one stroke weight on a square grid, and replace diagonals with right-angled steps.
Keep such letters for short words; use a plain sans-serif for running text.

images.alt: Two rows of black capital letters A to Z on white, each built only from thick horizontal and vertical strokes, with square counters and no curves or diagonals.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg, alphabet in Stijl letters, about 1919, as reproduced in Baljeu (1974). Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Typeface_Theo_van_Doesburg.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons marks the image public domain. Van Doesburg died in 1931, so the design is public domain in the Netherlands; made about 1919, it is public domain in the United States under either the pre-1931 publication rule or the life-plus-70 rule. The scan is a plain reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

references.title: Anatomy of a Murder poster
references.lede: Saul Bass cuts a body into flat black pieces, sets the title into the gaps, and lays it on a field of saturated yellow-orange above a red-orange cast panel.
references.summary: A black cut-paper body with the title set in its joints, on flat orange and red panels. Saul Bass, 1959.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons scan (2650 × 3925 px, stored here at 1080 × 1600). The scan is of a US one-sheet with the Columbia copyright line and the National Screen Service notice at the foot. No museum copy was checked.

styles.note: A canonical example of the graphic core: a figure reduced to flat cut-paper planes, hand-cut lettering, and a few flat printed colors. The orange is more saturated than the style’s muted range.

context: Theatrical poster for Otto Preminger’s film, released by Columbia Pictures in 1959. Commons credits the artwork to Saul Bass. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AnatomyMurder2.jpg).

The foot of the poster reads “Copyright 1959 by Columbia Pictures Corporation” and “Country of Origin U. S. A.”. Commons states that a search of the US Copyright Office catalog found no renewal. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AnatomyMurder2.jpg).
The film’s score is by Duke Ellington, as the poster credits. [Wikipedia: Anatomy of a Murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomy_of_a_Murder).
observed: The upper two thirds is a flat yellow-orange panel. A black human figure lies across it at an angle, cut into separate pieces for the head, torso, arms, and legs.
The title words “ANATOMY OF A MURDER” sit in the gaps between the body pieces, in hand-drawn, uneven capitals. “OTTO PREMINGER’S” runs above in a smaller hand-drawn line.
The panel edges are slightly irregular, as if cut from paper, and the panel does not line up exactly with the one below it.
The lower panel is a flat red-orange field with the cast names in outlined capitals.
A line at the top reads “Last year’s No. 1 best-seller…This year’s No. 1 motion picture.” in a bold grotesque. Credits at the foot mix a grotesque with a serif line.
A thin off-white margin surrounds both panels. Bass’s signature runs vertically at the right edge of the upper panel.
interpretation: The poster shows the cut-paper method at its most reduced: one silhouette, two flat colors, and lettering that is drawn rather than set. The figure is geometric but still hand-made.
Measured on the stored scan, the accent chroma is 0.80. That is well above the style’s muted range: Bass’s film posters are a saturated branch of the graphic core.
borrow: Break a figure or object into flat pieces and put the heading into the gaps between them.
Stack two flat color panels with slightly misaligned, hand-cut edges instead of ruled boxes.

images.alt: Film poster: a black cut-paper body lies across a yellow-orange panel with the words Anatomy of a Murder set in the gaps between its limbs; below, a red-orange panel lists James Stewart, Lee Remick, Ben Gazzara, Arthur O’Connell, Eve Arden, and Kathryn Grant in outlined capitals.
images.caption: Saul Bass, US theatrical poster for *Anatomy of a Murder*, 1959. Scan from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AnatomyMurder2.jpg), marked public domain (not renewed).

rights.statement: Commons license: {{PD-Art|PD-US-not renewed}}. The poster was published in the United States in 1959 with a notice; Commons reports that a Copyright Office catalog search found no renewal, so it entered the US public domain after 28 years. The country of origin is the United States. This catalogue did not repeat the renewal search.

references.title: Android 5.0 Lollipop
references.lede: The Android release that shipped Material Design in 2014, rebuilding the system interface around flat color, paper-like dialogs, and ink-colored accents.
references.summary: Android’s 2014 system interface: a white dialog with a soft shadow over a dimmed list, teal accents, and all-capital text buttons.

creator.name: Google and the Android Open Source Project

evidence.note: Opened the Wikimedia Commons screenshot *Android proxy settings.png* (a Wi-Fi proxy dialog on Android 5, uploaded by Amrav, 2015) as a 500 × 889 rendering, and an AOSP home-screen screenshot (*Android 5.1-pkp-file-01-08-2024.png*, 960 × 1707 rendering) on 28 September 2026. The home screen still mixes older icons, so the dialog is the stored example.

styles.note: The first system-wide release of the style. Its settings dialogs show the elevation, accent color, and text-button rules on a working interface.

context: Wikipedia: “One of the most prominent changes in the Lollipop release is a redesigned user interface built around a design language known as Material Design, designed to retain a paper-like feel.” Android 5.0 was unveiled at Google I/O on 25 June 2014, its source code was released on 3 November 2014, and the Nexus 6 was the first phone to ship with it. [Wikipedia: Android Lollipop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_Lollipop).

The same article quotes Matías Duarte: “unlike real paper, our digital material can expand and reform intelligently. Material has physical surfaces and edges. Seams and shadows provide meaning about what you can touch.”
observed: A white dialog with square corners floats over a list that the system dims to dark gray. A soft shadow separates the dialog from the list.
One teal accent colors the checked checkbox, the active text field underline, and the two text buttons, CANCEL and SAVE, which are set in medium all-capital letters with no button outline.
Text fields are a single underline with a small gray label above. The status bar is black, and the navigation bar shows flat outline glyphs of a triangle, a circle, and a square.
interpretation: The dialog is the style at its most basic: one opaque sheet at a high elevation, one accent hue, and text buttons instead of boxed buttons. It follows the dialog rules in the [guidelines](ref:material-design-guidelines-2014) exactly.
borrow: Mark the focused text field and the confirming actions with the same single accent color, and leave every other control gray.

images.alt: Android phone screenshot: a white dialog titled Guest_User with a checked teal checkbox, Proxy set to Manual, underlined fields for proxy hostname and port, and teal CANCEL and SAVE text buttons, over a dimmed settings list.
images.caption: Wi-Fi proxy dialog in Android 5 (Lollipop), screenshot by Amrav, 2015, from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Android_proxy_settings.png), CC BY-SA 4.0. The interface is Android Open Source Project software under the Apache License 2.0.

rights.statement: Borderline tier A, for the curator to confirm. The screenshot is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 by its uploader, Amrav. The interface shown is not public domain: it is Android Open Source Project code, which Google releases under the Apache License 2.0. The status bar shows a carrier name.

references.title: Angular Material (AngularJS) documentation website, 2016
references.lede: The 2016 home page of Google’s Material library for AngularJS, with a blue side navigation and flat gray tiles.
references.summary: Blue side navigation with all-capital items, a pale gray header bar, and flat gray tiles with Material icons. 2016.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear example of a Material 1 documentation layout: a saturated blue navigation drawer, all-capital medium labels, Material system icons, Roboto, and a header bar that casts a thin shadow. The tiles themselves are flat.

references.notice: The live site now documents the end of long-term support for AngularJS Material, which ended in January 2022.
observed: A blue navigation drawer on the left holds a red Angular shield, the name “Angular Material” in white, and sections in white all-capital labels with small chevrons.
A pale gray header bar reads “Introduction” and casts a thin shadow over the white content area.
The content is Roboto on white, with four flat light gray tiles (GETTING STARTED, DEMOS, CUSTOMIZATION, API REFERENCE), each with a gray Material icon and an all-capital label.
Links in the tiles are a red-pink accent color.
interpretation: The page measures shadows on only 8 % of its boxes, with a median blur of 7.5 px and offset of 2 px. Most of its boxes are flat gray tiles and navigation rows, so the shadow share falls far below the specimen.
borrow: Put navigation on the primary color and content on white, and use gray tiles with a single icon and an all-capital label for primary links.

images.alt: Angular Material documentation in 2016: a blue left navigation with a red Angular shield logo and all-capital section labels, a gray header bar reading Introduction, and flat gray tiles with icons for Getting started, Demos, Customization, and API reference.
images.caption: [Wayback Machine copy of material.angularjs.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20160529050309/https://material.angularjs.org/latest/), 29 May 2016.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Angular Material 12 documentation website
references.lede: Google’s Angular component library, documented in its own Material 2 components: an indigo app bar, a white raised button, and Roboto on pale gray.
references.summary: Indigo app bar and hero, a white raised button with a soft shadow, and Roboto text on pale gray.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A small cookie notice covers part of the lower left corner.

styles.note: Clear example of Material 2: an indigo primary app bar with a soft shadow, a small white raised button, Roboto throughout, and a pale gray ground. It passes every metric of the fingerprint.

references.notice: This is the archived documentation for version 12 (2021). The current Angular Material site uses Material 3.
observed: A full-width indigo app bar holds the white labels Material, Components, CDK, and Guides, a version menu reading 12.2.13, and a GitHub link. A soft shadow falls from the bar onto the hero.
The hero is the same indigo, with a large pale Angular shield behind the bold white title “Angular Material” and the line “Material Design components for Angular”.
A small white “Get started” button has slightly rounded corners and a soft shadow.
Below, three columns of gray Roboto text (High quality, Versatile, Frictionless) sit on a pale gray ground.
A white cookie notice with a soft shadow covers part of the lower left corner. Its OK, GOT IT button is indigo text in all capitals.
interpretation: The page measures a shadow on 55 % of its boxes, a median blur of 3 px and offset of 2 px (a 1 dp Material 2 surface), a 4 px median radius, and a chromatic share of 0.46.
borrow: Let the primary color of the app bar continue into the hero, and separate the two only by the bar’s shadow.

images.alt: Angular Material 12 documentation home: an indigo app bar and hero with the title Angular Material over a pale Angular shield, a white Get started button, three columns of gray text, and a small cookie notice at lower left.
images.caption: First viewport of [v12.material.angular.io](https://v12.material.angular.io/). The live site at material.angular.io now uses Material 3.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Apple iOS 7 website, 2013
references.lede: Apple’s launch page for iOS 7: very thin type on white and the new flat icons, under the old glossy navigation bar.
references.summary: Ultra-thin “iOS 7” headline and a phone showing the flatter iOS 7 icons; the navigation bar is still glossy. September 2013.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 20 September 2013, and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. Nothing covers the page. The headlines are images, so their weight is not measured.

styles.note: Borderline: the thin type and flatter icons show the iOS 7 turn to flat design, but the page has few color fills, the navigation bar is glossy, and the icons keep soft gradients.

observed: A gray navigation bar with a top highlight, vertical dividers, and a rounded search field runs across the top.
Under a thin gray rule, “iOS 7” and the line “The mobile OS from a whole new perspective.” are set in very thin, large dark gray type, centered on white.
A white iPhone lies at an angle below. Its screen shows the iOS 7 home screen: rounded-square icons in bright colors, with simple glyphs and soft gradients, on a dark blue starry wallpaper.
interpretation: Measured: 7% of screenshot pixels are saturated, and 65% of boxes have a 1 px border, so the capture fails the color and border ranges. The glossy navigation bar is an image the extractor cannot see.

The page shows the flat turn in type and icons before Apple removed the gloss from its site navigation; NN/g dates Apple’s fully flat navigation to 2015 ([NN/g](ref:nngroup-flat-design-article-2015)).
borrow: Use a very thin weight at a very large size for a single headline on white, and let the colored content carry the color.

images.alt: Apple iOS 7 page of September 2013: a glossy gray navigation bar, the headline iOS 7 and a subtitle in very thin dark gray type on white, and a white iPhone at an angle showing colorful iOS 7 app icons.
images.caption: First viewport of the [Wayback Machine copy of apple.com, 20 September 2013](https://web.archive.org/web/20130920043843/http://www.apple.com/ios/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot of an archived copy, captured for commentary.

references.title: Apple Liquid Glass
references.lede: Apple’s 2025 design material, which adds refraction and moving highlights to translucent glass across all its platforms.
references.summary: A translucent, refracting glass layer for controls and navigation on every Apple platform. 2025.

evidence.note: Inspected two Apple Newsroom images in scratchpad copies: Apple-WWDC25-Liquid-Glass-hero-250609 and Apple-WWDC25-Liquid-Glass-Home-Screen-clear-look-250609 (both 1960 × 1102). The screens in these images are small, so the refraction is not visible at this size. Not stored.

styles.note: Related branch, partial fit. It keeps the frosted, floating layer but adds refraction and specular edges, which the style’s rubric treats as a separate confusion.
Clear: Apple’s announcement of the design language that defines the style.

context: Apple describes Liquid Glass as a “translucent material” that “reflects and refracts its surroundings”, whose color “is informed by surrounding content”. It is used for controls, navigation, app icons, widgets, the Lock Screen, and Control Center. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/06/apple-introduces-a-delightful-and-elegant-new-software-design/).

The HIG separates Liquid Glass, a layer for controls and navigation that floats above content, from the standard materials (ultra-thin to thick blur) used in the content layer. It offers a regular and a clear variant, and suggests a 35 % dark dimming layer under clear glass on bright content. [Apple HIG: Materials](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials).

Wikipedia and [Everyday UX](https://www.everydayux.net/glassmorphism-apple-liquid-glass-interface-design/) (2025) treat Liquid Glass as a development of glassmorphism that adds real-time lensing and motion. [Wikipedia: Liquid Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Glass).
observed: Home-screen image: a MacBook desktop with a pale green photo wallpaper. Calendar, weather, reminders, and podcast widgets are clear, rounded glass tiles with thin light edges; the photo shows through almost unblurred.
The Dock is a clear glass strip with monochrome icons.
Hero image: a TV, MacBook, iPad, iPhone, and Watch together. On the iPad, widgets and the Dock are translucent over a blue-and-teal wave wallpaper.
interpretation: Liquid Glass is the largest deployment of the frosted layer since Big Sur, but its clear variant blurs less than classic glassmorphism and relies on lensing, which the stored rubric lists as a counter-trait.
borrow: Keep glass for the navigation and control layer only, and leave content surfaces opaque or in lighter standard materials.

rights.statement: Apple press images and software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple visionOS glass material
references.lede: Windows in Apple’s headset are made of a system glass that blurs the real room behind them.
references.summary: visionOS windows use an adaptive frosted glass over the physical surroundings. Apple, 2023.
references.made: 2023 (visionOS unveiled June 5, 2023; HIG visionOS guidance added June 21, 2023)

evidence.note: Read the HIG Materials page (through its JSON data and in Claude in Chrome) and inspected its image visionos-materials-window-example@2x.png (1184 × 746) and the Apple Newsroom image Apple-WWDC23-Vision-Pro-VisionOS-230605 (1960 × 1102) in scratchpad copies. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit. The glass, blur, radii, and opacity levels match, but the backdrop is a real room, not vivid color. NN/g and Everyday UX use it as a current example.
Partial fit: the precursor glass material of visionOS, before the refractive, lensing edge of Liquid Glass.

context: The HIG says visionOS windows “generally use an unmodifiable system-defined material called glass” that lets light, the current Environment, virtual content, and physical objects show through. Glass adapts to the luminance behind it, so visionOS has no separate Dark Mode. [Apple HIG: Materials](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials).

It advises: “Prefer translucency to opaque colors in windows.” The thin material marks interactive elements, regular separates sections such as a sidebar, and thick makes a dark element on top of regular. Vibrancy is applied to text and symbols on the glass.

NN/g writes that the Apple Vision Pro “uses glassmorphic SwiftUI materials in translucent UI overlays”. [NN/g 2024](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/glassmorphism/). Apple says the 2025 [Liquid Glass](ref:apple-liquid-glass-2025) design was “inspired by the depth and dimensionality of visionOS”.
observed: HIG diagram: a large window with rounded corners floats in a beige living room. The room behind it is blurred to soft shapes of furniture and a red object.
The window has a darker sidebar (regular), a dark text-field bar at the top (thick), and a lighter button at the lower right (thin). All are translucent.
Newsroom image: the App Store window floats in a room; a vertical, pill-shaped tab bar at its left edge is translucent and shows the wall behind it.
The window’s content (a star field with a constellation bear) is opaque; the glass appears in the chrome and control areas.
interpretation: visionOS moves the style off the gradient and onto the world: the backdrop becomes the user’s own room. It keeps the three-level opacity hierarchy that web glassmorphism uses.
borrow: Define three glass thicknesses and give each one a job: thin for controls, regular for sections, thick for dark overlays.

rights.statement: Apple documentation and press images; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Aquatic Park Bathhouse, San Francisco
references.lede: A WPA bathhouse of 1936–39 on San Francisco Bay, built like a white ocean liner with rounded decks, ship railings, and portholes.
references.summary: White rounded decks, pipe railings, portholes, and a curved glass corner. William Mooser II and III, San Francisco, 1936–39.

source.label: Library of Congress: HABS CAL,38-SANFRA,157, Aquatic Park Bathhouse

creator.name: William Mooser II and William Mooser III, architects; Works Progress Administration

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected two Historic American Buildings Survey photographs through their Commons copies at 1920 px: [general view, front and side](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_VIEW,_FRONT_AND_SIDE_-_Aquatic_Park_Bathhouse,_Beach_Street,_West_of_Polk_Street,_San_Francisco,_San_Francisco_County,_CA_HABS_CAL,38-SANFRA,157-1.tif) and [front elevation](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FRONT_ELEVATION_-_Aquatic_Park_Bathhouse,_Beach_Street,_West_of_Polk_Street,_San_Francisco,_San_Francisco_County,_CA_HABS_CAL,38-SANFRA,157-2.tif). The cars in the photographs date them to about the 1980s. The Library of Congress API returned HTTP 429 (rate limit), so the facts come from Wikipedia and Living New Deal.

styles.note: A canonical Streamline Moderne building: long horizontal decks, rounded ends, ship railings, and portholes on a smooth white wall.

context: Designed by William Mooser II and III, begun in 1936 and completed in January 1939 as a WPA project, with murals by Hilaire Hiler. [Wikipedia: Aquatic Park Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquatic_Park_Historic_District); [Living New Deal](https://livingnewdeal.org/sites/maritime-national-historical-park-aquatic-park-san-francisco-ca/).

The district became a National Historic Landmark District in 1987. The building now houses the San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park’s Maritime Museum. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquatic_Park_Historic_District).
observed: The two-storey white block has a fully rounded end; a curved wall of large glass panes wraps the ground-floor corner.
Upper decks step back like a ship’s superstructure; each deck has a rounded end and a pipe railing of three horizontal rails.
Four round portholes with thick frames line the ground-floor wall; smaller portholes flank the entrance.
Groups of three short horizontal grooves (speed lines) sit beside the windows and on the upper wall.
Ship details on the roof: ventilator cowls, masts, a flagpole, and an oval name board shaped like a ship’s transom reading “MARITIME MUSEUM”.
The walls are smooth and unornamented; the only relief is on the dark stone entrance surround.
interpretation: The building shows almost the whole rubric at once: horizontal decks, rounded ends, railings as parallel lines, and portholes, all on a white ground. The ship metaphor is literal because the building faces the bay.
borrow: Stack horizontal bands that each end in a semicircle, and run three thin parallel rules along the top edge of each band, like a railing.
Use groups of three short horizontal rules beside an element as a speed-line mark.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a white two-storey building shaped like a ship: rounded decks with pipe railings, round portholes along the wall, a curved glass corner, masts on the roof, and cars parked along the street.
images.caption: General view, front and side. Historic American Buildings Survey, HABS CAL,38-SANFRA,157-1, [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/ca1404.photos.016582p/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_VIEW,_FRONT_AND_SIDE_-_Aquatic_Park_Bathhouse,_Beach_Street,_West_of_Polk_Street,_San_Francisco,_San_Francisco_County,_CA_HABS_CAL,38-SANFRA,157-1.tif).

rights.statement: HABS photographs are works of the United States government and are in the public domain; Commons marks the file public domain. The building was completed in 1939, before December 1990, so it has no architectural copyright in the United States.

identifiers.commons: File:GENERAL VIEW, FRONT AND SIDE - Aquatic Park Bathhouse, Beach Street, West of Polk Street, San Francisco, San Francisco County, CA HABS CAL,38-SANFRA,157-1.tif

references.title: Armchair, model no. 718 F/B
references.lede: Otto Wagner’s bentwood armchair of about 1902: ebonized beech, a square upholstered seat and back panel, and aluminium sabots on the feet.
references.summary: Black bentwood frame, square leather panels, and aluminium feet. Otto Wagner for Jacob & Josef Kohn, c. 1902.

source.label: Minneapolis Institute of Art: Armchair, model no. 718 F/B, 98.276.302

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Minneapolis Institute of Art photograph of object 98.276.302 (560 × 800 px). The leather colour in the photograph may not be original; the museum record does not say.

styles.note: Partial fit: black and metal with square panels and no ornament, as in Wagner’s bank interiors, but the frame is a bentwood curve and the photographed upholstery is bright red.

context: Mia records the chair as designed by Otto Wagner and made by Jacob & Josef Kohn, c. 1902, in ebonized beechwood with aluminium sabots and leather. [Mia 98.276.302](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/60713/armchair-model-no-718-fb-otto-wagner).

Mia’s label says the chair precedes a variant armchair of 1904–1906 designed for the Postal Savings Bank in Vienna, that Kohn and the rival firm Gebrüder Thonet produced the form in several variations, and that Wagner was the first of his colleagues to use aluminium in interior elements and furniture. [Mia 98.276.302](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/60713/armchair-model-no-718-fb-otto-wagner). See [the Postal Savings Bank](ref:wagner-austrian-postal-savings-bank).
observed: The frame is black: a continuous bentwood rail forms the back and both arms and comes down as the front legs.
The seat and the back panel are square-cut and upholstered in smooth red leather; the back panel is framed by the black rail and two uprights.
A ring of bentwood joins the four legs below the seat.
Each leg ends in a bright metal sleeve (sabot), which stands out against the black wood.
interpretation: Metal caps at the points of wear are functional, but Wagner shows them as a deliberate accent, like the aluminium bolts on his bank façade. Black with bright metal is the palette of his bank interiors.
The curved bentwood rail links this chair to the Thonet tradition more than to the square lattice of Hoffmann and Moser, so it is a partial fit.
borrow: Use black as the main colour, with one bright metallic accent at edges and endpoints.
Frame one square panel with a thin black line, and keep the panel plain.

images.alt: Armchair with a black bentwood frame curving round the back and arms, a square red leather seat and back panel, a ring stretcher between the legs, and bright aluminium caps on the feet.
images.caption: Otto Wagner for Jacob & Josef Kohn, armchair model no. 718 F/B, c. 1902. Minneapolis Institute of Art, 98.276.302, The Modernism Collection, gift of Norwest Bank Minnesota. Image from [Mia](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/60713/armchair-model-no-718-fb-otto-wagner), rights status Public Domain.

rights.statement: Mia gives the rights status of this object as Public Domain. Otto Wagner died in 1918, and the chair was made c. 1902, so the design is in the public domain in Austria and in the United States.

references.title: Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society season ticket, 1890
references.lede: Walter Crane’s season ticket for the society that named the movement: a designer and a workman shake hands inside a framed woodcut-style panel.
references.summary: Brown-ink ticket with a framed panel of two craftsmen and hand-drawn capitals with middle dots. Walter Crane, 1890.

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A image 2006AC9526 of E.4164-1915 through the V&A IIIF service at 1200 × 935 px, saved only in a scratch folder. The object data come from the V&A API record O1024286.

styles.note: A primary document of the movement: Crane’s ticket for the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, with a framed figure panel and hand-drawn capitals.

context: The V&A describes it as “Walter Crane. Season ticket, The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, 1890”, process engraving, 77 × 133 mm, given by Emslie John Horniman. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1024286/).

The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, which gave its name to the movement, was formed in 1887 with Walter Crane as president and held its first exhibition at the New Gallery, London, in November 1888. [Wikipedia: Arts and Crafts movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_and_Crafts_movement).
observed: The card is printed in one dark brown ink on cream.

On the left, a square panel with a double-line frame shows a young man in a tunic and a bearded workman in an apron shaking hands over a small tree, with laurel sprays and acanthus leaves behind them.
Banners in the panel read “THE ARTS & CRAFTS EXHIBITION SOCIETY”, and ribbons at the foot read “121. REGENT ST.” and “·THE·NEW·GALLERY·”.

A vertical rule divides the panel from the right half, where “·SEASON· ·TICKET· ·1890·”, “ADMIT”, and “DURING THE PERIOD OF THE EXHIBITION ERNEST RADFORD SECRETARY” are hand-drawn in capitals with middle dots between words.
A dotted box leaves space for the holder’s name. “A&CES” is written at the lower left.
interpretation: The ticket confirms the framed panel and the double-rule frame of the rubric, but all its lettering is capitals. The style’s hand lettering is often capitals with middle dots, not mixed case.
The one-colour brown print is a cheaper, reproductive version of the Kelmscott look, useful as a model for small formats.
borrow: Separate words in a capital heading with middle dots (·) instead of spacing them out.
Divide a card into a framed picture panel and a lettered text half with a single vertical rule.

rights.statement: The work is in the public domain (Crane died in 1915), but the V&A licenses its images for non-commercial use only, which is not an open license. No image is stored.

references.title: Atomic War! #1, page 6
references.lede: A 1952 war-comic page of the kind Pop art enlarged: six panels with speech balloons, a yellow caption box, and the sound effects BANG! BANG!, ARRRRGH!, and a siren’s WHEEEE.
references.summary: Six comic panels with balloons, a yellow caption box, and sound effects in flat printed color. Ace Comics, November 1952.

creator.name: Ken Rice (artist, per Commons); Ace Comics (publisher)

evidence.note: Inspected the Internet Archive scan of the printed comic, [atomic-war-01](https://archive.org/details/atomic-war-01), page image n5 (960 × 1402 px), which is the page Commons files as AtomicWar0106.jpg. The Commons original could not be downloaded (HTTP 429); its metadata was read.

styles.note: Partial fit: source material, not Pop art. It shows the comic devices Pop art borrowed (panels, balloons, caption boxes, sound effects, black ink lines) at their original size, where the Ben-Day dots are too fine to see.

context: *Atomic War!* was an Ace Comics series of four issues, November 1952 to February 1953, about a fictional atomic war between the Soviet Union and the United States set in 1960. Commons credits this page to Ken Rice. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AtomicWar0106.jpg).
Lichtenstein’s war paintings, such as [Whaam!](ref:lichtenstein-whaam-1963), came from DC war comics of 1962, not from this series. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaam!).
observed: Six rectangular panels in three rows, each with a thin black border and white gutters between them.
Speech balloons are white ovals with black outlines and pointed tails. They hold hand-lettered capitals, with some words in heavier letters (“INLAND”, “ALL”, “AT ONCE!”).
The last panel has a yellow caption box across the top: “HIGH ABOVE THE UNSUSPECTING CITY, THE WAIL OF SIRENS SUDDENLY MINGLED WITH CHURCH BELLS!”
“BANG! BANG!” is lettered in red with a black outline next to a firing pistol; “ARRRRGH!” sits in a white balloon.
A red ribbon with the letters “WHEEEE…EEE” growing larger winds across an aerial view of Manhattan.
Color is flat and printed: mustard uniforms, pink skin, pale blue and green walls. Black ink lines and solid black shadows model the faces.
The paper is yellowed, and the colors are slightly off-register at some edges. No dot pattern is visible at this scan size.
interpretation: Compared with the Pop paintings, the source page is small, crowded, and busy. Lichtenstein’s change was to isolate one panel, enlarge it, simplify the color to primaries, and make the printing dot visible as a motif.
The heavy words inside balloons and the sound effect that grows along a ribbon are lettering devices that transfer directly to screen headings.
borrow: Mark stressed words in a balloon with heavier letters, as comic letterers do, instead of with color.
Let a sound-effect word grow in size along a path to show sound moving across a panel.

images.alt: Comic page with six panels: soldiers in mustard uniforms struggle with a spy at a radar board, speech balloons in capitals, the sound effects BANG! BANG! and ARRRRGH!, and a last panel of Manhattan from the air with a yellow caption box and a red ribbon reading WHEEEE.
images.caption: *Atomic War!* #1, November 1952, page 6, art credited to Ken Rice by Commons. Scan from the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/atomic-war-01); the same page is [AtomicWar0106.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:AtomicWar0106.jpg) on Commons.

rights.statement: Commons marks this page with the template PD-US-no-renewal and states that the copyright of this US comic, first published in 1952, was not renewed and has expired. The renewal was not checked here against the Copyright Office records. The country of origin is the United States. The stored image is the Internet Archive scan, which carries no license statement; a faithful scan of a public-domain two-dimensional work adds no new US copyright. A curator may prefer to replace it with the Commons file.

references.title: Austrian Postal Savings Bank, Vienna
references.lede: Otto Wagner’s bank of 1904–1906: a façade of square stone plates held by visible bolts, and a banking hall under a gridded glass vault.
references.summary: Square stone plates with bolt heads, aluminium details, and a banking hall under a vault of square glass panes. Otto Wagner, Vienna, 1904–1906.

evidence.note: Inspected the Wien Museum photographs (3500 px wide) of a 1908 booklet about the building, Wien Museum inv. 115662/2, which contains photographs of the public entrance and of the banking hall. I did not inspect a modern photograph, so present colours and later changes are not recorded here.

styles.note: A clear example in architecture: the façade and the banking hall are built from repeated squares and grids, with the fixings shown as ornament.

context: Wikipedia: the building was constructed between 1904 and 1906 in reinforced concrete and opened on 17 December 1906; an extension followed in 1910–1912. The façade is covered with square marble slabs; the bolts that articulate it were long thought decorative, but material analysis shows that they secure the thin slabs over a bed of mortar. Wagner used aluminium for the bolts, the portico columns, and the heating fans. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Postal_Savings_Bank).

The Wien Museum holds a 1908 booklet, “Das K. K. Oesterreichische Postsparkassenamt in Wien”, printed on paper, 23.8 × 15.9 cm, with Otto Wagner named as architect. [Wien Museum 115662/2](https://sammlung.wienmuseum.at/en/object/641443-das-k-k-oesterreichische-postsparkassenamt-in-wien/).
Mia’s label notes that Wagner designed an armchair for the bank in 1904–1906; see [the related model 718 armchair](ref:wagner-armchair-model-718).
observed: In the booklet’s photograph of the public entrance, the lower walls are clad in large stone plates, each marked with round bolt heads at regular intervals; the upper storeys carry a denser field of bolt heads.
The name “K. K. POSTSPARKASSENAMT” runs in one line of thin applied capitals, with small dots after each K.
