A flat glass canopy on thin columns covers the entrance; the windows behind it are divided into small square panes.
In the photograph of the banking hall, a curved glass vault is divided into a regular grid of rectangular panes by thin bars, and a flat glass ceiling of square panes covers the side aisles.
The floor is laid in bands and fields of small tiles. Slim cylindrical fans stand along the counters, and a clock and a date board sit on the axis of the end wall.
The booklet page frames each photograph with a border of small open rings, and sets the caption “EIN TEIL DES KASSENSAALES” in capitals between two small open squares.
interpretation: Wagner uses the grid at every scale, from the stone plates to the glass vault, and treats the fixings as the ornament. The building shows the style’s square module without the gold and the figurative motifs of the painters.
The 1908 booklet is itself a small Secession print: a ring border, a centred caption in capitals, and two open squares as end marks.
borrow: Mark a panel with a regular pattern of small dots, like bolt heads, to give it texture without drawing.
Frame an image with a border of small open rings, and close a caption with a small open square at each end.
Divide a large surface into a fine, even grid of thin lines, as in the glass vault.

images.alt: Booklet page with a black and white photograph of the banking hall: a high vault of gridded glass panes over an empty hall with columns, counters, and a patterned floor, framed by a border of small rings, with the caption Ein Teil des Kassensaales.
images.caption: Page from “Das K. K. Oesterreichische Postsparkassenamt in Wien”, 1908, showing the banking hall. Wien Museum, inv. 115662/2, image from the [Wien Museum Online Sammlung](https://sammlung.wienmuseum.at/en/object/641443-das-k-k-oesterreichische-postsparkassenamt-in-wien/), CC0, cropped to the right-hand page.

rights.statement: The Wien Museum releases this image under [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) and asks users to name the author, the photographer, and the Wien Museum. The building is by Otto Wagner, who died in 1918, and the booklet was printed in 1908, so the works shown are in the public domain in Austria and in the United States. The Wien Museum record does not name a photographer.

references.title: Ball Clock
references.lede: Twelve black balls on thin rods radiate from a white disc: the atomic starburst of 1950s graphics turned into a wall clock.
references.summary: Black balls on thin metal rods around a white hub, with triangle and lozenge hands. Irving Harper for George Nelson Associates and Herman Miller, 1948–69.

source.label: Art Institute of Chicago: Ball Clock, 1999.678

evidence.note: Inspected, in the scratchpad only, the Art Institute of Chicago photograph of 1999.678 at 843 × 671 px (the largest size served for this in-copyright object), a frontal view on gray. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: a product, not graphic design, but its ball-and-rod starburst is the atomic motif that the style’s graphics and textiles repeat.
Partial fit: a product, not a sign or building, but its ball-and-rod form is the atom motif that Googie signs repeat.

context: The Art Institute of Chicago dates the clock 1948–69 and credits Irving Harper (1916–2015) and George Nelson Associates, manufactured by Herman Miller Inc.; materials chrome, black enameled metal, and ebonized wood; Orbit Fund. [AIC 1999.678](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/154134/ball-clock).

The museum’s text places it in the Chronopak series of electric clocks that Harper designed at George Nelson Associates and says that, though abstract, it “suggests both the structure of the atom and the iconic asterisk symbol that abounded in the 1950s”. [AIC](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/154134/ball-clock).
observed: Twelve black spheres sit at the ends of thin metal rods that radiate evenly from a central white disc.
The hands are black: the hour hand ends in a triangle and the minute hand in a thin lozenge shape. There are no numerals.
The photograph shows the clock straight on against a flat gray background.
interpretation: The clock is the three-dimensional version of the starburst and ball-and-stick motifs in 1950s prints: a circle, radial lines, and dots with nothing else.
borrow: Use a ring of dots on thin radial lines around a plain disc as a starburst motif.
Give pointers or markers simple geometric ends: a triangle, a lozenge, a circle.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Art Institute of Chicago does not mark the object as public domain, and Irving Harper died in 2015.

references.title: Beach Culture no. 5
references.lede: An issue of the surf and culture magazine that Carson art-directed before Ray Gun, with mirrored, overlapping, and cropped display type.
references.summary: Painted cover by Gary Baseman; inside, mirrored giant letters across the gutter and spaced capitals overprinted on a blurred photo. David Carson, 1991.

source.label: Display Graphic Design Collection: Beach Culture No. 5, Feb/March 1991

evidence.note: Inspected five photographs (1600 × 1280 each) of one copy offered by Display in scratchpad copies: the cover and four interior spreads. The copy has no collection number. Not stored.

styles.note: Precursor and partial fit: the layouts break the grid and overlap type as in Ray Gun, but the letterforms are clean and the grounds are mostly plain paper.

context: Carson became art director of Beach Culture in 1989; the magazine ended after six issues. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)).

Display lists the issue as no. 5, February/March 1991, edited by Neil Feineman and published by Surfer Publishing Group, with a cover by Gary Baseman. It quotes Steven Heller: “Letter forms overlap, overprint, smash, and are otherwise covered by black, mortised, random bands.” [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/beach-culture-no-5-feb-march-1991-david-carson).

Display quotes Carson (Under Pressure, 2018) calling Beach Culture his best editorial work and saying he was already doing the Ray Gun kind of work there. [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/beach-culture-no-5-feb-march-1991-david-carson).
observed: The cover is a red, black, and white brush painting by Gary Baseman. The masthead is blue condensed slab capitals, stacked, with a yellow box around the issue number.
A cover line, “life on the pro tour”, is set in blue lowercase letters stepped down the page one or two at a time.
The “hanging at carmine st.” spread sets huge grey and black sans-serif letters mirrored and upside down across the gutter; one word is cut in half by the page edge.
“the song chant of the bush by wayne lynch” is a heavy lowercase sans-serif with wide word spaces, cropped by a photograph at the gutter.
A spread titled “romeo void” spaces single large letters in cells of thin rules; body text is a small typewriter-like face in narrow columns, next to blurred halftone images.
“GRACELAND, PARADISE GARDEN, AND ST. COCA COLA” is set in widely spaced capitals whose lines overlap each other over a blurred photograph.
interpretation: Beach Culture shows the step before grunge: the layout is already broken and intuitive, but the type is not yet damaged. Its wide letterspacing is closer to [New Wave typography](style:new-wave-typography), which marks the boundary between the two styles.
borrow: Mirror or invert one oversized word so it reads as shape before it reads as text.
Let two lines of spaced capitals overlap over a blurred photograph.

rights.statement: No image is stored. David Carson is living, so the design is in copyright. Photographs by their sources. The cover painting is by Gary Baseman.

references.title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
references.titleBreak: Beat the Whites|with the Red Wedge
references.lede: El Lissitzky’s Civil War poster turns a political slogan into pure geometry: a red triangle drives into a white circle on a black field.
references.summary: A red wedge pierces a white circle; the slogan runs on diagonals in black, outline, and red capitals. El Lissitzky, Vitebsk, 1919–1920.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Russian State Library scan published on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Klinom_Krasnym_Bej_Belych.JPG) (3360 × 2688 px, viewed at 1920 px). The Commons record names the Russian State Library as the holding institution and gives no call number.

styles.note: The founding image of the style’s graphic language: red and black on paper, a diagonal wedge, a circle, and rotated block capitals.

context: Lissitzky made the poster during the Russian Civil War, in which the Bolshevik “Reds” fought the anti-Bolshevik “Whites”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_the_Whites_with_the_Red_Wedge).

The imprint at the bottom reads “№ 19 Литиздат. Политуправления Запфронта” (lithographic publishing office of the Political Administration of the Western Front) and “Уновис”, the group around Kazimir Malevich in Vitebsk. The sheet measures 48.8 × 69.2 cm according to the Commons record.

Wikipedia records that the art historian Maria Elena Versari connects the image to Italian Futurism, and that Nikolai Kolli built a “Red Wedge” monument in Moscow in 1918 with the same symbol. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_the_Whites_with_the_Red_Wedge).
observed: The format is landscape. The ground is unprinted cream paper, framed by a thin black rule.

A large red triangle enters from the upper left and points into a white circle that sits on a black field. The black field is cut by a diagonal edge that runs from the top center to the bottom center.
Small red and black splinters, bars, and a gray stippled rectangle scatter around the point of impact.
“КЛИНОМ” runs down to the right in heavy black sans-serif capitals. “КРАСНЫМ” follows in outline capitals on a steeper diagonal.
“БЕЙ” is set in red capitals inside the white circle, and “БЕЛЫХ” is set in outline capitals on a gray stippled block on the black field.
The only hue is an orange-red. Everything else is black, gray tint, and paper.
interpretation: The poster states the style’s whole grammar in one sheet: one hue, a diagonal thrust, elementary shapes that carry the meaning, and words that follow the direction of the shapes instead of a baseline.
The screenshot measurement finds exactly one hue and 9% chromatic area, inside the style’s fingerprint for `color.hues` and `color.chromaticShare`.
borrow: Let one red shape point at the most important element on the page, and make everything else black, gray, or paper.
Rotate each word of a short heading to a different angle so that the words follow the shapes.
Split the ground into a light and a dark field with one diagonal edge.

images.alt: Landscape poster on cream paper: a large red triangle from the upper left points into a white circle set on a black field, with scattered small red and black bars and Russian words in black, outline, and red capitals set on diagonals.
images.caption: El Lissitzky, *Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge*, 1919–1920, lithograph. Russian State Library, image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Klinom_Krasnym_Bej_Belych.JPG).

rights.statement: Commons marks the scan {{PD-Art|PD-old-auto-expired}} (Public Domain Mark). Lissitzky died on 30 December 1941. Under Article 1281 of the Russian Civil Code, as summarized in the Commons template PD-Russia-expired, works of authors who died before 1 January 1952 are in the public domain in Russia in 2026, including the four-year extension for authors who worked during the Great Patriotic War. The poster was published before 1931, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Biba op-art mini-dress
references.lede: A long-sleeved jersey mini-dress from the London boutique Biba, printed with nested diamonds in brown and black.
references.summary: A high-necked mini-dress in brown jersey with a black print of concentric diamonds. Biba, London, 1965.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A photograph of its copy, T.159-1986 (1040 × 1600 px), on a dress form against a blue backdrop, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: An op print of nested diamonds on a mass-market dress. Partial fit: the colours are brown and black, not black and white.

context: The V&A catalogues the dress with the style “Op art” and says it “was produced during the short lived Op Art fashion trend of 1965”. A horizontal-stripe version was also made. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O133328/).

The V&A notes that “while true optical art was often stark white and black, other colourways were used”, and that Biba used a brown and black textile here. It quotes Barbara Hulanicki on prints that washed out to “faded grey Op-Art print dresses”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O133328/).
Physical description: straight-cut mini-dress with a high neck and long sleeves, brown jersey with black op-art geometric print, back zip. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O133328/).
observed: The print is a grid of concentric diamonds made of alternating brown and black bands of equal width.
Where four diamond centres meet, the bands turn into small checkerboards, and between them the bands form large X shapes.
The pattern covers the body, sleeves, and roll collar with no plain area.
interpretation: The structure is pure op: one banded unit repeated edge to edge, with checks where the fields meet. The brown ground softens the contrast, so the vibration is weaker than in a black and white print.
The V&A’s own note makes the scope of this style explicit: black and white is the core, and colourways such as this are commercial variants.
borrow: Tile concentric diamonds so that their corners meet and form checkerboards and X shapes between them.
For a softer op field, keep the black and replace the white with one mid-tone.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A photograph is not openly licensed, and the rights in the Biba print are unverified.

references.title: Bjango website, 2011
references.lede: The app studio Bjango’s home page, archived June 2011: dark gray plates held by small screws, with beveled buttons and embossed labels.
references.summary: Dark screwed-on plates, beveled buttons, embossed navigation, and a recessed email field.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The archived page may lack some images or scripts that the live page had.

styles.note: Clear: each panel is a metal-gray plate with a screw at every corner, buttons are beveled, labels are embossed, and the email field is an inset well.

observed: The page is dark charcoal. A large framed banner and three smaller plates sit on it with soft drop shadows.
Each gray plate has a small dot like a screw head at each corner and a light top edge.
Navigation words (iPhone, iPad, Mac, Articles, Help) are light gray with a dark shadow, as if embossed.
The footer buttons are rounded rectangles with a vertical gradient; the email field is recessed into a darker well with a Join button at its end.
A band of dark jagged shapes above a purple footer suggests a mountain silhouette.
interpretation: No CSS surface was measured: the page has 0 styled boxes in the viewport and 100% image share, so every bevel and shadow is a bitmap. The measurement sees none of the texture, because the page draws it with bitmap background images; see the style synthesis.
borrow: Put a small screw head in each corner of a panel to make it read as a mounted plate.
Recess a single email field into a darker well with the button attached to its end.

images.alt: Archived Bjango page: a dark charcoal background with the bjango logo, embossed navigation links, a framed banner for the game Sideways, three gray plates with screw heads linking to iPhone, iPad, and Mac apps, and beveled footer buttons.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20110622074312/http://bjango.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Björk, “All Is Full of Love” music video
references.lede: Chris Cunningham’s video of two white robots with Björk’s features, assembled and kissing in a clinical white room.
references.summary: Two white humanoid robots in a white, Japanese-styled lab. Directed by Chris Cunningham, 1999.

source.label: Wikipedia: All Is Full of Love

evidence.note: Based on Wikipedia and Media Art Net descriptions. No still of at least 800 px from a named copy was inspected.

styles.note: Partial fit: the humanoid robot and white-lab future of the period. The palette is white and clinical, not chrome or candy plastic.

context: The video was directed by Chris Cunningham and premiered in April 1999; post-production was by Glassworks. Cunningham described a white environment with “a Japanese feel to it”. It won MTV Video Music Awards for Breakthrough Video and Best Special Effects in 2000 and was on permanent exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art. [Wikipedia: All Is Full of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Is_Full_of_Love).
Media Art Net describes two humanoid robots being assembled, kissing, and falling in love. [Media Art Net](http://www.medienkunstnetz.de/works/all-is-full-of-love/).
interpretation: The cyborg is one of the style’s image motifs. This video shows its sincere, tender version around 1999: the machine as beautiful, not threatening.
It is close to the white, minimal side of the period and is useful as an edge case for the Y2K rubric.
borrow: Pair white glossy surfaces with a cool, soft light to suggest a clean-room future.
next: Inspect stills from a museum or distributor source and add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The video belongs to its rights holders (Björk, One Little Indian, and Chris Cunningham).

references.title: Blank Banshee 0 cover art
references.lede: A low-polygon 3D head floating in a purple-to-cyan gradient under a wide italic title.
references.summary: Low-poly game-style head on a purple-to-cyan gradient. 2012.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 × 1200 cover on the album’s [Bandcamp page](https://blankbanshee.bandcamp.com/album/blank-banshee-0), in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear on two diagnostics: a smooth purple-to-cyan gradient and an early 3D render. Wikipedia names the album, with Floral Shoppe, as a turning point of the genre.

context: Wikipedia: “In September [2012], Blank Banshee released his debut album, Blank Banshee 0,” which Bandwagon called a “progressive record” that, along with Floral Shoppe, “reconfigured what it means to make vaporwave music.” [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave).
observed: The background is a vertical gradient from violet at the top to bright cyan at the bottom, with no texture.
A flat-shaded, low-polygon female head with angular brows and pink lips floats in the centre, cut off at the neck.
BLANK BANSHEE runs across the top in white, heavy, extended italic capitals with an A that has no crossbar.
interpretation: The most economical statement of the style: one dated 3D object and one gradient. The head reads like a late-1990s console character model.
borrow: Use a single two-stop violet-to-cyan gradient behind one untextured 3D object, with no other decoration.

rights.statement: Copyrighted album art. No image is stored here.

references.title: Blech club night ticket
references.lede: A Designers Republic ticket for the Warp Records club night Blech, mixing manga, Japanese katakana, coded labels, and LCD-style type.
references.summary: Lime ticket with a big-eyed manga face, katakana, a pixel “BL-3CH” code, and a pink warning arrow. The Designers Republic, 1996–97.

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object E.50-2022 (image 2025PD1388, 1600 × 1298) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The V&A record has no description; the name Warp Records comes from the context below, not from the ticket.

styles.note: Partial fit: the Designers Republic’s Japanese-pop, coded-label side of Y2K graphics. Interface-like labels and LCD type are present; chrome and translucency are not.

context: The V&A holds the ticket as E.50-2022, titled “Blech”, by The Designers Republic, UK, 1996–7, given by The Designers Republic. [V&A E.50-2022](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1681781/blech-ticket-the-designers-republic/).
Wikipedia says The Designers Republic is sometimes associated with popularizing the Y2K look. [Wikipedia: Y2K aesthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_aesthetic).
observed: The ground is flat lime green. A large manga-style face with huge blue eyes, white highlights, and freckles fills the lower two thirds.
The heading “BLECH:” is in heavy orange-red sans-serif capitals, followed by katakana in bright blue.
A purple-edged box holds “BL-3CH” in a dotted, LCD-like pixel face; next to it are outlined rounded pictogram characters.
Small type reads “FORMAT: DISCOCLUB PASS”, “ADMITS ONE. PRICE £4.00”, and “THIS TICKET VALID MAY 11 ONLY” in magenta.
A pink double-headed arrow at right carries “WARNING! THIS PASS MUST BE SURRENDERED ON ENTRY” set vertically, and a small round “DR” badge sits at top right.
interpretation: The ticket treats a club pass like a product label from a Japanese future: format codes, model numbers, warnings, and trademark signs. This coded-label habit is the graphic side of the style’s “interface as device” layout.
It shows the flat, bright end of Y2K graphics before gloss and chrome became common in print.
borrow: Add fake model codes, format labels, and warnings in small capitals around a main image.
Set a short code in a dotted LCD face inside a thin outlined box.
Mix Latin headings with a second script or pictograms as texture.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London; the design belongs to The Designers Republic.

references.title: Bookplate for Otto Zuckerkandl
references.lede: Koloman Moser’s square bookplate of 1906 fits every letter into a ruled band, and sets one frontal figure on the central axis between them.
references.summary: Square black frame, capitals packed into ruled bands, and a frontal figure on the axis. Koloman Moser, Vienna, 1906.

source.label: MAK Collection Online: Exlibris für Otto Zuckerkandl, KI 9136-3859

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the MAK photograph of the impression MAK KI 9136-3859 (1671 × 1680 px). The MAK also holds the Wiener Werkstätte design sheet for the same bookplate (KI 12558-1), which I looked at only as a small image.

styles.note: A clear example of the geometric phase: a square format, thick ruled frame and bands, capitals stretched to fill each band, and strict symmetry in black on white.

context: The MAK records the bookplate as designed by Koloman Moser in Vienna in 1906 for Otto Zuckerkandl, printed from a block on paper, 8.5 × 8.5 cm. The plate is signed “KM”. It came to the museum with the Artur Wolf collection in 1933. [MAK KI 9136-3859](https://sammlung.mak.at/en/collect/exlibris-fuer-otto-zuckerkandl_134107).
A design sheet for the same bookplate carries the Wiener Werkstätte stamp. [MAK KI 12558-1](https://sammlung.mak.at/en/collection_online?id=collect-236484).
Moser co-founded the Wiener Werkstätte with Josef Hoffmann in 1903 and left it in 1907. [Wikipedia: Koloman Moser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koloman_Moser).
observed: The print is square, in black ink on cream paper, inside a thick hand-cut black frame.
“EX” and “LIBRIS” sit in two ruled bands at the top; “OTTO” and “ZUCKERKANDL” sit in two bands at the bottom.
The capitals are drawn from straight strokes and full circles, and are stretched or compressed so that each word fills its band from edge to edge. The U is drawn as a V.
A frontal female figure stands on the central axis in a dark rectangular robe. She holds a bowl, a snake curves over her head, and its tail ends in a spiral at the bottom.
The figure’s rectangle cuts through the lower band rules, so the image and the lettering lock together.
A small square mark with a dot sits at the lower right of the central field.
Wide areas of the central field are left blank.
interpretation: This is the Secession lettering rule in its plainest form: the text is set by the frame, not by a font. Each line takes the full width, whatever the letter count, so letter widths change from line to line.
The snake and spiral keep a trace of the curved early style, but they stay inside the figure’s rectangle. The page as a whole is built from squares and bands.
borrow: Put headings in full-width ruled bands, and stretch or condense the capitals so each word fills its band.
Let one central element break through a band rule to join image and text.
Use a single small square mark as a signature or end mark.

images.alt: Square black and white bookplate: the words Ex Libris at the top and Otto Zuckerkandl at the bottom in capitals packed into ruled bands, with a frontal woman holding a bowl, a snake arching over her head, standing in the middle.
images.caption: Koloman Moser, bookplate for Otto Zuckerkandl, 1906. MAK Vienna, KI 9136-3859, image from the [MAK Collection Online](https://sammlung.mak.at/en/collect/exlibris-fuer-otto-zuckerkandl_134107), Public Domain Mark 1.0.

rights.statement: The MAK marks this image with the [Public Domain Mark 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/) (“The image can be downloaded and used freely”). Koloman Moser died in 1918, and the bookplate dates from 1906, so the work is in the public domain in Austria and in the United States.

references.title: BRATATAT T-shirt
references.lede: A screen-printed T-shirt after Roy Lichtenstein: two firing gun barrels, red and yellow flames, a blue dot field, and the sound effect BRATATAT.
references.summary: A white T-shirt printed with blue Ben-Day dots, red and yellow flames, and a red sound effect. After Roy Lichtenstein, probably 1981.

creator.name: Roy Lichtenstein (artist); Fruit of the Loom, Screen Stars label (manufacturer)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, T.591-1997 (1400 × 2076 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: The comic-panel idiom on a garment: a coarse blue dot field, black key lines, flat red and yellow, and a sound effect. It is later than the style’s era but reuses a 1964 image.

context: The V&A describes a printed cotton T-shirt, probably made by Screen Stars (Fruit of the Loom) in the USA, probably in 1981, and probably made for a Lichtenstein exhibition that year. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O301462/).

The V&A says the design extends the final panel of Lichtenstein’s 1964 painting *As I Opened Fire*, which was based on 1962 comic panels by Jerry Grandenetti. The shirt omits the caption that crops the painting, and its dots differ from the painting. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O301462/).
observed: A large oval of blue dots on white runs diagonally across the front of the shirt. The dots are coarse and widely spaced.
Two gun barrels in black and white point up and to the right; red and yellow flames with black outlines stream from them.
“BRATATAT” is printed in red capitals with a black outline and a jagged, uneven baseline across the chest.
A small patch of magenta dots shades the gun mounts at lower left.
The shirt is sleeveless (the sleeves appear to have been cut off) and is stained at right.
interpretation: The shirt shows how the style survives reproduction on cheap media: three flat inks, a coarse dot screen, and black line, which is also how it survives on screens.
The dot field is an oval with a soft edge made by the dots themselves, not a gradient.
borrow: Give a dot field a shaped edge, such as an oval or a diagonal band, instead of filling the whole panel.
Set a sound-effect word at an angle along the direction of motion.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design is © Estate of Roy Lichtenstein.

references.title: Braun ET66 calculator, 1987
references.lede: The pocket calculator by Dieter Rams and Dietrich Lubs that inspired the iPhone’s Calculator app.
references.summary: A black calculator with round keys, the physical model for the iOS Calculator. Braun, 1987.

creator.name: Dieter Rams and Dietrich Lubs for Braun AG

evidence.note: Based on the Powerhouse Collection record 2012/33/1 and Cult of Mac (2013). The record’s image was not inspected.

styles.note: Not an example of the style: the physical object that an interface imitated. It shows that the style also borrowed from restrained modern products, not only from leather and wood.
Partial fit: a later Braun product by Rams and Lubs that keeps the plain housing and round keys of the product core, but in black plastic and outside the era.

context: Powerhouse Collection: Braun ET66 calculator, made 1987, designed by Dieter Rams and Dietrich Lubs, manufactured by Braun AG and made in Hong Kong; “black plastic, including a case, with round numeric and function keys.” [Powerhouse, 2012/33/1](https://collection.powerhouse.com.au/object/428164).

Cult of Mac (John Brownlee, 2 May 2013): “the Braun ET66 pocket calculator, first released in 1987 … inspired iOS’s own calculator app.” [Cult of Mac](https://www.cultofmac.com/news/buy-a-replica-of-the-classic-braun-calculator-that-inspired-ioss-calculator-app).
interpretation: An interface can imitate an object that is itself plain. The iOS calculator kept the ET66’s round-key layout and color accents, not a material texture.

rights.statement: Design by living and recent designers; the museum states that image copyright is held by the Powerhouse. No image is stored here.

references.title: Brushed-metal windows in Mac OS X
references.lede: A second Aqua window style with a brushed-aluminium texture, used for QuickTime Player, iTunes, the Finder, and Safari.
references.summary: Brushed-aluminium window frames with sunken buttons. Apple, QuickTime 4 (1999) to Mac OS X Leopard (2007).
references.made: First in QuickTime Player 4 (1999); widest use in Mac OS X Panther (2003); merged into one gray window style in Leopard (2007)

evidence.note: No image was inspected. Based on Wikipedia, which cites Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines and Daring Fireball.

styles.note: A precursor material: a metal texture tied to real devices, before the leather, wood, and paper of 2007–2013.

context: “Brushed-metal windows had a thick frame with a metallic texture or dark-gray background and sunken buttons and inner frames.” “Apple recommended brushed-metal windows for applications that mimic real-world devices (such as iTunes) or are used to interface with such devices (such as iSync).” [Wikipedia: Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_(user_interface)).

“Brushed Metal had first appeared in QuickTime Player 4.” Panther used it more, “especially to the Finder and Safari web browser.” In Leopard, Aqua and brushed-metal windows “obtained the same metal-like, gray look.” [Wikipedia: Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_(user_interface)).
Wikipedia links the change to Apple’s industrial design: “In 2003 and 2004, Apple moved to the use of brushed aluminium … The design of Aqua changed accordingly.”
interpretation: Apple’s own rule tied the texture to device-like apps. That is the logic of the later style: the material says what kind of object the app is.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Butcher Billy website
references.lede: An illustrator’s portfolio page: an edge-to-edge grid of pop-art comic covers and panels, many of them mock superhero covers titled “Post-Punk Comics”.
references.summary: A gapless grid of flat-colored, black-outlined comic pastiches under a small red logo block.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Borderline: the page is a grid of pop-art comic images with flat primaries, heavy black outlines, captions, and cover lettering, but the style lives in the artworks, not in the page’s own interface, and no Ben-Day dots are visible.

observed: A white header bar holds a red block with the white logotype “BUTCHER BILLY” and a gray link “contact the art dealer”.
The rest of the viewport is a gapless grid of square and double-width tiles, each an artwork.
The large tile at left shows a kiss between two masked figures in flat blue, red, yellow, and skin tone with black outlines, and the words “LOVE WILL TEAR US APART.” in cream condensed capitals.
Several tiles copy 1960s comic covers, with a price box (“60¢”), an issue number, a title band such as “Post-Punk Comics”, and a caption box at the foot.
Other tiles use huge outlined lettering, such as “WHY SO SERIOUS?” in orange on black and “IDOL” in red on yellow.
Colors are flat. There are no gradients in the artworks shown.
interpretation: The artworks follow the romance and superhero branches of the idiom closely, with Lichtenstein-like close-ups and lettering. The page itself is only a grid, so it shows the Warhol layout of repeated units more than any interface device.
The extractor sees almost none of this: the images hold 87% of the page, CSS hues measure 2, and there are no CSS borders or patterns.
borrow: Tile comic panels edge to edge with no gutters, and mix single and double-width tiles.
Use a small solid red block for the logotype and let the images carry the color.

images.alt: Butcher Billy portfolio page: a red logo block on a white bar above a gapless grid of pop-art comic images, including a masked couple kissing with the words Love Will Tear Us Apart, several fake 1960s comic covers titled Post-Punk Comics, and the words Why So Serious? in orange.
images.caption: First viewport of [butcherbilly.com](https://www.butcherbilly.com/), captured 28 September 2026.

references.title: C. F. A. Voysey Society website
references.lede: A plain society site that takes its title lettering, its red, and its cream from Voysey himself, and frames its news in thin olive rules.
references.summary: Voysey-style red capitals on a cream band, Georgia text, red links, and olive-ruled boxes.

creator.name: The C. F. A. Voysey Society

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear in type and colour: hand-drawn Arts and Crafts capitals in red, an old-style serif, cream grounds, and ruled boxes. It has no pattern.

observed: The title “THE·C·F·A·VOYSEY·SOCIETY” runs across a cream band in dark red hand-drawn capitals with small round letters set high and middle dots between words.
Below it a pale navigation bar with a slight gradient holds grey sans-serif labels divided by thin vertical rules.
An italic serif quotation from Voysey is centred under the navigation.
Body text is a dark old-style serif on white. Links are dark red.
The News box and the search box have thin olive rules; the News box has a light grey ground. Headings inside it are olive sans-serif.
The right column shows the orange-brown cover of the Society’s journal, The Orchard, and a black-and-white photograph of Voysey.
interpretation: The site shows the style with almost no pattern: red lettering, a serif text face, italic for the quotation, and rules. That supports the rubric’s type and colour traits more than its pattern trait.
Measured: two chromatic hues, accent chroma 0.54, no shadows, no capitals in the running text (the title is an image), and 1 px borders. It fails only `color.patternShare`.
borrow: Draw the title in a single dark red with middle dots between words, and leave the rest of the page in a plain serif.
Frame secondary content in a thin rule of a dye colour such as olive instead of a card with a shadow.

images.alt: C. F. A. Voysey Society home page: a cream band with the title in dark red hand-drawn capitals, a pale navigation bar, an italic quotation, serif body text, an olive-ruled News box, a journal cover, and a photograph of Voysey.
images.caption: First viewport of [voyseysociety.org](https://www.voyseysociety.org/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners, and the pattern images belong to their rights holders. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Cabaret Fledermaus bar room, Vienna
references.lede: Josef Hoffmann’s cabaret of 1907 for the Wiener Werkstätte: a black and white checkerboard floor, a bar clad in white square tiles, and walls of multicoloured majolica tiles.
references.summary: Checkerboard floor, a white-tiled bar, and a wall mosaic of coloured majolica tiles. Josef Hoffmann and the Wiener Werkstätte, Vienna, 1907.
references.made: 1907 (opened 19 October 1907; in use at this address until 1913)

evidence.note: The interior no longer exists. I inspected the Wien Museum photograph (3500 px wide) of Wiener Werkstätte postcard no. 75, “Cabaret Fledermaus, Barraum”, 1907, colour lithography, attributed to Josef Hoffmann (inv. 101968/25). The postcard is a drawing, not a photograph, so proportions and colours may be stylized. No image is stored.

styles.note: A clear example: the checkerboard floor and the square-tiled bar are the style’s signature surfaces, and the postcard’s lettering is packed into ruled bands.

context: German Wikipedia: the cabaret opened on 19 October 1907 in the basement of Kärntner Straße 33, corner of Johannesgasse, on the initiative of Fritz Wärndorfer. Josef Hoffmann planned the interior and the Wiener Werkstätte carried it out; Klimt, Kokoschka, Moser, Czeschka, and others took part. The Werkstätte also designed posters, postcards, cutlery, and ushers’ badges. The most striking element was a mosaic of 7,000 majolica tiles on the walls, the bar, and the cloakroom. The cabaret stayed at this address until 1913. [Wikipedia (German)](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabaret_Fledermaus).

The Wien Museum records postcard no. 75, “Cabaret Fledermaus, Barraum”, as by Josef Hoffmann, 1907, colour lithography on paperboard, 14.1 × 9.1 cm, published by the Wiener Werkstätte (?). [Wien Museum 101968/25](https://sammlung.wienmuseum.at/en/object/177264-postkarte-der-wiener-werkstaette-nr-75-cabaret-fledermaus-barraum/).
observed: On the postcard, the floor is a large black and white checkerboard drawn in perspective.
The bar counter is a block clad in white square tiles with black joints; a few tiles are coloured.
The rear walls are covered to about two-thirds of their height in a mosaic of rectangular tiles in blue, yellow, orange, green, red, and gray, with figures, flowers, and vessels on some tiles.
The upper wall and ceiling are plain white, with a row of oval yellow lamps along the top of the tile band.

The drawing sits in a thin black frame. Two ruled bands at the bottom hold “CABARET FLEDERMAUS” and “WIEN · KÄRNTNERSTRASSE 33” in capitals that fill each band from edge to edge; a small square monogram sits at the lower right.
interpretation: The room puts the style’s pattern where the rubric says it belongs: in bands and zones (floor, bar, lower wall), with plain white above.
The many-coloured tiles break the black, white, and gold rule. They show that the Werkstätte used full colour in small modules, while the structure stayed black and white.
borrow: Use a black and white checkerboard as a ground band or footer, with plain white above it.
Draw a block as a grid of white squares with black joints, and colour only a few squares as accents.
Close a card with two ruled bands of packed capitals, like the postcard’s address line.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Wien Museum makes this postcard image available only on request, because rights must be cleared with the copyright holder. Josef Hoffmann died in 1956, so his work is protected in Austria until the end of 2026.

references.title: Café De Unie, Rotterdam
references.lede: J. J. P. Oud’s 1925 café front, rebuilt in 1986: the building is a billboard of flat colored planes, yellow bars, and square capitals.
references.summary: Black, red-orange, white, blue, and yellow planes with capital lettering on a café facade. J. J. P. Oud, 1925; reconstruction 1986.
references.made: 1924–1925 (original on the Coolsingel, destroyed 1940); reconstruction 1985–1986 on the Mauritsweg

evidence.note: Inspected a 2009 photograph of the reconstruction by “Ad” on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WLANL_-_Adfoto_-_Caf%C3%A9_De_Unie,_JJP_Oud_(1925).jpg) (1920 × 2560 px, viewed at 1600 px). No image is stored. The photograph shows the 1986 reconstruction, not the 1925 building.

references.notice: The original building was destroyed on 14 May 1940. The existing facade is a reconstruction on a different street.

styles.note: De Stijl applied to a commercial front: flat rectangles in primaries, black, and white, with lettering built into the composition.

context: Oud designed the café for the Coolsingel in Rotterdam in 1924–1925. It was destroyed on 14 May 1940 and reconstructed in 1985–1986 by the architect Carel Weeber on the Mauritsweg. [archiweb](https://www.archiweb.cz/en/b/cafe-de-unie).
archiweb names Theo van Doesburg as a co-author; this record does not rely on that claim.
observed: A black band near the top carries “DE UNIE” in large light gray-blue capitals, with “CAFE” set vertically at both ends and a yellow bar above.
Below it a large red-orange plane carries raised lines that form nested right angles.
Yellow bars frame the upper window band and the lower windows; the lower windows have yellow inner frames.
A vertical sign reads “DE • UNIE” in blue capitals with a yellow strip; a tall blue sign at the left reads “CAFE RESTAURANT” twice.
The ground floor is framed in bright blue; the rest of the facade is white.
A dark later storey rises behind the facade, and ordinary brick buildings stand on both sides.
interpretation: The facade treats architecture as a graphic panel, which makes it the closest pre-war precedent for a De Stijl website or sign system.
The red is closer to orange in this photograph, which may reflect the reconstruction, weathering, or the camera.
borrow: Build the name into the composition as one rectangular plane among others.
Use thin yellow bars as frames and dividers between larger black, red, and white planes.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is CC BY-SA 2.0, but Oud died in 1963, so his design is protected in the Netherlands until 2034. Dutch freedom of panorama would probably permit exterior photographs; the lead curator can decide.

identifiers.commons: File:WLANL - Adfoto - Café De Unie, JJP Oud (1925).jpg

references.title: Calyx furnishing fabric
references.lede: Lucienne Day’s Festival of Britain fabric hangs cup and bowl shapes on thin stems across a terracotta ground, in flat and scratched-texture color.
references.summary: Abstract cup and bowl shapes on thin stems, in teal, lime, dark green, and cream on terracotta linen. Lucienne Day for Heal’s, 1951.

source.label: Victoria and Albert Museum: ‘Calyx’, furnishing fabric, T.329:2-1999

evidence.note: Inspected, in the scratchpad only, the V&A photograph of T.329:2-1999 (1200 × 900 px from the V&A image server), which shows the whole piece laid flat on a table. Also looked at the V&A image of the collage design CIRC.285-1955 (O85223), which uses a brown ground. Neither image is stored.

styles.note: A defining British example of the style’s biomorphic, plant-derived abstraction: flat and textured shapes in muted teal, lime, and cream on a warm earth ground.

context: The V&A catalogues T.329:2-1999 as a furnishing fabric of screen-printed linen, designed by Lucienne Day in 1950 and manufactured in 1951, 62 × 63 cm, given by Heal & Son Ltd. and acquired in 1995 with the Heal’s archive. It describes “abstracted calyx motifs in blues, greens and undyed, on a terracotta ground”. [V&A O33775](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O33775/).

The V&A record for the design (CIRC.285-1955, watercolour, gouache and collage, 1951) says that Day made Calyx for a room by her husband Robin Day in the Homes and Gardens Pavilion of the 1951 Festival of Britain, that Heal’s produced it, and that she acknowledged the influence of Klee and Miró. [V&A O85223](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O85223/).
The V&A image credits read “Design © Robin and Lucienne Day Foundation”. Lucienne Day lived from 1917 to 2010. [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1551026).
observed: The ground is a terracotta-brown linen with a visible weave.

Cup, bowl, and cone shapes hang from thin vertical stems in teal, lime green, dark green, and cream. Some are flat color; others are filled with a scratched or speckled cream texture, or with dark horizontal hatching.
Smaller stacked half-circles in cream run down some stems like beads.
A dotted cream line crosses the pattern on a diagonal.
The shapes are spread with a lot of open ground between them; nothing is outlined.
The selvedge at the left carries a printed line naming Heal’s, the design, and Lucienne Day.
interpretation: Calyx is close to the style’s textile band: plant forms abstracted into cups and cones, flat printed color, and scratched texture instead of shading.
The terracotta ground shows that a warm dark ground works as well as cream when the motifs are light.
borrow: Hang a few flat cup, cone, and half-circle shapes on thin stems and leave open ground between them.
Fill some shapes with a scratched or speckled texture instead of a gradient.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design is in copyright (Lucienne Day died in 2010); the V&A credits the design to the Robin and Lucienne Day Foundation and the photograph to the V&A.

references.title: Camera+ website, 2012
references.lede: The site for tap tap tap’s iPhone camera app, archived January 2012: a dark leather-grain page with a gray card, a film strip, and a price tag on a string.
references.summary: Dark leather grain, a textured gray card, a curling film strip, and a hanging “On sale” tag.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The archived page may lack some images or scripts that the live page had.

styles.note: Clear: a leather-grain background, a film strip and a hanging price tag without function, and embossed type on a textured card.

observed: The page background is a very dark gray with a fine pebbled grain like leather.
A large gray card with a paper-like grain and a soft top-lit gradient holds the headline “It’s all about one thing… great photos!” in dark gray with a light lower edge.
A strip of film with sprocket holes curves across the bottom of the card, carrying sample photos.
A green “On sale” tag hangs on a string from a beveled gray “Buy Now” button with a red “99¢” label.
The app icon is a photoreal camera lens in a dark rounded square; an iPhone 4 with a reflection shows the camera screen.
interpretation: It passes the gradient, shadow, and radius metrics (vertical gradients on 15% of boxes, shadows on 82%), but color and surface pattern shares are 0. The measurement sees none of the texture, because the page draws it with bitmap background images; see the style synthesis.
borrow: Hang a small tag on a string from a buy button for a sale price.
Use a curved film strip as a carousel frame for photos.

images.alt: Archived Camera+ page: a dark leather-grain background, a camera-lens app icon, a gray textured card with the headline It’s all about one thing… great photos!, a Buy Now button with a green On sale tag on a string, an iPhone 4 showing the camera, and a curved film strip of photos.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20120103083712/http://campl.us/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Campbell’s Soup Cans
references.lede: Andy Warhol’s thirty-two canvases, each a single Campbell’s soup can in the same format, one for each variety the company then sold.
references.summary: Thirty-two identical-format paintings of soup cans, hung as a grid. Andy Warhol, 1962.

source.label: MoMA: Andy Warhol, Campbell’s Soup Cans, 1962

evidence.note: MoMA’s collection page blocks scripts, and no open image of at least 800 px was found. Description relies on Wikipedia and on the MoMA record as quoted in search results.

styles.note: The founding packaging work of American Pop: a product label repeated as a grid of flat, uniform panels. Partial fit: it has no dots or comic devices.

context: The series has 32 paintings, each showing a different variety of Campbell’s soup in a uniform 20 × 16 inch format. It was first shown in July 1962 at the Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, and the Museum of Modern Art acquired the canvases in 1996. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campbell%27s_Soup_Cans).

Wikipedia quotes MoMA that Warhol “was careful to maintain an exceptional uniformity among the canvases and to minimize the visibility of brushstrokes or other signs of his own hand.” [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campbell%27s_Soup_Cans).
In 1967 Campbell’s promoted its soup with a paper dress printed after the series: [“Souper” paper dress](ref:campbells-souper-paper-dress-1967).
interpretation: The series defines the product branch of Pop art: an everyday package isolated, enlarged, and repeated, with the hand of the painter hidden.
For a screen layout, it suggests identical cards in a strict grid in which only the label text changes.
borrow: Build a catalogue grid of identical product cards and change only the name on each card.
Keep the product front-on and centered in every cell, with no perspective or shadow.
next: Inspect an image at least 800 px wide and add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, and the Campbell’s label is a trademark of the Campbell’s Company.

references.title: China Club sign and invitation
references.lede: April Greiman’s identity for the China Club restaurant in Los Angeles: a round neon sign with spaced, doubled letters, and a tilted opening invitation with rules, triangles, and a squiggle.
references.summary: Round black neon sign with spaced “C H I N A  C L U B” in white and blue and a red squiggle; a black-and-red tilted invitation. April Greiman, 1980.

source.label: People’s Graphic Design Archive: Signage for China Club

references.made: 1980 (invitation dated by the People’s Graphic Design Archive; the sign is undated there)

evidence.note: Inspected two People’s Graphic Design Archive images: a night photograph of the sign (1118 × 1098) and a photograph of the opened invitation ([item 1819](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/1819/china-club-invitation), 970 × 1452). Not stored. The owners of the physical objects are not stated.

styles.note: Clear example of the style in three dimensions: spaced letters, a doubled offset layer, bars, and loose geometric marks, carried into neon and a die-cut card.

context: The People’s Graphic Design Archive credits the sign and the invitation to April Greiman for the China Club, California, and dates the invitation 1980. [Sign](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/4146/signage-for-china-club), [invitation](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/1819/china-club-invitation).
The invitation lists April Greiman and Jayme Odgers among the credits and gives the address 8338 W Third Street, Los Angeles.
observed: The sign is a black disc on a pale wall, with two dark bars behind it at an angle.
“CHINA” and “CLUB” are white neon capitals with wide spaces between the letters, set on a rising diagonal. A blue copy of each letter sits slightly offset behind it.
A red and yellow neon squiggle rises from the top left edge of the disc.
The invitation is a folded card with a trapezoid outline, black above and red below.
On the invitation, event details sit on thin parallel rules that tilt; the year is set as “1  9  8  0” with wide spaces. The credits on the red half run upside down along diagonal rules.
White triangles, round punched holes, a thin wavy line, and short rules are scattered over both halves.
interpretation: The offset blue copy in the neon is the sign-maker’s version of an overprint: two film layers that do not quite register. The invitation uses tilted rules as a staff for spaced type, as in Weingart’s covers.
borrow: Set a short name in spaced capitals on a diagonal, with an offset second colour behind it.
Put event details on tilted hairline rules instead of a straight list.
Use one free squiggle as a counterpoint to straight bars.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design belongs to April Greiman or her client; the photographs’ owners are not stated.

references.title: Chrysler Airflow, 1934
references.lede: The first full-size American production car shaped by wind-tunnel streamlining: a rounded body, a waterfall grille, and headlamps set into the front.
references.summary: A rounded sedan with a curved waterfall grille, faired headlamps, horizontal chrome louvres, and a triple bumper. Chrysler, 1934.

creator.name: Chrysler Corporation (designer Oliver Clark; engineers Carl Breer, Fred Zeder, Owen Skelton)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected AlfvanBeem’s 2011 photograph of a 1934 Chrysler CU Airflow Eight sedan at the Louwman Museum, The Hague, on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1934_Chrysler_CU_Airflow_8_Sedan.JPG), at 1920 px.

styles.note: The car that brought streamlining to American production cars: rounded body, waterfall grille, and horizontal chrome lines. Its commercial failure is part of the style’s story.

context: Built 1934–1937, fewer than 29,600 made. Designer Oliver Clark worked with the Chrysler engineers Carl Breer, Fred Zeder, and Owen Skelton; the team ran wind-tunnel tests with the cooperation of Orville Wright. Wikipedia calls it the first full-size American production car to use streamlining as a basis for a sleeker automobile. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Airflow).

First-year sales were 10,839; Chrysler’s conventional sedans outsold it about 2.5 to one, and most historians say buyers disliked its looks. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Airflow).
observed: The body is one rounded mass: the hood curves down into the grille, and the fenders swell around the wheels in continuous curves.
The grille is a curved “waterfall” of many thin vertical chrome bars that follows the rounded nose.
The headlamps sit in the front, flush with the body, one pair stacked above a smaller pair on each side.
Three horizontal chrome louvre panels with rounded ends run along the side of the hood.
The bumper is three parallel chrome bars.
This car is painted metallic bronze. A mural photograph behind it shows a dark Airflow beside a streamlined train.
interpretation: The Airflow puts the horizontal speed line on a moving object: the three-bar bumper and hood louvres are the same parallel lines that later decorate buildings and graphics. Its failure shows that streamlining sold best as a surface style, not as an engineering shape.
borrow: Use three parallel horizontal bars with rounded ends as a bumper-like rule under a heading.
Stack short rounded bars as a louvre motif beside a panel.

images.alt: Bronze 1934 Chrysler Airflow sedan in a museum, seen from the front right: a rounded body, a curved grille of vertical chrome bars, headlamps set into the nose, chrome louvres on the hood side, and a triple chrome bumper. A large black-and-white photograph of another Airflow and a streamlined train hangs behind it.
images.caption: 1934 Chrysler CU Airflow Eight sedan, Louwman Museum. Photograph by AlfvanBeem, 2011, CC0, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1934_Chrysler_CU_Airflow_8_Sedan.JPG). The mural behind the car is a museum display photograph.

rights.statement: The photographer dedicated the photograph to the public domain (CC0). A production car is a useful article: its shape is not protected by copyright in the United States, its country of origin, and any 1934 design patents have long expired. The display photograph in the background is incidental.

references.title: Chuck Person’s Eccojams Vol. 1 cassette
references.lede: Daniel Lopatin’s 2010 cassette of slowed loops, packaged to look like the box of the 1993 game Ecco the Dolphin.
references.summary: Proto-vaporwave cassette whose J-card borrows the Ecco the Dolphin game box. 2010.

evidence.note: Relies on Wikipedia. The only image found was a 599 × 383 J-card scan in the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release/88ba5807-ba5d-41a5-bcff-14dc672688e3/cover-art), below the size needed to observe it.

styles.note: A precursor: Wikipedia credits it and Far Side Virtual with the musical template, and its game-box packaging set the habit of quoting 1990s consumer products. Partial fit, because it has none of the later pastel palette.

context: Released in August 2010 on cassette by The Curatorial Club. Wikipedia: “With packaging that resembled the 1993 video game Ecco the Dolphin, the album inspired a host of suburban teens and young adults to formulate what would become vaporwave.” [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave).
Lopatin had released several of the loops earlier on YouTube as sunsetcorp, from his audio-visual album Memory Vague (2009). [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave).
interpretation: The packaging is appropriation of a specific commercial object, not a new graphic language. That act of quoting a mass-market product is what the style kept.

rights.statement: Copyrighted packaging that reuses Sega game artwork. No image is stored here.

references.title: Ciné-dancing, Aubette, Strasbourg
references.lede: Van Doesburg’s cinema and dance hall of 1926–1928, reconstructed: walls and ceiling covered with large colored squares set on the diagonal.
references.summary: Tilted red, yellow, blue, green, and gray squares in relief across walls and ceiling. Theo van Doesburg, 1926–1928, reconstructed.
references.made: 1926–1928; covered over in 1938; reconstructed in the 1990s and 2000s

evidence.note: Inspected a photograph of the reconstructed room by the Commons user Clostridium ([File:Aubette cine dancing doesburg.JPG](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Aubette_cine_dancing_doesburg.JPG), 1024 × 768 px, viewed at 960 px). The photograph shows the present reconstruction, not the 1928 surfaces.

styles.note: Partial fit, Elementarism: flat primaries, gray, and white in rectangular panels, but the main structure is diagonal, the branch the style record treats as related, not core.

context: Theo van Doesburg, Sophie Taeuber-Arp, and Jean Arp decorated the Aubette entertainment complex on Place Kléber in 1926–1928. Van Doesburg did two cafés and two dance halls. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubette_(building)).

The decorations were covered over in 1938. The cinema and staircase became historic monuments in 1985, and renovations were completed in 1994 and 2006. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubette_(building)).
Wikipedia describes the scheme as an orthogonal composition in primary colors; the photograph shows the panels turned 45°, so that description does not match this room.
observed: Raised bands divide the walls and ceiling into large squares turned 45°, so every edge runs on the diagonal.
The squares are painted red, yellow, dark blue, green, gray, and off-white; two red panels sit on the ceiling.
A metal balcony and stair cross the left wall; a straight rail hung from the ceiling carries a row of conical metal lamps.
Low booths with white panels edged in black stand on a blue floor.
The warm lighting of the photograph shifts the whites and yellows toward cream.
interpretation: The room is van Doesburg’s counter-composition in space: the same flat colored planes as neoplasticism, turned against the orthogonal architecture. It is the clearest built example of the diagonal that divided him from Mondrian.
Use it as a contrast case for the fingerprint: a diagonal grid in the De Stijl palette should read as Elementarism.
borrow: For a single dramatic room or section, rotate a De Stijl grid 45° against an orthogonal frame, and keep everything else square.

images.alt: Interior of a large hall whose walls and ceiling are divided into big squares turned 45°, painted red, yellow, dark blue, green, and gray; a metal balcony and stair, a row of hanging conical lamps, and low white booths on a blue floor.
images.caption: Ciné-dancing of the Aubette, Strasbourg, designed by Theo van Doesburg in 1926–1928, as reconstructed. Photograph by Clostridium on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Aubette_cine_dancing_doesburg.JPG), released into the public domain.

rights.statement: The photographer released the photograph into the public domain (PD-self on Commons). The design is by Theo van Doesburg, who died in 1931, so it is public domain in France and the Netherlands; interiors finished in 1928 are not protected in the United States. The reconstruction copies his design and adds no new authorship that this record relies on.

references.title: Coca-Cola Building, Los Angeles
references.lede: Robert V. Derrah wrapped five industrial buildings in one ocean-liner facade for the Coca-Cola bottling plant on Central Avenue.
references.summary: A long white hull with rows of portholes, rivet lines, a bridge on the roof, and Coca-Cola script. Robert V. Derrah, Los Angeles, 1939.

source.label: Library of Congress: HABS CAL,19-LOSAN,31, Coca-Cola Bottling Company

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Historic American Buildings Survey general view (HABS CAL,19-LOSAN,31-1, taken between 1972 and 1977) through its [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_VIEW_-_Coca-Cola_Bottling_Company,_1334_South_Central_Avenue,_Los_Angeles,_Los_Angeles_County,_CA_HABS_CAL,19-LOSAN,31-1.tif) at 1920 px.

styles.note: The most literal ocean-liner building of the style: a whole factory block drawn as a hull, with portholes, rivets, a bridge, and horizontal bands.

context: Robert V. Derrah designed a Streamline Moderne facade in 1939 that joined five existing industrial buildings; the building mimics an ocean liner with portholes, a catwalk, and a bridge. It is Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 138, designated 5 February 1975. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca-Cola_Building_(Los_Angeles)).
observed: The block runs the full length of the street as one smooth white hull with a fully rounded corner.
Rows of round portholes of two sizes pierce the wall; some are grouped in pairs and threes.
Horizontal lines of rivets and two thin raised bands sweep along the wall and curve around the corner.
A darker band forms the base, like a waterline.
On the roof, a stepped bridge carries a flat oval sign with the Coca-Cola script.
A door with a rounded top, shaped like a ship’s hatch, sits in the wall. Script lettering “Coca-Cola Bottling Co.” is the only other sign.
interpretation: The building uses streamlining as a brand image: a factory turned into a ship suggests speed, cleanliness, and modernity. The long flat wall shows how repeated portholes and a few parallel bands carry a large surface without ornament.
borrow: Carry a long panel with only a few parallel horizontal rules and a row of circles; round one end.
Use a darker base band under a light surface, like a waterline.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a long white factory building shaped like a ship's hull, with rows of round portholes, rivet lines, a rounded corner, and a bridge-like structure on the roof carrying a Coca-Cola sign.
images.caption: General view. Historic American Buildings Survey, HABS CAL,19-LOSAN,31-1, [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/ca0218.photos.012085p/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:GENERAL_VIEW_-_Coca-Cola_Bottling_Company,_1334_South_Central_Avenue,_Los_Angeles,_Los_Angeles_County,_CA_HABS_CAL,19-LOSAN,31-1.tif).

rights.statement: HABS photographs are works of the United States government and are in the public domain; Commons marks the file public domain. The building dates from 1939, before December 1990, so it has no architectural copyright in the United States. The Coca-Cola script is a trademark that appears as part of the building.

identifiers.commons: File:GENERAL VIEW - Coca-Cola Bottling Company, 1334 South Central Avenue, Los Angeles, Los Angeles County, CA HABS CAL,19-LOSAN,31-1.tif

references.title: Collection of elements in neumorphic style
references.lede: A 2020 stock-vector sheet of neumorphic knobs, toggles, sliders, and menus, now the lead image of the Wikipedia article.
references.summary: Vectorium’s stock sheet of soft UI controls on one pale gray surface with a single blue accent.

evidence.note: Opened the Commons 1280 px rendition of `File:Neumorphism.jpg` (original 2000 × 2000). The Freepik source page returned HTTP 403, so its license and date were not checked there.

styles.note: A clear catalogue of the style’s control grammar: every knob, switch, slider, and menu is molded from one pale gray surface, and one blue marks selection.

context: Commons gives the source as Freepik (“collection-elements-neumorphic-style_8507495”), the author as Vectorium, the date as 2020, and a CC BY-SA 4.0 license. It was uploaded on 21 October 2020 by the user Le Paragone, not by the author.

A second file, `File:Neumorphism-fixed.jpg` (uploaded 29 January 2026 by Awesomecat), corrects the misspelled “Accept” button; the English Wikipedia article [Neumorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neumorphism) uses it.
observed: About thirty controls on a light gray square: two large dials with tick marks, a round knob in a blue ring, a pie selector, a nine-dot grid, toggles, sliders, dropdowns, a “Pop Up” card, media buttons, and round icon buttons.
Every control is the same gray as the background, with a white highlight at upper left and a soft gray shadow at lower right. Inputs, slider tracks, and the “Name” field are pressed in.
One mid blue fills the selected items, progress segments, and the “Cancel” button. Icons and text are dark gray.
Corners are fully round on pills and buttons and about 20 px on cards. Type is a geometric sans-serif (Montserrat-like).
interpretation: Stock sheets like this spread the style as ready-made parts. It follows the recipe closely and shows how the style favors physical controls (dials, knobs, rockers) over text.

rights.statement: Commons records CC BY-SA 4.0, but the file was uploaded by a third party from Freepik, whose own license does not grant CC BY-SA. The license claim is doubtful, so the image is not stored.

references.title: Comicraft website
references.lede: The comic-lettering foundry’s home page opens on a full-width comic panel with halftone shading, a speech balloon, and a sunburst background.
references.summary: A comic panel hero with visible halftone dots, black ink lines, a speech balloon, and a yellow navigation bar.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. The hero is a slideshow; the capture shows one slide.

styles.note: Clear example: halftone dot shading, heavy black ink lines, a speech balloon with lettering, a sunburst, and yellow and red. The panel is a contemporary comic drawing, not a Lichtenstein pastiche, and the palette leans orange rather than blue.

context: The site sells comic-book fonts; its navigation lists Word Balloons, Sound Effects, Character Voices, and Display Fonts. [Comicraft](https://www.comicbookfonts.com/).
observed: A bright yellow navigation bar holds the logo “The World’s Greatest Comic Book Fonts!” in red and yellow outlined letters, and menu items in a condensed comic font.
The hero is one comic panel: a hippo in a shirt and tie beside a woman on a sofa, drawn with black ink lines.
The figures are shaded with visible halftone dots in orange, red, and green.
A large white speech balloon with a black outline reads “Thru Thick and Thin?” in hand-lettered type.
Behind the panel, an orange sunburst of rays and paint splashes fills the width of the page.
A boxed “#5 2026” issue badge and an “Approved by the Comicraft Authority” seal copy comic-cover devices.
Below the hero, two flat yellow buttons read “WHAT’S NEW” and “MOST POPULAR” in black italic capitals.
interpretation: The halftone dots and heavy outlines are inside the hero image, so the extractor cannot see them: `surface.patternShare` is 0.06, `color.patternShare` is 0, and the median CSS border is 1 px. The page is a clear example by the rubric but fails those metrics for that reason.
Shadows cover 14% of boxes but with a 1 px offset and 1 px blur; they are not the hard offset shadows of neo-brutalism.
borrow: Put the main statement in a speech balloon over the hero image, not in a separate heading.
Use comic-cover furniture, such as an issue number box or a seal, as small secondary badges.

images.alt: Comicraft home page: a yellow navigation bar over a comic panel of a hippo in a shirt and tie and a woman on a sofa, shaded with halftone dots, with a large speech balloon reading Thru Thick and Thin? on an orange sunburst background.
images.caption: First viewport of [comicbookfonts.com](https://www.comicbookfonts.com/), captured 28 September 2026.

references.title: Composition with Large Blue Plane, Red, Black, Yellow, and Gray
references.lede: A 1921 Mondrian in which one bright blue plane takes the upper right, balanced by a small red strip, a black block, and a yellow square at the opposite edges.
references.summary: A large blue plane at upper right against gray and white, with red, black, and yellow at the edges. Piet Mondrian, 1921.

source.label: Dallas Museum of Art: Composition with Large Blue Plane, Red, Black, Yellow, and Gray

evidence.note: Inspected the Dallas Museum of Art photograph on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Piet_Mondrian_-_Composition_with_Large_Blue_Plane,_Red,_Black,_Yellow,_and_Gray_-_1984.200.FA_-_Dallas_Museum_of_Art.jpg) (7028 × 8465 px, viewed at 960 px), object 1984.200.FA. The photograph includes the white frame edge and a color checker strip at the top, which the stored copy crops off. Catalogue facts are from the museum’s record on Google Arts & Culture.

styles.note: A textbook neoplastic composition: one dominant primary plane, small opposing color planes at the far edges, gray and white fields, and black lines that stop short of some edges.

context: Oil on canvas, 60.33 × 49.85 cm. Dallas Museum of Art, Foundation for the Arts Collection, gift of Mrs. James H. Clark, 1984.200.FA. [Google Arts & Culture](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/composition-with-large-blue-plane-red-black-yellow-and-gray/CwE7U9R78Q2UOQ).

The museum’s text quotes Mondrian: “Color exists only through another color, dimension is defined by another dimension.” [Google Arts & Culture](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/composition-with-large-blue-plane-red-black-yellow-and-gray/CwE7U9R78Q2UOQ).
observed: A bright blue plane covers the upper right, about a third of the canvas; a black line divides its lower part into two smaller blue cells.
A narrow orange-red strip runs down part of the left edge beside a black rectangle.
A small pale yellow square sits at the bottom right, below a white cell.
The rest of the surface is light gray and white; the grays differ slightly from plane to plane.
The black lines are thick and even. The top-left line stops before the left edge, and the lowest vertical line stops above the bottom edge.
“PM ’21” is painted at lower left.
interpretation: The painting shows the rubric’s balance by opposition in its clearest form: the one large color plane is answered by three small ones in the far corners.
Lines that stop short of the edge keep the grid from reading as a closed table, which is a detail most web imitations miss.
borrow: Give one primary most of the color area and use the other two only as small accents in the opposite corners.
End some divider lines a little before the container edge.

images.alt: Abstract painting: a large bright blue plane at upper right, divided by black lines, light gray and white planes at left and below, a narrow red strip and a black block at the lower left edge, and a small yellow square at the bottom right.
images.caption: Piet Mondrian, Composition with Large Blue Plane, Red, Black, Yellow, and Gray, 1921. Dallas Museum of Art, 1984.200.FA. Photograph from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Piet_Mondrian_-_Composition_with_Large_Blue_Plane,_Red,_Black,_Yellow,_and_Gray_-_1984.200.FA_-_Dallas_Museum_of_Art.jpg), public domain; the color checker strip is cropped off.

rights.statement: Commons marks the museum photograph PD-Art with PD-old-auto-expired: Mondrian died in 1944, so the work is public domain in the Netherlands since 2015. Painted in 1921, it is public domain in the United States as a work published before 1931, and also under the life-plus-70 rule if it counts as unpublished.

identifiers.commons: File:Piet Mondrian - Composition with Large Blue Plane, Red, Black, Yellow, and Gray - 1984.200.FA - Dallas Museum of Art.jpg

references.title: Composition with Yellow, Red, Black, Blue, and Gray
references.lede: One of the first paintings in Mondrian’s mature neoplastic manner: a white square at the center, ringed by black, gray, and primary planes, divided by black lines of one weight.
references.summary: White center square, red strip at left, yellow at top and right, a dark blue plane below, black lines. Piet Mondrian, 1920.

source.label: Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam: Compositie met geel, rood, zwart, blauw en grijs

evidence.note: Inspected the Wikimedia Commons image (from RKD image 218858; 1000 × 860 px, viewed at 960 px) of the painting in the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, object A 9864. The Stedelijk collection page renders with JavaScript and returned no text to the fetch tool.

styles.note: A canonical neoplastic painting of 1920: only horizontal and vertical lines, flat primaries with black, white, and several grays, and an asymmetric balance around a white center.

context: The Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam holds the painting as object A 9864, dated 1920. [Wikidata Q24058759](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q24058759) gives the same number and date.

Commons lists it with Mondrian’s works of his second Paris period, 1920–1937. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Piet_Mondriaan_-_Composition_with_yellow,_red,_black,_blue_and_gray_-_A_9864_-_Stedelijk_Museum_Amsterdam.jpg).
observed: A large white square fills the center; a flat yellow plane sits above it and a dark, grayish blue plane below it.
A tall red strip runs down the left edge; two large black planes flank the white square at left and top right.
A second yellow plane stands at the right, above small light-gray cells; gray planes fill the corners.
Black lines of about the same width divide every plane; several run to the edge of the canvas, and some stop short of it at the top and bottom.
The initials and date “PM 20” are painted at lower left.
Paint texture and fine cracks are visible in the white and gray planes.
interpretation: The blue is dark and gray, the red is a warm earth red, and black and gray planes cover as much area as the primaries. The pure, bright primaries of later “Mondrian” pastiche are not yet here.
The composition is centered on the white square but not symmetric: the color planes are distributed to the edges, which fits the rubric’s asymmetric balance.
borrow: Put a large neutral plane at the center and push the colors to the edges.
Use black planes as well as black lines, so black carries weight, not only structure.

images.alt: Abstract painting: a large white square in the center, yellow planes above it and at the right, a dark grayish blue plane below it, a red strip along the left edge, two black planes, and light gray cells, all divided by black horizontal and vertical lines.
images.caption: Piet Mondrian, Composition with Yellow, Red, Black, Blue, and Gray, 1920. Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, A 9864. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Piet_Mondriaan_-_Composition_with_yellow,_red,_black,_blue_and_gray_-_A_9864_-_Stedelijk_Museum_Amsterdam.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons marks the image PD-Art with PD-old-auto-expired: Mondrian died in 1944, so his work is public domain in the Netherlands and the EU since 2015. The painting dates from 1920; it is public domain in the United States as a work published before 1931, and also under the life-plus-70 rule if it counts as unpublished.

identifiers.commons: File:Piet Mondriaan - Composition with yellow, red, black, blue and gray - A 9864 - Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam.jpg

references.title: Composition XXII
references.lede: Theo van Doesburg’s version of the neoplastic canvas: flat rectangles that meet edge to edge, with no black lines between them.
references.summary: Ochre, gray-green, white, black, blue, and red rectangles abutting without lines. Theo van Doesburg, 1920–1922.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Theo van Doesburg, Composition XXII (Van Abbemuseum)

references.made: June–July 1922 per the Commons record (after Hoek’s catalogue); older exhibition catalogues date it 1920

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image (1447 × 1532 px, viewed at 1280 px) of the painting in the Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven. The Commons record cites the museum’s old collection site as its source; the current museum record was not checked.

styles.note: Partial fit: orthogonal flat planes in an asymmetric balance, but without the black dividing lines, and with an ochre yellow and a gray-green that are not in Mondrian’s strict palette.

context: Oil on canvas, 45.5 × 43.3 cm, Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven, bought in 1966. The first owner was Thijs Rinsema of Drachten, who acquired it from van Doesburg in 1922. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Composition_XXII.jpg).
Exhibition catalogues listed on Commons date it 1920, 1920–1922, or about 1925. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Composition_XXII.jpg).
observed: A large ochre-yellow square fills most of the upper left and center.
Two gray-green planes sit at the top right and the lower left; off-white strips run down the left edge and at the right.
Two black rectangles, one at right and one below the ochre square, touch other planes directly.
A dark blue plane fills the lower right, and a red strip runs along the bottom left edge.
There are no lines: every plane meets its neighbor edge to edge. Canvas texture shows through the paint.
interpretation: This is the same grammar as Mondrian’s 1920–1921 canvases with the black lines removed. It shows that the lines are Mondrian’s signature more than a rule of the whole movement.
The earthy ochre and the gray-green show that the strict primaries were a direction, not yet a fixed rule, in van Doesburg’s painting of these years.
borrow: Tile a layout with flat rectangles that touch without gaps or borders, and let one large plane dominate.
Use black as a solid block among colored blocks instead of as lines.
