images.alt: Abstract painting of flat rectangles that meet without lines: a large ochre-yellow square, gray-green and off-white planes, two black rectangles, a dark blue plane at lower right, and a red strip along the bottom left.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg, Composition XXII, 1920–1922. Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Composition_XXII.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons marks the image public domain. Van Doesburg died in 1931, so his work is public domain in the Netherlands and the EU. Painted by 1922, it is public domain in the United States as a work published before 1931, and also under the life-plus-70 rule if it counts as unpublished.

references.title: Crak! Now, Mes Petits… Pour la France!
references.lede: Roy Lichtenstein’s offset poster for his 1963 Leo Castelli exhibition: a woman fires a rifle under the sound effect CRAK!, with a speech balloon and a line of exhibition text below.
references.summary: Yellow, red, and black offset print with dot-tinted skin, a speech balloon, and a black sound effect. Roy Lichtenstein, 1963.

source.label: V&A: Crak! Now, Mes Petits…Pour La France, E.229-1985

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, E.229-1985 (1400 × 933 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: A Pop exhibition poster printed with the same means as a comic: three inks, a dot tint, black key lines, a speech balloon, and a sound effect.

context: The V&A records it as a colour offset lithograph poster, 535 × 718 mm, printed in the United States in 1963, given by Steef Davidson. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O74122/).

The catalogue raisonné lists the work as RLCR 812: an offset lithograph in an edition of 300, published by Leo Castelli Gallery and printed by Colorcraft, New York, in yellow, red, and black. It announced Lichtenstein’s exhibition at Castelli from 28 September to 24 October 1963. [RLCR 812](https://www.lichtensteincatalogue.org/catalogue/entry.php?id=296).
That exhibition included [Whaam!](ref:lichtenstein-whaam-1963) and [Drowning Girl](ref:lichtenstein-drowning-girl-1963). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crak!).
observed: The image is one panel with a black border. A line of gray sans-serif text runs below it: “Roy Lichtenstein · September 28 - October 24, 1963 · Leo Castelli 4 E.77 N.Y.”
The woman’s face, hand, and the sky behind her are filled with red dots on the paper color.
Her beret is flat dark red. The smoke and the ground are flat yellow with black outlines.
“CRAK!” is drawn in huge black letters with broken, angular strokes inside a white cloud shape.
A white speech balloon at lower right holds black hand-lettered capitals: “NOW, MES PETITS… POUR LA FRANCE!” The last words are heavier.
Outlines are black and of even weight. Only yellow, red, and black ink appear on the off-white paper.
interpretation: The poster proves that the style works with three inks. Red dots give a pink, and paper white does the rest.
The exhibition line under the panel is the only set type. The panel carries the message, and the facts sit outside it.
borrow: Build a whole page from three inks: one primary for flat fills, one for dot tints, and black for lines and lettering.
Put the essential facts in one plain line under the panel, outside the artwork.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is © Estate of Roy Lichtenstein; the catalogue raisonné states “© 2026 Roy Lichtenstein Foundation. All Rights Reserved.”

references.title: Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design poster
references.lede: Katherine McCoy’s recruiting poster for Cranbrook: a central column of paired words in spaced grotesque, laid over a violet and blue collage and framed by labeled boxes and dotted lines.
references.summary: Paired words (“form/content”, “art/science”) in letterspaced grotesque over a two-colour collage, with boxed labels and dotted diagonals. Katherine McCoy, 1989.

source.label: V&A: The Cranbrook Graduate Program in Design, Michigan, E.599-1998

references.made: 1989 (V&A production date; the V&A description also says “early 1990s”)

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object E.599-1998 (image 2014HE4886, 1258 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example of the American academic branch: letterspacing, weight changes inside words, layers, and bars, used to carry an argument about reading.

context: The V&A holds the poster as E.599-1998, offset lithograph on card, 71.3 × 56 cm, printed by Signet in Michigan, given by the Design Museum. McCoy was chair of the Cranbrook graduate design program. [V&A E.599-1998](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O120192/).

The V&A says “Words are paired into couples such as ‘art / science’, ‘language / thought’ and ‘global / local’. The word couplings operate both as information and as design elements.” [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O120192/).
Designhistory.org places Cranbrook directly after New Wave in its sequence of design after modernism. [designhistory.org](http://www.designhistory.org/PostModern_pages/NewWave.html).
observed: A central column of word pairs runs down the sheet, each pair set as one word (“formcontent”, “mythologytechnology”, “artscience”). The first word is regular weight and the second bold, and all are widely letterspaced.
The column overprints a collage split into violet on the left and blue on the right: machine parts, a book, a face, and fragments of other posters.
“cranbrook” is set white on a black box at the top left. “The Graduate Program in Design” runs across the top in a large spaced grotesque that the word pairs overlap.
Labels in small boxes (“program”, “design”, “see”, “read”, “image”, “text”) sit at the corners, some white on black and some outlined, joined by dotted vertical and diagonal lines.
A violet-to-blue gradient fills the top band, and small paragraphs of text float inside it at different positions.
interpretation: The poster uses New Wave means (spacing, weight contrast inside a word, overprint, boxed labels) for a theory of reading. It is later and denser than Weingart’s work and points toward deconstruction, but its letterforms stay clean.
borrow: Join two words and change the weight at the join.
Letterspace a centered column of short phrases and let it overprint an image.
Label the corners of a composition with small boxed words and join them with dotted lines.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Katherine McCoy is living, so the design is in copyright.

references.title: CRED app and the Synth framework
references.lede: An Indian credit-card payments app that moved its whole product to a dark neumorphic interface and open-sourced the framework in 2021.
references.summary: CRED’s dark, soft-shadowed app interface and Synth, its open-source neumorphic component library for Android and iOS.

evidence.note: Inspected the Synth README banner (2560 × 1280, hosted on i.imgur.com), which shows CRED app screens on phones. The blog post was read from its Wayback capture of 26 January 2021; the live URL now redirects to the CRED home page. The app itself and the blog’s video were not inspected.

styles.note: A shipped consumer product, not a concept, that applied the style across the whole app. It is the dark variant: controls and panels share one charcoal surface and rise from it with soft shadows.

context: CRED’s blog post “World, meet Synth: Open-sourcing our Neumorphic UI framework” (18 January 2021) says the style “piqued the interest of a few of our designers”, who mocked it up “as a side project”, and that the company then decided “to not just have a few screens but the entire product adopt the Neumorphic aesthetic”.

It adds: “we had to optimize for lights, shadows, gradients, and more in our framework.” Synth was released for Android and iOS under the Apache 2.0 License; the Android repository was created on 12 January 2021.
The Synth README says the library “works over base color concept and derives light and dark colors from base color itself”.
observed: Three phones rendered as dark charcoal slabs on a charcoal background, tilted diagonally.
Pill buttons (“Add new”, “View details”) and header chips rise from the dark surface with soft dark shadows and faint light edges. A “Pay more” button is filled blue.
Credit-card images and notification cards are in saturated colors (green, mustard, purple, terracotta), which break the single-surface rule.
Text is a light, lowercase geometric sans-serif in pale gray; the “synth by CRED” logotype is a copper gradient.
interpretation: The strongest evidence found that the style reached a large production app, and it shows the dark variant that most concepts skip. The colored cards are content (the user’s credit cards); the chrome around them keeps to one surface.
borrow: Derive the light and dark shadow colors from one base color, as Synth does, so a theme change keeps the relief consistent.
next: Capture current CRED app screens or the Synth sample app to check whether the app still uses the style.

rights.statement: The Synth code is Apache 2.0, but the banner is hosted outside the repository and shows third-party marks (American Express, Axis Bank, Google), so it is not stored.

references.title: CSS backdrop-filter property
references.lede: The CSS property that blurs whatever lies behind an element, which made frosted glass practical on the web.
references.summary: The web platform feature behind glassmorphism: blur and other filters applied to an element’s backdrop.

creator.name: CSS Working Group (Filter Effects Module Level 2)

references.made: Safari 9 with the -webkit- prefix (2015-09-30); Chrome 76 (2019-07-30); Firefox 103 (2022-07-26); Baseline September 2024

evidence.note: Read the MDN page and the MDN browser-compatibility data (bcd.developer.mozilla.org) on 2026-09-28. A CSS property has no single appearance, so the level stays documented.

styles.note: The enabling technology. The style’s web spread in 2020–2021 followed Chrome’s support in 2019.

context: MDN: “The backdrop-filter CSS property lets you apply graphical effects such as blurring or color shifting to the area behind an element.” The element or its background must be transparent or partly transparent for the effect to show. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/backdrop-filter).

Browser support per MDN compatibility data: Safari 9 (2015) with the `-webkit-` prefix and Safari 18 (2024) without it; Chrome 76 (July 2019); Edge 17 prefixed (2018) and 79 (2020); Firefox 103 (July 2022). MDN marks the feature Baseline 2024.

It is specified in the CSS Filter Effects Module Level 2 draft. The [Hype4 generator](ref:hype4-glassmorphism-generator) and most glassmorphism tutorials use `backdrop-filter: blur()` with an `rgba()` fill.
interpretation: The dates explain the style’s timing: the name arrived in 2020, a year after Chrome shipped the property, and the web examples of 2020–2021 needed a fallback for Firefox until 2022.
borrow: Always pair `backdrop-filter` with a fill that is readable on its own, because the blur may be absent or turned off.

rights.statement: MDN text is CC BY-SA 2.5 by Mozilla contributors; only facts and a short quotation are used here.

references.title: Cyclamen (“Whiplash”) wall hanging by Hermann Obrist
references.lede: The embroidery that gave the whiplash line its name: a cyclamen plant, from roots to flowers, drawn as long gold stems that loop and snap back across a plain gray-brown linen ground.
references.summary: Gold silk embroidery of looping cyclamen stems on gray linen. Hermann Obrist, Munich, 1895.

source.label: Münchner Stadtmuseum: Großer Wandbehang mit Seidenstickerei („Peitschenhieb“), T-49/63

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the museum’s own image of object T-49/63 from its online collection (2000 × 1316 px). The same file is on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:T-49-63_3_Obrist-H-Peitschenhieb-A4-ONLINE.jpg). Read the museum’s object page.

styles.note: The canonical whiplash line: a whole plant turned into long, swelling, looping strokes on a calm ground.

context: The Münchner Stadtmuseum records a large wall hanging with silk embroidery (“Peitschenhieb”, whiplash), designed by Hermann Obrist, dated 1895, linen with silk embroidery, 119 × 183 cm, inventory number T-49/63, in its fashion and textiles collection. [Münchner Stadtmuseum](https://sammlungonline.muenchner-stadtmuseum.de/objekt/grosser-wandbehang-mit-seidenstickerei-peitschenhieb-10035267).

Wikipedia dates the hanging, *Cyclamen*, to 1894 and says that a description in *Pan* magazine compared it to the “sudden violent curves generated by the crack of a whip”. The term “whiplash”, first used to ridicule the style, is now applied to the characteristic curve of Art Nouveau. [Wikipedia: Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau).
observed: The ground is a plain gray-brown linen with a fine horizontal weave, left empty around a central motif that fills about two thirds of the width.
The motif is embroidered in one colour, an olive gold silk with a slight sheen.
Long stems run mainly on a diagonal from lower left to upper right. Each one swings out, loops back in a tight hairpin turn, and runs back, so the stems cross one another several times.
The stems swell and taper, with small hooked spurs along their length.
At the lower right a tangle of thin roots and a bulb; at the upper left and centre, feathery leaves and closed flower buds; at the lower left a larger flower with folded petals.
The work has no border or frame line; the hemmed edge of the cloth is the only edge.
interpretation: This is the grammar’s first term in its purest form: one plant, one colour, and a line that carries all the movement. It has no symmetry and no straight line.
The single warm metallic colour on a neutral ground shows that the style does not need many colours; the curve alone identifies it.
borrow: Draw a divider or a background flourish as one long line that loops back on itself, and let its width swell and taper.
Put one ornamental figure in a single warm colour on a large, quiet neutral field.

images.alt: Rectangular gray-brown linen hanging with a large olive-gold silk embroidery of a cyclamen plant: long stems loop back and forth diagonally across the cloth, with roots at lower right and leaves and flowers along the stems.
images.caption: Hermann Obrist, wall hanging with silk embroidery (“Peitschenhieb”, *Cyclamen*), 1895. Münchner Stadtmuseum, Sammlung Mode / Textilien, T-49/63. Image: [Münchner Stadtmuseum](https://sammlungonline.muenchner-stadtmuseum.de/objekt/grosser-wandbehang-mit-seidenstickerei-peitschenhieb-10035267), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: The Münchner Stadtmuseum publishes the image under CC BY-SA 4.0; credit “Münchner Stadtmuseum, Sammlung Mode / Textilien”. Hermann Obrist died in 1927, so the design is in the public domain in Germany and Switzerland, and a work of 1895 is in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Dashon neumorphic dashboard
references.lede: A Webflow dashboard experiment in which the frame, sidebar, cards, and bars all rise from one pale surface.
references.summary: Webflow analytics-dashboard experiment: pale gray-blue cards with paired shadows and orange progress bars.

creator.name: Viktoria Kosmovich (as credited on the page)

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear. The whole dashboard is one pale surface; cards, search field, icon buttons, and the Logout button rise with white and gray shadows, and progress tracks are pressed.

observed: A large raised frame on a pale gray-blue page holds a sidebar and a grid of cards in the same color.
Four “Total Earns 2056” cards and four larger panels are raised; the active “Dashboard” item in the sidebar is a raised bar.
The search field, bell, gear, and user buttons at the top are small raised squares and pills.
Three progress tracks under “Best Selling Categories” are pressed wells with orange gradient fills. “on” in the Dashon logo is orange; text is dark navy sans-serif.
interpretation: A dashboard with few controls, one of the uses the style suits. The footer says it was “recreated for experimental purposes”, so it is a demonstration, not a product.
Measured: shadows on 84 % of boxes (median offset 4.2 px, median blur 15 px, none hard), borders on 4 %, median radius 10 px.

images.alt: Dashon dashboard experiment: a pale gray-blue raised frame with a sidebar, four raised Total Earns cards, raised Revenue and Sales panels, and pressed progress tracks with orange fills.
images.caption: First viewport of [Dashon dashboard experiment](https://neumorph-dashboard.webflow.io/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: De Stijl journal cover and advertisement page, 1922
references.lede: Van Doesburg’s typography for the journal: DE STIJL in black capitals over a large red NB, and an advertisement page in which thick black bars frame each notice.
references.summary: Black sans-serif capitals over a red NB, vertical text blocks, and ads framed by thick black bars. Theo van Doesburg, 1920–1922.

source.label: Geheugen van Nederland: Typografie voor De Stijl, omslag en een paar advertenties

references.made: 1920–1922 (the cover shown is for the fifth volume, 1922)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons copy (1200 × 1533 px, viewed at 960 px) of the Geheugen van Nederland image of a mounted sheet, 41 × 32.5 cm, in the Centraal Museum Utrecht on loan from the Dutch State (inventory AB4945 in the file name). Also compared the Commons scan of the 1921 cover from the 1968 facsimile reprint ([File:De Stijl - vierde jaargang 1921 001.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:De_Stijl_-_vierde_jaargang_1921_001.jpg)).

styles.note: The movement’s own journal: rectilinear sans-serif capitals, one flat primary, text turned vertical, and thick black bars as structure.

context: Commons records the object as “Typografie voor De Stijl, omslag en een paar advertenties” (typography for De Stijl, cover and some advertisements), printed matter, 1920–1922, 41 × 32.5 cm, Centraal Museum Utrecht, on loan from the Dutch State. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:De_Stijl_typography_by_Theo_van_Doesburg_AB4945.jpg).

The same cover layout, with “VIERDE JAARGANG 1921”, opens the fourth volume. Commons credits that cover to Theo van Doesburg and Piet Mondrian. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:De_Stijl_-_vierde_jaargang_1921_001.jpg).
Van Doesburg edited the journal from 1917 until his death in 1931. [Wikipedia: De Stijl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Stijl).
observed: The cover shows “DE STIJL” in black geometric sans-serif capitals printed over two tall red letters, “N” and “B”.
“VIJFDE JAARGANG 1922” sits at top right; a tall red numeral “1” stands in the middle.
A block of letter-spaced capitals, “INTERNATIONAAL MAANDBLAD VOOR NIEUWE KUNST WETENSCHAP EN KULTUUR REDACTIE THEO VAN DOESBURG”, runs vertically at the right.
“WEIMAR” runs vertically at the lower left above the line “LEIDEN ANTWERPEN PARIJS ROME”.

The advertisement page is divided into boxes by thick black bars: horizontal bars above and below some notices and vertical bars at the sides of others. The notices advertise Gispen, Valori Plastici, De Sikkel, and Mécano.
The sheets are mounted on a dark blue-black ground with the label “1921 / THEO VAN DOESBURG”.
interpretation: The red NB probably abbreviates Nieuwe Beelding, the Dutch name for neoplasticism (not checked against a source). The cover sets the movement’s program as a letter block under the title.
The advertisement page shows the painted grid translated into print: black bars do the work of rules and borders, and they stop short of each other instead of closing the boxes.
borrow: Set a short title in black capitals over one oversized letter in a primary.
Frame content blocks with thick black bars on only two sides, and let the bars stop short of each other.
Turn a secondary text block 90° and set it in letter-spaced capitals.

images.alt: Two printed sheets on a dark ground. Above, a journal cover with DE STIJL in black capitals over a large red N and B, a red numeral 1, and a vertical block of small capitals. Below, an advertisement page where thick black bars frame notices for Gispen, Valori Plastici, De Sikkel, and Mécano.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg, typography for De Stijl: cover of the fifth volume (1922) and an advertisement page. Centraal Museum Utrecht, on loan from the Dutch State. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:De_Stijl_typography_by_Theo_van_Doesburg_AB4945.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons marks the image PD-old. Van Doesburg died in 1931 and Mondrian in 1944, so the design is public domain in the Netherlands. It was published in 1921–1922, before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States.

identifiers.commons: File:De Stijl typography by Theo van Doesburg AB4945.jpg

references.title: De Stijl student site on Neocities
references.lede: A small Portuguese-language site about the movement whose header is itself a Mondrian-like composition of thick black bars and red, yellow, and blue planes.
references.summary: Thick black bars and primary planes as a page header, with primary-colored navigation tabs above plain text.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The page is 15 px wider than the viewport.

styles.note: Clear in the header: black horizontal and vertical bars that run off the edge, with flat red, yellow, and blue planes among white ones. The body below is plain text, and the page describes the movement as well as using it.

observed: The header is a white field divided by thick black vertical bars and one thick black horizontal bar that runs the full width of the page.
Some cells are filled with flat red, yellow, and blue; a blue plane sits at the far right, red and yellow planes at the left.
The title “De Stijl” is set in white sans-serif with a dark drop shadow over the composition.
Six navigation tabs sit in a row, filled red, blue, yellow, black, white, and gray, with small rounded corners.
Below, the heading “História” and a paragraph about Mondrian and the journal are set in gray Helvetica on white, followed by a bibliography.
interpretation: The header uses the style’s grammar directly: lines as solid bars, planes in the three primaries, and asymmetric placement. The rest of the page is a default text layout.

The black bars are drawn as filled boxes, not CSS borders, so `surface.border.medianWidth` measures 1 px although the visible lines are about 24 px thick. The tabs have a 4 px radius, which gives a round share of 0.86 among only 7 measured boxes. No heading is in capitals (uppercase share 0).
borrow: Draw the grid lines as solid black bars that run past the content edge, and fill only two or three cells with primaries.
Color the navigation items with the palette itself: one primary or non-color per item.

images.alt: Web page with a header of thick black horizontal and vertical bars dividing white cells, some filled red, yellow, and blue, and the title De Stijl in white. Below are six navigation tabs in red, blue, yellow, black, white, and gray, and a Portuguese text about Mondrian.
images.caption: First viewport of [destijl.neocities.org](https://destijl.neocities.org/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Dead & Company website
references.lede: The band’s site after its 2026 Golden Gate Park shows: fat, outlined concert-poster lettering and a stippled drawing on full-bleed yellow.
references.summary: Full-bleed yellow, pink and light-blue outlined display lettering, and a stippled Golden Gate Bridge.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: a full-bleed saturated ground, centered layout, and fat display lettering with echo outlines, but the letters stay legible and the body type is a clean geometric sans. The colors do not vibrate.

observed: A saturated golden yellow fills the whole viewport.
DEAD & COMPANY is centered at the top in very fat, tight capitals filled with pink, with a black outline and a black offset shadow.
GOLDEN GATE PARK sits below in tall condensed capitals filled with light blue and outlined in black, with an offset black shadow.
Smaller lines, CELEBRATING 60 YEARS OF THE GRATEFUL DEAD’S MUSIC and SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA, are in a wide black geometric sans.
A stippled drawing of the Golden Gate Bridge in light blue, green, and black, with a DEADCO blimp, fills the lower half.
The navigation at top right is plain black text and social icons.
interpretation: The page borrows the poster tradition of its own subject, the Grateful Dead, through lettering and a colored ground. It stops short of the style’s distortion and ornament.
Measured values: `color.chromaticShare` 0.73 and `type.centerShare` 1.0 pass; `color.hues` is 2, `surface.radius.median` is 0, and `color.patternShare` is 0, because the stipple is an image.
borrow: Give display lettering a fill color, a black outline, and an offset black shadow for a poster look that stays legible.
Use a saturated yellow as the page ground instead of white.

images.alt: Dead and Company home page: yellow background, pink outlined DEAD & COMPANY lettering, light-blue outlined GOLDEN GATE PARK lettering, a thank-you line in black, and a stippled drawing of the Golden Gate Bridge with a blimp.
images.caption: First viewport of [deadandcompany.com](https://deadandcompany.com/).

references.title: Delicious Library, 2004
references.lede: A Mac cataloguing app that showed books, films, and games as photoreal covers on a wooden bookshelf.
references.summary: Photoreal media covers on a wooden shelf. Delicious Monster, 2004.

creator.name: Delicious Monster (Wil Shipley and Mike Matas)

references.made: First released November 2004; Delicious Library 2 in 2008

evidence.note: The archived 2009 website ([capture](ref:delicious-monster-website-2009)) shows a small screenshot of the shelves, too small to describe. Based on Wikipedia and TechCrunch (2010).

styles.note: A precursor on the Mac: the wooden bookshelf that iBooks later resembled.

context: Delicious Monster was founded by Wil Shipley and Mike Matas; Matas left in 2005 to work for Apple. Delicious Library won Apple Design Awards, including Best Mac OS X User Experience (2005). [Wikipedia: Delicious Monster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delicious_Monster).
The software was first released in November 2004; Delicious Library 2 was released in 2008. [Wikipedia: Delicious Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delicious_Library).

TechCrunch (27 January 2010): “the bookshelf view in iBooks is nearly identical to the main bookshelf view used in Delicious Library.” [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2010/01/27/think-ibooks-looks-familiar-youre-not-the-only-one/).
interpretation: The link from this app to [iBooks](ref:ibooks-ipad-2010) through one designer shows how the style moved from independent Mac software into Apple’s own apps.

rights.statement: Delicious Monster software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Delicious Monster website, 2009
references.lede: The page for Delicious Library 2, archived June 2009: a wood-grain header with vector flowers above olive panels, and a screenshot of the app’s wooden shelves.
references.summary: Orange wood grain, vector flowers and a skyline, olive panels, and a shelf screenshot.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The archived page may lack some images or scripts that the live page had.

styles.note: Borderline: the wood-grain header matches the style’s materials and the page shows the app’s bookshelf, but the vector flowers and flat olive panels come from mid-2000s illustration, not from an object metaphor.

observed: A large rounded header shows orange and brown wood grain with a monster mascot, a “2.1” speech bubble, and a vector skyline with flowers and birds.
Below, olive green panels with thin yellow lines hold the navigation (Library, Company, Help, Buy $40, Download) in small capitals.
A yellow box holds a screenshot of Delicious Library 2 with book and comic covers on three wooden shelves.
Feature buttons are olive rectangles with small round icons, divided by a stem-like line with a blue flower.
interpretation: All metrics except radius fail: the wood grain and panels are bitmap images (49% image share), so no gradient, pattern, or shadow is measured.
borrow: Pair a real wood-grain header with the product’s own shelf screenshot to connect the site and the app.

images.alt: Archived Delicious Monster page: an orange wood-grain header with a monster mascot, a 2.1 badge, and a vector skyline with flowers, above olive panels with navigation, a screenshot of Delicious Library 2 showing covers on wooden shelves, and feature buttons.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20090618031638/http://www.delicious-monster.com/).
