references.title: DerekArt website
references.lede: Derek Yaniger’s shop header pairs a bouncing retro logotype with a band of hand-drawn squared spirals in cream, red, and black.
references.summary: A pink header, a bouncing hand-lettered logo, and a cream, red, and black pattern band with a lowercase slab slogan.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: the header and pattern band use the style’s bouncing hand lettering and a textile-like repeat confined to one band, but the prints below are loud and clashing, and the page is a shop.

observed: The header is flat dusty pink with a centered logotype, “*DEREKart!”, in red and black letters of mixed sizes that bounce off the baseline, with an asterisk star.
The menu below is dark geometric sans-serif capitals.
A full-width band alternates cream, red, and black blocks with hand-drawn squared spirals in black, red, and gray lines.
At the right end of the band, “can you dig it?” is set in a heavy, rounded lowercase face in cream on red.
Below, on white, “FEATURED PRINTS” heads three poster thumbnails in saturated blue, yellow, magenta, and green with dense cartoon figures.
interpretation: The band shows the rubric’s “pattern as a band” trait directly, and the logotype shows bouncing, mixed lettering.

The featured prints are closer to a psychedelic or tiki revival: saturated, crowded, and outlined. Measured: the CSS sees no chromatic color (the colors are all in images); the screenshot palette finds five hue families.
borrow: Confine a hand-drawn geometric repeat to one horizontal band under the header.
Let a logotype’s letters change size and bounce off the baseline.

images.alt: DerekArt shop home page: a dusty pink header with a bouncing red and black DerekArt logo and a menu, a band of cream, red, and black blocks with hand-drawn squared spirals and the words can you dig it, and three bright poster thumbnails under Featured Prints.
images.caption: First viewport of [derekart.com](https://derekart.com/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design, artwork, and content belong to the site’s owners and artists. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Design for a poster for La Section d’Or
references.lede: An ink design for an exhibition poster in which blocky right-angled capitals are stacked, stepped, and turned on their sides to fill a square.
references.summary: Black rectilinear capitals in stepped blocks and rotated words on a square sheet. Theo van Doesburg, about April 1920.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Theo van Doesburg, design for a poster for La Section d’Or

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image (1106 × 1140 px, viewed at 960 px), from Geheugen van Nederland. The object is Indian ink on transparent paper mounted on panel, 65 × 62.5 cm, RCE inventory AB4980, on loan to the Centraal Museum Utrecht. No printed copy of the poster was checked.

styles.note: Partial fit: the typography is fully orthogonal, in van Doesburg’s rectilinear letters, but the sheet is black on paper with no primary colors.

context: The inscriptions read “INTERNATIONALE TENTOONSTELLING LA SECTION D’OR”, “KUBISTEN EN” at top right, and “NEOKUBISTEN” at bottom left, signed “THEO V.D”. The design came to the Dutch State in 1981 with the Van Moorsel donation. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Design_for_a_poster.jpg).

Commons lists it in the exhibitions *De Stijl, 1917–1931: Visions of Utopia* and *Van Doesburg and the International Avant-Garde*. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Design_for_a_poster.jpg).
observed: All letters are black capitals built from thick horizontal and vertical strokes, like van Doesburg’s alphabet.
“LA” sits large at top left; “KUBISTEN” runs along the top right, and “EN” descends vertically at the right edge.
The center holds a stepped stack: a very heavy word, then “INTERNATIONALE” and “TENTOONSTELLING” in narrower letters, then another very heavy word.
“D’OR” sits in a large block at lower right; “NEO” is turned on its side at the left and “KUBISTEN” runs along the bottom left.
The transparent paper has yellowed and shows water stains; the signature “THEO V.D” is at bottom right.
interpretation: The words are placed as rectangular blocks that interlock across the square, so the text itself builds an asymmetric grid.
The heaviest words are hard to read, which shows how far van Doesburg put composition before legibility in 1920.
borrow: Treat each word as a rectangle and interlock the rectangles in a square field, turning one or two words 90°.
Vary letter width, not letter shape, to fit words to the blocks.

images.alt: Square ink design on yellowed paper: black blocky capitals built from right angles, arranged in stepped blocks, with some words running vertically; the words include LA, KUBISTEN, INTERNATIONALE, TENTOONSTELLING, D’OR, and NEO KUBISTEN.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg, design for a poster for La Section d’Or, about April 1920. Dutch State collection (RCE AB4980), on loan to the Centraal Museum Utrecht. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Design_for_a_poster.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons marks the image public domain. Van Doesburg died in 1931, so the design is public domain in the Netherlands; made in 1920, it is public domain in the United States under either the pre-1931 publication rule or the life-plus-70 rule.

identifiers.commons: File:Theo van Doesburg Design for a poster.jpg

references.title: Design Quarterly 133: “Does It Make Sense?”
references.lede: April Greiman’s issue of the Walker Art Center’s journal, made on a Macintosh as a single fold-out poster: a life-size bitmap self-portrait among layers of type, symbols, and video images.
references.summary: A fold-out issue with a pixelated nude self-portrait, spaced typewriter-style lines, symbols, and video stills. April Greiman, Walker Art Center, 1986.

source.label: People’s Graphic Design Archive: Design Quarterly #133

evidence.note: Inspected the People’s Graphic Design Archive photographs of the front and back of one opened copy (1440 × 474 and 1440 × 485) in scratchpad copies. The owner of the copy is not stated. Only the larger type is readable at this size. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example of the style’s move to the computer: layered fragments, spaced lines of type, and bars, made in MacDraw.
Partial fit: the early Macintosh bitmap self-portrait shows visible square pixels, but the layout is New Wave.

context: Walker Art Center text quoted by the People’s Graphic Design Archive says the usual 32 pages were treated as a two-foot-by-six-foot, double-sided fold-out, and that Greiman used MacDraw to combine video images and type and to tile pages into a pixelated, life-size double self-portrait. [People’s Graphic Design Archive](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/1804/does-it-make-sense-design-quarterly-133).
Greiman’s own page names Mildred Friedman as editor and says the type was set on a Macintosh and LaserWriter. [aprilgreiman.com](https://www.aprilgreiman.com/does-it-make-sense).
observed: The front is dark violet on cream. A life-size nude figure made of coarse bitmap dots lies across the whole sheet.
Around the figure float a spiral galaxy, hands, a brain, orbits, planet symbols, small photographs, and a black panel with a moon.
A bitmap block at the top right holds large pixel numerals and “the spiritual double” in a monospaced face.
A line of words runs along the bottom edge on a ruled scale: “proton . neutron . electron . moron . milli . micro …”, with wide gaps and full stops between the words.
“live where you can.” sits upside down on a white bar.
The back has large colour video stills, a yellow ground, a dot-screen cloud in orange, blue text in a slab face, and narrow columns of small text.
interpretation: The issue keeps the style’s layering, bars, and spaced lines, but the type is often monospaced or slab, and bitmap dots replace film screens. It is a partial fit that marks the end of the period and the start of digital postmodern design.
The monospaced lines here are one reason the fingerprint should not treat a small share of monospaced type as a counter-sign by itself.
borrow: Run a spaced-out line of words along a ruled scale at the page edge.
Build one large figure from coarse dots and lay small symbols over it.
Turn one short phrase upside down on a white bar.

rights.statement: No image is stored. April Greiman is living, so the design is in copyright. The photographs’ owner is not stated.

references.title: Dlia golosa (For the Voice)
references.lede: El Lissitzky’s design for thirteen poems by Vladimir Mayakovsky builds letters, bars, and a ship from type material in red and black, with a thumb index to find each poem.
references.summary: Red and black letterpress pages with giant stacked capitals, a diagonal black bar, and a stepped thumb index. Lissitzky and Mayakovsky, Berlin, 1923.

source.label: Josef Chladek: Dlia golosa (For the Voice), Gosizdat / Lutze and Vogt, 1923

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a photograph of an open copy on display at the Deutsches Buch- und Schriftmuseum, Leipzig, published by Karl432 on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Seiten_aus_dem_Gedichtband_Dlja_golosa_von_Wladimir_Majakowski_gestaltet_von_El_Lissitzky.jpg) (2816 × 2300 px, viewed at 1920 px). The photograph shows one spread, the opening of “Left March”. Other spreads are known only from the Commons category [Dlia Golosa](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Dlia_Golosa), which was not inspected page by page.

styles.note: The canonical constructivist book: red and black type material, stacked heavy capitals, a diagonal bar, and pictures built from rules.

context: The book collects thirteen of Mayakovsky’s poems for reading aloud. It was published by Gosizdat (the State Publishing House) in Berlin in 1923 and printed by Lutze & Vogt; it has 61 pages and measures about 13 × 19 cm. [Josef Chladek](https://josefchladek.com/book/el_lissitzky_vladimir_mayakovsky_-_dlia_golosa).

Lissitzky added a thumb index so that a reader could find a poem quickly. He compared his role to “an accompanying piano to a violin”. [Josef Chladek](https://josefchladek.com/book/el_lissitzky_vladimir_mayakovsky_-_dlia_golosa).

The Leipzig museum shows the book as an example of “Elementare Typografie”. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Seiten_aus_dem_Gedichtband_Dlja_golosa_von_Wladimir_Majakowski_gestaltet_von_El_Lissitzky.jpg).
observed: The left page shows a sailing ship drawn from black and red rules and bars. A red flag reads “РСФСР”, and the word “ЛЕВ” repeats on stepped red lines above it.
The right page opens “ЛЕВЫЙ МАРШ” (Left March). Two red slabs with black rules form a giant letter М; “ЛЕВЫЙ” runs vertically in black capitals inside the first slab.
A thick black bar runs diagonally from upper right to lower center. “МАТРОСАМ” (to the sailors) runs on a diagonal beside it in red serif capitals.
The first lines of the poem are set small in a black serif text face.
The thumb index along the right edge gives each poem a title in small black sans-serif capitals and a symbol in red or black: a dot, a square, a cross, a question mark, two circles.
The paper is off-white. The only colors are red and black.
interpretation: The spread shows that constructivist heavy capitals and bars came first from the type case: letters and pictures are built from the same rules and blocks.
Body text stays small and horizontal while display words rotate, which matches the style rule not to rotate body text.
borrow: Build a large initial letter or a simple picture from thick rules and blocks in red and black.
Give each section a short symbol and use the symbols as a visible index or tab bar.
Pair one steep black bar with a heading set on the same angle.

images.alt: An open book on a black background. The left page shows a ship built from black and red bars with a red flag. The right page has a giant red letter M built from slabs, the words Left March in Russian capitals, a thick black diagonal bar, and a stepped thumb index with small red and black symbols.
images.caption: El Lissitzky and Vladimir Mayakovsky, *Dlia golosa*, Berlin 1923, opening of “Left March”. Copy on display at the Deutsches Buch- und Schriftmuseum, Leipzig; photograph by Karl432, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Seiten_aus_dem_Gedichtband_Dlja_golosa_von_Wladimir_Majakowski_gestaltet_von_El_Lissitzky.jpg), CC0.

rights.statement: The photograph is CC0 1.0 by Karl432; Commons also marks the book PD-old-70-expired. The book was published in Berlin in 1923. Lissitzky died in 1941 and Mayakovsky in 1930, so the design and the poems are in the public domain in Germany and Russia, and publication before 1931 puts them in the public domain in the United States.

identifiers.commons: File:Seiten aus dem Gedichtband Dlja golosa von Wladimir Majakowski gestaltet von El Lissitzky.jpg

references.title: Dragonfly brooch by René Lalique
references.lede: Two enamelled dragonflies, their wings spread, curl around a pale stone in a gold loop, with carved blossoms hanging from their feet.
references.summary: Gold brooch with plique-à-jour dragonfly wings in green and blue enamel. René Lalique, c. 1900–1910.

source.label: Cleveland Museum of Art: Dragon Fly Brooch, 1964.448

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 1964.448 (3400 × 2525 px print file). Read the object record through the museum’s open-access API.

styles.note: Paris Art Nouveau jewellery: a Japonisme insect motif, translucent enamel in outlined cells, and looping gold lines.

context: The Cleveland Museum of Art records the brooch as gold with plique-à-jour and cloisonné enamels, 7.7 × 9.7 cm, French, c. 1900–1910, by René Lalique (1860–1945). [CMA 1964.448](https://clevelandart.org/art/1964.448).

The dragonfly is one of the insect motifs that the style took from Japanese prints (see [Art Nouveau](style:art-nouveau), lineage). Lalique later became the leading Art Deco glassmaker; compare his 1928 [Victoire mascot](ref:lalique-victoire-car-mascot-1928).
observed: Two dragonflies face each other in mirror image. Their long bodies run down in dark green and blue enamel with small cross bands, and their tails nearly meet at the bottom.
The four long wings spread diagonally to both sides. Fine gold veins divide each wing into many cells of translucent pale green enamel, with blue and turquoise patches near the body.
A matte gold loop, drawn as two crossing curves, frames a pointed oval stone of milky blue-green in the centre.
Three small carved blossoms in pale blue-green hang on short gold stems at the sides and the bottom.
The museum photograph shows the brooch on a dark gray gradient.
interpretation: The piece is symmetrical, but its lines are soft curves and long tapering strokes, not the straight rays of Art Deco.
Plique-à-jour enamel works like stained glass: coloured cells set in thin metal lines. It is the same outlined-cell language as the [Tiffany lamp](ref:driscoll-tiffany-pony-wisteria-lamp).
borrow: Divide a large shape into many small cells with thin lines of one colour, and vary the tint from cell to cell.
Frame a central element with two crossing curves instead of a closed rectangle.

images.alt: Gold brooch on a dark gray ground: two mirrored dragonflies with long green and blue bodies and spread, veined wings of pale green enamel, around a pointed oval milky blue stone, with small carved blossoms hanging below.
images.caption: René Lalique, dragonfly brooch, c. 1900–1910, gold and enamel. [Cleveland Museum of Art 1964.448](https://clevelandart.org/art/1964.448), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art marks the object and its image CC0. René Lalique died in 1945, so his work entered the public domain in France in 2016. A brooch made about 1900–1910 is in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Droplet typeface
references.lede: Hat Nguyen’s family of swollen, irregular display letters for T-26, named as a signature grunge font.
references.summary: Blobby, irregular sans-serif capitals and lowercase in Lite, Regular, and Extra weights. Hat Nguyen, T-26, 1996.

evidence.note: Inspected the Klingspor Museum specimen sheet for Hat Nguyen (a one-page PDF, rendered at about 900 × 1300) and the Fonts In Use render (779 × 176), in scratchpad copies. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: sources name it a signature grunge font, but its letters are swollen and irregular rather than eroded or torn.

context: The Awl, quoting T-26 founder Carlos Segura, names Hat Nguyen’s Droplet among the signature grunge fonts distributed by T-26. [The Awl](https://web.archive.org/web/20150925150838/http://www.theawl.com/2012/08/grunge-typography).

The Klingspor Museum sheet lists Droplet Lite, Droplet, and Droplet Extra as 1996 T-26 releases, also sold by Linotype. [Klingspor Museum](http://www.klingspor-museum.de/KlingsporKuenstler/Schriftdesigner/Nguyen/HNguyen.pdf).
T-26 still sells Droplet in four styles: Lite, Regular, Extra, and Closed, tagged “bloated”, “hybrid”, “ink”, and “organic”. [T-26](https://www.t26.com/fonts/253-Droplet).
observed: Droplet Lite is a thin, slightly wobbly sans-serif; Droplet and Droplet Extra are heavy, with swollen terminals and small, irregular counters.
Letter widths and stroke ends vary: the I has a hook, the Z and K are compressed, and the Extra weight’s counters close up into blobs.
Edges are smooth, not speckled or torn.
interpretation: Droplet shows that “grunge font” was also a market label for any irregular, hand-made-looking display face of the mid-1990s. For the eroded core of the style, prefer [Reactor](ref:reactor-typeface-fuse-1993) or [Trixie](ref:ff-trixie-typeface-1991).
borrow: Pair one swollen, irregular display face with a clean text face for a looser, inky mood without heavy damage.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The typeface is by Hat Nguyen and T-26.

references.title: Drowning Girl
references.lede: Roy Lichtenstein’s romance-comic close-up: a crying woman in a stylized wave, with a thought balloon that reads “I DON’T CARE! I’D RATHER SINK — THAN CALL BRAD FOR HELP!”
references.summary: A square close-up with dot-tinted skin, flat blue hair, heavy black waves, and a thought balloon. Roy Lichtenstein, 1963.

source.label: Roy Lichtenstein: A Catalogue Raisonné, Drowning Girl (RLCR 761)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the catalogue raisonné image of the Museum of Modern Art’s painting, MoMA 685.1971 (1180 × 1200 px), in a scratchpad. MoMA’s own page blocks scripts. No image is stored.

styles.note: A canonical romance-comic panel: dot-tinted skin, even black key lines, flat primary blue, and a thought balloon with hand-lettered capitals.

context: The catalogue raisonné gives acrylic, oil, and graphite pencil on canvas, 171.8 × 169.5 cm, and the source as *Secret Hearts* #83 (November 1962). The Museum of Modern Art acquired it in December 1971 (685.1971). [RLCR 761](https://www.lichtensteincatalogue.org/catalogue/entry.php?id=452).

It was shown in Lichtenstein’s September–October 1963 exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery, the show announced by the [Crak! poster](ref:lichtenstein-crak-poster-1963). [RLCR 761](https://www.lichtensteincatalogue.org/catalogue/entry.php?id=452).
Wikipedia reports that the work also borrows from Hokusai’s *The Great Wave off Kanagawa*. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drowning_Girl).
observed: The face, hand, and arm are filled with fine red dots on white; the lips are flat pink with a black outline.
The hair is solid ultramarine blue with black strands. No blue dots appear in the hair.
The water is a pattern of heavy black curls and white foam shapes on a pale blue dot field.
A white thought balloon with a scalloped outline and three small bubbles fills the upper left. It holds four lines of black hand-lettered capitals.
Tears are drawn as white drops with black outlines.
Black outlines vary from thick to very thick. There are no gradients or modeled shadows.
interpretation: The painting shows the romance branch of the idiom: close-up faces, a limited palette of dot-red skin and one solid primary, and text in a balloon, not a caption box.
Large black shapes carry as much of the design as the outlines do. The style is not only outline plus fill; solid black areas give it weight.
borrow: Use a scalloped thought balloon for a quote or testimonial, with small trailing bubbles.
Tint large areas with a pale dot field and reserve one strong solid color for the focal shape.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The catalogue raisonné states “© 2026 Roy Lichtenstein Foundation. All Rights Reserved.”

references.title: Easter ’67 poster
references.lede: Ian McLaren’s poster for the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament’s Easter 1967 march: a field of white dots on black that swell into a glowing disc under a plain grotesque headline.
references.summary: White dots that grow toward the centre of a black sheet, under “Easter ’67” in white sans-serif. Ian McLaren for CND, 1967.

creator.name: Ian McLaren (artist); Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (issuer)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A photograph of its copy, E.383-2021 (1110 × 1600 px), photographed on a wooden surface, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Clear graphic-design use of op art: a black and white dot field that swells by steps, with plain sans-serif type in a separate band.

context: The V&A catalogues the poster with the style “Op Art”, gives Ian McLaren as artist and the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) as issuer, and dates it 1967. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1664114/).
The V&A record has no further description. The event text on the poster lists Easter Saturday at Grosvenor Square, Easter Sunday at Ruislip, and an Easter Monday march to a rally in Trafalgar Square.
observed: The upper third is a solid black band with the CND symbol in a white disc and “Easter ’67” in large white grotesque capitals and lower case.
Four columns of small white sans-serif text give the organiser’s address and the times and places of the events.
The lower two thirds hold a square field of white dots on black. The dots are small at the edges and grow until they merge near the centre, so a bright, soft-edged disc appears.
The dot field seems to bulge toward the viewer. There is no colour.
interpretation: The poster follows the op rules for type and pattern: the text sits on solid black, apart from the field, and the field does the expressive work.
The swelling dot field can be read as a light or a blast, which gives the abstract device a message without adding a figure.
borrow: Scale a regular dot grid so that the dots grow toward a centre and merge into a bright disc.
Keep all text in a separate solid band above the pattern, set in one plain grotesque at two sizes.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design is probably in copyright, and the V&A photograph is not openly licensed.

references.title: Elegant Themes “Beautiful Flat Icons”
references.lede: A free set of 192 flat icons from 2013: objects built from solid shapes on colored circles, with short solid shadows.
references.summary: Round flat icons in muted blue, orange, red, teal, and slate, each object with a short hard-edged shadow. GPL, 2013.

evidence.note: Downloaded eight icons from [Category:Elegant Themes Circle Icons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Elegant_Themes_Circle_Icons) as 330 px renders of the SVG files (calendar, camera, chat, lightbulb, mail, music, rocket, tools), inspected them, and stored them as one contact sheet (1420 × 720) made for this record. Publication date and license read on the Elegant Themes post on 2026-09-28.

styles.note: Clear for the imagery facet: single objects drawn in solid fills on solid circles, with no gradients or gloss.

context: The post by Nick Roach, published 16 October 2013, offers “a 192 piece set of flat icons” in “full color and single color” versions, “completely free and Open Source under the GPL”.
Wikimedia Commons holds the SVG files under GPL-2.0 with the source and date above ([example](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Circle-icons-camera.svg)).
observed: Each icon is a solid circle in muted blue, orange, red, teal, or dark slate.
The objects (a calendar, a camera, a speech bubble, a light bulb, an envelope, a music note, a rocket, crossed tools) are built from solid shapes in white, cream, slate, red, and yellow.
Every object casts a short shadow down and to the right in a darker tint of the circle color. The shadow has a hard edge and no blur.
There are no gradients, highlights, or outlines. Corners of the shapes are slightly rounded.
interpretation: Measured with `tools/image-traits.py`; see the measurement file. The palette is softer than the Flat UI kit, which shows that flat design did not require fully saturated color.
The short solid shadows are the milder form of the 2013 long-shadow trend that NN/g criticises ([NN/g 2015](ref:nngroup-flat-design-article-2015)).
borrow: Draw icons as one object on one solid circle, with a single hard shadow in a darker tint of the circle color when you need a hint of depth.

images.alt: Eight round flat icons on white: a calendar on blue, a camera on orange, a speech bubble on blue, a light bulb on red, an envelope on blue, a music note on teal, a rocket on dark slate, and crossed tools on teal, each object with a short solid shadow.
images.caption: Eight icons from the set, arranged for this record from the [Wikimedia Commons SVG files](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Elegant_Themes_Circle_Icons) (GPL-2.0, Elegant Themes).

rights.statement: Elegant Themes released the icons as open source under the GPL ([post](https://www.elegantthemes.com/blog/freebie-of-the-week/beautiful-flat-icons-for-free)); Wikimedia Commons lists them under GPL-2.0. Credit: Elegant Themes. The contact sheet is a derivative arrangement under the same license.

references.title: Emerson Patriot radio
references.lede: Norman Bel Geddes’s Catalin table radio for Emerson: a grille of stacked horizontal bars beside a big round dial.
references.summary: A red Catalin case with a grille of cream horizontal bars and a large round dial. Norman Bel Geddes for Emerson, 1940.

source.label: Victoria and Albert Museum: Patriot Midget radio, W.31-1992

creator.name: Norman Bel Geddes (designer); Emerson Radio and Phonograph Corporation (manufacturer)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Daderot’s 2015 photograph of a Model 400 (FC-400) Patriot in the Museum für Angewandte Kunst Köln on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Radio_Model_400_(FC-400)_Patriot,_Norman_Bel_Geddes,_Emerson,_Catalin_case_-_Museum_f%C3%BCr_Angewandte_Kunst_K%C3%B6ln_-_Cologne,_Germany_-_DSC09461.jpg) at 1920 px. Read the V&A record for W.31-1992 (blue case, red and white grille) through the V&A API. The two copies differ in color.

styles.note: Partial fit: the case is a rectangle, as the V&A notes, but the grille of stacked horizontal bars and the round dial are streamline signs.

context: The V&A says Bel Geddes (1893–1958) helped define streamline styling, but chose a rectilinear case for the Patriot, a “Stars and Stripes” design made in red, white, and blue combinations and linked to Emerson’s 25th anniversary; the knobs are embossed with stars. [V&A O85202](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O85202/patriot-midget-radio-bel-geddes-norman/).

The V&A copy has a blue case, a grille of alternating red and white bands, and two blue knobs; it measures 19 × 26.5 × 13.6 cm. [V&A O85202](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O85202/patriot-midget-radio-bel-geddes-norman/).
observed: The Cologne copy has a glossy red case with slightly rounded edges and a cream handle on top.
The left half of the front is a grille of seven cream bars stacked horizontally with dark gaps between them; the bars are flat on the front and slightly rounded at the ends.
The right half holds a large round dial with a cream ring of numbers and a red pointer; the small text on the dial reads “Emerson Radio and Phonograph Corp. N.Y. U.S.A.”
Two white knobs, each embossed with a five-pointed star, sit below the dial.
interpretation: The radio reduces the style to two signs: parallel horizontal bars and a circle. The bars read as speed lines even on a still box. The V&A’s caution matters: the case itself is not streamlined.
borrow: Pair a block of stacked horizontal bars with one large circle in a two-part layout.
Use red, cream, and navy as flat plastic colors with no gradient.

images.alt: Front view of a red plastic table radio in a museum case: a grille of seven cream horizontal bars on the left, a large round dial with a cream number ring on the right, two white star-embossed knobs, and a cream handle on top.
images.caption: Emerson Model 400 Patriot, Museum für Angewandte Kunst Köln. Photograph by Daderot, 2015, CC0, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Radio_Model_400_(FC-400)_Patriot,_Norman_Bel_Geddes,_Emerson,_Catalin_case_-_Museum_f%C3%BCr_Angewandte_Kunst_K%C3%B6ln_-_Cologne,_Germany_-_DSC09461.jpg).

rights.statement: The photographer dedicated the photograph to the public domain (CC0), and notes that the radio is not subject to US copyright, only to a long-expired design patent. The radio is an American useful article. Norman Bel Geddes died in 1958.

identifiers.commons: File:Radio Model 400 (FC-400) Patriot, Norman Bel Geddes, Emerson, Catalin case - Museum für Angewandte Kunst Köln - Cologne, Germany - DSC09461.jpg

references.title: Emery Walker’s House website
references.lede: The house museum of Morris’s typographic adviser puts a woven Morris bird pattern behind its title and sets its headings in a red old-style serif.
references.summary: A full-width woven bird-and-flower pattern in indigo and salmon under white serif type, with red serif headings.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A cookie bar covers the bottom 60 px of the viewport.

styles.note: Clear: a dense Morris textile fills the hero, and the headings are a red old-style serif under a woodcut-style device.

observed: The logo is a square black-and-white woodcut-style device of a bird in interlaced vines, beside “EMERY WALKER’S HOUSE” in three lines of red serif capitals.
A thin grey rule runs above and below a row of small grey capital navigation labels.

The hero is a full-width photograph of a woven textile: pairs of salmon and cream birds among dense leaves and flowers on dark indigo. “Emery Walker’s House” and “7 Hammersmith Terrace” sit over it in large white serif type.
A slate-blue band below holds “The Arts & Crafts home, London” in dark blue old-style serif.
Three photo cards at the bottom carry headings such as “Explore The House” in large red serif on a pale band.
A white cookie bar with a black Accept button covers the bottom edge.
interpretation: The pattern is a photographic image, so `color.patternShare` measures 0 even though the hero is the densest area of the page; the site shows the limit of the metric.
Measured: square corners (radius 0), accent chroma 0.36, and a shadow share of 0.15 from the cookie bar and cards.
The red serif headings over cream and indigo come close to the rubric’s red headings on a dye palette.
borrow: Set white serif display type directly over a dark, dense textile image, and let the pattern do the work of a hero photograph.
Pair a square black-and-white device with a red serif wordmark.

images.alt: Emery Walker’s House home page: a red serif wordmark beside a black-and-white bird device, grey navigation, a hero of a dense indigo textile with salmon birds under large white serif type, and a slate-blue band reading The Arts & Crafts home, London.
images.caption: First viewport of [emerywalker.org.uk](https://www.emerywalker.org.uk/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners, and the pattern images belong to their rights holders. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Evernote for Android
references.lede: Nielsen Norman Group’s 2015 example of Material Design as “flat 2.0”: a mostly flat app with subtle shadows on the bar and the action button.
references.summary: A mostly flat note app with card panes and a shadowed round add button, cited by NN/g in 2015.

source.label: Nielsen Norman Group, Kate Moran, “Flat Design: Its Origins, Its Problems, and Why Flat 2.0 Is Better for Users” (27 September 2015)

evidence.note: Relies on the NN/g article text. Its screenshot of the app is only 512 × 446 px, too small to record visual detail.

styles.note: Partial fit, documented only: NN/g names it as Material-style flat 2.0, with shadows on the bar and the action button and a card metaphor.

context: NN/g calls “Google’s Material design language” “one example of flat 2.0 with the right priorities”, and says that the Evernote app for Android “provides a few subtle shadows on the navigation bar and the floating + button (add new). It also makes use of the card metaphor to display content as flat, layerable panes in a 3D space.” [NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/flat-design/).
interpretation: The article is the clearest statement of how Material relates to [flat design](style:flat-design): the fills stay flat, and a few shadows return only where they tell the user what can be touched.
next: Find a larger, dated image of the 2015 Android app, for example in a Wayback copy of evernote.com, before marking this reference observed.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The app belongs to Evernote. The screenshot on the NN/g page belongs to NN/g.

references.title: Evolution (Daniel Oliva Barbero)
references.lede: A textbook vaporwave collage: two cyan statues, an Ionic column carrying a glitched Windows logo, a pink Paint window, palms, a striped sun, and a pink grid over blue.
references.summary: Statues, column, glitched Windows logo, pink Paint window, palms, striped sun, grid floor. 2019.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1920 × 2560 rendering of the 8554 × 11405 file on Wikimedia Commons, in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear: it combines every diagnostic in one image, with pastel pink, violet, and cyan, a Windows 9x window, classical statues, palm trees, and a grid floor under a striped sun.

context: Commons lists it under CC BY 2.0 from Flickr, while the author’s description says CC BY 4.0 and that it was “created from” another Flickr work. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vaprwave_97346.png).
observed: A mauve sky frames a yellow-to-pink sun cut by horizontal pink stripes.
A pink-tinted Microsoft Paint window with a navy title bar, tool palette, and colour swatches overlaps the left side.
A cyan Ionic capital and column carry a glitched, pixelated Windows flag logo in the centre.
Two identical cyan-and-violet statues of a draped woman face each other, each holding a small hexagonal pattern.
Pale pink palm trees stand at both sides; a magenta grid floor on blue recedes to the horizon.
interpretation: The most complete single statement of the rubric found in open sources. It is also a warning: the style depends on quoting other people’s trademarks and interfaces.
borrow: Tint real classical figures in a single pastel duotone so they read as cut-outs rather than photographs.

rights.statement: The author released the file under an open license (CC BY 2.0 on Commons, CC BY 4.0 in the description), but a Microsoft Paint window and the Windows logo are central to the composition, so no image is stored here.

references.title: EXP.TYPO website, 2008
references.lede: The 2008 home page of EXP.TYPO, an experimental typography portfolio, built as one torn-paper collage around a distressed wordmark.
references.summary: A layered, eroded “EXPTYPO” wordmark over torn paper, tape stripes, ink splashes, and crumpled white paper.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 17 May 2008, and inspected. Nothing covers the page. The measurement found no HTML text, boxes, or images, so the design is drawn in a single background or plug-in layer that the extractor cannot see.

styles.note: Clear example of 2000s grunge web design: an eroded, overprinted wordmark in several faces on torn and crumpled paper. Named in Smashing Magazine’s “The Secrets of Grunge Design” (2008).

context: Smashing Magazine’s March 2008 article “The Secrets of Grunge Design” links exptypo.com among its examples. [Smashing Magazine](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2008/03/the-secrets-of-grunge-design/).
observed: The wordmark “EXPTYPO” is a heavy condensed sans-serif, printed several times with offsets, outlines, and scratches, so the letters look misregistered and eroded.
Outline numerals “12” and a stencil-like “2005” sit behind and above the wordmark; “RENEWAL” is set in a spaced, hand-drawn line below it.
Torn paper edges, brown and black ink stains, and a strip of yellow-and-black hazard tape fill the left half.
A small cut-out figure of a woman, flourishes, pencil lines, and two orange paint dots are collaged over the type.
The right half is plain crumpled white paper; no navigation or text is visible in the first viewport.
interpretation: The page is a Photoshop collage in the manner of 1990s grunge print, using the same moves (misregistration, several faces, tape, stains) on screen. Because everything is one image, the computed-style metrics measure nothing; judge it by the rubric.
borrow: Print a wordmark two or three times with small offsets and one outline copy, to fake a misregistered photocopy.
Keep half of the page as empty textured paper, so the collage has room.

images.alt: EXP.TYPO home page from 2008: a distressed, misregistered EXPTYPO wordmark over torn paper, brown ink stains, hazard-tape stripes, a small collaged figure, and the word RENEWAL, with crumpled white paper filling the right half.
images.caption: First viewport of the [Wayback Machine copy of exptypo.com, May 2008](https://web.archive.org/web/20080517055553/http://www.exptypo.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s author. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Expansion furnishing fabric
references.lede: Barbara Brown’s screen-printed furnishing fabric for Heal’s: black bands that narrow, bend, and converge so that the cloth seems to bulge.
references.summary: Black undulating stripes on white that pinch together and swell, in a large repeat. Barbara Brown for Heal’s, 1966.

creator.name: Barbara Brown (designer); Heal’s Wholesale & Export Ltd (manufacturer)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.269-1967 (1165 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: A clear op furnishing print: black and white stripes that change width by steps to suggest swelling and depth.

context: The V&A catalogues the fabric with the style “Op art” and describes screen-printed cotton satin “with wide stripes in optical black-and-white undulating stripes giving the illusion of three-dimensionality”, 108 × 48 in. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O224418/).

The V&A’s Heal’s records say that 1960s Heal’s furnishing textiles moved from sober geometry “through Pop and Op Art-inspired motifs” to flower-power florals, under design consultant Tom Worthington. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O46802/).
observed: Pure black on white. Three identical horizontal repeats fill the length.
In each repeat, vertical black bands pinch to hair-thin lines at the centre and widen into heavy wave shapes toward the edges.
At the top and bottom of each repeat, the bands fan out into points, so each repeat reads as a swelling drum or waist.
Selvedge printing along both edges gives the designer, the title, and the maker.
interpretation: Expansion uses the op device of progression: stripe width alone creates a curved surface on flat cloth.
It shows the style at furnishing scale, where one repeat is about the height of a person.
borrow: Make a band narrow toward a centre line and widen toward the edges to suggest a bulge.
Repeat one large, symmetric unit vertically so that the whole panel reads as one field.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Barbara Brown’s design is in copyright, and the V&A image is not openly licensed.

references.title: Explore with books, Book Week poster
references.lede: Paul Rand builds a child from torn and cut paper shapes, with an open orange book for a roof, and sets the words in a lowercase slab on a charcoal ground.
references.summary: A cut-paper child under an open orange book, with lowercase slab lettering on charcoal. Paul Rand, 1958.

source.label: Library of Congress: Explore with books, Nov. 2-8. Book week

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Library of Congress service image (808 × 1024 px) of the Library’s copy, Prints and Photographs Division, Artist poster filing series. The larger TIFF was not opened.

styles.note: Cut-paper figure, flat mustard, orange, olive-green, and blue, loose black line drawing over the shapes, and friendly lettering: the illustrative core of the style. The ground is dark, not cream.

context: The Library of Congress record gives the title as “Explore with books, Nov. 2-8. Book week”, the date as [1958], the place as [New York], the publisher as not identified, and the artist as Paul Rand (1914–1996). It forms part of the Library’s Artist poster filing series. [LoC 2015646529](https://www.loc.gov/item/2015646529/).
The same series holds the 1957 Book Week poster “Explore with books”, which the record says was designed by A&M Provensen. [LoC 2015646521](https://www.loc.gov/item/2015646521/).
observed: The ground is flat charcoal gray to the edges.
“explore with books nov. 2-8” runs across the top and “book week” across the foot, in a lowercase slab-serif in pale blue-gray and off-white.
A mustard square with a loosely drawn black circle stands for the sun.

A small figure with a round pink face and white glasses stands under a large open orange book worn like a roof. Its body is a yellow coat with a blue bow, and it holds a pink open book and a stack of red and green books.
The shapes have uneven, cut or torn edges. Thin black lines are drawn over them for the page edges, fingers, and buttons, and do not always follow the shapes.
The figure stands on a green rectangle with short black grass strokes. “Paul Rand” is signed in script at the lower right.
interpretation: The poster shows the overprint idea by hand: color shapes and a separate black line layer that do not register exactly.
The lowercase slab and the childlike figure show the playful side of the style. Measured on the stored image: three hue families, accent chroma 0.53, and a dark background.
borrow: Draw a thin black line layer over flat color shapes and let it drift off register.
Set a friendly heading in a lowercase slab-serif, and let one hand-signed word or signature balance it.

images.alt: Poster on charcoal gray: a cut-paper child with a round pink face and white glasses stands under a large open orange book, holding a pink book and a stack of red and green books, beside a mustard square sun; lowercase slab lettering reads explore with books nov. 2-8 and book week.
images.caption: Paul Rand, “Explore with books, Nov. 2-8. Book week”, [1958]. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, [2015646529](https://www.loc.gov/item/2015646529/); no known restrictions on publication.

rights.statement: Library of Congress rights statement: “No known restrictions on publication.” The poster was published in the United States (LoC date [1958]); no copyright notice is visible on the digitized sheet at the size checked, and a US work of that date published without notice is in the public domain. The Library does not state its reason, so this rests on the Library’s assessment.

references.title: Fall
references.lede: Bridget Riley’s 1963 painting of a single wave line repeated across the surface, with waves that tighten toward the bottom until the field seems to ripple.
references.summary: Hundreds of thin black and white vertical waves whose curves compress toward the base. Bridget Riley, Tate, 1963.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Tate’s image of T00616 (1196 × 1200 px) from media.tate.org.uk in a scratchpad. The artwork page renders most of its text with JavaScript; the medium was read from the page metadata. No image is stored.

styles.note: A canonical black and white op painting: one curved stripe repeated edge to edge, with a period that changes by steps to make the surface seem to move.

context: Tate lists *Fall*, 1963, as polyvinyl acetate paint on hardboard, collection number T00616, on display at Tate Britain in the Bridget Riley room. [Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/riley-fall-t00616).

Riley’s *Current* (1964), a painting of the same kind, was reproduced on the cover of [The Responsive Eye](ref:the-responsive-eye-catalogue-1965) catalogue in 1965. [David Zwirner](https://www.davidzwirner.com/news/2019/bridget-riley-s-paintings-continue-to-mesmerize-six-decades-on).
observed: Thin vertical black and white stripes of almost equal width fill the square surface to all four edges.
Every stripe follows the same wavy path. In the upper part the waves are long and gentle; toward the bottom they become shorter and sharper.
In the lowest band the waves are so tight that the stripes seem to vibrate and form moiré-like ridges.
The black is slightly warm and the white slightly off-white in the photograph. There is no other colour and no texture beyond the paint.
interpretation: *Fall* is the reference case for the style’s “progression and distortion” grammar: nothing changes except the period of one repeated curve.
It shows why op patterns need a fixed size on screen: the effect depends on the width of each stripe relative to the eye.
borrow: Repeat one wave path hundreds of times with a small horizontal offset, and shorten its period toward one edge.
Fill the whole panel edge to edge so that the field has no frame inside it.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is by a living artist, and Tate’s image is not openly licensed.

references.title: Far Side Virtual cover art
references.lede: James Ferraro’s 2011 cover: an iPad showing a cloud-sky face, pasted over a grainy New York street full of taxis.
references.summary: Tablet with a sky-collage face over a noisy Manhattan street; spaced multicolour title. 2011.

evidence.note: Inspected the 2000 × 1995 front cover of the Hippos in Tanks digital release in the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release/964ec492-5cf2-4635-a54a-0287007f956c/cover-art), in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: A precursor and the start of the “utopian virtual” branch. Partial fit: it quotes then-current tablets and stock imagery rather than 1980s–1990s media, and it has no pastel palette.

context: Wikipedia: Far Side Virtual “drew primarily on ‘the grainy and bombastic beeps’ of then-recent past media, such as Skype, Second Life, Windows XP and the Nintendo Wii,” and the utopian virtual offshoot it began “later became associated with the Frutiger Aero Internet aesthetic.” [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave). See [Frutiger Aero](style:frutiger-aero).
observed: A black tablet, tilted, fills the left half; its screen shows a face cut out of a blue sky with white clouds, with brush-stroke eyebrows and a red oval mouth.
The background is a Manhattan street with yellow taxis, overlaid with heavy colour noise.
A small copy of the same tablet sits at the upper right; smeared rainbow shapes and a blurred green-and-red blob float at the edges.
The title FARSIDEVIRTUAL runs along the bottom in widely spaced capitals, each letter a different primary colour.
interpretation: It shows the style’s irony toward consumer technology before the palette settled. The widely spaced title already anticipates the fullwidth-letter habit.

rights.statement: Copyrighted album art. No image is stored here.

references.title: Fastmail website, 2020
references.lede: Fastmail’s 2020 home page: a woman with long legs relaxes at a laptop on a balcony full of plants, in a flat yellow hero with a curved lower edge.
references.summary: A relaxed long-limbed figure among potted plants on a flat yellow field with a curved edge. 2020.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. No cookie box covers the page. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: a flat scene with a long-legged figure, potted plants, and oversized sneakers on a pale color field, but the skin is natural and some shapes carry a light grain.

references.notice: The live Fastmail site has changed since this 2020 capture.
observed: A dark navy bar holds the logo and navigation; a square blue “Sign up” button sits at the right.
The hero is a flat pale yellow field whose lower edge is a wide convex curve.
The heading “Email you can feel good about” is bold dark grey sans-serif; a square-cornered blue button reads “Try it free for 30 days”.
On the right, a woman with brown skin and long black hair sits with crossed legs in a white chair, holding a cup beside a pink laptop. Her shoes lie on the floor below.
Potted plants in pink and blue pots, a pale yellow city skyline, and trees surround her; some leaves and pots have a fine grain.
interpretation: The page takes the style’s plants, pastel field, and relaxed long-limbed figure and gives it a natural skin tone, a variant common after 2019.
borrow: End the hero color field with one wide convex curve instead of a straight edge.

images.alt: Fastmail home page, 2020: a pale yellow hero with the heading “Email you can feel good about” on the left and a long-legged woman relaxing at a pink laptop among potted plants and a pale skyline on the right.
images.caption: First viewport of [Fastmail](https://web.archive.org/web/20200701220517/https://www.fastmail.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: FF Trixie typeface
references.lede: Erik van Blokland’s scanned typewriter face of 1991, one of the first FontFonts, with blotched, filled, and uneven letters.
references.summary: A monospaced typewriter face with inky, clogged counters and ragged edges. Erik van Blokland, FontShop, 1991.

evidence.note: Inspected Eye’s photograph (951 × 627) of the spread in Eye 7 (1992) that shows Trixie beside LettError’s Beowolf, in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example of the style’s typewriter voice: damaged, inky letters that look reproduced rather than typeset.

context: Paul Barnes writes that Trixie was released in 1991 as one of the first FontFonts sold by FontShop, that it “revelled in distress and distortion”, and that it “was perfect for the age of grunge”. It appeared on CD covers and in the titles of The X-Files (1993). [Eye](https://eyemagazine.com/blog/post/variable-grunge).

Barnes says a typewriter borrowed from a friend called Beatrix was the starting point, and that LettError revised the design in 2023 as the variable font Neither Confirm Nor Deny. [Eye](https://eyemagazine.com/blog/post/variable-grunge).
Robin Kinross’s article “The digital wave” in Eye 7 (1992) showed Trixie beside Beowolf and BeoSans. [Eye](https://eyemagazine.com/blog/post/variable-grunge).
observed: The Eye 7 spread shows the Trixie lowercase and numerals very large on a teal page.
The letters are a monospaced slab-serif typewriter design with uneven stroke weight, ragged edges, and ink blots.
Several counters are filled or partly clogged: the a, e, g, o, p, q, 8, and 9 read as dark blobs.
A white dashed line runs along the baseline of each row; a small sample in upper and lower case sits in a white-on-dark box above.
On the facing page, LettError’s Beowolf shows the same B many times, each with a different jagged outline.
interpretation: Trixie is the calm end of grunge type: it imitates worn machine printing rather than tearing letters apart. It is the typewriter face that the style’s captions and data call for.
borrow: Use a worn typewriter face for captions, dates, and tables, where its damage stays readable.
Let some counters fill with ink at display sizes, but not at text sizes.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The typeface is by Erik van Blokland; the photograph is Eye’s.

references.title: Flagey Building, Brussels
references.lede: Joseph Diongre’s broadcasting house for Belgian radio, nicknamed the paquebot for its ship-like silhouette: curved facades of ribbon windows and a round tower.
references.summary: A curved pale yellow block with continuous ribbon windows and a round banded tower. Joseph Diongre, Ixelles, 1933–38.

evidence.note: Downloaded to a scratch folder and inspected Busoni’s 2013 photograph on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ancien_Institut_national_de_Radiodiffusion_-_vue_d%27ensemble.JPG) at 1280 px. No image is stored.

styles.note: A European paquebot building: curved facades, horizontal bands of windows, and a round tower like a ship’s funnel.

context: Joseph Diongre won a 1933 competition and the building was completed in 1938 as the headquarters of the National Institute of Radio Broadcasting (INR/NIR). Wikipedia calls it Streamline Moderne and gives the nickname “paquebot” (packet boat). Studio 4 is a noted concert hall. It is now the Flagey cultural centre. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagey_Building).
observed: A six-storey block with a pale yellow facade curves around the corner of the square in one continuous sweep.
Every floor has a continuous ribbon of windows separated by solid horizontal bands of the yellow wall, so the facade reads as stacked horizontal stripes.
A round tower rises from the curved corner; each of its floors is a ring of windows under a projecting band, and a lantern and mast sit on top.
Small round clocks sit on the facade near the top of the curve. The walls carry no applied ornament.
interpretation: Flagey shows a European version of the style: no chrome and no portholes, but curved corners, continuous horizontal bands, and a funnel-like tower make the ship reading.
borrow: Wrap a corner with one continuous curve and let horizontal bands run unbroken around it.
A stack of rings with projecting edges reads as a streamline tower or a progress indicator.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Joseph Diongre died in 1963, so the building is protected in Belgium until 2033. Belgian freedom of panorama would probably permit exterior photographs, and the Commons photograph is CC BY-SA 3.0; the lead curator can decide whether to upgrade.
