references.title: Flat UI Colors website, 2014
references.lede: A palette tool that is one grid of twenty solid color tiles, named Turquoise, Peter River, Alizarin, and so on.
references.summary: Twenty full-bleed color tiles with white uppercase names; the palette of the Flat UI kit. June 2014.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 5 June 2014, and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Clear: the whole page is solid, borderless color tiles in the canonical flat palette, with flat label buttons.

references.notice: The live site now offers many palettes in a different layout.
observed: A pale gray top bar holds small solid label buttons in pink, navy, and teal, and a white “CHOOSE FORMAT” dropdown.
Below it, a five-by-four grid of full-bleed tiles fills the rest of the viewport. Each tile is one solid color with its name in white uppercase at bottom left.

The rows read: Turquoise, Emerald, Peter River, Amethyst, Wet Asphalt; Green Sea, Nephritis, Belize Hole, Wisteria, Midnight Blue; Sun Flower, Carrot, Alizarin, Clouds, Concrete; Orange, Pumpkin, Pomegranate, Silver, Asbestos.
Tiles touch each other. There are no borders, gaps, or gradients.
interpretation: The twenty names match the color variables of [Designmodo’s Flat UI kit](ref:flat-ui-free-kit-designmodo) (for example `$turquoise: #1abc9c`, `$midnight-blue: #2c3e50`), so the page publishes the kit’s palette as a tool.
Measured: 62% of screenshot pixels are saturated, in 7 hue groups; no borders. The dropdown has a 1 px shadow, so 13% of boxes have a shadow and the capture fails the shadow range.
borrow: Pair each saturated hue with a darker partner of the same hue (Turquoise and Green Sea, Peter River and Belize Hole) for hover and pressed states.

images.alt: Flat UI Colors page of June 2014: a pale gray top bar with small label buttons and a Choose format dropdown above a grid of twenty solid color tiles named Turquoise, Emerald, Peter River, Amethyst, Wet Asphalt, and others.
images.caption: First viewport of the [Wayback Machine copy of flatuicolors.com, 5 June 2014](https://web.archive.org/web/20140605032117/http://flatuicolors.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot of an archived copy, captured for commentary.

references.title: Flat UI Free kit
references.lede: Designmodo’s free Bootstrap theme of 2013, which gave the flat web its best-known palette.
references.summary: Open-source Bootstrap theme with solid turquoise, emerald, blue, yellow, and red buttons, Lato type, and a named twenty-color palette.

evidence.note: Captured the live demo page [designmodo.github.io/Flat-UI](https://designmodo.github.io/Flat-UI/) with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 2026-09-28 and inspected it. The demo is the current release (2.3), not the first 2013 version; Wayback copies of the 2013 demo lost their CSS. License and palette read from the repository on 2026-09-28.

styles.note: Clear for surfaces and color: solid buttons in a named palette of saturated hues, no gradients or shadows. Its headings are bold (weight 700), which departs from the light Metro headings.

context: The README calls Flat UI “a beautiful theme for Bootstrap. We have redesigned many of its components to look flat in every pixel.” The repository was created on 3 March 2013 and had about 15,000 stars on 2026-09-28.
Released under the MIT License, © 2013–2018 Designmodo ([LICENSE](https://github.com/designmodo/Flat-UI/blob/master/LICENSE)).

The color variables name twenty swatches in pairs, for example `$turquoise: #1abc9c` and `$green-sea: #16a085`, `$peter-river: #3498db` and `$belize-hole: #2980b9`, `$wet-asphalt: #34495e` and `$midnight-blue: #2c3e50` ([_variables.scss](https://github.com/designmodo/Flat-UI/blob/master/app/styles/_variables.scss)).
The kit sets its base text in [Lato](ref:lato-typeface) (`$font-family-base`) and its demo titles in Helvetica Neue (`$font-family-demo`).
observed: A diamond logo made of flat blue and cyan facets with a white sparkle sits above the title “Flat UI” in heavy dark blue-gray type and a pale gray subtitle.
Section headings “Basic elements” and “Buttons” are bold dark blue-gray.

Eight buttons in two rows are solid fills: turquoise, yellow, silver gray, red, green, dark navy, blue, and a pale disabled gray. Each has white text and slightly rounded corners, with no border, gradient, or shadow.
The page ground is plain white.
interpretation: Measured: Lato sets 93% of the text; large headings weigh 700; 24% of boxes have a 2 px border, from outlined input fields further down; 5% of boxes have a shadow. Only 6% of screenshot pixels are saturated because the demo is mostly white, so the capture fails the color range as well as the heading-weight range.
The kit is the reference point for the web branch of flat design: the same palette names reappear on [Flat UI Colors](ref:flatuicolors-com-website-2014) and in this catalogue’s specimen colors.
borrow: Give each semantic role (primary, success, warning, danger, info) one saturated hue, and pair it with a darker partner of the same hue for the pressed state.
Use a dark blue-gray such as #2c3e50 for text and dark buttons instead of black.

images.alt: Flat UI demo page: a faceted blue diamond logo above the title Flat UI in heavy dark blue-gray type, then the headings Basic elements and Buttons and eight solid buttons in turquoise, yellow, gray, red, green, navy, blue, and pale gray.
images.caption: First viewport of the [Flat UI demo page](https://designmodo.github.io/Flat-UI/), captured 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Screenshot of the project’s own demo page, which is published from the MIT-licensed repository, © 2013–2018 Designmodo ([LICENSE](https://github.com/designmodo/Flat-UI/blob/master/LICENSE)). It shows only the kit’s own logo and components.

references.title: Floral Shoppe cover art
references.lede: Macintosh Plus’s album art: a Helios bust on a pink-and-black checkered floor beside a video still of the Twin Towers, with the title in green katakana.
references.summary: Helios bust, pink checkered floor, Twin Towers video still, green Japanese title. The genre’s template, 2011.

creator.name: Macintosh Plus (Ramona Langley, also known as Vektroid)

references.made: December 9, 2011 (digital release); 2012 cassette on Beer on the Rug

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 × 1180 front J-card scan of the 2012 Beer on the Rug cassette (catalogue BOTR009) in the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release/165a3396-c023-42f5-a1fb-174b262ef862/cover-art), in a scratchpad copy. Compared it with the 600 × 600 cover of the 2011 digital release in the same archive and with the current 1200 × 1200 Bandcamp art, a later variant in which the bust has no face and a compact-disc frame surrounds the image. Not stored.

styles.note: Wikipedia calls it the first album “properly considered of the genre” and its cover the image most associated with vaporwave: classical bust, pastel pink, checkered floor, Japanese text, and pre-2001 media.

context: Released digitally on December 9, 2011, by Beer on the Rug. Wikipedia says it “established a blueprint for the genre” and that some albums, “including Floral Shoppe, depict the intact Twin Towers on their covers.” [Wikipedia: Floral Shoppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floral_Shoppe); [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave).

The bust is a Roman copy of the head of Helios, which is itself public domain; the cover as a whole is a copyrighted composition. [Wikipedia: Helios (statue)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helios_(statue)).
observed: A cut-out marble head on a white plinth fills the left half of the square.
The background is flat salmon pink; a black-and-pink checkered floor recedes to a horizon at the lower right.
A blurred, orange-and-violet video still shows a city skyline with the Twin Towers over water.
The title is set in mint-green katakana and Latin capitals (MACプラス, フローラルの専門店) beside a green isometric cube icon and a green rule.
On the cassette card a Sega Saturn manual header and “compact disc 取扱説明書” sit at the top, and the spine runs a full rainbow gradient.
interpretation: Every later cliché is already here: statue, pink, checkerboard, Japanese title, degraded video, and a quoted consumer-electronics label. The composition is sparse and flat, closer to a desktop collage than a designed sleeve.
borrow: Pair one cut-out object with one degraded video frame on a flat pastel ground, and add a perspective checkerboard in the lower third.

rights.statement: Copyrighted album art. No image is stored here.

references.title: Flutter Neumorphic
references.lede: A Flutter UI kit from February 2020 that turned the two-shadow recipe into depth, intensity, and light-source settings.
references.summary: Idean’s open-source neumorphic widget kit for Flutter, with a playground for depth, intensity, and shape.
references.made: 2020–2021 (version 0.0.1 on 19 February 2020; version 3.2.0 on 11 November 2021, per pub.dev)

evidence.note: Inspected frames of the repository’s own `medias/playground.gif` (500 × 842). The stored image is its first frame. The showcase image `medias/showcase_1.png` was also viewed; it contains a third-party photograph and is not stored. Licence read through the GitHub API; dates from the pub.dev API.

styles.note: The kit is built for the style: every widget shares the surface color and gets a light and a dark shadow set by a depth value, positive to rise and negative to sink.

context: The README calls it “a complete, ready to use, Neumorphic ui kit for Flutter”. The repository was created on 19 February 2020, about ten weeks after [Malewicz named the style](ref:malewicz-neumorphism-article-2019).
Its style settings are named depth, intensity, surface intensity, light source, and shape (concave, convex, flat, emboss).
Released under the Apache License 2.0. It had about 2,200 GitHub stars on 2026-09-28, the most of any repository returned by a GitHub search for “neumorphic”.
observed: A rounded square in the center of a pale gray surface, the same color as the surface. A white glow sits to its upper left and a gray shadow to its lower right.
Two blue sliders at the top and left edges set the light direction.
A lower panel with “Style” and “Element” tabs and sliders for Depth (11), Intensity (0.86), and SurfaceIntensity (0.5). The tabs and panel are flat white and saturated blue, not neumorphic.
interpretation: The playground makes the grammar of the style explicit as parameters: one surface color, a light source, and a depth that sets the offset and blur of both shadows. The Material-style control panel below it shows how often the style was confined to a few hero elements.
borrow: Expose depth as one signed number, positive for raised and negative for pressed, and derive both shadows from it.

images.alt: Flutter Neumorphic playground: a pale gray rounded square rising from a pale gray surface with a white glow at upper left and a gray shadow at lower right, above a panel with blue sliders for depth, intensity, and surface intensity.
images.caption: First frame of the playground animation in [Flutter Neumorphic](https://github.com/Idean/Flutter-Neumorphic) by Idean. Apache License 2.0.

rights.statement: Image committed to the repository as documentation and covered by its Apache License 2.0, © Idean. It shows only the package’s own widgets. The stored file is one frame converted from the GIF.

references.title: Franco Grignani blog
references.lede: A blog about the designer Franco Grignani that frames its posts with his black and white graphics: a radial burst in the header and a band of diagonal stripes behind the cards.
references.summary: A black header with a white radial line burst and a striped portrait, above post cards on a field of diagonal black and white stripes.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The request for francogrignani.org redirected to this site. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Borderline: black and white radial lines and a diagonal stripe band carry the page, but a photographed face, a gold script signature, and card shadows are counter-traits.

context: Search results describe the blog as supervised by Daniela Grignani. This was not checked on the site itself. For the designer’s work, see the [Woolmark logo](ref:grignani-woolmark-logo-1964) and the [Alfieri & Lacroix page](ref:grignani-alfieri-lacroix-ad-1959).
observed: The header is solid black. At the left, white radial lines taper around an off-centre black hole, like a warped sunburst.

At the right, a photographed face is striped with light and shadow lines. At the centre, a gold handwritten signature sits over the line “the first blog about the man and the artist” in white sans-serif.
Below, a band of thick diagonal black and white stripes fills the page width. “the sign of our time” is set in black on a white label over the stripes.

White post cards with soft shadows sit on the stripe band: a black card with white condensed capitals, a black and white portrait, and a poster with red, green, and black stripes. A grey sidebar holds search and links.
A grey “Menu” button sits at the top left.
interpretation: The site borrows Grignani’s optical line work as page chrome. The diagonal stripe band behind the cards is the clearest op device on the page.
The screenshot is dark (palette lightness 0.27) while the CSS reads a white page (0.83), because the header and stripes are images. Card shadows give a shadow share of 0.16.
borrow: Put a band of heavy diagonal stripes behind a row of solid cards, so the pattern shows only in the gaps.
Use a warped radial burst of white lines on black as a header image.

images.alt: Franco Grignani blog home page: a black header with a white radial line burst at left, a gold signature at centre, and a striped portrait at right, above white post cards on a band of diagonal black and white stripes.
images.caption: First viewport of [francogrignani.info](https://www.francogrignani.info/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Franz Ferdinand website, 2006
references.lede: The band’s official site from the time of its Rodchenko-inspired second album, archived on 1 January 2006, frames the news in red bars under a tilted red banner.
references.summary: A red diagonal banner with the band name, red section bars with capitals, and a black stepped tower of halftone at the left edge, on a pale olive ground.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive copy of 1 January 2006 with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The `id_` form of the archive URL loads the raw archived page; images loaded. The site is a fixed-width table layout centered on black.

styles.note: Clear in its frame, generic in its content: the header, the section bars, and the left border use red and black, a diagonal, and capitals. The news text is ordinary small Arial. The band based the album cover of the time on [Rodchenko’s Lengiz poster](ref:rodchenko-lengiz-books-poster-1924).

context: Franz Ferdinand’s second album, *You Could Have It So Much Better* (2005), has a cover based on Rodchenko’s 1924 Lengiz poster. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Could_Have_It_So_Much_Better).
The archived news items on the page date from 5 to 9 December 2005.
observed: A red banner cuts across the top right on a diagonal. “Franz Ferdinand” is set on it in cream sans-serif letters that follow the slope.
Navigation links are set in small red capitals, each after a small red square.
Section headings such as “NEWS”, “LATEST PICS”, and “BAND BLOG” are set in white capitals on red bars with a thin black rule below.
A black stepped tower with square windows and a band of coarse black halftone dots runs down the left edge, leaning slightly.
The page ground is a pale olive-khaki; the content panels are white. Photographs are in color.
Body text is small black Arial with red links.
interpretation: The site shows how a 2005 web design carried the style: in sliced images for the header and borders, with HTML text left plain. The measurement sees only the HTML: `type.uppercaseShare` is 0.06 and `color.chromaticShare` is 0.03, because the capitals and the red areas are mostly images. The screenshot palette finds 3% red.
The khaki ground stands in for aged paper. The measurement counts one hue in the computed styles and two in the screenshot, where the khaki registers.
borrow: Put the site name on a diagonal band that cuts off one top corner.
Mark each section with a solid red bar that carries its title in white capitals.

images.alt: Archived Franz Ferdinand home page: a red diagonal banner with the band name at the top right, small red capital navigation links, red section bars titled News, Latest Pics, and Band Blog, and a black leaning tower with halftone dots down the left edge, on a pale olive ground.
images.caption: First viewport of the [1 January 2006 archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20060101020315/http://www.franzferdinand.co.uk/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to Franz Ferdinand and their rights holders. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Fruit Trees furnishing fabric
references.lede: Alexander Girard turns trees into symmetrical black stems hung with flat orange, pink, and olive circles, ovals, and squares on white cotton.
references.summary: Symmetrical black-stemmed trees with flat orange, pink, and olive fruit shapes in vertical repeats. Alexander Girard for Herman Miller, 1960.

source.label: Art Institute of Chicago: Fruit Trees (Furnishing Fabric), 1988.76

evidence.note: Inspected, in the scratchpad only, the Art Institute of Chicago image of 1988.76 at 843 × 574 px (the largest size the museum serves for this in-copyright object). The image shows a detail with four vertical repeats. Not stored.

styles.note: Flat geometric fruit and plant forms, a warm orange-pink-olive palette on white, and folk-derived pattern: Girard’s Herman Miller textiles are a core source for the style.

context: The Art Institute of Chicago dates the fabric 1960 and describes it as cotton, plain weave, screen printed; designed by Alexander Girard (1907–1993) and produced by Herman Miller, Inc., Zeeland, Michigan. The piece measures 104 × 132.5 cm with a repeat of 58.8 × 30.8 cm. Credit line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Alexander Girard; Alexander Demond Fund. [AIC 1988.76](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/71159/fruit-trees-furnishing-fabric).
The museum’s API marks the object as not public domain.
observed: The ground is white. Black stems branch symmetrically from a central trunk in each repeat, with small curled tips.
Fruit shapes hang from the branches: orange and pink circles, pale pink ovals, orange and pink squares and trapezoids, and olive-green ovals on the trunk.
The shapes are flat color with no outlines; the black line is only the stems.
The trees stand in vertical columns side by side, with narrow white gaps between them.
interpretation: Girard mixes circles and squares freely on a folk-like tree form. The palette is warm and saturated, but softened by the pale pink and the white ground.
This is the “pattern as a band” idea at textile scale: small flat shapes repeated in columns.
borrow: Build a symmetric plant from a thin black stem and flat, unoutlined circles, ovals, and squares.
Use orange, pale pink, and olive together on white for a warm but light repeat.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Alexander Girard died in 1993; the Art Institute of Chicago does not mark the object as public domain.

references.title: Game Boy Color in Atomic Purple
references.lede: Nintendo’s colour handheld in translucent purple plastic, which shows its circuit board, speaker, and button contacts through the shell.
references.summary: Translucent purple shell with visible electronics and a multicolored COLOR logo. Nintendo, 1998.

creator.name: Nintendo (development team led by Satoru Okada, per Wikipedia)

references.made: 1998 (Japan 21 October 1998; North America 18 November 1998, per Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Inspected Evan-Amos’s 2011 photograph of one Atomic Purple unit (Commons, original 1580 × 2580; viewed at 960 × 1568) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The photographed unit is privately owned; no museum copy was found.

styles.note: Clear: translucent candy-colored plastic that displays the technology inside, released the same year as the iMac G3.

context: Wikipedia says the Game Boy Color launched in Japan on 21 October 1998 and in North America on 18 November 1998. “Atomic Purple”, made from translucent purple plastic, was released at the same time as the other launch colors. [Wikipedia: Game Boy Color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Color).
observed: The whole shell is translucent lilac-purple. The green circuit board, the round speaker with its copper coil, screws, and contact pads show through it.
A black glass panel frames a gray screen. Below it “GAME BOY” is in gray italic capitals and “COLOR” in red, purple, green, yellow, and blue letters.
The buttons are dark gray; the A and B buttons are round and the Select and Start buttons are pill shapes.
Every outer corner of the case is rounded.
interpretation: Translucency here is a display of the machine itself: the inner technology becomes decoration. This is a central Y2K idea, shared with the [iMac G3](ref:imac-g3-bondi-blue-1998).
Clear purple is a frequent Y2K candy color; it sits between the blues and the pinks of the palette.
borrow: Show structure through a tinted translucent surface instead of hiding it.
Use pill-shaped secondary controls next to round primary controls.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is released into the public domain by its author, Evan-Amos, but the product design and logos belong to Nintendo. The lead curator can decide whether the photograph may be stored (tier A) on the argument that a utilitarian product is not copyrightable.

references.title: Game Center, iOS 4.1, 2010
references.lede: Apple’s social gaming app, dressed as a casino card table of green felt framed in wood.
references.summary: Green felt, a wooden table rim, and game chips. Apple, 2010.

evidence.note: No image of 800 px or more was found under a usable source. Based on Wikipedia and Fast Company (2012).

styles.note: A clear object metaphor: a card table with felt cloth and chips, pushed by Steve Jobs according to former Apple designers.

context: Game Center was released to the public on 8 September 2010 with iOS 4.1. Its developer preview “had a dark appearance with abstract colors”; the release changed to “a lighter ‘game board’ appearance with more skeuomorphic design elements.” [Wikipedia: Game Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Center).

A former Apple designer told Fast Company: “Steve pushed very hard to have everything—the felt-cloth table, the game chips—look like they would in real life.” [Fast Company, Austin Carr, “Will Apple’s Tacky Software-Design Philosophy Cause A Revolt?” (2012)](https://www.fastcompany.com/1670760/will-apples-tacky-software-design-philosophy-cause-a-revolt).
interpretation: The shift from an abstract dark preview to felt and wood at release shows the style as a deliberate late choice, not a default.
next: Find a large screenshot of the iOS 4–6 Game Center and inspect the felt and wood textures.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Garbo waste can
references.lede: Karim Rashid’s curvy polypropylene wastebasket for Umbra, one of the best-known blobjects of the late 1990s.
references.summary: Curvy molded polypropylene wastebasket with handle cut-outs, in bright and translucent colors. Karim Rashid for Umbra, 1995–1996.

source.label: Minneapolis Institute of Art: Garbo waste can, 2001.232

references.made: 1996 (Minneapolis Institute of Art and Nasjonalmuseet); the Philadelphia Museum of Art says designed 1995

evidence.note: Based on the Minneapolis Institute of Art record 2001.232 (no image published), the Nasjonalmuseet record OK-2002-0106, the Philadelphia Museum of Art record, and Metropolis (2016). No museum image of at least 800 px was inspected.

styles.note: Partial fit: a soft, curvy blobject in bright molded plastic from the Y2K period. It has no chrome or techno motifs.

context: Mia records a plastic waste can dated 1996, 33.2 × 26.7 × 25.1 cm, designed by Karim Rashid and made by Umbra, and says the “curvaceous, handled Garbo trash can is now a design icon, selling over two million units”. [Mia 2001.232](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/58170/garbo-waste-can-karim-rashid).

The Philadelphia Museum of Art gives “designed 1995”, polypropylene, translucent. [Philadelphia Museum of Art](https://philamuseum.org/collection/object/92596). Nasjonalmuseet in Oslo dates its copy 1996. [Nasjonalmuseet OK-2002-0106](https://www.nasjonalmuseet.no/en/collection/object/OK-2002-0106).

Metropolis (Misha Volf, 19 January 2016) describes an injection-molded polypropylene can released in 1996 in a “high-intensity color palette”, and says Rashid proposed in early meetings that it be translucent, “passing diffused light through its torso”. [Metropolis](https://metropolismag.com/viewpoints/karim-rashids-garbo-20/).
interpretation: Garbo is the blobject in domestic form: a cheap molded object made sensual through curves and color. It shows that the Y2K shape language reached everyday goods, not only electronics.
The shape and color are well documented, but no image was inspected, so no visual details are listed here.
borrow: Give functional openings, such as handles, soft rounded cut-outs instead of separate parts.
Let a container flare outward at the top, so the silhouette reads as a curve, not a box.
next: Find a museum image of at least 800 px (Cooper Hewitt, MoMA, or Philadelphia) and inspect it, then add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design belongs to Karim Rashid and Umbra; the Mia record marks rights as unknown.

references.title: Generalitat de Catalunya election information video
references.lede: An animated public-information video for the 2024 Catalan parliamentary election: long-legged figures in patterned clothes stand on a globe or carry a giant highlighter.
references.summary: Outlined, long-limbed figures with dotted and striped clothes on peach and pink. Government explainer video, 2024.

source.label: YouTube: Eleccions al Parlament de Catalunya – 12 de maig | ERTA

creator.name: Generalitat de Catalunya, Departament d’Acció Exterior i Unió Europea

evidence.note: Inspected two 1280 × 720 video frames on Wikimedia Commons: [frame 1](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corporate_Memphis_-_Generalitat_de_Catalunya_(2024),_1.png) and [frame 2](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corporate_Memphis_-_Generalitat_de_Catalunya_(2024),_2.png). The video itself was not watched. No image is stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: the Commons uploader gives it as an example of the style, and the figures have small heads, long limbs, and oversized objects, but they have black outlines and dot and stripe patterns, which the rubric lists as counter-traits.

context: The Commons description (in Catalan) calls it an example of the Corporate Memphis style used by the Generalitat de Catalunya in general videos in 2024, and gives the YouTube video as the source. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corporate_Memphis_-_Generalitat_de_Catalunya_(2024),_1.png).
Wikipedia notes that by 2023 the style was spreading from tech to other sectors while its popularity fell. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_Memphis).
observed: Frame 1: four figures stand around the curve of a dark plum globe on a flat peach background. Their bodies are tall and thin with small heads and small feet.
Their clothes have dot, check, and stripe patterns in pink and plum; every shape has a thin dark outline.
A red label reads “VOT EXTERIOR ERTA” and a subtitle runs along the bottom.
Frame 2: on flat pink, a woman in a beret and striped wide trousers holds a highlighter as long as her torso next to a desk calendar showing “maig 2”.
interpretation: It shows the style after its tech years: adopted by government communication, with outline and pattern added. The oversized object and the long thin figure remain; the non-natural skin and flat unoutlined fills are gone.
borrow: Put the key fact (a date, a place) on an oversized object that the figure holds or points to.

rights.statement: Commons tags the frames with the Generalitat’s attribution license, which covers content published on gencat.cat. These frames come from a YouTube video, so the tag may not apply; no image is stored.

references.title: Genesis soil intelligence website
references.lede: A climate-data company whose dashboard cards are frosted glass over a sunrise landscape photo.
references.summary: Frosted, rounded data cards and pill navigation over a landscape photo at sunrise.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. Found through the One Page Love glassmorphism collection (discovery only).

styles.note: Clear example: translucent, blurred cards with large radii float over the backdrop, and the content inside them stays flat. The backdrop is a photo, not abstract color.

observed: The backdrop is a photo of green hills under a sky that fades from blue at the top to peach and pink at the horizon.
Two large cards at the bottom (‘Resilience score’ and ‘Share of soils in good health’) are translucent and blurred: the hills behind them show as soft green and brown.
The cards have large rounded corners and a faint lighter edge. Their content is flat: a green gauge, colored bars, and white sans-serif type.
The navigation links sit in separate translucent pills; ‘Book a demo’ is a solid near-black pill.
The primary hero button is a solid dark red pill next to a white pill.
interpretation: Measured: 37 % of boxes use a backdrop blur and 77 % are rounded (median radius 12 px). No box has a CSS border, and 54 % have a gradient fill, so the light edge and the frosted look come from gradients and shadows. Chromatic share is only 0.10 because the photo backdrop is soft.
borrow: Put data cards in frosted glass over a large landscape photo, and keep the charts inside them flat and saturated.

images.alt: Genesis home page: a sunrise photo of green hills with a dark sans-serif headline, pill navigation at top right, and two frosted translucent data cards at the bottom showing a gauge of 6.5 and a bar chart.
images.caption: First viewport of [genesis.live](https://www.genesis.live/), captured 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Gerald McBoing-Boing
references.lede: UPA’s Oscar-winning short animated a Dr. Seuss story with flat, sparse drawings and limited movement, and set the look of mid-century “cartoon modern”.
references.summary: Animated short film by United Productions of America, directed by Robert Cannon, released by Columbia in 1950.

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article and its quotation from The New York Times. No frames of the film were inspected for this record.

styles.note: The source of the style’s “limited animation” trait: flat shapes, few in-betweens, and sparse backgrounds.

context: Gerald McBoing-Boing is a 1950 animated short directed by Robert Cannon and produced by United Productions of America. Columbia Pictures released it on 4 November 1950. Phil Eastman and Bill Scott adapted a story by Dr. Seuss. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_McBoing-Boing).
It won the 1950 Academy Award for Best Animated Short. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 1995. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_McBoing-Boing).

Wikipedia quotes The New York Times: Cannon “was primarily responsible for the drawings, strongly reminiscent of a [Saul] Steinberg cartoon”, and Bill Hurtz and Herb Klynn did the design and the color. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_McBoing-Boing).
interpretation: UPA’s films moved studio animation away from rounded, fully animated characters toward flat, graphic drawing. That link between print illustration and motion is why the style record names limited animation as a trait.
borrow: Animate by moving, cutting, and swapping flat shapes rather than by smooth tweening, as the style’s motion facet describes.
next: Inspect frames from a licensed copy of the film and record what they show.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The film’s copyright status was not checked.

references.title: Gilt bench by Louis Majorelle
references.lede: A Nancy window bench from the Majorelle firm: gilt wood that curves up into two arched, leaf-shaped ends carved with flowers.
references.summary: Gilt-wood bench with arched, upholstered ends and carved flower tops. Louis Majorelle, Nancy, c. 1900.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 1971.28 (3400 × 2587 px print file). Read the object record through the museum’s open-access API.

styles.note: Nancy School furniture: continuous curves, arched panel ends, and carved plant tops. It is a partial fit, because its gilding and Rococo echo are more courtly than the whiplash core.

context: The Cleveland Museum of Art records the bench as gilt wood, 75 × 118.1 × 40.7 cm, made in Nancy, France, c. 1900, by Louis Majorelle (1859–1926). [CMA 1971.28](https://clevelandart.org/art/1971.28).

The museum’s text says that French Art Nouveau furniture designers took inspiration from Rococo pieces of about 1750, that this bench shows the Majorelle firm’s version of that taste, and that it is now covered with a Japanese brocade of about 1900. [CMA 1971.28](https://clevelandart.org/art/1971.28).
observed: The frame is gilt all over. The seat rail curves gently and runs without a break into the two raised ends.
Each end is a tall panel with an arched top, divided by a central rib into two pointed, leaf-shaped fields of upholstery.
Carved flower heads sit at the top of each end, and small carved leaves sit where the legs meet the seat rail.
The four legs are slender and curve outward to small scrolled feet.
The brocade is pale pink and gold with small green and red floral sprigs, edged by a coral-orange braid that follows the curves of the panels.
interpretation: The arched, leaf-shaped end panels are a direct source for the style’s arched and leaf-cut panel shapes.
The upholstery is a later Japanese brocade, so its colours are not Majorelle’s choice; the frame and its carving are the evidence here.
borrow: Give a panel an arched top and split it with one central rib into two leaf-shaped fields.
Run a contrasting edge line around a curved panel so that the curve reads clearly.

images.alt: Long gilt-wood bench on four slender curved legs. Both ends rise into tall arched panels upholstered in pink and gold floral brocade and topped with carved flowers.
images.caption: Louis Majorelle, bench, c. 1900, gilt wood with later Japanese brocade. [Cleveland Museum of Art 1971.28](https://clevelandart.org/art/1971.28), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art marks the object and its image CC0. Louis Majorelle died in 1926, so his designs are in the public domain in France, and the bench, made about 1900, is in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Gismonda poster by Alphonse Mucha
references.lede: The life-size poster that made Mucha’s name: Sarah Bernhardt as a Byzantine noblewoman under a mosaic arch, in pastel ochres, rose, and slate blue, with flared hand-drawn capitals.
references.summary: Tall poster of Sarah Bernhardt under an arched mosaic halo, with hand-drawn lettering. Alphonse Mucha, Paris, 1894–95.

source.label: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Gallica: Gismonda. Sarah Bernhardt. Théâtre de la Renaissance (épreuve du tirage définitif)

creator.name: Alphonse Mucha; printed by Imprimeries Lemercier, Paris

references.made: Designed December 1894 for posting from 1 January 1895 (Wikipedia); BnF and Commons date this proof 1895

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a 960 × 2466 px copy of the BnF scan on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gismonda._Sarah_Bernhardt._Th%C3%A9atre_de_La_Renaissance_-_(affiche)_(%C3%89preuve_du_tirage_d%C3%A9finitif)_-_Mucha_-_btv1b90163096.jpg). The copy is the BnF proof of the final printing, shelf mark ENT DN-1 (MUCHA,Alphonse/3)-ROUL, printed in two sheets. Also compared the reduced *Maîtres de l’Affiche* plate 27 on [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alphonse_Mucha_-_Poster_for_Victorien_Sardou%27s_Gismonda_starring_Sarah_Bernhardt_-_Original.jpg).

styles.note: The founding Mucha poster: a figure framed by an arched halo, flowers in the hair, flared hand-drawn capitals, and soft pastel colours with dark outlines.

context: Wikipedia: Sardou’s *Gismonda* opened on 31 October 1894 at the Théâtre de la Renaissance. On 26 December Bernhardt ordered a new poster from the printer Lemercier to be ready by 1 January 1895; Mucha, who happened to be there correcting proofs, received the commission. The poster is a little more than two metres high. [Wikipedia: Alphonse Mucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mucha).

Wikipedia notes the arch behind the head, “almost like a halo”, which appears in all of Mucha’s later theatre posters, the Byzantine mosaic behind the head, and the delicate pastel colours, unlike the bright posters of the time. Its success led to a contract for six more Bernhardt posters. [Wikipedia: Alphonse Mucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mucha); [Wikipedia: Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau).
The Commons record of the BnF copy gives the size as 217 × 75 cm and the catalogue reference Rennert and Weill 3. [BnF catalogue](https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb40461484m).
observed: The format is very tall and narrow, about 1 : 2.9.
At the top, “GISMONDA” in dark blue capitals on an ochre mosaic band. The letters are hand-drawn, with flared strokes and an unusual G and A.
Behind the head, a round arch carries “BERNHARDT” in cream letters on an orange band, with a mosaic dome inside it. It acts as a halo.
Bernhardt stands in profile with a crown of pink orchids and long orange-red hair. She holds a tall palm branch in sage green.
Her robe and stole are covered in dense gold, ochre, and slate-blue brocade with birds and flowers; the lower half of the poster is mostly this fabric on a plain cream ground.
At the bottom, a curling banner reads “THÉÂTRE DE LA RENAISSANCE” in dark blue capitals. “IMPRIMERIES LEMERCIER, PARIS” is set small at lower right. A thin dark border frames the whole sheet.
Colours are muted: ochre, old gold, dusty rose, sage, slate blue, and cream, with dark blue-black outlines.
interpretation: The poster sets most of the style’s graphic rules: the arched medallion behind the head, the flower crown, the flared, legible hand lettering, the dark key line, and a pastel, earthy palette on a light ground.
Its whiplash is soft: curves appear in the hair, the palm, and the banner, while the frame stays a tall rectangle.
borrow: Put a round arch or halo behind the key figure or heading, and set a word along the arch.
Set a title in a band at the top and a short credit on a curling banner at the bottom, leaving the middle to the image.
Use a tall, narrow panel for a hero image.

images.alt: Tall narrow poster: Sarah Bernhardt in profile under a mosaic arch lettered BERNHARDT, wearing pink orchids in her hair and a long gold brocade robe, holding a palm branch; GISMONDA across the top and THEATRE DE LA RENAISSANCE on a banner at the bottom.
images.caption: Alphonse Mucha, *Gismonda*, poster for Sarah Bernhardt at the Théâtre de la Renaissance, proof of the final printing, Imprimeries Lemercier. Bibliothèque nationale de France, via [Gallica](https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b90163096) and [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gismonda._Sarah_Bernhardt._Th%C3%A9atre_de_La_Renaissance_-_(affiche)_(%C3%89preuve_du_tirage_d%C3%A9finitif)_-_Mucha_-_btv1b90163096.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file with the templates PD-France, PD-old-auto-expired (1939), and PD-US-expired. Mucha died in 1939, so the poster entered the public domain in France and the Czech Republic in 2010. It was published in 1895, so it is in the public domain in the United States. Gallica’s terms of use ask for a fee for commercial reuse of BnF reproductions; the lead curator should confirm that this does not affect the catalogue.

identifiers.commons: File:Gismonda. Sarah Bernhardt. Théatre de La Renaissance - (affiche) (Épreuve du tirage définitif) - Mucha - btv1b90163096.jpg

references.title: Going Under (Aggro Crab, 2020)
references.lede: A satirical dungeon-crawler about failed tech startups, whose characters and office spaces take the style’s colors and shapes into 3D.
references.summary: A 3D game that parodies startup culture with the style’s pastel palette, blob furniture, and bright-skinned characters. 2020.

evidence.note: Inspected two 1920 × 1080 screenshots from the Steam store API (a boss fight and the company lobby). No image is stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: a parody in 3D. It uses the style’s palette, pill-shaped furniture, and potted plants, and blue-skinned monsters, but it has painted texture and 3D light, not flat vector fills.

context: Steam describes it as “a satirical dungeon crawler about exploring the cursed ruins of failed tech startups”, with the player as an unpaid intern in the city of Neo-Cascadia. Developer Aggro Crab, publisher Team17, released 24 September 2020. [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/1154810/Going_Under/).
Reviews and essays describe its art as a parody of Corporate Memphis, for example [Merry-Go-Round Magazine](https://merrygoroundmagazine.com/going-under-reclaims-corporate-aesthetics/).
observed: The lobby screenshot shows pink and peach walls, a green floor with orange paths, and long yellow and purple pill-shaped benches.
Rounded teal trees stand in violet pots on red bases; giant soda cans float over a fountain.
The boss screenshot shows a violet brick room with a zig-zag stripe, and a large monster with blue arms and an orange body.
Surfaces carry a brushed, speckled texture and soft 3D shading.
interpretation: Going Under shows how recognizable the style became by 2020: a game could use its palette and props as shorthand for startup culture and make fun of it.
borrow: For a satirical or self-aware brand, keep the style’s palette and props but add texture to signal distance from it.

rights.statement: © Aggro Crab and Team17. No image is stored.

references.title: Google Material Theme (Material Design 2)
references.lede: The 2018 update that Google applied to its own apps: more white, rounder 4 dp corners, Google Sans headings, and colorful icons.
references.summary: Material Design 2 in Google’s products: white app bars, rounder corners, Google Sans, and a bottom app bar. 2018.

evidence.note: Relies on Wikipedia and on 9to5Google’s article of 26 April 2018. No image was inspected: the 9to5Google images did not load for scripts, and m2.material.io renders only with JavaScript.

styles.note: Documents the Material 2 branch of the style, in which white app bars and rounder corners replace the bold primary bar of 2014.

context: Wikipedia: “After the 2018 revamp, Google began redesigning most of their apps based on an updated set of principles and guidelines dubbed ‘Material Design 2’, which appeared on Android Pie.” The update emphasizes “white space, rounded corners, colorful icons, and bottom navigation bars”, and Google began to use Google Sans, a version of Product Sans. [Wikipedia: Material Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Material_Design).

9to5Google (Stephen Hall, 26 April 2018) lists the redesigned Gmail web client, Google Tasks, the Google I/O 2018 app, and Android P Settings, and notes “lots of white space” and “a much rounder radius on corners”. [9to5Google](https://9to5google.com/2018/04/26/what-is-material-design-2-examples-launch-io/).
interpretation: Material 2 keeps the elevation system but moves color out of the app bar and into icons and accents. This is why many Material 2 screens measure far less chromatic color than Material 1 screens.
next: Capture a dated Wayback copy of a Material 2 Google page, for example material.io in 2019, to observe the theme directly.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The products belong to Google.

references.title: Google Play store website, 2016
references.lede: The 2016 web store for Android apps, in French: a green section tab, white app cards with soft shadows on pale gray, and Roboto Light headings.
references.summary: White app cards with soft shadows on pale gray, a green section tab, a blue raised button, and Roboto Light headings. 2016.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The archive served the French edition. Four app icons in the first card row did not load, and a thin cookie strip covers the top edge.

styles.note: Clear example of Material 1 on the web: white cards at a low elevation on a pale gray ground, one saturated green for the current section, a blue raised sign-in button, and Roboto. Scrims over the carousel photos add gradients.

references.notice: The live Google Play store has a different design.
observed: A white header holds the Google Play logo, a long search field with a blue search button, and a blue raised “Connexion” button with square corners.
A solid green tab labeled “Applications” with a white Android glyph marks the section. Beside it, text tabs read Catégories, Accueil, Classements, and Nouveautés, with a gray underline under Accueil.
A carousel of three photographs runs edge to edge, with white titles over a dark gradient at the bottom of each photo.

Below, the heading “50 jeux incontournables” is set in large Roboto Light. A row of white app cards with soft, short shadows sits on a pale gray ground. Each card holds an icon, a title, a developer name, and gray stars.
Four of the seven app icons in the row did not load and show alt text. A thin dark cookie strip runs across the top of the page.
interpretation: The page measures a shadow on 36 % of its boxes, with a median blur of 4 px and offset of 2 px, which matches a 2 dp card. Its chromatic share is 0.01, because color is limited to the green tab, the blue buttons, and photographs. The gradient share of 0.14 comes from the scrims under the carousel captions, not from gradient fills on surfaces.
borrow: Put catalog items on identical white cards with a 2 dp shadow on a pale gray ground, and let only the item images carry color.

images.alt: Google Play in 2016, French edition: the Google Play logo and search field, a green Applications tab, a photo carousel, and a row of white app cards with soft shadows on a pale gray ground.
images.caption: [Wayback Machine copy of play.google.com/store/apps](https://web.archive.org/web/20160601095735/https://play.google.com/store/apps), 1 June 2016. The archive served the French edition.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Grateful Dead at the Avalon Ballroom (Skeleton and Roses)
references.lede: Alton Kelley and Stanley Mouse’s Family Dog poster of September 1966, which framed an old book illustration of a skeleton crowned with roses in banners of hand lettering.
references.summary: Mouse and Kelley, 1966. A rose-crowned skeleton inside red ribbons and blue frames of swelling lettering.

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object E.55-1999 (IIIF, 1200 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The imprint on this copy reads 26 (2), so it may be a second printing. The image is not stored.

styles.note: The Art Nouveau revival side of the style: a borrowed nineteenth-century illustration, symmetrical ribbons, and swollen hand lettering. Partial fit on color: red and blue on cream paper, with a white margin.

context: The V&A catalogues it as a psychedelic poster promoting the Grateful Dead and Oxford Circle at the Avalon Ballroom, offset lithography, 508 × 356 mm, by Alton Kelley and Stanley Mouse, San Francisco, 1966. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O111021/).

Wikipedia reports that Mouse and Kelley drew heavily on Art Nouveau graphics, in particular Alphonse Mucha and Edmund Joseph Sullivan, and credits the two with the skull-and-roses image for the Grateful Dead. Sullivan’s skeleton comes from a nineteenth-century edition of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám. [Wikipedia: Stanley Mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Mouse), [Wikipedia: Alton Kelley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alton_Kelley).
observed: A skeleton crowned and surrounded by red roses stands in a pale blue rectangle at the center. The drawing is fine black line with red and white roses.
GRATEFUL DEAD runs across a red ribbon at the top in black-outlined, swelling capitals. The ribbon ends curl down both sides and hold two Family Dog medallions.
SEPT 16 and SEPT 17 stand in large red script letters left and right of the image, symmetrically.
A blue cartouche at the bottom holds OXFORD CIRCLE in red and AVALON BALLROOM in blue on a white ribbon.
A bright blue border fills the space between the frames. Cream paper shows around the edge, and the ticket outlets at the bottom are set in plain type.
interpretation: The poster shows how much of the style is revival. The skeleton is Victorian book illustration, and the ribbons and medallions come from Art Nouveau and Victorian posters. The psychedelic part is the lettering and the crowding.
Its two-ink palette of red and blue is saturated but not vibrating, which is common in Family Dog posters.
borrow: Frame a central image with a ribbon banner and mirrored side elements.
Set dates or secondary facts as large, symmetrical ornaments rather than small text.
Combine one fine-line illustration with heavy, swollen display lettering for contrast.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. The imprint reads © Family Dog Productions 1966. Stanley Mouse is alive; Alton Kelley died in 2008.

references.title: Grateful Dead, Aoxomoxoa, album cover
references.lede: Rick Griffin’s cover for the Grateful Dead’s third album, 1969, adapted from a concert-poster painting, with the band name in large flowing capitals.
references.summary: Rick Griffin, 1969. Poster painting reused as an LP sleeve, with a palindrome title and flowing lettering.

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article and its sources. I found no image of at least 800 px from a museum or other citable holder, so I did not describe the cover beyond what the text states.

styles.note: The poster style carried onto a record sleeve by one of its main artists. Documented only; the fit is taken from the sources, not from inspection.

context: Aoxomoxoa is the Grateful Dead’s third studio album, released on 20 June 1969 by Warner Bros.-Seven Arts. The title is a palindrome made up by the cover artist Rick Griffin and the lyricist Robert Hunter. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aoxomoxoa).

According to Wikipedia, the artwork is adapted from a painting first made as a concert poster for the band. The bottom shows death, rebirth, and the cycle of life, with fertility symbols and Egyptian-based imagery; the top shows a sun that doubles as an egg; stylized censers stand at both sides. The words “Grateful Dead” are written in large, flowing capital letters. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aoxomoxoa).

Rolling Stone ranked it eighth among the best album covers of all time in 1991, as cited by Wikipedia. Griffin also designed the [Flying Eyeball](ref:flying-eyeball-hendrix-poster-1968) poster. [Wikipedia: Rick Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Griffin).
interpretation: The sleeve documents how the poster artists moved into album packaging, which carried the style far beyond San Francisco.
next: Find a citable image of an original 1969 sleeve, for example in a museum collection, and upgrade the evidence to observed.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The cover art is in copyright; Rick Griffin died in 1991.

references.title: Greyhound bus station, Huntington, West Virginia
references.lede: A late Greyhound terminal in the company’s streamline manner: a low granite-clad box with rounded corners, portholes, a ribbed canopy, and red neon capitals.
references.summary: Rounded corners, round windows, a racetrack-shaped ribbon window, and GREYHOUND BUS DEPOT in red neon. George D. Brown, Huntington, 1953.

source.label: Library of Congress: Streamline Moderne-style Greyhound Bus Station in Huntington, West Virginia

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Carol M. Highsmith’s 2015 photograph (Library of Congress LCCN 2015631799) through its [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Streamline_Moderne-style_Greyhound_Bus_Station_in_Huntington,_West_Virginia_LCCN2015631799.tif) at 1920 px. The date and architect come from Clio; SAH Archipedia refused the request (HTTP 403).

styles.note: Clear fit on form, late in date: rounded ends, portholes, a ribbon window with semicircular ends, and a ribbed canopy. Built in 1953, after the style’s main period.

references.notice: Built in 1953, after the main period of the style. It shows how long Greyhound kept the streamline look for its terminals.
context: Clio dates the station to 1953 and names the Charleston architect George D. Brown, who designed many Greyhound stations in the South and Midwest. The Tri-State Transit Authority bought and restored it in 1994. [Clio](https://theclio.com/entry/15652).
The Library of Congress title calls it a Streamline Moderne-style Greyhound bus station. [LOC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2015631799/).
observed: A low, long building clad in pinkish-brown speckled granite panels, with every outside corner rounded.
A taller block over the entrance rises in a curve toward the right and carries “GREYHOUND” and “BUS DEPOT” in red neon capitals with the running-dog emblem between.
Over the doors, a semicircular canopy is ribbed with several parallel horizontal bands.
A long ribbon window on the right ends in a semicircle, like a racetrack; round porthole windows sit on each side of the building.
Glass block fills the panels beside the doors; thin white coping runs along the roofline.
interpretation: The terminal is a compact catalogue of streamline elements for a roadside brand: rounded ends, parallel bands on the canopy, portholes, and a racetrack window. The red capitals on a warm ground show a transport palette other than cream and navy.
borrow: Give a long horizontal window or panel semicircular ends.
Ribbed canopies: stack three to five thin parallel bands on a rounded element to suggest speed.

images.alt: Color photograph of a low granite-clad bus station with rounded corners, round porthole windows, a long window with rounded ends, a ribbed semicircular canopy over glass doors, and red neon letters reading GREYHOUND BUS DEPOT with a running dog.
images.caption: Carol M. Highsmith, 2015. [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2015631799/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Streamline_Moderne-style_Greyhound_Bus_Station_in_Huntington,_West_Virginia_LCCN2015631799.tif).

rights.statement: Commons marks the photograph public domain; Carol M. Highsmith placed her Library of Congress photographs in the public domain. The building dates from 1953, before December 1990, so it has no architectural copyright in the United States. The Greyhound name and dog are trademarks shown as part of the building.

identifiers.commons: File:Streamline Moderne-style Greyhound Bus Station in Huntington, West Virginia LCCN2015631799.tif

references.title: Guimard Métro entrance, Porte Dauphine, Paris
references.lede: Hector Guimard’s cast-iron and glass station entrance: stalk-like green posts, a fan-shaped glass canopy like a dragonfly’s wings, and his hand-drawn “Métropolitain” sign.
references.summary: Green cast-iron stalks, a fan-shaped glass canopy, and flared METROPOLITAIN lettering. Hector Guimard, Paris, 1900.

source.label: Wikipedia: Paris Métro entrances by Hector Guimard

references.made: 1900–1913 for the series; most designs date from 1900, and the lettering reached its final form in 1902 (Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Guilhem Vellut’s photograph of the Porte Dauphine édicule, taken 25 March 2017, on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Metropolitain_entrance_by_Hector_Guimard_@_Porte_Dauphine_@_Paris_(32826231574).jpg) (1280 × 853 px copy of a 5472 × 3648 px original). Also compared Georges De Valkeneer’s 2015 night photograph of the Abbesses édicule on [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Abbesses_metro_station,_Paris_30_May_2015.jpg).

styles.note: The work that gave the style its French nickname, “Style Métro”: plant-stem ironwork, a winged glass canopy, and custom flared lettering in public use.

context: Wikipedia: Guimard designed the first generation of entrances to the Paris Métro between 1900 and 1913, mostly in 1900. He used cast iron set in concrete, painted green to look like weathered brass, and standard parts, including “M” cartouches and signs in his own lettering reading “Métropolitain” or “Métro”. His designs created the “Métro style” and popularised Art Nouveau. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_M%C3%A9tro_entrances_by_Hector_Guimard).

The roofed édicules, called *libellules* because they resemble dragonflies, had glass roofs and sometimes wall panels of enamelled lava. Two original type B édicules survive: Porte Dauphine, on its original site with its wall panels, and Abbesses, moved from Hôtel de Ville in 1974. Eighty-six Guimard entrances remain and are protected historical monuments. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_M%C3%A9tro_entrances_by_Hector_Guimard).
observed: The canopy is a fan of curved glass panes on thin iron ribs. It opens upward and outward at the front like a pair of wings.
Two slender green posts rise from the ground on each side, curve inward at the top, and carry the canopy; their tops branch into thinner tendrils.

Under the canopy, a pale yellow oval-ended plaque reads “METROPOLITAIN” in dark green capitals with flared strokes and unusual letter shapes: the O is narrow and pointed, and the letters vary in height.
The side and back walls are panels of ochre-orange enamel, each with a round-topped inner frame; above them runs a band of glass in a grid of thin green bars.
Colours are sea green iron, ochre and orange panels, a cream sign, and clear glass.
interpretation: The entrance applies the whiplash and the plant stem to industrial, standardised parts, which the style’s grammar names as a key difference from Arts and Crafts.
The sign is a model for Art Nouveau lettering: legible, but drawn by hand with curved, swelling strokes that match the ironwork.
borrow: Frame a heading in a pale plaque with rounded ends and a dark outline, set in flared display capitals.
Use a fan of thin curved lines as a header or canopy shape instead of a flat bar.
Pair sea green with ochre and cream.

images.alt: Métro entrance in a park in daylight: green cast-iron posts curve up to a fan-shaped glass canopy; a cream sign reads METROPOLITAIN in dark green flared letters; ochre-orange panels line the stairway walls below.
