references.title: Gustav Klimt | Wien 1900 Foundation website
references.lede: The foundation’s site opens with a black square logo of justified capitals and gold, on a finely patterned ground with square-cornered white panels.
references.summary: Black square logo of justified capitals with one gold line, on a patterned ground, with square panels and capital navigation.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. A cookie bar covers the bottom 90 px of the screenshot. The measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: the logo is a Secession device (a black square with capitals set to fill each line, and gold), and the ground is patterned, but the layout is asymmetric and the tiles use several colours.

observed: At the upper left, a black square holds “GUSTAV / KLIMT / WIEN 1900 / FOUNDA / TION” in white and gold capitals, right-aligned; “FOUNDATION” is broken over two lines to keep the block square.
The page ground is a fine cream and gray pattern of small interlocking marks, like a woven or diagonal lattice.
The navigation (FOUNDATION, COLLECTION, RESEARCH, PUBLICATIONS, SALON) is in spaced gold capitals on a white panel with square corners.
A Klimt painting fills a white-framed panel in the right column.
Below, two square-cornered tiles in slate blue, green, and blue carry large white capitals: “GUSTAV KLIMT-DATABASE / RESEARCH ONLINE” and “EDITION KLIMT / PUBLICATION”.
The layout is a left logo column and a wide right column, not a central axis.
interpretation: The logo is the closest the site comes to the style: a square block of capitals that are broken and aligned to fill the shape, with the words “WIEN 1900” in gold.

The fingerprint does not see the patterned ground: it is a CSS background image, and the extractor measured `surface.patternShare` and `color.patternShare` as 0. Text is left-aligned (`type.centerShare` 0.01) and only 17% of it is capitals. Square corners (radius 0) and one hue pass.
borrow: Make a logo as a black square of capitals set to fill each line, and break a long word to keep the block square.
Put square-cornered white panels on a finely patterned ground so the pattern frames the content.

images.alt: Klimt Foundation home page: a black square logo with the words Gustav Klimt Wien 1900 Foundation in white and gold capitals, on a finely patterned cream background, with a gold capital navigation bar, a Klimt painting in a white frame, and two coloured tiles for the database and a publication.
images.caption: First viewport of [klimt-foundation.com](https://www.klimt-foundation.com/en/), captured 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the Gustav Klimt | Wien 1900-Privatstiftung. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Handspring Visor Deluxe
references.lede: A Palm-style organiser sold in translucent candy colors, which the V&A links directly to the iMac G3.
references.summary: Translucent orange case with silver oval buttons and a frosted cradle. Handspring, 1999–2000.
references.made: 2000 (V&A); Wikipedia says the Visor line was released in September 1999

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object W.663:1 to 8-2001 (image 2008BT4277, 1600 × 1200) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear: translucent candy-orange plastic, visible circuit board, silver capsule buttons, and a frosted blob-shaped cradle.

context: The V&A says the Visor “was available in a range of translucent, coloured plastic cases, inside of which the complex computer technology is concealed. In this way, it is aesthetically related to the design of the Apple iMac G3”. The case is polypropylene. [V&A W.663-2001](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O59892/visor-deluxe-handheld-computer-handspring-international/).

Wikipedia lists the Visor Deluxe colors as translucent blue, green, and orange, and clear “Ice”, and gives a September 1999 release. [Wikipedia: Handspring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handspring_(company)).
observed: The case is translucent orange plastic. The circuit board and screws show through the lower part.
Fine horizontal ribs run down both sides of the frame around the greenish LCD screen.
Four round buttons and a central pill-shaped rocker are silver with a metallic sheen.
The device stands in a frosted, semi-clear cradle with a curved, lens-like front.
The stylus is a chrome tube with a white translucent tip.
interpretation: The Visor shows how quickly the iMac’s material language spread to small electronics: the same translucent color, now combined with small chrome parts.
The mix of warm translucent orange and cold silver is a compact version of the Y2K palette.
borrow: Combine a translucent warm color panel with small silver pill-shaped controls.
Use a frosted clear surface as a base or stand for a colored element.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London; the product design belongs to its maker.

references.title: Handspring website, 2000
references.lede: Handspring’s home page in August 2000, led by a large photograph of a translucent blue Visor.
references.summary: A translucent blue Visor on a textured blue swoosh, light serif VISOR heading, and rounded lilac tab headings.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. All images loaded.

styles.note: Borderline: the translucent candy product and the rounded tab shapes carry the style; the page around them is a plain white table layout. The page draws its graphics with images, so the CSS fingerprint measures flat, square, unshadowed boxes (see the style page). Judge it by the rubric.

observed: A large photograph at upper left shows a translucent blue Visor at an angle, with round silver buttons, on a blue textured surface that curves away in a swoosh.
“VISOR” is set in large serif capitals that fade from pale blue to dark blue; the tagline “whatever the heck you want it to be.” is in small blue sans-serif.
Three columns start with lilac tab bars whose ends are rounded: “places to go”, “things to buy”, and “news to know”, with the last word in heavy blue.
Product teasers pair small photos (an orange Visor, a thin modem, colored styluses, a leather case) with light lilac headings.
Small orange “GO” circles and square lilac and green buttons act as controls. A blue textured swoosh closes the layout at the bottom.
interpretation: The site sells the object that carries the style: the [Visor](ref:handspring-visor-deluxe-2000) in translucent candy colors. The page shows the product photo as the hero and repeats its blue and rounded shapes in the tab bars.
Measured: no CSS gradients, shadows, or radii; the pixel palette is mostly white with a strong blue accent.
borrow: Use a product photo on a curved band of color as the page header, and echo the curve in the footer.

images.alt: Archived Handspring home page: a translucent blue Visor handheld on a curved blue textured band at top left, a large VISOR heading and tagline, and three columns under rounded lilac tab bars with product photos and news links.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20000815053118/http://www.handspring.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to Handspring. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Hit Vibes cover art
references.lede: Saint Pepsi’s 2013 cover imitates an early-1980s record sleeve: a red square, floating parallelograms, a yellow wedge, and a thin swoosh on grainy grey.
references.summary: Mock-1980s sleeve: red square, drop-shadowed parallelograms, yellow wedge, grey grain. 2013.

evidence.note: Inspected the 900 × 900 front cover in the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release/ff881a14-c23e-4728-bfb9-7b11bb5b6ecd/cover-art), in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit, from the future-funk branch: it quotes 1980s commercial graphics, the [Memphis](style:memphis)-derived shapes Wikipedia lists among the style’s sources, but has no pastel gradient, statue, or digital chrome.

context: Wikipedia names Skylar Spence (formerly Saint Pepsi) among the most popular future funk artists, and lists Saint Pepsi among the performers at the first vaporwave festival in 2019. [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave).
observed: A large red square with a thin black outline sits on a grey, grainy ground.
A row of small red parallelograms with grey drop shadows crosses the top diagonally; a thin yellow wedge cuts down through the square.
A thin navy swoosh curves across the middle; HIT VIBES is printed faintly inside the square in large outline letters, and SAINT PEPSI in white thin italic capitals at the top left.
interpretation: Useful as a boundary case: it quotes the same 1980s source material as vaporwave through graphic pastiche, without the collage and digital artefacts.

rights.statement: Copyrighted album art. No image is stored here.

references.title: Horta Museum website, 2013
references.lede: The Horta Museum’s old language page: an ochre panel with a white outline and rounded corners, flared Art Nouveau capitals, a whiplash butterfly ornament, and three framed photographs of Horta’s ironwork and glass.
references.summary: Ochre rounded panel with flared HORTAMUSEUM capitals, a whiplash ornament, and three framed detail photographs on a tan ground.
references.made: Captured by the Wayback Machine on 14 January 2013

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 14 January 2013 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. The whole panel is drawn with images, so the computed-style measurement sees almost none of it.

styles.note: Clear: earthy ochre and brown on a light ground, a rounded panel with a light outline, flared Art Nouveau capitals, and a whiplash ornament.

references.notice: The live site at hortamuseum.be now uses a dark photographic home page with a modern serif wordmark. This record describes the 2013 archive copy.
observed: The page ground is a plain light tan. One centred panel sits near the top.
The panel is ochre with rounded corners, inside a white frame with rounded corners and a soft gray edge.
“HORTAMUSEUM” runs across the top in cream capitals with flared strokes and unusual forms: the M’s have curved middles and the U is pointed.
At the right end of the title, a cream line ornament of two looping, wing-like whiplash curves, like a butterfly.
A thin cream rule runs under the title.

Three photographs sit in a row with thin light frames: a stained-glass skylight with curved ironwork, a curved brass door handle on wood and marble, and a stone facade with swelling, carved window surrounds.
Below the photographs, “please choose your language” and the four language names in a brown serif.
A line of news links in plain brown Arial sits below the panel.
interpretation: The page follows the style’s rules more closely than the museum’s current site: an earthy palette on a light ground, a framed and outlined panel, a hand-drawn display face, and a single whiplash ornament.

Measured: the panel, frame, title, and ornament are all images. Computed styles report 5 boxes with radius 0, no borders, and no pattern; only the screenshot pixels show the warm palette (two hue families, accent chroma 0.39). Pages of this period can only be judged by the rubric.
borrow: Set a site title in flared display capitals with one whiplash ornament at its end, over a thin rule.
Show three detail photographs in a row, each with a thin light frame, inside one warm, rounded panel.

images.alt: Horta Museum language page from 2013: on a tan ground, an ochre panel with a white rounded frame holds the title HORTAMUSEUM in cream flared capitals with a butterfly-like whiplash ornament, three framed photographs of Horta ironwork, glass, and stone, and a row of language links.
images.caption: First viewport of [hortamuseum.be](https://web.archive.org/web/20130114061413/http://www.hortamuseum.be/), Wayback Machine copy of 14 January 2013.

rights.statement: Design, photographs, and content belong to the Horta Museum. Screenshot of an archived page captured for commentary.

references.title: Humaaans illustration library (Pablo Stanley)
references.lede: A free mix-and-match library of flat vector people by Pablo Stanley: interchangeable heads, tops, legs, and poses that anyone can assemble into scenes.
references.summary: Mix-and-match flat people with small heads and long legs. Free under CC0, and one of the main channels of the style.
references.made: 2018 (Commons gives 13 December 2018 for the uploaded parts)

evidence.note: Inspected 1280 px renderings of `Humaaans-standing-1.svg` and `Humaaans-sitting-1.svg` from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Humaaans_design_library) and stored the standing figure, flattened onto white.

styles.note: Clear fit in form: small head, long tapering limbs, flat fills, and no outlines. The stored figure has brown skin, not a non-natural color, which the library lets the user choose.

context: The Humaaans site states: “Free for commercial or personal use. CC0 Public Domain License.” It describes customizable hair, tops, pants, poses, and scene templates for success states, error states, onboarding, and landing pages. [Humaaans](https://www.humaaans.com/).

Wired (24 January 2021) quotes Pablo Stanley on his image banks of “flat, wacky SVGs” and his estimate that they were downloaded hundreds of thousands of times, and names such banks as a main cause of the style’s spread. [Wired](https://www.wired.com/story/corporate-memphis-design-tech/).

In August 2019 AIGA Eye on Design illustrated its article on the style with edited Humaaans figures, then licensed under CC BY 4.0. See [Katharina Brenner’s illustration](ref:brenner-big-tech-cartoons-illustration-2019).
observed: A standing woman in profile, turned to the right, with a long ponytail drawn as a wavy navy shape.
The head is a small, featureless oval; there are no eyes or mouth.
She wears a bright blue jacket, a pale grey top, and trousers in two tones of grey-teal, one tone per leg.
Hands are flat brown shapes with pointed fingers; shoes are dark navy blocks.
Every shape is a flat fill with no outline. Shading is one darker tone of the same color on the far sleeve and leg.
The seated figure uses the same system: a red jacket, blue trousers, and a pale grey ball as a seat.
interpretation: Humaaans turns the style into a kit. The parts join at fixed points, so any combination gives the same proportions, which is why the figures appear on so many unrelated products.
borrow: Use one darker tone of the same hue for the far arm and leg instead of shading.
Keep faces blank or nearly blank so that pose and color carry the expression.

images.alt: Flat vector woman in profile with a long wavy navy ponytail, a small featureless brown head, a bright blue jacket, grey-teal trousers, and navy shoes, on white.
images.caption: “Humaaans-standing-1” by Pablo Stanley, 2018. CC0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Humaaans-standing-1.svg), rendered at 1280 px and flattened onto white.

rights.statement: The Humaaans site states “CC0 Public Domain License”; the Commons file carries CC0. In 2019 AIGA credited the library under CC BY 4.0, so the license appears to have changed from CC BY to CC0. Credit: Pablo Stanley.

references.title: Hype4 Academy glassmorphism CSS generator
references.lede: The web tool from the style’s namer that turns blur and transparency sliders into a copyable glass-card CSS rule.
references.summary: Michał Malewicz’s Hype4 glassmorphism generator with its default glass-card CSS.

evidence.note: Read the page’s server-rendered HTML on 2026-09-28 and inspected its hero image glassmorphismHero.png (1602 × 870) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The interactive generator was not operated. The page is now branded SquarePlanet.

styles.note: Documents the style as code, from the person who named it. The CSS values it outputs are a direct recipe for the specimen.

context: The page calls itself “The original generator for Glassmorphism” and says it was “made by the person who created the glassmorphism name”. It credits Malewicz with coining the term and dates the [initial article](ref:malewicz-glassmorphism-article-2020) to November 2020. [Hype4 Academy](https://hype4.academy/tools/glassmorphism-generator).

Its default output (blur 20, refraction 0.15, depth 10) is `background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15)`, `backdrop-filter: blur(20px)`, `border-radius: 20px`, `border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.3)`, and a `0 8px 32px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` shadow with inset white highlights, plus 1 px gradient lines on the top and left edges.
It depends on the CSS [backdrop-filter](ref:css-backdrop-filter-property) property.
observed: Hero image: a dark ‘Settings’ panel with Blur value, Refraction, and Depth sliders sits over a black 3D keyboard with one red key.
The part of the keyboard behind the panel is blurred and dimmed; the part outside it is sharp.
The panel has large rounded corners and a thin, lighter edge. Slider tracks are white with lime-green fills and white round thumbs.
interpretation: The generator’s defaults (15 % white fill, 20 px blur, 20 px radius, 1 px white border at 30 %) sit inside the ranges in the style’s rules. The newer ‘refraction’ control and edge highlights move the output toward Liquid Glass.
borrow: Start a glass card from: 15 % white fill, 20 px backdrop blur, 20 px radius, 1 px border at 30 % white, and a 32 px soft shadow at 10 % black.

rights.statement: Hype4 Academy / SquarePlanet; copyrighted. Link and quotation only.

references.title: iBooks on the iPad, 2010
references.lede: Apple’s e-book app for the first iPad: a wooden bookshelf for the library and a bound book with stacked page edges for reading.
references.summary: A bookshelf library and a two-page book spread with page edges and a curling page turn. Apple, 2010.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1280 px copy of [File:1st-Gen-iPad-WiFi-iBooks.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1st-Gen-iPad-WiFi-iBooks.jpg) (Evan-Amos, 2011, public-domain photograph of a first-generation iPad showing the iBooks reading view). The photo shows the reading view only. The bookshelf view is documented, not observed. Not stored.

styles.note: The reading view imitates a bound book, and the library imitates a wooden bookshelf: a clear object metaphor from the core years of the style.

context: Apple announced iBooks with the iPad on 27 January 2010. In Book layout, “pages are turned by tapping or dragging the page, animated to imitate the appearance of a paper book.” [Wikipedia: Apple Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Books).
NN/g: “Ereaders, like iBooks and Kindle, were designed to look like physical bookshelves.” [NN/g: Skeuomorphism](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/skeuomorphism/).

On the day of the announcement, TechCrunch wrote that “the bookshelf view in iBooks is nearly identical to the main bookshelf view used in Delicious Library”; Wil Shipley noted that Mike Matas, a former Delicious Monster designer, worked on the iPad interface. [TechCrunch, MG Siegler, 27 January 2010](https://techcrunch.com/2010/01/27/think-ibooks-looks-familiar-youre-not-the-only-one/). See [Delicious Library](ref:delicious-library-2004).
observed: In landscape the screen shows two facing pages with a dark shadow in the gutter.
Thin stacked page edges run down the outer sides of both pages, as on a thick closed book block.
The pages are off-white; text is set in a serif face, justified and hyphenated.
A small bar at the top holds “Library” and table-of-contents buttons with a light bevel.
interpretation: The reading view carries non-functional detail from the physical book (page edges, gutter shadow) while the controls stay small and plain. It is a quieter case than the leather and felt apps.
borrow: Suggest a long document with stacked edge lines at the sides instead of a scroll bar.
Put a soft vertical shadow in the gutter of a two-column reading layout.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: iCal in Mac OS X Lion, 2011
references.lede: Apple’s desktop calendar in Lion, with a stitched tan leather top bar and torn paper edges, the most cited example of the style’s excess.
references.summary: Stitched leather and torn desk-calendar pages on the Mac. Apple, 2011.

source.label: Apple, “Mac OS X Lion: New features” (archived July 2011)

references.made: 2011 (Mac OS X Lion); renamed Calendar in OS X Mountain Lion (2012); leather removed in OS X Mavericks (2013)

evidence.note: Apple’s archived Lion features page describes the “streamlined new look” of iCal; its screenshot of the app is only 323 × 199 px, too small to describe. The leather design is documented by Fast Company (2012) and by the style record’s sources.

styles.note: The emblematic example of the style: a desk calendar with leather binding, stitching, and torn pages, all without function.

context: Apple’s Lion page said iCal “features a streamlined new look that gives you more room to browse and edit your events.” [Apple, archived July 2011](https://web.archive.org/web/20110727225723/http://www.apple.com/macosx/whats-new/features.html).

A former senior Apple UI designer told Fast Company that “iCal’s leather-stitching was literally based on a texture in his Gulfstream jet,” meaning Steve Jobs’s jet. [Fast Company, Austin Carr, “Will Apple’s Tacky Software-Design Philosophy Cause A Revolt?” (2012)](https://www.fastcompany.com/1670760/will-apples-tacky-software-design-philosophy-cause-a-revolt).

Wikipedia’s lead on skeuomorphs uses “a software calendar that imitates the appearance of binding on a paper desk calendar” as its virtual example, citing Wired (2012). [Wikipedia: Skeuomorph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeuomorph).
interpretation: The leather is decoration from a luxury interior, not from a calendar. That is why critics used it as the clearest sign of the style going too far.
next: Find an openly licensed or large archived screenshot of Lion iCal and inspect it.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Illustration for “Don’t Worry, These Gangly-armed Cartoons…” (Katharina Brenner)
references.lede: The hero image of AIGA Eye on Design’s 2019 article on the style: three flat figures with blue, violet, and orange skin reaching toward a browser window with a thumbs-down.
references.summary: Three gangly, flat figures with non-natural skin on mint green, around a thumbs-down browser window. Editorial illustration, 2019.

creator.name: Katharina Brenner, with figures by Pablo Stanley (Humaaans)

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 × 750 original (`Alegria_Hero-1.jpg`) from the AIGA article and stored it. The same image is on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corporate_Memphis_(2019).png), where the Wikipedia article uses it.

styles.note: Clear fit: long bendy limbs, small blank heads, violet, blue, and orange skin, flat fills with no outline, and a pale background. It is also the image that Wikipedia uses for the style.

context: The AIGA caption reads: “Image by Katharina Brenner. Illustrations are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Illustrations by Pablo Stanley, via humaaans design library. All illustrations have been edited.” [AIGA Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/dont-worry-these-gangley-armed-cartoons-are-here-to-protect-you-from-big-tech/).
The image is built from [Humaaans](ref:humaaans-illustration-library-2018) figures; the article itself is about Facebook’s [Alegria](ref:facebook-alegria-illustration-system-2017) and its imitators.
observed: The background is a flat mint green. A white browser window with a grey frame and three dots stands in the centre and shows a large navy thumbs-down.
A figure with violet skin walks in from the left in a yellow sweater and pale teal trousers, with long arms that end in small pointed hands.
A figure with orange skin in a blue top lunges toward the window with both arms raised; a single white tear marks the face.
A figure with pale blue skin and a long navy ponytail stands on the right in an orange jacket and pink trousers, one arm stretched out.
All shapes are flat fills without outlines; each garment has one darker tone for the far side.
interpretation: The image uses the style to comment on it: the cheerful figures react to a thumbs-down, the reverse of Alegria’s thumbs-up.
borrow: Put one interface object, such as a browser window, in the centre and let the figures react to it from both sides.
Use a single pale background color instead of white to hold several bright skin and clothing colors together.

images.alt: Flat illustration on mint green: three long-limbed figures with violet, orange, and pale blue skin walk and reach toward a white browser window that shows a large navy thumbs-down.
images.caption: Illustration by Katharina Brenner with Humaaans figures by Pablo Stanley, for [AIGA Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/dont-worry-these-gangley-armed-cartoons-are-here-to-protect-you-from-big-tech/), 2019. CC BY 4.0.

rights.statement: The AIGA caption states a CC BY 4.0 license for the illustrations; the Commons copy carries the same license. Credit: Katharina Brenner; figures by Pablo Stanley (Humaaans).

references.title: iMac G3 in Bondi Blue
references.lede: Apple’s first iMac put a computer in a rounded shell of translucent blue and frosted white plastic, and made see-through candy colors a mass-market look.
references.summary: Rounded translucent Bondi-blue and frosted-white casing, round puck mouse. Apple, designed by Jonathan Ive’s team, 1998.

creator.name: Apple, industrial design team led by Jonathan Ive

references.made: 1998 (announced 6 May 1998, on sale 15 August 1998 per Wikipedia; V&A gives 1998 and 1998–1999)

evidence.note: Inspected the two V&A photographs of object W.29:1 to 4-2008 (images 2009BX8549 and 2009BX8548, 1600 × 1200 each) in scratchpad copies. Not stored.

styles.note: The canonical Y2K object: translucent candy plastic, a blobby rounded shell, and a matching round mouse. Wikipedia’s Y2K article uses it as its blobject example.

context: The V&A says the iMac G3 “revolutionised the aesthetics of computers at the end of the 1990s and influenced the shapes and colours of all types of domestic electrical products”, because Ive housed it “in translucent coloured polycarbonate rather than giving it a standard grey box”. The museum’s copy is the first model, available only in Bondi Blue with a tray disk drive. [V&A W.29-2008](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O158296/imac-g3-personal-computer-ive-jonathan/).

Wikipedia gives the announcement as 6 May 1998 and first shipments as 15 August 1998. In January 1999 Apple replaced Bondi Blue with five colors: blueberry, strawberry, tangerine, grape, and lime. [Wikipedia: iMac G3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMac_G3).
Wikipedia’s Y2K aesthetic article calls the iMac G3 an example of the blobject design common in the aesthetic. [Wikipedia: Y2K aesthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_aesthetic).
observed: Side view: the back of the case is a large teardrop curve of translucent teal-blue plastic. Vent grilles, brackets, and cables show through it.
The lower part of the case and the front bezel are frosted, milky white plastic with fine vertical ribs.
Front view: a gray screen sits in a rounded white bezel with a small serif “iMac” name under it. Round translucent-blue speaker grilles flank a slot panel.
The keyboard has black keys in a frosted, blue-edged frame. The mouse is a round puck with a translucent blue rim and a clear top.
interpretation: The object sets the Y2K material grammar: saturated color that is also see-through, frosted white as the neutral, and technology shown as a pleasure instead of hidden in a gray box.
Its shapes are soft and continuous. Even the mouse is a disc. This is the blobject side of the style, without chrome.
borrow: Pair one saturated translucent color with a frosted white. Let a darker inner structure show through the colored layer.
Use fine parallel ribs on a pale surface to suggest molded plastic.
Make small controls round and give them the same translucent color as the main panel.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A photographs are © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The product design belongs to Apple. Public-domain photographs of the iMac exist on Wikimedia Commons, but the lead curator must decide whether an industrial product of 1998 counts as not copyrightable before any image is stored.

references.title: Inbox by Gmail
references.lede: Google’s experimental email client, launched in 2014 as one of the first full Material Design apps: a blue app bar, white cards, and a red action button.
references.summary: Blue app bar, bundled mail on white cards over pale gray, and a round red plus button. Google, 2014.

source.label: Official Gmail Blog: “An inbox that works for you” (22 October 2014)

evidence.note: Opened the two images in Google’s announcement post on 28 September 2026: *inbox-nexus6-500.png* (500 × 884, the app on a Nexus 6) and *bigtopblog_fullres.gif* (1000 × 592, a close-up of a Purchases bundle). Not stored.

styles.note: A clear example: blue primary app bar, white cards and list rows on pale gray, and a red floating action button in the lower right.

context: Sundar Pichai announced Inbox on the Official Gmail Blog on 22 October 2014 as “a completely different type of inbox”. [Gmail Blog](https://gmail.googleblog.com/2014/10/an-inbox-that-works-for-you.html).

Wikipedia: Inbox was announced on an invitation-only basis on 22 October 2014, released to the public on 28 May 2015, and shut down on 2 April 2019. [Wikipedia: Inbox by Gmail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inbox_by_Gmail).
observed: A bright blue app bar holds a hamburger menu, the white title “Inbox”, a pin toggle, and a search glyph. The status bar above it is a darker blue.

Messages sit in white rows on a pale gray ground, with gray section labels “Today” and “Yesterday”. A Purchases bundle is a white card with a soft shadow and square corners, holding flat gray inner tiles with product photos.
Bundle labels are colored words: brown “Purchases”, cyan “Promos”, each with a count on a light tint of the same color.
A round red action button with a white plus floats over the lower right corner of the list with a soft shadow.
interpretation: Inbox uses the accent rule in its textbook form: a blue primary and a red action button, with category colors used only for small labels.
borrow: Give each content category one hue and use it only for its label and a light tint behind the count.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The product and images belong to Google.

references.title: Invisible Creature website
references.lede: The studio’s home slider shows a Lakeshore Learning project: flat cut-shape stickers of vehicles, animals, and children on plywood, under a huge condensed title.
references.summary: Flat cut-paper stickers in teal, orange, green, yellow, and purple on wood, with a white ultra-condensed title.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The hero is the first slide of a rotating slider.

styles.note: Borderline: flat cut-shape figures, textured print fills, and several hues come from the mid-century children’s-book branch, but purple and bright green push the palette past the style’s warm, muted range, and a dark scrim covers the image.

observed: Die-cut sticker shapes cover a plywood background: a submarine in a teal pond with fish, a helicopter, a turtle, a truck, a child playing a xylophone on wheels, a pencil, and a rocket.
Each sticker is built from flat shapes in teal, orange, green, yellow, purple, and pink, with a white or colored border and speckled, screen-print-like texture in some fills.
Children are drawn as simple profiles with round heads and dot eyes.
A dark translucent scrim covers the whole image to make the title readable.
“LAKESHORE LEARNING” is set in very large white ultra-condensed capitals over the lower third, with a black “VIEW PROJECT” button and two yellow round arrow buttons.
interpretation: The illustration method matches the style’s children’s-book side: flat planes, rough print texture, and simple figures. The ultra-condensed display type and the purple are contemporary.
Measured: round-share 0.94 (the round buttons) and heading weight 700 pass; the CSS sees one hue and a high accent chroma from the yellow buttons.
borrow: Give flat illustrations a speckled print texture inside the shapes, not across the page.
Cut each figure out with a thin light border, like a sticker or cut paper.

references.title: iOS 7 interface
references.lede: Apple’s 2013 redesign that dropped the textures of earlier iOS for flatter icons and thinner type.
references.summary: Flatter icons, slimmer fonts, and redesigned apps in Apple’s mobile system. Jony Ive’s team, 2013.

creator.name: Apple (design team led by Jony Ive)

evidence.note: Wikipedia article read on 2026-09-28. The home screen is visible only small and at an angle in the capture of [Apple’s iOS 7 page](ref:apple-ios-7-website-2013), so the record is not marked observed.

styles.note: The turn of the most skeuomorphic mobile system to flat design; partial fit, because the icons keep soft gradients and the system uses translucent blurred panels.

context: iOS 7 was announced on 10 June 2013 and released on 18 September 2013. It “introduced a completely redesigned user interface, a design credited to a team led by Apple’s former senior vice president of design, Jony Ive” ([Wikipedia: iOS 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS_7)).
Wikipedia quotes the redesign as “sharper, flatter icons, slimmer fonts, a new slide-to-unlock function, and a new control panel that slides up from the bottom of the screen”.
Ive: “There is a profound and enduring beauty in simplicity, in clarity, in efficiency.”
Wikipedia’s article on [Letterpress](ref:letterpress-app-2012) states that Ive took inspiration from minimalist iOS apps, among them Letterpress, for the iOS 7 graphics.
interpretation: The style record lists Helvetica Neue as the iOS 7 face and treats iOS 7 as part of the flat turn. Its blurred panels also point toward [glassmorphism](style:glassmorphism).

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: iOS 7 interface
references.lede: Apple’s 2013 flat redesign, whose blurred Control Center and Notification Center panels Malewicz names as the start of background blur.
references.summary: The 2013 iPhone redesign that brought translucent, blurred layers to a mass-market interface.

creator.name: Apple (design team led by Jony Ive)

evidence.note: Relies on the Apple press release and on Malewicz’s text. The archived press release has no images, and the Wikipedia screenshots are non-free and below 800 px (237 × 420 and 365 × 274), so they were not used for observation.

styles.note: Precursor. Malewicz writes that background blur “was first widely introduced in 2013 with iOS 7”.

context: Apple’s press release: iOS 7 has “distinct, functional layers”, and “the use of translucency and motion makes even simple tasks more engaging”. It introduced Control Center and a Notification Center available from the Lock screen. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2013/06/10Apple-Unveils-iOS-7/).

Malewicz: background blur “was first widely introduced in 2013 with iOS 7”, and pulling down notifications showed icons that “fade out and blur under the new panel”. He adds that Apple later “greatly reduced the blurry-glass effect” on mobile. [Malewicz 2020](ref:malewicz-glassmorphism-article-2020).
Wikipedia credits the design to a team led by Jony Ive and describes flatter icons and new animations. [Wikipedia: iOS 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS_7).
interpretation: iOS 7 joined translucent blur to [flat design](style:flat-design). Glassmorphism keeps that pairing: flat content on a frosted layer.
next: Find an openly licensed or official high-resolution image of the iOS 7 Control Center and upgrade the evidence level.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Jefferson Airplane at the Fillmore Auditorium (BG-1)
references.lede: The first poster in Bill Graham’s Fillmore series, February 1966, before the psychedelic style formed: red calligraphy and a winged horse on flat yellow.
references.summary: Peter Bailey, 1966. Red bands and calligraphic lettering on full-bleed yellow, still legible and diagonal.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Jefferson airplane fillmore poster 1966.jpg

creator.name: Peter Bailey (per collector sources; Commons names Bill Graham)

references.made: 1966 (concerts 4–6 February); the printing shown is undated

evidence.note: Downloaded the Commons file (1091 × 1538 px, a photograph of one copy taken from an eBay listing) and inspected it. The copy carries the imprint “Creative Lithograph Co. 1” at lower left. Collector sources say the first printing read “Design Peter Bailey, East Wind Printers”, so this is probably a later printing.

styles.note: Partial fit, kept as the starting point: full-bleed saturated color and hand-drawn lettering, but the letters stay legible, the layout is diagonal, and there is no ornament or pattern. Compare Wilson’s [Otis Rush poster](ref:wes-wilson-otis-rush-grateful-dead-poster-1967) a year later.

context: Collectors call this poster BG-1, the first in the Bill Graham Fillmore series. Poster dealers attribute it to Peter Bailey and report that Graham had Bailey’s credit removed after the first copies; Wes Wilson designed BG-2 and most of the posters that followed. [Heritage Auctions](https://entertainment.ha.com/itm/music-memorabilia/posters/bg-1-jefferson-airplane-1966-fillmore-auditorium-concert-poster-signed-by-peter-bailey/a/41154-5225.s), [PosterCentral](https://blog.postercentral.com/2013/12/10/jefferson-airplane-1966-concert-poster-bg-1-very-first-printing/).

The Commons description says there are no copyright marks on the poster and names Bill Graham as author. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jefferson_airplane_fillmore_poster_1966.jpg).
The poster names the “Sights and Sounds of the Trips Festival”, the January 1966 event that preceded the Fillmore dances.
observed: The whole sheet is a flat golden yellow. All text and image are in one red ink.
THE JEFFERSON and AIRPLANE run in two broad red bands that climb diagonally from lower left to upper right. The letters are yellow, cut out of the bands, in a tall calligraphic hand with swashes.
A red winged horse with a rider, drawn over the frame of a biplane, crosses the bands at the center.
The concert details are in condensed sans-serif capitals, set at the same diagonal: BILL GRAHAM PRESENTS THREE DANCE CONCERTS at top left, FILLMORE AUDITORIUM and DONATIONS: $2 at lower right.
Nothing is centered and there is no border, frame, or background pattern.
interpretation: The poster has the style’s color habit, a single saturated ink over the whole sheet, but not its type or layout. It helps separate what the San Francisco posters added in 1966: lettering that fills shapes, symmetry, and ornament.
Measured with `tools/image-traits.py`, the scan has a chromatic share of 1.0 and 3 hues, which is closer to the style’s fingerprint than most of the later posters.
borrow: Cut display letters out of a solid colored band so the ground shows through them.
Use one strong ink on a saturated ground for a two-color scheme with no white.

images.alt: Yellow poster with two diagonal red bands carrying the words The Jefferson Airplane in yellow calligraphic letters, a red winged horse and biplane at the center, and concert details in red condensed type.
images.caption: A copy of BG-1 photographed for an eBay listing. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jefferson_airplane_fillmore_poster_1966.jpg), public domain (PD-US-no notice).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain under PD-US-no notice: a United States work published before 1978 without a copyright notice. I saw no notice on this copy. The first printing is not inspected; if it carried a notice, this tier needs review.

references.title: Jim Flora website
references.lede: The official Jim Flora site puts the illustrator’s small flat figures and a playful serif-script name on a pale butter-yellow header.
references.summary: Pink and black cut-shape children, a kite, and a dog on pale yellow, with a quirky display name and a charcoal menu bar.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: the header is a mid-century graphic composition, with flat two-color figures on warm paper and hand-drawn display lettering. The body below is a plain modern layout.

observed: The header ground is a flat pale butter yellow (#faeeb2 in the screenshot palette).

Small figures in flat pink and black play across it: a child on a scooter, a girl skipping rope, children tumbling, a boy flying a pink kite on a long line, and a pink dog. The figures are built from a few flat shapes with black details.
“Jim Flora” at upper left is a dark, high-contrast display face with curled terminals.
A full-width charcoal bar holds the menu in white geometric sans-serif capitals.
Below, on white, a black-and-white photograph of Flora at work sits next to two colorful thumbnails of his later work and body text in a humanist sans-serif.
interpretation: The header uses the style’s method at small scale: two flat printed colors, figures reduced to a few planes, and generous open paper around them.

Measured: the page’s CSS sees only one hue family and a heading weight of 400, and the round shapes are drawn in images. The screenshot palette finds two hue families. See the style synthesis for why the computed-style metrics miss this.
borrow: Scatter a few small flat figures across a warm pale header and leave most of it empty.
Limit the illustration to two printed colors, such as pink and black, on yellow paper.

images.alt: Jim Flora home page: a pale yellow header with the name Jim Flora in a dark curly display face and small pink and black figures of children, a kite, and a dog; a charcoal menu bar; below, a photograph of Flora drawing and thumbnails of his artwork.
images.caption: First viewport of [jimflora.com](https://www.jimflora.com/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design, artwork, and content belong to the site’s owners and artists. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Jimi Hendrix, John Mayall, Albert King (Flying Eyeball)
references.lede: Rick Griffin’s first Fillmore poster, February 1968: a winged eyeball in a ring of flames, under gothic, dripping lettering on a red ground.
references.summary: Rick Griffin, 1968. A winged eyeball in a flaming blue circle, with gold-outlined black lettering on red.

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object S.169-2021 (IIIF, 1067 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The image is not stored.

styles.note: A clear example: saturated red over the whole sheet against a blue central circle, a symmetrical medallion composition, and ornate lettering that is hard to read at a glance.

context: The V&A describes a “winged eyeball with three tentacles, one gripping a fanged skull, against a sky blue background within a central circle edged with flames”, with the rest of the poster red and “elaborate black and gold lettering”. It advertised the Jimi Hendrix Experience, John Mayall and the Bluesbreakers, and Albert King. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1376448/).

Griffin (1944–1991) began designing for Bill Graham in February 1968; the Flying Eyeball was the first of these posters and became one of his best-known works. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Griffin).
observed: The whole ground is a saturated red. BILL GRAHAM PRESENTS IN SAN FRANCISCO sits in small black capitals at the top.
JIMI HENDRIX and JOHN MAYALL are drawn in heavy black letters with gold outlines and inner gold details, in a spiky, gothic manner. EXPERIENCE and AND THE BLUESBREAKERS are thinner, looser lines.
A large circle of sky blue at the center is ringed by red, orange, and yellow flames that break its edge.
A white eyeball with a blue iris and red veins has white wings. Green tentacles curl around it; one holds a skull at left.
ALBERT KING and a large numeral 4 sit below the circle. The dates and venues are split left and right of the 4 in the same hand lettering.
interpretation: Red and blue are not strict complements, but the saturated red field against the blue circle has the same pull. The composition is a single medallion on the vertical axis, as the rubric describes.
The gold outline on black letters is the echo-outline device done with a metallic ink.
borrow: Put one saturated circle of a cool color inside a warm full-bleed ground.
Outline heavy display letters in a second, lighter color to separate them from a busy ground.
Split secondary information into mirrored columns around a central numeral or symbol.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. Rick Griffin died in 1991.

references.title: Jotform website
references.lede: Jotform’s home page: two flat figures at laptops sit inside pastel blob shapes on either side of a sign-up card.
references.summary: Flat figures in blue and yellow blobs around a centred sign-up card, with a heavy navy heading. Live site.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. No cookie box covers the page. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: flat figures with laptops sit in pastel blobs on a white page, but their proportions are ordinary and their skin is natural, so the gangly, non-natural figure is missing. A late, softened form of the style on a live site.

observed: A small orange overline, “EASIEST ONLINE FORM BUILDER”, sits above the heavy navy heading “Powerful forms get it done.”
In the centre, a white card with a thin border holds three full-width buttons: blue for Google, black for Apple, and orange for email.
On the left, a woman in a green top with a pink headset types on a laptop inside a bright blue blob; an orange cat sleeps on top of the blob.
On the right, a woman with brown skin and a navy bob works at a grey laptop in front of a yellow blob, with a green check mark badge.
Figures have faces with eyes and mouths and roughly natural proportions; fills are flat with small darker shadow shapes.
interpretation: The page keeps the style’s scene grammar (a figure, a device, a pastel blob, white space) after the gangly proportions went out of fashion. The measurement finds a median radius of 7 px and shadows on 9% of boxes.
borrow: Set each spot figure inside one saturated blob shape, and let one small object (a cat, a check mark) break the blob’s outline.

images.alt: Jotform home page: a heavy navy heading above a sign-up card with Google, Apple, and email buttons, flanked by two flat figures working at laptops inside blue and yellow blob shapes.
images.caption: First viewport of [Jotform](https://www.jotform.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: JotForm website, 2018
references.lede: JotForm’s 2018 home page: two flat figures work at desks on a hero split diagonally into flat green and blue fields.
references.summary: Flat figures at desks with a cat, plants, and a form card on a diagonal green and blue split. 2018.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. No cookie box covers the page. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: a flat vector office scene with oversized objects and no outlines, but the figures have ordinary proportions and natural skin, so the gangly figure is missing. Compare the [live site](ref:jotform-website).

references.notice: The live JotForm site has changed since this 2018 capture.
observed: The hero is split diagonally into a flat green left side and a flat blue right side.
A light-weight white heading reads “Easy-to-use online form builder for every business.”, with a square white “SIGN UP” button with orange text.
At the bottom left, a woman with yellow hair and a headset works at a monitor; an orange cat sleeps on top of it, and a small Statue of Liberty stands behind.
At the bottom right, a red-haired woman sits at a laptop next to a large “EVENT FORM” card and a San Francisco poster.
Everything is drawn in flat fills without outlines or texture; a floor lamp, plants, and blue window panes are simple geometric shapes.
interpretation: The page shows the flat office-scene genre that ran alongside Corporate Memphis. It shares the flat fills and props but not the distorted figure.
borrow: Split a hero into two flat color fields and give each side its own figure, to show two roles (the form maker and the form filler).

images.alt: JotForm home page, 2018: a hero split into flat green and blue fields, with a white heading and sign-up button, above two flat figures working at desks with a sleeping cat, plants, and an event form card.
images.caption: First viewport of [JotForm](https://web.archive.org/web/20180901004135/https://www.jotform.com/).
