references.title: KABOOM! UI website
references.lede: The demo site of a comic-book CSS framework: speech balloons, a sound-effect logotype, a dot-patterned background, and outlined buttons with hard shadows.
references.summary: Yellow hero with speech balloons and an outlined KABOOM! logotype, over a pale dot field and outlined panels with offset shadows.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Borderline: speech balloons, a sound-effect logotype, and a CSS dot field are Pop devices, but the dots are pale and small, the outlines are 2 px, and most blocks carry hard offset shadows.
Its structure is neo-brutalist: every box has a black border, hard unblurred shadows cover 43% of boxes, and radii are zero. It passes every neo-brutalism fingerprint metric.

context: The author describes KABOOM! UI as a CSS framework inspired by 1962 comic books, with buttons, cards, badges, speech bubbles, halftone backgrounds, ink borders, and offset shadows. [DEV Community](https://dev.to/gorupa/i-was-tired-of-boring-uis-so-i-built-a-css-framework-straight-out-of-a-1962-comic-book-mc1).
observed: The hero is flat pale yellow. A white oval speech balloon with a black outline and a tail reads “Holy CSS, Batman!”.
The logotype “KABOOM! UI” is set in a condensed, slanted comic face in black with a white inline and a black drop.
Two buttons read “GET THE KIT” (yellow) and “VIEW COMPONENTS” (steel blue); both have black outlines and hard black offset shadows.
Below the hero, the page background is a pale gray dot pattern on white.
A white panel with a steel-blue border carries a tilted “LIVE PREVIEW” label, a heading in comic capitals, and a second speech balloon with red text.
interpretation: The CSS dot field covers 39% of the page (`color.patternShare` 0.39), which passes the Pop fingerprint, but the extractor records `surface.patternShare` 0, a 2 px median border, and shadows on 43% of boxes.
The site shows how easily web Pop slides into neo-brutalism: once every block has an offset shadow, the Pop devices become decoration on a neo-brutalist frame.
borrow: Use an oval speech balloon with a tail as a tagline above the logotype.
Put the dot pattern behind content panels, and keep text on solid white.

images.alt: KABOOM! UI home page: a pale yellow hero with a speech balloon reading Holy CSS, Batman!, a slanted black KABOOM! UI logotype, two outlined buttons with hard shadows, and below it a white panel on a dotted background with another speech balloon.
images.caption: First viewport of [kaboom-ui-kit.pages.dev](https://kaboom-ui-kit.pages.dev/), captured 28 September 2026.

references.title: KDE Plasma 6 desktop
references.lede: A free-software desktop whose launcher and panel are blurred, translucent glass over a pink and blue wallpaper.
references.summary: Blurred translucent launcher and panel over a colorful wallpaper. KDE Plasma 6.4, 2025.
references.made: Plasma 6 released February 2024; screenshot of Plasma 6.4.5, 2025-10-20

evidence.note: Inspected the GPL-licensed screenshot [File:KDE Plasma 6.4.5 Light.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:KDE_Plasma_6.4.5_Light.png) (1920 × 1080, Breeze Light theme, dated 2025-10-20) and stored a 1600 px copy.

styles.note: Partial fit. Only the launcher and the panel are glass; the application windows are opaque and grey.

context: The Commons record describes the file as a screenshot of KDE Plasma 6.4.5 in the Breeze Light theme. It credits the software to KDE Plasma, the wallpaper to Krystian Zajdel, and the screenshot to User:Michio.kawaii, and gives the license as GPL. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:KDE_Plasma_6.4.5_Light.png).
The same desktop line appears earlier in the catalogue as [KDE Plasma 4](ref:kde-plasma-4-desktop), whose glossy widgets belong to [Frutiger Aero](style:frutiger-aero).
observed: The wallpaper is a soft, out-of-focus scene of blue ribbon-like coils on a pink-to-red ground.
The application launcher at the lower left is a large panel with rounded top corners. The pink wallpaper shows through it as a smooth, blurred pastel wash.
The taskbar along the bottom is a translucent, pale strip; the wallpaper tint shows through it faintly.
The System Settings and Dolphin windows are opaque light grey with thin borders and a small radius.
Icons are flat and blue; the type is a neutral sans-serif.
interpretation: Plasma uses glass the way Fluent Acrylic recommends: on transient and shell surfaces, not on document windows. Measured chromatic share of the stored image is 0.37, most of it from the wallpaper.
borrow: Keep glass for the shell (launcher, panel) and leave working windows opaque.

images.alt: KDE Plasma desktop with a blurred translucent application launcher at lower left over a pink and blue wallpaper, and two opaque grey windows.
images.caption: KDE Plasma 6.4.5, Breeze Light, screenshot dated 2025-10-20. Software by KDE, wallpaper by Krystian Zajdel. GPL. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:KDE_Plasma_6.4.5_Light.png).

rights.statement: Screenshot licensed under the GNU General Public License per [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:KDE_Plasma_6.4.5_Light.png). The depicted software is free software. The same basis as [KDE Plasma 4](ref:kde-plasma-4-desktop).

references.title: Kunsthalle Basel Kunstkredit 76-77 poster
references.lede: Wolfgang Weingart’s black-and-white exhibition poster for the Basel state art credit: cut photographs, dot screens, heavy black bars, and blocks of grotesque type that overlap and step.
references.summary: Grey collage of halftone photographs, black L-shaped bars, and stepped grotesque headings. Wolfgang Weingart, Basel, 1977.

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object E.473-2009 (image 2010EB0013, 1200 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example by the style’s founder. The V&A calls this poster an example of Weingart’s “new wave” or “swiss punk” style.

context: The V&A holds the poster as E.473-2009: lithograph, 128 × 90.5 cm, designed and printed in Switzerland in 1977. It is marked “Printed Design Weingart” and “Druck: Wassermann AG/Basel”, with the designer’s pencil signature. [V&A E.473-2009](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1155283/).

The V&A says Weingart is “credited with being the father of the ‘new wave’ or ‘swiss punk’” and describes the poster as “a collage effect of text, geometric forms and photographic images of architecture and objects”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1155283/).
observed: The poster uses only black, white, and greys. Halftone photographs of a machine part, crumpled paper, a draped figure, and the Kunsthalle facade are cut into rectangles that overlap.
“KUNSTHALLE” is set in small heavy black capitals next to a much larger “BASEL” in pale grey, which a black bar cuts across.
“KUNSTKREDIT” is very large and white on a grey band. The lines below change from grey to black to white.
Heavy black bars make an L-shaped frame at the top left, and parallel diagonal black bars fill the lower left corner.
Opening hours sit in white strips on black bars at the left. “Eintritt frei” and the tour times run vertically at the right beside a black arrow.
A coarse dot screen covers the machine photograph. A thin perspective grid and a small black cross lie over the figure.
“Ausstellung / 7. bis 30. Mai 1977” is white bold type on black blocks that step down.
The display lines are tightly spaced, not letterspaced.
interpretation: This is the style’s layer-and-screen side. Disorder comes from cut blocks, changes of value, and overlap, not from wide letterspacing. A fingerprint that needs wide heading tracking would miss works like this one.
The information stays readable because each block of text keeps a solid ground, even when the blocks themselves overlap.
borrow: Put short labels in white on black bars that come in from the page edge.
Let one large word be cut by a solid bar, and keep its partner word small and heavy.
Step a date line down across two or three black blocks.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Weingart died in 2021, so the design is in copyright.

references.title: Kunsthaus Graz
references.lede: Peter Cook and Colin Fournier’s “Friendly Alien”: an art museum in a blue acrylic blob with nozzle-shaped skylights.
references.summary: A dark-blue acrylic blob with a grid of light points and nozzle skylights, among red tiled roofs. Peter Cook and Colin Fournier, Graz, 2003.

creator.name: Peter Cook and Colin Fournier (spacelab); BIX media facade by realities:united

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons photograph [Graz Kunsthaus vom Schlossberg 20061126.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Graz_Kunsthaus_vom_Schlossberg_20061126.jpg) by Marion Schneider and Christoph Aistleitner (26 November 2006, CC BY-SA 2.5), viewed at 1280 × 853 in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: blob architecture at the end of the period, with a glossy blue translucent skin and a pixel light facade. It is architecture, so type and interface traits do not apply.

context: Wikipedia: the museum by Colin Fournier and Peter Cook opened in 2003, the year Graz was European Capital of Culture. Its skin is made of “iridescent blue acrylic panels”, and the BIX media facade by realities:united uses 930 individually dimmable fluorescent lamps. The building is nicknamed the “Friendly Alien” and is an example of blob architecture. [Wikipedia: Kunsthaus Graz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunsthaus_Graz).
observed: A long, bulging, dark-blue shell sits among steep red tiled roofs. It has no straight edges except at its base.
The glossy skin reflects the sky in lighter blue patches and is dotted with a regular grid of small light points.
About fifteen tube-shaped skylights with round, pale openings rise from the top and point in one direction.
A flat glass box with a thin roof line projects from one end, and a round porthole sits on the side of the shell.
interpretation: The Kunsthaus is the blobject scaled up to a building: one continuous glossy form in a single saturated color, with technical details (nozzles, pixel lights) added like device parts.
Its contrast with the old town is the point, in the same way the iMac contrasted with gray office computers.
borrow: Place one glossy, rounded shape in saturated blue against an old or plain background.
Overlay a regular grid of small light dots on a curved dark surface to suggest a screen.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is CC BY-SA 2.5, but the building is a recent architectural work by living architects. Austrian freedom of panorama would probably allow exterior photographs; the lead curator can decide whether to store one.

references.title: Ladybug screen print
references.lede: Charley Harper reduces a ladybug to a red half-disc with two black dots, set against a gray ground with stylized grass stems.
references.summary: A red half-disc ladybug with black dots, thin black legs, and tan grass on gray. Charley Harper, 1959.

evidence.note: Based on the Cincinnati Art Museum record. The museum serves only a 600 × 446 px image, below this catalogue’s 800 px threshold for observed evidence, so the observations below are provisional. Not stored.

styles.note: Harper reduces animals to flat geometric planes, a core trait of the illustrative side of the style.

context: The Cincinnati Art Museum catalogues Ladybug as a color screen print by Charley Harper (American, 1922–2007), dated 1959; composition 32.9 × 47 cm on a 38.7 × 52 cm sheet; Gift of the Estate of Charley Harper; accession number 2009.67. [Cincinnati Art Museum](https://collection.cincinnatiartmuseum.org/objects/26803/ladybug).
Harper’s serigraphs grew out of his bird paintings for *Ford Times* in the 1950s. [Charley Harper Art Studio](https://www.charleyharperartstudio.com/ford-times-retrospective).
observed: From the 600 px museum image: a large red shape, a half-disc with a straight edge, carries two black circles. A small black head with cream eyes sits at its straight edge.
Thin black legs and antennae are drawn as straight segments.
Tan grass stems and seed heads rise at the left beside a black vertical bar, on a flat gray ground with a few speckled dark patches.
interpretation: The insect is built from a circle cut in half and two dots: the reduction to a few flat planes that the style’s rubric names.
The saturated red is an exception to the muted palette, used as a single accent on gray.
borrow: Reduce a creature to one geometric shape plus two or three details.
Use one saturated accent on a quiet gray or cream ground.
next: Find an image of this print or another 1950s Harper serigraph at 800 px or more, and review the observations.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Charley Harper died in 2007; the work is in copyright.

references.title: Lato typeface
references.lede: The free humanist sans-serif of 2010 that became a default text face of the flat web.
references.summary: Semi-rounded humanist sans-serif in weights from hairline to black. Łukasz Dziedzic, 2010, Open Font License.

evidence.note: Inspected a 960 × 1152 render of the specimen [File:Lato-font.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lato-font.png) (by Gtk3, 2012, PD-textlogo) and stored it. Its use in the Flat UI kit was read in the kit’s `_variables.scss` and measured on its demo page.

styles.note: The base font of the [Flat UI kit](ref:flat-ui-free-kit-designmodo) and one of the free web faces that the style record names for the flat web; the web counterpart of Segoe in Metro.

context: “Lato is a humanist sans-serif typeface designed by Łukasz Dziedzic. It was released in 2010.” It was made for a Polish bank, shelved, and released the same year under the SIL Open Font License ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lato_(typeface))).
After it was added to Google Fonts it became, by August 2018, the third most served font there, after Roboto and Open Sans. It has nine weights from hairline to black, each with an italic.

Designmodo’s Flat UI kit sets `$font-family-base: "Lato", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif` and ships Lato Light, Regular, and Black ([_variables.scss](https://github.com/designmodo/Flat-UI/blob/master/app/styles/_variables.scss)). Lato set 93% of the text measured on the kit’s demo page.
observed: The specimen shows “Lato” large in a dark brown regular weight, italic and bold italic pairs (Aa Ee Nn), a very large pale gray “a”, and the word “Humanist” in teal.
A teal band below holds the lowercase alphabet in dark type and the figures 0–9 in white.
Letters have open apertures and slightly rounded stroke ends. The a is double-storey and the g is single-storey.
interpretation: Measured with `tools/image-traits.py`; see the measurement file. Lato gave web designers a free, warm sans-serif with light and black weights, which let them follow both the light-heading Metro look and the bold-heading look of the Flat UI kit.
borrow: For a flat interface on the web, pair a humanist sans-serif such as Lato in Light for large headings with Regular for text.

images.alt: Lato type specimen: the word Lato in large dark type, italic and bold italic letter pairs, a large gray letter a, the word Humanist in teal, and a teal band with the lowercase alphabet and the figures 0 to 9.
images.caption: Lato specimen by Gtk3, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lato-font.png) (PD-textlogo).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons tags the specimen {{PD-textlogo}}. The Lato fonts are released under the SIL Open Font License.

references.title: Lattice basket (Gitterwerk)
references.lede: Josef Hoffmann’s basket for the Wiener Werkstätte is cut from plated sheet metal perforated with a grid of squares, so the grid is the whole structure and the only ornament.
references.summary: Nickel-plated metal pierced with a square grid, with a stepped handle. Josef Hoffmann for the Wiener Werkstätte, c. 1905–1910.

evidence.note: Downloaded the Minneapolis Institute of Art photograph of object 98.276.65 (800 × 598 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. It is not stored. Other museums hold silver and painted versions of Hoffmann’s lattice baskets that differ in shape, for example the [Chazen Museum of Art, 2012.32.3.2a-b](https://chazen.wisc.edu/collection/24790/gitterwerk-basket/), which I did not inspect.

styles.note: A clear example of Hoffmann’s square lattice (Gitterwerk), the object type behind his nickname “Quadratl-Hoffmann”.

context: Mia records the basket as designed by Josef Hoffmann and made by the Wiener Werkstätte, c. 1905–10, in nickel-plated brass, 15.24 × 26.04 × 13.97 cm to the handles, marked “Wiener Werkstätte / JH”. [Mia 98.276.65](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/7097/basket-josef-hoffmann).

Mia’s label: Hoffmann designed various household objects in gitterwerk, or gridwork; the gridded sheets of base metal were the structure of the objects as well as their decoration, and they were made affordably and often nickel- or silver-plated. [Mia 98.276.65](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/7097/basket-josef-hoffmann).
Koloman Moser designed objects in the same technique; see [Moser’s lattice bud vase](ref:moser-gitterwerk-bud-vase).
observed: The basket is a low vessel of bright plated metal pierced with a regular grid of square holes.
In plan the wall steps in and out in shallow curves and corners, so the grid bends around a scalloped outline.
A flat lattice handle rises in straight segments and steps down at each side, like a stepped arch.
The top edge and the base are plain metal strips; every other surface is grid.
interpretation: The grid is used as a material, like a fabric, and the shape comes from folding it. This is the plainest statement of the square as the module of the style.
The shine of the plating is the one luxury. In a flat design the same effect can come from a gold or silver line.
borrow: Use a square-hole grid as a full panel texture with a plain border strip at the top and bottom.
Step a frame line in right-angled segments instead of curving it.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Mia gives the rights status as Unknown. Josef Hoffmann died in 1956, so his designs are protected in Austria until the end of 2026.

references.title: Lattice bud vase (Gitterwerk)
references.lede: Koloman Moser’s small vase for the Wiener Werkstätte is a box of white-painted sheet metal pierced with a regular grid of square holes, with two lattice loops as handles.
references.summary: White-painted metal pierced with a grid of small squares, around a glass liner. Koloman Moser for the Wiener Werkstätte, c. 1904–1906.

source.label: Minneapolis Institute of Art: Bud vase, 98.276.247a, b

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Minneapolis Institute of Art photograph of object 98.276.247a, b (372 × 800 px, the largest rendition the museum serves without an application). Other Gitterwerk vases by Moser differ in shape and colour.

styles.note: A clear example: the square lattice is both structure and ornament, in plain white, with no applied decoration.

context: Mia records the bud vase as designed by Koloman Moser and made by the Wiener Werkstätte, c. 1904–1906, in painted metal and glass, 21.59 × 7.62 × 5.08 cm, stamped “Wiener Werkstätte” on the bottom. [Mia 98.276.247a, b](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/6990/bud-vase-koloman-moser).

Mia describes Gitterwerk (gridwork) objects as made from sheets of base metal perforated with a grid, so that the grid is both the structure and the decoration. Hoffmann used the same technique; see [Hoffmann’s lattice basket](ref:hoffmann-gitterwerk-basket). [Mia 98.276.65](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/7097/basket-josef-hoffmann).
observed: The body is a tall, narrow rectangular box of white-painted metal, perforated with a regular grid of small square holes of equal size.
Two tall loops of the same perforated strip rise from the two long sides and end in round arches, like two handles side by side.
A clear glass liner shows through the holes.
The holes run in straight rows and columns up to the edges; the metal between them forms thin bars of equal width.
The paint is chipped in places along the edges and at the base.
interpretation: The object is the style’s square lattice with nothing else added: one module, repeated, gives the whole form. The only curve is the arch at the top of each loop.
White paint rather than silver keeps it flat and graphic, close to a printed grid.
borrow: Use a grid of small square cut-outs with bars of equal width as a border, a background band, or a frame.
Let a lattice band stand alone on a plain white ground, without shadows or gloss.

images.alt: Narrow white metal vase pierced all over with a grid of small square holes, with two tall arched loops of the same lattice rising from the top, photographed on a gray gradient.
images.caption: Koloman Moser for the Wiener Werkstätte, bud vase, c. 1904–1906. Minneapolis Institute of Art, 98.276.247a, b, The Modernism Collection, gift of Norwest Bank Minnesota. Image from [Mia](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/6990/bud-vase-koloman-moser), rights status Public Domain.

rights.statement: Mia gives the rights status of this object as Public Domain. Koloman Moser died in 1918, and the vase was made c. 1904–1906, so the design is in the public domain in Austria and in the United States.

references.title: Le Cercle Guimard website
references.lede: The Guimard society’s site sets its news column on a full-page repeat of a Guimard-style textile: pink swirls, blue whiplash scrolls, and yellow blossoms.
references.summary: White news panel on a pink, blue, and yellow whiplash pattern, with a green spiral logo and a rounded display serif.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. The request for lecercleguimard.fr redirected to the English home page.

styles.note: Clear: the page background is a whiplash textile repeat, the logo is a curling plant spiral, and the headings use a soft, flared display face. Only the slate-blue header is plain.

observed: A slate-blue header holds a pale green logo: a spiral seed or bud shape above “Le Cercle Guimard” in small capitals.
The navigation is set in a light serif in capitals, in white on the slate blue.
Below the header, the whole page background is a repeat pattern: dense pale pink swirls, large sky-blue whiplash scrolls, coral spiral bosses, and yellow flower clusters.
A white main panel holds the news list. News headlines are set in a rounded, calligraphic serif (Gabriela per the measurement) in slate blue.
The “News” heading is flanked by two small drawn plant sprigs that curl outward.
A small side panel has an orange-brown title bar reading “Social networks”. News thumbnails have thin gray frames.
interpretation: The site uses the style the way a Guimard interior would: pattern on the ground, a calm reserved panel for content. The measurement cannot see the pattern because it is a background image (`patternShare` 0, `imageShare` 0.57).

Measured: square panels (radius median 0), thin 1 px borders on 54% of boxes, faint shadows on 11%, and one measured colour family plus the pattern colours in pixels. The fingerprint’s radius and pattern metrics fail for reasons the rubric does not require.
borrow: Put the ornament on the page ground as one repeated textile, and keep content in a plain, light, outlined panel on top.
Flank a section heading with two small drawn sprigs instead of a rule.

images.alt: Le Cercle Guimard home page: a slate-blue header with a green spiral logo and serif navigation, above a white news panel on a pink, blue, and yellow whiplash textile pattern.
images.caption: First viewport of [lecercleguimard.fr/en](https://www.lecercleguimard.fr/en/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Leather notepad illustration, 2013
references.lede: A Photoshop drawing of a stitched leather notepad with ruled paper and a pen, made to illustrate skeuomorphism.
references.summary: Stitched brown leather, ruled paper, a chrome pen, and gold script. Openly licensed, 2013.

evidence.note: Inspected the full 687 × 1108 px original from Wikimedia Commons. It is an amateur demonstration, not a shipped interface.

styles.note: Shows the full vocabulary of the style in one image: leather grain, stitching, ruled paper, a photoreal pen, and embossed gold type. It is a demonstration, not a historical product.

context: The Commons description: “This is a leather notepad created in photoshop. It includes a pen, paper, and gold embroidery. This is a classic example of skeuomorphism: making a simulation of a real life object.” [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Leather_Notepad.png).
observed: A brown leather cover with a fine grain and a lighter dashed stitch line inset from the edges and along a pocket seam.
A sheet of white paper with pale blue horizontal rules, a red margin rule on each side, and punched holes along the left edge.
A silver and dark gray pen with strong highlights lies over the paper and casts a shadow.
The word “Notes” in gold italic script with a dark drop shadow sits on the leather pocket.
interpretation: The image repeats the iOS and Lion notepad vocabulary (see [Notes](ref:ios-notes-legal-pad)) without any interface controls, so its measurements show material color and texture alone.
borrow: Mark a panel edge with a dashed stitch line 6 to 10 px inside the border, in a lighter tone of the leather.
Use a red margin rule and pale blue rules for a note surface.

images.alt: A brown stitched leather notepad holding a sheet of ruled white paper, with a silver pen clipped at the top left and the word Notes in gold script on the lower pocket.
images.caption: “Leather Notepad” by TTerlizz, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Leather_Notepad.png), CC BY-SA 3.0.

rights.statement: Own work by TTerlizz, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0 on Wikimedia Commons. The depicted work is the uploader’s own drawing under the same license, not a public-domain work; this is a borderline use of tier A for review.

references.title: Lef journal, issue 4
references.lede: Alexander Rodchenko’s cover for the journal of the Left Front of the Arts splits its huge block-letter title into red and black halves.
references.summary: Giant square block capitals ЛЕФ, red above and black below, with a stepped poem, a red 4, and a black bar. Rodchenko, 1924.
references.made: 1923–1924 (Art Institute of Chicago, for the set of seven issues)

evidence.note: Viewed the Art Institute of Chicago image of the cover of issue 4 from its complete set, 2009.485 (843 × 1194 px), in a scratch folder. No image is stored. The issue number is read from the cover; the year of issue 4 (1924) is not stated on the museum record.

styles.note: A canonical constructivist journal cover: red and black on paper, giant block capitals, a heavy black bar, and stepped text.

context: The Art Institute of Chicago holds a complete set of the seven issues of *Lef*, 1923–24, with “2-color zincograph wrappers designed by Aleksandr Rodchenko” and contributions by Mayakovsky, Pasternak, Kruchenykh, Khlebnikov, Babel, Osip Brik, Tretyakov, and others. [Art Institute of Chicago](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/199233).
The same record lists illustrations by Rodchenko, Liubov Popova, Klutsis, Varvara Stepanova, and Anton Lavinskii. [Art Institute of Chicago](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/199233).
observed: The lower half of the cover carries “ЛЕФ” in giant square block capitals. The top half of each letter is red and the bottom half is black, split on one horizontal line.
A thick vertical black bar runs down the left side of the upper half.
A poem in heavy black sans-serif lowercase steps down and to the right in short lines. The words “Лефа” and “вперед” are picked out in red.
“ДАЛЬШЕ!” is set in small red spaced capitals at the top left. A large red “4” sits at the top right.
The paper is a warm, slightly flecked tan. Red and black are the only inks.
interpretation: The cover has no diagonal. Its movement comes from the stepped poem and the split between red and black, which shows that the style’s energy can come from scale and color alone.
The block letters are built from rectangles, like the letters Lissitzky assembled from type material in [Dlia golosa](ref:lissitzky-dlia-golosa-1923), published the same year.
borrow: Set a short masthead in giant square capitals and split it horizontally into red and black.
Highlight the key words of a paragraph in red instead of bold or italic.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Rodchenko died on 3 December 1956. Under Article 1281 of the Russian Civil Code his works stay protected in Russia until at least the end of 2026, and until the end of 2030 if he counts as having worked during the Great Patriotic War (life + 70 + 4 years). The museum marks the object as not in the public domain.

references.title: Lengiz “Books” poster
references.lede: Alexander Rodchenko’s advertisement for the Leningrad State Publishing House, with Lilya Brik calling out the slogan, is the most copied image of Soviet constructivism.
references.summary: A photographed Lilya Brik shouts “Books in all branches of knowledge” through a cupped hand. Alexander Rodchenko, 1924 (some sources: 1925).
references.made: 1924 (Wikipedia); 1925 in some dealer and reproduction listings

evidence.note: Based on text sources only. No museum record with an image of a printed copy was found: MoMA refuses automated access, and the Art Institute of Chicago and the V&A do not list the poster. Search results describe a photomontage and gouache design in a private collection, which may differ from any printed version.

styles.note: The best-known constructivist advertisement: a cut-out photograph joined with geometric type, used here to promote reading.

references.notice: No image of an identified copy was inspected. Treat the visual description as unverified until a museum record is checked.
context: Wikipedia calls it “likely his most famous poster, an advertisement for the Lengiz Publishing House sometimes titled ‘Books’”, made in 1924, with the slogan “книги по всем отраслям знания” (books in all branches of knowledge). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Rodchenko).

The woman in the photograph is Lilya Brik. Franz Ferdinand based the cover of their 2005 album *You Could Have It So Much Better* on the poster. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Rodchenko).
interpretation: The poster’s long afterlife in album covers and advertising shows that its combination of a cut-out photograph and constructivist type is how many people recognize the style today.
next: Find a museum record with an image of a printed copy (for example the Merrill C. Berman Collection or MoMA) and upgrade the evidence level.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Rodchenko died on 3 December 1956, so his works stay protected in Russia until at least the end of 2026, and until the end of 2030 if he counts as having worked during the Great Patriotic War. The poster was published before 1931, so it is probably in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Letterpress word game
references.lede: Loren Brichter’s 2012 iPhone game of colored letter tiles, drawn after Windows Phone and cited as an inspiration for iOS 7.
references.summary: A 5 × 5 board of flat letter tiles that turn blue or red as players claim them. Atebits, 2012.

evidence.note: Wikipedia article read on 2026-09-28. A Wayback copy of atebits.com/letterpress (30 November 2012) shows a small promotional image of the board; it is too small to count as observed and was not kept.

styles.note: A link between Metro and iOS 7: its interface borrows from Windows Phone, and Apple’s designers cited it for iOS 7.

context: Letterpress is a turn-based word game developed by Loren Brichter and published by Atebits, released for iOS on 24 October 2012. Players claim letter tiles on a 5 × 5 grid; claimed tiles take the player’s color ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letterpress_(video_game))).
“For graphics and the user interface, he took inspiration from the Windows Phone.”
It won a 2013 Apple Design Award, and “Apple designer Jony Ive took inspiration from minimalist iOS apps, among them Letterpress, while designing graphics for iOS 7.”
The Verge described the interface as “barren” with “natural-feeling animations”.
interpretation: It shows the flat grammar moving from Microsoft to Apple’s platform through a third-party app, before [iOS 7](ref:ios-7-interface-2013).

rights.statement: Software and graphics © Atebits and their successors. No image is stored here.

references.title: LOVE stamp
references.lede: The first US Love stamp: an eight-cent issue of 1973 on which Robert Indiana adapted his stacked LOVE image for the United States Postal Service.
references.summary: Robert Indiana’s stacked LOVE on an eight-cent US postage stamp, 1973.

creator.name: Robert Indiana, for the United States Postal Service

evidence.note: The [National Postal Museum page](https://postalmuseum.si.edu/exhibition/art-of-the-stamp-the-artwork-love/love-1973) and the Smithsonian collection record return HTTP 403 to scripts. The only open image found is a 451 × 287 px copy on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lovestamp.png), too small for observation.

styles.note: Pop art’s word-as-image carried into mass print on hundreds of millions of stamps. Partial fit: it has no dots, key lines, or comic devices.

context: In 1973 the United States Postal Service commissioned a stamp design from Indiana and released the eight-cent LOVE stamp before Valentine’s Day. It was unveiled at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and 425 million were printed over the next two years. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_(image)).

The image began as a 1964 card that Indiana sent to friends, and in 1965 a red, blue, and green version was chosen for the Museum of Modern Art’s Christmas card. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_(image)).
The Commons file gives the issue date as 26 January 1973. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lovestamp.png).
A 1967 screenprint of the same image is [Love](ref:indiana-love-screenprint-1967).
interpretation: The stamp shows how far the Pop idiom travelled into everyday print by the early 1970s: a gallery image reduced to postage size still reads because it is one word in four flat colors.
borrow: Test a Pop headline at icon size: a stacked word in flat color should still read at 40 px.
next: Inspect an image at least 800 px wide, for example through the National Postal Museum in a browser, and add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Commons marks its copy public domain with the template PD-textlogo (too simple for copyright), not with a US government or postal rationale, and its source is a cleaned-up web image. The design reproduces Robert Indiana’s LOVE, a privately authored image. The rights need a curator’s decision.

references.title: Love, screenprint
references.lede: Robert Indiana’s LOVE in a 1967 screenprint: four red slab-serif letters stacked two over two, with a tilted O, on flat blue and green.
references.summary: Stacked red slab-serif capitals on flat blue and green, with a tilted O. Robert Indiana, 1967.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.579-1968 (1200 × 1456 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: The type branch of the style: a single word in stacked slab-serif capitals, flat saturated color, and no modeling. Partial fit: it has no dots, outlines, or comic panel.

context: The V&A records a colour screenprint on paper, 65 × 50 cm, printed by Editions Domberger in 1967. It calls the image one of the iconic images of American Pop Art and notes that it was used for a US postage stamp. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O76309/).

A sister print in the V&A (CIRC.576-1968) belongs to a set of four called “Love Wall”, made for a portfolio published in Germany for the exhibition *Formen der Farbe*. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O157118/).
The 1973 US stamp is recorded as [LOVE stamp](ref:love-stamp-1973).
observed: The letters L, O, V, and E are stacked in a square, LO above VE, and fill the image to its edges.
The letters are flat red slab-serif capitals. The O is tilted to the right, and its counter is a green oblong.
The spaces between the letters are flat blue in the top half and flat green in the bottom half.
Red and green, and red and blue, meet at hard edges with no outline between them.
A wide unprinted white margin fills the bottom of the sheet.
interpretation: Indiana’s contribution to the idiom is the word as image: sign-painter lettering, enlarged until the letters become the whole composition.
The red against blue and green vibrates at the edges, so the image stays loud without any black line.
borrow: Stack a short word in heavy slab-serif capitals into a square and let it fill the panel.
Tilt one letter to give a static block of type a single point of movement.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A credits a sister print “Copyright ARS, New York & DACS, London 2001”. Robert Indiana died in 2018.

references.title: Lovelace Soft UI for Home Assistant
references.lede: A December 2019 theme that brought the style to real smart-home dashboards, in a very faint form.
references.summary: Open-source neumorphic card styles for the Home Assistant Lovelace dashboard, with light and dark modes.

evidence.note: Inspected the repository’s own `images/screenshot.png` (3349 × 1796), which shows the light and dark themes in two browser windows. The stored image is a crop of the light window without the browser toolbar. The screenshot may be more recent than 2019. Licence and dates read through the GitHub API.

styles.note: Partial fit. The README calls it “a neumorphic theme” and its CSS gives each card a white shadow up-left and a gray shadow down-right on the page color, but the shadows are so faint that the cards read as soft floating tiles.

context: The README calls it “a neumorphic theme for Home Assistant Lovelace” with “elegant soft shadows, light & dark modes”.
Its light theme sets `box-shadow: -5px -5px 15px #ffffff, 5px 5px 15px #ebebeb` and `border-radius: 15px` on every card, and a pressed state `inset -4px -4px 5px #ffffff, inset 4px 4px 5px #ebebeb`.
The repository was created on 27 December 2019, two weeks after the style was named. MIT License, © 2019 ilzq. About 890 GitHub stars on 2026-09-28. The project is now archived.
In the dark window of the same screenshot, cards are near-black tiles on a dark gray page and an active button has an amber outline.
observed: A near-white page (#f7f8fa) with square tiles in the same color: two small icon buttons, two larger tiles (“Study / Off”, “Stared / On”), and two icon tiles next to scene titles.
Each tile has a very soft gray shadow that is strongest at the lower right. The white highlight at upper left is barely visible against the near-white page.
The active tile has a 2–3 px blue outline, and the thumbs-up and star icons are blue. All other icons and text are slate gray.
Corners are rounded at roughly 15 px. Type is a medium-weight sans-serif (Roboto-like).
interpretation: A real smart-home dashboard, one of the uses the style is known for. It shows the common problem of the style on a near-white page: the light shadow disappears, and only a soft drop shadow remains. The blue outline on the active tile adds the contrast that the shadows alone cannot give.
Measured with `tools/image-traits.py`: the page color covers about 97 % of the image.
borrow: Mark the active state with the accent color as well as a pressed shadow, so it survives on screens where the shadows vanish.

images.alt: A near-white Home Assistant dashboard with rounded square tiles in the page color and very soft shadows; one tile labeled Stared On has a blue outline, and scene tiles show a GitHub logo and a remote-control icon.
images.caption: Light theme, cropped from the README screenshot of [Lovelace Soft UI](https://github.com/qiz-li/lovelace-soft-ui). MIT License. The GitHub mark and Material Design icons are incidental.

rights.statement: Image committed to the repository and covered by its MIT License, © 2019 ilzq. It shows the theme applied to Home Assistant’s own interface; the crop removes the browser frame.

references.title: Lustre vase by Walter Crane for Maw & Co.
references.lede: A squat earthenware vase in ruby lustre on which Walter Crane wrapped a spiral band with a reclining figure around a field of scrolling leaves.
references.summary: Ruby-red lustre on cream earthenware: a spiral band with a figure and scrolling leaves. Walter Crane for Maw & Co., 1889.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 2017.208 (3283 × 3400 px). Only one side of the vase is shown.

styles.note: Partial fit: shown at the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society and drawn in flat outline, but its diagonal, flowing band is looser than the movement’s symmetrical repeats.

context: Cleveland calls Crane one of the leading figures of the British Arts and Crafts movement. This vase is one of a series he designed for Maw & Co. around 1889, when they were first listed in the catalogue of the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/2017.208).
The ruby-red lustre surface is a hallmark of Maw’s work and refers to 15th- and 16th-century Spanish lustreware. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/2017.208).
Cleveland lists it as earthenware, 22.4 × 22.7 cm, Britain, 1889. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/2017.208).
observed: The vase has a wide, flattened body, a narrow neck, and a cup-shaped mouth.
The decoration is in one colour: ruby-red lustre on a cream, slightly speckled ground.
A broad band, outlined by two red lines, spirals around the body. Inside it a nude figure with long hair reclines, drawn in thin red lines.
Outside the band, oval cartouches hold stylized leaves, surrounded by small scrolls and dots.
All decoration is flat outline and fill, without shading.
interpretation: The flat outline drawing and the look back to Renaissance lustreware fit the movement. The diagonal band with a figure is closer to Crane’s book illustration than to the static repeats of Morris’s textiles.
Read with [Strawberry Thief](ref:morris-strawberry-thief-textile), it shows that the movement’s red can be a strong, glossy ceramic red as well as a printed madder.
borrow: Use a single warm red on cream for both pattern and figure, and let the line weight carry the hierarchy.
Frame a figure inside a band with a double line, and fill the rest of the field with small, repeated leaf cartouches.

images.alt: Squat earthenware vase decorated in ruby-red lustre on cream: a spiral band with a reclining nude figure crosses the body, and scrolling leaf cartouches fill the rest.
images.caption: Walter Crane for Maw & Co., vase, 1889. Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Katharine Lee Reid, 2017.208. [Open-access image](https://clevelandart.org/art/2017.208), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art releases the image as CC0. Walter Crane died in 1915, and the vase dates from 1889, so the design is in the public domain in the United Kingdom and the United States.

references.title: macOS Big Sur interface
references.lede: Apple’s 2020 desktop redesign: frosted Control Center tiles and notifications over a vivid wave wallpaper.
references.summary: Translucent, blurred Control Center and notifications over a saturated wallpaper. Apple, 2020.

evidence.note: Inspected two Apple Newsroom press images in scratchpad copies: the Control Center close-up (apple_macos-bigsur_controlcenter_06222020, 1306 × 1306) and the Notification Center close-up (apple_macos-bigsur_notificationcenter_06222020, 1306 × 1306). Not stored. The operating system was not run.

styles.note: Malewicz’s naming article and Everyday UX both name Big Sur as the moment the style entered a mainstream desktop. Its Control Center matches every diagnostic trait.

context: Apple’s press release describes a menu bar with “a new translucent material”, an all-new Control Center, and a redesigned Notification Center with widgets. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2020/06/apple-introduces-macos-big-sur-with-a-beautiful-new-design/).

Wikipedia says Big Sur “features new blurs to establish a visual hierarchy” and was the first macOS user interface redesign since OS X Yosemite. [Wikipedia: macOS Big Sur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS_Big_Sur).

Malewicz writes that Apple “recently brought transparent-blurs back with Mac OS Big Sur” and suggests that this may be why Apple chose a colorful default wallpaper. [Malewicz 2020](ref:malewicz-glassmorphism-article-2020).
observed: The wallpaper is a set of large, smooth waves in blue, white, orange, red, and magenta.
Control Center is one large translucent panel with rounded corners. Inside it, tiles for Wi-Fi, Do Not Disturb, Display, Sound, and Now Playing are lighter translucent rounded rectangles.
The blue and orange of the wallpaper show through the panel as soft color. No wallpaper edges are sharp behind it.
Sliders are white pills on a darker translucent track. Controls use flat blue discs and SF-style sans-serif text.
Notification cards are translucent blue-tinted rounded rectangles. The widgets below them are opaque white or dark grey, so both treatments appear side by side.
interpretation: Big Sur’s Control Center is the clearest large-platform example of the web recipe: glass inside glass, flat content, and a wallpaper chosen to make the blur visible. The opaque widgets show the rule of opacity for hierarchy.
borrow: Nest lighter translucent tiles inside a translucent panel to group controls without borders.
Pair glass surfaces with a wallpaper of large, smooth color areas, not a detailed photo.

rights.statement: Apple press images and software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Man with a Movie Camera poster
references.lede: The Stenberg brothers’ poster for Dziga Vertov’s film spins a dancing woman and a spiral of credits over skyscrapers seen from steep angles.
references.summary: A spiral of white capitals on black around a cut-out dancing figure, over tilted red, yellow, and green skyscrapers. Vladimir and Georgii Stenberg, 1929.

source.label: Digital Library of Early Soviet Cinema: Man with a Movie Camera [Poster]

evidence.note: Viewed an 800 × 1243 px image from the Digital Library of Early Soviet Cinema, whose record credits the image to Kinopoisk. The physical copy is not identified, so the level stays documented. MoMA lists a copy as object 217943 ([MoMA](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/217943)); the MoMA page refused automated access (HTTP 403) and was not read.

styles.note: Partial fit: a canonical constructivist film poster in its composition and lettering, but it is the colorful exception the style record names. It uses several hues and drawn, tonal imagery.

context: The Digital Library of Early Soviet Cinema describes it as “a constructivist poster by the Stenberg brothers” advertising Dziga Vertov’s documentary *Man with a Movie Camera* (1929). [Digital Library of Early Soviet Cinema](https://cdm15851.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p15851coll19/id/33/).
The imprint names the producer VUFKU. The poster is signed “2 СТЕНБЕРГ 2” at the lower left, the brothers’ usual signature.
observed: In the image viewed, a woman’s figure, drawn from photographs, dances with arms spread across the sheet. Her head is upside down near the center and her legs fall toward the lower right.
A black circle and a spiral band of white capitals turn around her, carrying the credits and “ФИЛЬМ БЕЗ СЛОВ” (film without words).
“ЧЕЛОВЕК С КИНО АППАРАТОМ” curves in large white capitals on a black band from the left edge to the lower right.
Skyscrapers in red, yellow, teal green, and beige, drawn with gridded windows, tilt in from every edge in steep perspective.
The ground is black.
interpretation: The poster keeps the style’s grammar of rotation, cut-out figures, and heavy capitals, but replaces red and black with a multicolor palette. The measured fingerprint rule `color.hues = 1` would reject it, which the record accepts as the style’s known exception.
borrow: Set a line of credits on a circular or spiral path around a central figure.
Frame a subject with architecture seen from steep upward and downward angles to create vertigo.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Georgii Stenberg died in 1933, but Vladimir Stenberg died in 1982, so the joint work is protected in Russia until at least 2052. The Digital Library of Early Soviet Cinema marks its image “Public Domain”, which does not account for Vladimir Stenberg’s term.

references.title: Marilyn Diptych
references.lede: Andy Warhol’s fifty repeated Marilyn Monroe heads on two canvases: a grid in flat color on the left, fading black and white on the right.
references.summary: Fifty silkscreened faces in a grid, colored on one panel and black on the other. Andy Warhol, 1962.

evidence.note: Tate serves images of this work only up to 256 px wide; larger sizes return HTTP 403. The 256 px image confirms only the two-panel grid, which is too small for observation. Description relies on Tate’s record and Wikipedia.

styles.note: The key source for the style’s grid of repeated units and for the Warhol color variant. Partial fit: it has no dots, key lines, or comic devices.

context: Tate gives the medium as alkyd ink, acrylic paint, oil ground, and graphite on two canvases. [Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/warhol-marilyn-diptych-t03093).

Warhol made the work in 1962, shortly after Monroe’s death in August. It repeats fifty images from a publicity still for the 1953 film *Niagara* by Gene Kornman: colored portraits on the left panel and fading black-and-white impressions on the right. Tate acquired it in 1980. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Diptych).

Warhol described silkscreening as picking a photograph, blowing it up, transferring it in glue onto silk, and rolling ink across it, so that each image is the same but slightly different. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Diptych).
A later screenprint of the same head is [Marilyn Monroe (Marilyn)](ref:warhol-marilyn-screenprint-1967).
interpretation: The diptych gives the style its second layout: not one enlarged panel but a strict grid of identical units, like goods on a shelf or frames on a contact sheet.
The contrast between the two panels depends on print variation. On screen, the equivalent is a grid in which units vary slightly in ink density or registration.
borrow: Repeat one image in a tight grid with no gutters, and vary only its color or density from cell to cell.
Pair a colored grid with a monochrome grid of the same unit.
next: Inspect an image at least 800 px wide and add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts; Warhol died in 1987.

references.title: Marilyn Monroe (Marilyn), shocking pink colourway
references.lede: One of Andy Warhol’s ten 1967 Marilyn screenprints: a publicity photograph reduced to black, laid over flat blocks of hot pink, yellow, and peach.
references.summary: A face screenprinted in black over flat hot pink, yellow, and peach. Andy Warhol, 1967.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.123-1968 (1200 × 1198 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: The Warhol branch of the style: flat off-register color blocks under a black photographic screen, in hot pink and yellow instead of process primaries. It has no dots, outlines, or comic devices, so it fits the color grammar more than the panel grammar.

context: The V&A records a screenprint on paper, 91.4 × 91.6 cm, printed by Aetna Silkscreen Products Inc./Du-Art Displays and published by Factory Additions, New York, 1967. The print is one of a portfolio of ten colourways; this one is described as shocking pink, yellow, and peach. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O72301/).
The V&A notes that every print and painting Warhol made of Marilyn used the same publicity photograph by Gene Kornman for the 1953 film *Niagara*. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O72301/).
The painted version of the motif is [Marilyn Diptych](ref:warhol-marilyn-diptych-1962).
observed: The background is a flat hot pink that fills the square to the edges.
The hair is a flat yellow shape; the face is a flat peach shape with no modeling.
A black screen of the photograph gives the eyes, brows, nose, mouth, and the shadowed side of the face and neck.
Eyelids are a brighter pink block, and the lips are dark red under the black.
The color blocks do not align exactly with the black layer: the yellow runs past the hair outline at the right edge.
interpretation: Warhol replaces the drawn key line with a black photographic layer, and the process primaries with a hotter palette. The style record’s Warhol variant comes from works like this.
The misregistration is part of the look: flat color and line are two separate layers that do not quite meet.
borrow: For a Warhol variant, set a black high-contrast image over flat blocks of hot pink, yellow, and peach.
Offset one color block a few pixels from the black layer to suggest a printing misregister.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts; Warhol died in 1987.

references.title: Marina Apollonio website
references.lede: The artist’s own site opens on a black and white field of concentric rings that tighten into one side, under a plain sans-serif name and menu.
references.summary: A wide panel of black and white concentric rings that crowd together, with light grey sans-serif type on white.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Clear in imagery: a wide black and white ring field that changes by steps, with plain sans-serif text kept off the pattern. A soft shadow under the next panel is a counter-trait.

context: The site describes Apollonio as an Italian artist of the optical and kinetic movement (page title: “Artista Italiana del movimento Ottico/Cinetico”). The Peggy Guggenheim Collection held a retrospective, *Marina Apollonio: Beyond the Circle*, from October 2024 to March 2025. [Peggy Guggenheim Collection](https://www.guggenheim-venice.it/en/whats-on/exhibitions/marina-apollonio-beyond-the-circle/).
observed: “Marina Apollonio” sits at the top left in a light, dark-grey geometric sans-serif on two lines. The menu at the right (biografia, eventi, opere, contatti) uses the same face in black.
Below, a panel almost the full width of the page shows a large half-disc of concentric black and white rings of equal width.
The centre of the rings is off to the upper middle, so the rings crowd together on one side and spread out on the other, and the disc seems to tilt in depth.
A white panel with a soft grey shadow starts at the bottom edge of the viewport.
interpretation: The page shows the simplest web form of the style: an artwork reproduction used as a hero field, with the interface reduced to a small neutral sans-serif.

The fingerprint misses most of this. The rings are an image, so the pattern metrics read 0; the body text is #666 grey, so the text contrast is 5.7; and the soft shadow under the next panel gives a shadow share of 0.55. The screenshot palette gives lightness 0.69 and no hues.
borrow: Offset the centre of a set of concentric rings so that they crowd on one side and suggest a tilt.
Keep the name and menu small and plain above the field, so the pattern carries the page.

images.alt: Marina Apollonio home page: the artist’s name in light grey sans-serif at top left and a four-item menu at right, above a wide panel of black and white concentric rings whose centre is off to the upper middle.
images.caption: First viewport of [marinaapollonio.com](https://www.marinaapollonio.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Material Design color palette
references.lede: The 2014 palette of 19 hues, each in ten shades from 50 to 900 and most with four accent shades, from which Material apps took one primary and one accent.
references.summary: Nineteen saturated hues in numbered shades, with 500 as the primary and A200 as a typical accent. Google, 2014.

evidence.note: Read the hex values in the HTML text of the Material Design 1 color page on 28 September 2026. No image was inspected: the page draws its swatches in HTML.

styles.note: The palette sets the style’s color grammar: one bold 500 shade for the app bar, a darker 700 for the status bar, and a contrasting accent.

context: The page says: “Color in Material Design is inspired by bold hues juxtaposed with muted environments, deep shadows, and bright highlights.” [Color](https://m1.material.io/style/color.html).

The 19 hues and their 500 shades are: Red #F44336, Pink #E91E63, Purple #9C27B0, Deep Purple #673AB7, Indigo #3F51B5, Blue #2196F3, Light Blue #03A9F4, Cyan #00BCD4, Teal #009688, Green #4CAF50, Light Green #8BC34A, Lime #CDDC39, Yellow #FFEB3B, Amber #FFC107, Orange #FF9800, Deep Orange #FF5722, Brown #795548, Grey #9E9E9E, and Blue Grey #607D8B.
Each hue runs from 50 to 900. Indigo, for example, runs from #E8EAF6 to #1A237E and adds accents A100 #8C9EFF, A200 #536DFE, A400 #3D5AFE, and A700 #304FFE.

The page describes a scheme in which the primary color fills the toolbar and status bar, and a secondary color accents the floating action button. The later edition of the page names the accent a “secondary” color.
interpretation: Almost every hue has the same brightness at 500, so any two can be swapped without redesigning the screen. This is why Material apps of 2015 look like one family in many colors.
borrow: Choose one 500 shade for the app bar, its 700 shade for the top edge, and an A200 accent from a hue at least 90 degrees away on the color wheel.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Color values are facts. The page text is under the Apache License 2.0 unless otherwise specified.

references.title: Material Design guidelines, first edition
references.lede: Google’s own specification for Material Design: the document that defines sheets of material, resting elevations, the color palette, and the floating action button.
references.summary: Google’s 2014 design specification, illustrated with flat colored sheets, soft shadow diagrams, and component sheets.

creator.name: Google, design team led by Matías Duarte

references.made: 2014 (published at Google I/O, 25 June 2014; revised until 2018)

evidence.note: Read the introduction, elevation and shadows, material properties, and color pages at m1.material.io on 28 September 2026. Opened the introduction illustration (2320 × 1248) and the elevation diagram *whatismaterial-3d-elevation1.png* (1520 × 960) from the site’s image store, and the Wikimedia Commons component sheet *Material Design.svg* rendered at 960 × 1707.

styles.note: The source document of the style. Its illustrations use the style’s own grammar: flat color, sheets at named heights, soft shadows, and a round action button.

context: The guidelines name three principles: “Material is the metaphor”, “Bold, graphic, intentional”, and “Motion provides meaning”. Their stated goal is to “create a visual language that synthesizes classic principles of good design with the innovation and possibility of technology and science.” [Introduction](https://m1.material.io/material-design/introduction.html).

The material properties page says that material is 1 dp thick, that “material casts shadows”, and that “shadows are never approximated by coloring material”. [Material properties](https://m1.material.io/material-design/material-properties.html).

The elevation page gives resting elevations for Android: card 2 dp, app bar 4 dp, floating action button 6 dp, with higher values for menus, the navigation drawer, and dialogs. [Elevation and shadows](https://m1.material.io/material-design/elevation-shadows.html).

Google first published the specification at google.com/design/spec when it announced Material Design at Google I/O on 25 June 2014. The m1.material.io copy now says “Material 1 is no longer maintained”. [Wikipedia: Material Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Material_Design).
observed: The introduction illustration is four flat rectangles and one circle in shades of cyan and teal, stacked with no outlines and no shadows. Only the tone changes from sheet to sheet.

The elevation diagram shows two near-white cards on a pale gray ground. The upper card has a larger, softer shadow than the lower card. A side view on the right marks heights of 2 dp, 6 dp, and 8 dp with dashed lines.

The component sheet shows a red app bar with a darker red status bar, blue raised buttons with all-capital labels, a blue toggle, an underlined text field, a white dialog with a large soft shadow, and a round blue action button with a plus sign in the lower right.
interpretation: The guidelines are both the rulebook and a specimen. They show the grammar in its purest form, with no product content, so they are the best source for token values.

The introduction illustration shows the flat half of the style, and the elevation diagram shows the paper half. Together they explain why Material is called flat 2.0 ([Evernote for Android](ref:evernote-android-2015)).
borrow: Give every surface a named elevation and derive its shadow from that height, instead of choosing shadows one by one.
Show layered structure with tones of one hue when shadows are not available, as the introduction illustration does.

images.alt: Diagram on a pale gray ground: two white cards on the left, the upper one with a larger soft shadow, and on the right a side view of two thin sheets at heights marked 2dp, 6dp, and 8dp.
images.caption: Elevation diagram from the [Material Design 1 guidelines, Elevation and shadows](https://m1.material.io/material-design/elevation-shadows.html). Google, Apache License 2.0.

images.alt: Flat illustration of overlapping rectangles and a circle in five shades of cyan and teal, with no outlines or shadows.
images.caption: Introduction illustration from the [Material Design 1 guidelines](https://m1.material.io/material-design/introduction.html), resized. Google, Apache License 2.0.

images.alt: Phone screen of Material components: a red app bar titled Page title, blue raised buttons labeled NORMAL and PRESSED, toggles, an underlined text field, a white Permissions dialog with a soft shadow, checkboxes, radio buttons, a slider, and a round blue plus button.
images.caption: Component sheet based on the 2015 Google specification, from [Wikimedia Commons: Material Design.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Material_Design.svg), rendered and resized. Author given as Google Inc. Tagged PD-ineligible and Apache License 2.0.

rights.statement: Borderline tier A, for the curator to confirm. The work is not public domain. The m1.material.io pages state: “All content and code on this site are licensed under the Apache 2 license unless otherwise specified”. The first two images come from that site. The Commons component sheet is tagged both PD-ineligible and Apache License 2.0 (Google Inc., 2015).

references.title: Material Design Lite
references.lede: Google’s 2015 library of Material components in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, for websites that did not use a framework.
references.summary: Google’s framework-free Material component library, with dashboard, blog, and portfolio templates. 2015.

evidence.note: Opened the template previews *dashboard_2x.jpg* and *general_2x.jpg* (1786 × 966 each) from the repository’s docs/_assets/templates folder on 28 September 2026. Not stored. getmdl.io returned HTTP 403 to scripts.

styles.note: A Google implementation of the style for the web. Its templates show drawers, cards with soft shadows, tab bars with an accent underline, and Roboto.

context: The README describes MDL as “an implementation of Material Design components in vanilla CSS, JS, and HTML” and says that it is now in limited support, with development moved to Material Components for the web. It also says that the old getmdl.io documentation site is gone. [README](https://github.com/google/material-design-lite).
The GitHub API gives the license as Apache 2.0 and the creation date as 14 January 2015.
observed: Dashboard template: a dark blue-gray navigation drawer with a round avatar, white Roboto labels, and a cyan band that marks the selected item.
The content area is pale gray with a white header bar and a white card that has a soft shadow and square corners. The card holds two flat ring charts in lime green and cyan.
General template: a full-bleed photo above a blue-gray tab bar with all-capital labels, where a pink underline marks the active tab.
interpretation: The templates show how the style moved from phones to the web: the drawer and app bar stay, and the card becomes the main unit of a desktop layout.
borrow: Mark the active tab with a 2 px accent underline, and keep the tab labels in medium all-capital letters on the primary color.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The repository is under the Apache License 2.0. The general template’s photograph may have its own rights, so the catalogue links to the previews only.

references.title: Material Design product icons
references.lede: Google’s rules for app icons as shapes of cut and folded paper, lit from above, with the 2014 Gmail envelope as the model.
references.summary: App icons drawn as folded paper with flat color, soft fold shading, and a thin edge shadow. Google, 2014.

source.label: Google, Material Design 1 guidelines: Icons, Product icons

evidence.note: Opened the product icon definition image *style-logos-product-intro-definition.png* (1520 × 960) and three 720 × 720 anatomy and lighting diagrams from the Material Design 1 icons page on 28 September 2026. Not stored.

styles.note: The imagery facet of the style: product icons use the same paper metaphor as the interface, with flat color, clean folds, and soft light from above.

context: The Material Design 1 icons page describes product icons as the visual expression of a brand’s product and defines their anatomy, a keyline grid, lighting at 45 degrees from the top left, and rules for folds and shadows. [Icons](https://m1.material.io/style/icons.html).
observed: The Gmail envelope is a flat red M over a pale gray paper envelope with rounded outer corners.
The folds of the envelope show as flat facets of slightly different grays, with a soft shadow under the red M.
A thin, slightly darker line along the bottom edge suggests that the paper has thickness. There is no gloss and no texture.
interpretation: Product icons are the one place where Material draws light and shade inside an image. They still read as flat color, because the shading is limited to large facets and short soft shadows.
borrow: Build an emblem from two or three flat paper layers. Shade only the folds and the edge where one layer lies on another.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The m1.material.io site is under the Apache License 2.0 unless otherwise specified, but the product icons are Google trademarks, so the catalogue links to them only.

references.title: Material Design system icons
references.lede: Google’s set of simple 24 dp interface glyphs, drawn on one grid with the same stroke, corners, and flat gray fill.
references.summary: A grid of flat gray interface glyphs with 2 dp strokes and square-cut geometry. Google, 2014.

evidence.note: Opened the system icon overview *style-icons-system-intro.png* (1520 × 730) from the Material Design 1 icons page on 28 September 2026. Checked the repository date and license through the GitHub API for [google/material-design-icons](https://github.com/google/material-design-icons).

styles.note: The standard glyph set of the style. Every Material 1 and 2 app bar, list, and action button uses these icons or ones drawn to the same rules.

context: The Material Design 1 icons page separates product icons (see [Material product icons](ref:material-product-icons-2014)) from system icons, which are simple glyphs for actions and objects. It shows the system icons on a keyline grid. [Icons](https://m1.material.io/style/icons.html).

Google publishes the icons in the repository google/material-design-icons under the Apache License 2.0. The GitHub API gives the creation date as 8 October 2014. [GitHub](https://github.com/google/material-design-icons).
observed: Seventy-two icons in six rows, all in one mid-gray (about #757575) on a near-white ground.
Strokes have one weight throughout. Ends are cut square, and corners of outlined shapes are slightly rounded.
Glyphs mix solid shapes (camera, envelope, bookmark) with outlines (heart, cloud, circle with plus). None has a gradient, a highlight, or a shadow.
interpretation: The icons carry the flat half of the style. Depth in Material belongs to surfaces, not to glyphs, so an icon stays flat even when it sits on a raised button.
borrow: Draw interface icons on a 24 px grid with one stroke weight and square ends, and color them with the secondary text color (black at 54 %) instead of pure black.

images.alt: Grid of seventy-two flat gray interface icons in six rows, including a printer, globe, pin, camera, shopping cart, envelope, bell, heart, cloud, arrows, and a plus sign.
images.caption: System icon overview from the [Material Design 1 guidelines, Icons](https://m1.material.io/style/icons.html). Google, Apache License 2.0.

rights.statement: Borderline tier A, for the curator to confirm. The icons are not public domain, but Google licenses them under the Apache License 2.0, both in the [icon repository](https://github.com/google/material-design-icons) and on m1.material.io (“All content and code on this site are licensed under the Apache 2 license unless otherwise specified”).

references.title: Material-UI website, 2018
references.lede: The 2018 home page of Material-UI, the React library for Material Design, with a blue app bar and a dark snackbar announcing version 3.
references.summary: Blue app bar, a dark snackbar with a pink CLOSE action, a blue folded-ribbon logo, an outlined button, and flat gray panels. 2018.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

references.title: Mercury Weather website
references.lede: A weather app’s page with translucent chips and quote cards, edged in thin light lines, over a dark teal and violet glow.
references.summary: Translucent bordered chips and cards on a dark teal-to-violet glow, for an Apple-platform weather app.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Clear example: translucent chips and cards with hairline light borders and large radii over a colored glow. The glass is dark and tinted rather than white.

observed: The background is a dark glow: teal at the upper left, deep violet on the right, and near-black at the edges.
Four feature chips (‘Hyper-local forecasts’, ‘Beautiful charts’, ‘Trip forecast’, ‘All Apple devices’) are dark translucent pills with a thin light border.

borrow: For dark glass, use a 1 px light border at low opacity on every chip and card, and let one teal and one violet glow provide the color.

references.title: Metro UI CSS website, 2013
references.lede: An open-source CSS framework that rebuilt Windows 8 Metro for the web, shown in its own tiles.
references.summary: Blue top bar, a magenta note, and blue, green, and yellow tiles with light white titles and line icons. May 2013.

source.label: metroui.org.ua, Metro UI CSS home page

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 23 May 2013, and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. Nothing covers the page. The page shows photographs of the three team members.

styles.note: Clear: square solid tiles in blue, green, and yellow with light white titles and single-color line icons; the framework imitates Windows 8 Metro by design.

references.notice: The live site has been redesigned many times since 2013.
context: The page describes Metro UI CSS as “a set of styles to create a site with an interface similar to Windows 8 Metro UI”. A photo caption names Sergey Pimenov as author and team leader.
The repository [olton/metroui](https://github.com/olton/metroui) was created on 9 March 2012 and is released under the MIT License (GitHub API, read 2026-09-28).
observed: A full-width blue bar holds a white four-square logo, “Metro UI CSS 0.95-a”, and white menu words.

A pale gray panel has the light heading “Metro UI CSS” over a solid magenta bar with white text: “Developed with the advice of Microsoft to build the user interface and include:”. Below it are check-marked features.
Three short red and black bars mark slide positions. Two thin circled arrows are the slide controls.
A pale blue panel says “project is looking for a sponsor” in light crimson type, with a crimson circled arrow.
Three square tiles in blue, green, and yellow have light white titles (Simple, Sufficient, Responsive) and white line icons.
Team photographs sit on pale blue cards with captions.
interpretation: Measured: headings weight 200 (Segoe UI Semilight), no radius, no shadow, no gradient, and 7 hue groups in the screenshot. 47% of boxes have a 1 px border, mostly the pale frames around photographs and panels.
It is a direct translation of the Metro grammar into web components: tiles, light headings, and circled-arrow controls.
borrow: Build a tile as a solid rectangle with a light title at top left and a one-color glyph at bottom right.

references.title: Micha Klein, Artificial Beauty “Venus”
references.lede: A digitally built portrait from Micha Klein’s 1998 series Artificial Beauties: a flawless face in front of floating 3D crystals, lens flares, and electric color.
references.summary: An idealised digital portrait against purple 3D crystals and neon light streaks. Micha Klein, 1998, Cibachrome on aluminium.

source.label: Kunsthuizen: Micha Klein, Arteficial beauty Venus

evidence.note: Inspected the image on the Kunsthuizen art-lending page for this print (840 × 864, series no. 5 of the edition), in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: late-1990s digital-render imagery with 3D crystals, lens flares, and electric purple, blue, and pink. It has no chrome, plastic, or type.

context: Kunsthuizen describes an original 1998 photograph from Klein’s series Artificial Beauties, as exhibited at the Groninger Museum: a Cibachrome print on aluminium behind perspex, 75 × 75 cm. [Kunsthuizen](https://www.kunsthuizen.nl/kunstwerken/venus-micha-klein/).

Klein (1964–2026) studied at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie and graduated in 1989 with the first degree there in computer graphics. The Groninger Museum held a ten-year retrospective of his digital work in 1998. [Micha Klein: About](https://www.michaklein.com/about); [Digicult (2006)](https://digicult.it/digimag/issue-014/the-multimedia-colours-of-micha-klein/); [Metropolis M](https://metropolism.com/nl/feature/i-m-micha-klein-1964-2026/).
observed: A woman with red hair and bare shoulders faces the viewer; her skin is smooth and even, like a retouched render.
Behind her float faceted purple and violet crystals of different sizes, some translucent.
The background swirls with electric blue, cyan, magenta, and orange streaks and fractal-like filaments.
Small star-shaped lens flares sparkle at the lower left and upper right.
interpretation: This is the image side of Y2K: 3D software used for its own sake, with rendered crystals, flares, and a perfected artificial face. The Y2K style record cites Evan Collins, [in the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/may/19/year-2000-y2k-millennium-design-aesthetic), linking the aesthetic to new CAD tools that allowed layered transparencies and lens flares.
The palette of violet, electric blue, and hot pink matches the style’s accent colors.
borrow: Use a few floating rendered crystals or gems with sharp facets as background motifs.
Add small four-point sparkle flares at the corners of an image.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is © the estate of Micha Klein.

references.title: Michèle Vasarely Foundation website
references.lede: The Michèle Vasarely Foundation’s home page: a full-screen black, white, and grey grid of squares that buckles and breaks, with small black pill buttons at the edges.
references.summary: A full-bleed grey and white square grid that distorts toward the centre, with black pill links in white sans-serif.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Clear: a black, white, and grey square grid fills the whole viewport and distorts by steps, and all text sits in solid black pills with plain sans-serif. The pattern is an image, so the pattern metrics read zero.

observed: The whole viewport is one image: a regular grid of grey squares separated by white lines.
Inside a large central rectangle the squares shrink, tilt, and break into black and white fragments, circles, and rhombs, so the grid seems to buckle toward the viewer.
A few pencil notes are visible at the right edge, so the image appears to be a scan of a drawing or study.

Ten navigation links (Michèle Vasarely Foundation, Vasarely, Yvaral, About, EN; Instagram, Certificate Request, Catalogue Raisonné, Contact, Newsletter) sit in small black rounded pills with white sans-serif text along the top and bottom edges.
There is no colour.
interpretation: This is the closest live match to the style’s web rules: one op field edge to edge, and text only on solid black panels, never on the pattern.

The measurement cannot see the pattern because it is an image: `color.patternShare` and `surface.patternShare` are 0, and the CSS lightness is 0.17 because the page ground is black behind the image. The screenshot palette gives lightness 0.57 and no hues.
The rounded pills are a modern interface habit that the op rubric neither asks for nor forbids.
borrow: Use one black and white field as the full-screen ground and push all navigation to small solid-black labels at the edges.
Distort only a central area of a regular grid so that the rest of the field frames the effect.

images.alt: Michèle Vasarely Foundation home page: a full-screen grey and white grid of squares that breaks into black and white fragments in the centre, with small black pill links in white text along the top and bottom edges.
images.caption: First viewport of [vasarely.com](https://vasarely.com/).
