references.title: Microsoft Bob, 1995
references.lede: A Windows shell that showed programs as objects in the rooms of a house, the extreme early case of the metaphor.
references.summary: A house with rooms; a pen and paper opens the word processor. Microsoft, 1995.

evidence.note: The only image found is a 288 × 216 px non-free screenshot on Wikipedia, too small to describe. Based on Wikipedia.

styles.note: A precursor: the whole computer becomes a set of household objects. It uses the metaphor fully but predates the material textures and bevels of 2007–2013.

context: Released on 10 March 1995 and discontinued in early 1996. “Microsoft Bob presented screens showing a house, with rooms that the user could visit containing familiar objects corresponding to computer applications, such as a desk with pen and paper and a checkbook. Clicking on the pen and paper would open the system’s word processor.” [Wikipedia: Microsoft Bob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Bob).

Wikipedia’s skeuomorph article names Bob as the extreme case of the desktop metaphor, “representing different programs as objects in a home.” [Wikipedia: Skeuomorph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeuomorph).
interpretation: Bob shows the metaphor without the later material realism. Its failure is a common warning against a metaphor that makes actions harder.

rights.statement: Microsoft software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Microsoft Fluent Acrylic material
references.lede: Microsoft’s frosted-glass brush for Windows apps: blur, tint, and noise over the desktop, three years before the style had a name.
references.summary: Fluent Design’s translucent Acrylic brush and its documented recipe. Microsoft, 2017 onward.
references.made: 2017 (Fluent Design System; first shipped in the Windows 10 Fall Creators Update, October 2017, per Wikipedia); documentation page updated 2026

evidence.note: Read the documentation page (ms.date 2026-08-29) and inspected two of its images in scratchpad copies: the Windows 11 context menu over a colorful wallpaper (acrylic-transient-context-menu.png, 1591 × 871) and the recipe diagram (acrylic-recipe-diagram.jpg, 1920 × 1080). Not stored.

styles.note: NN/g and t3n name Acrylic as glassmorphism under another name, and Malewicz quotes it in the naming article. It is the style’s material in a shipping design system.

context: The page defines Acrylic as “a type of Brush that creates a translucent texture” that adds depth and helps establish visual hierarchy. Background acrylic shows the desktop and other windows; in-app acrylic shows content inside the app. [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/style/acrylic).

Guidance: use background acrylic for transient surfaces such as context menus and flyouts; avoid layering several acrylic surfaces and placing acrylic panes edge to edge; do not place accent-colored text on acrylic. Acrylic falls back to a solid color when the user turns off transparency effects, in Battery Saver mode, in High Contrast mode, and on low-end hardware.

The text gives the recipe as “background, blur, exclusion blend, color/tint overlay, noise”. The diagram labels the layers Desktop background, Gaussian blur, Luminosity blend, Tint/Color blend, and Noise texture; the two labels for the blend layer differ.

Fluent Design (codename Project Neon) was introduced by Microsoft in 2017 with five components: light, depth, motion, material, and scale. [Wikipedia: Fluent Design System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluent_Design_System). Microsoft’s [materials overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/signature-experiences/materials) calls Acrylic “a semi-transparent material that replicates the effect of frosted glass”.
observed: Context-menu screenshot: a File Explorer window sits on a wallpaper of blurred violet, magenta, red, blue, and cyan light.
The context menu is a pale, pink-tinted translucent panel. The wallpaper colors show through it as soft washes, with no detail.
The menu has rounded corners, a thin light edge, and a soft shadow. Its icons and text are dark and flat.
Recipe diagram: five slanted sheets in a stack, from a saturated blue ‘desktop’ through a blurred sheet, a grey blend sheet, a light-blue tint, and a grey noise texture.
interpretation: Acrylic is the style before its name, fixed as an engineering recipe. The noise layer is Microsoft’s addition; web glassmorphism usually leaves it out.
borrow: Add a faint noise texture over the blur and tint so that large glass areas do not look like a plain gradient.
Give every glass surface a solid fallback for reduced-transparency settings.

rights.statement: Microsoft documentation and images; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Mindtwitch Interactive website, 2008
references.lede: A 2008 portfolio site for interactive designer Michael Boucher, dressed in aged paper, rusted metal, torn edges, and stencil tabs.
references.summary: Stained parchment panels with torn edges on dark leather, rusty bands, red stencil tabs, and a taped photograph.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 9 March 2008, and inspected. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Borderline: a clear example of later grunge web surfaces (stains, torn paper, rust, tape), but its HTML type is clean Georgia and Trebuchet, with damage only in image headings.

context: Smashing Magazine’s March 2008 article “The Secrets of Grunge Design” links mindtwitch.com among its examples. [Smashing Magazine](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2008/03/the-secrets-of-grunge-design/).
observed: The page sits on a dark brown leather texture. The central column is made of stained, yellowed parchment with torn, curled edges.
A frayed cloth and paper strip at the top carries the “mindtwitch” wordmark with a red star and the tagline “CREATIVELY TWISTED”.
Navigation tabs are dark red with beige stencil capitals (“CREATIONS”, “EXPERIENCE”, “THE BLOG”).
A rusted metal band runs across the page below the tabs and again at the foot.
A photograph of a figure in a gas mask is mounted in a white frame held by strips of tape.
The heading “Creations” is a red brush script over a faded, larger copy of itself; body text is a plain serif list in black, blue, and red.
interpretation: The measurement finds only two families (Trebuchet MS and Georgia) and no pattern share, because every texture is a bitmap image (image share 1.0). This is typical of 2000s grunge web design: surfaces carry the style, and HTML type stays conventional.
borrow: Tear the edges of a content panel with an image mask and let a faded, oversized copy of the heading sit behind the heading.

images.alt: Mindtwitch home page from 2008: a stained parchment column with torn edges on dark leather, red navigation tabs with stencil lettering, a rusty metal band, a taped photograph of a person in a gas mask, and a red script heading Creations over a list of services.

references.title: Mister Tambourine Man
references.lede: Martin Sharp’s screen-printed homage to Bob Dylan, 1967: a face in dark glasses inside a halo of concentric circles, also used as the cover of Oz magazine.
references.summary: Martin Sharp, 1967. Red-orange target circles fill a black ground around a patterned face and cut-up lettering.

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object E.7-1968 (IIIF, 1067 × 1600 px, with the poster about 750 × 1150 px inside a white margin) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The V&A copy is worn at the edges. The image is not stored.

styles.note: Clear on density and motif: concentric circles fill the whole sheet and the title is broken up into patterned letters. Partial fit on color: red-orange, black, and silver, not a pair of vibrating complements.

context: The V&A catalogues it as a colour screen print, 760 × 511 mm, inspired by Bob Dylan. The image appeared on the cover of the October–November 1967 issue of the London magazine Oz. The museum describes “a hallucinogenic frenzy of lettering and circles” that plays with Dylan’s song titles and lyrics. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O76010/).

Sharp (1942–2013) was an Australian artist and an editor of Oz; he also made the covers for Cream’s Disraeli Gears and Wheels of Fire. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Sharp). See also [Oz no. 4](ref:oz-magazine-4-cover-1967).
observed: Hundreds of concentric-circle targets in red-orange on black fill the sheet from edge to edge, at many sizes.
A face in large dark glasses fills the middle. It is printed in silver halftone covered with small red-orange marks.
The left lens carries the hand-lettered words BLOWING IN THE MIND in red-orange.
A larger silver target with a fine radiating pattern sits above the forehead like a third eye.
The title at the bottom is cut into pieces and partly covered by circles, so only parts such as MIST and URINE MAN can be read. The letters are filled with small patterns.
interpretation: The concentric circles are the entoptic motif of the rubric used as an all-over texture. The effect is the same visual buzz as Moscoso’s stripes, but it comes from pattern density instead of complementary color.
A dark ground is unusual for the style. It shows that saturated pattern can carry the look without a light or colored field.
borrow: Scatter concentric-ring targets at many sizes as an all-over background texture.
Put a short phrase inside a small enclosed shape of the main image, as with the lens here.
Let pattern cut through a display word, and keep enough of it to read.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. Martin Sharp died in 2013.

references.title: Mondriaanhuis website
references.lede: The museum in Mondrian’s birthplace in Amersfoort frames its photographs with offset black lines and uses flat yellow buttons and gray-blue planes.
references.summary: Offset black line frames around photos, flat yellow buttons, a gray-blue plane, and capitals in the navigation.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The request redirected to the Dutch home page, https://www.mondriaanhuis.nl/nl/.

styles.note: Borderline: the logo and photographs are framed by offset black horizontal and vertical lines, and the buttons are flat yellow, but the lines are thin, photographs dominate, and there is no red or blue plane.

observed: The logo is a rectangle of black lines that overlap and extend past their corners, with a small gray-blue plane and the words AMERSFOORT and MONDRIAANHUIS in capitals.
The navigation is set in small letter-spaced capitals: PLAN JE BEZOEK, ZIEN EN DOEN, OVER HET MONDRIAANHUIS, TICKETS.
Two flat yellow buttons with square corners read “Koop Tickets” and “Webshop”.
A news panel in gray-blue overlaps a photograph of a museum room; thin dark lines run along and past the edges of the photographs.
A large photograph shows a canal street in Amersfoort with the text “Ontdek Piet Mondriaan in zijn geboortehuis”.
interpretation: The site quotes the style through lines that run past their corners, as in Mondrian’s paintings, and through flat yellow, but it is mostly a photograph-led museum site.
Measured: 3 px median border, 3 hues, 0.24 uppercase share, and no rounded corners; the chromatic share is 0.04 because photographs and white dominate.
borrow: Frame an image or a logo with black lines that overshoot the corners instead of a closed box.

references.title: Mondrian Generator (mondriangenerator.com)
references.lede: A browser tool that draws random Mondrian-like compositions, with controls in black-outlined boxes and flat yellow and black buttons.
references.summary: Generated black-line compositions beside square, outlined control panels with yellow and black buttons.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The first capture with a 3-second wait showed an empty canvas; the kept capture waited 9 seconds. A cookie bar covers the bottom 35 px.

styles.note: Borderline: the page exists to produce the style, and its controls use square black-outlined boxes and flat yellow and black, but the composition itself is a generated image and the page chrome uses thin outlines.

observed: A black top bar holds the title “Mondrian Generator” in white bold sans-serif and small navigation links.
At left, two white panels with thin black outlines hold settings: black label cells, light gray option cells, and flat yellow buttons with black text.
At right, a generated composition in a portrait format shows many black-outlined rectangles, several filled red, yellow, blue, or black, the rest white.
The page background is a light gray with a faint texture; no control has rounded corners.
A dark cookie bar with a blue Accept button runs along the bottom edge.
interpretation: The generated compositions follow the grammar loosely: they subdivide into many small cells, which is closer to Mondrian’s 1918–1919 grids than to the few large planes of 1920–1921.
The composition is drawn as an image (image share 0.71), so computed styles see only the controls: 1 px outlines, 2 hues, and a 0.08 round share from a few small elements.
borrow: Put tool controls in square cells with 1 px black outlines and one yellow action color; keep the working area white.

references.title: Morire typeface
references.lede: Harriet Goren’s sketchy, vibrating typeface, drawn over one weekend in an experimental type workshop and soon used throughout Ray Gun.
references.summary: A grunge font of sketch lines and shadows, named after a Monteverdi song and sold by T-26. Harriet Goren, c. 1993–94.

source.label: Sharan Shetty, “The Rise And Fall Of Grunge Typography”, The Awl (2012), archived copy

evidence.note: Based on The Awl’s interview with Goren. The only image found, The Awl’s sample, is 600 × 103 px, too small to describe the letterforms. T-26 stopped selling the font in 2004, so no current specimen was found.

styles.note: Clear example by documentation: The Awl and Wikipedia name it one of the signature grunge fonts, and Carson used it in Ray Gun.

context: Goren told The Awl she designed the whole typeface over one weekend in 1993 or 1994, in an experimental typography course taught by P. Scott Makela at the Center for Creative Imaging in Camden, Maine. [The Awl](https://web.archive.org/web/20150925150838/http://www.theawl.com/2012/08/grunge-typography).

Makela suggested she send it to David Carson; a few months later she found Morire “emblazoned all over the pages” of Ray Gun, credited and used on a cover. [The Awl](https://web.archive.org/web/20150925150838/http://www.theawl.com/2012/08/grunge-typography).

The Awl says the design was inspired by Monteverdi’s song “Sì ch’io vorrei morire” and is “all sketch and shadows, as though the letters are in perpetual and subtle vibration”. [The Awl](https://web.archive.org/web/20150925150838/http://www.theawl.com/2012/08/grunge-typography).

T-26 distributed Morire and stopped in 2004. Wikipedia, citing The Awl, lists Morire with Hat Nguyen’s Droplet and Eric Lin’s Tema Cantante as “signature grunge fonts”. [The Awl](https://web.archive.org/web/20150925150838/http://www.theawl.com/2012/08/grunge-typography); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge#Graphic_design).
interpretation: Morire shows how the style spread: a quickly made, deliberately rough font moved from a workshop to Ray Gun to a commercial foundry within months.
borrow: Draw display letters as clusters of loose sketch lines, so that their edges seem to vibrate.
next: Find a specimen or Ray Gun page that shows Morire at 800 px or more, and record the issue that used it on the cover.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The typeface is by Harriet Goren.

references.title: Morris & Co. Sussex armchair
references.lede: A light, ebonized country armchair with turned spindles and a rush seat, sold by Morris & Co. as cheap, plain furniture.
references.summary: Ebonized turned spindles and rails with a rush seat. Morris & Co., late 19th century.

evidence.note: Inspected the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum photograph of 2004-29-2 through its [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22Sussex%22_Chair,_late_19th_century_(CH_18700699).jpg) (2848 × 3457 px; viewed at 1280 px wide). Cooper Hewitt’s site was not opened; the object data come from the Commons record. The museum credits only Morris & Co., not a designer.

styles.note: Partial fit: Morris & Co. furniture that shows the movement’s plain, vernacular side, with no pattern.

context: Cooper Hewitt describes an ebonized beech armchair with turned back sections, supports, and legs, and a rush seat set into the frame; 95 × 54.5 × 56 cm; late 19th century; made by Morris & Co.; Gift of Arthur Sanderson & Sons, Ltd. [Commons record of the Cooper Hewitt image](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22Sussex%22_Chair,_late_19th_century_(CH_18700699).jpg).
observed: The frame is thin, turned wood stained black, with fine ring turnings on the posts and legs.
The back has three horizontal rails over a row of thin spindles; the middle spindle is crossed by a short bar with a small bead.
The arms are straight rails ending in round knobs, carried on short baluster-turned supports.
The seat is woven rush in natural straw colour, inside a square frame with black corner blocks.
There is no carving, inlay, or pattern.
interpretation: The chair shows that Morris & Co. sold plain, vernacular goods alongside its dense patterns. It belongs to the movement’s ideals rather than to the patterned graphic core that this record describes.
It is close to the plain [Ashbee kettle](ref:ashbee-silver-kettle-1900): honest material and structure with no applied ornament.
borrow: Use thin, repeated vertical lines, like spindles, as a quiet structural rhythm.
Pair near-black with one natural material colour, such as straw.

images.alt: Black turned-wood armchair with thin spindles and rails in the back, straight arms ending in round knobs, and a woven natural rush seat, on a grey background.
images.caption: Morris & Co., “Sussex” armchair, late 19th century. Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, 2004-29-2. [Commons copy of the museum photograph](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22Sussex%22_Chair,_late_19th_century_(CH_18700699).jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons tags the Cooper Hewitt image {{PD-old-100-1923}}. The chair is a late 19th-century design whose makers died more than 100 years ago, and it was made before 1900, so it is in the public domain in the United Kingdom and the United States. Cooper Hewitt’s own image terms were not checked.

references.title: MTV International rebrand, 2015
references.lede: MTV’s international on-air identity of June 2015, which critics described as pastel, badly 3D-modelled, and borrowed from vaporwave and seapunk.
references.summary: Broadcast identity with pastel 3D idents, drawn from Tumblr microcultures. June 2015.

source.label: Motherboard: What the Hell Is MTV’s New Rebrand About?

creator.name: MTV International (creative lead Sean Saylor, per Motherboard)

evidence.note: Relies on Motherboard and Wikipedia. No still or video of the idents was inspected.

styles.note: The best-documented corporate adoption: Wikipedia says the rebrand was “heavily inspired by vaporwave and seapunk.” Its appearance is documented, not observed here.

context: Clinton Nguyen, Motherboard, June 25, 2015: the new look is “pastel-swatched, bad 3D modeling, and visual features drawn directly from Tumblr-born microcultures,” with the slogan changed to “I am my MTV.” Sean Saylor, MTV’s vice-president of creative and marketing, is quoted on refreshing the look constantly. [Motherboard](https://www.vice.com/en/article/53989n/what-the-hell-is-mtvs-new-rebrand-about).

Wikipedia: on the same day that MTV International introduced the rebrand, Tumblr launched Tumblr TV “with an explicitly MTV-styled visual spin.” Motherboard’s Jordan Pearson wrote that the style’s cynical impulse is “co-opted and erased.” [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave).
interpretation: The point at which the style became a brand look for the kind of company it satirised. The criticism is part of the record: a corporate use of vaporwave reads as either knowing or tone-deaf.
next: Find a still or archived ident at useful size and upgrade the evidence to observed.

rights.statement: Copyrighted broadcast identity. No image is stored here.

references.title: Musée de l’École de Nancy website
references.lede: The Nancy School museum’s site pairs a flared Art Nouveau wordmark with a soft sage-green panel and photographs of Majorelle’s villa and collections.
references.summary: Flared Art Nouveau wordmark on sage green, beside a photograph of the Villa Majorelle.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. The request redirected to /accueil.

styles.note: Borderline: the wordmark is drawn in Art Nouveau letterforms and the palette is moss and olive green, but the layout and body type are a plain modern sans-serif grid.

observed: A sage-green panel fills the left half of the hero. It holds “MUSÉE DE L’ÉCOLE DE NANCY” in dark teal capitals with flared, curving strokes and an unusual M and N.
Below the wordmark, a thin dark rule and a menu of capitals with arrows in a plain sans-serif.

references.title: Museu del Modernisme de Barcelona website
references.lede: The Barcelona Modernisme museum frames its page between two columns of trencadís mosaic and uses a looping, swelling MM monogram.
references.summary: Page framed by orange and red flower-mosaic columns, with a curving MM monogram and gray condensed type.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page.

styles.note: Borderline: the Catalan branch. The mosaic columns and the looping monogram carry the style, but the colours are saturated red and orange and the type is a condensed sans-serif.

observed: Two vertical columns of broken-tile mosaic in orange, red, and yellow with white flowers frame the page at left and right.
The logo is an MM monogram of two looping, swelling strokes in white and red.
“MUSEUM OF MODERNISM BARCELONA” is set in white and red sans-serif capitals on a gray band; the navigation uses a condensed gothic face.
The hero banner shows two stained-glass women with flowers in the Mucha manner, around a red panel with white sans-serif type.
Below, thin gray rules and a carousel of cards.

Measured: square boxes, 3 px borders on 68% of boxes, few shadows, three colour families, and accent chroma 0.63, above the fingerprint’s muted range.
borrow: Frame a page between two narrow ornamental columns and keep the content column plain.
Draw a monogram from two looping strokes that swell and thin.

references.title: Nausea book jacket, New Classics series
references.lede: Alvin Lustig draws a knot of loose calligraphic strokes twice, once in black and once in white, slightly offset on an olive jacket.
references.summary: Offset black and white brush strokes and lowercase italic serif titles on olive. Alvin Lustig for New Directions, c. 1952.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Nausea.jpg (photograph by Karen Horton)

evidence.note: Inspected, in the scratchpad only, the 1280 px Commons rendition of Karen Horton’s photograph of a copy of the jacket (original 2478 × 2859 px). The copy shows edge wear at the top. No museum copy was checked.

styles.note: Partial fit: Lustig’s New Directions jackets are central to the style’s graphic core, and this one shows hand-drawn marks and an off-register double image, but it uses only olive, black, and white.

context: The Commons caption credits the jacket design to Alvin Lustig for the New Classics series published by New Directions, c. 1952. The photograph is by Karen Horton and is licensed CC BY 2.0. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nausea.jpg).

Lustig lived from 1915 to 1955. [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q4738169). Sartre’s novel was first published in French in 1938; Lloyd Alexander translated it into English. [Wikipedia: Nausea (novel)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausea_(novel)).
observed: The jacket is flat olive-brown.
“nausea” at upper left and “sartre” at lower left are lowercase italic serif in off-white.

The center holds an abstract knot of strokes: straight bars, hooks, arcs, and a V shape. Each stroke is drawn twice, once in black and once in off-white, with the two copies offset by a few millimetres.
“lustig” is signed in small black script at the right of the knot.
There is no frame or rule; the strokes float on the olive ground.
interpretation: The offset black and white copies read like a two-color print out of register, the same effect the style uses as overprint.
The lowercase italic title and the loose marks show how Lustig paired quiet book type with expressive, hand-made imagery.
borrow: Draw a mark twice in two colors and offset the copies slightly to suggest a print out of register.
Set titles in lowercase italic serif and let the image do the loud work.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is CC BY 2.0 (Karen Horton), but the jacket design itself has not been shown to be in the public domain: its US publication, notice, and renewal status were not checked.

references.title: Neumorphic for SwiftUI
references.lede: A March 2020 SwiftUI package whose demo is a catalogue of raised and pressed shapes in light and dark modes.
references.summary: Costa Chung’s open-source SwiftUI modifiers for soft outer and inner shadows.

evidence.note: Inspected the README demo image (1000 × 800) hosted on user-images.githubusercontent.com. Licence and dates read through the GitHub API.

styles.note: A clear specimen sheet of the style: squares, circles, rings, and buttons raised from and pressed into one surface, in a light and a dark version.

context: The README says it is “a SwiftUI utility to build Neumorphism Soft UI”, written because in SwiftUI “we can’t easily create inner shadow”.
MIT License. It had about 1,000 GitHub stars on 2026-09-28. Later versions add text fields, sliders, pickers, and accessibility helpers for contrast.
observed: Two iPhone frames side by side: one pale blue-gray, one dark charcoal.
In each, a pressed square and a pressed circle, a raised ring and a pressed ring, three small squares (raised, pressed, flat), a wide “Soft Button”, and a round heart button.
The light version has white highlights at upper left and blue-gray shadows at lower right; the dark version uses a slightly lighter edge and a black shadow.
One red circular button with a white heart is the only color. Text is gray system sans-serif.
interpretation: The paired light and dark sheets show that the effect holds on a dark surface only when the highlight is a lighter gray, not white.

rights.statement: The code is MIT-licensed, but the demo image is hosted outside the repository and includes an iPhone frame, so it is not stored.

references.title: Neumorphism Day and Night
references.lede: A Webflow experiment with raised buttons and a day/night toggle under a rising yellow sun.
references.summary: Webflow experiment: raised gray buttons and tabs, a soft toggle, and a white content card.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline. The buttons, toggle, and inactive tabs are clear neumorphic shapes on a pale gray surface, but the main content card is plain white with a drop shadow.

observed: A pale gray page with a large yellow sun rising behind a curved horizon at the top.
Five raised buttons in the page color (Launch, Menu, Apple, Play, and an icon button), each with a white glow above and a gray shadow below.
A soft pill toggle labeled “Day”, and three tabs: the active one white, the others raised gray.
A large white card with placeholder rich text fills the lower half.

Measured: shadows on 87 % of boxes (median offset 9.9 px, median blur 15 px, none hard), borders on 33 %, median radius 20 px.

references.lede: The demo of a 2020 open-source Bootstrap kit, set on a pale blue-gray surface with raised buttons and round icon wells.
references.summary: Themesberg’s Bootstrap UI kit demo: raised buttons and round icon badges on one blue-gray surface.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear. Buttons, the logo tile, and round icon badges are the page color and rise with a white highlight and a gray shadow. Many components also carry a faint 1 px border.

context: Source code: [themesberg/neumorphism-ui-bootstrap](https://github.com/themesberg/neumorphism-ui-bootstrap), created on 7 May 2020, MIT License.
observed: A pale blue-gray page (about #e6e6ee in the screenshot). A square “N” logo tile, the “Upgrade to PRO”, “Docs v1.0”, and “Download” buttons are raised in the same color.
Three large round badges with dark icons rise from the surface above “Over 200 components”, “10+ sections”, and “5 example pages”.

A dark “Featured on Product Hunt” badge covers the lower right corner. A small GitHub star button shows 893.

Measured: shadows on 71 % of boxes (median offset 4.2 px, median blur 7 px, none hard), borders on 68 %, median radius 8.8 px.

references.title: Neumorphism.io
references.lede: The CSS shadow generator that spread the style’s recipe, itself built on one pale gray surface.
references.summary: Adam Giebl’s neumorphism generator: a demo shape, sliders, and the paired box-shadow code.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear. The demo shape and the control panel share the gray page color and rise from it with a white glow and a gray shadow. The tool is also the most-used source of the style’s CSS.

context: The source is on GitHub as [adamgiebl/neumorphism](https://github.com/adamgiebl/neumorphism), created on 29 December 2019, BSD-3-Clause, about 6,200 stars on 2026-09-28.
observed: A pale gray page (#e0e0e0). A large rounded square in the same gray sits at the left with a white glow at upper left and a gray shadow at lower right.
A raised panel in the same gray holds sliders for Size, Radius, Distance, Intensity, and Blur, and four shape buttons (flat, concave, convex, pressed).
A dark navy code box shows `box-shadow: 20px 20px 60px #bebebe, -20px -20px 60px #ffffff`.
Headings and labels are a navy sans-serif. A small dark GitHub button at top right shows 6,162 stars.
interpretation: The generator states the style’s rule as code: two shadows with equal and opposite offsets and a blur three times the offset. [CSS-Tricks](ref:css-tricks-neumorphism-and-css-2020) names it as the generator of the trend.
Only the demo and the panel carry shadows; the text below is plain, so the page-level shadow share is low.
Measured: shadows on 11 % of boxes (median offset 28.3 px, median blur 60 px, none hard), borders on 25 %, median radius 6 px.
borrow: Set the blur to two or three times the offset and derive both shadow colors from the surface color, as the generator does.

images.caption: First viewport of [neumorphism.io](https://neumorphism.io/).

references.title: Neuropol typeface
references.lede: Ray Larabie’s wide, rounded-square techno face, first given away as freeware in 1996 and widely used in the years around 2000.
references.summary: Very wide techno sans-serif built from rounded squares, with cut horizontal strokes. Ray Larabie, 1996.

source.label: Typodermic Fonts: Public domain fonts, Neuropol

evidence.note: Inspected Typodermic’s specimen image for Neuropol (1800 × 160) from its public-domain page, and the specimen for its chrome variant Neurochrome (1352 × 120).

styles.note: Clear: the wide techno type of the grammar, made in the period and spread as free software. Its companion Neurochrome renders the same letters as 3D chrome.

context: Typodermic dates Neuropol to 1996 and says the design was influenced by Brendel Type Studio’s Digital Sans (1974). Its sister face Neurochrome (1997) was Neuropol “rendered in Lightwave, a 3D modeling program, applying extrusion, beveling, and reflections to make it look like chrome”. [Typodermic: Public domain fonts](https://typodermicfonts.com/public-domain/#neuropol).

Fonts In Use calls Neuropol “a wide, starkly futuristic typeface” based on rounded squares, like the earlier techno fonts Microgramma, Digital, and Chimes; it was redrawn as Neuropol X in 2004. [Fonts In Use: Neuropol](https://fontsinuse.com/typefaces/175126/neuropol).

Larabie released his Larabie Fonts freeware from 1996. A modified Neuropol was used in the wordmark of the 2006 Winter Olympics in Turin. [Wikipedia: Ray Larabie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Larabie).
observed: The letters are very wide and low. Round letters such as C, D, and O are built from rounded rectangles with straight sides.
Stroke ends are cut flat; the horizontal strokes of E and F stop short of the stem ends and look like separate bars.
The A is a pointed triangle without a crossbar at the apex, and the lowercase a, b, c, d, and e repeat the rounded-rectangle bowl.
Strokes have one even weight, and spacing is generous.
In the Neurochrome specimen the same forms are extruded and bevelled, with black-and-white reflections that read as chrome.
interpretation: Neuropol is the Y2K techno heading face in its free, amateur-web form. Its spread through freeware explains why the wide rounded-square look was everywhere around 2000, on game menus, club flyers, and personal websites.
Neurochrome shows the typical Y2K move of turning a flat face into a 3D chrome render.
borrow: Set short headings in a wide rounded-square face, uppercase, with extra letter spacing.
For a hero word, add a chrome treatment: a vertical silver gradient with a hard highlight line near the middle.

images.alt: Typeface specimen in black on white: the letters A B C D E F and a b c d e set in Neuropol, very wide letters built from rounded rectangles with flat cut stroke ends.
images.caption: Neuropol specimen from [Typodermic Fonts’ public-domain page](https://typodermicfonts.com/public-domain/#neuropol), resized. The font is dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0.

rights.statement: Typodermic states that Neuropol and its other early fonts are “released under the official CC0 1.0 Universal public-domain dedication, with no rights reserved”. The stored specimen image shows only the font’s glyphs and comes from the same public-domain page.

references.title: New York World’s Fair poster by Joseph Binder
references.lede: Joseph Binder’s poster for the 1939 fair: the Trylon and Perisphere in airbrushed light, with a streamlined train and liner on the horizon and slanted capitals.
references.summary: Trylon and Perisphere in searchlights over a red streamlined train and liner, with forward-slanting capitals. Joseph Binder, 1938–39.

source.label: Christie’s: Joseph Binder, New York World’s Fair 1939

references.made: 1938 (dated 20 July 1938 on Commons), for the 1939 fair

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_Binder_New_York_World%27s_Fair_1939_The_World_of_Tomorrow.jpg), a scan from a Christie’s lot, at 1280 × 1939 px. I did not open the Christie’s page.

styles.note: Partial fit: the streamlined train and liner, the white speed swoosh, and the forward-slanting capitals are streamline; the vertical searchlight composition is Art Deco.
Late Art Deco poster: a monumental vertical axis, radiating searchlight beams, and airbrushed gradients on deep blue.

context: Poster for the 1939 New York World’s Fair, whose theme was “The World of Tomorrow”. The printer’s line reads “Made in U.S.A. by … Grinnell Litho. Co. Inc. N.Y.C.” (read on the scan). Commons dates the design 20 July 1938. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_Binder_New_York_World%27s_Fair_1939_The_World_of_Tomorrow.jpg).
observed: The ground is deep blue, lighter toward the bottom.
A tall yellow and white spire (the Trylon) rises at left of center beside a large glowing yellow-white sphere (the Perisphere) on a pale green-blue mound.
Pale blue searchlight beams cross the sky in diagonals; a formation of small red aircraft flies at upper left.
A white swoosh curls around the base of the sphere like a speed trail.
Along a red horizon line, a long streamlined red train runs left and a red ocean liner with rows of lit portholes sits at right; a skyline of lit windows rises at far left.
“NEW YORK WORLD’S FAIR” is set in white condensed sans-serif capitals that slant forward; “THE WORLD OF TOMORROW” and “1939” below are in pale blue.
The small line “© N.Y.W.F.” is printed at lower left.
interpretation: The poster places streamlined transport at the base of an Art Deco monument: the vertical beams belong to Deco, while the horizontal train, liner, and slanted capitals carry the streamline idea of speed. It fits the style record’s view of Streamline Moderne as a late branch of Art Deco.
borrow: Slant condensed capitals forward and let one line of them run the full width.
Draw a thin horizontal band of vehicles or shapes along a horizon line under a large calm field.

images.alt: Poster on deep blue: a tall yellow-white spire and a glowing sphere lit by crossing searchlights, red aircraft at upper left, a red streamlined train and ocean liner on the horizon, and the slanted words New York World's Fair, The World of Tomorrow, 1939.
images.caption: Joseph Binder, New York World’s Fair 1939. Scan from a Christie’s lot via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joseph_Binder_New_York_World%27s_Fair_1939_The_World_of_Tomorrow.jpg), marked PD-US-not renewed.

rights.statement: Commons tags the scan PD-US-not renewed: the poster was first published in the United States (printed by Grinnell Litho, New York) and, per that tag, its copyright was not renewed. The poster carries a “© N.Y.W.F.” notice, so its public-domain status rests on non-renewal, which I did not check in the renewal records. Binder died in 1972; because the country of origin is the United States, the Austrian term does not apply. The lead curator should confirm or downgrade to tier D.

identifiers.commons: File:Joseph Binder New York World's Fair 1939 The World of Tomorrow.jpg

references.title: News at 11 cover art
references.lede: Cat System Corp.’s 9/11 album: a VHS-degraded American flag in a rounded TV frame, with a Japanese obi strip down the left edge.
references.summary: VHS-smeared flag in a CRT frame, Japanese obi strip, weather-channel logos. 2016.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 × 1200 cover on the album’s [Bandcamp page](https://catsystemcorp.bandcamp.com/album/news-at-11), in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The creator’s name comes from the Commons file [Cat System Corp. - News at 11 cassette artwork (flag only).jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_System_Corp._-_News_at_11_cassette_artwork_(flag_only).jpg).

styles.note: Partial fit, from the signalwave and mallsoft branches: VHS degradation, a CRT frame, and Japanese text are clear, but the palette is dark red, white, and blue instead of pastel.

context: Wikipedia: “One vaporwave album that directly interrogates 9/11 is News at 11 (2016) by Cat System Corp.” The label is Geometric Lullaby; the release date is September 11, 2016. [Wikipedia: Vaporwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave); [Wikipedia: News at 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_at_11_(album)).
observed: A waving American flag, smeared and colour-shifted like a worn VHS frame, fills a rounded-rectangle screen shape on black.
NEWS AT 11 sits below in white, narrow, pixel-like capitals.
A white obi strip on the left carries vertical katakana, a small flag, CATCORP and LOCAL 11 WEATHER logos, track lists in serif capitals, and the Geometric Lullaby logo.
interpretation: It shows the style’s darker side: the same devices (Japanese packaging, broadcast artefacts) used for mourning instead of play. The obi strip imitates Japanese import records.
borrow: Add a narrow vertical strip of small, dense label text beside a large image to imitate an import-record obi.

rights.statement: Copyrighted album art. No image is stored here.

references.title: Newsstand, iOS 5 and 6
references.lede: A special iOS folder that showed downloaded magazines and newspapers on wooden shelves.
references.summary: Wooden shelves for magazines and newspapers. Apple, iOS 5 to iOS 8, 2011–2015.
references.made: Introduced with iOS 5 (October 2011); shelves replaced in iOS 7

evidence.note: Inspected a 960 px copy of [File:Apple Newsstand on iOS 6 on an iPhone 3GS.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_Newsstand_on_iOS_6_on_an_iPhone_3GS.jpg) (Delicje, 2021, CC BY-SA 4.0), a slightly blurred photo of the empty Newsstand folder on iOS 6. Not stored.

styles.note: Newsstand turned a folder into a shop shelf of light wood, the same bookshelf metaphor as iBooks.

context: Newsstand “emulated a newsagent’s shop, with virtual shelves that held and presented each newspaper and magazine that had been downloaded.” It was “a visual shelf accessible directly on the iOS home screen, similar in style to iBooks,” available from iOS 5. [Wikipedia: Newsstand (software)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsstand_(software)).
observed: The open folder shows two shelves of pale, grained wood with a light front lip.
A pale header strip carries the name “Newsstand” in dark bold type and a small beveled “Store” button.
The Newsstand icon is a small set of empty wooden shelves in a rounded square.
An empty-state message sits on the shelf as a pale blue card.
interpretation: A folder with no physical counterpart is given one: a shop shelf. The material carries the meaning, so the wood covers the full width.
borrow: Show an empty collection as an empty shelf with a single card on it.

rights.statement: The photograph is CC BY-SA 4.0 by Delicje, but its main subject is Apple’s copyrighted interface. No image is stored here.

references.title: Nicecard
references.lede: A Webflow landing page for a fictional credit card, in the dark variant of the style.
references.summary: Dark Webflow landing page: raised charcoal pill buttons, orange headline, and floating 3D cards.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A “Made in Webflow” badge sits at the lower right.

styles.note: Borderline. The navigation and hero pills are dark neumorphic shapes (charcoal on charcoal, lit edge above, dark shadow below), but the main image is floating 3D cards and many elements carry outlines.

observed: A charcoal page. “The future of credit cards is nice ;)” is set in large bold orange sans-serif; the body is lorem ipsum.
Navigation pills (Home, Features, Pricing) and the “View pricing” button are charcoal on charcoal with a faint light edge and a dark shadow; “Home” has an orange outline.
“Discover features” is an orange gradient pill. White App Store and Google Play badges sit below.
Three 3D credit cards (black, silver, orange) float at the right with glossy highlights.
interpretation: Evidence for the dark variant on the web, comparable to the [CRED app](ref:cred-app-synth-neumorphic-ui). The measurement finds outlines on most boxes, so the fingerprint rejects it.
Measured: shadows on 37 % of boxes (median offset 5.7 px, median blur 6 px, none hard), borders on 82 %, median radius 0 px.

references.title: Nightwave Plaza
references.lede: An online vaporwave radio whose player is a Windows 9x desktop over a faded anime still of stacked CRT computers.
references.summary: Windows 9x player windows and taskbar over a muted pink-and-teal anime still of old computers.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: the site calls itself “Online Vaporwave Radio”, and it combines Windows 9x chrome with a faded 1980s-style anime image in dusty pink and teal. The CSS bevels pass the shadow and radius metrics.

observed: The background is a muted anime still of stacked beige computer units and CRT monitors, one labelled TOSHIBA EX-500, with orange, pink, and teal screens showing large pixel characters.
A grey Windows 9x player window with Play and like buttons and a pink checkered album thumbnail sits in the centre, partly covered by a News dialog with a navy title bar and a Close button.
A grey Windows 9x taskbar runs along the bottom with task buttons and a clock.
interpretation: The measurement finds hard shadows on 56% of boxes with a 1.4 px median offset and zero radius: the same bevel values as [Agora Road](ref:agora-road-website). The pastel colour is all in the background image, so gradient share is 0.
borrow: Put a faded, low-contrast image behind crisp, unfaded Windows 9x windows; the contrast between the two keeps the text readable.

references.title: Nine Collages: The New Graphics by Weingart
references.lede: Weingart’s poster and order form for his own series of nine hand-printed collages, laid out as a sheet of framed panels around one large collage.
references.summary: Black on white: a grid of framed collages with stepped lines, dot patterns, arcs, and crosses, and a vertical order form. Wolfgang Weingart, 1974–75.

source.label: Letterform Archive: Legacies of Swiss Style, Part 2—Wolfgang Weingart

evidence.note: Inspected Letterform Archive’s photograph of the Archive’s copy (2496 × 3000) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example. The small collages collect the style’s marks: spaced letters, stepped lines, dot fields, heavy bars, and halftone fragments.

context: Letterform Archive says the Nine Collages series came from darkroom experiments of the 1960s and early 1970s with “hand-cut films, barely-legible type, and the deliberate overlap of halftones to produce moiré effects”. [Letterform Archive](https://letterformarchive.org/news/from-the-collection-legacies-of-swiss-style-part-2-wolfgang-weingart/).
The poster text offers the collages, 59 × 49 cm, for sale by post from Basel, and its biography says Weingart taught typography at the School of Design in Basel from 1968.
observed: The title is set in heavy grotesque capitals across the top: “NINE COLLAGES: THE NEW GRAPHICS BY WEINGART”.
Thin rules divide the sheet into panels of different sizes. Each small panel shows one collage and a bold caption such as “COLLAGE 5/1974”.
Collage 6 is made of spaced letters and dots (“1 8 9-1”, “E”, “T”, “H”) scattered on white. Collage 5 has a stepped line, a small grid, arcs, and “STO?”.
The large central collage is a black flame-like shape that holds halftone photographs of a cemetery, a garden, and a woman, with black dots, short rays, and a white cross.
The sale text uses bold capitals with a much larger price. The order form at right is set vertically, with “Order Form” in large type.
The biography at the bottom left is set in a typewriter face.
interpretation: The poster shows that the style can use a plain framed grid as a container, as long as what happens inside the frames breaks it.
The typewriter biography is one of the few monospaced passages in Weingart’s work here; it is a small caption, not the main voice.
borrow: Frame small experiments in a grid of thin rules, with one bold caption under each.
Set a form or call to action vertically along one edge.
Scatter a few spaced letters and dots in open white space as a quiet panel next to dense ones.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Photograph by Letterform Archive. Weingart died in 2021, so the design is in copyright.

references.title: Ninety Parallel Sinusoids with Linearly Increasing Period
references.lede: A. Michael Noll’s early computer-generated image: ninety parallel wave lines whose period shortens across the sheet, made to approximate Bridget Riley’s Current.
references.summary: Ninety black sine curves stacked in parallel, with waves that tighten from left to right. A. Michael Noll, Bell Labs era, 1964.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its print, E.34-2011 (1210 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: A computer plot built to reproduce the op effect of Riley’s wave paintings: parallel black lines on white whose period changes by steps.

context: The V&A describes a photographic print of a computer-generated image first created in 1964, and quotes Noll: “The top sinusoid was expressed mathematically and then repeated again and again. The result closely approximates the op-art painting ‘Current’ by Bridget Riley.” [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1193786/).
Riley’s *Current* (1964) is the painting reproduced on the cover of [The Responsive Eye](ref:the-responsive-eye-catalogue-1965).
observed: About ninety thin black curves run in parallel across a white sheet, in a block with a white margin.
Toward the left the curves are nearly straight; toward the right the waves become shorter and steeper.
Where the curves turn steeply at the right, the gaps between them narrow and the lines seem to shimmer.
There is no text, no tone, and no colour.
interpretation: Noll shows that the Riley effect is a rule: one curve, repeated with a fixed offset, with a period that changes linearly. This makes it the most direct reference for generating op patterns in code.
The image sits where op art meets early computer art, and that link is a natural fit for screen design.
borrow: Generate an op field from one function: repeat a sine curve with a fixed vertical offset and shorten its period across the width.
Keep a wide white margin around the line block so that the field reads as an object.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is by a living artist, and the V&A image is not openly licensed.

references.title: Nintendo website, 2001
references.lede: Nintendo’s home page of August 2001, framed as a periwinkle console with rounded corners, dark side rails, and pixel-font labels.
references.summary: Periwinkle device-like frame with rounded corners, dark rails, pixel type, and orange capsule buttons around game promotions.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. All images loaded.

styles.note: Clear: the page is built as a device, with a rounded periwinkle casing, dark control rails, pixel labels, and small capsule buttons. It has little chrome. The page draws its graphics with images, so the CSS fingerprint measures flat, square, unshadowed boxes (see the style page). Judge it by the rubric.

observed: The whole page sits in one periwinkle frame with rounded outer corners and angled cut-outs, like the housing of a handheld device, on a light gray ground.
Dark charcoal rails with dotted texture run across the top and down both sides and hold the navigation.
Main navigation (“GAMES”, “SYSTEMS”, “NEWS”, “NSIDER”, “DOWNLOADS”) is in orange pixel-style capitals; side labels such as “TOP TEN” and “PLAYER’S CHOICE” run vertically.
Small controls are capsule-shaped orange and gray buttons with pixel labels, such as “CODE BANK”, “GAME FINDER”, and “SUBMIT”.
Content panels have rounded ends and stacked list rows, each with a small icon and an orange arrow tab.
Game art and a purple Game Boy Advance fill the panels; Mario stands at top left with a pixel speech bubble.
interpretation: This is the style’s “interface as device” layout on the web: the page is drawn as a piece of hardware, with rails, ports, and buttons.
Measured: no CSS gradients, shadows, or radii, because the frame is sliced images; the pixel palette has three hues.
borrow: Frame a whole page as a device housing: one rounded outer shape, dark rails for navigation, and capsule buttons.
Set small labels in a pixel font and run side labels vertically.

images.alt: Archived Nintendo home page: a periwinkle, round-cornered frame with dark dotted rails and orange pixel navigation, a Super Smash Bros. Melee banner, lists of news with icons, featured game sites, a poll, and a Pokémon Crystal sweepstakes panel.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20010822153959/http://www.nintendo.com/).

references.title: NN/g, “Flat Design: Its Origins, Its Problems, and Why Flat 2.0 Is Better for Users”
references.lede: A usability firm’s definition of flat design, its dating, and its main usability cost.
references.summary: Nielsen Norman Group, 2015: flat design defined by the absence of 3D effects, dated to about 2012, criticised for weak click signifiers.

evidence.note: Article text read on 2026-09-28. The page metadata gives the author (Kate Moran) and the publication date (27 September 2015, modified 6 January 2018). The article’s screenshots were not inspected at full size.

styles.note: An authoritative UX source that defines the style, dates it, names Metro as its main origin, and names flat 2.0 and Material Design as its successors.

context: Definition: flat design is “defined by the absence of glossy or three-dimensional visual effects in the graphical elements of a web page”, and is “commonly interpreted as a reactionary movement against 3D, skeuomorphic, and realistic design styles”.

Origins: “The release of Microsoft’s Metro design language and Windows 8 in 2011 was particularly influential in popularizing flat design.” Microsoft’s documentation called the style “authentically digital”.
It uses Apple’s home page as a benchmark: glossy tabs in 2007, a glossy bar in 2012, and an “entirely flat” navigation bar in 2015.
Main problem: “the lack of signifiers on clickable elements”, which causes click uncertainty.

It names “semi flat”, “almost flat”, or “flat 2.0” as a later branch with subtle shadows and layers, calls long shadows (popular around 2013) “flat 2.0 gone wrong”, and calls Google’s Material Design “flat 2.0 with the right priorities”.
interpretation: The source for the style’s dating, its reaction against skeuomorphism, and the rule not to remove every signifier from links and buttons. Its account of flat 2.0 supports treating Material Design as a related branch.

rights.statement: © Nielsen Norman Group. Link and quotation only.

references.title: Notes on iPhone, to iOS 6
references.lede: Apple’s iPhone notes app as a yellow ruled pad with a leather top and handwriting-style type, used until 2013.
references.summary: Lined, textured paper, a leather binding strip, and Marker Felt type. Apple, until 2013.
references.made: Until 2013 (Wikipedia); the Mac version followed in OS X Mountain Lion (2012)

evidence.note: Based on Wikipedia and NN/g. The NN/g article shows an image of the early iOS notepad, but it was not saved or measured here.

styles.note: A clear object metaphor: a paper notepad with ruled lines, textured paper, and a leather binding.

context: “Until 2013, both applications used a strongly skeuomorphic interface, with a lined, textured paper design; the Mountain Lion version placed this inside a leather folder.” Notes could use three fonts: Noteworthy, Marker Felt, and Helvetica. [Wikipedia: Notes (Apple)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notes_(Apple)).
NN/g: “This early iOS notepad design mimics a traditional paper notepad with textured lines and leather binding.” [NN/g: Skeuomorphism](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/skeuomorphism/).
interpretation: The handwriting face is part of the metaphor. The style record keeps it to places where the object would carry handwriting.
next: Inspect a large screenshot of iOS 6 Notes and record the paper color and rule spacing.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Obey Giant website
references.lede: Shepard Fairey’s studio site opens with a full red panel of white condensed capitals beside a black-and-white photograph of one of his murals.
references.summary: A red half-screen with the slogan in white condensed capitals, a black navigation bar, and a desaturated street photograph.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the first viewport. The measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: a contemporary propaganda aesthetic that Wikipedia traces to Russian Constructivism. The hero has the red field, white capitals, and black-and-white photograph, but no diagonal, and the featured mural brings in several hues.

context: Wikipedia states that Fairey “began appropriating the Russian Constructivist style utilized in Soviet-era propaganda during his time in San Diego”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepard_Fairey).
observed: The left half of the first viewport is a solid red panel. It carries “MANUFACTURING QUALITY DISSENT SINCE 1989” in large white condensed capitals, a small kicker in the same face, and a white outlined button “READ LATEST NEWS”.
The right half is a black-and-white photograph of a building, looking up at a steep angle, with a colored mural that reads “PEACE”. Only the mural is in color.
A dark bar across the top holds the star logo in a circle and the navigation in small gray condensed capitals.
Corners are square. There are no shadows except a dark overlay on the navigation bar.
interpretation: The site passes five of seven fingerprint metrics: one hue, 19% chromatic area, 38% uppercase text, square corners, and few shadows. It fails `type.headingWeight` because the condensed display face (Knockout) is set at weight 400, although it reads as heavy, and `color.gradientShare` (0.08) because of the overlay on the photograph.
The upward view of the building echoes the steep camera angles of Rodchenko’s photography, but the page itself stays orthogonal.
borrow: Split the first screen into a solid red text panel and a black-and-white photograph.
Set a two-line slogan in condensed capitals and a single outlined button, with nothing else in the panel.

images.alt: Obey Giant home page: a solid red left half with the slogan Manufacturing Quality Dissent Since 1989 in white condensed capitals and an outlined button, and on the right a black-and-white upward view of a building with a colorful Peace mural.
images.caption: First viewport of [obeygiant.com](https://obeygiant.com/), captured 28 September 2026.

references.title: Obey Giant website, 2010
references.lede: The 2010 version of Shepard Fairey’s site, on black, labels every section with a slanted red tab in italic capitals.
references.summary: A red OBEY block logo, slanted red section tabs with white italic capitals, and hatched red rules on a black page.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive copy of 27 May 2010 with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The page is a fixed-width layout centered on black; the tabs and rules are images.

styles.note: Borderline: red, black, and white only, with capitals and slanted tabs, but on a black page with small body text and no large diagonal composition. See the [live site](ref:obeygiant-website).

context: Wikipedia states that Fairey “began appropriating the Russian Constructivist style utilized in Soviet-era propaganda during his time in San Diego”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepard_Fairey).
observed: The logo is a red rectangle with “OBEY” in heavy white italic capitals, followed by a strip of black-and-white photographs of street posters.
Section labels such as “HEADLINES”, “ATTENTION”, “PROPAGANDA”, “ENGINEERING”, and “INDUSTRIES” sit on red tabs whose right edge is cut on a diagonal, in white italic capitals.
Red diagonal hatching forms the rules between the sections of the right column.
Navigation and link lists are set in white bold capitals. Article titles are red capitals.
Body text is small white Arial on black. Thumbnails of Fairey’s posters add cream, yellow, and red.
interpretation: The site shows the propaganda vocabulary of the style (red labels, capitals, words like “propaganda” and “engineering” as section names) applied to a 2010 blog layout. The red is drawn in images, so the computed measurement finds only 2% chromatic area and 11% uppercase text; the fingerprint cannot see the tabs.
The diagonal survives only in small details: the cut edge of each tab and the hatched rules.
borrow: Cut the end of each red label on a diagonal to give a static list a sense of direction.
Use a band of diagonal red hatching as a section divider.

images.alt: Archived Obey Giant home page on black: a red OBEY logo block beside a strip of street-poster photos, red slanted section tabs such as Headlines, Attention, and Propaganda in white italic capitals, red diagonal hatched rules, and news posts in small white text with red titles.
images.caption: First viewport of the [27 May 2010 archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20100527200015/http://obeygiant.com/).

references.title: Oeta – 1956
references.lede: Victor Vasarely’s screenprint after a 1956 composition: a black and white grid of squares that shears and twists, between large black and white rhombs on a grey ground.
references.summary: A black-square grid that distorts into rhombs, with large tilted black and white blocks on grey. Victor Vasarely, screenprint, 1959.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.682-1965 (1267 × 1600 px), with a colour bar at the side, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Vasarely’s black and white period in print: a regular grid of squares that bends into rhombs to suggest folding and depth.

context: The V&A describes a colour screenprint on paper, 55.5 × 36.8 cm, made in France in 1959, acquired in 1965. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O71746/).

The V&A calls Vasarely (1908–1997) one of the leading artists of the movement later named Op art, whose aim was to make a static surface seem to move, and notes his use of cheap screenprinting for multiples. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O71746/).
observed: A mid-grey rectangle sits on a white sheet. On it, a wide band holds a grid of black squares on white.
In parts of the grid the squares rotate or shear into rhombs, so the band seems to fold and ripple.
Large black squares and black-and-white rhombs, tilted at different angles, sit above and below the grid.
Only black, white, and one grey appear.
interpretation: Oeta shows the checkerboard as a surface under stress: a few units change shape, and the whole plane seems to bend.
The grey ground is the one step in the value scale that the style record allows.
borrow: Take a strict grid of black squares and shear a few rows or cells into rhombs to suggest a fold.
Use one mid-grey as a ground to separate a black and white pattern from a white page.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Vasarely died in 1997, so the work is in copyright until 2067 in France.

references.title: Office.com website, 2013
references.lede: A red-orange Office 365 panel and light Segoe headings on a white page with blue link lists.
references.summary: Solid red-orange hero panel with a light white headline and a flat green button, over three columns of light headings. April 2013.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 1 April 2013, and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. Nothing covers the page. The headings render in a light Segoe-like face.

styles.note: Clear: a solid red-orange panel with a flat green button and light headings; the rest is white space, light headings, and blue text links.

observed: A dark gray top bar holds the white Office logo. Below it, uppercase navigation has the active item in red-orange.
The search field is a thin gray outline with a red-orange magnifier glyph.

A solid red-orange panel holds the Office 365 logo, the headline “Transform how you run your business with Office 365” in large light white type, and a square green “Try it for free” button. A photograph fills its right half.
Three columns have large light headings: “What’s New in Office?”, “Get Templates”, and “Office for Home Use”. Each has a picture and a list of blue text links.
A pale gray band at the bottom holds more headings.
interpretation: Measured: headings weight 400 in Segoe UI and Segoe UI Light; 16% of screenshot pixels are saturated; no shadows or gradients. 33% of boxes have a 1 px border, from the search field and hairline dividers on a page with only 9 filled boxes.
borrow: Put one saturated panel at the top of an otherwise white page, and set its headline in a light weight at large size.

references.title: Okeechobee Music & Arts Festival website
references.lede: A Florida festival site whose hero is a giant spiral of lime-green and gray rings behind a warped, bulging wordmark.
references.summary: Huge lime and gray concentric rings, a perspective-warped black wordmark, and a magenta sign-up box.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. A magenta sign-up box covers about a sixth of the viewport and hides part of the wordmark; it does not dim the page.

styles.note: Borderline: the concentric rings and warped wordmark are psychedelic motifs, but the palette is lime and neutral gray, not complements, and the type is a condensed grotesque.

observed: Broad concentric rings of lime green and mid gray fill the whole viewport, centered left of middle.
The black wordmark OKEECHOBEE runs across the rings in heavy condensed capitals whose letters grow and shrink as if seen on a bulging surface.
Music & Arts Festival and Sunshine Grove · Florida are set at right in a black condensed sans.
Navigation items are gray pill-shaped buttons at top right, with one in purple.
A magenta rectangle with a black outline asks READY TO JOIN THE OMF FAMILY? above a lime pill button.
interpretation: The page uses the entoptic ring motif at full scale, and the warped wordmark borrows the style’s habit of bending letters to a shape. Its lime and magenta accents clash, but the gray field keeps it cooler than a period poster.
Measured values: the rings are drawn as an image, so `color.chromaticShare` from computed styles is 0.14 while the screenshot measures 0.53; `color.patternShare` is 0 and `type.centerShare` is 0.14.
borrow: Use concentric rings at viewport scale as the hero ground.
Warp a wordmark so letter height follows an imagined curved surface.
Shape navigation as pills to echo the round forms of the hero.
