references.title: Op-art paper dress
references.lede: A disposable dress of bonded-fibre paper from the Scott Paper Company, printed all over with a black and white op-art check.
references.summary: A sleeveless shift printed edge to edge with a distorted black and white checkerboard. Scott Paper Company, USA, 1966.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, T.30-1992 (1200 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: The black and white op check moved straight onto a cheap mass-market garment: an all-over field of squares that compress and expand.

context: The V&A catalogues the dress with the style “Op art” and describes “a repeating black and white op art printed pattern” on bonded fibre paper. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O147891/).

The V&A says Scott Paper Company invented the paper dress in 1966 as a marketing tool: for one dollar a buyer got the dress and coupons for Scott paper products, and the company received about half a million orders in under a year. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O147891/).
A later promotional paper dress with a Pop print is [the Campbell’s “Souper” dress](ref:campbells-souper-paper-dress-1967).
observed: A sleeveless A-line shift with a round neck and two patch pockets, photographed flat on black.
The whole surface carries one black and white print: checkerboard bands in which the squares change size, alternating with rows of small open squares inside larger ones.
Where fine checks meet coarse checks, the rows seem to bend and bulge.
The print runs across the seams and pockets without matching them. A plain white band finishes the hem.
interpretation: The dress applies the op rule of one unit changed by steps: the square is the only motif, and only its size and grouping change.
As a throwaway paper product, it shows how quickly the gallery look of 1965 became a mass-market print.
borrow: Build a pattern from one square unit whose size changes by steps across bands.
Let an all-over pattern run through seams, pockets, or panel edges, so that the field reads as continuous.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is not openly licensed, and the rights in the print are unverified.

references.title: Optik Art earrings
references.lede: A pair of square earrings in white acrylic, screen-printed with nested black squares and rings, from Wendy Ramshaw and David Watkins’s Optik Art Jewellery.
references.summary: White perspex squares turned on point and printed with concentric black squares and circles. Ramshaw and Watkins, London, 1963–65.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A photograph of the pair T.338E&F-1982 (1600 × 1308 px), on black, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Black and white op geometry at the smallest scale: rings and squares nested so that figure and ground swap. Partial fit: a single motif, not an all-over field.

context: The V&A describes the pair as screen-printed acrylic (perspex) and base metal: an opaque white square with a screen-printed black op-art design. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1194608/).

The V&A’s record of a related ring says that Ramshaw and Watkins began Optik Art Jewellery in 1963, “inspired by Op-Art”. They screen-printed black and white patterns onto acrylic sheets and sliced the sheets into pieces, and Fenwicks of Bond Street commissioned collections. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O145843/).
observed: Each earring is a flat square turned 45 degrees, with a black ground.
Inside, a white ring holds a black square on point, which holds a smaller white ring and a black square: circles and squares alternate inward.
Where a circle crosses a square, the white areas split into crescents and triangles, so figure and ground alternate.
The edges of the acrylic show as thin white lines.
interpretation: The earrings reduce op art to one emblem, much like Vasarely’s square-in-circle units, and make it a cheap fashion product.
Screen printing on a sheet and cutting it into pieces is the same industrial logic that made op prints easy to reproduce.
borrow: Nest alternating circles and squares in black and white so that the crossings make crescents and triangles.
Turn a square badge or icon 45 degrees to give a static motif tension.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The designs are in copyright, and the V&A photograph is not openly licensed.

references.title: Otis Rush, Grateful Dead, Canned Heat at the Fillmore
references.lede: Wes Wilson’s Fillmore poster of February 1967: a woman’s profile whose hair becomes rippling bands of lettering that fill the whole sheet.
references.summary: Wes Wilson, 1967. Band names swell inside flowing hair, in pink, gray, and black on white.

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object E.527-2004 (IIIF, 1183 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. Catalogue data read on the V&A and Library of Congress records. Cooper Hewitt (1979-34-28) returned HTTP 403 to scripts, so its record is known only through its 2018 blog post. The image is not stored.

styles.note: The type trait in its purest form: Wilson’s lettering bends and swells until the band names become the hair of the figure. The palette is the exception: pale pink and gray on white, not vibrating complements.

context: The V&A catalogues it as psychedelic poster #51 by Wes Wilson, colour offset lithograph, 56.7 × 34.6 cm, and describes it as a “pink, green and black image of a female face in profile” with the text “within her hair”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O108984/).

The Library of Congress holds a copy printed by West Coast Lithograph Co., gift of Bill Graham (POS - US .W5578, no. 8). [LoC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2014647489/). Cooper Hewitt holds another (1979-34-28) and describes “pale pink and grey” rather than intense hues, a “dense, crowded composition”, and lettering that blurs into the undulating strands of the image. [Cooper Hewitt](https://www.cooperhewitt.org/2018/10/23/deliberately-disorienting/).

Wilson (1937–2020) designed Bill Graham’s Fillmore posters in 1966 and 1967 and is credited with the melting, moving lettering; he took the space-filling block letters of Alfred Roller as a model. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Wilson).
observed: A woman’s face in profile looks left from the lower middle of the sheet. Her face is drawn in dotted contour lines like a topographic map.
Her hair streams to the right as alternating bands of black, pink, gray, and white. Each band carries lettering: OTIS RUSH, GRATEFUL DEAD, THE CANNED HEAT BLUES BAND, the dates, and FILLMORE.
The letters are hand-drawn, with round counters and swollen strokes. They stretch to fill each band, so that letter height changes along a word.
The ground is white paper. Color is limited to pale pink, mid gray, and black.
Only the top line, BILL GRAHAM PRESENTS IN SAN FRANCISCO, and the ticket outlets at the bottom are in a plain sans-serif.
The imprint at lower left reads “Wes Wilson ©1967 Bill Graham” with number 51 and the printer, West Coast Lithograph Co.
interpretation: This is the rubric’s type rule taken to the limit: the lettering is the image. It also shows that the color rule is not universal. Many Wilson posters use two or three soft inks on white.
The two plain lines at top and bottom work as the legible frame around an illegible center, a useful model for screens.
borrow: Set display words inside flowing bands and let the band shape set the letter height.
Keep one plain line of practical text above and below a free display area.
Draw a face or object in contour lines so it matches the rhythm of the lettering.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. The poster carries a © 1967 Bill Graham notice.

references.title: Oz magazine no. 4, cover
references.lede: The cover of London Oz, May 1967, drawn by Hapshash and the Coloured Coat: a face whose streaming hair fills the page in gold and black on yellow.
references.summary: Hapshash and the Coloured Coat, 1967. Streaming gold hair and a starry cloak on yellow, with magenta OZ mastheads.

source.label: Victoria and Albert Museum: Oz no. 4 (National Art Library)

creator.name: Hapshash and the Coloured Coat (signed on the cover)

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image 2016JC9259 of this copy (IIIF, 1198 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The signature “Hapshash and the Coloured Coat” runs along one strand of hair; the V&A record names no designer. The image is not stored.

styles.note: The style applied to a magazine cover: full-bleed saturated yellow, flowing Art Nouveau hair that fills the page, and swollen lettering in a clashing magenta.

context: The V&A holds this issue as “OZ Magazine. Number 4, May 1967”. Its record says that Richard Neville and Martin Sharp launched London Oz in 1967, and that Sharp and the designer Jon Goodchild made it “one of the most visually dazzling Psychedelic publications of its time”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1328452/).
Hapshash and the Coloured Coat designed covers for Oz, according to the V&A record for their later “Tantric Lovers” Oz cover. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1155465/).
observed: A bright lemon-yellow ground covers the page, with a faint pattern of scalloped curves and stippling.
A woman’s face in grayscale halftone looks out from the left edge, cut off by the page.
Her hair streams right and up in broad bands of ochre-gold outlined in black, with fine parallel lines inside. It fills most of the cover.
A black shape inside the hair is scattered with gold stars and ends in a winged form at upper right. A small cloud contains zodiac signs.
OZ appears twice, at top left and bottom left, in fat black letters filled with magenta, with pointed, bat-wing counters. The price 2/6 is lettered at top right.
interpretation: The cover shares its main device with Wilson’s [Otis Rush poster](ref:wes-wilson-otis-rush-grateful-dead-poster-1967): hair as a flowing field that organizes the page. Here the field carries imagery instead of words.
Magenta mastheads on yellow and gold give the one clashing accent, a pattern that suits a site header.
borrow: Use one flowing shape, such as hair or smoke, to fill the page and lead the eye.
Repeat a short fat wordmark in two corners in a single clashing accent color.
Crop a photographic face at the edge and let drawn forms grow out of it.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The cover design is in copyright; Michael English died in 2009 and Nigel Waymouth is alive.

references.title: Pacific Wave, Museo Fortuny poster
references.lede: April Greiman’s poster for an exhibition of California graphic design in Venice: a stippled wave photograph, pink and black fields with irregular white holes, and tilted bitmap type.
references.summary: Pink, black, and yellow fields with white blob-shaped holes, a dotted gradient wave, and tilted bitmap “pacific wave” lettering. April Greiman, 1987.

source.label: V&A: Pacific Wave, Museo Fortuny, E.1499-2010

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object E.1499-2010 (image 2011EN9649, 1200 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: the tilted type, gradient bars, and layered fields belong to the style, but the letters are rough bitmaps and type plays a small part.

context: The V&A holds the poster as E.1499-2010, colour offset lithograph, 98.5 × 68 cm, and describes it as a poster for “Pacific Wave”, an exhibition of California graphic design at the Museo Fortuny, Venice, September 1987. [V&A E.1499-2010](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1176678/).
observed: A yellow bar runs across the top and down the right side, fading through red to blue.
Large black and hot-pink fields fill the sheet. Irregular white shapes with soft, blob-like edges cut holes through them.
A photograph of a breaking wave is rendered in coarse white stipple over a yellow-red-blue gradient panel.
“pacific wave” runs on a rising diagonal in white bitmap letters with broken, ragged edges, followed by dotted lines. A second, smaller copy sits on the pink field.
Small text runs vertically in narrow black and pink strips at the left.
interpretation: This is the style at its most digital. The ragged bitmap letters come near the grunge counter-rule, but they are low-resolution output, not deliberate damage. Treat it as the edge of the style, not a model for it.
borrow: Run a gradient bar around two edges of a composition as a frame.
Set a title on a steep diagonal and repeat it smaller in another layer.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. April Greiman is living, so the design is in copyright.

references.title: Panic Coda 2 website, 2012
references.lede: Panic’s page for the web editor Coda 2, archived August 2012: a photoreal leaf with water drops on a textured navy band.
references.summary: A dew-covered leaf on dark navy texture, a paper-clipped logo, and a gray device-like strip of tabs.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The archived page may lack some images or scripts that the live page had. A flat blue bar in the middle is probably an image that the archive did not load.

styles.note: Borderline: a textured band, photoreal objects, and a paper clip, but the middle of the page is flat gray and black.

observed: The top band is dark navy with fine diagonal lines like brushed fabric.
A large photoreal green leaf with water drops, the Coda icon, hangs over the band’s lower edge onto the gray page.
The Panic logo tab at the top left is held by a paper clip; the links have photoreal icons of a crate, a question mark, and a box.
A gray strip at the bottom holds red, orange, and green glossy buttons and tab thumbnails with a riveted metal Panic tile.
A flat two-tone blue bar in the middle is probably an image or animation that the archive did not load.
interpretation: It passes 4 of 6 metrics: patterned surfaces on 64% of boxes and gradients on 31%. Color pattern share is 0.26 and shadow share 0.18, both under the provisional minimums.
borrow: Let a photoreal object overlap the edge between a textured header and a plain body, so the object seems to sit on the page.

images.alt: Archived Coda 2 page: a dark navy textured band with a large dew-covered green leaf, a paper-clipped Panic logo tab, links with photoreal icons, a flat blue bar, two text columns, and a gray strip of glossy buttons and document thumbnails on black.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20120808132653/http://panic.com/coda/).
