references.title: Panic Transmit website, 2011
references.lede: Panic’s page for the Mac FTP app Transmit 4, archived May 2011: a photoreal delivery truck, a paper-clipped logo tab, and chrome lettering.
references.summary: A photoreal truck, a paper clip on the logo, embossed chrome lettering, and photoreal icons.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The archived page may lack some images or scripts that the live page had.

styles.note: Borderline: the objects are fully skeuomorphic (a truck for file transfer, a paper clip on the logo tab, chrome lettering), but the page body is plain light gray with no material texture.

observed: The top band is a dark gradient with a large photoreal yellow and purple truck, the app’s icon.
A white Panic logo tab at the top left is held by a drawn paper clip.
The links Download, Get Help, and Buy Now each have a photoreal icon: a hard disk with a green arrow, a glossy question mark, and a wooden crate.
The word “Features” is set in outlined chrome script with a bevel and shadow.
Below, a screenshot of the Transmit window shows a gray gradient toolbar and red callout dots.
interpretation: Vertical gradients cover 94% of boxes, but no box has a measured shadow and the pattern shares are 0. The page’s depth is in its illustrations.
borrow: Clip the logo to the page with a drawn paper clip, as on a document.
Let one large photoreal object carry the metaphor and keep the text area plain.

images.alt: Archived Transmit page: a dark band with a large photoreal yellow truck with a purple cargo box, a paper-clipped Panic logo tab, Download, Get Help, and Buy Now links with photoreal icons, a blue headline about Transmit 4, chrome Features lettering, and a screenshot of the app window.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20110531073504/http://www.panic.com/transmit/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Peacock and Dragon woven wool
references.lede: A heavy woven wool hanging by William Morris in which peacocks, dragons, and palmettes mirror each other in a strict, static repeat.
references.summary: Mirrored peacocks and dragons in green, salmon, red, and blue on a light ground. William Morris, woven wool, 1878.

source.label: Cleveland Museum of Art: Peacock and Dragon, 1953.330

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 1953.330 (2752 × 3400 px).

styles.note: A Morris woven textile with a strictly mirrored, dense repeat of birds and plants in muted dye colours.

context: Cleveland describes it as a weft-faced compound twill in wool, 206.6 × 174.7 cm, woven at Merton Abbey, Surrey, in 1878. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/1953.330).

Morris wanted textiles that worked like medieval wall hangings and brought warmth to cold rooms; Cleveland calls this one the closest he came to that ideal. A room from Damascus that he saw at a London dealer the same year partly inspired the motifs. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/1953.330).

The design was sold in five colourways. George Willis Pack bought this piece between 1878 and 1886 for his house on Euclid Avenue, Cleveland. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/1953.330).
observed: Two large birds with spread wings face each other across a central palmette; the whole field is a mirror-symmetrical repeat, two units wide.
A band of red-winged birds with dark blue heads crosses the middle of each unit.
Colours are olive and sage green, salmon pink, a stronger red, and slate and dark blue on a cream ground.
Stems, leaves, and feathers are flat shapes with no shading. The twill weave gives a diagonal texture to every colour.
Plain ground shows only as thin lines around the shapes.
interpretation: The piece matches the rubric’s dense, symmetrical, lattice-based repeat, but its colours are softer and lighter than the deep indigo of the printed cottons.
The layout comes from medieval and Near Eastern woven silks, which fits the movement’s look back to pre-industrial models.
borrow: Build a large mirrored unit around a central plant and cross it with a narrow band of smaller motifs.
Use a soft green and salmon palette with one small, stronger red accent.

images.alt: Woven wool panel with a dense pattern of mirrored peacocks, dragons, and palmettes in olive green and salmon pink on cream, crossed by bands of small red and dark blue birds.
images.caption: William Morris, Peacock and Dragon, 1878. Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. Philip White, 1953.330. [Open-access image](https://clevelandart.org/art/1953.330), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art releases the image as CC0. William Morris died in 1896, and the work dates from 1878, so it is in the public domain in the United Kingdom and the United States.

references.title: Pennsylvania Railroad S1 locomotive at the 1939 World’s Fair
references.lede: Raymond Loewy’s shroud for the longest steam locomotive ever built: a bullet nose with a round headlamp and speed lines that run the whole length of engine and tender.
references.summary: A dark bullet-nosed steam locomotive with parallel speed lines along its length. Raymond Loewy for the Pennsylvania Railroad, 1939.

creator.name: Raymond Loewy (shroud); Pennsylvania Railroad, Altoona Works (builder)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected two Gottscho-Schleisner photographs of No. 6100 at the New York World’s Fair: [PRR S1.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PRR_S1.jpg) (Library of Congress reproduction number LC-G613-35557, dated 15 July 1939) and [gsc.5a18640](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:World%27s_Fair,_railroad_exhibit_locomotives._LOC_gsc.5a18640.jpg), both at 1920 px on Commons. The stored image is the first.

styles.note: Loewy’s best-known streamline design: a bullet nose, a round headlamp, and groups of parallel speed lines along a very long horizontal body.

context: Built at the Pennsylvania Railroad’s Altoona Works and completed on 31 January 1939; Raymond Loewy designed the streamlined shell. At 140 ft 2½ in with tender it was the longest reciprocating steam locomotive ever. At the 1939 New York World’s Fair it ran on a roller platform at 60 mph under the lettering “American Railroads”, part of a combined 27-railroad exhibit. It served from 1939 to 1946 and was scrapped in 1949. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad_class_S1).
observed: The locomotive is very long and low; the photograph is more than twice as wide as it is tall and still crops the tender.
The front is a rounded bullet nose with a large round headlamp in a ring at its center.
Groups of two and three thin bright lines run from the nose back along the whole engine; the tender carries the same parallel lines and the words “AMERICAN RAILROADS” in spaced capitals.
The shell is a smooth, dark, glossy surface; small star-shaped badges are the only other marks.
A railing encloses the exhibit, and the fair’s disc-shaped canopy and a lighting mast appear at right.
interpretation: The S1 is the rubric’s speed line in its purest form: a few parallel lines drawn along a long dark body, meeting at a round headlamp. It also shows that the style works on a dark ground, not only on cream.
borrow: Start a group of parallel lines at a circular element and run them to the far edge of the layout.
Space the capitals of a long label widely so it reads as a band.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a very long streamlined steam locomotive behind a railing: a rounded bullet nose with a round headlamp, thin parallel lines along the whole body and tender, and the words American Railroads on the tender.
images.caption: PRR S1 No. 6100 at the New York World’s Fair, 15 July 1939. Gottscho-Schleisner, Inc., Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-G613-35557, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PRR_S1.jpg).

rights.statement: Commons marks the Gottscho-Schleisner photograph public domain; the Library of Congress lists no known restrictions on that collection. A locomotive is a useful article, not protected by copyright in the United States, its country of origin. Raymond Loewy died in 1986; the shroud’s shape is not a separable artwork.

references.title: Pioneer Zephyr brochure, 1934
references.lede: The Burlington’s brochure for “Burlington’s Streamline Motor Train”: script lettering trailed by speed lines, a winged-god badge, and photographs of the stainless-steel train.
references.summary: Red script with trailing speed lines, a round Zephyrus badge, and photographs of the stainless train. Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad, 1934.

creator.name: Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad; printed by Gusdorf-Warren Printing Company, Chicago (Commons)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons scan of the front, middle, and back of one copy (scanned from an eBay item, per Commons) at 1920 × 756 px; each page is about 530 × 740 px in that image. Small body text was not fully legible.

styles.note: Period transport graphics in the style: script and capitals with trailing horizontal speed lines, a round badge, and the word “Streamline” in the title.

context: Commons says the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad issued the brochure to announce the Pioneer Zephyr’s entry into regular service, which began on 11 November 1934. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1934_Pioneer_Zephyr_brochure.JPG).

The back page credits the Edw. G. Budd Manufacturing Company as builder, Paul Cret as consulting architect for the interior, and Holabird & Root as consulting architects for the train’s styling (read on the scan). See also [Pioneer Zephyr](ref:pioneer-zephyr-1934).
observed: The cover title “The Zephyr” is set in large red script; thin horizontal lines trail from the left of the letters.
Below it, “Burlington’s Streamline Motor Train” is set in black sans-serif on a pale pink band.
A round badge shows the wind god Zephyrus in the clouds above a train with speed lines, ringed in red.

A photomontage runs from a stagecoach and an old steam locomotive at upper left to the nose of the stainless Zephyr at lower right; white capitals list “Stainless Steel”, “Diesel Engine”, and technical features.
The inside spread has red serif italic headings, a large pale-blue winged Zephyrus with a train in profile, and photographs of the train.
The back page ends with the red Burlington Route box and the slogan “Everywhere West” in red italic with a trailing underline.
interpretation: The brochure shows speed lines as a graphic device in 1934, attached to script lettering and a badge. The photomontage from stagecoach to streamliner states the style’s theme: speed as progress.
borrow: Trail three to five thin horizontal lines from the first letter of a display word.
Set a round emblem on a band of speed lines as a logo.

images.alt: Three pages of a 1934 railroad brochure side by side: an inside spread with red italic headings and a pale-blue winged figure above a train, a cover with red script reading The Zephyr, Burlington's Streamline Motor Train, and a photomontage of old and new trains, and a back page with photographs, text, a route map, and the slogan Everywhere West.
images.caption: Pioneer Zephyr brochure, Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad, 1934: inside spread, cover, and back. Scan via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1934_Pioneer_Zephyr_brochure.JPG), marked PD-US-not renewed.

rights.statement: Commons tags the scan PD-US-not renewed: a United States publication of 1934; the uploader reports searching the renewal records and finding no renewals for the railroad. I did not see a copyright notice on the scanned pages, but the small print was not fully legible. The Burlington Route mark is a trademark.

references.title: Pioneer Zephyr, 1934
references.lede: The Burlington’s stainless-steel diesel train of 1934: a sloping, rounded nose and sides fluted with horizontal lines.
references.summary: A polished stainless-steel train with a rounded, sloping nose, a grilled dome, and horizontal fluting. Budd Company for the Burlington, 1934.

creator.name: Budd Company; exterior design by Albert Gardner Dean with Paul Philippe Cret and John Harbeson (Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Daderot’s 2014 photograph of the train at the Museum of Science and Industry, Chicago, on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pioneer_Zephyr_-_Museum_of_Science_and_Industry_(Chicago)_-_DSC06911.JPG), at 1280 × 1920 px.

styles.note: A founding object of American streamlining: a rounded, sloping nose, polished metal, and horizontal fluting along the sides.

context: Built by the Budd Company in 1934 of stainless steel joined by shotwelding; exterior design by Albert Gardner Dean with the architects Paul Philippe Cret and John Harbeson. On 26 May 1934 it ran non-stop from Denver to Chicago, 1,015 miles in 13 hours 5 minutes, and appeared at the Century of Progress fair. It entered service on 11 November 1934. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pioneer_Zephyr).
The train was donated to the Museum of Science and Industry, Chicago, in 1960. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pioneer_Zephyr).
observed: The nose slopes back and rounds over into a dome covered by a grille of curved ribs, with a large round headlamp on top.
The cab windows form a curved band across the front.
Several thin parallel ridges run horizontally around the nose and continue along the sides as fluting.
The skirt below curves forward to a blunt, rounded lower edge.
The whole surface is polished stainless steel with visible rivet lines; the only color is a black and red “Burlington Route” sign on the nose.
interpretation: The fluting turns the speed line into structure: the parallel ridges that stiffen the steel also give the train its look. Many later graphics draw the same few parallel lines to mean stainless steel and speed.
borrow: Use a band of four to six thin parallel lines that wraps a rounded corner and continues along the edge.
Set one small saturated badge on a large field of silver-gray.

images.alt: Front three-quarter view of a polished stainless-steel train in a museum hall: a rounded, sloping nose with a ribbed grille dome and a large headlamp, a curved band of cab windows, horizontal ridges wrapping the nose, and a black and red Burlington Route sign.
images.caption: Pioneer Zephyr at the Museum of Science and Industry, Chicago. Photograph by Daderot, 2014, CC0, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pioneer_Zephyr_-_Museum_of_Science_and_Industry_(Chicago)_-_DSC06911.JPG).

rights.statement: The photographer dedicated the photograph to the public domain (CC0). A train is a useful article: its shape is not protected by copyright in the United States, its country of origin. The Burlington Route sign is a trademark shown as part of the object.

identifiers.commons: File:Pioneer Zephyr - Museum of Science and Industry (Chicago) - DSC06911.JPG

references.title: PlayStation website, 2000
references.lede: Sony’s PlayStation region-choice page of October 2000: the logo on a globe inside orbit rings, with region names in spaced capitals on black.
references.summary: The PlayStation logo on the Earth, circled by white orbit rings that end in the controller symbols, on black.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. It is a short region-choice page; most of the viewport is black.

styles.note: Borderline: a gateway page with Y2K motifs (orbit rings, space, widely spaced capitals) but no chrome or plastic, and very little content. The page draws its graphics with images, so the CSS fingerprint measures flat, square, unshadowed boxes (see the style page). Judge it by the rubric.

observed: A photograph of the Earth sits at the top center of a black page, with the PlayStation logo in a white-edged square over it.
White orbit rings curve around the globe. Their ends carry the four controller symbols (cross, circle, square, triangle) in blue, red, and green circles.
Region names such as “NORTH AMERICA”, “EUROPE”, “JAPAN”, and “AUSTRALASIA” are in small white bold capitals next to the symbols.
“WELCOME TO THE WORLD OF PLAYSTATION®” runs below in small capitals with very wide letter spacing.
interpretation: The orbit ring is one of the style’s image motifs. Here it turns a region chooser into a small solar system.
The widely spaced capitals are drawn as images, so the measured letter spacing and uppercase share are 0.
borrow: Arrange a few choices on orbit rings around a central logo.
Set one welcome line in small capitals with very wide letter spacing.

images.alt: Archived PlayStation gateway: on black, the Earth with the PlayStation logo, circled by white orbit rings ending in the cross, circle, square, and triangle symbols, next to region names, with a widely spaced welcome line below.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20001027223903/http://www.playstation.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to Sony Computer Entertainment. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Pocket “rainbow reader” illustration in Firefox
references.lede: A spot illustration shipped in Firefox’s Pocket panel: a person reading on a laptop while a rainbow loops out of the screen and over their raised legs.
references.summary: A reader on a laptop under a looping rainbow; flat pastel fills with black line details. Firefox source, about 2020.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1280 × 1045 rendering of the SVG from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Firefox_Browser_%E2%80%93_Rainbow-reader.svg) and stored it, flattened onto white. The Commons uploader placed it in Category:Corporate Memphis.

styles.note: Partial fit: a flat spot illustration of a person with a long bending leg in a software panel, but the hands, shoes, and face are drawn with black lines and the skin is white.

context: Commons gives the source as the Pocket panel image folder of the Firefox source code, the author as “Mozilla Foundation et al.”, the date as 2020, and the license as MPL 2.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Firefox_Browser_%E2%80%93_Rainbow-reader.svg).
observed: A figure lies on its front with a green sweater and reads a white laptop outlined in black.
A pale blue leg runs from the bottom left and bends up; the foot in a red shoe is drawn with black lines.
A wide rainbow of light blue, teal, yellow, red, and pink bands loops from the laptop screen over the figure in an S-curve.
The hair is a solid black mass; the face is white with a few black lines. Pink key shapes sit on the laptop keyboard.
interpretation: It shows how the style reached browser chrome and empty states: one figure and one oversized, impossible object in a small panel. The black hand-drawn line details make it a looser, sketch-like variant.
borrow: Let a single flowing shape (a rainbow, a ribbon) come out of the device the figure uses, to show the feature’s effect.

images.alt: Flat illustration: a person in a green sweater lies reading a laptop, with a pale blue leg raised behind, while a wide rainbow of blue, teal, yellow, red, and pink loops out of the screen in an S-curve.
images.caption: “Firefox Browser – Rainbow-reader”, Mozilla, 2020. MPL 2.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Firefox_Browser_%E2%80%93_Rainbow-reader.svg), from the Firefox source, flattened onto white.

rights.statement: Distributed in the Firefox source code under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, per Wikimedia Commons. Credit: Mozilla. Firefox and Pocket are trademarks of Mozilla.

references.title: Podcasts app, 2012
references.lede: Apple’s first standalone podcast app, whose player showed an animated reel-to-reel tape deck.
references.summary: A reel-to-reel tape deck that spins with playback. Apple, 2012, removed March 2013.

source.label: The Next Web, Matthew Panzarino, 21 March 2013

references.made: 2012 (announced at WWDC 2012 as part of iOS 6); tape deck removed 21 March 2013

evidence.note: No image was inspected. Based on The Next Web and Gizmodo reports of the March 2013 update, and on Wikipedia.

styles.note: An extreme object metaphor from the style’s last year: an analog tape machine for a download app, with motion that follows the real reels.

context: A standalone Apple Podcasts app was announced at WWDC 2012 as a feature of iOS 6. [Wikipedia: Apple Podcasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Podcasts).

In the update of 21 March 2013, “Gone are the fat tape-machine style buttons and the reel-to-reel imitation scrubber.” [The Next Web](https://thenextweb.com/news/apple-updates-podcasts-app-with-custom-stations-on-the-go-playlists-and-less-skeuomorphic-design).

[Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/apples-podcasts-app-no-longer-has-horrible-reel-to-reel-5991798) reported the same change under the headline “Apple’s Podcasts App No Longer Has Horrible Reel-to-Reel Skeuomorphism.”
interpretation: The object had no link to how podcasts are made or delivered. It shows the style used as nostalgia, and its removal three months before iOS 7 marks the end of the period.
next: Find and inspect a screenshot of the 2012 player.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Poolsuite
references.lede: A web radio and lifestyle brand that frames its player as a classic Mac window on a pale pink desktop.
references.summary: Pale pink desktop, classic Mac-style player window with TV static, and a dock of pixel icons.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: pastel pink, square retro-OS windows, TV static, and a 1997 clock match the style, but the source is summer and classic Mac leisure culture, with no statues, gradients, or Japanese text. The brand does not call itself vaporwave on this page.

observed: The desktop is flat pale pink with a faint dot texture.
A cream window with a thin black outline, a close box, and the POOLSUITE wordmark frames a video area showing black-and-white TV static and a file name “commercials_88.wmv”.
Below the video, a now-playing panel and square transport buttons in pale blue and pink.
A dock of square buttons with small pixel icons (a cocktail, a CD, a camera, a sunscreen bottle) runs along the bottom; a clock at the top right reads MON 28 SEP 1997.
interpretation: The measurement finds hard shadows on 60% of boxes and zero radius, but a median offset of 11 px, because the main window casts a large offset shadow rather than a thin bevel.

images.alt: Poolsuite home page: a cream classic-Mac-style player window showing TV static on a pale pink desktop, with square transport buttons and a dock of pixel icons along the bottom.
images.caption: First viewport of [poolsuite.net](https://poolsuite.net/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Poppy plate from Mucha’s Documents décoratifs
references.lede: A plate from Alphonse Mucha’s 1902 pattern book: a frieze of pink poppies on tall stems above ochre and sea-green leaves, with two small studies of the same flower made into flat repeat patterns.
references.summary: Lithographed plate of poppy friezes and patterns in pink, ochre, and sea green on buff. Alphonse Mucha, Paris, 1901–2.

source.label: Cleveland Museum of Art: Documents Decoratifs: Oriental Poppies, 1969.236

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of print 1969.236 (2400 × 3400 px print file). Read the object record through the museum’s open-access API. The plate is numbered “PL. 38” at its upper right; Cleveland titles it “Oriental Poppies” and lists a separate print 1969.237 as “Plate 38”, which this record did not inspect.

styles.note: A teaching sheet for the style: one plant shown as a frieze, a dense field, and a stylized repeat, in the earthy pastel palette.

context: The Cleveland Museum of Art records the print as a lithograph from *Documents Décoratifs*, 1901–2, by Alphonse Mucha (1860–1939). [CMA 1969.236](https://clevelandart.org/art/1969.236).

Wikipedia: *Documents Décoratifs* is a series of seventy-two plates published as a book in 1902 by the Librairie Centrale des Beaux-Arts. The plates show how floral, vegetal, and natural forms can be used in decoration and decorative objects. Mucha taught decoration at the Académie Colarossi from about 1900. [Wikipedia: Alphonse Mucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mucha).
observed: The sheet has a wide plain buff margin. The design sits in a rectangle with a thin ochre border line.
The lower two thirds is a frieze: three large pink poppies and several buds on tall, thin, vertical stems, against a pale peach ground.
Sea-green leaves with jagged edges fill the base of the frieze, over a tangle of ochre-gold leaf outlines. At the very bottom, small ochre spirals run along a sea-green band.
Top left: a dense field of pink poppies with ochre and blue-gray curving leaves on a sage-green ground.
Top right: the poppy reduced to a flat repeat of tomato-red cells separated by pale yellow, branching lines with green centres.
Every shape has a thin ochre or dark red outline. The colours are soft: dusty pink, plum, ochre, sea green, and sage.
interpretation: The plate shows the style’s method in three steps: the natural plant, a decorative field, and a flat pattern. The frieze is calm and vertical; the whiplash appears only in the leaves.
The palette matches the style’s grammar closely: dusty rose, ochre, and moss or sea green on a cream ground, with outlines instead of shading.
borrow: Use one flower at three scales: a hero frieze, a small dense field, and an abstract repeat for backgrounds.
Outline every coloured shape in ochre instead of black to keep a warm, soft contrast.

images.alt: Lithographed plate on buff paper, numbered PL. 38: a frieze of pink poppies on tall stems above sea-green leaves on a peach ground, with a small panel of pink poppies on sage green and a small red-and-yellow flat pattern above it.
images.caption: Alphonse Mucha, plate 38 of *Documents Décoratifs*, 1901–2, lithograph. [Cleveland Museum of Art 1969.236](https://clevelandart.org/art/1969.236), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art marks the print and its image CC0. Alphonse Mucha died in 1939, so his work entered the public domain in the Czech Republic and France in 2010. The book was published in 1902, so it is in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I
references.lede: Gustav Klimt’s square portrait of 1907 sets a naturalistic face and hands in a field of gold covered with squares, spirals, eyes, and checkered strips.
references.summary: A square canvas of gold and silver leaf, with the sitter’s dress and chair built from squares, spirals, and eye motifs. Gustav Klimt, Vienna, 1907.

source.label: Wikipedia: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I

evidence.note: Inspected a 1280 × 1279 px rendition of the Neue Galerie New York photograph on Wikimedia Commons. Gold and silver leaf photograph differently under different light, so the colours are approximate.

styles.note: Clear for the gold and the geometric ornament: a square format, grids of small squares, and a checkered strip, around a flat figure. It is denser and richer than Secession graphics, which keep wide plain areas.

context: Wikipedia: an oil painting on canvas with gold leaf by Gustav Klimt, completed between 1903 and 1907, commissioned by the sitter’s husband, Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer. It is described as the final and most fully representative work of Klimt’s golden phase. It was stolen by the Nazis in 1941, restituted to Maria Altmann in 2006, and sold the same year. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Adele_Bloch-Bauer_I).

The Commons file page gives the medium as oil, silver, and gold on canvas, 140 × 140 cm, and the location as the Neue Galerie New York. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gustav_Klimt,_1907,_Adele_Bloch-Bauer_I,_Neue_Galerie_New_York.jpg).
observed: The canvas is square. The left half is an almost plain field of speckled gold, with two small silver squares.
Behind the sitter, a panel is filled with small squares, each outlined and holding a dot or a smaller square, some in red.
The dress is a tall field of gold triangles and almond-shaped eyes, and the chair and sleeves carry spirals, circles, and flat rectangles of gold and silver.
A narrow black and white checkered strip runs along the lower left, above a band of flat green.
Only the face, shoulders, and hands are painted naturalistically; everything else is flat pattern.
The signature “GUSTAV / KLIMT” is lettered in a small square at the lower right, with “19 / 07” below.
interpretation: The painting shows where the style’s gold comes from. The square motifs and the checkered strip match the Wiener Werkstätte vocabulary, while the eyes and spirals are Klimt’s own.
The signature in a small square box is the same device as the monograms on Werkstätte objects and posters.
borrow: Leave one large area in flat gold or a gold tint, and concentrate pattern in one zone beside it.
Use a grid of small outlined squares, each with a dot, as a panel texture.
Put a signature or date in a small square box of stacked capitals.

images.alt: Square gold painting: a pale-faced woman with dark hair sits in a gold dress covered in eyes and triangles, against a background panel of small outlined squares and gold spirals; the left half is speckled gold with a checkered strip and a green band at the lower left.
images.caption: Gustav Klimt, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I, 1907. Neue Galerie New York. Photograph via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gustav_Klimt,_1907,_Adele_Bloch-Bauer_I,_Neue_Galerie_New_York.jpg), public domain (PD-Art).

rights.statement: The Commons file carries “PD-Art | PD-old-auto-1923 | deathyear=1918”. Gustav Klimt died in 1918, so the painting is in the public domain in Austria; the Commons licence text also states that it is in the public domain in the United States (published before 1931). The photograph is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

identifiers.commons: File:Gustav Klimt, 1907, Adele Bloch-Bauer I, Neue Galerie New York.jpg

references.title: Poster for the 13th Secession exhibition
references.lede: Koloman Moser’s poster of 1902 stacks three flat, frontal figures above a block of lettering set between checkered bands, all on one central axis.
references.summary: Three symmetrical figures above packed capitals and blue and white checkered bands, framed in brown. Koloman Moser, Vienna, 1902.

source.label: Gallica (BnF): Ver Sacrum V Jahr, XIII Ausstellung … Secession, affiche, Kolo Moser

evidence.note: Inspected the Bibliothèque nationale de France copy (Gallica btv1b52506931h) at 554 × 1600 px through IIIF, and the Commons copy of the same scan at 960 × 2772 px. The MAK holds two copies (PI 118-1, 177 × 70 cm, and PI 118-2, 94.4 × 32 cm); I did not inspect their images at full size, so differences between sizes are not recorded.

styles.note: A clear example: strict symmetry, capitals packed into ruled bands, checkerboard bands, and a frame, with flat colour. It uses two accent colours (blue and ochre brown), one more than the rubric’s limit.

context: The MAK records the poster as designed by Koloman Moser for the Vienna Secession, printed by Albert Berger, Vienna, 1902, in lithography. The inscription gives the exhibition dates as 1 February to 16 March 1902. [MAK PI 118-2](https://sammlung.mak.at/en/collect/plakat-zur-xiii-ausstellung-d-vereinigung-bildender-kuenstler-oesterreichs-secession-ver-sacrum-v-jahr_53970), [MAK PI 118-1](https://sammlung.mak.at/en/collect/ver-sacrum-v-jahr-xiii-ausstellung-d-vereinigung-bildender-kuenstler-oesterreichs_71619).
The Museum of Modern Art holds a copy as “Ver Sacrum (Sacred Spring) (Poster for the Thirteenth Secession exhibition)”, 1902. [MoMA 133907](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/133907).
observed: The format is tall and narrow. An ochre-brown frame surrounds a white field.

Three identical women stand on the central axis, one above and two below. Each has a large blue and black disc of hair, a white face, and a narrow, flat, rectangular body with a teardrop-shaped panel of small triangles.
A thin white circle is drawn around the upper figure’s head.
A column of blue squares runs down the centre between the lower figures.

Below, “VER / SACRUM / V. / JAHR” is lettered in blue and “XIII. AUSSTELLUNG / D. VEREINIGUNG / BILDENDER KÜNST / LER ÖSTERREICHS / SECESSION” in brown. Every line is ruled above and below, and the capitals fill each line from edge to edge; words break where the line ends.
Bands of blue and white checkerboard squares separate the text blocks and frame “VER SACRUM”.
Opening hours and the entry price sit in two more ruled brown lines; a row of small triangles closes the bottom. The printer’s line “LITH. v. DRUCK A. BERGER WIEN, VIII/2” runs under the frame.
interpretation: This is the style in one sheet: figure and letters become modules on one grid, and the checkerboard bands work as rules between text blocks.
Breaking words to fill the line, as in “KÜNST / LER”, shows that the block shape mattered more than word breaks.
borrow: Put a thin band of small checkerboard squares between text blocks, like a rule.
Rule every heading line and let the capitals fill it edge to edge.
Repeat one flat figure or icon three times on a central axis.

images.alt: Tall poster in blue, ochre, black, and white: three identical flat women with large blue and black hair discs stacked symmetrically, above blocks of capitals reading Ver Sacrum V. Jahr and XIII. Ausstellung der Vereinigung bildender Künstler Österreichs Secession, separated by blue and white checkered bands.
images.caption: Koloman Moser, poster for the 13th exhibition of the Vienna Secession, 1902. Bibliothèque nationale de France, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ver_Sacrum_V_Jahn,_XIII_Ausstellung._Secession._affiche,_Kolo_Moser.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: The Commons file page gives the source as Gallica btv1b52506931h and applies CC0 and PD-US. Koloman Moser died in 1918, and the poster was published in 1902, so the work is in the public domain in Austria and in the United States. The MAK’s own photographs of its copies are CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and are not used here.

identifiers.commons: File:Ver Sacrum V Jahn, XIII Ausstellung. Secession. affiche, Kolo Moser.jpg

references.title: Poster for the 16th Secession exhibition
references.lede: Alfred Roller’s poster of 1903 packs heavy, rounded capitals into a solid block under a field of repeated three-part emblems.
references.summary: Heavy black capitals packed into a block, with long black strokes and a repeated red three-shield emblem. Alfred Roller, Vienna, 1903.

source.label: Leopold Museum Online Collection: Poster for the 16th Exhibition at the Vienna Secession, Inv. 3027

evidence.note: Inspected the Leopold Museum photograph of its copy, Inv. 3027 (992 × 3017 px), which is not open for download. The stored image is a smaller Commons scan from a printed reproduction (459 × 1359 px); its red is more saturated than the salmon red of the Leopold copy.

styles.note: Clear for lettering and pattern: capitals packed into a solid block, a repeated three-part emblem, and black with one accent colour. The long curved strokes from the S of SECESSION keep a trace of the early curvilinear phase.

context: The Leopold Museum records the poster as designed by Alfred Roller and printed in colour lithography by Albert Berger, Vienna, 1902/03, 95 × 31.4 cm, signed and dated “ALFRED ROLLER.1903” on the stone. Its text says Roller combined simplifying flat stylization with a high degree of ornamental abstraction, and that distorted lettering was typical of Viennese posters around 1900. [Leopold Museum Inv. 3027](https://onlinecollection.leopoldmuseum.org/en/object/1246-poster-for-the-16th-exhibition-at-the-vienna-secession/).
Alfred Roller (1864–1935) was an Austrian painter, graphic designer, and set designer, and a member of the Vienna Secession. [Wikipedia: Alfred Roller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Roller).
observed: The poster is tall and narrow, on cream paper inside a thin black frame.
“SECESSION” runs across the top in black letters; the descending strokes of its S letters continue as three long black curves that sweep down through most of the height.
Behind the curves, a regular grid of red emblems repeats: each emblem is three small shield or pentagon shapes, two above and one below.

The lower third is a dense block of heavy, rounded black capitals: “16. AUSSTELLUNG / D. VEREINIGUNG / BILD. KÜNSTLER / ÖSTERREICHS”, then three lines with the months “JÄNNER FEBRUAR 1903”, the daily opening hours, and “EINTRITT 1 KRONE”, and “VER SACRUM 6. JAHR”.
The letters are packed with almost no space between them and are stretched so that each line is full width; spirals fill the ends of short lines.
Small red rectangles mark the divisions between the text blocks.
interpretation: Roller turns the text into a texture: the lettering block reads first as a black field and only then as words. It is the strongest example of the style’s tight, block-filling capitals.
The three-part emblem repeats the Secession habit of grouping three small squares or shields as a mark.
borrow: Set a short, important text block in heavy capitals with minimal spacing so it reads as one black shape.
Repeat a small three-part emblem on a regular grid as a quiet background pattern in one accent colour.

images.alt: Tall poster on cream paper: the word Secession across the top, three long black curves falling from its S letters over a grid of small red three-shield emblems, and a dense block of heavy black capitals with the exhibition details at the bottom.
images.caption: Alfred Roller, poster for the 16th exhibition of the Vienna Secession, 1903. Scan from a printed reproduction by Luc Devroye, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_Roller_Poster_Secession_XVI.png), public domain (PD-Art). Colours differ from the original.

rights.statement: The Commons file carries the PD-Art template. Alfred Roller died in 1935, and the poster was published in 1903, so the work is in the public domain in Austria and in the United States. The Leopold Museum’s photograph is not released for download and is not stored.

references.title: Poster stamp for the Cologne exhibition, 1907
references.lede: Joseph Maria Olbrich’s advertising stamp puts a tower in a diamond of laurel, and fits the exhibition text into ruled bands of squared capitals.
references.summary: A laurel diamond over stacked, ruled bands of tightly packed capitals, in one gray ink. Joseph Maria Olbrich, 1907.

source.label: MAK Collection Online: Werbemarke zur Kölner Ausstellung 1907, KI 21484-3-311

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the MAK photograph of the stamp MAK KI 21484-3-311 (1198 × 1680 px). The photograph is soft and shows JPEG blocking, so fine details of the laurel and the tower figure are uncertain.

styles.note: Clear for the lettering and layout: symmetrical, framed, with capitals packed into ruled bands. It is a German commission by one of the founders of the Secession.

context: The MAK records the object as a poster stamp (Werbemarke) designed by Joseph Maria Olbrich in 1907, printed in collotype, 4.5 × 3.1 cm. The text reads “Mai / Kölner / October / Ausstellung / veranstaltet v. d. A. G. Flora / Kunst und Kunstgewerbe / wechselnde Ausstellungen”. It is part of an album of poster stamps from the Werner J. Schweiger collection. [MAK KI 21484-3-311](https://sammlung.mak.at/en/collect/werbemarke-zur-koelner-ausstellung-1907_276583).

Olbrich (1867–1908) was one of the founders of the Vienna Secession. [Wikipedia: Joseph Maria Olbrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Maria_Olbrich). He completed the Secession building in 1898. [Wikipedia: Secession Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession_Building).
observed: The stamp is printed in one dark gray ink on pale paper, with perforated edges.
A border of small scallops and dots frames the upper field.
A diamond (a square set on its point) made of dense laurel leaves holds a tall tower with a figure on top, on the central axis.
Below, the text sits in five ruled bands. “KÖLNER” and “AUSSTELLUNG” are large; smaller capitals in the lower bands fill each band from edge to edge.
“MAI” and “OCTOBER” sit in small boxes at the two ends of the “KÖLNER” band. The small words “v. d. A. G.” and “und” are set at a smaller size between larger words.
The capitals are narrow and geometric; the U is drawn as a V.
interpretation: Olbrich uses the same devices as the Vienna posters: a frame, a central emblem, and text blocks in which letter size and width change so that every line is full. The laurel echoes the laurel dome of his Secession building.
Because it is a single-colour miniature, the stamp shows how much of the style is carried by structure and lettering alone.
borrow: Give a small badge or card a central emblem in a square set on its point, with the text in full-width ruled bands below it.
Set small connecting words (and, of, from) in a much smaller size between large words, so the line stays justified.

images.alt: Gray perforated poster stamp: a diamond of laurel leaves around a tower, above ruled bands of capitals reading Mai, Kölner, October, Ausstellung, veranstaltet v. d. A. G. Flora, Kunst und Kunstgewerbe, wechselnde Ausstellungen.
images.caption: Joseph Maria Olbrich, poster stamp for the Cologne exhibition, 1907. MAK Vienna, KI 21484-3-311, image from the [MAK Collection Online](https://sammlung.mak.at/en/collect/werbemarke-zur-koelner-ausstellung-1907_276583), Public Domain Mark 1.0.

rights.statement: The MAK marks this image with the [Public Domain Mark 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Joseph Maria Olbrich died in 1908, and the stamp was issued in 1907, so the work is in the public domain in Germany, Austria, and the United States.

references.title: Printed flannel with chevrons
references.lede: A surviving swatch of Varvara Stepanova’s geometric flannel print, made when constructivist artists turned to designing textiles for Soviet factories.
references.summary: Wine-red and olive-brown interlocking chevrons on a natural cotton ground. Varvara Stepanova, 1924, V&A.

evidence.note: Viewed the V&A photograph of the swatch T.213-2016 (1600 × 1443 px through the museum’s IIIF service) in a scratch folder. No image is stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: a productivist textile from the constructivist circle. It shares the flat, repeated geometry and diagonal movement, but it uses two muted hues instead of red and black and has no type.

context: The V&A describes the swatch as printed cotton flannel, about 22 × 23–25 cm, “with geometric design of wine red and dull olive-brown chevrons on a pale fawn natural colour ground”, made in Russia in 1924. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1371413/).

After an official appeal in 1923, Stepanova, Popova, and Rodchenko designed prints for the Soviet textile industry. The V&A notes that rural buyers preferred floral prints, so surviving samples are rare. Stepanova’s grandson Alexander Lavrentiev gave the swatch to the V&A director Martin Roth in 2014. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1371413/).
observed: Rows of chevrons point alternately up and down, in a wine red and an olive green-brown.
Pale bands of the unprinted ground run on two diagonals between the chevrons, so the pattern reads as a lattice of zigzags.
The edges are cut and slightly frayed; the flannel nap softens the edges of the print.
interpretation: The swatch shows the style’s diagonal energy transferred to an all-over repeat. The color is quieter than in the posters, which suggests that the red-and-black rule belongs to print, not to every constructivist medium.
Compare [Popova’s design with stars in circles](ref:popova-stars-in-circles-textile-design), which keeps red and black.
borrow: Build a background pattern from two interlocking chevrons and let the gaps between them form a diagonal lattice.
Use a muted red with an earthy second color for a quieter version of the style.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Stepanova died in 1958, so her designs are protected in Russia until the end of 2028 or later (life + 70, plus 4 years if she worked during the Great Patriotic War). The V&A image is shown under the museum’s own terms.

references.title: Propellerhead Reason, 2000
references.lede: Music software drawn as a studio equipment rack, with a back panel of animated patch cables.
references.summary: A virtual rack of synthesizers and effects with riveted panels and patch cables. Propellerhead, 2000.

source.label: Sound On Sound, Derek Johnson and Debbie Poyser, review (March 2001)

evidence.note: No image was inspected. Based on the Sound On Sound review (March 2001) and Wikipedia.

styles.note: The audio branch of the style: hardware imitated down to rack rails, rivets, knobs, and cables. It predates the Apple period and continued through it.

context: Reason first released in 2000. “Reason simulates a recording studio with virtual cables and representations of a subtractive synthesizer, sampler and drum machine.” [Wikipedia: Reason Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_Studios).

Sound On Sound: devices “appear as graphic units in a rack”; “flipping the on-screen image reveals a back-panel view of the virtual hardware, complete with animated pluggable cabling.” Audio cables are red, effects cables green, and Gate and CV leads yellow. The mixer’s look “owes a lot to Mackie’s LM3204.” [Sound On Sound, March 2001](https://www.soundonsound.com/reviews/propellerhead-software-reason).

Wikipedia’s skeuomorph article names audio software that emulates “physical musical instruments and audio equipment complete with buttons and dials” as an extreme example. [Wikipedia: Skeuomorph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeuomorph).
interpretation: Here the metaphor carries function: the cable view is how users route signals. It is the strongest case for the style’s claim that familiar objects teach.
next: Find an openly licensed screenshot of Reason 1–6 and inspect it.

rights.statement: Propellerhead software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.

references.title: Ray Gun Bryan Ferry interview in Zapf Dingbats
references.titleBreak: Ray Gun Bryan Ferry interview|in Zapf Dingbats
references.lede: The 1994 Ray Gun spread in which David Carson set a whole Bryan Ferry interview in the symbol font Zapf Dingbats.
references.summary: Justified columns made entirely of dingbat symbols, with giant dingbats over the headline. David Carson, Ray Gun, 1994.

source.label: Sharan Shetty, “The Rise And Fall Of Grunge Typography”, The Awl (2012), archived copy

references.made: 1994 (The Awl); issue number not stated by the sources

evidence.note: Inspected a 1100 × 697 photograph of the opened spread, posted on the Process & Skills student blog (2013), in a scratchpad copy; The Awl’s own copy is 640 px wide. The owner of the photographed copy and the issue number are not stated. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example of the style’s attitude: legibility is abandoned on purpose. Partial fit for its surface, because the dingbats are clean and the ground is not dirty.

context: The Awl says Carson disliked a Ray Gun article on Bryan Ferry and set the entire spread in Zapf Dingbats, in a 1994 issue. [The Awl](https://web.archive.org/web/20150925150838/http://www.theawl.com/2012/08/grunge-typography).
Wikipedia cites the Ferry interview as the example of Ray Gun’s not always readable “grunge typography”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Gun_(magazine)).
observed: The right-hand page and most of the left are justified columns made entirely of Zapf Dingbats symbols: stars, circles, triangles, crosses, and arrows.
A grey rectangle sits behind part of the dingbat text and crosses the gutter.
The headline “bryan ferry” is a lowercase serif, partly covered by a large maroon four-lobed dingbat and a yellow-green photograph of Ferry in an armchair.
A large olive asterisk-like dingbat and a row of grey stars and flowers act as display ornaments.
The photo credit under the picture is the only readable text.
interpretation: The spread is grunge as a gesture rather than as a texture: it uses a clean, standard font to make text unreadable. It belongs in the collection for its intent and for how often it is cited, not for its surfaces.
borrow: Use a symbol font as a grey texture that has the rhythm of text, in a decorative area only.
Enlarge single dingbats to poster size and let them cover a headline.

rights.statement: No image is stored. David Carson is living, so the design is in copyright. Photographs by their sources.

references.title: Ray Gun no. 12, “The LA episode”
references.lede: A Ray Gun issue from the turn of 1993–94, with Deborah Harry interviewing L7 on the cover and headlines inside that are scattered, doubled, blurred, and sprayed.
references.summary: Green masthead bar over L7, scattered outline letters over body text, and a blurred, doubled “Mazzy Star” headline with yellow spray. David Carson, Ray Gun no. 12.

source.label: Display Graphic Design Collection: Ray Gun, No. 12

evidence.note: Inspected five photographs (1600 × 1279 each) of one copy offered by Display in scratchpad copies: the cover and four interior spreads. The copy has no collection number. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example: headlines are scattered, blurred, doubled, and sprayed over body text, while the cover stays comparatively plain.

context: Display lists the issue as no. 12, 10 × 12 inches, 108 pages, art direction by David Carson, with L7 interviewed by Deborah Harry, and features on Mazzy Star, Redd Kross, Moby, and Yo La Tengo. [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/ray-gun-no-12-december-january-1993-david-carson).
Wikipedia’s issue list dates no. 12 to December 1993/January 1994, with L7 on the cover. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Gun_(magazine)).
observed: The cover is a full-bleed colour photograph of L7 with a bright green masthead bar reading “R AYGUN,” in heavy black sans-serif with an odd gap and a trailing comma.
Cover lines are a condensed sans-serif in white capitals, right-aligned in a narrow column.
The Bad Religion spread scatters large serif capitals, some in outline, across a brown duotone band photograph and over the body text; a brown splash surrounds one letter.
Pull-quote lines are set in several sizes and faces and overlap the text columns.
The Mazzy Star headline is blurred, doubled, and scratched, repeated across both pages, with yellow spray-paint marks over the body text.
The Mazzy Star body text is an italic serif set in a tilted, bending column; the photograph has a rough black border.
The Redd Kross opener uses a spiky decorative serif for the headline and byline over a red duotone photograph of sneakers.
interpretation: This issue shows how grunge damage is concentrated in headlines and ornaments. Body text stays set in conventional serifs and a typewriter face, even when it is tilted or overlapped.
borrow: Repeat a headline twice with a slight offset and blur, as a misregistered print.
Scatter the letters of one heading across a spread in mixed outline and solid capitals.
Add one spray or stain mark in a muted accent colour over body text, not over the headline.

rights.statement: No image is stored. David Carson is living, so the design is in copyright. Photographs by their sources.

references.title: Ray Gun, premiere issue
references.lede: The first issue of the music magazine Ray Gun, November 1992: painted and scratched covers, typewriter lists, and spreads where text is layered until it turns into texture.
references.summary: Scratched yellow cover with a red condensed masthead, typewriter band list, and overprinted, collaged spreads inside. David Carson, Ray Gun no. 1, 1992.

source.label: Display Graphic Design Collection: Ray Gun, Premiere Issue, November 1992

evidence.note: Inspected eight photographs (1600 × 1279 each) of one copy offered by Display, a design collection and bookshop, in scratchpad copies: the cover, six interior spreads, and one further collaged page with the masthead. The copy has no collection number. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example: the first issue of the magazine that defines the style, with scratched, overprinted, and hand-lettered type over painted and photocopied grounds.

context: Ray Gun was a music magazine first published in Santa Monica in 1992, with Marvin Scott Jarrett as publisher and David Carson as art director. Wikipedia describes its editorial pages as a “chaotic, abstract ‘grunge typography’ style”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Gun_(magazine)).

Display lists the issue as no. 1, November 1992, 10 × 12 inches, 100 pages, with Carson credited as design consultant. Its first page reads “Raw by choice. Immediate by necessity. Alternative by design.” [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/ray-gun-premiere-issue-november-1992-david-carson).

Features include Henry Rollins, Sonic Youth (photographed by Spike Jonze), The Lemonheads, and The Prodigy. [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/ray-gun-premiere-issue-november-1992-david-carson).
observed: The cover is a scraped yellow, white, and black painted surface with pencil scrawl, paint spatter, and a heavy black scribble.
Two black-and-white face fragments are cut into rough rectangles and pasted into the paint.

The masthead “rAY GUn” is a red condensed sans-serif in mixed case, with letters of different heights; “PREMIERE ISSUE” is blue hand lettering; the band list is a typewriter face, indented in an uneven zigzag.
The Sonic Youth opener layers strips of contact-sheet film, overprinted serif and sans-serif lines, and blue text until lines collide.
A second Sonic Youth spread has large blue hand-painted words over a page of body text, facing a painted face on red gingham with a scrawled title.
One spread overprints lines of text in several faces until the headline area becomes a solid black mass.
A music-video feature sets its body in a condensed typewriter face, justified in narrow columns, facing a cropped blue duotone photograph.
Headlines break words across lines and space them down the page (“lov / i / ng / the / rock / star”).
interpretation: The issue shows the whole grammar at once: damaged grounds, several unrelated faces per spread, and body text used as a texture. The typewriter lists and captions are the stable voice among the noise.
borrow: Set a list of names in a typewriter face with alternating indents instead of a clean column.
Overprint a headline in several faces and colors until part of it becomes a black mass, and keep the body text clean beside it.
Paste photo fragments with rough rectangular edges onto a painted or scratched ground.

rights.statement: No image is stored. David Carson is living, so the design is in copyright. Photographs by their sources.

references.title: Reactor typeface, FUSE poster
references.lede: Tobias Frere-Jones’s distressed sans-serif for the experimental type magazine FUSE, shown on its FUSE poster as white capitals that break up line by line.
references.summary: White eroded capitals on a black, smeared photographic ground, with a yellow line at the foot. Tobias Frere-Jones, FUSE, 1993.
references.made: 1993 (Fonts In Use; poster credit line); released by Font Bureau in 1996

evidence.note: Inspected the FUSE poster for Reactor as reproduced in Typographica’s review of the FUSE 1–20 book (1647 × 2340), and the Fonts In Use type sample (856 × 194), in scratchpad copies. The FUSE issue number was not confirmed. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example: a font drawn damaged, whose distress grows as more text is set.

context: Fonts In Use says Frere-Jones designed Reactor in 1993 for Neville Brody and Jon Wozencroft’s FUSE; Font Bureau released it in 1996, and it is no longer sold. [Fonts In Use](https://fontsinuse.com/typefaces/26615/fb-reactor).

Chris Hamamoto describes Reactor as “inspired by a burning building and its ruins”, with lowercase letters that contain copies of other characters extending into their neighbours, adding distress “the more type is set”. [Typographica](https://typographica.org/typography-books/fuse-1-20/).

Wikipedia’s list of Frere-Jones typefaces calls Reactor (1993–96) “an example of the ‘grunge typography’ style of the 1990s”, citing Ellen Lupton. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_typefaces_designed_by_Tobias_Frere-Jones).
observed: The poster is black with a grey, smeared photographic texture in the upper half and a dark photograph of machinery or wreckage at the foot.

Five lines of white capitals, cropped at both page edges, read like an incident report: “…WER LOSS IN ENGINE 3”, “…TIONAL DOWN 95 POI…”, “…ORE INTEGRITY SUSP…”, “…RNAL STRUCTURE DAM…”, “…LTIPLE SKULL FRACTU…”.
The first line is only lightly rough; each following line has more specks, torn edges, and stray fragments, until the letters in the last line are hard to separate.
A final line, “I CAN HEAR IT NOW”, is set in yellow in the same face with little damage.
The small credit line reads “F REACTOR ® 1993 FONTSHOP INTERNATIONAL © 1993 TOBIAS FRERE-JONES” in a plain monospaced face.
In the Fonts In Use sample, the capitals are a narrow humanist sans-serif with ragged, splintered edges and doubled strokes.
interpretation: Reactor makes distress a function of the text, not a filter: the more you type, the worse it gets. The poster shows the style’s link between damage and content.
borrow: Increase distress down a stack of display lines, so the page seems to decay as it is read.
Crop display lines at both edges of the page, as if the text continues off-screen.

rights.statement: No image is stored. © 1993 Tobias Frere-Jones and FontShop International, per the poster’s credit line.

references.title: Red Blue Chair
references.lede: Rietveld’s armchair of square battens and two flat boards: a red back, a blue seat, and a black frame whose cut ends are painted yellow.
references.summary: Red back, blue seat, black batten frame with yellow ends. Gerrit Rietveld, designed 1917–1918, colored about 1923.
references.made: Designed 1917–1918; painted in its known colors in the early 1920s (about 1923 per MoMA)

evidence.note: Inspected a photograph by Daderot of the copy in the Museum für Angewandte Kunst Köln, labeled “Roodblauwe Stoel … G. A. van de Groenekan, Utrecht NL, 1918, lacquered wood” ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Armchair_Roodblauwe_Stoel,_designed_by_Gerrit_T._Rietveld,_G._A._van_de_Groenekan,_Utrecht_NL,_1918,_lacquered_wood_-_Museum_f%C3%BCr_Angewandte_Kunst_K%C3%B6ln_-_Cologne,_Germany_-_DSC09583.jpg), 3222 × 4039 px, viewed at 1280 px). Many copies exist and they differ. The MoMA page returned 403 to the fetch tool; MoMA facts come from its catalogue text as shown in search results.

styles.note: The movement’s best-known object: separate bars and boards that overlap without joining, each painted one color, in the primaries and black.

context: Wikipedia dates the design to 1917 and states that the chair was not painted in its distinct colors until the early 1920s, and that several versions are held in collections. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_and_Blue_Chair).
MoMA dates its copy 1918–1923, painted wood, 86.7 × 66 × 83.8 cm, and states that the red, yellow, blue, and black scheme was applied around 1923. [MoMA](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/4044).
observed: The back is a flat red board set at a steep slant; the seat is a flat dark blue board set at a shallower slant.
The frame is made of square black battens that cross each other and run past every joint.
Every cut end of a batten is painted yellow, which makes small yellow squares at the ends.
The armrests are flat black boards resting on the frame.
In this museum photograph the chair stands on a white plinth in front of a frosted window.
interpretation: The chair applies the painting rule to an object: lines become battens, planes become boards, and the joints are left visible as overlaps rather than hidden.
The yellow ends show how a primary can be used as a point accent that marks where a line ends.
borrow: Mark the ends of lines or bars with a small square of a primary.
Let structural bars cross and overshoot, and keep flat panels in single colors.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is CC0, and Commons notes that the chair, as a utilitarian object, is not protected by US copyright. Rietveld died in 1964, and in the Netherlands and the EU applied art is protected until 2035, so the chair is treated as link only.

references.title: Red House, Bexleyheath
references.lede: The red-brick house that Philip Webb and William Morris designed in 1859 as Morris’s home, an early building of the movement.
references.summary: Red brick, steep tiled roofs, round and pointed windows, and a conical well house. Philip Webb and William Morris, 1859–60.

evidence.note: Inspected a 2004 photograph of the garden front by the Wikipedia user Velela on [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Red_House,_Bexleyheath.JPG) (1296 × 972 px; viewed at 1280 px wide). The interior was not inspected.

styles.note: The movement’s founding house: vernacular red brick and medieval forms, built as the setting for Morris’s craft work.

context: Webb and Morris co-designed the house in 1859 as a family home for Morris; it was completed in 1860. Wikipedia calls it an early example of what came to be known as the Arts and Crafts movement. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_House,_Bexleyheath).

Morris called it “very medieval in spirit”. Burne-Jones and Rossetti helped decorate it, and while living there Morris helped form Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. and began his first wallpaper designs. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_House,_Bexleyheath).
It became a Grade I listed building in 1950, and the National Trust bought it in 2003. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_House,_Bexleyheath).
observed: The walls are red brick; the steep roofs are dark tile, with red ridge tiles and tall red chimney stacks.
A square wing with a pyramidal roof carries a small lead-covered turret.
Windows vary: tall narrow sashes, a large multi-pane window under a pointed brick arch, two round windows, and white sash windows. The door sits in a deep pointed arch.
In the lawn in front stands a well house with a steep conical tiled roof on timber posts over a round brick base.
Climbing plants cover much of the lower walls.
interpretation: The house carries the movement’s ideas in building form: local materials, visible structure, and medieval arches used for a small home. Its red brick and dark tile match the warm end of the style’s dye palette.
The asymmetrical plan and mixed windows are the architectural side of the style; they have no direct equivalent in the graphic rubric.
borrow: Combine one warm, dark red with a deep grey-brown and a strong green for a palette taken from brick, tile, and planting.
Mix a few distinct window shapes, round and arched, as a motif set.

images.alt: Red-brick house with steep dark tiled roofs, tall chimneys, round windows, pointed arches, and climbing plants, with a well house under a conical tiled roof on the lawn in front.
images.caption: Red House, Bexleyheath, garden front with the well house, photographed June 2004 by Velela. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Red_House,_Bexleyheath.JPG), public domain.

rights.statement: The photographer released the photograph into the public domain (Commons). The building was completed in 1860 and its architects died in 1896 and 1915, so it is not protected by copyright.

references.title: Reeder website, 2011
references.lede: The site for the RSS reader Reeder, archived October 2011: two panes of speckled paper with pale debossed type.
references.summary: Speckled paper texture, a debossed logo, and a thin pane divider. Nothing else.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The archived page may lack some images or scripts that the live page had.

styles.note: Borderline: the paper texture and debossed type are the style, but the page shows only those two traits.

observed: The whole viewport is pale warm-gray paper with small specks, split into two panes by a thin dark line.
The logo “reeder” with a star and feed waves is a slightly darker gray, pressed into the paper with a light lower edge.
Three links (for iPhone, for iPad, for Mac) are pale gray text on the paper.
A small gray ribbon at the bottom reads “MADE@GLORIA!”.
interpretation: It passes the shadow and radius metrics but fails the pattern and gradient metrics: the paper is one bitmap image, measured as 100% image share.
borrow: Use a speckled paper texture and a debossed logo alone for a very quiet version of the style.

images.alt: Archived Reeder page: two panes of pale speckled paper separated by a thin line, with a pale gray debossed reeder logo and three faint links for iPhone, iPad, and Mac.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20111002015721/http://reederapp.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Reflect notes website
references.lede: A note-taking app shown as a dark, translucent window that a violet light glows through.
references.summary: A dark glass app window under a violet eclipse glow, with a pill-shaped translucent navigation bar.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. A Superdesign article names Reflect as a glassmorphism example; that claim was not relied on.

styles.note: Borderline: the app window is dark translucent glass that the violet glow shows through, but the page is mostly near-black and uses small radii.

observed: The page is near-black navy. A bright violet and white ring of light, like an eclipse, sits behind the top edge of an app window.
The app window is dark and translucent: the violet glow shows through its middle column as a soft haze.
The window has rounded corners and a thin light border. Inside it, a sidebar, a note, and a calendar use grey and white sans-serif text.
The top navigation links sit in one dark pill with a thin border. ‘Start free trial’ is a violet button with a light border.
interpretation: Measured: blur share 0.21, median radius 6 px, 27 % of boxes bordered, and 62 % with gradient fills. It fails five of six metrics, so the glass effect here comes from one large element rather than many cards. It is the dark, glow-lit variant of the style, close to the look of many AI and developer-tool sites.
borrow: Put a single bright glow behind the top edge of a dark glass panel so that the light seems to pass through it.

images.alt: Reflect home page: the headline ‘Think better with Reflect’ above a violet eclipse glow, which shines through a dark translucent app window with a sidebar, a daily note, and a calendar.
images.caption: First viewport of [reflect.app](https://reflect.app/), captured 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Rietveld Schröder House, Utrecht
references.lede: Gerrit Rietveld’s house of 1924: white and gray wall planes, black frames, and a few linear elements in the primaries, arranged as separate slabs and bars.
references.summary: White and gray slabs, black window frames, and a yellow post and red bars. Gerrit Rietveld, Utrecht, 1924.

evidence.note: Inspected a 2010 photograph of the street front by User:Husky on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rietveld_Schr%C3%B6derhuis_HayKranen-20.JPG) (4515 × 3010 px, viewed at 1280 px). No image is stored. The museum’s website showed a cookie box over its home page in a headless capture.

styles.note: The movement’s best-known building: planes and bars that overlap without joining, white and gray surfaces, and small primary accents.

context: Rietveld built the house in 1924 for Truus Schröder-Schräder and her three children. The facades have white and gray surfaces, black window and door frames, and linear elements in primary colors. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rietveld_Schr%C3%B6der_House).

The upper floor uses sliding and revolving panels to open or divide the space. The house was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on 2 December 2000 and is run by the Centraal Museum. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rietveld_Schr%C3%B6der_House).
observed: The house is a composition of flat white and gray wall slabs and thin roof slabs that project past the walls.
A tall yellow post stands at the left corner and runs above the roof edge; a black steel post supports a balcony at the center.
Red appears in thin horizontal bars at the upper right window and in a short vertical element at the ground floor right.
Window frames are black; a cantilevered white balcony slab with a black railing projects over the entrance.
The house joins the end wall of a brick terrace with pitched roofs, which makes its flat planes stand out.
interpretation: The house turns the painting rule into space: each plane and bar is a separate element with its own color, and the primaries are used as thin accents while white and gray carry the mass.
It shows that the style’s primaries can be very small in area and still dominate.
borrow: Let panels overlap and project past each other instead of meeting in closed corners.
Keep large areas white and gray, and use primaries only for thin structural elements such as posts, bars, or rules.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is CC BY 3.0, but Rietveld died in 1964, so the building is protected in the Netherlands until 2035. Dutch freedom of panorama (Article 18 of the Auteurswet) and the United States exclusion of pre-1990 buildings would probably permit exterior photographs; the lead curator can decide whether to upgrade to tier A.

references.title: Riga Art Nouveau Centre website
references.lede: The Riga museum’s site crowns a plain blue-and-white layout with a drawn header of Jugendstil masks and flared lettering.
references.summary: Drawn Jugendstil header with masks and hand-lettered name, over a blue and white serif layout.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. A cookie notice covers the bottom sixth of the viewport.

styles.note: Borderline: the header is a drawn Art Nouveau facade ornament with flared hand lettering, but the rest of the page is a plain blue grid.

observed: The header is a blue line drawing on pale blue of two large female masks with stylized hair, flanking a dark blue panel with “RĪGAS JŪGENDSTILA CENTRS” in hand-drawn, flared capitals and a curling ornament below.
The navigation sits on white in a serif (Lora), in mid-blue capitals separated by small snowflake-like ornaments.
The main area is a photograph of the museum’s spiral staircase with painted Art Nouveau wall decoration, next to a dark blue information column.
Two overlay labels in yellow serif with yellow triangles sit over the photograph.
A cookie notice covers the bottom sixth of the viewport.
interpretation: Only the header and the photograph carry the style. The blue palette is closer to the Riga facades than to the grammar’s moss and ochre.
Measured: square boxes (radius median 0), 1 px borders on half the boxes, no shadows, two colour families, and accent chroma 0.52.
borrow: Draw the site header as a line illustration in one colour and set the name inside it in hand-drawn flared capitals.
Separate navigation items with a small ornament instead of a bar.

images.alt: Riga Art Nouveau Centre home page: a blue line-drawn header with two stylized masks and hand-lettered museum name, a serif navigation bar, a photograph of a painted spiral staircase, and a dark blue information column.
images.caption: First viewport of [jugendstils.riga.lv](https://jugendstils.riga.lv/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Roboto
references.lede: Christian Robertson’s grotesque for Android, redesigned in 2014 to be the voice of Material Design.
references.summary: A neutral grotesque with open curves and straight-sided rounds, in weights from Thin to Black. Google, 2011, redesigned 2014.

evidence.note: Opened the Wikimedia Commons weight sample *Roboto weights.png* by Blythwood (26 December 2014) as a 960 × 1338 rendering on 28 September 2026. The sample has no R, i-dot close-up, or figures, so it does not show which of the two Roboto versions it uses.

styles.note: The style’s typeface. The Material 1 and 2 type scale is defined in Roboto, and the 2014 redesign was announced with Material Design.

context: Christian Robertson designed Roboto in house at Google for Android 4.0 in 2011. On 25 June 2014 Matías Duarte announced at Google I/O that Roboto was redesigned for Android 5.0: dots and punctuation became rounded, the leg of R became straight, and the family became “slightly wider and rounder”. [Wikipedia: Roboto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roboto).
The family was released under the Apache License, and most variants were later relicensed under the SIL Open Font License. [Wikipedia: Roboto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roboto).
observed: The phrase “Semi-fast” repeats six times in orange-red on a pale cream ground, from a hairline Thin weight to a heavy Black.
The round letters (S, e, a) have fairly straight sides and open apertures. The a has a small bowl and a straight stem.
Weights grow evenly. In the Black weight the counters of e and a close to small slits.
interpretation: Roboto is neutral enough to disappear into an interface. That fits Material, where hierarchy comes from size, weight, and elevation, not from a characterful font.
borrow: Use only Regular and Medium for interface text, and Light or Regular for large display lines, as the Material type scale does.

images.alt: The word Semi-fast set six times in orange-red Roboto on a cream background, from very thin at the top to very heavy at the bottom.
images.caption: Roboto weight sample by Blythwood, 2014, from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Roboto_weights.png), resized. CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: The sample image is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 by its author, Blythwood. It shows only letterforms. Typeface designs are not protected by copyright in the United States, Roboto’s country of origin, and the font itself is under the Apache License 2.0 or the SIL Open Font License.

references.title: S.S. United States poster
references.lede: Lester Beall loops a single red arrow around the word NEWEST and the ship’s two funnels, on cream paper between heavy black and blue bands.
references.summary: A red looping arrow, flat red and blue funnels, and heavy condensed type on cream. Lester Beall for United States Lines, 1952.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: 1951 SS United States Travel Poster by Lester Thomas Beall (1).jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the 1280 × 1751 px Commons rendition of the scan (original 1358 × 1858 px). Commons names the Smithsonian National Museum of American History (nmah_1102295) as the source, but that page returned HTTP 403 to scripts and to WebFetch, so the museum record was not read.

styles.note: Partial fit: American corporate modernism of the early 1950s, with flat shapes on cream paper, a gestural arrow, and mixed type. The palette is red, blue, and black rather than the style’s warm earth tones.

context: The Commons description says Lester Beall designed the poster for United States Lines as part of his wider graphic design for the ship’s identity, and that the line advertised the SS United States as the largest and fastest passenger ship built in the United States. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1951_SS_United_States_Travel_Poster_by_Lester_Thomas_Beall_(1).jpg).
Beall lived from 1903 to 1969. [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q6531814).
observed: A black band at the top carries “S.S. UNITED STATES” in heavy slab-like capitals, cream with the upper half tinted blue, and “NEW YORK ★ HAVRE ★ SOUTHAMPTON” in widely spaced geometric sans capitals.
The middle is cream paper. A thin red line loops once around the word “NEWEST” and ends in an arrowhead at the upper right.
“NEWEST” is set in thin, tall, slightly italic capitals; “…LARGEST AND FASTEST AMERICAN SHIP” below is a bold condensed sans.
Two raked funnels are flat red with blue caps, black bands, and a soft dark edge on one side. Below them the superstructure is drawn in gray outline with rows of windows and dots.
A black hull band crosses the lower third. A blue band at the foot holds “UNITED STATES LINES” in heavy condensed black capitals.
A small signature is visible at the upper right corner.
interpretation: The single looping arrow is a hand gesture laid over otherwise mechanical drawing: the mix of the drawn and the engineered that marks American graphic modernism of the period.
Four typefaces in one poster, from thin display to heavy condensed, show the style’s loose, mixed typography. Measured on the stored image: cream background (#f1e6d2), accent chroma 0.54.
borrow: Let one thin colored line loop around a heading and exit as an arrow.
Frame a cream field between a heavy dark top band and a colored bottom band.

images.alt: Travel poster: S.S. United States in heavy capitals on a black band, a cream field where a thin red arrow loops around the word Newest above two flat red funnels with blue caps, a gray line drawing of the ship’s decks, a black hull band, and United States Lines in heavy black capitals on a blue band.
images.caption: Lester Beall, poster for the S.S. United States, United States Lines, 1952. Scan from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1951_SS_United_States_Travel_Poster_by_Lester_Thomas_Beall_(1).jpg), marked public domain (no notice).
