references.title: Sam Xie portfolio
references.lede: A software engineer’s portfolio on a pale gray gradient with a soft raised button and a white 3D bird.
references.summary: Personal portfolio: pale gray surface, a raised pill button, a raised panel, and a monochrome 3D render.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline. The pale gray surface, the raised “Browse products” pill, and the raised panel below follow the style, but the first viewport is mostly type and a 3D render, and the shadows are small.

context: The site’s template is published as [samzx/soft-portfolio](https://github.com/samzx/soft-portfolio) (created 1 May 2020), described as “a neumorphic inspired website”.
observed: A pale gray page with a faint diagonal gradient. “Sam Xie” is set in a very large, bold, near-black sans-serif.
A “Browse products” pill in a lighter gray with a soft shadow is the only control.
A large white 3D render of a bird in flight fills the right half.
The top edge of a wide panel in a lighter gray with round corners rises from the bottom of the viewport.
interpretation: One of the few personal sites found that still use the style. The monochrome 3D bird matches the surface; the open-source template it derives from calls itself “a neumorphic inspired website”.
Measured: shadows on 71 % of boxes (median offset 4.5 px, median blur 4 px, none hard), borders on 0 %, median radius 20 px.

images.alt: Sam Xie portfolio home page: a pale gray page with the name in large black type, a soft raised Browse products pill, a white 3D bird in flight, and the top of a raised panel.

references.title: San Francisco Oracle, vol. 1 no. 10, cover
references.lede: The front page of the Haight-Ashbury underground newspaper, October 1967: a mandala of rings and checkerboards in magenta, violet, and turquoise on newsprint.
references.summary: October 1967. Concentric mandala, swollen ORACLE masthead, and warped checkerboards in three inks on newsprint.

source.label: Internet Archive: San Francisco Oracle Vol. 1 No. 10 (Daniel D. Teoli Jr. Archival Collection)

creator.name: The Oracle of the City of San Francisco (Allen Cohen, editor); cover artist not identified

evidence.note: Downloaded page 1 of the Teoli scan (2704 × 4073 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The cover is signed at lower center with a name I could not read, dated ’67. The Letterform Archive scans of other issues on Internet Archive are stream-only. The image is not stored.

styles.note: A clear example in newsprint: every part of the page is patterned, the masthead swells to fill an arch, and magenta, violet, and turquoise sit side by side.

context: The Oracle was an underground newspaper published in 12 issues from September 1966 to February 1968 in the Haight-Ashbury, edited by Allen Cohen with Michael Bowen as art director. Wikipedia calls it “arguably the outstanding example of psychedelia” in the underground press. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Oracle).

From issue 6 the paper was printed at Howard Quinn Printers, where its artists perfected the split-fountain rainbow effect by damming the ink fountain to feed several colors at once. The print run peaked at about 125,000. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Oracle).
The Internet Archive item states a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license from the scanning collector. That license covers the scan, not the 1967 artwork.
observed: ORACLE fills an arch across the top in fat turquoise letters with violet shadows and outlines. THE CITY OF SAN FRANCISCO curves above it in smaller letters.
A large mandala of concentric rings, lobes, and interlocking circles fills the middle. Its center is a small target of tight rings.
Warped checkerboards in magenta, violet, turquoise, and paper color fill every corner and recede like a tunnel.
An embracing couple drawn in rough outline stands at the bottom center, under a figure-eight sign.
The inks are magenta, violet, and turquoise on yellowed newsprint. Prices, the date, and the issue number are lettered by hand into the pattern.
interpretation: This page meets all four diagnostics of the rubric: complementary colors side by side, a swollen masthead, a symmetrical central medallion, and rings and patterns that fill the background.
Low-cost three-ink newsprint produced the same effect as the poster work, which suggests the look depends on arrangement more than on premium printing.
borrow: Arch a fat masthead over a central mandala and let pattern fill the rest.
Use a warped checkerboard that recedes toward the center to give depth without shading.
Letter small facts, such as price and date, into the pattern instead of into a separate box.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The cover artwork is in copyright or of unknown status; the artist is not identified. The CC BY-NC-ND license on the Internet Archive item applies to the scan only.

references.title: Sci-Arc “Changing Concepts” poster
references.lede: April Greiman’s lecture-series poster for the Southern California Institute of Architecture: pixel type in black squares, dot-screen gradients, and a spaced-out subtitle.
references.summary: Orange-to-blue gradient panels, a dotted Vitruvian figure, “sci-arc” in pixel letters on black squares, and “concepts of s p a c e”. April Greiman, 1986.

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object E.1500-2010 (image 2011EN9653, 1200 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The smallest text is not readable at this size.

styles.note: Clear example from the late, digital phase: letterspacing, weight changes inside a phrase, dot screens, and overlapping panels, with early bitmap letters.

context: The V&A holds the poster as E.1500-2010, colour offset lithograph, 91.5 × 61 cm, published in the United States in 1986, and describes it as the “Sci-Arc Changing Concepts poster”. [V&A E.1500-2010](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1176682/).
observed: Overlapping rectangles in orange, magenta, pale yellow, and cyan fade into each other as gradients.
A white dotted drawing of a Vitruvian figure in a circle and square fills a panel that is covered by a regular grid of dots.
A small orange-framed photograph of broken classical fragments sits at the centre.
“sci-arc” is set in blocky pixel letters, one letter on each black square, with wide gaps between the squares.
“changing / concepts of s p a c e / in architecture / and art” is set flush left in lines that change weight, and “space” is spaced out letter by letter.
A lecture list at the top right runs on thin rules, with black numbered squares and black bars at the right edge.
A column of small photographs runs down the left edge. Fields of scattered dots cover the orange ground.
interpretation: The poster keeps the Basel habits (steps, bars, screens, spacing) and replaces film halftones with computer dot patterns and bitmap letters. It sits at the point where New Wave turns into digital design.
The pixel letters are clean, not distressed, so the counter-rule on damaged letterforms still holds.
borrow: Set a short name one letter per solid square, with gaps between the squares.
Letterspace only one word in a phrase to make it the subject.
Put a list on hairline rules and end each row with a black bar at the page edge.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. April Greiman is living, so the design is in copyright.

references.title: Se7en title sequence
references.lede: Kyle Cooper’s opening titles for David Fincher’s 1995 film: hand-scratched letters that jitter and smear over close-ups of a killer’s notebooks.
references.summary: Scratched white credits flicker over notebooks, razor blades, and film leader in dark brown and green. Kyle Cooper, R/GA, 1995.

evidence.note: Inspected Art of the Title’s grid of nine stills (1080 × 452, each still about 360 px wide) in a scratchpad copy. The moving sequence was not watched. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example of the style in motion: scratched, smeared, jittering letters mixed with a plain sans-serif over grimy close-ups.

context: Art of the Title says the typography was hand-etched into black scratchboard and manipulated during film transfer “to further smear and jitter it”, then cut up and reassembled. [Art of the Title](https://www.artofthetitle.com/title/se7en/).

Cooper says he and Fincher “decided to use hand-drawn [type] mixed with Helvetica”, because the titles came “from the mind of the killer”. [Art of the Title](https://www.artofthetitle.com/title/se7en/).

The sequence was assembled mostly by hand as a traditional film optical; the notebooks were designed by Clive Piercy and John Sabel. Art of the Title reports that the New York Times called it “one of the most important design innovations of the 1990s”. [Art of the Title](https://www.artofthetitle.com/title/se7en/).
observed: Credits are white on dark frames: small plain sans-serif capitals (“NEW LINE CINEMA PRESENTS”, “CASTING BY”) beside larger hand-scratched names.
The title “SE7EN” is rough, uneven white capitals over a blurred notebook page.
Some credit words are doubled or ghosted, with letters shifted against each other.
Images are extreme close-ups of hands, notebooks with dense handwriting, cut photographs, a razor, and a dollar bill with “IN GOD” cut out.
The palette is near-black with sepia, olive, and dirty green.
interpretation: Se7en carries the grunge vocabulary into film and fixed it as a horror and thriller convention. The mix of neutral Helvetica with scratched letters matches the style’s rule of clashing faces.
borrow: Mix a neutral sans-serif with scratched, hand-drawn letters in the same credit line.
Animate display type with small frame-to-frame jitter and ghosting, and keep the timing short.

rights.statement: No image is stored. © New Line Cinema; stills via Art of the Title.

references.title: Secession Building, Vienna
references.lede: Joseph Maria Olbrich’s exhibition house of 1898: white cubic blocks with flat pylons around a dome of pierced metal laurel leaves.
references.summary: White cubic volumes, square pylons, and a pierced dome of laurel leaves. Joseph Maria Olbrich, Vienna, 1898.

evidence.note: Inspected two Wien Museum photographs (3500 px wide): the plate “Das Haus der Secession in Wien, Seitenansicht” from the Wiener Bauten-Album, 1899–1900 (inv. 54584/14), and a postcard of about 1905 by Deutsch’s Postkartenverlag (inv. 309795). Both are black and white, so they do not show the colour of the dome.

styles.note: Partial fit: the movement’s own building, with cubic masses, square pylons, and a laurel dome, but its 1898 relief ornament of trees and leaves belongs to the early floral phase.

context: Wikipedia: the building was completed in 1898 by Joseph Maria Olbrich as an architectural manifesto for the Vienna Secession. It holds Gustav Klimt’s Beethoven Frieze. The motto “Der Zeit ihre Kunst. Der Kunst ihre Freiheit” is written above the entrance. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession_Building).

The Wiener Bauten-Album plate is captioned “Das Haus der Secession in Wien. Architekt: Joseph Olbrich C. M. Erbaut 1898. Seitenansicht.” It was a supplement to the Wiener Bauindustrie-Zeitung, 1899/1900. [Wien Museum 54584/14](https://sammlung.wienmuseum.at/en/object/127802-1-friedrichstrasse-12-secession-seitenansicht-wiener-bauten-album-blatt-nr-38-beilage-zur-wiener-bauindustrie-zeitung/).
observed: The front block is a white cube with sharp corners. Four flat pylons rise from its top and frame a round dome.
The dome is a pierced ball of metal leaves, dark against the sky in both photographs.
The side wall of the front block carries tall stylized trees in low relief, with leafy crowns at the top corners, and small bands of square dots under the windows.
The long exhibition wing behind is plain white with large windows, small laurel wreaths in relief, and a row of glass roof lanterns.
Two tall flagpoles with ring tops stand in front of the side wall.
The plate is printed on cream paper with a thin ruled frame and centred captions in spaced capitals.
interpretation: The massing already shows the geometric turn: cubes, flat pylons, and a single round form on the axis. The plant reliefs still belong to the floral early Secession, which this catalogue files under [Art Nouveau](style:art-nouveau).
The dome is the one rich, textured element on a plain white building; in flat design it corresponds to one gold or patterned element on a white ground.
borrow: Set one round or gold element on the central axis, framed by plain square blocks.
Use small rows of square dots as a band under a heading or a window-like panel.

images.alt: Black and white plate of the Secession building from the side: a white cubic front block with four pylons around a leafy dome, relief trees on the wall, a long white exhibition wing with glass roof lanterns, and two tall flagpoles, with printed captions below.
images.caption: “Das Haus der Secession in Wien”, side view, Wiener Bauten-Album plate 38, 1899–1900, unknown photographer. Wien Museum, inv. 54584/14, image from the [Wien Museum Online Sammlung](https://sammlung.wienmuseum.at/en/object/127802-1-friedrichstrasse-12-secession-seitenansicht-wiener-bauten-album-blatt-nr-38-beilage-zur-wiener-bauindustrie-zeitung/), CC0, cropped to the sheet.

rights.statement: The Wien Museum releases this image under [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/). The building is by Joseph Maria Olbrich, who died in 1908, and the plate was printed in 1899–1900, so the works shown are in the public domain in Austria and in the United States.

references.title: Shag website
references.lede: The artist Shag fills the home page with one of his paintings: a flat, stylized 1950s living room in brown, orange, olive, and black under an orange bar.
references.summary: A flat painted lounge scene with an Eames-style chair, a starburst, and a cat, under a burnt-orange menu bar.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: a contemporary revival of the illustrative core, with flat planes, a warm brown-orange-olive palette, atomic and biomorphic props, and stylized figures. The page is a full-bleed image slider, so the style is in the artwork, not in the page layout.
Partial fit: the painted lounge scenes use the Atomic Age starburst and space-age props, but the page itself is a plain image slider.

observed: A burnt-orange bar at the top holds a white hand-drawn “SHAG” logotype with swept strokes and spaced white capitals for the menu.

The rest of the viewport is one painting: a room with a brown wood wall, a sideboard with rows of circles, a harlequin-diamond vase, a framed square painting in red, orange, and olive, and an orange starburst panel.
A stylized red-haired woman with a guitar reclines on a black lounge chair with an ottoman. The figure is nude and drawn with flat planes and no detail.
A white cat with green eyes sits on the ottoman, a black bird figure stands on a side table, and an orange oval rug lies on the floor.
All forms are flat color areas with sharp edges and flat cast shadows; there are no gradients.
Four slider dots sit at the right edge and a down-arrow at the bottom.
interpretation: The painting collects the style’s motifs in one place: a starburst, circles, harlequin diamonds, an Eames-type chair, and a flat, geometric figure.

Measured: CSS color metrics see only the orange bar (accent chroma 0.85) and a 0.57 shadow share from the slider controls. The screenshot palette has an accent chroma of 0.73, above the style’s muted range.
borrow: Use one burnt-orange bar with white spaced capitals above a full-bleed flat illustration.
Draw cast shadows as flat darker shapes, not blurs.

images.alt: Shag home page: a burnt-orange top bar with a white hand-drawn Shag logo and menu, above a flat painting of a 1950s living room with a red-haired woman on a black lounge chair, a white cat, a black bird figure, an orange rug, and a starburst panel.
images.caption: First viewport of [shag.com](https://www.shag.com/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design, artwork, and content belong to the site’s owners and artists. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Shipboard Girl
references.lede: Roy Lichtenstein’s offset lithograph of a smiling blonde woman at a ship’s rail, in red, blue, and yellow dots and flat color with black key lines.
references.summary: A close-up face in red dots, yellow hair, blue dot sky, and a solid blue block. Roy Lichtenstein, offset lithograph, 1965.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.649-1967 (1400 × 1810 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: A clear example of the full process palette: red and blue dot fields, flat yellow and blue, and heavy black outlines on white paper.

context: The V&A records an offset lithograph on paper, sheet 69 × 51.5 cm, printed by Graphic Industries, Inc. and published by Leo Castelli, New York, 1965, signed “R Lichtenstein”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1034308/).
observed: The face and neck are covered in red dots on white; the hair is flat yellow with thick black strands.
Two blue dot fields fill the sky at the top and the area behind the shoulder.
A solid ultramarine block with white horizontal stripes sits at lower right.
The lips are flat red with a white highlight shape and a black outline.
A ship’s rail and a rope net are drawn in thick black lines over white.
The image is printed with a wide white margin. There are no speech balloons or words in the image.
interpretation: This print shows the balance of the idiom: roughly equal areas of dot tint, flat color, and white, held together by black.
The dots are large enough to see as dots at print size, which is the scale the style record asks for on screen.
borrow: Use red dots for a warm tint and blue dots for a cool tint, and never mix them in one shape.
Leave generous white around a dense panel so that the dots do not fill the whole page.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is © Estate of Roy Lichtenstein.

references.title: Side chair by Hector Guimard
references.lede: A pearwood chair whose back posts rise, split, and flow into a leaf-shaped leather panel, with no joint or edge left straight.
references.summary: Pearwood chair with a pointed leaf-shaped leather back and flowing carved posts. Hector Guimard, Paris, c. 1907.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 1985.96 (2272 × 3400 px print file). Read the object record through the museum’s open-access API.

styles.note: Paris Art Nouveau furniture by the designer of the Métro entrances: the frame reads as one carved plant stem that divides and joins.

context: The Cleveland Museum of Art records the chair as pearwood with a tooled leather back and seat, 108 × 45.4 × 50.4 cm, French, c. 1907, by Hector Guimard (1867–1942). [CMA 1985.96](https://clevelandart.org/art/1985.96).

Wikipedia: after visiting Horta’s [Hôtel Tassel](ref:horta-hotel-tassel-staircase-1893), Guimard built the Castel Béranger (1895–1898), among the first Paris buildings in the new style, and his [Métro entrances](ref:guimard-paris-metro-entrance-1900) brought it to the visitors of the 1900 Exposition. [Wikipedia: Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau).
observed: The back is a pointed, inverted-triangle shield with curved sides, filled with a brown leather panel edged by a row of brass nails.
The two back posts swell as they rise, bend inward, and merge into the top rail; carved grooves run along them like the veins of a stem.
A single central splat drops from the back panel, splits into a narrow pointed opening, and joins the seat rail.
The front seat rail dips in the middle and carries a small carved scroll ornament.
The legs taper and flare slightly into small pad feet. No edge on the frame is straight.
The photograph shows the chair in three-quarter view on a gray ground.
interpretation: The chair turns the rubric’s leaf-shaped panel into structure: the back is literally a leaf held up by its stalk.
The palette is only wood brown, leather brown, and brass, which fits the style’s earthy colours.
borrow: Shape a card or badge as a pointed shield with softly curved sides.
Carry a thin groove or line along a curved edge so the edge reads as a stem.

images.alt: Tall wooden side chair on a gray ground, in three-quarter view. The back is a pointed leaf shape filled with brown leather and edged with brass nails, carried on curved carved posts, above a brown leather seat.
images.caption: Hector Guimard, chair, c. 1907, pearwood and tooled leather. [Cleveland Museum of Art 1985.96](https://clevelandart.org/art/1985.96), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art marks the object and its image CC0. Hector Guimard died in 1942, so his work entered the public domain in France in 2013. A chair made about 1907 is in the public domain in the United States. The Met, by contrast, marks its Guimard objects as not public domain; this record relies on Cleveland’s CC0 statement and the author’s death date.

references.title: Silver Diner website
references.lede: A diner chain’s site whose header carries the brand’s streamline mark: a script name between two sets of triple speed lines on navy.
references.summary: A navy header with the Silver Diner script between triple white speed lines, uppercase navigation, and a red top band.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. A cookie banner covers the bottom 70 px and an accessibility button sits at lower right; neither hides the header.

styles.note: Borderline: the logo and header use triple horizontal speed lines and a navy, red, and white palette, but the rest of the first screen is a full-width food photograph with square corners.

context: Silver Diner is a restaurant chain in the diner tradition; its logo draws the name in tall script between horizontal speed lines. The site states no designer.
observed: A red band at the top carries “SAVE SILVER DINER! LEARN MORE” in spaced serif capitals.
The navy header centers the “Silver Diner” logo in tall, condensed white script; three parallel white lines run out from each side of the name almost to the header’s full width.
The navigation below is in white sans-serif capitals: Menus, Locations, About, Specials, Rewards, Contact. An “ORDER NOW” button at right is a white rectangle with square corners.
The rest of the viewport is a slider photograph of pancakes with chocolate sauce and raspberries on a red booth background.
interpretation: The speed lines live in the logo image, so the measurement cannot see them: color.patternShare and surface.patternShare are 0. The header is centered (type.centerShare 0.87), and every box has square corners (radius median 0). The site passes only the uppercase and gradient metrics of the fingerprint.
It is the clearest live website found for this style. Real sites use streamline as a logo and a palette, not as a layout.
borrow: Run three thin parallel rules out from both sides of a centered wordmark to the edges of the header.

images.alt: Silver Diner home page: a red top band, a navy header with the white Silver Diner script between triple horizontal speed lines, uppercase white navigation, and a large photograph of pancakes with chocolate sauce and raspberries.
images.caption: First viewport of [silverdiner.com](https://www.silverdiner.com/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design, logo, and photographs belong to Silver Diner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Silver kettle by C. R. Ashbee
references.lede: A plain, hand-hammered silver kettle by the founder of the Guild of Handicraft, with an ivory handle, a green stone finial, and heart-shaped piercings in the foot.
references.summary: Hand-hammered silver with an ivory grip, a chrysoprase finial, and pierced hearts. C. R. Ashbee, 1900.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 1976.23 (3400 × 3208 px). The museum record has no description; the maker attribution, date, and materials come from its tombstone data.

styles.note: Partial fit: Arts and Crafts metalwork with visible hammer marks and a simple stone setting, but none of the movement’s pattern.

context: Cleveland lists the kettle as silver with an ivory handle and chrysoprase finial, 28.6 × 25.7 cm, by Charles Robert Ashbee (1863–1942), England, 1900. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/1976.23).

Ashbee founded the Guild and School of Handicraft in the East End of London and moved the guild to Chipping Campden in 1902. Wikipedia describes the guild’s work as plain surfaces of hammered silver, flowing wirework, and coloured stones in simple settings. [Wikipedia: Arts and Crafts movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_and_Crafts_movement).
observed: The body is a squat, rounded pot on a flared foot. Small dents from hammering break up the reflections on every surface.
A tall loop handle of two thin silver rods ends in teardrop-shaped tabs soldered to the shoulder. The grip is a spindle of pale ivory.
The lid finial is a green stone held in a small silver wire cage.
Heart shapes are pierced through the foot ring.
There is no engraved or chased ornament on the body.
interpretation: The kettle shows the movement’s surface trait, visible handwork, without its pattern. It is closer to the plain, square branch than to Morris’s textiles.
The only ornament is structural: the pierced foot, the handle tabs, and the stone. That is the movement’s idea of ornament that stays secondary to the thing it decorates.
borrow: Let a hand-made surface texture stand in for ornament: one quiet texture over a plain form.
Mark a small detail with a simple cut-out shape, such as a heart, instead of applied decoration.

images.alt: Round silver kettle on a flared foot with a tall looped handle and an ivory grip, a green stone knob on the lid, and heart-shaped holes cut in the foot. The surface shows small hammer marks.
images.caption: Charles Robert Ashbee, kettle, 1900. Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of the Womens Council of the Cleveland Museum of Art, 1976.23. [Open-access image](https://clevelandart.org/art/1976.23), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art releases the image as CC0. Ashbee died in 1942, so the design entered the public domain in the United Kingdom at the end of 2012. It was made in 1900, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Skeuomorph Mobile Banking
references.lede: The Dribbble concept that started the trend: a banking app molded out of one pale blue-gray surface.
references.summary: Alexander Plyuto’s viral 2019 banking-app concept, the usual starting point of neumorphism.
references.made: 2019 (posted 5 November 2019, per the Wayback copy of the shot page)

evidence.note: Opened the shot’s main image (`frame_8_4x.png`, 1600 × 1200) from cdn.dribbble.com, found through the Wayback capture of 15 November 2019. The live Dribbble page returned an empty body to scripts. Only the first image of the shot was inspected; the other images in the shot were not.

styles.note: The shot that [Malewicz](ref:malewicz-neumorphism-article-2019), [CSS-Tricks](ref:css-tricks-neumorphism-and-css-2020), and Wikipedia name as the origin of the style. Cards, buttons, and wells rise from or sink into one pale surface.

context: The description reads: “Let’s imagine that we live in a dimension where skeuomorph is still alive and continued its evolution in mobile interfaces. What would applications look like then? Here is my vision.” A later update links a Figma file, “Skeuomorph Style Guide”.
The Wayback capture of 15 November 2019 shows 129,538 views and 2,644 likes. Malewicz wrote in December 2019 that the shot “gained over 3000 likes and pushed the trend forward”.
In 2019 Dribbble credited the shot to “Alexander Plyuto for Heartbeat Agency”; search results in 2026 show the name “Oleksandr Plyuto”.
observed: Two phone-sized panels and a settings card on a pale blue-gray background. The panels, cards, and buttons have the same color as the background.

Each raised shape has a white highlight on its upper left and a soft blue-gray shadow on its lower right. The credit-limit bar, the active tab in the bottom bar, and the back/menu button pair look pressed in.
A large round chart is carved into the surface with ridges between segments. One segment is a raised orange wedge with a gradient; a small red button sits in its center.
Two accents break the monochrome: a glossy red rocker switch with ridges (“OFF”) and an iridescent patch on the credit card.
Type is a geometric sans-serif in dark navy, bold for “Statistic” and “Balance”, regular for labels. The card number uses a monospaced face.
interpretation: This is neumorphism before its name. The surface recipe is already complete, but the red rocker switch, the chip, and the iridescent foil keep objects from [skeuomorphism](style:skeuomorphism). Later work dropped them and kept only the pale surface and the paired shadows.
borrow: Carve a chart into the surface as a pressed dial and raise only the selected segment, so that selection reads as height.

rights.statement: © Alexander Plyuto / Heartbeat Agency. Link only.

references.title: Slack website, 2018
references.lede: Slack’s 2018 home page: four flat, long-limbed people work around an oversized chat window beside the serif headline “Where Work Happens”.
references.summary: Flat figures with long limbs and natural skin around an oversized chat window; light hatch texture. 2018.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. No cookie box covers the page. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: the figures are flat and long-limbed and act around an oversized interface, but their skin is natural and parts carry a hatch texture. Wired names Slack among the brands that use the style.

references.notice: The live Slack site has changed since this 2018 capture.
context: Alice Lee made the illustration voice and library for Slack from January 2017, citing Mary Blair and Charley Harper, with “organic, imperfect shapework; bold colors and warm tone”. [Alice Lee](https://www.byalicelee.com/slack).
Wired (2021) lists Slack among the brands that use the style. [Wired](https://www.wired.com/story/corporate-memphis-design-tech/).
observed: On the left, a large chat window titled “#project-mobile” shows colored squares and grey placeholder lines, with a dark plum bar at its left edge.

Four people stand, kneel, and walk around it: a red-haired woman in a blue jacket and a yellow and green skirt, a kneeling woman writing on the window, and a man in a green sweater holding up a chart.
Skin tones are natural browns and peach. Limbs are long and figures are about eight heads tall; faces have small features.
The kneeling woman’s top and the man’s trousers carry a fine grid or hatch texture.
On the right, “Where Work Happens” is set in a heavy serif, with an email field and a square indigo button.
interpretation: It shows the style’s layout and gesture (people acting on a giant interface) without its non-natural skin. The heavy serif headline and square button also depart from the style’s rounded sans-serif interface.
borrow: Put the figures around an oversized version of the product’s own window so the illustration explains the product.

images.alt: Slack home page, 2018: four flat, long-limbed people with natural skin work around a large chat window on the left; the heavy serif headline “Where Work Happens” and an email sign-up on the right.
images.caption: First viewport of [Slack](https://web.archive.org/web/20180531232743/https://slack.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Sleep Cycle App – Neumorphism Redesign
references.lede: An unofficial January 2020 redesign of a sleep-tracking app, made while the trend was weeks old.
references.summary: Devanta Ebison’s Dribbble concept: an alarm, a sleep journal, and a bar chart pressed into a pale surface with one coral accent.
references.made: 2020 (posted 2 January 2020, per the Wayback copy of the shot page)

evidence.note: Opened the shot’s image (`dribbble__2x_4x.png`, 1600 × 1200) from cdn.dribbble.com, found through the Wayback capture of 4 January 2020. The live Dribbble page returned an empty body to scripts.

styles.note: A clear example: phones, buttons, tabs, and chart tracks all share one pale surface and differ only by soft raised or pressed shadows; one coral accent marks values and the main action.

context: The designer wrote: “Wanted to try my hand at this new design style called neumorphism because it’s been trending for the past few weeks. This was a fun exercise, but I don’t know if this style will stand the test of time.”
It is a fan concept. Sleep Cycle AB did not make it. The Wayback capture of 4 January 2020 shows 32,152 views and 334 likes.
observed: Three tilted phones on a very pale gray-blue background. The phone bodies, buttons, and tabs are the same color as the background and are shaped by white highlights and soft gray shadows.
The clock display “10:00” sits in a pressed rectangular well; the HR and MIN buttons are raised circles.
The segmented control (Days, Weeks, Months) is a pressed track with a raised pill for the selected item. The chart bars are coral fills inside pressed tracks.
One accent color, a soft coral, fills the “Set alarm” button, the chart bars, the progress rings, and the active tab icon.
Text is a rounded geometric sans-serif in slate gray, bold for figures.
interpretation: A textbook statement of the style two months after [Plyuto’s shot](ref:plyuto-skeuomorph-mobile-banking-2019): the object details are gone, only surface, shadow, and one accent remain. The designer’s own doubt about its future is an early sign of the reaction against it.
borrow: Draw bar-chart tracks as pressed wells and fill them with the accent, so the empty part of each bar stays readable without gridlines.

rights.statement: © Devanta Ebison. Link only.

references.title: Smart Calendar App (Dribbble shot)
references.lede: A 2020 Dribbble concept for a calendar app in candy colors, cited in the article that named the style.
references.summary: Three frosted phone screens with light edges over a pink and lilac glow. Paperpillar, 2020.
references.made: 2020 (the screens show August 2020; cited by Malewicz in November 2020)

evidence.note: Inspected the shot image named in the page’s structured data (1600 × 1200, Dribbble CDN) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored. The page was read in Claude in Chrome; the cookie banner was not accepted. The exact post date was not visible on the page.

styles.note: A clear concept example from the Dribbble wave, cited by Malewicz for its 1 pt semi-transparent white outline that simulates the glass edge.

context: The Dribbble description reads “Calendar App exploration using some candy colors.” The shot is credited to Ghani Pradita for Paperpillar. [Dribbble](https://dribbble.com/shots/13842720-Smart-Calendar-App).
Malewicz calls it “a clear representation of this trend” and notes that it “may be on the verge of readability in some places”. [Malewicz 2020](ref:malewicz-glassmorphism-article-2020).
observed: The background is a soft glow of coral pink at the top fading into lilac at the upper right and white at the bottom.
Three tall phone screens are frosted panels: pink-tinted and translucent in their upper parts, near-opaque white in their lower cards.
Each panel and card has large rounded corners and a thin, lighter edge.
Colorful gradient spheres (Task, Notes, Event) sit on the third screen; the glass itself carries no imagery.
Text is a geometric sans-serif in dark plum. The primary buttons (‘Mulai’ and a plus button) are solid dark plum pills and discs.
interpretation: The shot matches all four diagnostic traits and also the ‘opaque primary action’ rule. It shows the Dribbble version of the style: presentation panels floating over a generated glow, not a real app screen.
borrow: Use near-opaque white for reading surfaces and more transparent tinted glass for headers.
Make the one primary button solid and dark so it reads through all the glass.

rights.statement: © Ghani Pradita / Paperpillar. No image is stored here.

references.title: Sony Memory Stick Walkman NW-MS7
references.lede: An early digital music player shaped as a flattened silver capsule, with a translucent blue front and chrome earbuds.
references.summary: Silver capsule body, translucent blue face, wide techno “MS WALKMAN” lettering, chrome earbuds. Sony, 2000.

source.label: V&A: Sony Memory Stick Walkman NW-MS7, W.665:1 to 14-2001

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object W.665:1 to 14-2001 (image 2006AF4293, 1271 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear: silver metallic plastic, a translucent blue panel, a rounded capsule form, chrome earbuds, and wide rounded techno lettering.

context: The V&A describes a “flattened cylinder form on grey/silver plastic, incorporating a LED display”. The player stored up to 80 minutes of music on a Memory Stick instead of a cassette. [V&A W.665-2001](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O60018/sony-memory-stick-walkman-nw-personal-stereo-sony-corporation/).
observed: The body is a long rounded capsule in pale silver plastic. The ends are rounded and the sides curve.
A translucent royal-blue panel runs down the front. It narrows in the middle and holds the LCD, the name, and a window for the Memory Stick.
“MS WALKMAN” is set in wide, rounded, extended capitals; smaller labels such as “PORTABLE MEMORY STICK PLAYER” are in small spaced capitals.
The earbuds are polished chrome with black rims and show sharp highlight lines.
interpretation: This is the chrome side of Y2K in a product: silver as the base material, one saturated translucent color, and a wide techno wordmark.
The hourglass-shaped blue panel on the capsule reads like a device interface drawn as an object.
borrow: Put a translucent color panel on a silver base, and taper it so the base shows at the edges.
Set a short product name in wide rounded capitals, with small spaced capitals as secondary labels.
Use polished chrome with one hard highlight line for small accessories or icons.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London; the product design and the Walkman name belong to Sony.

references.title: Sparton Nocturne radio, model 1186
references.lede: Walter Dorwin Teague’s floor radio for Sparton: a disc of blue mirror glass more than a metre across, crossed by a chrome ladder of horizontal bars.
references.summary: A large blue mirror-glass disc with a vertical chrome frame of horizontal bars, a round dial, and chrome feet. Walter Dorwin Teague for Sparton, 1935.

creator.name: Walter Dorwin Teague (designer); Sparton Corporation, Jackson, Michigan (manufacturer)

references.made: 1935 (unveiled at the New York Radio Exposition, September 1935)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Wmpearl’s 2014 photograph of the Wolfsonian–FIU copy on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Radio,_Nocturne,_Model_1186,_c._1935,_Sparton_Corporation,_Jackson,_Michigan.JPG) at 1920 px. The Decorative Arts Trust caption identifies the Wolfsonian copy as XX1990.168, from the lobby of the Park Central Hotel, Miami Beach; I did not read the Wolfsonian record itself.

styles.note: Partial fit: the big circle and chrome horizontal bars are streamline, but the vertical frame and luxury mirror glass are closer to Art Deco.

context: Unveiled at the New York Radio Exposition in September 1935, the Nocturne was made of midnight-blue Tufflex mirror glass, satin chrome steel, and painted wood, 46 in high and 43¼ in wide, priced at $350 to $375. About two dozen survive; copies are in the Wolfsonian–FIU and the Dallas Museum of Art. [Encyclopedia of Design](https://encyclopedia.design/2023/04/28/nocturne-model-1186-designed-by-walter-dorwin-teague/).

The Wolfsonian copy (XX1990.168) came from the lobby of the Park Central Hotel, Miami Beach. [Decorative Arts Trust](https://decorativeartstrust.org/transatlantic-connections-influencing-miamis-wolfsonian/xx1990-168_001/).
observed: A large disc of dark blue mirror glass stands on edge; a chrome band runs around its lower half.
A vertical chrome frame crosses the disc from top to bottom, filled with thin horizontal chrome bars at regular spacing.
In the upper part, a round dial in a chrome ring sits between the bars, with a row of five round chrome knobs below it.
In the lower part, the bars cover a dark speaker cloth.
Two chrome feet with rounded ends hold the disc. The mirror reflects the gallery around it.
interpretation: The Nocturne sits between the two styles: the circle and the horizontal chrome bars belong to streamlining, while the vertical axis, symmetry, and luxury glass point to Art Deco. It is useful as a boundary case.
borrow: Put a ladder of thin horizontal rules inside a circle to make a badge or hero mark.
Use chrome-gray rules on navy for a night version of the palette.

images.alt: A large round disc of blue mirror glass on chrome feet, crossed vertically by a chrome frame with horizontal bars, a round dial and five knobs near the top, and speaker cloth behind the bars at the bottom. The mirror reflects a museum gallery.
images.caption: Sparton Nocturne, model 1186, Wolfsonian–FIU. Photograph by Wmpearl, 2014, CC0, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Radio,_Nocturne,_Model_1186,_c._1935,_Sparton_Corporation,_Jackson,_Michigan.JPG). Other museum objects appear in the reflection.

rights.statement: The photographer dedicated the photograph to the public domain (CC0). The radio is an American useful article, not protected by copyright in the United States. Walter Dorwin Teague died in 1960. Objects reflected in the mirror are incidental.

identifiers.commons: File:Radio, Nocturne, Model 1186, c. 1935, Sparton Corporation, Jackson, Michigan.JPG

references.title: Stained-Glass Composition IV
references.lede: Three tall leaded-glass windows for a house in Alkmaar, made in the movement’s first year: small rectangles of white, yellow, blue, and dark glass arranged in mirrored patterns.
references.summary: Three leaded windows of small white, yellow, blue, green, ochre, and dark rectangles. Theo van Doesburg, 1917.

source.label: Kröller-Müller Museum: Stained-glass composition IV for the De Lange House, Alkmaar

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image (1396 × 2135 px, viewed at 1600 px) from Geheugen van Nederland (urn:gvn:ICN01:3492), which shows all three windows on a dark ground. The Kröller-Müller page was found by search and not read.

styles.note: Partial fit: an early De Stijl work that is strictly orthogonal and built from flat colored rectangles, but uses green, ochre, and brown glass and a mirrored, near-symmetric layout that the mature style drops.

context: Jan de Lange commissioned the windows for his house at Wilhelminalaan 2, Alkmaar, where they were installed from early September 1917. Each window measures 287 × 56.5 cm. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_139.jpg).

The windows passed to the Dutch State (RCE R5533–R5535) and have been on loan to the Kröller-Müller Museum, Otterlo, since 1991. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_139.jpg).
Wikidata records the work as [Q2460532](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2460532), dated 1917.
observed: Three tall, narrow panels stand side by side on a dark ground.
Each panel is filled with small rectangles of white glass and of yellow, blue, and very dark glass, divided by thin black lead lines.
The two outer panels repeat the same pattern as mirror images of each other.
The middle panel uses green, ochre, and dark blue glass instead of yellow.
The rectangles form L-shapes and bars that recur down each panel; there are no curves or diagonals.
A small monogram sits at the bottom right.
interpretation: The windows show the style before Mondrian’s large planes: a dense rhythm of small rectangles, closer to a pattern than to a balanced composition.
The lead lines play the part that black lines play in the paintings, which may be one source of the style’s black grid.
borrow: Repeat a small set of rectangular motifs down a tall strip, and mirror the strip for side panels.
Use thin dark dividers between many small cells for a textured band, and keep large planes for main content.

images.alt: Three tall leaded-glass window panels on a dark ground, each filled with small white, yellow, blue, and dark rectangles; the outer panels mirror each other and the middle panel uses green and ochre glass.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg, Stained-Glass Composition IV, 1917, for the De Lange House, Alkmaar. Dutch State collection, on loan to the Kröller-Müller Museum. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_139.jpg) via Geheugen van Nederland, public domain.

rights.statement: Commons marks the image PD-old. Van Doesburg died in 1931, so the work is public domain in the Netherlands; made in 1917, it is public domain in the United States.

references.title: Staircase hall of the Hôtel Tassel, Brussels
references.lede: Victor Horta’s stair hall, one of the first Art Nouveau interiors: an exposed iron column that branches like a plant stem, whiplash railings, and painted tendrils that sweep up the wall.
references.summary: Iron column branching into tendrils, whiplash railings, and painted wall curves. Victor Horta, Brussels, 1892–93.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Henry Townsend’s September 2002 photograph of the stair hall on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tassel_House_stairway.JPG) (1700 × 1440 px). The colours are warm and strongly saturated in this photograph and may not match the paint exactly. The house is a private office and was not visited.

styles.note: The founding building of the Brussels core: whiplash iron, wall painting, and structure fused into one curving interior.

context: Wikipedia: Horta designed the house for the scientist Émile Tassel and built it in 1892–1893. With Paul Hankar’s house of the same years it is considered one of the first Art Nouveau buildings. A steel-and-glass middle section links a street block and a garden block; it holds the stairs and landings and brings light down from a glass roof. Horta designed every detail, including woodwork, stained glass, mosaic floors, and furniture. [Wikipedia: Hôtel Tassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_Tassel).

Since 2000 the house has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site “Major Town Houses of the Architect Victor Horta (Brussels)”. The Hôtel Tassel influenced Hector Guimard, who built the Castel Béranger in Paris after he saw it. [Wikipedia: Hôtel Tassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_Tassel); [Wikipedia: Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau).
observed: A slender iron column, painted gray-green with thin gold bands, stands at the foot of the stair. At its top it splits into curling iron tendrils that hold the beam above.
The stair turns in a smooth curve. Its polished wooden handrail follows the curve without a break.
The iron balustrade is a web of dark, looping whiplash lines between vertical bars; a similar railing on the upper landing continues the pattern.
The wall beside the stair carries painted olive-green tendrils that swirl up and to the left over a peach and salmon ground, with parallel bands that follow the rake of the stair.
The floor is a pale mosaic with large, curving pink lines.
Colours are warm peach, salmon, and cream, with gray-green iron and brown wood.
interpretation: Here the whiplash is not applied ornament but structure: the column, the railing, and the wall painting are the same line in iron and paint.
The palette of gray-green iron, warm plaster, and wood is the source of the style’s moss-and-terracotta colour pair.
borrow: Let a thin vertical element split at its top into curling branches where it meets a horizontal one.
Run a painted flourish diagonally across a wall or a hero area so that it follows the direction of movement, as the tendrils follow the stair.

images.alt: Interior stair hall: a curving staircase with a wooden handrail and dark iron whiplash railings, a gray-green iron column that branches into tendrils at the top, and olive-green painted swirls on a peach wall.
images.caption: Stair hall of the Hôtel Tassel, Brussels, by Victor Horta, 1892–93. Photograph by Henry Townsend, September 2002, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tassel_House_stairway.JPG), released into the public domain. A radiator and a modern light fitting are visible.

rights.statement: The photographer released the photograph into the public domain (Commons template PD-self). Victor Horta died in 1947, so his work entered the public domain in Belgium in 2018. A building finished in 1893 is not protected by copyright in the United States.

references.title: Stasher website, 2018
references.lede: The 2018 home page of a London luggage-storage service: three yellow-skinned figures with long bent limbs haul oversized suitcases across a line-drawn city.
references.summary: Yellow-skinned, gangly figures straining under giant luggage below a pill-shaped search bar. 2018.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. A thin blue notice bar at the top covers about 5% of the page. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: non-natural yellow skin, small heads, long bending limbs, oversized objects, and flat fills without outlines on a white page. The overlapping translucent fills and dot patches are a small departure.

references.notice: The live Stasher site now uses a photograph and has changed since this 2018 capture.
observed: A thin blue bar at the top reads “Remember to book online…”. Below, “Stasher” in bold blue and the heading “Luggage Storage. Everywhere.” are centred.
A wide white search bar with fully rounded ends holds fields for location, drop-off, pick-up, and number of items, and a pill-shaped blue button “Find Luggage Storage”.
Below, a man carries an orange suitcase larger than his torso on his back, a woman in an orange dress drags a huge green bag, and a boy holds a red case.
All three have yellow skin, small heads, and long bent arms and legs; hair is red or coral. Fills are flat and overlap as darker translucent areas; some clothes have fine dot patterns.
Behind them, a city skyline is drawn in thin grey lines on white.
interpretation: It follows the rubric almost point by point: oversized objects, non-natural skin, gangly effort poses, white page. The search bar and button are pills, as the rubric expects, while the measurement shows the rest of the page with square boxes.
borrow: Make the product’s object (here, luggage) absurdly large so that the figures’ effort tells the problem the service solves.

images.alt: Stasher home page, 2018: the heading “Luggage Storage. Everywhere.” and a pill-shaped search bar above three yellow-skinned, long-limbed figures straining to carry oversized suitcases in front of a line-drawn city.
images.caption: First viewport of [Stasher](https://web.archive.org/web/20180614205120/https://stasher.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owner. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Stoclet Palace, Brussels
references.lede: Josef Hoffmann’s house for Adolphe Stoclet, 1905–1911: flat white stone planes edged with metal mouldings, with interiors by the Wiener Werkstätte and a mosaic frieze by Klimt.
references.summary: Flat stone planes framed by bands of metal moulding, and tall windows of small square panes. Josef Hoffmann, Brussels, 1905–1911.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1280 × 853 px rendition of a 2015 exterior detail photograph by Fred Romero on Wikimedia Commons ([Bruxelles - Palais Stoclet (11)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bruxelles_-_Palais_Stoclet_(11).jpg), CC BY 2.0). It shows part of the tower and a window bay, not the whole house. The house is private and closed to visitors, so I saw no interior. No image is stored.

styles.note: A clear example of the late geometric phase: flat planes outlined by continuous bands, and windows of small squares. The style record lists Belgium for this building.

context: Wikipedia: the house was designed by Josef Hoffmann for the financier Adolphe Stoclet and built between 1905 and 1911 in the Vienna Secession style. It was the first residential project of the Wiener Werkstätte. Its features include geometric volumes, symmetry, straight lines, concrete covered with marble plaques, and mosaic friezes by Gustav Klimt. It is still owned by the Stoclet family and not open to visitors. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoclet_Palace).
Wikipedia: the house has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009. The UNESCO listing is [Stoclet House, 1298](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1298/), which I did not open.
observed: The wall is faced with large flat, pale stone plates with fine joints.
Every edge of the wall is outlined by a continuous band of dark metal moulding with a repeated, stepped pattern, so each plane reads as a framed panel.
A tall bay holds three narrow windows, each divided into many small square panes by white bars.
Three sculpted heads sit in square recesses above the windows, inside the moulding frame.
A black metal railing of squares and spirals stands on the roof edge above.
interpretation: Outlining every plane with a thin band is the architectural version of the style’s ruled frames on paper. The building has little ornament apart from these edges.
Wikipedia’s Wiener Werkstätte article calls the house a pioneering work of Art Deco; the continuous edge bands point toward that later style.
borrow: Outline each panel with a thin, patterned or dark band instead of a shadow or a fill change.
Divide a tall narrow element into a column of small squares.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photograph is CC BY 2.0, but the building is by Josef Hoffmann, who died in 1956, so his work is protected in Austria until the end of 2026. Belgian freedom of panorama may permit exterior photographs; the lead curator can decide whether to upgrade to tier A after 2026.

references.title: Strawberry Thief furnishing textile
references.lede: William Morris’s best-known printed cotton: thrushes and strawberries mirrored across an indigo ground, with almost no plain ground left.
references.summary: Mirrored thrushes, strawberries, and flowers in red, yellow, green, and white on indigo. William Morris, designed 1883.

source.label: Cleveland Museum of Art: Strawberry Thief, 1937.696

references.made: Designed 1883; this length printed at Merton Abbey, about 1936

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art open-access image of object 1937.696 (3400 × 3035 px). The museum dates this length “c 1936” and gives its place as Merton Abbey, so it is a late printing of the 1883 design.

styles.note: A core Morris & Co. printed textile: a flat, dense, mirror-symmetrical repeat of birds and plants in dye colours on indigo.

context: The Cleveland Museum of Art calls it perhaps the most recognizable of Morris’s textiles. It shows the thrushes that ate the fruit in the garden at Kelmscott Manor. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/1937.696).

Morris perfected the indigo-discharge process with this design: the whole cloth was dyed blue, then bleached and block-printed, here with more colours than any of his other textiles. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/1937.696).
Cleveland describes this length as plain-weave cotton, discharge printed, 88.3 × 99.1 cm, printed at Merton Abbey about 1936. [Cleveland Museum of Art](https://clevelandart.org/art/1937.696).
observed: The ground is a deep indigo blue. Plain blue shows only in narrow gaps between motifs.
Pairs of thrushes face each other across a vertical axis; the pattern is a mirrored, turnover repeat.
Motifs are red strawberries, pink and salmon flowers, sage and olive leaves, and pale blue-white acanthus leaves, with yellow stems.
Each motif has a dark outline and flat fills. Speckles on the birds’ breasts give texture, not shading.
A plain indigo band runs down both edges. Printed white capitals on the right edge read “…PANY 449 OXFORD STREET LONDON W.”
interpretation: This is the clearest case of the rubric’s dense all-over repeat: the mirror axis makes the pattern static and symmetrical, and the colours are those of indigo, madder, and weld.
The red here is a light, warm red on dark blue. It is used for fruit and flowers, not for text.
borrow: Mirror a motif pair around a vertical axis and fill the gaps with leaves until only thin lines of ground show.
Use a dark indigo field with small, bright accents of madder red and weld yellow.

images.alt: Printed cotton with a dark indigo ground covered by mirrored pairs of speckled thrushes, red strawberries, pink flowers, and green and pale blue leaves. A plain blue band runs down each side.
images.caption: William Morris, Strawberry Thief, designed 1883, printed about 1936. Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. Henry Chisholm, 1937.696. [Open-access image](https://clevelandart.org/art/1937.696), CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art releases the image as CC0. William Morris died in 1896. The design dates from 1883, so it is in the public domain in the United Kingdom and the United States.

references.title: Study for the painting “Intake”
references.lede: Bridget Riley’s black poster-colour study of 1964: wavy black and white bands that tighten into one corner.
references.summary: Black and white curved bands that narrow and bunch toward the top right corner. Bridget Riley, study for Intake, 1964.

source.label: V&A: Study for the painting “Intake”, CIRC.237-1965

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.237-1965 (1552 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: A clear black and white Riley study: stripes that change width and direction by steps, so the flat sheet seems to flow.

context: The V&A catalogues the drawing with the style “Op Art”: pencil and black poster colour on paper, 26.3 × 29.4 cm, acquired by the V&A Circulation Department in 1965. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1036839/).

The V&A’s general Riley text also says she designed the Woolmark logo while at an advertising agency. That claim conflicts with the usual attribution of the logo to [Franco Grignani](ref:grignani-woolmark-logo-1964), and it is not repeated here as fact. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1036839/).
observed: Alternating black and white bands run from the lower left toward the top right corner inside a square.
At the lower left the bands are broad and gently curved; toward the top right they narrow, bend more, and converge.
The bands are flat and hard-edged, painted in solid black with no tone.
A narrow grey mount shows around the square.
interpretation: The study isolates the core op device of the style: a stripe field that changes width by steps until the eye reads movement and depth.
Its hand-painted scale shows that Riley’s effects were planned in small studies before the large paintings.
borrow: Run a stripe field diagonally and let it converge into one corner to create a strong direction.
Change stripe width and curvature together, not separately, so that the field seems to turn in space.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is by a living artist, and the V&A image is not openly licensed.

references.title: Suwannee Hulaween festival website
references.lede: A Florida festival site whose hero wordmark uses melting, swollen letters with a cyan echo outline over a dark, glittering photo.
references.summary: Swollen white letters with a cyan outline on a dark bokeh photo, and a dense psychedelic lineup poster below.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: the wordmark is close to Wes Wilson’s lettering, and the lineup poster is dense and patterned, but the page ground is a dark photograph and the interface is plain.

observed: The hero is a dark photograph of out-of-focus magenta and cyan points of light.
HULAWEEN is centered in very large white letters that swell and taper, with blobby terminals and a cyan echo outline.
The dates above and LIVE OAK FL and SPIRIT OF THE SUWANNEE MUSIC PARK below are in a white serif with soft, flared shapes.
Three outlined buttons in green sit below, in a wide sans.
A light-blue panel below holds a lineup poster: dense jungle plants, flowers, and figures in green, pink, and blue around the same lettering, with band names in condensed capitals.
The navigation bar is black with spaced green capitals.
interpretation: The page keeps the style in its display lettering and in the poster image, and uses a conventional dark festival interface for everything else.
Measured values: `color.chromaticShare` 0.34 fails because the photo ground is dark; `color.hues` 5 and `type.centerShare` 0.93 pass; `color.patternShare` is 0.
borrow: Give swollen white display letters a single cyan outline to lift them from a dark ground.
Pair a psychedelic wordmark with a soft, flared serif for secondary lines.

images.alt: Hulaween home page: a dark sparkling photo with the word HULAWEEN in large swollen white letters with a cyan outline, the dates and location in white, three green outlined buttons, and below it part of a colorful lineup poster.

references.title: tailwindcss-neumorphism demo
references.lede: A 2020 Tailwind CSS plugin demo in which every form field, button, and toggle is molded from the page.
references.summary: Tailwind plugin demo: pressed inputs, raised pill buttons, and soft toggles on pale blue.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear. Inputs are pressed wells, buttons and the select are raised pills, and toggles and progress tracks are soft, all in the page color.

context: The plugin repository [sambeevors/tailwindcss-neumorphism](https://github.com/sambeevors/tailwindcss-neumorphism) was created on 4 June 2020.
observed: A pale blue page (about #edf2f6 in the screenshot). “Full name” and “Email” inputs are pressed pills with inner shadows; the select and the “Submit” button are raised pills.
A round home button and a “Buy gift card” pill with a faint gradient sit below.
Three thin progress tracks carry red, yellow, and green fills; three toggles are soft pills, two filled blue and green.
Labels are small uppercase letter-spaced sans-serif in slate; a raised “Card title” card starts at the bottom.
interpretation: A compact specimen of raised versus pressed states in real form controls. The three saturated progress colors go beyond the one-accent rule.
Measured: shadows on 85 % of boxes (median offset 3.4 px, median blur 4.8 px, none hard), borders on 0 %, median radius 12.6 px.
borrow: Make every input a pressed well and every button a raised pill; the difference alone tells a user what can be typed into and what can be pressed.

images.alt: tailwindcss-neumorphism demo: a pale blue form with pressed pill inputs, a raised select and Submit button, a round home button, colored progress bars, and soft toggles.
