references.title: Tamagotchi
references.lede: Bandai’s egg-shaped virtual pet, sold as “the tiny pet from cyberspace”, made a pocket blobject out of a digital toy.
references.summary: Pink egg-shaped plastic toy with a small LCD and bead chain, on a blister card. Bandai, 1996–1997.

creator.name: Aki Maita and Akihiro Yokoi, for Bandai

references.made: 1997 (V&A copy); first released in Japan on 23 November 1996 per Wikipedia

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object B.239-1997 (image 2006AE9151, 1200 × 1600), which shows the toy in its blister pack, in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: an egg-shaped blobject in candy pink and lime with a clear plastic bubble, marketed as coming from cyberspace. The card art is hand-drawn, not techno.
Partial fit: a candy-pink egg toy with hand-drawn card art of a cute digital pet, but the photographed object shows no character face.

context: The V&A calls it “one of the biggest toy fads of the late-1990s” and describes an egg-shaped virtual pet “made from pink and green plastic” with an LCD screen and a metal chain, sealed in a clear bubble pack printed in five languages. [V&A B.239-1997](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O37315/tamagotchi-video-game-yokoi-akihiro/).

Wikipedia gives the Japanese release as 23 November 1996 and the United States release as 1 May 1997, and says nearly 40 million units had sold by spring 1998. [Wikipedia: Tamagotchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamagotchi).
observed: The toy is a hot-pink egg with a lime-green face ring printed with numbers and a small square LCD in the center.
A silver bead chain loops from its top.
The blister pack is a clear plastic bubble with ribbed, rounded edges on a white card.
The card shows the Tamagotchi name in hand-drawn magenta capitals and three loose crayon-style drawings of an egg hatching; the slogan reads “The tiny pet from cyberspace”.
interpretation: The object, not the packaging, carries the style: a soft egg in candy colors that holds a digital creature. It predates the iMac, so it shows the candy blobject already in toys in 1996–97.
The crayon card art is a counter-example to the techno side of Y2K.
borrow: Frame a small pixel display inside a rounded, brightly colored shape.
Use a clear, ribbed plastic bubble as a frame for a product image.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London; the toy and its packaging belong to Bandai.

references.title: Textile design with stars in circles
references.lede: Lyubov Popova’s design for a printed fabric repeats red stars inside black overlapping ovals and changes them from solid to line as the pattern moves across.
references.summary: Solid and outlined red stars in a lattice of black ovals on paper. Lyubov Popova, 1923, Tretyakov Gallery.

source.label: Wikidata: Tissu imprimé à motif d’« étoiles dans un cercle »

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a gallery photograph by Sukkoria on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fabric_design_%C2%AB_stars_in_circles_%C2%BB_by_Lyoubov_Popova_-_Rouge_Grand_Palais.jpg) (3228 × 2256 px, viewed at 1920 px), taken in the exhibition *Rouge. Art et utopie au pays des Soviets*, Grand Palais, Paris, 2019. The photograph is slightly soft and taken through glazing. Wikidata names the State Tretyakov Gallery as the collection; no inventory number is recorded.

styles.note: Partial fit: constructivist textile design, the branch that applied the style to industrial production. It keeps the red-and-black palette and elementary shapes but has no type and no diagonal composition.

context: Wikidata records the work as a design by Lyubov Popova, dated 1923, in the collection of the State Tretyakov Gallery. [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q65965662).

In 1923 an official appeal asked artists to design prints for the Soviet textile industry. Popova, Varvara Stepanova, and Alexander Rodchenko were among the first to respond. [V&A, T.213-2016](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1371413/). See [Stepanova’s printed flannel](ref:stepanova-printed-flannel-1924).
observed: A lattice of overlapping black outlined ovals covers the sheet in staggered rows.
Each oval holds a five-pointed star in a magenta-red. In the left part the stars are solid; toward the right they become open pentagrams drawn in thin red lines.
The red stars and the black ovals overlap, so the stars appear to pass behind and in front of the lattice.
The ground is unpainted off-white paper. Red and black are the only colors.
interpretation: The design reduces a textile print to the same two inks as the posters and uses the change from solid to outline as its only variation, a rule-based system rather than decoration.
The star is a Soviet emblem. The style record advises against using such emblems as decoration today; the geometry and the solid-to-outline change are the parts to reuse.
borrow: Make a pattern from one elementary shape and one outline lattice, and let the shape change from solid to outline across the surface.
Limit a pattern to one hue plus black on an unprinted ground.

images.alt: A framed sheet with a pattern of black overlapping ovals, each holding a red five-pointed star. The stars are solid on the left and become thin red line pentagrams on the right.
images.caption: Lyubov Popova, textile design with stars in circles, 1923. State Tretyakov Gallery, shown at the Grand Palais, Paris, in 2019. Photograph by Sukkoria, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fabric_design_%C2%AB_stars_in_circles_%C2%BB_by_Lyoubov_Popova_-_Rouge_Grand_Palais.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Photograph © Sukkoria, CC BY-SA 4.0, attribution required. Popova died in 1924, so the design is in the public domain in Russia and, as the work of an author who died more than 70 years ago, in the United States whether or not it counts as published.

identifiers.commons: File:Fabric design « stars in circles » by Lyoubov Popova - Rouge Grand Palais.jpg

references.title: The Craftsman, February 1915
references.lede: Gustav Stickley’s magazine of the American movement opens its issue with a heavy masthead between two joiner’s-compass devices and a woodcut initial.
references.summary: Heavy condensed capitals between two compass devices, a woodcut initial, and dense old-style text. The Craftsman, 1915.

source.label: Internet Archive: The Craftsman 1915-02, Vol. 27, Issue 5

creator.name: Gustav Stickley (publisher); The Craftsman Publishing Co.

evidence.note: Inspected page 459, the first text page of the issue, in the Internet Archive microfilm scan (1468 × 2006 px, greyscale), saved only in a scratch folder. The scan is black and white, so colour cannot be judged. The printed cover, on [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Craftsman_vol._XXVII_no._5,_Feb._1915_cover.jpg), could not be downloaded because of repeated HTTP 429 rate limits and was not inspected.

styles.note: Partial fit: the American branch. Heavy capitals, a device, and a woodcut initial over dense text, without the British pattern.

context: Stickley founded The Craftsman in October 1901 to promote the American Arts and Crafts movement; the first issue’s cover story was on William Morris. The last issue appeared in December 1916. [Wikipedia: The Craftsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Craftsman_(magazine)).

This issue is Volume XXVII, Number 5, February 1915, published by the Craftsman Publishing Co.; its opening article is “My People” by Robert Henri. [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/sim_craftsman-an-illustrated-monthly-magazine_1915-02_27_5).
observed: “THE CRAFTSMAN” runs across the top in heavy, condensed, slightly irregular capitals.
A black device stands at each end of the masthead: a joiner’s compass shape with the words “Als ik kan” in a small panel.
Under it, a line of small bold capitals gives the publisher, volume, date, and number.
The article title “MY PEOPLE:” BY ROBERT HENRI is in bold capitals; an editor’s note follows in smaller type.
A square black woodcut initial T, with a small landscape inside it, opens the text.
The text is a single wide column of dark old-style serif with tight spacing and narrow margins.
interpretation: The page shares the British private-press habits of a device, a woodcut initial, and a dark text block, but its masthead lettering is a condensed display face, not a blackletter or Venetian roman. That is typical of the American branch, which the style record treats as related.
The Dutch motto “Als ik kan” (“as I can”) in the devices states the craft ideal in the masthead itself. Its history was not checked for this record.
borrow: Frame a masthead between two matching square devices.
Open an article with a square woodcut-style initial that holds a small picture.

rights.statement: The issue was published in the United States in 1915 and is in the public domain there. The Internet Archive microfilm scan carries no rights statement, so no image is stored.

references.title: The End of Print: The Graphic Design of David Carson
references.titleBreak: The End of Print:|The Graphic Design of David Carson
references.lede: The 1995 monograph on David Carson by Lewis Blackwell, with an introduction by David Byrne, whose cover mixes blurred, mirrored, and substituted letters over photo fragments.
references.summary: Cover with a blurred, mixed-font title, a mirrored “CARSON”, and yellow, blue, and orange photo panels. Lewis Blackwell and David Carson, 1995.

source.label: Design Reviewed: The End of Print, Laurence King, 1995

references.made: 1995 (Design Reviewed; Chronicle Books edition, ISBN 0-8118-1199-9, per Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Inspected Design Reviewed’s scan of the Laurence King edition cover (1600 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. The interior was not seen. Design Reviewed’s page returned 403 to scripts and was read through WebFetch. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example: the book that fixed the style’s name and reputation, with a cover title made of blurred, mirrored, and mismatched letters.

context: Design Reviewed lists the book as published by Laurence King in 1995, designed by David Carson, 245 × 285 mm. [Design Reviewed](https://designreviewed.com/artefacts/the-end-of-print-the-graphic-design-of-david-carson-laurence-king-1995/).
Wikipedia lists the US edition as Chronicle Books, 1995, ISBN 0-8118-1199-9. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)).
An Internet Archive lending copy is catalogued as “The end of print: the graphic design of David Carson” by Lewis Blackwell. [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/endofprintgraphi0000blac).
observed: The cover is divided into pale yellow, deep blue, and orange panels, with photo fragments of a machine part and an astronomical chart labelled “Mercury” and “Venus”.
“THE END OF PRINT:” mixes letters from different serif and blackletter-like faces; several letters are blurred, doubled, or mirrored, and a thin rule runs under the line.
“DATUM” is printed upside down in a heavy sans-serif beside a vertical rule.
“THE GRAPHIC DESIGN OF DAVID CARSON” uses substituted and reversed letters: a numeral 1 for I, a reversed E, and a mirrored S in “CARSON”.
“CARSON” is very large white serif capitals over a blue photograph; the author lines are a spaced sans-serif and an italic serif.
interpretation: The cover is milder than the Ray Gun pages but carries the core traits: mixed faces within one word, damaged or mirrored letters, and type laid over photographic fragments.
borrow: Replace a few letters in a title with glyphs from other faces, or mirror them, and keep the word readable.
Blur or double one or two letters in a display line instead of the whole line.

rights.statement: No image is stored. David Carson is living, so the design is in copyright. Photographs by their sources. Scan by Design Reviewed.

references.title: The Matrix website, 2000
references.lede: The official site of The Matrix in December 2000: a black page with the green film logo, spaced capital menu items, and film stills.
references.summary: Black page with the green MATRIX logo, small spaced capitals, film stills of the cast in fog, and a red-pill button.

evidence.note: Captured from the Internet Archive with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Two image boxes in the center column did not load (probably Flash or ad slots); they cover less than a quarter of the page.

styles.note: Borderline: the cyber side of the period (black, digital green, spaced techno capitals). It has no chrome, candy color, or rounded plastic. The page draws its graphics with images, so the CSS fingerprint measures flat, square, unshadowed boxes (see the style page). Judge it by the rubric.
Clear: the official site of a core cyberpunk film, with a black page, glowing green capitals, and spaced techno type.

observed: The page is black. A film still of the three main characters walking out of fog between dark skyscrapers fills the left column and repeats at the right.
“MATRIX” is at the top in thin, glowing green capitals.
Menu items such as “ENHANCED VERSION”, “GET FLASH”, “SOUNDTRACK”, and “SHORTCUTS” are small white capitals with wide spacing.
“HACK THE MATRIX” is in green condensed capitals; a book cover sits in a green glowing outline with “PREORDER HERE”.
A red pill in a red target circle and a gold Warner Bros. shield sit below. A red banner reads “NOT A SOUND / NOT A WARNING”.
interpretation: The site shows the dark, cyber end of the Y2K range around 1999–2000: glowing green type and spaced capitals, but film photography instead of rendered objects.
It is useful as an edge case between Y2K and later cyberpunk revivals.
references.notice: The live site no longer exists. This is an archived copy of the HTML page; the site’s separate Flash version was not captured.

images.alt: Archived Matrix site: black page, film still of three figures in long coats walking out of fog between skyscrapers on both sides, a thin green MATRIX logo, small spaced white menu capitals, a book in a green glow, a red pill in a target, and a red banner.
images.caption: First viewport of the [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20001206212800/http://whatisthematrix.warnerbros.com/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to Warner Bros.. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: The Miller Blues Band at the Matrix (Neon Rose #2)
references.lede: Victor Moscoso’s Neon Rose poster of January 1967: a photographed dancer inside nested stripes of magenta and cyan that seem to flicker.
references.summary: Victor Moscoso, 1967. Magenta and cyan contour stripes vibrate around a photo-collage figure on orange-red.

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object E.624-2004 (IIIF, 1165 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The Library of Congress record for its copy has no online image. The image is not stored.

styles.note: The color trait in its purest form: two complements of similar value in tight alternating stripes, so the edges seem to move. Moscoso learned this from Josef Albers.

context: The V&A catalogues it as Neon Rose #2, a colour offset lithograph “depicting a photograph of a nude model posing in a Salome-style costume circa 1920s”, signed by the artist. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1023103/).

The Library of Congress copy (POS - US .M6775, no. 5) is 51 × 36 cm and was published by Neon Rose, San Francisco. It names the venue as the Matrix, Fillmore near Lombard. [LoC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2014647491/).

Moscoso (born 1936) studied at Cooper Union and Yale. Wikipedia attributes his vibrating colors to his teacher Josef Albers and notes that he was the first rock poster artist to use photographic collage. His Neon Rose posters advertised the Matrix club. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moscoso).
observed: An orange-red border surrounds an arched field of alternating magenta and light cyan stripes.
The stripes follow the outline of a central standing figure and repeat outward like contour lines, then fall straight down to the bottom edge.
The figure is a halftone photograph printed in magenta over the orange-red, so the body reads as one warm color against the cool stripes.
THE MILLER BLUES BAND arches over the head in orange-red hand-drawn capitals with small serifs. A smaller arched line above gives the dates and the venue, with stars as separators.
Every part of the sheet is colored. There is no white paper and no black.
interpretation: This is the rubric’s color rule exactly: magenta and cyan of similar lightness in thin alternating bands. The flicker comes from the edges, not from any single color.
The contour stripes act as echo outlines around the figure, the same device that the rules recommend for display type.
borrow: Repeat an outline outward in two alternating colors of similar value to make a vibrating halo.
Print a photograph in one flat color and let the ground carry the complement.
Arch a title over the main figure to keep the composition on its vertical axis.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. Victor Moscoso is alive.

references.title: The Move and Pink Floyd at UFO
references.lede: Hapshash and the Coloured Coat’s screen print for the UFO club, London, 1967: a winged woman falling through gold sunburst rays, with lettering that melts from magenta to yellow.
references.summary: Hapshash and the Coloured Coat, 1967. Gold sunburst on white, with rainbow-blended swollen lettering.

creator.name: Hapshash and the Coloured Coat (Michael English and Nigel Waymouth)

references.made: 1967 (The Move on 26 May, Pink Floyd on 2 June)

evidence.note: Downloaded the V&A image of object E.1708-1991 (IIIF, 1067 × 1600 px) to a scratch folder and inspected it. The V&A image shows the sheet rotated 180°; the observations below use reading orientation, with the imprint at top left. The image is not stored.

styles.note: The London branch of the style: swollen, melting lettering with a two-ink rainbow blend, radiating rays, and Art Nouveau patterning. Partial fit on color: much white paper and a metallic gold instead of complements.

context: The V&A catalogues it as a silkscreen poster by Michael English and Nigel Waymouth (Hapshash and the Coloured Coat) for The Move and Pink Floyd at UFO, Great Britain, 1967. It describes “pink through orange to yellow rainbow lettering with gold on white ground” and an upside-down woman with butterfly wings. The inscription at top left reads “1007 © UFO 1967”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O129217/).

Hapshash’s silkscreen posters advertised London happenings, clubs, and concerts and helped start the sale of posters as art. The V&A owns many originals and held the retrospective “Cosmic Visions: Psychedelic Posters from the 1960s” in 2000–2001. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hapshash_and_the_Coloured_Coat).
observed: Broad rays of metallic gold radiate from the center of the sheet across white paper.
A woman in white silhouette falls head-down through the middle. Her butterfly wings and robe are filled with scale, bubble, and droplet patterns cut out of the gold.
Two blocks of swollen, rounded lettering sit lower left and lower right. Each blends from magenta at the top through orange to yellow at the bottom.
Sprays of fine gold dots soften the edges of the rays near the figure.
There is no rectangle or frame. The rays run off every edge.
interpretation: The magenta-to-yellow lettering is the split-fountain rainbow effect that the rubric names, done in screen print. It carries all the color on a sheet that is otherwise gold and white.
The sunburst is the radiating-ripple motif in its simplest form, a useful background for a hero area.
borrow: Run one warm two-color blend through the display lettering and keep everything else flat.
Use a full-bleed sunburst of broad rays as the ground behind a central figure.
Fill a silhouette with a repeating scale or bubble pattern instead of shading.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The V&A image is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, and the design is in copyright. Michael English died in 2009; Nigel Waymouth is alive.

references.title: The Peacock Skirt, Beardsley’s illustration for Salome
references.lede: Aubrey Beardsley’s black-and-white plate for Oscar Wilde’s Salome: a woman seen from behind in a vast robe of peacock-feather scales, joined to a second figure by long hairlines that end in feather eyes.
references.summary: Pen-and-ink figures with a peacock-feather robe, dotted clouds, and long hairline curves. Aubrey Beardsley, London, 1894.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a 960 × 1338 px copy of a line reproduction on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Beardsley-peacockskirt.PNG), sourced there from humanitiesweb.org. It is a clean black-and-white reproduction, not a museum photograph, so the physical copy it shows is not known. Commons credits another copy to the Harvard Art Museums, which hold the original drawing; that record was not read.

styles.note: Partial fit: British graphic Art Nouveau with peacock ornament, long curving lines, and Japonisme, but in black and white rather than the earthy palette.

context: Wikipedia: *The Peacock Skirt* is an 1893 pen-and-ink illustration, first reproduced as a wood engraving in the first English edition of Wilde’s *Salome* (Elkin Mathews and John Lane, 1894), and later as a line block. It was the second of ten plates. The original drawing was bequeathed to the Fogg Art Museum, Harvard, in 1943. The print measures 178 × 127 mm. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Peacock_Skirt).

Wikipedia notes the influence of Whistler’s Peacock Room and of Japanese woodblock prints, and says the refined curving lines anticipate the Art Nouveau aesthetic. The Art Nouveau article names Beardsley, whose drawings featured “the curved lines that became the most recognizable feature of the style”, as a key influence, and says the Maison de l’Art Nouveau showed his posters. [Wikipedia: The Peacock Skirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Peacock_Skirt); [Wikipedia: Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau).
observed: The image is pure black line and solid black on white, framed by a double rule.
At left, a woman seen from behind wears a robe that swells into a huge teardrop shape. Its lower half is solid black filled with white scale and feather-eye patterns.
Long, very thin lines hang from her headdress and shoulders in wide curves and end in small feather-eye pendants.
A headdress of peacock feathers spreads above her head; a small stylized peacock sits at upper left in a cloud of dotted lines.
At right, a second figure in a pleated, layered tunic turns toward her, drawn in fine parallel lines.
Large areas of the sheet are left empty white between the figures.
interpretation: Beardsley shows how far the style can go with only line: the curve, the peacock motif, and the contrast of dense pattern with empty ground carry everything.
It is a partial fit for the [Art Nouveau](style:art-nouveau) grammar, which expects earthy colours; it belongs to the British source of the style more than to its Paris core.
borrow: Contrast one very dense patterned mass with a large empty ground.
Use a hairline curve that ends in a small ornament, such as a feather eye or a bud, as a connector or divider.

images.alt: Black-and-white illustration in a double-ruled frame: a woman seen from behind in a huge black robe patterned with white peacock-feather scales, with a peacock headdress, facing a figure in a pleated tunic; thin curving lines with feather-eye pendants hang between them.
images.caption: Aubrey Beardsley, *The Peacock Skirt*, plate for Oscar Wilde’s *Salome*, 1894. Line reproduction from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Beardsley-peacockskirt.PNG), public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired). Beardsley died in 1898, and the plate was published in 1894, so it is in the public domain in the United Kingdom and the United States.

references.title: The Responsive Eye
references.lede: William C. Seitz’s catalogue for the Museum of Modern Art’s 1965 exhibition of optical art, with Bridget Riley’s Current printed edge to edge on the cover.
references.summary: A cover filled with fine black and white wave stripes, overprinted with the title in several colours. MoMA, 1965.

source.label: UbuWeb: scan of The Responsive Eye (MoMA, 1965)

creator.name: William C. Seitz (author); Joseph Bourke Del Valle (designer); The Museum of Modern Art

evidence.note: Downloaded the UbuWeb PDF scan and inspected the cover and the first pages as extracted page images (2538 × 2793 px) in a scratchpad. The faint colophon reads as the third printing, 1966. MoMA’s own exhibition page returned HTTP 403. No image is stored.

styles.note: The exhibition catalogue that fixed op art in public view, with a black and white Riley wave field as its cover.

context: The title page reads “The Responsive Eye, by William C. Seitz, The Museum of Modern Art, New York”, in collaboration with the City Art Museum of St. Louis, the Contemporary Art Council of the Seattle Art Museum, the Pasadena Art Museum, and the Baltimore Museum of Art. [UbuWeb scan](https://ubu.com/historical/responsive/ResponsiveEyeMOMA1965.pdf).

Seitz’s acknowledgments say that the exhibition was announced in November 1962, and that “the catalogue was designed by Joseph Bourke Del Valle of the Museum’s Department of Publications”. [UbuWeb scan](https://ubu.com/historical/responsive/ResponsiveEyeMOMA1965.pdf).

David Zwirner says that Seitz included Riley’s *Current* (1964) and *Hesitate* (1964), and that “the eye-popping black-and-white squiggles of Riley’s Current adorned the catalogue cover”. [David Zwirner](https://www.davidzwirner.com/news/2019/bridget-riley-s-paintings-continue-to-mesmerize-six-decades-on).
observed: The whole cover is filled with thin vertical black and white stripes that wave; the waves tighten toward the left and right edges and toward the middle.
“THE RESPONSIVE EYE” is set four times in condensed sans-serif capitals, overprinted in yellow, magenta, green, and red, slightly offset from one another across the middle.
The coloured letters take on the stripes of the ground, so the title seems to vibrate and blur.
The title page inside is plain: “The Responsive Eye” in a black condensed grotesque, with the author and publisher in small serif capitals on white.
interpretation: The cover shows the style’s rule for type on pattern in its display form: large letters may carry the stripes, while the inside pages keep text on plain white.
The offset colour overprints are a graphic-design addition to Riley’s black and white field, and they go beyond the style’s one-accent rule.
borrow: Fill a cover or hero panel with one black and white wave field, edge to edge.
Let display letters show the pattern through them, and move all reading text to a plain page.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The catalogue is © The Museum of Modern Art, 1965, and the cover reproduces a work by a living artist.

references.title: The Source, a psychedelic art store in Washington, D.C.
references.lede: A 1967 news photograph of customers in a store that sold psychedelic posters and objects, showing how far the San Francisco style had spread within a year.
references.summary: Marion S. Trikosko, 21 April 1967. Posters, hangings, and a light fixture in a Washington head shop.

creator.name: Marion S. Trikosko, U.S. News & World Report

evidence.note: Downloaded the Library of Congress service image (1024 × 697 px) and inspected it. The photograph is black and white, so it shows composition and lettering but not color.

styles.note: Context, not an exemplar: posters in the style hang on the walls of a commercial store in Washington, D.C., in April 1967.

context: The Library of Congress titles it “Customers at ‘The Source,’ a psychedelic art store with rock posters and other images on the walls, 2151 K St., N.W. Washington, D.C.”. The job log caption reads “Hippies and Teenie-Boppers”. It is part of the U.S. News & World Report Magazine Photograph Collection. [LoC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2024640512/).

Wikipedia notes that the San Francisco posters were torn down as soon as they went up and were soon reprinted for sale, with poster shops opening locally and nationwide. [Wikipedia: Wes Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Wilson).
observed: A low room with fluorescent ceiling lights. Posters, prints, and hangings cover the walls.
At upper left hangs a vertical poster with a large central medallion and hand-drawn lettering.
Further back, a poster with a large stylized face and wavy lettering hangs near a dark cloth decorated with dots.
A large photographic poster of a man’s face fills the upper right.
Customers browse. Two men crouch at a display in the center, and a table of flat prints stands at left.
interpretation: The photograph shows the posters as retail goods on the East Coast only months after the first Fillmore and Avalon posters, which supports the account that the style spread through poster sales as much as through concerts.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a small store with posters and hangings on every wall, customers browsing, and two men crouching at a display in the center.
images.caption: Marion S. Trikosko, 21 April 1967. [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2024640512/), no known restrictions on publication. The posters on the walls are third-party works shown incidentally.

rights.statement: Library of Congress: “No known restrictions on publication” (U.S. News & World Report Magazine Collection). The posters on the walls are copyrighted works shown incidentally in a documentary photograph of the store.

references.title: The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (Kelmscott Chaucer)
references.lede: The Kelmscott Press’s great folio: a woodcut title and a Burne-Jones picture framed in dense borders of white vine on black, with blackletter text in two columns.
references.summary: Dense white-on-black vine borders, woodcut lettering, and two columns of Chaucer type. William Morris and Edward Burne-Jones, 1896.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: The Kelmscott Chaucer, Cantor Arts Center copy (Google Art Project)

creator.name: William Morris (design and borders); Edward Burne-Jones (illustrations); Kelmscott Press

evidence.note: Inspected the opening spread of the Iris & B. Gerald Cantor Center for Visual Arts copy (Stanford; Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Nathaniel J. Kendall) through its Google Art Project image on Commons (4501 × 3304 px; viewed at 1280 px wide). Also inspected page 29 of the [Boston Public Library copy](https://archive.org/details/worksofgeoffreyc00chau_0) on Internet Archive (2036 × 3000 px) to check the use of red; that page is not stored.

styles.note: The canonical private-press book: dense framed borders, woodcut lettering, blackletter text, and red side notes on the text pages.

context: The Kelmscott Press, founded by William Morris and Emery Walker, published 53 books in 66 volumes between 1891 and 1898. Its books imitated 15th-century printing, and its best known is the large folio of Chaucer with many wood engravings. [Wikipedia: Kelmscott Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelmscott_Press).

Morris set smaller spaces between words and lines to make a dense block of text, with large outer margins for shoulder notes. [Wikipedia: Kelmscott Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelmscott_Press).
The Boston Public Library catalogue record on Internet Archive notes “Side notes and headings in red”. [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/worksofgeoffreyc00chau_0).

The Cantor copy measures 17.25 × 12.2 × 2.9 in. and is catalogued as an illustrated book with woodcuts. [Commons record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:William_Morris_-_The_Works_of_Geoffrey_Chaucer_(The_Kelmscott_Chaucer)_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).
observed: On the left page, the title “the works of Geoffrey Chaucer now newly imprinted” is cut as white lettering on a black ground of fine vines, inside a rectangular panel.
Both pages have wide borders of white vine leaves and grapes on black, so dense that almost no black ground shows.

On the right page, a Burne-Jones picture of a man in a garden sits in its own framed panel. Above it, white capitals on black read “HERE BEGINNETH THE TALES OF CANTERBURY AND FIRST THE PROLOGUE THEREOF”.
Below the picture a large ornamented initial W opens two columns of blackletter verse.
The frames are single black lines around each panel, not double rules. All corners are square.

This spread is printed only in black. On page 29 of the Boston copy, the text is in two plain columns without borders, with small leaf fleurons, ornamented initials, and a red side note, “The Knyghtes Tale”, in the outer margin.
interpretation: The book supports the rubric’s framed, dense layout, but it separates two modes: heavily bordered opening spreads and plain two-column text pages where red is kept for small side notes.
The title lettering is in lowercase and the headings are in capitals, so the style does not require mixed-case headings.
borrow: Save a dense border for the opening screen or section start, and keep reading pages plain.
Put short red notes in the outer margin next to a dense black text block.

images.alt: Open Kelmscott Chaucer: the left page has the title in white woodcut lettering on black vines inside a wide border of white vine leaves and grapes; the right page has a framed Burne-Jones picture of a man in a garden, a white-on-black heading, a large ornamented initial, and two columns of blackletter verse, all in a matching border.
images.caption: Kelmscott Press, The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, 1896, opening spread. Iris & B. Gerald Cantor Center for Visual Arts, Stanford. [Google Art Project image on Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:William_Morris_-_The_Works_of_Geoffrey_Chaucer_(The_Kelmscott_Chaucer)_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons tags the image {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-1923}}: a faithful photograph of a two-dimensional public-domain work. Morris died in 1896 and Burne-Jones in 1898; the book was published in 1896.

identifiers.commons: File:William Morris - The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (The Kelmscott Chaucer) - Google Art Project.jpg

references.title: TokyWoky website, 2020
references.lede: The 2020 home page of a French community-platform startup: small flat figures with long legs gather on a grey platform in front of an oversized browser window.
references.summary: Small long-legged flat figures around a giant tilted browser window, next to a bold blue heading. 2020.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. No cookie box covers the page. Wayback redirected to a copy without the `if_` flag, but no archive toolbar appears in the screenshot. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: long-legged figures with small heads act around an oversized interface, the style’s standard scene, but the skin is natural and the platform and screen use soft gradients.

context: The live address now redirects to a Skeepers brand-community page, which returned “Error 403 Forbidden” to `tools/capture.mjs` on 28 September 2026.

On the right, a large tilted browser window in light grey shows a red-framed portrait and grey text bars.

“Mr. Tom Froese” at upper left is a pink connected script logotype.

Put a faint script signature behind a sans-serif heading as a texture.

references.title: Trellis wallpaper
references.lede: Morris’s first wallpaper design: climbing roses and birds on a square wooden trellis, drawn flat on an open cream ground.
references.summary: Roses, blue birds, and insects on a square trellis, on open cream. William Morris, designed 1862.

creator.name: William Morris, Morris & Company, and Philip Webb (as the Met lists them)

evidence.note: Inspected the Metropolitan Museum of Art image DT255077 of sheet 23.163.4h, through its CC0 [Wikimedia Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trellis_MET_DT255077.jpg) (3239 × 4000 px; viewed at 1280 px wide). The Met’s own collection API refused scripted access (HTTP 403), so the object data come from the Commons record of the Met upload. The Met lists William Morris, Morris & Company, and Philip Webb as artists. Webb is often credited with the birds, but that record does not say so.

styles.note: A founding Morris & Co. pattern, but an open one: flat, outlined motifs on a square lattice with much plain ground, not the dense repeat of the later work.

context: The Met record gives the date as designed 1862, first produced 1864; the medium as block-printed wallpaper; and the sheet size as 68.6 × 54.6 cm. It was bought with the Edward C. Moore Jr. Gift, 1923. [Wikimedia Commons record of the Met upload](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trellis_MET_DT255077.jpg).

Morris began his earliest wallpaper designs while he lived at [Red House](ref:red-house-bexleyheath) (1860–1865). [Wikipedia: Red House, Bexleyheath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_House,_Bexleyheath).
observed: A square trellis of grey-brown laths, with wood grain and nail heads, divides the sheet into large open squares.
Thorny green rose stems climb across the trellis with sage-green leaves and salmon-red roses.
Four blue birds in different poses perch or fly among the stems. Small brown insects float in the open squares.
The ground is a plain cream; roughly half of the sheet shows it.
Every shape has a dark outline and flat fills. Stippling on the stems and birds adds texture, not shading.
“MORRIS & Cº” is printed in small capitals on the right margin, beside colour-registration marks.
interpretation: The prospect notes describe Arts and Crafts pattern as dense and symmetrical. Trellis is neither: it is open, and the birds break the symmetry. The lattice is visible here instead of hidden.
The palette is lighter than the later indigo-discharge cottons such as [Strawberry Thief](ref:morris-strawberry-thief-textile): cream, sage, salmon, and pale blue.
borrow: Show the grid itself as a motif, like a trellis, and let plants cross it at irregular points.
Leave a light, open ground and use a few outlined, flat motifs for a calmer version of the style.

images.alt: Wallpaper sheet with a grey-brown square trellis on a cream ground, climbing thorny rose stems with salmon-red roses and green leaves, blue birds, and small brown insects. Morris & Co. is printed in the right margin.
images.caption: William Morris (with Philip Webb), Trellis wallpaper, designed 1862, first produced 1864. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 23.163.4h. [Commons copy of the Met image](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trellis_MET_DT255077.jpg), CC0.

rights.statement: The Metropolitan Museum of Art released the image as CC0 (Commons template Cc-zero, from the Met Open Access upload). Morris died in 1896 and Webb in 1915; the design dates from 1862, so it is in the public domain in the United Kingdom and the United States.

references.title: Typografische Monatsblätter covers, 1972–1973
references.lede: Wolfgang Weingart’s series of covers for the Swiss trade journal TM, which break its grid with stepped blocks, spaced-out letters, and heavy bars.
references.summary: Grey and white journal covers: Akzidenz-Grotesk set in steps, arcs, and very wide letterspacing, with black bars and arrows. Wolfgang Weingart, 1972–73.

source.label: Letterform Archive: Legacies of Swiss Style, Part 2—Wolfgang Weingart

evidence.note: Inspected Letterform Archive’s photographs of seven covers held by the Archive (Nr. 1, 5, and 12 of 1972; Nr. 2, 3, 6.7, and 10 of 1973), 1996 to 2965 px wide, in scratchpad copies. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example. The covers are the first public statement of the style, and Letterform Archive connects them with the name “Swiss Punk”.

context: The TM editorial board asked Weingart, a new board member, to design fifteen covers for the 1972 and 1973 print runs. The covers are set in Akzidenz-Grotesk and have “a conspicuous variety of line weights, imbalanced asymmetries, and stepped text blocks intersected by bold rectilinear shapes”. [Letterform Archive](https://letterformarchive.org/news/from-the-collection-legacies-of-swiss-style-part-2-wolfgang-weingart/).

Jan Tschichold wrote to the editor that he hoped this was the last issue with a Weingart cover, and later called Weingart “the anti-typographer”. [Letterform Archive](https://letterformarchive.org/news/from-the-collection-legacies-of-swiss-style-part-2-wolfgang-weingart/).
The cover of Nr. 6.7/1973 carries the name of April Greiman, Weingart’s student; see [her later work](ref:greiman-your-turn-my-turn-poster-1983).
observed: Nr. 2/1973: a quotation in small capitals with very wide gaps between the letters fills four lines; below it, “NACHRICHT” in heavy capitals runs up in an arc, each letter rotated.

Nr. 1/1972: “Typographie realisiert Sprache” in large black grotesque is cut into cells by thin vertical rules; a narrow text column at right ends each line with a black rectangle of a different length.

Nr. 5/1972: “SPRACHE:” in heavy condensed capitals, then lines in a regular grotesque, each underlined by a grey bar. Weight changes inside one line (“Darstellungs-zeichen.”), and the last word “Gebärden.” is letterspaced.
Nr. 12/1972 and Nr. 3/1973: grey or white panels with stepped edges overlap the text blocks, and a justified line opens into very large word gaps.
Nr. 6.7/1973: “A P R I L   G R E I M A N” and “F E E L I N G   T Y P O G R A P H Y” in thin capitals with very wide letterspacing, around a centered photograph.
Nr. 10/1973: large heavy type in mixed sizes, a black arrow bar, black dots, a triangle, and small rotated text on a thin angled line.
Each cover keeps the same footer, the three journal names with bold initials, and a number at the top.
interpretation: The series is a catalogue of the style’s type moves inside one fixed frame: wide tracking, rotation, stepping, weight changes, and bars. The fixed footer and number show that the disorder is controlled.
The palette is almost only black, grey, and paper, so colour is not needed for the style.
borrow: Keep a fixed header and footer, and change only the middle composition from issue to issue.
Set a quotation in small capitals with gaps of one or two letter widths between the letters.
End lines of a narrow column with black bars of different lengths instead of a clean rag.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Photographs by Letterform Archive. Weingart died in 2021, so the designs are in copyright.

references.title: unDraw illustration library (Katerina Limpitsouni)

references.summary: Free flat vector scenes with one changeable accent color. A main source of the style on startup sites. Documented.

styles.note: Documented fit: Wired names unDraw with Freepik and Adobe’s library as image banks that let non-illustrators use the style. The illustrations were not inspected for this record.

references.title: USSR Russische Ausstellung poster, Zurich
references.lede: El Lissitzky’s poster for a Soviet exhibition in Zurich fuses two young faces into one photomontage and runs the museum’s name up a red bar.
references.summary: Photomontage of two merged heads above a cut-out exhibition building, with red capitals and a vertical red band. El Lissitzky, 1929.

source.label: Plakatsammlung der Schule für Gestaltung Basel, object 6370

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the scan that the Basel Poster Collection contributed to [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CH-000957-X-8308_Lissitzky.jpg) (2921 × 4096 px, viewed at 1920 px). Copy: Plakatsammlung der Schule für Gestaltung Basel, accession number CH-000957-X:8308.

styles.note: A canonical constructivist photomontage poster: black-and-white photographs cut and combined with red block capitals, a red bar, and a diagonal architectural fragment.

context: The poster advertised the Russian exhibition at the Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich from 24 March to 28 April 1929. The Commons record gives the size as 125 × 90.5 cm, the technique as intaglio, and the printer as Gebr. Fretz AG, Zurich. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CH-000957-X-8308_Lissitzky.jpg).
The poster is signed in the lower left corner “el Lissitzky Moskau”. The source photographs are not credited on the sheet.
observed: A red band runs down the full left edge. “KUNSTGEWERBEMUSEUM ZÜRICH” is set in it in black spaced capitals, reading upward.
Two photographed heads, a young man and a young woman, are merged into one face with two sets of eyes and mouths. They look up and to the right against a gray sky.
“USSR” is set in red condensed capitals across the forehead.

Below the heads, a cut-out photograph of a modern building with black slabs, white planes, and diagonal supports forms the base. “RUSSISCHE” in gray and “AUSSTELLUNG” in large red condensed capitals sit on its black face.
The dates “1929 24 MÄRZ–28 APRIL” are set in white sans-serif at the lower right.
Apart from the red, the poster is printed in black and gray tones on a warm paper.
interpretation: The merged heads are a direct example of the style’s photomontage: the photograph is a raw material to cut, double, and scale, not a window.
The red is limited to type and one bar, but the bar spans the full height, so it organizes the page. The measurement finds one hue and 12% chromatic area.
The sheet is dark overall because the photographs fill it, unlike the paper-white ground of the earlier letterpress work.
borrow: Put the organization’s name in a full-height colored band on one edge, set in spaced capitals and turned 90 degrees.
Set a short label in red capitals directly on a black-and-white photograph.
Crop a building or object photograph along its own diagonals and use it as a base for the heading.

images.alt: Portrait poster: two merged black-and-white faces of a young man and woman look upward, with USSR in red capitals across the forehead. Below, a cut-out photograph of a modern building carries the words Russische Ausstellung in gray and red capitals. A red band on the left edge reads Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich.
images.caption: El Lissitzky, *USSR Russische Ausstellung*, Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich, 1929. Plakatsammlung der Schule für Gestaltung Basel, CH-000957-X:8308, image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CH-000957-X-8308_Lissitzky.jpg).

rights.statement: Commons marks the scan {{PD-Art-two|PD-old-auto|PD-US-not renewed}} (Public Domain Mark). The poster was published in Zurich in 1929. Lissitzky died in 1941, so the design is in the public domain in Switzerland (life + 70 years) and in Russia, and it was published before 1931, so it is in the public domain in the United States. The source photographs are uncredited; Lissitzky is commonly credited with the photomontage.

references.title: Van Doesburghuis website
references.lede: The foundation site for Theo van Doesburg’s studio house in Meudon arranges its content in flat red, yellow, and bright blue panels with square corners.
references.summary: Flat red, yellow, and bright blue panels on gray, an axonometric drawing, and bold Futura text.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The requested URL https://www.vandoesburghuis.com/ redirected to the English home page.

styles.note: Borderline: flat primary panels with square corners, but no black dividing lines, a bright sky blue instead of a primary blue, lowercase type, and a photograph.

context: The page states that the foundation runs the studio house that Theo van Doesburg designed for himself and Nelly van Doesburg in Meudon-Val-Fleury at the end of the 1920s. [vandoesburghuis.com](https://vandoesburghuis.com/en/).
observed: A red bar runs across the top of the page with a notice about opening days.
A white column on a light gray background holds rectangular panels: a red language panel, a yellow panel with a black-and-white axonometric drawing of the house, and a bright blue navigation panel.
A bright blue welcome panel and a large color photograph of the white house with tall steel windows fill the right column.
Navigation and headings are set in bold Futura in lowercase or sentence case; the current item is yellow on blue.
No panel has rounded corners, a shadow, or a gradient.
interpretation: The site takes the palette and flat rectangles from the movement but not the black line grid, so it reads as color blocking more than as a neoplastic composition. The axonometric drawing adds diagonals, which belong to van Doesburg’s later Elementarism and his architectural drawings.
Computed styles find 2 hues (red and bright blue); the yellow is mostly in the image. There are no CSS borders to measure.
borrow: Separate navigation, language choice, and intro text into flat panels of one primary each, and keep every corner square.

images.alt: Web page with a red notice bar, a red language panel, a yellow panel with a black-and-white axonometric drawing of a house, a bright blue navigation panel, a bright blue welcome panel, and a photograph of a white modernist house with tall windows.
images.caption: First viewport of [vandoesburghuis.com](https://vandoesburghuis.com/en/).

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s authors. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Vaporesources
references.lede: A Neocities collection of old computer graphics, introduced by a CRT monitor on a grid floor, a broken marble head, and letter-spaced magenta capitals.
references.summary: Sage-green page with a CRT on a grid floor, a marble head, and spaced magenta serif capitals.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear on imagery and type, not on palette: a CRT monitor on a receding grid, a fragment of a classical head, spaced capitals, and an embedded vaporwave track, but on a sage-green ground instead of pastel pink.

observed: A narrow column with a thin black outline is centred on a flat sage-green page.
At the top, a photograph shows a beige AT&T CRT monitor standing on a receding blue-and-white grid floor.
WELCOME TO VAPORESOURCES is set in bold magenta Times capitals with a space between every letter.
A cut-out fragment of a classical marble head sits below, above a spaced blue “G a l l e r y” link and a small Bandcamp player.
interpretation: The spaced heading is typed with a space between each letter, not set with CSS letter-spacing, so the measured heading tracking is 0. The grid floor is inside a photograph, so pattern share is 0 too.

images.alt: Vaporesources home page: sage-green background, a narrow outlined column with a CRT monitor photographed on a grid floor, the spaced magenta heading WELCOME TO VAPORESOURCES, a marble head fragment, a Gallery link, and a small music player.

references.title: Vaporwave Guide (Neocities)
references.lede: A fan-made beginner’s guide to vaporwave on a hot pink page, with a collage of the Windows 95 logo, Game Boys, palms, and Japanese text.
references.summary: Hot pink page, mint headings, default blue links, and a Windows 95 collage with vertical Japanese text.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: a fan site that describes the genre and uses it too, with a saturated pink ground, a collage of the Windows 95 logo, Game Boys, palms, and drink bottles, and vertical Japanese text. The CSS is plain, so the fingerprint cannot see the style; it lives in the image and the colour.

observed: The whole page is flat hot pink; the title “Vaporwave Guide” and the welcome line are mint green, bold, and underlined.
Six centred links in default blue underlined text list labels, artists, images, albums, a guide, and credits.

A wide collage below shows a glitched Windows 95 logo and wordmark, a column of Game Boy handhelds, fruit-drink bottles, palm trees, blue statues, and vertical pink Japanese text over a pink-and-green sky.
interpretation: It is the style at its most amateur: all of it sits in one pasted image and a background colour. The measurement sees only flat colour and no shadows.

images.alt: Vaporwave Guide home page: hot pink background, mint-green underlined title, a column of blue links, and a collage of the Windows 95 logo, Game Boys, drink bottles, palms, and vertical Japanese text.
images.caption: First viewport of [thevaporwaveguide.neocities.org](https://thevaporwaveguide.neocities.org/).

references.title: Vaporwave wallpaper (Mike Grauer Jr)
references.lede: A free 3D-rendered desktop wallpaper: a striped orange sun over a magenta plain crossed by a warped ribbon grid, under a starry violet sky.
references.summary: Striped sun, magenta plain, warped teal-green grid, violet starry sky. Free wallpaper, 2018.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1920 × 1080 rendering of the 7680 × 4320 original through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vaporwave_WP3_Print.jpg) and stored a reduced copy.

styles.note: Partial fit: the author calls it a vaporwave wallpaper and it has the grid floor and striped sun, but it has no collage, statue, or software chrome, and the grid-and-sun scene alone is shared with synthwave. The violet sky, not black, keeps it on the vaporwave side.
Partial fit: the striped sun over a magenta grid plain is the core synthwave scene, but the violet sky is softer than its usual black night.

context: The author’s description reads: “A new Vaporwave wallpaper! It is free and put under Creative Commons.” The CC BY 2.0 license was confirmed by Commons’ Flickr review bot on December 14, 2023. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vaporwave_WP3_Print.jpg).
observed: The upper half is a flat violet sky full of small white stars.
A large orange-to-yellow sphere with thin horizontal gaps across its lower half sits left of centre on the horizon.
The ground is a magenta plain, lighter toward the horizon, covered by a grid of twisted ribbons in green, teal, and pink that rises into jagged peaks at the right.
interpretation: A clean example of the grid-and-sun motif that vaporwave shares with synthwave. The rubric separates them by the sky: violet and pastel here, black in synthwave.
borrow: Cut three or four horizontal gaps through the lower half of a sun disc to get the striped-sun motif without a separate stripe layer.

images.alt: 3D-rendered landscape: a striped orange sun on the horizon, a magenta plain crossed by a warped green and teal ribbon grid rising into peaks, and a violet sky with stars.
images.caption: Vaporwave wallpaper by Mike Grauer Jr, 2018. CC BY 2.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vaporwave_WP3_Print.jpg), from [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/mike_grauer/26310058937/).

rights.statement: Published by the author under CC BY 2.0 on Flickr; license reviewed on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vaporwave_WP3_Print.jpg). Credit: Mike Grauer Jr.

references.title: vaporwave.neocities.org
references.lede: A small 2014 personal page: a white column on a cyan-to-pink gradient, a katakana greeting, spaced lowercase, and a clip-art crab with sunglasses and a soda.
references.summary: White column on a cyan-to-pink gradient, katakana welcome, letter-spaced subtitle, clip-art crab. 2014.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. The update log on the page dates it to October 2014.

styles.note: Clear: a pastel cyan-to-pink gradient behind the whole page, a Japanese greeting, a letter-spaced subtitle, and dated clip art. The only capture that passes the gradient metric.

observed: The page background is a vertical gradient from pale cyan at the top to pink at the bottom.
A white column with thick black top and bottom rules holds the heading ようこそ, the spaced subtitle “W e l c o m e  t o  h e l l”, and a monospace update log dated October 2014.
A clip-art illustration shows a red crab in black sunglasses holding a soda can with a straw.
Three small monospace links (Dream, Hell, Chats) sit at the top left.

references.title: Vertigo business cards
references.lede: April Greiman’s business cards for the Los Angeles shop Vertigo: a letterspaced wordmark on a tilted bar, with stripes, dots, and diagonal lines that change from card to card.
references.summary: Four cards with “V e r t / g o” on a tilted bar, a black triangle for the V, and stripes, dots, and checks. April Greiman, 1980.

source.label: People’s Graphic Design Archive: Vertigo business cards

evidence.note: Inspected the People’s Graphic Design Archive image (901 × 1500), a black-and-white photograph of four cards, probably reproduced from a publication; the owner of the physical cards is not stated. Not stored. Colours are not visible.

styles.note: Clear example of Greiman’s California New Wave at the scale of stationery: wide letterspacing, tilted bars, and scattered geometric marks.

context: The People’s Graphic Design Archive credits the cards to April Greiman for the client Vertigo/Lynda Weinman, printed by McCoy Printing, and dates them 1980. [People’s Graphic Design Archive](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/3133/vertigo-business-cards).
observed: Each card carries the wordmark “Vertigo” on a tilted rectangular bar. The V is a solid black triangle, a slash replaces the i, and a black dot follows the o.
The letters of the wordmark are spaced wide apart.

The four cards have different grounds: black vertical stripes that extend past the card edge, a dark card with round holes or dots, a light card with thin diagonal lines and circles, and a card with a pattern of rounded squares.
Addresses are set in small bold grotesque, some lines tilted or letterspaced (“L o s  A n g e l e s”).
Small words such as “gifts”, “paper”, and “fashion acces.” run along diagonal lines.
interpretation: The cards turn a small identity into a system of variations: one tilted, spaced wordmark stays fixed while the surfaces change. This is the style’s move from the poster to everyday print.
borrow: Put a letterspaced wordmark on a slightly tilted solid bar.
Replace one letter with a geometric mark (a triangle, a slash, a dot).
Keep the mark fixed and change the surface pattern across a set of cards.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design belongs to April Greiman or her client; the photograph’s owner is not stated.

references.title: Vertigo poster
references.lede: A white line spiral on flat red-orange pulls two small figures into its center, under hand-cut capitals that lean and bounce.
references.summary: A white spiral and black silhouettes on flat red-orange, with rough hand-cut capitals. Saul Bass, 1958.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons restoration (2703 × 4189 px, stored here at 1032 × 1600). Adam Cuerden restored the scan on Commons by removing fold marks and blemishes. No museum copy was checked.

styles.note: Hand-cut lettering, flat silhouettes, and one flat printed ground: the Bass branch of the graphic core. Partial fit: only one hue, and it is saturated.

context: Theatrical poster for Alfred Hitchcock’s film, released by Paramount in 1958. Commons credits the artwork to Saul Bass and cites Adrian Curry’s [Movie Poster of the Week](http://mubi.com/notebook/posts/movie-poster-of-the-week-alfred-hitchcocks-vertigo) column. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vertigomovie_restoration.jpg).

The foot of the poster carries “Copyright 1958 Paramount Pictures Corporation. Country of Origin U.S.A.”. Commons states that a Copyright Office catalog search found no renewal. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vertigomovie_restoration.jpg).
observed: The whole sheet is one flat red-orange field inside a thin off-white margin.
A large spiral of fine white lines fills the middle. Its lines cross into a lattice at the outer turns.
At the center a black silhouette of a man and a line drawing of a woman fall together over a small red-orange ellipse.
“JAMES STEWART”, “KIM NOVAK”, and “IN ALFRED HITCHCOCK’S MASTERPIECE” are black capitals with rough, cut edges and uneven letter widths.
“VERTIGO” at the foot is in wide, heavy black capitals with notched, hand-cut strokes, between single quotation marks.
The credit block below the field is a condensed grotesque on off-white.
interpretation: The lettering is the most transferable part: capitals cut or drawn by hand, with uneven widths and a slight bounce, next to a plain grotesque for the credits.
Measured on the stored image, the accent chroma is 0.69 with one hue family. The poster is flatter and more saturated than the warm, multi-hue textile side of the style.
borrow: Draw the heading as rough, hand-cut capitals and set the small print in a plain grotesque.
Put a single line-drawn motif (a spiral, a starburst) on a flat colored ground and let it carry the page.

images.alt: Film poster on flat red-orange: a large white line spiral with a black silhouette of a man and a line drawing of a woman falling at its center; black hand-cut capitals name James Stewart and Kim Novak at the top and Vertigo at the bottom.
images.caption: Saul Bass, US theatrical poster for *Vertigo*, 1958, restored scan by Adam Cuerden. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vertigomovie_restoration.jpg), marked public domain (not renewed).

rights.statement: Commons gives the reason in the permission field: a Copyright Office catalog search found no renewal of the 1958 US copyright, so the poster art entered the US public domain 28 years after publication. The country of origin is the United States. The license tag on the page is {{PD-art|PD-old-auto-1964}}, which does not match that reason; the non-renewal claim is the operative one. This catalogue did not repeat the renewal search.

references.title: Veshch/Gegenstand/Objet cover, issue 1–2
references.lede: El Lissitzky’s cover for the trilingual Berlin review builds its title from stencil-like black letters and a steep black bar with a circle, all printed on red.
references.summary: Black geometric capitals, a tilted black bar, a black disc, and outline numerals on a red cover. El Lissitzky, Berlin, 1922.

creator.name: El Lissitzky (cover); El Lissitzky and Ilya Ehrenburg (editors)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the cover image on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Weschch_1-2.jpg) (1218 × 1600 px, viewed at 1200 px). Commons credits the image to the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and names the Mayakovsky Museum, Moscow, as the holding institution; no inventory number is given.

styles.note: A canonical constructivist cover: a steep black bar, a circle, and letters built from bars and blocks. It inverts the usual palette and prints black on a red ground.

context: *Veshch’/Gegenstand/Objet* was an international review of modern art published in Berlin by El Lissitzky and Ilya Ehrenburg in 1922. Its title gives the word for “object” in Russian, German, and French. Issue 1–2 appeared in March–April 1922 and issue 3 in May 1922; there were no further issues. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veshch%27/Gegenstand/Objet).
Commons describes the print technique as zinc printing (Zinkdruck). [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Weschch_1-2.jpg).
observed: The whole cover is a flat, slightly mottled red. All type and shapes are printed in black.

A thick black bar runs steeply from the upper left to the lower center and turns at its foot into a short horizontal. “OBJET” runs along it, reading upward, and “GEGENSTAND” sits in the foot, both in red letters reversed out of the black.
“ВЕЩЬ” is set in large black letters built from bars and blocks, with stencil-like gaps. The letter В is doubled by an offset shadow.
The issue number “№ 1·2” is drawn in outline and solid strokes with thin rules that cross the black bar.
A solid black disc sits beside the foot of the bar. “BERLIN 1922” is stacked at the top of the bar in small heavy letters.
A small stepped block of text in three languages runs diagonally at the lower left.
interpretation: The cover uses the same vocabulary as [Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge](ref:lissitzky-beat-the-whites-red-wedge-poster), a diagonal bar and a circle, but turns it into a masthead. The letters are drawn as constructions, not set from a font.

The red ground covers the whole cover, so the measurement finds 69% chromatic area, above the website fingerprint’s maximum of 0.6. Print covers and posters by Klutsis show that a full red field belongs to the style.
borrow: Print black type and shapes on a full red ground for a cover or hero, and reverse small labels out of the black shapes in red.
Run the secondary title words along the edge of a steep bar.

images.alt: Red magazine cover: a steep black bar with the words Objet and Gegenstand, a black disc, the Russian title ВЕЩЬ in large black block letters, and the issue number 1·2 drawn with outlines and thin rules.
images.caption: El Lissitzky, cover of *Veshch’/Gegenstand/Objet* 1–2, Berlin 1922. Image by the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek, from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Weschch_1-2.jpg).

rights.statement: Commons marks the image {{PD-old-70-1923}} (Public Domain Mark). The cover design is by Lissitzky, who died in 1941, so it is in the public domain in Germany and Russia, and it was published in 1922, so it is in the public domain in the United States. The co-editor Ilya Ehrenburg died in 1967, but none of his text appears on the cover.

references.title: Vienna on the Path to Modernism exhibition website
references.lede: The Japanese site for the 2019 exhibition Wien Modern sets its English title in a framed block of Secession-style capitals, with gold date panels over a Klimt painting.
references.summary: A framed logo of squared, stacked capitals and gold date panels over a full-width Klimt painting. Tokyo and Osaka, 2019.

source.label: artexhibition.jp: ウィーン・モダン クリムト、シーレ 世紀末への道

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. Nothing covers the page. The exhibition closed in December 2019; the site is kept as an archive. The measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: the logo and the gold date panels are drawn in the Secession manner, but most of the viewport is a painting and the navigation is an ordinary dark bar.

context: The exhibition “Vienna on the Path to Modernism” (ウィーン・モダン クリムト、シーレ 世紀末への道) ran at the National Art Center, Tokyo, from 24 April to 5 August 2019, and at the National Museum of Art, Osaka, from 27 August to 8 December 2019. [The National Art Center, Tokyo](https://www.nact.jp/exhibition_special/2019/wienmodern2019/).
observed: At the upper left, the English title “VIENNA ON THE PATH TO MODERNISM” is set in a thin-ruled rectangle: “VIENNA” across the top, “ON”, “THE”, “PATH”, and “TO” stacked in narrow columns, and “MODERNISM” across the bottom, with small dots between words.
The capitals are thin and geometric; the O of “MODERNISM” is drawn small and raised, as in Secession lettering.
Beside it, the Japanese title sits in a second ruled box of the same height.
The background is Klimt’s painting Pallas Athene (1898), cropped to the full width, with a gold helmet and a dark blue ground.
At the lower right, two panels in gray and gold give the Osaka and Tokyo dates in large serif figures, each with a small checkered square at one corner.
A gold rule strip runs across the upper left, and a dark bar with a gold-outlined ticket button carries the navigation at the bottom.
interpretation: The site uses the style as a brand for the exhibition: the lettering, the ruled boxes, the gold, and the small checkered corners come from Secession graphics, and the rest is a standard museum layout.

Measured: square corners (radius 0), one hue, no heading tracking, and a surface pattern share of 0.19 pass. Most text is Japanese, so `type.uppercaseShare` (0.03) does not apply, and the text is not centered (`type.centerShare` 0.19).
borrow: Stack short words in narrow columns inside a ruled rectangle, with full-width words above and below, to make a square title block.
Mark the corner of an information panel with a small checkered square.

images.alt: Exhibition home page: Klimt’s gold-helmeted Pallas Athene fills the screen; at the upper left, a ruled box of stacked thin capitals reads Vienna on the Path to Modernism beside the Japanese title; gold and gray date panels sit at the lower right above a dark navigation bar.
images.caption: First viewport of [artexhibition.jp/wienmodern2019](https://artexhibition.jp/wienmodern2019/), captured 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the exhibition organizers; the painting image is credited on the page to Wien Museum / Foto Peter Kainz. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Voysey block-printed silk bed cover
references.lede: A bed cover by C. F. A. Voysey with rows of mirrored orange flowers on blue, held in a cream scroll lattice and edged by denser borders.
references.summary: Mirrored orange flowers and cream scrolls on blue, with patterned side borders. C. F. A. Voysey, designed about 1888.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Bed cover, LACMA AC1995.250.46

creator.name: C. F. A. Voysey (designer); G. P. and J. Baker, Ltd.

evidence.note: Inspected the Los Angeles County Museum of Art image of AC1995.250.46 through its [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bed_cover_LACMA_AC1995.250.46.jpg) (1536 × 2032 px; viewed at 1280 px wide). LACMA’s own collection page was not opened; the object data come from the Commons record.

styles.note: A Voysey textile with a flat, outlined, mirrored repeat on a lattice, in indigo, orange, and cream.

context: LACMA dates it England, about 1895, designed about 1888, block-printed silk, 234.95 × 177.8 cm, Gift of Ellen and Max Palevsky, and names Voysey and G. P. and J. Baker, Ltd. [Commons record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bed_cover_LACMA_AC1995.250.46.jpg).

Wikipedia notes that many of Voysey’s patterns rely on rhythmically contrasted areas of flat, clear colour bounded by dark or pale outlines, with plants and birds as the positive shapes. [Wikipedia: C. F. A. Voysey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._F._A._Voysey).
Commons files the image under Art Nouveau patterns as well as Voysey textiles.
observed: The central field has a medium blue ground covered by horizontal rows of orange tulip-like flowers, each pair mirrored across a vertical axis.
Round orange seed heads alternate with the flowers.
Cream stems curl into symmetrical scrolls and figure-eight knots between the rows.
A side border on each edge has a denser cream interlace with orange pods, separated from the field by thin orange lines.
Motifs have flat fills and dark or pale outlines, without shading. The silk shows creases and some fading.
interpretation: The work fits the rubric’s flat, symmetrical, lattice-based repeat. The orange and blue are lighter and warmer than Morris’s madder and indigo.
The curling scrolls explain why Commons also files it under Art Nouveau: the curves are there, but each is mirrored and locked into rows.
borrow: Mirror each motif pair and stack the pairs in rows to keep a lively curve static.
Edge a field with a narrower, denser border and separate the two with a thin line in the accent colour.

images.alt: Block-printed silk bed cover with a blue ground, rows of mirrored orange tulip-like flowers and round seed heads joined by cream scrolling stems, and a denser cream-and-orange border down each side.
images.caption: C. F. A. Voysey for G. P. and J. Baker, bed cover, designed about 1888, printed about 1895. Los Angeles County Museum of Art, AC1995.250.46. [Commons copy of the LACMA image](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bed_cover_LACMA_AC1995.250.46.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons tags the image {{PD-LACMA}}, LACMA’s public-domain image release. Voysey died in 1941, so his designs entered the public domain in the United Kingdom at the end of 2011; the work was made before 1900, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Voysey Tulip wallpaper
references.lede: A pale Voysey wallpaper in which tulips rise between huge curling leaves, much closer to Art Nouveau curves than to Morris’s static repeats.
references.summary: Cream tulips and large S-curved leaves in pale green and blue-grey. C. F. A. Voysey, 1893–95.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Tulip, Cooper Hewitt 1980-73-32 (Google Art Project)

evidence.note: Inspected the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum image of sidewall 1980-73-32 through its Google Art Project copy on Commons (2180 × 3501 px; viewed at 1280 px wide). Cooper Hewitt’s own site was not opened.

styles.note: Partial fit: flat, outlined Voysey pattern, but its long S-curves and pale colours point toward Art Nouveau.

context: The Google Art Project data on Commons give the title Tulip, the date 1893–95, the medium block-printed on paper, the type sidewall, the museum number 1980-73-32, and the credit Gift of Dr. Francis J. Geck, Cooper Hewitt. [Commons record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Francis_Annesley_Voysey_-_Tulip_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg).

Wikipedia says Voysey’s early work in wallpapers and fabrics was in an Arts and Crafts style and that he made an important contribution to the Modern Style, the British form of Art Nouveau. Mackmurdo introduced him to wallpaper design, and some early patterns use restrained versions of Mackmurdo’s swirling motifs. [Wikipedia: C. F. A. Voysey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._F._A._Voysey).
observed: Large pale-green leaves with jagged edges curl in long S-shapes across the whole width of the paper.
Cream tulips with yellow-tipped petals stand on thin straight stems between the leaves.
Behind them, a blue-grey ground is striped with thin pale lines that follow the curves.
All shapes have olive outlines and flat fills.
The colours are pale: cream, light green, blue-grey, and a little yellow. There is no red and no dark ground.
The pattern repeats vertically, but the large curves run diagonally and are not mirrored.
interpretation: This paper contradicts two claims in the prospect record: the pattern is not symmetrical, and the colours are not deep dye tones. It supports the confusion with [Art Nouveau](style:art-nouveau), which Voysey himself fed.
It still shares the movement’s flat drawing with firm outlines.
borrow: Use one very large, curling leaf shape as the structure of a pattern and set small upright flowers against it.
Build a pale, quiet version of the style from cream, light green, and blue-grey.

images.alt: Wallpaper length with cream tulips on thin stems between large pale-green leaves that curl in long S-curves, on a blue-grey striped ground, all outlined in olive.
images.caption: C. F. A. Voysey, Tulip, sidewall, 1893–95. Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, 1980-73-32. [Google Art Project image on Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Francis_Annesley_Voysey_-_Tulip_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg), public domain.

rights.statement: Commons tags the Google Art Project image {{PD-Art-two-auto|1941}}: a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work whose author died in 1941. Voysey’s designs entered the public domain in the United Kingdom at the end of 2011; the paper dates from 1893–95, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.

identifiers.commons: File:Charles Francis Annesley Voysey - Tulip - Google Art Project.jpg

references.title: Vuetify 1.5 documentation website
references.lede: The archived home page of Vuetify 1.5, a Material Design component framework for Vue: a blue hero with three raised white cards.
references.summary: A blue hero with a light-weight title, outlined buttons, and three white cards lifted by large soft shadows.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: white cards on a blue field with soft shadows, all-capital buttons, and Roboto follow the style, but the hero is a vertical blue gradient and the card shadows are larger than Material’s resting elevations.

references.notice: This is the archived documentation for version 1.5. The current Vuetify site uses Material 3.
observed: A yellow strip at the top says that Vuetify 1 has reached end of life. Below it is a white bar with the Vuetify logo.
The hero is blue, lighter toward the bottom. A large round white logo sits beside the title “Material Design Component Framework” in light Roboto.
A white GET STARTED button with blue all-capital text stands beside two outlined buttons, GITHUB and GET HELP.
Three white cards with square corners and large soft shadows show an illustration, a wireframe, and a dark terminal window, each above a bold title and centered text.
interpretation: The page measures a shadow on 45 % of its boxes, but with a median blur of 22 px and offset of 12 px, and a gradient share of 0.62 from the hero. It fails three fingerprint metrics for those reasons.
borrow: Put three raised white cards across the seam between a colored hero and the page below, so that the shadows carry the change of level.
