references.title: Whaam!
references.lede: Roy Lichtenstein’s two-canvas war comic: a fighter plane fires on the left, and the target explodes on the right under the sound effect WHAAM!
references.summary: A comic panel blown up to 4 m: Ben-Day blue sky, black key lines, a yellow caption box, and a red and yellow explosion. Roy Lichtenstein, 1963.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Tate’s image of the painting, Tate T00897 (1536 × 660 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: The canonical comic-panel painting: Ben-Day dot fields, even black outlines, a yellow caption box, and a huge outlined sound effect.

context: Tate gives the medium as acrylic paint and oil paint on canvas. [Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/lichtenstein-whaam-t00897).

The diptych was first shown at the Leo Castelli Gallery, New York, in 1963 and bought by the Tate Gallery in 1966. Lichtenstein adapted it from several comic-book panels; the main source is a panel drawn by Irv Novick for a 1962 war comic. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaam!).
The exhibition poster for the same 1963 Castelli show is [Crak!](ref:lichtenstein-crak-poster-1963).
observed: Two canvases side by side, each framed as one comic panel; the thin gap between them acts as a gutter.
The sky on both canvases is a field of small, even blue dots on white. The plane’s shadows use a lavender dot tint.
Every shape has a black outline of even weight. Clouds, smoke, and flames are closed shapes with flat fills.
A yellow caption box with a black outline sits at top left and holds hand-lettered capitals: “I PRESSED THE FIRE CONTROL… AND AHEAD OF ME ROCKETS BLAZED THROUGH THE SKY…”.
“WHAAM!” runs down the right canvas in tall yellow slanted capitals with black outlines.
The explosion is flat red and yellow with white and black; bundles of black speed lines radiate from it.
The rocket trail is a band of parallel red, yellow, and black stripes.
interpretation: Whaam! shows every device in the style record at once: dot tints, key lines, a caption box, a sound effect, and speed lines. It is the best single reference for the comic-panel branch.
The dots are used only as tints for sky and shadow. Figures, flames, and lettering stay solid, which keeps the image legible at a distance.
borrow: Split a hero into two panels with a narrow white gutter, and let one action continue across the gap.
Use one dot tint for the whole background and keep the foreground in solid flat color.
Put a short narration in a yellow outlined caption box in the top corner.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The painting is © Estate of Roy Lichtenstein; Lichtenstein died in 1997.

references.title: WikiCon Brasil 2022 visual identity figure (Isadora Pinheiro)
references.lede: A figure from the visual identity of the WikiCon Brasil 2022 conference: a woman with yellow skin, huge block limbs, and a tiny head, holding up a phone.
references.summary: Yellow skin, tiny head, giant block arms and flared red trousers, with thin black outlines. Conference identity, 2022.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: WikiCon Brasil 2022 – Ícone – Ser humano 4

creator.name: Isadora Pinheiro (User:Zaphyrza), for Wiki Movimento Brasil

evidence.note: Inspected a 1280 × 3101 rendering of the SVG from Wikimedia Commons and the first page of the [identity PDF](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WikiCon_Brasil_2022_-_Identidade_Visual.pdf). Stored the figure, flattened onto white and reduced.

styles.note: Partial fit: non-natural yellow skin, a tiny head, and huge limbs match the style, but every shape has a thin black outline, which the rubric lists as a counter-trait. It shows the outlined variant used after 2020.

context: Commons describes the file as an icon of the visual identity of WikiCon Brasil 2022 and credits Isadora Pinheiro (User:Zaphyrza) as author, under CC BY-SA 4.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WikiCon_Brasil_2022_-_%C3%8Dcone_-_Ser_humano_4.svg).

The identity PDF names Wiki Movimento Brasil as organizer, with support from the Wikimedia Foundation, the Goethe-Institut, nic.br, and cgi.br. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WikiCon_Brasil_2022_-_Identidade_Visual.pdf).
observed: The figure is about four times as tall as it is wide. The head is a small yellow circle with a black bun of hair, and one curved line marks the ear.
A white shirt forms one huge rounded arm that bends up to hold a white phone above the head; three short lines show the phone’s flash.
The trousers are two long orange-red trapezoids that flare to the floor, over yellow ankles and white shoes with thin laces.
All shapes are flat fills in yellow, orange-red, white, and black, each with a thin black outline.
interpretation: The proportions are more extreme than Alegria’s: the body is built from a few large geometric blocks. The outline and the limited palette point toward the later, more graphic variants of the style.
borrow: Exaggerate one limb into a large block that holds the key object, and keep the head as a small circle.

images.alt: Tall flat figure with thin black outlines: a small yellow head with a black bun, a huge white arm raising a phone, flared orange-red trousers, and white shoes, on white.
images.caption: “WikiCon Brasil 2022 – Ícone – Ser humano 4” by Isadora Pinheiro, 2022. CC BY-SA 4.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WikiCon_Brasil_2022_-_%C3%8Dcone_-_Ser_humano_4.svg), flattened onto white.

references.title: Wikimedia Foundation research report cover with Humaaans figures
references.lede: The title slide of a 2019 Wikimedia Foundation design research report: bold black type on the left and two Humaaans figures passing an image card in front of a pale app window on the right.
references.summary: Two flat Humaaans figures in front of a grey wireframe window, beside bold sans-serif titles. Research slide deck, 2019.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Android Microcontributions Phase 1 & 2 Findings Report

creator.name: Daisy Chen, Wikimedia Foundation Product Design Strategy

evidence.note: Inspected the 1280 × 720 rendering of page 1 of the PDF on Wikimedia Commons and stored it. Only the title slide was reviewed.

styles.note: Clear fit in use: stock [Humaaans](ref:humaaans-illustration-library-2018) figures as a spot illustration in white space next to a wireframe interface, the typical layout of tech decks and landing pages.

context: Commons describes the file as user research on what motivates and retains Wikipedia editors who use the section editor in the Android app, by Daisy Chen, under CC BY-SA 4.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Android_Microcontributions_Phase1%262_Findings_Report.pdf).
The slide credits its image to humaaans.com.
observed: The left half has a short rule and a heavy black sans-serif title, “Android Microcontributions”, with three bullet lines and the author’s name.
On the right, a pale grey browser window shows grey placeholder lines and circles like a wireframe list.
Two figures stand in front of it: one in a blue top and red trousers holds out a blue image card, the other in a red jacket and navy trousers reaches for it.
The figures have small blank heads, long limbs, and flat fills without outlines; the page is white.
interpretation: It shows the style as off-the-shelf corporate furniture: free figures added to a research deck to make it friendly, with no custom drawing.
borrow: Pair one flat figure scene with a wireframe window behind it to signal “product” without showing a real screen.

images.alt: Title slide: bold black text “Android Microcontributions” on the left; on the right two flat long-limbed figures pass a blue image card in front of a pale grey wireframe browser window.
images.caption: Title slide of “Android Microcontributions Phase 1 & 2 Findings Report” by Daisy Chen, Wikimedia Foundation, 2019. CC BY-SA 4.0. Figures from Humaaans. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Android_Microcontributions_Phase1%262_Findings_Report.pdf).

rights.statement: Released under CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons. The figures are from Humaaans by Pablo Stanley (CC0). Credit: Daisy Chen, Wikimedia Foundation.

references.title: Wikiwave 00000
references.lede: A Commons user’s vaporwave collage about Wikipedia: tilted browser windows, a glowing ringed planet, katakana, and a sunset room with a checkered floor.
references.summary: Open-licensed vaporwave collage: floating browser windows, planet, katakana, checkered floor, glitch. 2020.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1920 × 1554 rendering of the 2100 × 1700 original on Wikimedia Commons and stored a reduced copy.

styles.note: A clear, if amateur, example that uses almost every diagnostic: floating software windows, a pink-purple-orange sunset, a checkered floor, katakana, and glitch text. Chosen because it is openly licensed, not because it is canonical.

context: The file page describes it as “an example of vaporwave art,” made by the uploader and “partially based on” the CC BY-SA images of Wikipe-tan and the Wikipedia logo. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wikiwave_00000.png).
observed: Three Wikipedia browser windows float at a steep angle at the upper left, with article titles such as “Where Is My Mind?” and “Thanatos”.
A yellow ringed planet with pink spots glows at the upper right against a starry violet sky.
The centre shows a large white serif W, the katakana ウィキペディア above it, and “the surreal encyclopedia” below in widely spaced lowercase.
A room with dark columns, a glowing cyan pool, and a black-and-violet checkered floor recedes toward an orange sunset.
Two white-outlined anime girls stand at the left and right edges; “[citation needed]” repeats in cyan, pink, and yellow with scan-line and colour-offset glitches.
Film grain covers the whole image.
interpretation: It shows that the style can be applied to any institution by swapping the quoted interface; here the quoted software is Wikipedia’s own skin.
borrow: Tilt two or three stacked software windows in perspective at a corner of a hero image, so the interface itself becomes collage material.

images.alt: Violet and pink collage with tilted Wikipedia browser windows, a yellow ringed planet, a large white W with katakana above it, anime girls at both sides, a glowing pool on a checkered floor, and glitched “citation needed” text.
images.caption: “Wikiwave 00000” by AtikaAtikawa, 2020. CC BY-SA 4.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wikiwave_00000.png).

rights.statement: Released by the author under CC BY-SA 4.0 on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wikiwave_00000.png). Based partly on CC BY-SA images of Wikipe-tan and the Wikipedia logo. The Wikipedia marks are trademarks of the Wikimedia Foundation. Credit: AtikaAtikawa.

references.title: William Morris Archive website
references.lede: The University of Iowa’s edition of Morris’s writings frames its blackletter title with Morris wallpaper and stacks its main links as blocks of dye colour.
references.summary: A Morris Troy blackletter title between Morris pattern corners, a slate navigation bar, and gold, ochre, indigo, and madder link blocks.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Clear: Morris pattern bands, a blackletter title set in a revival of Morris’s own Troy type, and flat blocks in dye colours. The navigation is in sans-serif capitals.

observed: The header is pale grey. Cut-outs of a Morris floral pattern in indigo, green, and pink fill its left and right corners.
“William Morris Archive” is set in a dark slate blackletter.
A slate-blue bar holds white sans-serif capitals: POETRY, PROSE, NONFICTION, TRANSLATIONS, DRAMA, BOOK ARTS.
A red italic serif “Welcome” heads a short text in a small sans-serif.
Four square-cornered blocks stack under it in yellow ochre, brown ochre, dark indigo, and madder red, each with an underlined spaced-capital link.
A portrait of Morris with a soft shadow sits on the right, and a strip of the same pattern runs along the bottom of the viewport.
interpretation: The measurement names the title font “Morris Troy”, a digital revival of the Kelmscott Press’s Troy type.

Measured: two hues, accent chroma 0.40, square corners, no shadows, and an uppercase share of 0.46 from the navigation and the link blocks. The uppercase share is one reason the fingerprint now allows capitals up to 0.5.
borrow: Stack primary links as flat, square blocks in a dye palette: ochre, brown, indigo, and madder.
Use a pattern as corner or border ornament around a centred blackletter title, and keep the content area plain.

images.alt: William Morris Archive home page: a pale header with Morris floral pattern in the corners around a blackletter title, a slate navigation bar with white capitals, four stacked link blocks in ochre, brown, indigo, and red, and a portrait of Morris.
images.caption: First viewport of [morrisarchive.lib.uiowa.edu](https://morrisarchive.lib.uiowa.edu/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners, and the pattern images belong to their rights holders. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: William Morris Society in the United States website
references.lede: A standard modern template with one Morris wallpaper panel behind a framed portrait and a serif capital heading.
references.summary: A Morris floral wallpaper panel, a framed portrait, serif capitals, and a white card with a soft shadow.

creator.name: William Morris Society in the United States

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens.

styles.note: Borderline: a Morris wallpaper panel and serif capitals, but the layout is a modern template with soft shadows and spaced sans-serif labels.

observed: A Morris floral wallpaper in sage, cream, and yellow fills a panel on the left third of the page.
A black-and-white photograph of Morris sits in a thick white frame with a soft drop shadow, overlapping the panel.
On the right, a white card on light grey holds a small spaced-capital label in salmon, “WILLIAM MORRIS” in large dark serif capitals, and body text in a sans-serif.
The “ABOUT US” button is slate blue with spaced white capitals and a soft shadow.
The navigation uses small, spaced sans-serif capitals.
interpretation: The pattern is decoration beside a modern card layout. The soft shadows and spaced sans-serif labels are counter-signs in the rubric.
Measured: shadow share 0.27, one chromatic hue, and a median border of 6 px from the photo frame.
borrow: Put a wallpaper panel behind a framed image instead of using a plain background colour.

images.alt: William Morris Society in the United States home page: a sage floral wallpaper panel at left behind a framed black-and-white portrait of Morris, and a white card with WILLIAM MORRIS in large serif capitals and an About Us button.
images.caption: First viewport of [morrissociety.org](https://morrissociety.org/), 28 September 2026.

rights.statement: Design and content belong to the site’s owners, and the pattern images belong to their rights holders. Screenshot captured for commentary.

references.title: Windows 8 logo
references.lede: Pentagram’s 2012 Windows logo: the waving four-color flag redrawn as a flat, single-color window in perspective.
references.summary: Four flat light-blue panes in perspective beside a plain sans-serif wordmark. Pentagram for Microsoft, 2012.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1920 × 420 render of [File:Windows logo and wordmark - 2012–2015.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windows_logo_and_wordmark_-_2012%E2%80%932015.svg) and stored a 1600 px copy. Pentagram’s project page read on 2026-09-28; it lists Paula Scher as partner.

styles.note: Clear: the brand mark itself drops gradient, gloss, and the four colors for one flat hue, and Pentagram ties it to Metro’s “authentically digital” rule.

context: Pentagram writes that the Windows logo gained “a 3D effect with a gradient” for Windows XP and became a “pearl” for Vista, and that the new logo “reflects the sleek, modern ‘Metro’ design language”.

Pentagram: “One guideline of Metro is that the graphic or interface must appear ‘authentically digital’ – that is, it should not appear to be material or three-dimensional using gradients or effects.” The logo instead “suggests dimensionality using the classic principle of perspective”.
Commons dates the logo to February 2012, with the Windows 8 Consumer Preview.
observed: Four panes of one flat light blue form a window seen in perspective: the left panes are shorter and narrower than the right panes.
A white cross of even width separates the panes.
The wordmark “Windows” is a plain humanist sans-serif in the same blue, with no effects.
interpretation: Measured with `tools/image-traits.py`; see the measurement file. The logo shows the rule of the style at the scale of a brand mark: depth by drawing (perspective), never by rendering (gradient or shadow).
Compare the gradients and glossy orbs of the Aero era in [Windows 7](ref:windows-7-aero-interface).
borrow: When a flat mark needs depth, draw it with geometry, such as perspective or overlap, and keep each shape one solid color.

images.alt: Windows logo of 2012: four light-blue panes forming a window in perspective, separated by a white cross, beside the word Windows in the same blue.
images.caption: Windows logo and wordmark, 2012–2015, from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windows_logo_and_wordmark_-_2012%E2%80%932015.svg) (PD-textlogo).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons tags the logo {{PD-textlogo}}: simple geometric shapes and text, below the threshold of originality in the United States. It is a Microsoft trademark; it appears here only to identify and discuss the design.

references.title: Windows 8.1 Calculator app
references.lede: A Metro-style app that shows the grammar at small scale: gray key tiles, thin numerals, and one green key.
references.summary: Flat gray key rectangles with thin white numerals on charcoal, and one solid green equals key. Windows 8.1, 2013.

evidence.note: Inspected [File:Windows 8.1 Calculator.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Windows_8.1_Calculator.png) (1920 × 1080; first uploaded 24 October 2013, retaken in 16:9 in April 2022) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear for the Metro branch: flat rectangles, thin type, and color used only for the one primary key.

context: Commons describes it as “Windows 8.1’s additional Metro-style calculator app in standard mode”.
Microsoft published the Windows Calculator source under the MIT License in 2019 ([microsoft/calculator](https://github.com/microsoft/calculator), repository created 28 January 2019).
observed: The ground is a flat charcoal. Three mode names at top (Standard, Scientific, Converter) are thin type; the active one is white and the others gray.
The display is a slightly lighter gray panel with a thin green line along its top edge and a very thin, very large white “0” at right.
Keys are flat mid-gray rectangles with square corners, separated by narrow dark gaps. Digits and operators are thin white or gray glyphs.
The equals key is the only color: a solid green rectangle with a white sign.
A separate column of memory and function keys is set apart by a wider gap, not by a line.
interpretation: It shows how Metro handles a dense control surface with almost no color: one hue marks the primary action, and space groups the rest.
borrow: In a dense control grid, keep every key the same neutral fill and give only the primary action a saturated color.
Group controls with a wider gap instead of a rule or box.

rights.statement: Commons tags the screenshot as MIT-licensed, but Microsoft’s 2019 MIT release is the Windows 10 Calculator source, and I could not confirm that it covers the Windows 8.1 app. No image is stored here.

references.title: Windows 8.1 Start screen (geometric version)
references.lede: The tile grid of the Windows 8.1 Start screen, with names, icons, and pictures removed so that only the colored rectangles remain.
references.summary: Grid of solid-color tiles in four sizes on a charcoal ground, under a thin white “Start” title. Windows 8.1, 2013.

evidence.note: Inspected [File:Start81.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Start81.png) (1366 × 768, dated 2013-12-12) and stored it. Commons describes it as the Start screen “without text, backgrounds, and other non-geometric material”, so it is an edited image, not a raw screenshot.

styles.note: Clear, and the core of the Metro branch: a grid of solid colored rectangles with light type and no chrome.
Partial fit: a precursor with tiles in four sizes and narrow, even gaps, but square corners and saturated fills.

context: Wikipedia names Windows 8 as one of the products that adopted Metro after Windows Phone 7, and says that flat colored “live tiles” came from early Windows Phone studies ([Wikipedia: Metro (design language)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_(design_language))).
NN/g names Metro and Windows 8 as the main influence that made flat design popular ([NN/g 2015](ref:nngroup-flat-design-article-2015)).
observed: The ground is a flat charcoal gray. The title “Start” is set in large, thin white type at top left.
Group labels “essential” and “internet” are lowercase, light, white, and smaller.
Tiles come in four sizes: small squares, medium squares, wide rectangles, and one large square. All have square corners and are separated by narrow even gaps.
Tile colors include blue, royal blue, cyan, crimson, green, lime, purple, violet, orange-red, orange, and a dark slate.
Each tile brightens slightly from left to right and has a faint lighter edge. The effect is subtle next to the color change between tiles.
A user tile at top right shows the name “Wikipedia” and a plain white square.
interpretation: Measured with `tools/image-traits.py`; see the measurement file. The image strips the Start screen to its structure: size, color, and gap.
The faint gradient on each tile belongs to Windows 8.1. The strict no-gradient rule of this record is stricter than Metro was in practice.
borrow: Lay out navigation as tiles in two or three sizes on one grid, with one even gap, and give each destination its own saturated color.
Label groups with small lowercase words instead of boxes or rules.

images.alt: Windows 8.1 Start screen with text and icons removed: a charcoal ground with the thin white title Start, lowercase group labels essential and internet, and a grid of solid tiles in blue, crimson, green, purple, lime, cyan, orange, and slate in several sizes.
images.caption: Windows 8.1 Start screen reduced to its geometry, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Start81.png) (PD-simple).

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons tags this image {{PD-simple}}: it consists only of simple geometric shapes and short text, which are not protected by copyright. Commons also marks the Wikipedia name as a trademark. Credit: Microsoft, via Wikimedia Commons.

references.title: Windows Azure website, 2013
references.lede: Microsoft’s cloud site in full Metro dress: a faceted blue hero, large light tabs, and three solid color tiles.
references.summary: Orange, magenta, and purple tiles with white text under a cyan faceted hero, and a lime-green call to action. February 2013.

evidence.note: Captured with `tools/capture.mjs` (headless Chrome, 1440 × 900) on 28 September 2026 from the Wayback Machine copy of 14 February 2013, and inspected. The screenshot shows the first viewport; the measurement covers up to four screens. Nothing covers the page. Segoe UI is not installed on the capture machine, so text that the archive did not serve as a web font renders in a fallback sans-serif. A capture of the 31 May 2013 copy showed a blank hero and was deleted.

styles.note: Clear: square-cornered solid tiles in orange, magenta, and purple, a lime button, and a cyan hero, with large light lowercase tabs and no outlines.

references.notice: The address now leads to Microsoft Azure, which has a different design.
observed: A dark slate top bar holds the Windows Azure wordmark and a square PORTAL button.
Under small uppercase gray navigation, three large lowercase tabs read welcome, features, and case studies. The active tab is cyan.
A cyan square with the words “Free trial” and a white circled arrow fills the top right corner.
The hero is a field of blue and cyan triangular facets. The headline “A rock-solid cloud platform for blue-sky thinking” is large white type, next to a lime-green “try it free” rectangle.
Three square-cornered tiles in orange, magenta, and dark purple each hold a white title, one short line, and a white circled arrow.
The footer is plain gray link columns on white, divided by thin gray rules.
interpretation: Measured: 26% of screenshot pixels are saturated, in 3 hue groups; no box has rounded corners, and 17% of boxes have a 1 px border. The computed-style color share is only 0.03, because the tiles and hero are drawn in ways the extractor does not count as filled boxes. The white page frame casts one large soft shadow (85 px blur), so the capture fails the shadow range.
Each facet in the hero is a single flat tint, so the hero suggests depth without a gradient.

references.title: Windows Phone 7 and the Metro interface
references.lede: The 2010 phone operating system that introduced Metro by name, with a Start screen of flat colored live tiles.
references.summary: Start screen of flat live tiles in one accent color on black or white, large type, and panoramic hubs. Microsoft, 2010.

evidence.note: Wikipedia articles on Windows Phone 7 and on Metro read on 2026-09-28. The only interface image found was a 481 × 207 non-free crop of the Music + Video hub on English Wikipedia, too small to count as observed.

styles.note: The first product in which Microsoft named and shipped Metro; the origin of the tile grammar of this record.
Partial fit: a precursor with Metro live tiles on one grid, but square corners and saturated fills.

context: Windows Phone 7 was released worldwide on 21 October 2010 and in the United States on 8 November 2010. “It was designed with the distinct flat-style Metro interface.” ([Wikipedia: Windows Phone 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Phone_7)).

The home screen, “Start screen”, is made up of live tiles that link to apps, contacts, and other items and update in real time. The default theme is dark; users can choose a light theme and an accent color, and tiles appear in that color.

Metro “was formally introduced as Metro during the unveiling of Windows Phone 7 in 2010”. Its designers cite transport signage as inspiration, and it uses Segoe fonts, including a Segoe WP family made for the phone ([Wikipedia: Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_(design_language))).

The Industrial Designers Society of America gave Windows Phone 7 a Gold Interactive award, a People’s Choice award, and Best in Show at IDEA 2011 ([Wikipedia: Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_(design_language))).
interpretation: The single-accent tile grid is the most compact statement of the style: content and type instead of chrome, and color as the only surface treatment.

references.title: Wipeout 2097 graphics by The Designers Republic
references.lede: The PlayStation anti-gravity racing game whose logos, team brands, and packaging by The Designers Republic defined a techno, club-culture future.
references.summary: Futuristic racing game with a full brand system of team logos, packaging, and in-game type by The Designers Republic. Psygnosis, 1996.

creator.name: Psygnosis (developer); The Designers Republic (graphics and promotional art)

references.made: 1996 (PlayStation, Europe, 18 October 1996, per Wikipedia); PC and Saturn ports 1997

evidence.note: Based on Wikipedia and The Designers Republic’s project page. The studio’s page loads its images with scripts and returned no images to a plain fetch. No image of at least 800 px was inspected.

styles.note: A documented source of the look: Wikipedia’s Y2K article names The Designers Republic as sometimes credited with popularizing it, and Wipeout is their best-known work. Its visual traits are not observed here.

context: Wipeout 2097 was developed by Psygnosis; “the promotional art was designed by Sheffield-based The Designers Republic.” The game and its soundtrack “drew heavily on the ‘future UK’ aesthetic of the 1990s—a style defined by techno-inspired visuals and the rise of electronic music and rave culture.” [Wikipedia: Wipeout 2097](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wipeout_2097).
The Designers Republic lists the Wipeout series as a project. [The Designers Republic: Wipeout](https://www.thedesignersrepublic.com/project/wipeout).
Wikipedia says The Designers Republic is sometimes associated with popularizing the Y2K aesthetic. [Wikipedia: Y2K aesthetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_aesthetic).
interpretation: Wipeout gave the late-1990s future a corporate identity: fictional racing teams with logos and sponsor language, treated like real consumer brands. The coded, branded surface of later Y2K graphics follows from this.
It sits at the start of the period, before translucent plastic and chrome web graphics, so it counts as a precursor here.
borrow: Invent a small family of brand marks, each with its own color and code, to populate a futuristic interface.
next: Inspect the packaging and in-game graphics from an archival source (for example the V&A or a museum game collection) and add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The game belongs to Sony Interactive Entertainment (Psygnosis); the graphics belong to The Designers Republic.

references.title: Woolmark logo
references.lede: The International Wool Secretariat’s Woolmark of 1964: a skein of wool drawn as three looped bands of black and white stripes.
references.summary: Three interlaced loops of tapering black stripes on white. The Woolmark, 1964, attributed to Franco Grignani.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the AGI reproduction of the mark (1600 × 1457 px) in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Op-art line work compressed into a trademark: parallel black stripes that taper and curve so that a flat mark seems to turn. Partial fit: a single emblem, not an all-over field.

context: Woolmark says that the International Wool Secretariat announced a design competition in 1963, and that the winning design, “a stylised skein of wool”, was “the work of a Milanese designer named Francesco Saroglia”. [Woolmark](https://www.woolmark.com/industry/certification/celebrating-60-years/).

AGI attributes the mark to Franco Grignani: he sat on the jury, entered under the alias Francesco Seraglio, and won. [AGI](https://a-g-i.org/design/woolmark). AIGA Eye on Design says the mark was claimed by Grignani in 1975. [AIGA Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/the-hypnotic-mind-bending-work-of-italian-designer-franco-grignani/).
The V&A’s Riley records instead say that Bridget Riley designed the Woolmark logo. No other source checked here supports that. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1036839/).
observed: Three looped bands interlace to form a rounded triangle with a small open triangle at the centre.
Each band is made of five or six parallel black stripes separated by white gaps. The stripes taper to points at their ends.
The stripes thicken on the outer curve and thin on the inner curve, so each loop seems to twist.
The mark is pure black on white, with no outline or tone.
interpretation: The Woolmark carries Grignani’s optical research into a trademark: tapering parallel lines make the flat mark read as a turning, three-dimensional skein.
It shows how op line work can survive at small sizes when the stripes are few and heavy.
borrow: Draw a mark from a few parallel stripes that taper to points, so that it seems to twist.
Keep op motifs for icons to five or six heavy stripes; fine lines break up at small sizes.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Woolmark is a registered trademark of The Woolmark Company, and Grignani died in 1999.

references.title: Worker Men and Women: Everyone Vote in the Soviet Elections
references.titleBreak: Worker Men and Women:|Everyone Vote in the Soviet Elections
references.lede: Gustav Klutsis multiplies one photographed raised hand into a crowd of hands and sets the slogan in white capitals on the diagonal across a solid red field.
references.summary: A giant black-and-white photographed hand over a crowd of raised hands, with white condensed capitals on the diagonal across a red field. Gustav Klutsis, 1930.

evidence.note: Viewed the Art Institute of Chicago image of its copy, 2011.876 (843 × 1199 px, the size the museum serves for works not in the public domain), in a scratch folder. No image is stored.

styles.note: A canonical Klutsis photomontage poster: one red field, cut-out black-and-white photographs, and heavy condensed capitals on the diagonal.

context: The Art Institute of Chicago records the poster as color offset lithograph on cream wove paper, 119.7 × 84.7 cm, 1930, and marks it as not in the public domain. [Art Institute of Chicago](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/199171).

The same museum holds a 1930 gelatin silver print with red gouache by Klutsis, *We Shall Fulfill the Country’s Coal Debt* ([2011.872](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/199147)), which shares its title with his 1930 poster ([2011.865](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/199166)) and shows the photographic stage of his method.
observed: The ground is a solid red from edge to edge.
A giant photographed hand, cut out along its outline, rises diagonally from the lower right to the upper left and fills most of the sheet.
At its wrist, the hand dissolves into a photomontage of many smaller raised hands and faces of workers.
“РАБОЧИЕ и РАБОТНИЦЫ” runs down to the right in white condensed capitals, with oversized initial letters.
“ВСЕ НА ПЕРЕВЫБОРЫ СОВЕТОВ” runs up to the right at the lower left on the same diagonal, ending in a large “СОВЕТОВ”.
The signature “КЛУЦИС” runs vertically in small capitals at the right edge.
The only hue is the red; the photographs are black and white, and the type is the cream of the paper.
interpretation: Here red is the whole ground, not an accent, which is the upper end of the style’s range for chromatic area. The poster shows the style at its most photographic, about 1930.
The single hand that becomes many hands is the core device of Klutsis’s photomontage: repetition and scale turn a document into a slogan.
borrow: Use one full-bleed red field with a single large cut-out photograph and white type.
Set a two-part slogan on one diagonal axis, one part above and one below the image, with oversized initials.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Klutsis was shot in 1938 and posthumously rehabilitated on 25 August 1956. Under Article 1281 of the Russian Civil Code the term for a rehabilitated author runs from the rehabilitation, so his works stay protected in Russia until the end of 2026 and enter the public domain there on 1 January 2027 (see the Commons template PD-Russia-expired). The poster was published in 1930, before 1931, so it is probably in the public domain in the United States. Recheck in 2027 for tier A.

references.title: Your Turn My Turn poster
references.lede: April Greiman’s 3-D poster for a furniture design symposium at the Pacific Design Center: red and cyan type, dot screens, and wedges in a tilted, layered field.
references.summary: Tilted “Your Turn My Turn” in red and cyan offsets, dot-screen panels, yellow wedges, and a spaced “1 9 8 3”. April Greiman, 1983.

source.label: People’s Graphic Design Archive: Your Turn My Turn, Pacific Design Center event

references.made: 1983 (People’s Graphic Design Archive; the poster is dated © 1983)

evidence.note: Inspected the People’s Graphic Design Archive image (1440 × 2188), a flat photograph of one copy; the owner is not stated. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example. It has almost every trait in the rubric: tilted and stepped lines, dot screens, overlapping layers, wedges and bars, and spaced numerals.

context: The People’s Graphic Design Archive lists the poster as offset lithography, 24 × 36 in, for PDC2 Pacific Design Center / Westweek, and says it was a 3-D poster issued with glasses. [People’s Graphic Design Archive](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/738/your-turn-my-turn-pacific-design-center-event), [second record](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/1422/your-turn-my-turn-3-d-poster).
The poster names the event “The International Contract Furniture Design Symposium during WestWeek”, 18 and 19 March, Pacific Design Center, Los Angeles.
observed: “Your Turn” and “My Turn” are set in a heavy italic grotesque at a slight tilt, each letter printed twice in dark red and cyan with an offset, as in anaglyph 3-D.
Small copies of “turn” and “you” float upside down and mirrored around the main words.
A panel of coarse dark-red dot screen fills the upper left. A field of red, white, and cyan spray dots spreads over a dark panel at the right.
Yellow and blue wedges and a black diagonal band cross the sheet. A red-grey photograph of the Earth sits at the lower left.
“1  9  8  3” is set as separate numerals stepping up across the dark panel.
Sponsor lists are set small on a yellow panel at an angle; the event details at the lower left are flush left in blue and pink italics, each line stepped to the right.
“P D C 2” sits in small separate squares at the top left.
interpretation: The poster shows how Greiman’s California work adds colour and depth to Weingart’s structure: the dot screens and wedges stay, but the palette moves to cyan, pink, and yellow, and the overprint becomes a literal 3-D effect.
borrow: Print a display word twice in two colours with a small offset.
Space out a year into single numerals that step across a panel.
Tilt a small-print list as a block and keep its lines parallel to the panel edge.

rights.statement: No image is stored. April Greiman is living, so the design is in copyright. The photograph’s owner is not stated.

references.title: “$100,000 Reward! The Murderer of our late beloved President” broadside
references.lede: The War Department’s reward broadside of 20 April 1865 for Lincoln’s assassin and two accomplices, set in condensed gothics and fat slab capitals under three mounted photographs.
references.summary: Letterpress reward broadside with a pointing hand, condensed sans, and fat slab lines. Washington, 1865.

source.label: Library of Congress: $100,000 reward! The murderer of our late beloved President, Abraham Lincoln, is still at large

evidence.note: Inspected the Library of Congress photograph (cph 3g05341) through its [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:$100,000_reward!_The_murderer_of_our_late_beloved_President,_Abraham_Lincoln,_is_still_at_large_LCCN96521960.jpg) at 1145 × 1463 px. The image is a transparency of the copy in “Miscellaneous Items in High Demand” with a colour bar and gray scale beside it. LoC catalogues other copies (for example [rbpe.00000800](http://www.loc.gov/item/rbpe.00000800/)), which may differ.

styles.note: Centred lines in several wood and metal display faces, a printer’s pointing hand, and a rule, in black on paper. Partial fit: the three photoprints are not typical of the letterpress bill.

context: The Library of Congress catalogues the item as 1 print (broadside): text and 3 photoprints, 1865, and marks it “No known restrictions on publication.” [LoC 96521960](https://www.loc.gov/item/96521960/).
The broadside is dated “War Department, Washington, April 20, 1865” and is signed by Edwin M. Stanton, Secretary of War.
observed: Three albumen portraits in black-bordered mounts sit across the top, captioned SURRAT., BOOTH., and HAROLD. in small capitals.
A pointing hand engraving points at “$100,000 REWARD!” set in a tall condensed sans-serif with a thick-and-thin rule below.
“THE MURDERER” runs in a very large, very condensed sans-serif. The next line returns to a condensed mixed-case sans.
“IS STILL AT LARGE.” is set in a black slab or Clarendon capital, and the three reward lines in a wide fat slab with bracketed serifs.
Every display line is centred and spans the sheet. Small roman text in justified paragraphs fills the lower third.
Black ink on buff paper, with folds, stains, and uneven inking in the big letters.
interpretation: The sheet shows how a government notice used the commercial poster’s range of faces. Width does the work: condensed letters for the long line, a wide slab for the short repeated “REWARD”.
The photographs are an exception that marks the 1860s. Most bills of the period used small stock cuts or no images.
borrow: Use a repeated phrase in one face as a vertical rhythm, and change only the number in front of it.
Put a pointing hand before the key line instead of a colour change.

images.alt: Aged buff broadside photographed on black with a colour bar at right. Three framed portrait photographs sit at the top. Below, centred lines of black display type read $100,000 Reward!, The Murderer of our late beloved President, Abraham Lincoln, is still at large, and three reward amounts, above small paragraphs of text.
images.caption: War Department reward broadside, Washington, 20 April 1865. Library of Congress, cph 3g05341, through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:$100,000_reward!_The_murderer_of_our_late_beloved_President,_Abraham_Lincoln,_is_still_at_large_LCCN96521960.jpg). No known restrictions.

rights.statement: The Library of Congress states “No known restrictions on publication.” Commons tags the file {{PD-old-100-1923}}. It is a United States government work published in 1865.

identifiers.commons: File:$100,000 reward! The murderer of our late beloved President, Abraham Lincoln, is still at large LCCN96521960.jpg

references.title: “ACM President’s Letter: Pixel Art” (Goldberg and Flegal, 1982)
references.lede: Adele Goldberg and Robert Flegal of Xerox PARC published the term “pixel art” in a two-page letter in *Communications of the ACM*.
references.summary: The first published use of the term “pixel art”. Communications of the ACM 25 (12), December 1982, pages 861–862.

creator.name: Adele Goldberg and Robert Flegal, Xerox Palo Alto Research Center

evidence.note: Based on the citation in the Wikipedia article on pixel art. The ACM Digital Library page returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool, so the letter text was not read.

styles.note: The source of the style’s name, which the style record cites for the date of the term.

context: Wikipedia says the term *pixel art* was first published in a journal letter by Adele Goldberg and Robert Flegal of Xerox PARC in 1982, and that the practice goes back at least to Richard Shoup’s SuperPaint system of 1972, also at Xerox PARC. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel_art).

Wikipedia cites it as “ACM president’s letter: Pixel Art”, *Communications of the ACM* 25 (12), December 1982, pages 861–862, doi 10.1145/358728.358731, marked free to read. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel_art).
interpretation: The name comes from computer research, not from games. It was used for pictures edited pixel by pixel on bitmap displays like those at Xerox PARC.
next: Read the letter on the ACM Digital Library in a browser, and record what it says about pixel art.

rights.statement: Journal text published by the ACM. The Wikipedia citation marks it free to read, which is not an open license. Link and metadata only.

references.title: “Bericht Mouvement Dada”, Mécano no. 4/5, 1923
references.lede: A mock advertisement in Mécano answers the press’s question about the color of van Doesburg’s socks at the Dutch Dada evenings, with pointing hands, heavy rules, and letters that change case inside words.
references.summary: Mock notice with mixed-case headings, heavy rules, vertical side lines, and four pointing hands. Van Doesburg, Mécano, 1923.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Theo van Doesburg, Bericht Mouvement Dada (from Mécano no. 4/5)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons scan (1327 × 1769 px original, viewed at 1200 px). It is scanned from a reproduction in the book *Holland’s bankroet door dada* (Amsterdam: Ravijn, 1995, ISBN 9072768418), not from an original copy of the magazine. Text from the reverse side shows through the paper.

styles.note: Dada typography as a joke advertisement: case and size change inside words, stock pointing hands act as images, and heavy rules divide the page.

context: Commons describes the page as “Bericht Mouvement Dada”, from *Mécano* no. 4/5 White, Blanc, Wit, Weiß (1923, published January 1924), by Theo van Doesburg, tagged PD-old. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Bericht_Mouvement_Dada.jpg).

The notice refers to the Dada soirées in Holland of 1923, which van Doesburg gave with Kurt Schwitters. See [the soirée program](ref:van-doesburg-schwitters-kleine-dada-soiree-1922) and [another Mécano page](ref:van-doesburg-mecano-red-chroniek-1922).
observed: The heading “BERICHT MOuveMEnt DadA” changes size and case inside the words: large capitals, small capitals, and lowercase in one line.
Heavy black rules run under the heading and under each display line. Thinner rules underline the smaller lines.
Display lines are in several sans-serif styles: a light wide grotesque, a condensed capital line, and a very heavy bold for “DEZE SOKKEN NIET WIT”.
Four pointing-hand cuts appear: two point inward at the bold line, and two small ones stand vertically at the sides.
Two lines run vertically up the margins: “Zoo lang de voorraad strekt” at left and “20 FR. FRANCO THUIS” at right.
The page is black on white with no second color. Text from the reverse shows faintly through.
interpretation: The page borrows the layout of a shop notice and fills it with a joke, which is a typical Dada move against commercial print. The type is clean, and the disorder is in the case changes and the content.
borrow: Write a notice in the voice of an advertisement, with pointing hands aimed at the key line.
Run short side labels vertically up both margins.
Underline each display line with a heavy rule of a different length.

images.alt: Black-and-white magazine page headed BERICHT MOuveMEnt DadA, with lines of sans-serif type underlined by heavy rules, four printed pointing hands, vertical text in both margins, and the bold line DEZE SOKKEN NIET WIT.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg, “Bericht Mouvement Dada”, *Mécano* no. 4/5, 1923. Scan from a 1995 reproduction via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_Bericht_Mouvement_Dada.jpg), PD-old.

rights.statement: Commons tags the image PD-old. Van Doesburg, a Dutch author, died in 1931, so the page is public domain in the Netherlands. It was published in 1923 or January 1924, so it is public domain in the United States (works published before 1931). A faithful scan from a 1995 book adds no new copyright under the PD-Art principle that Commons applies.

identifiers.commons: File:Theo van Doesburg Bericht Mouvement Dada.jpg

references.title: “Large Stock of Dry Goods at Auction!” broadside
references.lede: A Boston shop-closing bill of 1862 that turns a sale notice into a ladder of decorated, extended, condensed, and fat display faces.
references.summary: Auction broadside with a shaded decorated headline, extended Egyptians, and a pointing hand. Boston, 1862.

source.label: Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection: Large stock of dry goods at auction!

evidence.note: Inspected the Library of Congress scan (Printed Ephemera Collection, Portfolio 69, Folder 50; 2582 × 3441 px).

styles.note: A commercial jobbing bill: centred lines, about ten display faces, a decorated shaded headline, and a pointing hand, in black on paper.

context: LoC catalogues the bill as 1 p., 30 × 22.5 cm, Boston, 1862, subject “Auction.” [LoC 2020770660](https://www.loc.gov/item/2020770660/).

The text announces that C. McCauley of Hanover Street will close out his stock at auction from Thursday, 17 July, with M. E. Brown as auctioneer. The imprint reads “Geo. B. Hamlin, Printer, 131 Hanover Street, (Opposite the Blackstone Bank,) Boston.”
observed: “DRY GOODS” is set in a decorated letter with a black drop shade, a white face, a row of dots, and a dark band at the top of each letter.
“LARGE STOCK OF” and “AT AUCTION!” use a wide sans-serif capital, and a single rule closes the head.
“C. McCAULEY,” is a tall condensed slab; “No. 122 Hanover Street, Boston,” a mixed-case fat Clarendon.
“DOMESTIC GOODS!” is an extended Egyptian with very wide letters, and “AND A GENERAL STOCK OF” a small wide sans-serif above it.
A pointing hand leads into the line about accommodation for ladies.
Body paragraphs mix roman and bold for single phrases. The display lines are centred, and the paragraphs are justified.
Black ink on white paper, with show-through from the back of the sheet.
interpretation: The bill shows how a printer turned an ordinary trade notice into a spectacle with stock faces alone. The decorated headline is the only costly letter, and it goes on the product, not the shop name.
The change between wide and condensed faces is as strong as the change in size.
borrow: Spend the one decorative face on the single word that sells, and keep the rest in plain heavy faces.
Pair a small wide line with a big wide line below it as a two-step heading.

images.alt: Black-and-white auction broadside. Centred lines read Large Stock of, Dry Goods in a dotted shaded decorative letter, At Auction!, C. McCauley, No. 122 Hanover Street, Boston, and Domestic Goods! in very wide letters, with paragraphs of smaller text and a pointing hand.
images.caption: “Large Stock of Dry Goods at Auction!”, Boston, 1862. Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection, [2020770660](https://www.loc.gov/item/2020770660/).

rights.statement: The Library of Congress says that, with a few exceptions, it “is not aware of any U.S. copyright protection … or any other restrictions in the materials in the Printed Ephemera Collection.” The bill was published in the United States in 1862, so it is in the public domain.

references.title: “Men of Color, To Arms! To Arms!” recruiting broadside
references.lede: A three-sheet Philadelphia recruiting broadside of 1863 that changes typeface on almost every line, from tall condensed gothics to spurred Tuscans and expanded slabs.
references.summary: Black-letterpress recruiting broadside with a dozen wood-type faces, every line centred. Philadelphia, 1863.

source.label: National Museum of African American History and Culture: object 2012.133

creator.name: Frederick Douglass and others (text); U.S. Steam-Power Book and Job Printing Establishment, Philadelphia (printer)

evidence.note: Inspected the NMAAHC photograph through its [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NMAAHC-2012_133_001_-_MEN_OF_COLOR_To_Arms!_To_Arms!.jpg) at 1518 × 3000 px. The copy is NMAAHC object 2012.133, printing ink on rag paper, 238.1 × 117.5 cm.

styles.note: A textbook wood-type broadside: centred lines, one face and size per line, display capitals in black, and small roman text between the big lines.

context: NMAAHC describes the object as a large three-sheet broadside that promotes the enlistment of Black men in the Union Army, printing ink on rag paper, 1863, and lists Frederick Douglass as author. [NMAAHC 2012.133](https://nmaahc.si.edu/object/nmaahc_2012.133).

The foot line names the printer: “U. S. Steam-Power Book and Job Printing Establishment, Ledger Buildings, Third and Chestnut Streets, Philadelphia.” The list of signers includes Frederick Douglass, Octavius V. Catto, and William Whipper.
observed: About twenty display lines are stacked and centred, and each spans nearly the full width of the sheet.

The faces change from line to line: very condensed sans-serif capitals (“MEN OF COLOR”, “FAIL NOW, & OUR RACE IS DOOMED”), a heavy slab with bracketed serifs (“NOW OR NEVER”), condensed French Clarendons with spurred serifs (“SILENCE THE TONGUE OF CALUMNY”), Tuscan-style letters with split serifs (“VALOR AND HEROISM”), and a very wide expanded slab (“STRIKE NOW!”).
Long condensed lines and short wide lines sit next to each other, so the width of the letter changes to fill the measure.
Small roman and bold text runs as one or two full-width lines between the display lines.
Black ink on off-white rag paper. There is no second colour, no image, and no ornament except one rule above the imprint.
Ink coverage is uneven in the large letters, with grain and lighter patches, and the sheet joins are visible.
The names of the signers sit in seven columns at the foot, in small bold roman.
interpretation: The broadside shows the poster grammar at its plainest: no pictures, only a ladder of lines in which the face, width, and size carry the emphasis. Each slogan gets its own letter, so the reader scans from shout to shout.
The mix of condensed and expanded widths for lines of different length is the practical logic of wood type, which came in many widths of each style.
borrow: Stack short centred statements, and give each one its own face and width so that it fills the line.
Put one line of small text between two display lines to set the rhythm loud, quiet, loud.

images.alt: Tall black-and-white letterpress broadside. Centred lines of capitals in many different heavy typefaces read Men of Color, To Arms! To Arms!, Now or Never, Three Years' Service!, Valor and Heroism, We Appeal to You!, and Strike Now!, with small text lines between them and columns of names at the foot.
images.caption: “Men of Color, To Arms! To Arms!”, Philadelphia, 1863. National Museum of African American History and Culture, 2012.133, through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NMAAHC-2012_133_001_-_MEN_OF_COLOR_To_Arms!_To_Arms!.jpg). Public domain.

rights.statement: Commons tags the file {{PD-US-expired}} and names the NMAAHC object page as source. The broadside was published in the United States in 1863, and Frederick Douglass died in 1895.

identifiers.commons: File:NMAAHC-2012 133 001 - MEN OF COLOR To Arms! To Arms!.jpg

references.title: “ulm”, journal of the Hochschule für Gestaltung, 1958–1968
references.lede: The school’s journal, laid out by Anthony Froshaug and later Tomás Gonda: lowercase grotesque titles on pale card, with small multilingual text in columns.
references.summary: Lowercase “ulm” titles in a bold grotesque, pale grey covers, small text in narrow columns, and black-and-white photographs. HfG Ulm, 1958–1968.

creator.name: Hochschule für Gestaltung Ulm; layout by Anthony Froshaug (issues 1–5) and Tomás Gonda (issues 6–21)

evidence.note: Inspected the HfG-Archiv photograph of the issue set HfG-AR Sti M 0284 at 960 × 904 px through museum-digital. It shows issues 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8/9, 14/15/16, 17/18, and 21 fanned out. The text in it is too small to read.

styles.note: The school’s own print voice: lowercase grotesque, pale grey stock, small exact text, and documentary photographs.
Partial fit: flush-left grotesque and column grids, used with Ulm’s lowercase and very small text.

context: The HfG-Archiv record gives Tomás Maldonado as the main editor (1958–1967), Gui Bonsiepe as editor and writer (1962–1968), Anthony Froshaug as designer of the layout of the first five issues (1958), and Tomás Gonda as designer of issues 6 to 21 (1962). [museum-digital 2088573](https://global.museum-digital.org/object/2088573).

Issues 1 to 5 appeared in a square format (28 × 29.7 cm) in German, English, and French. After a break of more than three years, “ulm 6” came out in October 1962 in A4, in German and English only. The last issue, “ulm 21”, appeared in April 1968. There were 14 issues in total. [museum-digital](https://global.museum-digital.org/object/2088573).
observed: Each cover title is the lowercase word “ulm” with the issue number, in a bold grotesque, flush left near the top.
Most covers are white, off-white, or light grey card. One later issue is black.
“ulm 1” carries a wide black-and-white photograph of the school buildings, with three narrow columns of small text below.
“ulm 6” carries a grid of small black-and-white photographs.
There is no color other than black and grey on the covers that are visible.
interpretation: The journal applies the product rules to print: lowercase, small sizes, one grey family, and photography as documentation. Its grid ties it to the Swiss style, while its quiet scale and lowercase titles are typical of Ulm.
borrow: Set a lowercase title in a bold grotesque with a number, and keep all other text small.
Use pale grey stock instead of pure white.

rights.statement: The museum-digital record marks the image “RR-P” (rights reserved). Photograph by Ernst Fesseler for Museum Ulm/HfG-Archiv. Froshaug died in 1984 and Gonda in 1986, so the layouts are protected. No image is stored.

references.title: 391, no. 13: “Ce numéro est entouré d’une dentelle rose”, 1920
references.lede: Francis Picabia opens an issue of his Paris Dada magazine 391 with a mock machine drawing whose parts carry hand-lettered phrases at several angles.
references.summary: A line drawing of wheels and a crank with hand-lettered captions at several angles, a roman headline, and large serif 3 9 1. Picabia, Paris, 1920.

source.label: Gallica, Bibliothèque nationale de France: 391, no. 13, July 1920

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons copy of the Gallica scan ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Francis_Picabia,_391,_n._13,_July_1920.jpg), 906 × 1337 px original; the stored 960 px Commons thumbnail is slightly upscaled). The physical copy is the BnF copy digitized on Gallica, ark bpt6k891104w, view f9. The Gallica page itself was not opened.

styles.note: A page from Picabia’s Dada magazine: mock-technical drawing, phrases at several angles, and unrelated roman, Didone, and hand-lettered type. Partial fit: no photomontage and no second color.

context: Commons records the page as *Ce numéro est entouré d’une dentelle rose*, from *391*, no. 13, July 1920, taken from Gallica (BnF), with the license PD-old-auto-expired (death year 1953). [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Francis_Picabia,_391,_n._13,_July_1920.jpg).
Picabia published *391* from 1917 to 1924, in Barcelona, New York, Zürich, and Paris. [Wikipedia: 391 (magazine)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/391_(magazine)).
observed: The headline “Ce numéro est entouré d’une dentelle rose.” (This issue is surrounded by pink lace) is set in a light roman at the top.
A drawing in thin and heavy black lines shows circles, a crank-shaped bar, dashed circles, and a circle with a slash, like a parody of a machine diagram.

Hand-lettered capitals follow the lines of the drawing: “LA PEINTURE EST FAITE POUR LES DENTISTES” runs vertically, “FAR-NIENTE BEAU PARTI” runs horizontally, and “LA COULEUR DE LA LUNE” runs along the diagonal bar.

A block of hand-lettered capitals runs vertically at the right: “Vraiment cela m’est impossible de faire paraître ‘Cannibale’ régulièrement, c’est trop idiot. J’espère que vous accepterez pour cette fois ‘391’.”
“FRANCIS PICABIA.” is set in small roman capitals. The title “3 9 1” is set at the foot in very large, widely spaced high-contrast Didone numerals.
The paper is plain off-white, with folds, a round library stamp at the bottom, and pencil notes at top right. Only black ink is used.
interpretation: The page shows the Paris branch of Dada: the disorder comes from the joke machine and the angled phrases, not from a case of mixed type. The huge Didone numerals against the hand lettering give the clash of faces.
borrow: Let short labels follow the lines of a drawing, so the text turns with the shapes.
Set a short title in very large, widely spaced Didone numerals at the foot of the page.

images.alt: Magazine page with a line drawing of circles, a crank-shaped bar, and a slashed circle, hand-lettered French phrases running along its lines and vertically at the right, a roman headline at the top, and large serif numerals 3 9 1 at the foot.
images.caption: Francis Picabia, page from *391*, no. 13, July 1920. Bibliothèque nationale de France, [Gallica](http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k891104w/f9.image), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Francis_Picabia,_391,_n._13,_July_1920.jpg), PD-old-auto-expired.

rights.statement: Commons tags the image PD-old-auto-expired (death year 1953). Picabia, a French author, died in 1953, so the 70-year term ended at the end of 2023. French wartime extensions do not lengthen it, because 50 years plus the extensions ends before 2023. The page was published in 1920, so it is public domain in the United States.

references.title: A Psalm for the Wild-Built (cover)
references.lede: The cover of Becky Chambers’s first Monk and Robot novella, a widely read work of solarpunk fiction about a tea monk and a robot.
references.summary: Cover art by Feifei Ruan, design by Christine Foltzer, for Becky Chambers’s solarpunk novella. Tordotcom, 2021.

source.label: Reactor (Tor.com): Revealing A Psalm for the Wild-Built by Becky Chambers

references.made: Cover revealed 22 September 2020; book published 13 July 2021 (Reactor)

evidence.note: Based on the publisher’s cover-reveal post, the Wikipedia article on the solarpunk genre, and the Wikidata edition item. The cover image was not inspected, so no visual traits are recorded.

styles.note: The cover of one of the best-known solarpunk novels. The fit rests on the book’s documented genre; its cover has not been inspected.

context: Reactor (then Tor.com) revealed the cover on 22 September 2020 and credits “Art by Feifei Ruan; Design by Christine Foltzer”. The book was published on 13 July 2021. In the story, a tea monk meets a robot that wants to know “what do people need?”. [Reactor](https://reactormag.com/cover-reveal-a-psalm-for-the-wild-built-by-becky-chambers/).

Wikipedia’s solarpunk article says that in 2018 Becky Chambers agreed to write two solarpunk novellas for Tor Books, and that she published *A Psalm for the Wild-Built* (2021) and *A Prayer for the Crown-Shy* (2022). [Wikipedia: Solarpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solarpunk).
Wikidata has an item for the Tor hardcover edition with a cover-artist statement. [Wikidata Q107583570](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q107583570).
Feifei Ruan sells signed prints of the cover art. [Feifei Ruan shop](https://www.feifeiruan.shop/product-page/print-a-psalm-for-the-wild-built).
interpretation: The novellas are among the most widely read solarpunk fiction, so their covers are among the images most people meet first for the genre. A curator should inspect the cover before it is used as visual evidence.
next: Inspect a large image of the cover (at least 800 px on the long side) and add observed traits.

Consider a record for the cover of *A Prayer for the Crown-Shy* (2022), after you check its cover credits on [Reactor](https://reactormag.com/cover-reveals-a-prayer-for-the-crown-shy-by-becky-chambers/).

rights.statement: No image stored. The cover art is a 2020–2021 copyrighted work by Feifei Ruan for Tordotcom (Macmillan).

references.title: A Solarpunk tower
references.lede: Three generations tend raised beds on the roof terrace of a planted residential tower, under a canopy of solar panels on a branching steel column.
references.summary: Rooftop garden, solar canopy, and a train on a viaduct in warm evening light. The.lemonaut.ukr with Scandinavian101, 2024.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 3000 × 3329 px PNG, viewed at 1442 × 1600 px).

styles.note: A textbook scene of the style: food grown on a roof, visible solar panels, public rail, and people of several ages working together in daylight.

context: The uploader dates the file 4 September 2024 and says it was made in collaboration with Scan101 (Scandinavian101). Commons lists it in the categories Solarpunk, City farms, Rooftop gardens, and Art by Commons users. [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Solarpunk_tower.png).
observed: In the foreground, wooden raised beds hold carrots, beet, lettuce, strawberries, and dill. A watering can stands on a tiled path.
An older woman sits on a stool and holds a leaf, a child looks over the bed, and a younger woman in gardening gloves looks out over the city.
Overhead, angled glass solar panels sit on a steel column that branches like a tree and has round holes along its trunk.
At right, a tall tower has open orange balconies with plants and laundry. Its base is clad in a mosaic of blue, violet, green, and gold triangles.
Behind, a park, a train on a viaduct, and pale tower blocks stand under a light blue sky.
The drawing has thin dark outlines, flat colour with soft painted shading, and a grain texture. The light is warm and low, with orange tones on the left side of each figure.
interpretation: The image joins all the diagnostic traits of the style: plants, visible renewables, public transport, and daily life. The tree-shaped solar column is the style’s typical hybrid of organic form and technology.
The faceted mosaic on the tower base plays the role that stained glass plays in other solarpunk art. The warm evening palette shifts the style’s gold toward orange.
borrow: Put a practical task (gardening, repair) in the foreground and the sustainable city in the background, so the scene reads as lived-in.
Draw infrastructure with organic structure, for example a support column that branches like a tree.

images.alt: Illustration of a rooftop garden: an older woman, a child, and a young woman by wooden raised beds, under angled solar panels on a tree-like steel column, beside a tower with planted balconies and a mosaic base.
images.caption: The.lemonaut.ukr with Scandinavian101, “A Solarpunk tower”, 2024. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Solarpunk_tower.png), CC BY 4.0.

rights.statement: Commons: self-published work by The.lemonaut.ukr, licensed CC BY 4.0. Credit: The.lemonaut.ukr and Scandinavian101, via Wikimedia Commons.

references.title: A Tumultuous Assembly. Numerical Sensibility
references.lede: A words-in-freedom plate in which F. T. Marinetti builds a shouting figure from giant letters and surrounds it with tilted columns of printed numbers, prices, and tables.
references.summary: A figure built from huge letters, hooks, and numbers among tilted columns of tabular type. F. T. Marinetti, 1919.

source.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Une Assemblée tumultueuse. Sensibilité numérique (1995.511.2)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Met’s image as uploaded to [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Tumultuous_Assembly._Numerical_Sensibility_(Une_Assembl%C3%A9e_tumultueuse._Sensibilit%C3%A9_num%C3%A9rique)_published_in_Les_mots_en_libert%C3%A9_futuristes_MET_DP371750.jpg) (original 3917 × 3127 px; a 1280 × 1022 px rendering was inspected and stored). The physical copy is the Met’s sheet, accession number 1995.511.2, as stated in the Commons record.

styles.note: Words in freedom with the Futurist love of numbers: tables, prices, and giant digits at many angles, assembled into a figure.

context: Letterpress, 26.7 × 33.0 cm, published in 1919 in *Les mots en liberté futuristes*. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Drawings and Prints, 1995.511.2, gift of W. Michael Sheehe, 1995. [Commons record from the Met](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Tumultuous_Assembly._Numerical_Sensibility_(Une_Assembl%C3%A9e_tumultueuse._Sensibilit%C3%A9_num%C3%A9rique)_published_in_Les_mots_en_libert%C3%A9_futuristes_MET_DP371750.jpg).
The same book contains [Le Soir, couchée dans son lit](ref:marinetti-le-soir-couchee-dans-son-lit-1919).
observed: At the center, a standing figure is built from a giant black “P”, a long black hook like an arm or a mouth, the word “ANCHUZ” in heavy capitals, and a large “5” as the legs.
Inside the hook, small columns of text run along its length.
Columns of tiny numbers and words, like tables or price lists, are pasted at many angles across the whole sheet.
Large isolated letters and numbers stand around the edges: “MA”, “T”, “A5”, “M”, “Z”, “1”, “10”, “1918 918!”.
At right, letters such as “O”, “ZZ”, and “E” are set inside black discs, and a clock face appears among them.
Prices and quantities such as “50 mila”, “50.000”, “5000”, and “del 100 per 100” are set in medium sizes at different tilts.
Printed in black only on buff paper with a center fold.
interpretation: The page treats a crowd as data: the “assembly” is made of numbers, statistics, and prices, and the shouting figure at the center is a typographic puppet. It anticipates the mechanical figures of the 1920s that the style record describes.
The tilted tables show how even dense, small text can become texture and motion when it is set at angles.
borrow: Build a figure or mascot from giant letters and numbers.
Use tables of small numbers as a tilted background texture behind large type.
Put single letters inside solid circles as accents.

images.alt: Black letterpress on buff paper: a figure built from a giant letter P, a long black hook, the word ANCHUZ, and a large 5 stands among tilted columns of tiny numbers and tables. Large letters and numbers, digits in black discs, and a clock face surround it.
images.caption: F. T. Marinetti, *Une Assemblée tumultueuse. Sensibilité numérique*, published 1919 in *Les mots en liberté futuristes*, letterpress. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1995.511.2. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_Tumultuous_Assembly._Numerical_Sensibility_(Une_Assembl%C3%A9e_tumultueuse._Sensibilit%C3%A9_num%C3%A9rique)_published_in_Les_mots_en_libert%C3%A9_futuristes_MET_DP371750.jpg), CC0.

rights.statement: The Metropolitan Museum of Art released the image under CC0 through its Open Access programme. Marinetti was Italian and died in 1944, more than 70 years ago, so the work is public domain in Italy. It was published in 1919, before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States.

identifiers.commons: File:A Tumultuous Assembly. Numerical Sensibility (Une Assemblée tumultueuse. Sensibilité numérique) published in Les mots en liberté futuristes MET DP371750.jpg

references.title: Adobe Blog, “Brutalist Web Designers Eschew Rules for UX Best Practices”
references.lede: An early trade article that credits Pascal Deville with codifying brutalist web design and quotes his reasons.
references.summary: Adobe’s 2016 article on the brutalist web movement, with quotes from Pascal Deville of brutalistwebsites.com.

evidence.note: Article text read on 2026-10-02. The date comes from the URL path (2016/12/01). No byline was found in the extracted text. The embedded animation was not inspected.

styles.note: Dated attestation of the name and of Deville’s role. Partial fit: it describes both the plain and the deliberately difficult branches.

context: “One of the first people to codify brutalist web design was Pascal Deville,” creative director at Freundliche Grüsse and founder of [Brutalist Websites](ref:brutalist-websites-directory).

Deville: many designers explain it “as a kind of a minimalist movement. They want to get rid of all the creative elements and stuff you can add to a website today.” Others come from punk or hardcore culture, “where things are very rough”.
Deville also calls it a push against UX design that “has become a style that is very dominated by how Google and Apple do stuff”.
The article frames brutalist sites as “rougher, more basic — and at the same time more difficult to navigate”, which mixes in the antidesign branch.
interpretation: Good for dating and for motive. Its description of difficulty belongs to antidesign, which [NN/g (2017)](ref:nngroup-brutalism-antidesign-article-2017) later separated.

rights.statement: © Adobe. Link and quotation only.

references.title: Akira
references.lede: Katsuhiro Otomo’s 1988 animated film of his manga, set in a Neo-Tokyo of densely drawn night towers, through which motorcycles leave trails of colored light.
references.summary: The founding work of Japanese cyberpunk: a detailed night Neo-Tokyo and light trails from speeding bikes. Katsuhiro Otomo, Tokyo Movie Shinsha, 1988.

creator.name: Katsuhiro Otomo (director); Tokyo Movie Shinsha (animation studio)

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia articles on the film and on cyberpunk, read as wikitext on 2026-10-02. No image of the film was inspected for this record.

styles.note: The style record names Akira as one of the two works that set the look of cyberpunk. The British Film Institute calls it a vital cornerstone of the genre.

context: Wikipedia: “The Japanese cyberpunk subgenre began in 1982 with the debut of Katsuhiro Otomo’s manga series Akira, with its 1988 anime film adaptation (also directed by Otomo) popularizing the subgenre.” [Cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk).

The film was animated by Tokyo Movie Shinsha and distributed by Toho. Wikipedia: “The British Film Institute describes Akira as a vital cornerstone of the cyberpunk genre, along with Blade Runner and Neuromancer.” [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira_(1988_film)).

Dave Kehr of the *Chicago Tribune* praised its “animation-specific ideas: Vehicles leave little color trails as they roar through the night”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira_(1988_film)).
interpretation: Akira adds speed and violence to the night city of [Blade Runner](ref:blade-runner-1982). Its light trails are an early form of the style’s motion: light that smears as it moves.
It ties the style to Japan and to animation, which later games and anime continued.
borrow: Show motion as a trail of colored light behind a moving element, not as a blur of the whole scene.
Draw a city as a mass of many small lit windows to suggest scale and density.
next: Find an inspectable image (for example a museum-held poster or cel) and upgrade the evidence level.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The film, its posters, and its stills are in copyright. This record does not name the rights holders.

references.title: Anja Kaiser, Balance presents Siren poster, Club Culture Festival 2017
references.lede: A lilac festival poster with a sharp blackletter “Balance pres.”, wide and stretched sans-serif names, an op-art ray disk, and blurred black shapes.
references.summary: Lilac ground, blackletter and stretched grotesque type, a black-and-white ray disk, motion-blurred marks. Anja Kaiser, Leipzig, May 2017.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2019): “Acid Graphics” Are the New Psychedelia

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px image `Anja-Kaiser-Balance-p-Siren-Poster.jpg` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) published with the article, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image as the magazine published it, not a named physical copy. The caption reads “Anja Kaiser, Balance Presents Siren Poster”.

styles.note: Partial fit: blackletter, stretched type, an op-art ray disk, and flyer density, but on a light lilac ground with no chrome. Flat-color club-poster branch.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) shows the poster in its 2019 article on acid graphics, with the caption “Anja Kaiser, Balance Presents Siren Poster”.

The poster text names the Club Culture Festival, Institut fuer Zukunft in Leipzig, Laurel Halo, and The Empire Line, and lists the funders, among them the European Commission and the Kulturstiftung des Freistaates Sachsen.
observed: The ground is a flat pale lilac with a black frame.
“Balance pres.” is set very large in a sharp, angular blackletter at the top.
Performer names are set in a wide, horizontally stretched sans-serif in capitals. The date and venue run vertically down the right edge.
A black-and-white disk of radiating lines with a small checkered center sits in the middle, like an op-art target.
Motion-blurred black marks and a faint, gray 3D-rendered form overlap the type.
Small text, logos, and notes fill the lower edge.
interpretation: The poster has the typographic grammar of the trend, blackletter against stretched grotesques with an op-art figure, without its chrome or black ground. It shows that the name covers a wider club-poster practice than the chrome core.
borrow: Combine one blackletter line with names in a horizontally stretched grotesque.
Use a radial op-art disk as the central image of a type-led poster.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright. The rights holder is the designer or the client.

references.title: Anja Kaiser, Cry Baby club poster, Institut fuer Zukunft
references.lede: A Leipzig club poster in orange, black, and gray: a huge blackletter “Cry Baby”, vertical stretched grotesque capitals, and grainy silver shapes like petals.
references.summary: Black blackletter over orange and black halves, gray stretched capitals, grainy silver forms. Anja Kaiser, for Institut fuer Zukunft, Leipzig.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2019): “Acid Graphics” Are the New Psychedelia

references.made: Not stated (before September 2019). The poster gives the date “Oct 9” without a year.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px image `Anja-Kaiser-2-Cry-Baby.jpg` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) published with the article, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image as the magazine published it, not a named physical copy. The caption reads “Anja Kaiser, Cry Baby”.

styles.note: Partial fit: blackletter display type, stretched capitals, and flyer density, but flat color on a half-orange ground and no chrome. It belongs to the flat-color club-poster branch.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) shows the poster in its 2019 article on acid graphics, with the caption “Anja Kaiser, Cry Baby”.
The poster text names Institut fuer Zukunft, An den Tierkliniken 38, 04103 Leipzig, and the performers Mykki Blanco, Yves Tumor, Perera Elsewhere, and Neele.
observed: The upper half is flat red-orange and the lower half near-black. A gray vertical band at the right carries the time and address, set sideways.
“Cry Baby” fills the upper half in a very large black blackletter, with tight, overlapping letters.
Gray capitals in a wide grotesque run vertically and are cut by the edges: “MYKKI BLANCO” down the right side and other letters at the left.
Grainy, silver-gray shapes like petals or leaves cross both halves.
The line-up at the bottom is set in a heavy orange grotesque, with small notes such as “live SHAME” between the names.
There is no chrome type and no green.
interpretation: The poster shows the type side of the trend: blackletter against stretched grotesques, set huge and cut by the edges. Eye on Design includes it under acid graphics. It lacks the chrome core of this record, so it marks the edge of the style.
borrow: Set one huge blackletter word against a vertical stretched grotesque, and let both run off the edges.
