Split the ground into two flat halves and let the display type cross the split.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright. The rights holder is the designer or the client.

references.title: Apple Event September 2019: iPhone 11 Pro display slide
references.lede: An early Apple summary slide that already uses a grid of tiles in mixed sizes, but with square corners.
references.summary: Square-cornered dark tiles of mixed sizes with large figures and words, behind a presenter on stage. September 2019.

source.label: Apple Summary Slides (fan archive): Apple Event September 2019

evidence.note: Inspected the 1920 × 1080 WebP `[Apple Event September 2019]-[iPhone]-[iPhone 11 Pro (1)].webp` from the fan archive [Apple Summary Slides](https://apple-summary-slides.vercel.app/events/apple-event-september-2019) (Ricky Zhang), which says that all images are screenshots of Apple event videos. The copy is a frame of the event video, not an Apple press file. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit, as a precursor: mixed tile sizes, narrow gutters, and one large figure per tile, but the corners are square or barely rounded.

context: Apple introduced iPhone 11 Pro at its event on 10 September 2019. The fan archive starts its collection of summary slides with this event.
observed: The frame is a photo of the stage: a presenter stands in front of a large screen that shows the slide, so the slide is seen in perspective and partly covered.
Dark tiles of several sizes fill the screen with narrow, even dark gutters. Their corners are square or only very slightly rounded.
Tiles hold large white figures with small labels (“1200 nits peak brightness”, “458 pixels per inch”, “15%”), large words (“OLED”, “HDR”), and pictures of the phone and of abstract texture.
“Wide color” is filled with a rainbow gradient. “Haptic Touch” sits in a tile of orange and pink concentric rings.
interpretation: The content rules of the bento grid are present here, one year before Apple rounded the tiles. Compare the rounded tiles of [WWDC 2020](ref:apple-wwdc-2020-ios-14-summary-slide). The square tiles connect the form to the tile grids of [Metro](ref:windows-8-1-start-screen).
borrow: Mix figure tiles with picture tiles so that the eye moves between numbers and images.

rights.statement: Frame of an Apple event video; copyrighted by Apple Inc. The fan archive states “All rights reserved by Apple Inc.” No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple Event September 2022: Apple Watch Ultra summary slide
references.lede: A light summary slide for Apple Watch Ultra in which one product color, safety orange, carries every key figure across pale grey tiles.
references.summary: Pale grey rounded tiles and black-and-white photo tiles with large orange figures, around a central watch. September 2022.

source.label: Apple Summary Slides (fan archive): Apple Event September 2022

evidence.note: Inspected the 1920 × 1080 WebP `[Apple Event September 2022]-[Apple Watch]-[Apple Watch Ultra].webp` from the fan archive [Apple Summary Slides](https://apple-summary-slides.vercel.app/events/apple-event-september-2022) (Ricky Zhang), which says that all images are screenshots of Apple event videos. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear: rounded tonal tiles of many sizes with one fact each, and one accent color for the figures.

context: Apple introduced Apple Watch Ultra at its event on 7 September 2022, the same event as the [iPhone 14 Pro slide](ref:apple-event-2022-iphone-14-pro-summary-slide).
observed: Pale grey tiles with large rounded corners sit on an off-white ground with narrow even gutters. About twenty tiles range from small pills (“ECG”, “LTE”, “Blood oxygen”) to a tall central tile with three views of the watch.
Key figures and words are set very large in bold orange: “60 hrs battery life”, “GPS”, “2000 nits”, “EN13319”. Labels are small and black.
Four tiles are black-and-white photographs (mountains, divers, a storm) with the orange figure set over the photo.
“WR100” and “MIL-STD 810” are set in a monospaced face, in blue and in black with orange.
Product photos of the watch and its bands are cropped by the tile edges.
interpretation: The slide shows how the look takes a brand accent: the tiles stay neutral, and one product color marks every figure. The black-and-white photo tiles keep the accent the only color on the slide.
borrow: Choose one accent from the product and use it only for figures and key words.
Desaturate photo tiles so that the accent figure on them stays the strongest color.

rights.statement: Frame of an Apple event video; copyrighted by Apple Inc. The fan archive states “All rights reserved by Apple Inc.” No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple Event September 2022: iPhone 14 Pro summary slide
references.lede: The dark version of Apple’s summary grid for iPhone 14 Pro, with a large product tile in the middle and violet gradient type.
references.summary: Near-black rounded tiles on black around a large purple iPhone 14 Pro, with violet gradient headings. September 2022.

source.label: Apple Summary Slides (fan archive): Apple Event September 2022

evidence.note: Inspected the 1920 × 1080 WebP `[Apple Event September 2022]-[iPhone]-[iPhone 14 Pro].webp` from the fan archive [Apple Summary Slides](https://apple-summary-slides.vercel.app/events/apple-event-september-2022) (Ricky Zhang), which says that all images are screenshots of Apple event videos. The copy is a frame of the event video, not an Apple press file. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear: the dark variant of the core look, often cited as the model for the bento trend.

context: Apple introduced iPhone 14 Pro at its event on 7 September 2022. Deck.gallery lists the Apple Event Product Summary 2022 among four Apple bento decks ([Deck.gallery](https://www.deck.gallery/blog/apple-bento-grid-decks-roundup/)).
observed: The ground is black and the tiles are a slightly lighter near-black, with large rounded corners and narrow even gutters.
About twenty tiles of different sizes fill the frame. The largest tile, in the center, shows the top of a deep purple iPhone 14 Pro with its camera, cropped by the tile edge.
Several key words are set large in bold type filled with a violet or blue gradient: “ProMotion”, “Always-On display”, “Ultra Wide”, “48MP”, “Action mode”.
Smaller tiles carry white labels with one image each: a green battery ring, a MagSafe charger, four phone colors, an A16 Bionic chip.
Numbers appear as large blue headings with white labels: “1600 nits”, “2000 nits”.
interpretation: The dark slide shows that the look is not a color scheme. What stays the same as the light slides is the rounded tonal tile, the narrow gutter, the mixed sizes, and the one-fact-per-tile rule.
borrow: On a dark ground, use tiles only a few steps lighter than the ground and keep color for the type and the product.
Fill the key word of a tile with the product color as a gradient.

rights.statement: Frame of an Apple event video; copyrighted by Apple Inc. The fan archive states “All rights reserved by Apple Inc.” No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Materials (Liquid Glass)
references.lede: The HIG page that defines where Liquid Glass belongs: a functional layer for controls and navigation that floats above an opaque content layer.
references.summary: Apple’s rules for Liquid Glass: controls only, regular and clear variants, and a dimming layer.
references.made: 2025 (Liquid Glass section added with the June 2025 update; text read in October 2026)

evidence.note: Read the page text through its JSON data endpoint (developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials.json) on 2026-10-02, because the HTML page renders with JavaScript. The page’s example images were not inspected.

styles.note: The primary written source for the style’s rules: glass only on the control layer, two variants, and legibility measures.

context: “Liquid Glass forms a distinct functional layer for controls and navigation elements — like tab bars and sidebars — that floats above the content layer.” Content can “scroll and peek through from beneath these elements”.

“Don’t use Liquid Glass in the content layer.” The exception is transient controls such as sliders and toggles, which take on the glass look while a person uses them. “Use Liquid Glass effects sparingly.”

The regular variant “blurs and adjusts the luminosity of background content”. The clear variant “is highly translucent” and is for components over photos and videos. Over bright content, “consider adding a dark dimming layer of 35% opacity”.

Standard materials (blur, vibrancy, and blending modes) stay in use for structure in the content layer, beneath the glass. All quotes: [Apple HIG: Materials](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials).
interpretation: The rule that glass belongs only to controls is what separates the style from glassmorphism, where glass cards carry the content.
borrow: Choose the glass variant by what sits behind it: regular over text and mixed content, clear only over media, with a dimming layer when the media is bright.

rights.statement: Apple documentation; copyrighted. Quoted briefly. No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple Icon Composer
references.lede: Apple’s 2025 tool for building layered app icons from Liquid Glass, with controls for specular light, blur, translucency, and shadow.
references.summary: Apple’s icon tool, which exposes the glass material as sliders. 2025.

evidence.note: Inspected the Apple Newsroom image Apple-WWDC25-Liquid-Glass-Icon-Composer-250609 (1960 × 1102, large_2x variant) in a scratchpad copy. A press render. Not stored.

styles.note: Names the parts of the material in its own interface: specular, blur, translucency, dark, and shadow, applied to stacked layers.

context: Apple: Icon Composer annotates “layers for multiple rendering modes, with advanced features that include blurring, adjusting translucency, testing specular highlights, and previewing icons in various tints”. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/06/apple-supercharges-its-tools-and-technologies-for-developers/).

Apple: “the Dock, app icons, and widgets have all been crafted from multiple layers of Liquid Glass … with specular highlights”. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/06/apple-introduces-a-delightful-and-elegant-new-software-design/).
observed: A Mac window with three parts over a blue wave wallpaper: a layer list on the left, a large preview of the Podcasts icon in the middle, and an inspector on the right.
The icon is built from stacked translucent layers: a blue rounded square, two pale rings, and a white figure. Each layer has a lit rim, and the rings show the blue square through them.
The inspector has a “Liquid Glass” group with Mode (Individual), Specular (on), Blur 21.8 %, Translucency 50 %, Dark 42 %, and Shadow (Neutral, 50 %).
The toolbar is a row of separate capsules: appearance toggle, grid, light angle (34°), and zoom (50 %). Small previews at the bottom show the icon in default, dark, and mono looks.
The sidebar and inspector are light, translucent panels inset in the window with rounded corners.
interpretation: The tool turns the material into a short list of parameters with a single light direction. This is close to how a CSS version must work: a fill, a blur, a highlight angle, and a shadow.
borrow: Fix one light angle for the whole interface, and place every specular highlight on the edge that faces it.

rights.statement: Apple press image of copyrighted software and icons. No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple Music on macOS Tahoe 26
references.lede: The Music app in macOS Tahoe 26: opaque album content under a floating glass sidebar and a floating glass player bar.
references.summary: Album art runs under a floating glass sidebar and player capsule. Apple, 2025.

evidence.note: Inspected the Apple Newsroom image Apple-WWDC25-macOS-Tahoe-26-Apple-Music-250609 (1960 × 1306, large_2x variant) in a scratchpad copy. A press render. Not stored.

styles.note: A clear case of the two layers: opaque content, with glass only on the sidebar, the player controls, and the Dock.

context: Apple: in macOS Tahoe 26 “the Dock, sidebars, and toolbars have been refined, bringing greater focus to a user’s content”. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/06/macos-tahoe-26-makes-the-mac-more-capable-productive-and-intelligent-than-ever/).

The HIG: Liquid Glass “forms a distinct functional layer for controls and navigation elements — like tab bars and sidebars — that floats above the content layer”. [Apple HIG: Materials](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/materials).
observed: A MacBook screen with a blue wave wallpaper, a transparent menu bar, and glass calendar and weather widgets on the desktop.
The Music window is opaque white with a large black “Home” title and rows of square album art with rounded corners.
The sidebar is a separate rounded panel inset inside the window, lighter than the content, with a faint pink and blue glow from the content beside it. Its selected item is a grey capsule.
A white player capsule floats over the lower row of album art, inset from the window edges. The art shows faintly through its edges.
The Dock is a long glass strip inset from the screen edge, with a lit upper rim.
interpretation: Here the glass is quiet. The style shows mainly in the floating, inset shapes and the content that runs under them, not in strong transparency.
borrow: Float the media player as a capsule above the scrolling content instead of docking it as a full-width bar.

rights.statement: Apple press image of copyrighted software and third-party album art. No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple WWDC 2020: iOS 14 summary slide
references.lede: The keynote slide that summarizes iOS 14 as a grid of rounded dark tiles around a large gradient “iOS” tile.
references.summary: Rounded dark grey tiles of many sizes on black, one feature each, around a central gradient iOS tile. WWDC 2020.

source.label: Apple Summary Slides (fan archive): Apple WWDC 2020

evidence.note: Inspected the 1920 × 1080 WebP `[WWDC 2020]-[iPhone]-[iOS 14].webp` from the fan archive [Apple Summary Slides](https://apple-summary-slides.vercel.app/events/wwdc-2020) (Ricky Zhang), which says that all images are screenshots of Apple event videos. The copy is a frame of the event video, not an Apple press file. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear and early: rounded tiles of many sizes fill one grid with even gutters, one feature per tile, with the main tile in the center.

context: Apple held WWDC 2020 online from 22 June 2020 and announced iOS 14 in the keynote. The fan archive files the slide under that event.
iOS 14 itself introduced home-screen widgets in small, medium, and large sizes; one tile of the slide shows them.
observed: The ground is black. About fifteen tiles in dark grey fill the frame, with narrow even gutters and large rounded corners.
Tiles differ in size: a wide central tile, tall tiles at the right, and small squares at the left. The tiles line up on shared column and row edges.
The central tile is filled with an orange, pink, and violet gradient and carries a large white “iOS” in a bold sans-serif.

Each other tile shows one feature as an icon, an interface fragment, or a product illustration, with a short white label at the bottom: “Translate app”, “App Clips”, “Car keys”, “App Library”, “Widgets on the Home Screen”.
There are no outlines and no visible shadows. Tiles differ from the ground only by tone.
interpretation: This slide already has every trait of the core look, two years before design articles named it. The dark tile on a black ground is the night version of the light grey slides that followed.
borrow: Put the product name in the center tile and let feature tiles of mixed sizes surround it.
Label each tile with one short line at the bottom, centered under its picture.

rights.statement: Frame of an Apple event video; copyrighted by Apple Inc. The fan archive states “All rights reserved by Apple Inc.” No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple WWDC 2022: iOS 16 summary slide
references.lede: The light version of Apple’s keynote summary grid: pale grey rounded tiles on an off-white ground, with device mockups cut off by the frame.
references.summary: Pale grey rounded tiles and phone mockups of mixed sizes on off-white, one feature each. WWDC 2022.

source.label: Apple Summary Slides (fan archive): Apple WWDC 2022

evidence.note: Inspected the 1920 × 1080 WebP `[WWDC 2022]-[iPhone]-[iOS 16].webp` from the fan archive [Apple Summary Slides](https://apple-summary-slides.vercel.app/events/wwdc-2022) (Ricky Zhang), which says that all images are screenshots of Apple event videos. The copy is a frame of the event video, not an Apple press file. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear: the light variant of the core look, with tonal tiles on a pale ground and mixed sizes on one grid.

context: Apple announced iOS 16 in the WWDC 2022 keynote on 6 June 2022. Deck.gallery compares the WWDC 22 product highlights with other Apple summary decks ([Deck.gallery](https://www.deck.gallery/blog/apple-bento-grid-decks-roundup/)).
observed: The ground is an off-white. Tiles are a slightly darker pale grey with large rounded corners and narrow even gutters.

Five columns of different widths hold tiles of different heights. Large iPhone mockups run off the top and bottom edges of the frame and are labeled with a heading outside the device (“Live Activities”, “Notification views”, “Multilayered photo effect”).
A central tile carries a large white “iOS” on a blue, green, and yellow gradient. One tile in the top row is black with a colored-confetti pattern and the white “Pay Later” logo.
Labels are short, in a dark sans-serif, centered at the top of each tile: “Next generation of CarPlay”, “Quick Note”, “Redesigned Home app”.
Icons are simple and colored: a yellow note, a green field, an orange house, a blue-green shield.
interpretation: The light ground and pale grey tiles are the version that Apple product pages and most web bento grids copy. The device mockups that break the tile edge are a variation: the grid holds, but some content sits on the ground.
borrow: On a light ground, separate tiles by a small step in grey, not by lines or shadows.
Let one or two large device images span several rows and sit on the ground between tiles.

rights.statement: Frame of an Apple event video; copyrighted by Apple Inc. The fan archive states “All rights reserved by Apple Inc.” No image is stored here.

references.title: Apple WWDC 2022: M2 chip summary slide
references.lede: A specification slide in which every tile holds one large number in gradient type around a central image of the chip.
references.summary: Pale grey rounded tiles with very large orange-to-violet numbers around a dark M2 chip. WWDC 2022.

source.label: Apple Summary Slides (fan archive): Apple WWDC 2022

evidence.note: Inspected the 1920 × 1080 WebP `[WWDC 2022]-[Mac]-[Apple M2 Chip].webp` from the fan archive [Apple Summary Slides](https://apple-summary-slides.vercel.app/events/wwdc-2022) (Ricky Zhang), which says that all images are screenshots of Apple event videos. The copy is a frame of the event video, not an Apple press file. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear: the number-per-tile form of the core look, with very large figures and short labels in tiles of mixed sizes.

context: Apple announced the M2 chip in the WWDC 2022 keynote on 6 June 2022. Deck.gallery describes the smallest tiles of these decks as holding specs such as “chip names, screen sizes, battery hours” ([Deck.gallery](https://www.deck.gallery/blog/apple-bento-grid-decks-roundup/)).
observed: Pale grey rounded tiles on an off-white ground, with narrow even gutters. The tiles form a symmetrical grid: a large central square, wide tiles at the outer edges, and small squares in pairs.
The central tile shows a black square chip with the Apple logo and “M2” in silver, with an orange, pink, and violet glow around it.
Almost every other tile holds one figure set very large in a bold sans-serif: “24GB”, “40%”, “15.8 trillion”, “18%”, “35%”, “20 billion”, “100GB/s”.

The figures and some headings are filled with a gradient that runs from orange at the left of the slide to pink and violet at the right. The small labels under them are dark grey or black and much smaller.
Two tiles show simple line drawings of CPU and GPU cores in the same gradient colors.
interpretation: This is the slide that the type marker of the record describes: the figure is the content, and its size states its importance. The gradient type is the only ornament.
borrow: Set one figure per tile at five to ten times the label size, with the unit attached (GB, %, GB/s).
Run one gradient across all figures on the slide, so that the color moves with position, not with the tile.

rights.statement: Frame of an Apple event video; copyrighted by Apple Inc. The fan archive states “All rights reserved by Apple Inc.” No image is stored here.

references.title: ASDF Graphics, “Acid Font – Acid Graphics Typography”
references.lede: A commercial display typeface sold under the name “acid graphics typography”, shown in acid yellow-green on black with spiky, wide, sharp-cut letters.
references.summary: Sharp, wide, spiky display letters in acid yellow-green on black, with stars and rings. ASDF Graphics, specimen dated MMXXI.

source.label: MasterBundles: ACID FONT – ACID GRAPHICS TYPOGRAPHY

references.made: The specimen reads “MMXXI” (2021). MasterBundles gives the listing date as 24 February 2023.

evidence.note: Inspected the first product image (`acid-font-screenshoot-1--569.jpg`, 1820 × 1214 px) from the MasterBundles page in a scratch folder. Not stored. The Creative Market listing of the same font returned HTTP 403.

styles.note: The trend name used as a product label. The specimen shows the market version of the style: acid green on black, sharp spiky letters, curved text, stars, and dense small text.

context: MasterBundles lists the product under Fonts › Blackletter, as “ACID FONT – ACID GRAPHICS TYPOGRAPHY”, created by ASDF Graphics, with OTF files. [MasterBundles](https://masterbundles.com/asdf-graphics/acid-font-acid-graphics-typography/).
The same title appears on Creative Market and Creative Fabrica, which shows that “acid graphics” works as a market label for this kind of face.
observed: The ground is near-black with a grainy noise texture.
All type and ornament are in one acid yellow-green.
The word “ACID” is set large in the center in wide letters with sharp, angled cuts and spurs. Two outline copies sit above and below it.
“A DISPLAY TYPEFACE” runs around an arch on a curved baseline.
Long, thin four-point stars, circular rose ornaments, chains of rings, and checkered bars fill the corners and margins.
Small blocks of justified capitals sit in the upper corners.
A photograph of a Baroque ceiling fresco fills the arch behind the type.
interpretation: The specimen is a stock version of the style: one acid green on black, spiky letters, ornaments, and dense micro text. It does not use chrome. The name on the product is evidence that the label is in commercial use.
borrow: Set a secondary line on a curved path around the main image.
Fill the margins with small spiky stars and ring chains in the accent color.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The font and its product images are commercial and in copyright (ASDF Graphics). The background photograph shows a third-party fresco.

references.title: Astro Motel sign, Fresno
references.lede: A motel sign on Fresno’s Motel Drive: a spire topped by a ring with radiating spikes, over a panel with “astro” in neon script and “MOTEL” in tube capitals.
references.summary: A tapering spire with an orbit ring and spikes over a script-and-capitals neon panel with upswept ends. Fresno, California, photographed 1987.

source.label: Library of Congress: John Margolies, Astro Motel sign, Motel Drive, Fresno, California, 1987

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected John Margolies’s 1987 color slide, Library of Congress LC-MA05-1478, 702 × 1024 px, in a scratchpad. Not stored.

styles.note: A space-age motel sign: a spire, an orbit ring with star spikes, a panel with upswept ends, and a name in neon script over tube capitals.

context: The Library of Congress record gives only the title, the date of the photograph (1987), and the Margolies category “Motel signs.” It does not date or attribute the sign. [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2017703592/).
observed: A tall tapering spire, lined with rows of bulbs on one edge, rises from a stuccoed base.
At the top, a ring seen almost edge-on surrounds a frame of crossed bars, and thin spikes radiate from the ring like a starburst or an orbit diagram.
The main panel is dark maroon with pale tube lettering: “astro” in a connected lowercase script with a long cross-stroke, and “MOTEL” below it in wide capitals drawn as double-line tubes.
Pale wings at both ends of the panel slope up and out, so the top edge is wider than the base.
The whole sign stands against a deep blue sky; the sign colors are pale pink, maroon, and cream. The neon is not lit.
interpretation: The ring and spikes combine the orbit of the atom symbol with a starburst: one compact space-age emblem at the top of a pylon, read from far down the road.
borrow: Pair one script word with a second word in wide capitals, both drawn as double-line outlines.
Flare the ends of a sign panel up and out, so the top edge is longer than the base.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Margolies photograph has “No known restrictions on publication” (Library of Congress), but the Library notes that works shown in the photographs may have their own rights. The sign is the main subject and its designer, date, and copyright status are unknown. If it was erected before 1978 without a copyright notice it is probably in the public domain; this was not checked.

references.title: Bento (bento.me) link-in-bio pages
references.lede: A Berlin web app of 2022–2026 that let anyone build a personal page as a grid of rounded tiles in several sizes, and took its name from the layout.
references.summary: Personal link pages made of rounded white tiles in mixed sizes beside a profile column. Bento, Berlin, 2023.

source.label: Tech.eu: Sequoia-backed Bento boxed up by Linktree (Dan Taylor, 2023-06-06)

references.made: 2022–2026 (founded 2022, public launch February 2023 according to Tech.eu; shut down 2026-02-13)

evidence.note: Inspected the Wayback Machine copy of the co-founder’s page [bento.me/selim of 2023-09-27](https://web.archive.org/web/20230927080251/https://bento.me/selim), captured at 1440 × 900 on 2026-10-02. Only the first screen was inspected. An archived copy of [bento.me/bento](https://web.archive.org/web/20230319014443/https://bento.me/bento) shows only “No profile found” and was not used. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear for the layout: tiles of several sizes with large radii and wide even gaps. The tiles have a hairline edge and a faint shadow, which the core look omits.

context: Tech.eu reports that Bento was founded in Berlin in 2022, backed by Sequoia’s Arc programme, launched publicly in February 2023, and was acquired by Linktree in June 2023, with the whole team joining Linktree.

AlternativeTo reported on 2025-12-21 that Bento would shut down on 2026-02-13 and that its links would redirect to Linktree ([AlternativeTo](https://alternativeto.net/news/2025/12/bento-to-shut-down-in-2026-as-linktree-takes-over-and-offers-migration-path/)).

Taplink describes the editor: “You can make each block large, small, horizontal, vertical, or square”, with “almost no design settings” ([Taplink](https://taplink.at/en/blog/bento-me.html), updated 2026-04-29).
observed: The page is white. A left column holds a round profile photo, the name “Sélim” in large bold black type, and the line “Builder and bento fanatic” in grey.
The right two thirds hold a two-column grid of white tiles with large rounded corners, wide even gaps, a very light grey hairline edge, and a faint shadow.
Tiles come in at least three sizes: tall link tiles with a small icon, a title, and a grey domain; a large square photo tile; and short wide tiles with one line of text.
Section headings (“Find me on the internet ↓”, “Get to know me ↓”) sit on the white ground between groups of tiles, not inside a tile.
A small violet “Create Your Bento” button sits at the bottom left.
interpretation: The product is named after the layout, which shows how widely the word “bento” was attached to tile grids by 2022–2023. Its tiles are white on white, so a hairline and a faint shadow replace the tonal step of the Apple slides.
borrow: Offer each block in a few fixed shapes (small, wide, tall, large square) on a two- or four-column grid, so that users cannot break the grid.
Keep the identity column fixed beside the grid on wide screens and above it on narrow screens.

rights.statement: Bento software and user content; copyrighted by their owners. The profile photo shows a private person. No image is stored here.

references.title: Berlin Friedrichstraße Utopia 2048
references.lede: A bird’s-eye matte painting of central Berlin in 2048: terraced green hills over the railway, solar roofs, canals for swimming and solar boats, and an airship in a clear sky.
references.summary: Aerial painting of a planted, solar-roofed Berlin around Friedrichstraße station. Aerroscape and Lino Zeddies, 2023.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Berlin_Friedrichstra%C3%9Fe_Utopia_2048_small_file.jpg) (original 7098 × 5315 px, viewed at 1600 × 1198 px).

styles.note: A wide daylit solarpunk city: planted terraces, solar roofs, a turbine-topped tower, rail, bicycles, and clean water, in bright green and sky blue.

context: Realutopien, a project of Reinventing Society e. V., publishes the image as “Berlin Friedrichstraße Utopia 2048 by Lino Zeddies & Aerroscape, CC BY-SA 4.0”, with other “Utopia 2048” views by Aerroscape (Singapore, Landleben, Vehlefanz). [Realutopien](https://realutopien.info/visuals/berlin-friedrichstrasse-utopia-2048/).

The Commons upload is dated 6 May 2023 and describes “a futuristic, sustainable Berlin - with lots of solar power, trees and greenery, airships, walkable streets, clean water”. A Commons reviewer confirmed the license on 7 October 2023. [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Berlin_Friedrichstra%C3%9Fe_Utopia_2048_small_file.jpg).
observed: The view looks east over Bahnhof Friedrichstraße, whose arched train shed carries blue solar panels. The Fernsehturm stands on the horizon.
A hill of stepped, planted terraces with buildings rises behind the station. Two towers in the distance are wrapped in trees.
At right, a tall slab is clad in solar panels and planting and carries two vertical-axis wind turbines on its roof.
The Spree runs through the foreground with swimmers, a small solar boat, and steps down to the water. Streets are full of pedestrians, cyclists, and market stalls, with no cars visible.
Arched pedestrian bridges, a monorail-like train, an airship marked “art by aerroscape”, and a hot-air balloon fill the scene.
The palette is saturated leaf green and clear sky blue, with cream and terracotta buildings. The rendering is a detailed, semi-realistic digital painting, not outlined.
interpretation: The painting shows the architectural branch of solarpunk: an existing city retrofitted, not replaced. Historic buildings stay, and green and solar layers grow over them.
Its realistic matte-painting finish differs from the outlined, flat illustration in the style’s core, but its colour and content match the grammar closely.
borrow: Use a high, wide viewpoint over a recognizable place to show change at city scale.
Keep the existing landmarks and add planting, solar roofs, and water access around them.

images.alt: Aerial painting of Berlin with a solar-roofed Friedrichstraße station, a terraced green hill, a river with swimmers and solar boats, crowds of cyclists and walkers, the TV tower on the skyline, and an airship in a blue sky.
images.caption: Aerroscape and Lino Zeddies, “Berlin Friedrichstraße Utopia 2048”, 2023. [Realutopien](https://realutopien.info/visuals/berlin-friedrichstrasse-utopia-2048/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Berlin_Friedrichstra%C3%9Fe_Utopia_2048_small_file.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0. Existing Berlin buildings appear as part of the painted cityscape.

rights.statement: Realutopien: “Berlin Friedrichstraße Utopia 2048 by Lino Zeddies & Aerroscape, CC BY-SA 4.0”. The site’s default license is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, but this image is marked CC BY-SA 4.0, and a Commons license review confirmed it on 2023-10-07.

references.title: Blade Runner
references.lede: Ridley Scott’s 1982 film set in a rain-soaked Los Angeles of 2019, whose dark, neon-lit, high-tech but decaying city became the visual model for cyberpunk.
references.summary: The founding image of the cyberpunk city: rain, neon, giant advertising, and noir darkness. Ridley Scott, with Syd Mead as concept artist, 1982.

creator.name: Ridley Scott (director); Syd Mead (concept artist); Lawrence G. Paull (production designer); Jordan Cronenweth (cinematographer)

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article, read as wikitext on 2026-10-02. No image of the film was inspected for this record.

styles.note: The style record names Blade Runner as one of the two works that set the look of cyberpunk. Wikipedia calls it “a foundational work of the cyberpunk genre”.

context: Wikipedia: “Hailed for its production design depicting a high-tech but decaying future, the film is often regarded as both a leading example of neo-noir cinema and a foundational work of the cyberpunk genre.” [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_Runner).

Scott used Edward Hopper’s *Nighthawks* and the French comics magazine *Métal Hurlant* as mood sources, and drew on the landscape of “Hong Kong on a very bad day”. He hired Syd Mead as concept artist. Production designer Lawrence G. Paull and art director David Snyder realized Scott’s and Mead’s sketches. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_Runner).

Wikipedia notes that the film’s look, “in particular its overall darkness, preponderance of neon lights and opaque visuals”, made it a popular reference point for video games. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_Runner).
interpretation: The film fixed the core of the style’s imagery: night, rain, neon, and advertising on a scale that dwarfs people. Most later works quote it, including [Cyberpunk 2077](ref:cyberpunk-2077-video-game-2020).
Its link to film noir explains why the style is dark and lit by small, hard sources instead of daylight.
borrow: Keep most of the frame dark and let a few signs, screens, or advertisements carry all the light.
Pair high-tech elements with signs of wear and decay so that the future looks used.
next: Find an openly licensed or museum-documented still, or a production design drawing, that can be inspected, and upgrade the evidence level.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The film, its posters, and its stills are in copyright. This record does not name the rights holders.

references.title: Bosco Verticale, Milan
references.lede: Two residential towers in Milan’s Porta Nuova district whose cantilevered balconies hold trees, shrubs, and more than ninety plant species.
references.summary: Twin residential towers planted with trees on every balcony. Boeri Studio, Milan, 2014.

creator.name: Boeri Studio (Stefano Boeri, Gianandrea Barreca, and Giovanni La Varra)

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article and the Wikidata item. The only usable Commons photograph, [Milan skyline with Unicredit Tower and Bosco Verticale.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Milan_skyline_with_Unicredit_Tower_and_Bosco_Verticale.jpg) by Daniel Case (2016), shows one tower from far away, about 200 px wide in a 1600 px view. Commons holds very few photographs of the building, probably because Italy has no freedom of panorama. Another Commons file titled “Il Bosco Verticale Milano” shows only reflections in a glass facade.

styles.note: The best-known planted tower, often cited as a real-world model for solarpunk’s buildings wrapped in trees. Partial fit: it is luxury housing with no visible renewables or handwork.

context: Wikipedia: two residential skyscrapers in the Porta Nuova district, designed by Boeri Studio (Stefano Boeri, Gianandrea Barreca, and Giovanni La Varra), 116 m and 84 m tall, inaugurated in 2014. Over ninety plant species, including tall shrubs and trees, grow on the facades. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosco_Verticale).
Wikidata records architect Stefano Boeri, inception 2014, and opening on 10 October 2014. [Wikidata Q2501413](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2501413).
It won the International Highrise Award on 19 November 2014 and the CTBUH “Best Tall Building Worldwide” award in 2015. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosco_Verticale).
Architizer’s 2022 article on solarpunk architecture, cited in the style record, describes towers wrapped in planted terraces of this kind.
observed: In Daniel Case’s distant view, the tower is a dark rectangular block whose facade is broken by irregular light balcony edges and dense dark green planting on every floor. A crane stands on the roof.
interpretation: The building made the image of a tree-covered tower familiar worldwide, and solarpunk illustration repeats it often, for example in the skyline of [Berlin Friedrichstraße Utopia 2048](ref:aerroscape-zeddies-berlin-friedrichstrasse-utopia-2048).
Critics of greenwashing note that such towers are expensive housing. That is why this record calls it a partial fit.
borrow: Stagger planted balconies so that greenery breaks the outline of a rectangular block.

rights.statement: No image stored. The building (2014) is a protected architectural work, and Italy has no freedom of panorama.

references.title: Braun Cosmolux sun lamp, 1964
references.lede: A folding sun lamp by Dieter Rams, Reinhold Weiss, and Dietrich Lubs for Braun: a light-grey steel case with a square frame of tubes, hinged on a flat aluminium tray.
references.summary: A light-grey enamelled case with a square frame around the tubes, hinged on a flat aluminium base. Braun, 1964.

creator.name: Dieter Rams, Reinhold Weiss, and Dietrich Lubs, designers; Braun, manufacturer

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s primary image 2021MW4323 of object W.5-2020 at 1600 × 1201 px, through the V&A IIIF service.

styles.note: A small appliance in the Braun grammar: one light-grey finish, a rounded-rectangle frame, a visible hinge, and a tiny logo.

context: The V&A credits Dieter Rams, Reinhold Weiss, and Dietrich Lubs, dates the lamp 1964, and gives anodised aluminium, enamelled steel, and plastic. It describes five glass tubes in an enamelled steel case “hinged on an aluminum base”, metal “pierced at the bottom to prevent overheating”, and a timer dial on the right side. It came as a gift of Michael and Mariko Whiteway. [V&A W.5-2020](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1554431/).
observed: The case and the base are the same light grey. The case is a box with one strongly rounded rear corner.
A square frame with rounded inner corners surrounds three horizontal white tubes and a small central lamp.
The case turns on one round pivot on a flat bracket. The base is a shallow tray with a short dark foot strip.
A small “braun” logo sits on the edge of the tray. A dark socket for the cable is set into the side.
interpretation: The lamp shows the style’s rounded rectangle at small scale: one radius for the frame, one finish for all parts, and the mechanism left visible.
borrow: Use one rounded-rectangle frame to hold the working part, and leave the hinge or joint visible.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The V&A allows non-commercial use of its images under its own terms, not an open license. The design is by living or recently deceased designers. No image is stored.

references.title: Braun M 140 hand mixer, 1960s
references.lede: A Braun hand mixer credited to Dieter Rams and Reinhold Weiss: an off-white plastic body with a cut-out handle, a slotted vent, and orange accents on the switch and one beater.
references.summary: Off-white plastic body, cut-out handle, slotted vent, and orange on the switch and one beater. Braun, 1960–1970.

source.label: Victoria and Albert Museum, CIRC.343:1 to 7-1974

creator.name: Dieter Rams and Reinhold Weiss, designers; Braun, manufacturer

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s primary image 2019MA6040 of object CIRC.343:1 to 7-1974 at 1600 × 1600 px, through the V&A IIIF service. The V&A gives a date range, not a model year.

styles.note: Braun’s domestic line: a plain light housing, a slotted vent as the only texture, and orange used only where the hand acts.

context: The V&A lists Dieter Rams and Reinhold Weiss as designers, Braun as manufacturer, Kronberg and Barcelona as places of origin, and 1960–1970 as the date. It describes an “off white plastic casing” with “a rectangular gap at the top to accommodate the hand” and an end “triangular in cross section with horizontal ventilation slots”. The object came as a gift of the manufacturer. [V&A CIRC.343:1 to 7-1974](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1227045/).
observed: The body is one off-white plastic volume with softly rounded edges and a rectangular opening for the hand.
A recessed panel of parallel slots marks the vent on the sloping end.
The sliding switch and the collar of one beater are orange. The other collar is white. There is no other color.
The model name “M 140” and the “braun” logo are printed small in black on the side.
interpretation: The mixer moves the radio grammar into the kitchen: one pale shell, slots for air, small black type, and color only on the switch.
borrow: Color the control that the user moves, and nothing else.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The V&A allows non-commercial use of its images under its own terms, not an open license. The design is by living or recently deceased designers. No image is stored.

references.title: Braun RT 20 table radio, 1963
references.lede: Dieter Rams’s table radio for Braun: a white steel face, tilted slightly back, with a circle of slots for the speaker and a column of grey knobs.
references.summary: White powder-coated face with a circular slot grille, grey knobs in a column, and a red tuning line. Rams for Braun, 1963.

creator.name: Dieter Rams, designer; Braun AG, manufacturer

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s primary image 2007BR3160 of object W.13-2007 at 1600 × 1067 px, through the V&A IIIF service.

styles.note: A clear case of the Braun grammar: a white face, perforation as the only texture, small lowercase labels, and one red signal on the scale.

context: The V&A describes an “oblong beechwood box with a white powder-coated sheet steel fascia tilted slightly backwards”, pierced with slots that form a circular loudspeaker, and says the speaker is concealed “with only pierced lines to indicate its presence”. [V&A W.13-2007](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O152458/).
The record transcribes the control labels in lowercase German: “höhen, tiefen, volumen, ein aus, phono, lang, mittel, ukw, sender”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O152458/).
observed: The front is one flat white panel inside a pale wood box. Its edge folds over the top with a small radius.
On the left, horizontal black slots of different lengths form a circle, split by a narrow vertical gap.
Three grey cylindrical knobs stand in a column in the centre, with a tiny label above each. Five small grey push buttons and one larger knob form a row along the bottom.
A tall, narrow tuning scale on the right carries fine black numerals and one red horizontal line, the only color on the face.
A small black “braun” logo sits above the knob column.
interpretation: The RT 20 shows the style’s one-signal rule: grey and white everywhere, and red only where the user reads the station.
borrow: Draw a circle from parallel lines of different lengths instead of a filled shape.
Give one thin line the only accent color, where the user reads a value.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The V&A allows non-commercial use of its images under its own terms, not an open license. The design is by living or recently deceased designers. No image is stored.

references.title: Braun SK 55 Phonosuper radiogram, 1956
references.lede: Hans Gugelot and Dieter Rams’s radio-phonograph for Braun: a white metal box between wooden ends, under a clear acrylic lid, the type nicknamed “Snow White’s coffin”.
references.summary: White metal top and front, wooden end panels, a clear acrylic lid, and slotted speaker grilles. Gugelot and Rams for Braun, 1956.

creator.name: Dieter Rams and Hans Gugelot, designers; Braun AG, manufacturer

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s primary image 2006AC4504 of object W.51-1978 at 1600 × 1373 px, through the V&A IIIF service. The record names the model SK55. Other copies of the SK 4 family differ in details.

styles.note: The founding object of the Braun program and the Ulm collaboration: a plain white housing, slotted grilles, and controls set out in rows.

context: The V&A record names the object “Phonosuper, radiogram, SK55” with the other title “Schneewittchensarg (snow white coffin)”, dates it 1956, credits Dieter Rams and Hans Gugelot as designers and Braun AG as manufacturer, and gives metal, wood, and acrylic plastic, 24 × 58 × 29 cm. [V&A W.51-1978](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O168285/).

The HfG-Archiv says the SK 4 of 1956, developed by Gugelot with Rams and HfG staff, became “an icon of West German post-war design” as the “Snow White Coffin”. [HfG-Archiv](https://hfg-archiv.museumulm.de/en/exhibition/hans-gugelot-100-en/).
observed: The top deck and the front are white or very light grey metal. Two end panels are pale wood with visible grain.
A clear, flat acrylic lid spans the two wooden ends and is propped open on a thin metal stay.
The front carries three rectangular fields of thin horizontal slots for the speakers. There is no other texture.

The turntable sits in a recessed square plate on the left. On the right, three small black knobs, a row of five black piano keys, and a small white dial with a red dot sit on one axis beside a narrow tuning scale.
A small lowercase “braun” logo sits above the knobs. Edges are crisp, with only a slight rounding.
interpretation: The object replaces the wooden radio cabinet with a white instrument box. Wood stays only as two end planes, so the white face, the slots, and the controls carry the design.
borrow: Group controls into one ordered block and leave the rest of the surface plain.
Use a field of parallel slots as the only texture on a large white panel.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The V&A allows non-commercial use of its images under its own terms, not an open license. The design is by living or recently deceased designers. No image is stored.

references.title: Braun T 1000 world receiver, 1963
references.lede: Dieter Rams’s portable short-wave radio for Braun: an aluminium case with a perforated speaker panel, a dark tuning scale, and a front flap that holds the manual.
references.summary: Silver aluminium case, finely perforated speaker panel, dense rows of small controls, and one orange button. Rams for Braun, 1961–1963.

source.label: Victoria and Albert Museum, W.12:1 to 3-2007

creator.name: Dieter Rams, designer; Braun AG, manufacturer

references.made: 1963 (V&A date field); the V&A brief description says 1961

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s primary image 2007BR3164 of object W.12:1 to 3-2007 at 1067 × 1600 px, through the V&A IIIF service.

styles.note: The technical end of the Braun program: an aluminium housing, a perforated panel, controls on a strict grid, and one orange signal.

context: The V&A dates the object 1963 in its production fields, while its brief description says “West Germany, 1961”. It is an “oblong aluminium radio with drop down flap on the front, revealing dials and controls”, 24.5 × 36.2 × 13.4 cm. [V&A W.12:1 to 3-2007](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O168288/).

The V&A notes that the complex wavebands needed “a thick user manual, stored in the drop-down cover”, and that the aerials and dials give it “the character of a piece of military or surveillance equipment”. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O168288/).
observed: The case is matte silver aluminium with slightly rounded vertical edges and a black top strip with a bar handle.
A tall panel on the left is covered in very fine, regular perforation.
A black tuning scale fills the upper right with rows of small white numerals. Two large white knobs sit at its right edge, one with a red dot.
Below, five dark knobs, four toggle switches, and three round sockets line up in three rows. A column of four white round buttons ends in one orange button.
The open front flap holds the printed manual.
interpretation: The T 1000 shows that the style can carry dense controls. The density stays calm because every part sits on the same rows and columns and the color is held back.
borrow: Use a finely perforated panel next to a dense control area to give the eye a rest.
Put many small controls on a strict grid, and give color to one button only.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The V&A allows non-commercial use of its images under its own terms, not an open license. The design is by living or recently deceased designers. No image is stored.

references.title: Brutal theme (WordPress)
references.lede: Justin Jackson’s open-source WordPress theme, made to carry the plain-page ideas of his essay “This is a web page”.
references.summary: A 2016 one-column WordPress theme: monospace body, small headings, square bullets, no decoration.

creator.name: Justin Jackson, after a design by Kyle Fox

evidence.note: Read the README and `style.css` on GitHub on 2026-10-02. Repository created 27 September 2016 (GitHub API). The bundled `screenshot.png` is only 600 × 450 px, so the look is not recorded as observed.

styles.note: Partial fit: a one-column monospace page with tiny headings, but with a set font (Roboto Mono) and a fixed column instead of raw defaults.

context: README: “A brutalist WordPress theme”, “inspired by two of my essays”: [This is a web page](https://justinjackson.ca/words.html) and “I’m a fucking websmaster”. “The original design came from Kyle Fox.”

`style.css` sets `font-family: 'Roboto Mono', monospace; font-size: 16px; max-width: 46em`, `h1 { font-size: 1.5em }`, `h2 { font-size: 1.2em }`, `h3 { font-size: 1em }`, and square list bullets. Theme tags: one-column, light.
[NN/g (2017)](ref:nngroup-brutalism-antidesign-article-2017) cites Justin Jackson’s blog for “the black and blue Monospace typography often seen in brutalist sites”.
Licensed under the GNU General Public License.
interpretation: Shows how small the type scale of the style is: here the largest heading is only 1.5 times the body.

rights.statement: The code is GPL-licensed. No image is stored.

references.title: Brutalist (Pelican theme)
references.lede: A static-site theme that applies Copeland’s brutalist guidelines: readable, accessible, fast, underlined links.
references.summary: A 2018 Pelican theme written after reading brutalist-web.design. It follows the rules more than the default look.

evidence.note: Read the README and `static/css/main.css` on GitHub on 2026-10-02. Repository created 28 August 2018 (GitHub API). The README cover image shows only the theme name and the Pelican logo, so it is not evidence of the look. The demo site was not captured.

styles.note: Partial fit: it follows the guidelines of the style, but uses Lato and dark gray links instead of default type and link blue.

context: README: “After reading David Bryant Copeland’s [Brutalist Web Design](ref:copeland-brutalist-web-design-guidelines) a few weeks ago, I was inspired to try and apply those design principles to a Pelican theme.” Its stated features include “Clean, readable, accessible, and fast” and “W3C validated”.
`main.css` sets `font-family: "Lato", sans-serif` on the body and underlined links in `#232a2e`, with `#39739d` on hover.
No license file is reported by the GitHub API.
interpretation: Evidence that the guidelines travel without the default look. A capture would show whether the result still reads as [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design).

rights.statement: No license stated. Link only.

references.title: Cadillac Eldorado Biarritz, 1959
references.lede: The 1959 Cadillac convertible, remembered for the tallest tail fins of the period: sharp fins with twin bullet tail lights over a jewel-like chrome grille.
references.summary: Pointed tail fins with twin red bullet lights, a chrome grille of small studs, and jet-exhaust bumper pods, in flamingo pink. General Motors, 1959.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected two CC0 photographs of one restored car at a 2025 show by “Charles from Port Chester, New York” on Wikimedia Commons, at 1920 px: the rear view (stored) and the front three-quarter view ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cadillac_Eldorado_Biarritz_(1959)_(54801176727).jpg)). The pink paint is this car’s finish; the color is not documented as original.

styles.note: Partial fit: a car, not a sign or building, but its tail fins and jet-exhaust lights are the jet-age source of Googie’s upswept angles, which the style record names as an influence.

context: Wikipedia: the 1959 Cadillac is remembered for its huge sharp tailfins with dual bullet tail lights, two rooflines, and new jewel-like grille patterns with matching deck-lid panels. GM lowered, lengthened, and widened its 1959 styling in response to Virgil Exner’s redesign at Chrysler. [Wikipedia: Cadillac Eldorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadillac_Eldorado).
The Googie style record and Wikidata list jet aircraft and the Space Age as influences on Googie. [Wikipedia: Googie architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Googie_architecture).
observed: Two tall fins rise from the rear fenders and end in sharp points that lean back past the trunk.
Each fin carries a pair of red, pointed bullet-shaped tail lights, one above the other, set in chrome.
The rear bumper ends at each side in a large round chrome pod with a dark center and a small chevron, like a jet exhaust.
Between the pods, a wide grille of small chrome studs in rows spans the back; a matching panel sits on the deck lid.
The body is flamingo pink with a white leather interior and bright chrome trim.
Spectators and food trucks at the show stand in the background.
interpretation: The fins carry the same upswept, pointed line as Googie roofs and sign pylons, and the bullet lights read as rocket exhausts: the car is a product version of the style’s jet imagery.
It is a partial fit: the style is defined by signs and buildings, and the car has no starbursts, neon, or script signs.
borrow: End a horizontal bar with a sharp upswept point, like a fin, instead of a rounded cap.
Use a tight grid of small studs or dots as a chrome-like texture strip, not a gradient.

images.alt: Rear view of a pink 1959 Cadillac Eldorado convertible on grass: two tall pointed tail fins with twin red bullet lights, a wide chrome studded grille between round chrome bumper pods, and an Eldorado license plate. People and vans are in the background.
images.caption: Cadillac Eldorado Biarritz (1959), rear view, photographed 31 August 2025 by Charles from Port Chester, New York, CC0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cadillac_Eldorado_Biarritz_(1959)_(54802366150).jpg). The people and vehicles behind it are incidental.

rights.statement: Photograph: CC0 1.0 (Wikimedia Commons). Car: a United States useful article whose shape is not protected by copyright. Cadillac and Eldorado are General Motors trademarks, used here only for commentary. People in the background are small and not the subject.

references.title: Caribbean Motel, Wildwood Crest
references.lede: A 1958 Doo Wop motel on the Jersey Shore with a cantilevered ramp, slanted glass walls, plastic palm trees, and a rooftop neon sign in connected script with a star.
references.summary: Slanted lounge glass, a floating ramp, a C-shaped pool, and a script “Caribbean” neon sign. Wildwood Crest, New Jersey, 1958.

source.label: Library of Congress: HABS NJ-1186, Caribbean Motel, 5600 Ocean Avenue, Wildwood Crest

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected all nine HABS NJ-1186 measured drawing sheets (1997, 1024 px versions) in a scratchpad. No photograph was inspected, so color is documented, not observed.

styles.note: A Wildwood Doo Wop motel, the East Coast branch of Googie: a levitating ramp, lean-in glass, fake palms, and a neon script sign with a star.

context: HABS significance statement: a well-preserved Wildwood motel with original 1950s features, a “levitating” concrete ramp, lean-in and lean-out glass walls on the second-floor lounge, colorful lighting, a C-shaped swimming pool, and a large neon sign that required the town to liberalize its ordinances. The first owner claimed to have originated fake palm trees in the Wildwoods. [Library of Congress, HABS NJ-1186](https://www.loc.gov/item/nj1486/).

The drawings won fourth place in the 1997 Charles E. Peterson Prize. The title sheet credits Timothy Wagner, Laura West, and Donna Zarzycki of Kent State University. Its text names the style “Populuxe,” “Googie,” or “Doo-Wop.” [Library of Congress, HABS NJ-1186](https://www.loc.gov/item/nj1486/).
Wikipedia gives Wildwood, New Jersey, its own section as a Googie district. [Wikipedia: Googie architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Googie_architecture).
observed: The title sheet sets “THE CARIBBEAN MOTEL” in widely spaced outline capitals, the drawings’ own graphic, not the motel’s.
The sign detail sheet draws the rooftop sign: “Caribbean” in a connected, slanted script built from a double outline like a neon tube, with a small five-point star over the letters.
The plan is an L of two-storey room wings around a C-shaped pool with a fan-shaped deck; a curved ramp rises from the pool deck.
The elevations show a flat roof, long balconies with thin railings, and a glass lounge on the corner whose walls lean in and out in section.
Sculpted palm trees stand on the pool deck in the elevations.
interpretation: The sign detail is the clearest record here of the style’s type: a connected script drawn as a continuous tube, with a star as punctuation.
The leaning glass walls make a room into a sign, the same idea as the upswept Los Angeles coffee shops at a seaside scale.
borrow: Draw a one-word name in connected script with a double outline, as if bent from neon tube, and add one small star.
Set a slanted glass-like panel at an angle against straight horizontal bands.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The building (1958, United States) is not protected as architecture, but the drawings are 1997 student work donated to HABS, not U.S. Government work, and the Library of Congress advises that “images copied from other sources may be restricted.” Peterson Prize entrants sign a copyright release form; its terms were not checked. The neon sign is a separate work whose rights were not checked. The lead curator can upgrade to tier A if the release puts the drawings in the public domain.

references.title: Chase The Sun (G. Casqueiro)
references.lede: A frame from a short Blender animation: a cyan neon wireframe valley runs toward a glowing yellow sun under a violet-to-magenta sky.
references.summary: Cyan neon wireframe valley and peaks, yellow sun, violet-magenta sky. Blender animation, 2019.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1920 × 1080 still [Synthwave cyberspace sunset (low res).jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave_cyberspace_sunset_(low_res).jpg), a frame of the video, and stored a reduced copy. The video itself was not played.

styles.note: The Outrun landscape in motion: a glowing wireframe floor and peaks that lead to a sun on the horizon, under a violet and magenta sky.

context: The author describes it as a “First animation test with Blender 2.8 Beta and Eevee”, made by following a Ducky 3D tutorial, with the music “Mt Fuji” by Timecrawler 82 (CC BY 3.0). [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chase_The_Sun.webm).

The video comes from [Vimeo 315911655](https://vimeo.com/315911655). A Commons reviewer confirmed the CC BY-SA 3.0 license on Vimeo on 10 December 2019. Commons files both the video and the still under Category:Synthwave.
observed: The sky shades from deep indigo at the upper left through magenta to a pale lilac at the upper right.
A large yellow sun, half hidden, sits at the centre of the horizon with a pink halo.
A cyan wireframe of low-polygon facets fills the lower two thirds: a flat valley floor in the centre and sharp peaks on both sides. Every edge glows.
The valley converges on the sun, and the glow turns almost white near the horizon. There is no text, car, or palm tree.
interpretation: It shows the symmetrical horizon composition and the glow surface of the style with nothing else. Cyan, not magenta, carries the grid here, so it is a useful counterpart to the magenta grids of [the j4p4n banner](ref:j4p4n-synthwave-banner-2018).
borrow: Center the vanishing point on the sun and let the grid glow brighten toward the horizon.
Frame a central path with jagged wireframe peaks on both sides to make a symmetrical hero.

images.alt: 3D render: a cyan glowing wireframe valley with sharp peaks on both sides leads to a yellow sun on the horizon, under a sky that shades from indigo to magenta and lilac.
images.caption: Frame of *Chase The Sun* by G. Casqueiro, 2019. CC BY-SA 3.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave_cyberspace_sunset_(low_res).jpg), from [Vimeo](https://vimeo.com/315911655).

rights.statement: Published by the author under CC BY-SA 3.0 on Vimeo; license reviewed on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chase_The_Sun.webm) on 10 December 2019. Credit: G. Casqueiro.

references.title: Cyberpunk 2077
references.lede: CD Projekt Red’s open-world role-playing game set in Night City, a dystopian Californian metropolis of megabuildings, neon signs, and body modification.
references.summary: A dense night city of pink and cyan neon, Japanese signs, and haze, with chrome and cyberware. CD Projekt Red, 2020.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected eight 1920 × 1080 px screenshots from the Steam store listing (app 1091500) in a scratch folder. The observations come mainly from the street scene with a fenced lookout. The screenshots are publisher marketing images and may differ from play.

styles.note: The style’s current flagship: the Aesthetics Wiki uses it as its lead image, and its Night City shows the neon-on-black palette, signs, and cyborg bodies at full scale.

context: Wikipedia: “Cyberpunk 2077 is a 2020 action role-playing game developed by CD Projekt Red and published by CD Projekt. Based on Mike Pondsmith’s Cyberpunk tabletop game series, the plot is set in the fictional cyberpunk metropolis of Night City in California”. Pondsmith served as a consultant. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk_2077).

Wikipedia: the team used “four distinct visual styles—austere Entropism, colourful Kitsch, imposing Neomilitarism, and opulent Neokitsch” to build Night City, and drew on Syd Mead’s “vibrant colours and materialism”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk_2077).
The style record notes that the Aesthetics Wiki uses Cyberpunk 2077 as its lead image. See [Cyberpunk](style:cyberpunk).
observed: In the street scene, tall dark buildings and elevated structures close the sky. Haze lit orange and red fills the space between them.
A vertical magenta neon sign hangs at upper left. A tree of small pink lights and a vertical sign beginning “BE” glow at right.
A fence of black bars in the foreground is backlit by a bright cyan light from below. Japanese signs, including “営業”, appear in the distance.

Other screenshots show a scratched black car with a white checker stripe, police vehicles with red and blue lights, and characters with visible implants: a gold line on a woman’s face and a metal arm.
Not all screenshots are nocturnal: a garage scene is lit by work lights and shows a wedge-shaped car in blue, white, yellow, and red blocks.
interpretation: The game shows the style as a full environment rather than a graphic layer: neon light, haze, and dark mass do the work, and the HUD sits on top.
Its range of sub-styles (Kitsch, Neomilitarism) shows that the look is not one palette. The pink-and-cyan street is only one register of it.
borrow: Use haze or a soft gradient of colored light between dark masses to give depth to a dark layout.
Light one foreground element from behind with cyan so it reads as a silhouette.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Cyberpunk 2077 and its screenshots are © CD Projekt. The screenshots were viewed on the Steam store page only.

references.title: Darren Oorloff, Pleasure Planet “Pure Romance” artwork
references.lede: A square artwork of chrome mannequin heads in a warped checkerboard room, with a pink gradient sphere, warped stripes, and a vertical title strip.
references.summary: Chrome heads, warped checkerboards, a red-pink sphere, and wavy stripes. Darren Oorloff, featured on @acidgraphix.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2019): “Acid Graphics” Are the New Psychedelia

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px image `Darren-Oorloff-PP-Pure-Romance.jpg` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) published with the article, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image as the magazine published it, not a named physical copy. The caption reads “Darren Oorloff, PP, Pure-Romance, as featured on @acidgraphix”. The square format suggests a record cover, but the source does not say so.

styles.note: Partial fit: chrome heads, warped op-art checkerboards, and glitch cuts as the article describes, but with pink and red, not acid green, and no chrome lettering.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) shows the work in its 2019 article on acid graphics, with the caption “Darren Oorloff, PP, Pure-Romance, as featured on @acidgraphix”.
observed: Black-and-white checkerboards cover the floor and walls of a room and bend in perspective.
Two bald mannequin heads in profile face each other. Their surfaces are rendered as dark, reflective metal.
A red-to-violet gradient sphere sits on the checkerboard floor, and a red-pink doorway glows in the back wall.
A strip at the left holds “PLEASURE PLANET” in condensed capitals running vertically, “PURE ROMANCE” in italic capitals, the kanji 愛, and a panel of wavy red stripes.
Diagonal glitch cuts split the image near the left edge.
interpretation: The work shows the op-art and chrome-figure side of the trend that Eye on Design lists, with a pink palette that brings it close to vaporwave. It is a boundary case for this record.
borrow: Bend a checkerboard into a room to give a flat layout depth.
Run the title vertically in a narrow strip beside the image.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright. The rights holder is the designer or the client.

references.title: David Bryant Copeland, “Guidelines for Brutalist Web Design”
references.lede: A short manifesto that reads brutalism as truth to the web’s materials: content, links, buttons, and the browser.
references.summary: Copeland’s guidelines: readable content, underlined links, buttons that look like buttons, scrolling, and speed.

evidence.note: Page text read on 2026-10-02. The update date is on the page. The first publication year is not stated there: a Pelican theme from August 2018 cites it, so it existed by then. The page was not captured; it is listed as a capture candidate.

styles.note: The best-known written statement of the raw core, cited by Smashing Magazine and by theme authors.

context: The guidelines: “Content is readable on all reasonable screens and devices. Only hyperlinks and buttons respond to clicks. Hyperlinks are underlined and buttons look like buttons. The back button works as expected. View content by scrolling. Decoration when needed and no unrelated content. Performance is a feature.”
“A website’s materials aren’t HTML tags, CSS, or JavaScript code. Rather, they are its content and the context in which it’s consumed.”
“By default, a website that uses HTML as intended and has no custom styling will be readable on all screens and devices.” The site itself does not use default styles.
[Smashing Magazine (2020)](ref:smashing-split-personality-brutalist-web-2020) and the [Brutalist Pelican theme](ref:brutalist-pelican-theme) both cite it.
interpretation: It turns the look into rules about behavior. That makes it the basis for the `do` and `dont` rules of [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design), more than for its colors.
borrow: Underline every link and make every button look pressable. Let only those two things respond to clicks.

rights.statement: © David Bryant Copeland. Link and quotation only.

references.title: David Rudnick, Turbo Warehouse Series compilation sleeve
references.lede: A record sleeve shown in a clear plastic bag: a pale pink insert crammed with mixed display type, a wavy rendered texture, and a woodcut, with a yellow sticker and a two-euro coin.
references.summary: Dense mixed display type on a pink insert, a wavy metallic texture, a plastic bag, and a yellow sticker. David Rudnick, Turbo TWR72, before September 2016.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2016): David Rudnick’s Portfolio is a Codex for Electronic Music Design

references.made: Before September 2016 (the article does not date it)

evidence.note: Inspected the 1000 × 1000 px image `David-Rudnick-Turbo-Warehouse-Series.png` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/david-rudnicks-portfolio-is-a-codex-for-electronic-music-design/) published, in a scratch folder. Not stored. It is a staged product image, not a named physical copy.

styles.note: Partial fit: flyer density, mixed and stretched display faces, and a rendered wavy metal texture, in pale pink and black instead of acid green, with no chrome lettering.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/david-rudnicks-portfolio-is-a-codex-for-electronic-music-design/) (Emily Gosling, 5 September 2016) shows this image among works captioned “David Rudnick, Turbo Warehouse Series”. It says that Rudnick “mainly designs for electronic music clients, creating posters and sleeve designs”, and names the record label Turbo among his partners.
The insert reads “TWR72”, “COMPILATION TURBO”, and “Warehouse Series?” and lists Gingy & Bordello, Sei-A, Joe Farr, and Randomer.
observed: A clear, wrinkled plastic bag holds a pale gray sleeve with a large black square-and-triangle mark, on a black ground.
A pale pink insert covers the left half. It is crammed with display lines in at least six faces: a bold grotesque, a heavy italic, a thin wide sans, a squared bracket face, a serif, and a stencil.
“REAL ESTATE” runs vertically down the insert in very tall, thin letters that are cut by horizontal bars.
A panel near the top holds a gray, wavy rendered texture like liquid metal. A woodcut of two figures under a tree sits below it.
A yellow sticker at the upper right reads “100% Turbo Commodity Warehouse Series: Real Estate for Real Value”. A two-euro coin lies on the lower right.
interpretation: The sleeve shows the self-referential, ironic packaging of the trend: dense flyer type, stretched letters, a rendered liquid texture, and props such as a coin and a sticker. It lacks the black ground and the acid green of the core.
borrow: Stack many display faces in one narrow column, each on its own line, like a flyer line-up.
Use a rendered liquid-metal texture as one small panel among type panels.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright (David Rudnick and Turbo Recordings).

references.title: David Rudnick, Turbo Warehouse Series poster for Sei A
references.lede: An acid-green record poster packed with black panels, sliced italic capitals, a barcode, a woodcut, and a track list, like a 1990s rave flyer.
references.summary: Acid green and black, sliced italic “REAL E$TATE” and “TURBO”, barcode, dense panels. David Rudnick, Turbo 151, before September 2016.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2016): David Rudnick’s Portfolio is a Codex for Electronic Music Design

references.made: Before September 2016 (the article does not date it)

evidence.note: Inspected the 900 × 1336 px image `SeiAPoster.png` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/david-rudnicks-portfolio-is-a-codex-for-electronic-music-design/) published, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image of the poster as the magazine published it.

styles.note: The flyer side of the style at full strength: one acid green with black, horror vacui, mixed display faces, and sliced, slanted capitals. It has no chrome.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/david-rudnicks-portfolio-is-a-codex-for-electronic-music-design/) (Emily Gosling, 5 September 2016) shows this image among works captioned “David Rudnick, Turbo Warehouse Series”. It says that Rudnick “mainly designs for electronic music clients, creating posters and sleeve designs”, and names the record label Turbo among his partners.
The poster text names Turbo 151, the Warehouse Series, the artist Sei A, and three tracks: “Blades of Brazil”, “Swoon”, and “Made of Something”.
observed: The whole sheet is a flat acid green, framed by a black border.
Black panels of different sizes tile the sheet edge to edge, like a flyer or a cereal box.
“REAL E$TATE” and “TURBO” are set in very heavy, slanted capitals that are sliced through by thin horizontal cuts.
Other lines use a heavy grotesque (“Warehouse Series”), a thin wide sans (“SEI-A”), a squared techno face (the track list), and a condensed italic.
A barcode, small triangle arrows, stars, and a black-and-green woodcut of robed figures fill the side panels.
Small ironic texts, such as “THE HEAVY-HEAVY SOUND OF PROPERTY SPECULATION”, sit between the large words.
interpretation: This is the rave-flyer root of the style, redrawn with a cynical text about property and clubs. It shows the acid green, the density, and the mixed display faces. It does not show the chrome type, so it marks the flyer side of the core.
borrow: Tile the page edge to edge with black panels on one acid green, and give each panel one job.
Slice heavy italic capitals with thin horizontal cuts for speed.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright (David Rudnick and Turbo Recordings).

references.title: DawnLike 16 × 16 roguelike tileset
references.lede: DragonDePlatino’s open tileset for roguelike games draws walls, floors, furniture, and monsters on a 16-pixel grid in one 16-color palette.
references.summary: Top-down dungeon rooms of 16 × 16 tiles in the DawnBringer 16-color palette. DragonDePlatino, 2014, CC BY 4.0.

source.label: OpenGameArt: DawnLike - 16x16 Universal Rogue-like tileset v1.81

creator.name: DragonDePlatino, with the DawnBringer 16 palette by DawnBringer

evidence.note: Downloaded the sample map `Dungeon_0.gif` from the OpenGameArt page (640 × 480 px, already enlarged 2×) and inspected it enlarged again to 1280 × 960 px. The file has exactly 16 colors.

styles.note: Hand-placed square pixels on a fixed tile grid, a 16-color palette, flat palette-step shading, and sprites with dark outlines.

context: DragonDePlatino writes that the project began in autumn 2013 as DawnHack, a tileset for NetHack, and grew into a general tileset for roguelike games. [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/dawnlike-16x16-universal-rogue-like-tileset-v181).

The page tags the set “16x16” and “16 Color” and requires users to credit DawnBringer, “that mad color-bending genius” who made the palette that the pack uses. [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/dawnlike-16x16-universal-rogue-like-tileset-v181).
The author says that he used the DawnBringer 16 palette as a personal challenge. [OpenGameArt comments](https://opengameart.org/content/dawnlike-16x16-universal-rogue-like-tileset-v181).
observed: Three dungeon areas seen from above on a near-black purple ground (#140c1c).
Walls are rows of blue-gray bricks with a pale cyan top edge and a dark outline, drawn as a thick frame around each room.
Floors are gray brick tiles. One room has a brown dirt floor with an orange rubble edge.
Small sprites stand on the tiles: a knight, a skeleton, a chest, barrels, a bed, a table, candles on the walls, a beetle, and a cat.
Every edge is stepped. There is no anti-aliasing and no gradient: shading uses two or three flat steps of one hue.
The measured image has 12 colors above a 2 percent share and a low mean chroma (0.11), with small saturated accents of cyan and orange.
interpretation: A clear example of the style’s tile grammar: every object fits a 16-pixel cell, and one shared palette makes walls, monsters, and props read as one world.
The palette is muted and dark rather than the saturated console look. This shows that a fixed small palette, not high saturation, is the core trait.
borrow: Choose one published 16-color palette and draw every element with it.
Frame panels with a two-tone edge, a light top line, and a dark outline, as the walls do here.

images.alt: Pixel-art map of three dungeon rooms seen from above. Blue-gray brick walls with pale cyan tops enclose gray brick floors, a brown dirt area, a knight, a skeleton, barrels, a bed, candles, and a beetle, on a near-black ground.
images.caption: DragonDePlatino, DawnLike sample map “Dungeon”, palette by DawnBringer, from [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/dawnlike-16x16-universal-rogue-like-tileset-v181), CC BY 4.0. Enlarged 2× with nearest-neighbor scaling and saved as PNG.

rights.statement: OpenGameArt lists the license as CC-BY 4.0. Attribution instructions: “If you use this tileset you must accredit DawnBringer.” Credit: DragonDePlatino (art) and DawnBringer (palette).

references.title: Dear Alice (Chobani advertisement)
references.lede: A one-minute 2D animated advertisement in which a grandmother’s letter to her granddaughter narrates a future of farms under solar panels and green cities.
references.summary: Hand-drawn animated ad of a solarpunk farming future, scored by Joe Hisaishi. The Line for Chobani, 2021.

creator.name: The Line, directed by Bjørn-Erik Aschim

evidence.note: Based on the studio’s project page and the Looper article (2023). The film was not watched and no still was inspected.

styles.note: The style record names this advertisement as the model for solarpunk motion, and Looper calls it a one-minute summary of the genre.

context: The Line, a London animation studio, lists “Dear Alice” for client Chobani: director Bjørn-Erik Aschim, June 2021, length 1:00, music by Joe Hisaishi, art director Antoine Perez, producer Samia Ahmed, animation lead Bishoy Gendi.
