The studio describes it as “a love letter from a grandmother to a granddaughter and an optimistic vision of the future of farming”. [The Line](https://thelinestudio.com/work/chobani).

Looper says the opening images show sustainable farming combined with modern technology, “such as a cow grazing while solar panels are overhead”, and that the view then pulls out to a city whose buildings incorporate greenery. It says the ad “distills the genre into one minute”. [Looper, 15 November 2023](https://www.looper.com/1446464/what-is-solarpunk-dear-alice-ad-explained/).

Joe Hisaishi is known for his scores for Studio Ghibli films, and press coverage compared the ad’s look with Ghibli. [Nerdist](https://nerdist.com/article/dear-alice-solarpunk-anime-short-studio-ghibli-composer/).
interpretation: The ad brought the solarpunk look to a mass audience and fixed its motion grammar: slow pans across fields, wind in grass and leaves, and soft daylight.
It is also a brand film for a food company, so it shows the greenwashing risk that the style’s rules warn about.
borrow: Use slow camera moves and natural motion (wind, light, grazing animals) in place of fast cuts.
next: Watch the film and describe its palette and framing from the video, with a timestamp for each observation.

rights.statement: No image stored. The film is a 2021 commercial work owned by Chobani and The Line.

references.title: Denny’s Coffee Shop, Monrovia, postcard
references.lede: A Tichnor Brothers linen postcard of a Denny’s in Monrovia, California: a yellow roof that sweeps up into a pointed prow, a glass front with stone panels, and a stacked pole sign.
references.summary: A yellow upswept prow roof over a glass coffee shop, a red “COFFEE SHOP” panel, and a “24” chevron sign, in airbrushed postcard color. Tichnor Brothers, about 1959–1960s.

source.label: Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers collection #3974, via Digital Commonwealth

references.made: Boston Public Library: ca. 1930–1945. The name Denny’s dates from 1959 (Wikipedia), so the card is probably 1959 or later.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the front of the Boston Public Library scan (Tichnor Brothers collection #3974, accession 06_10_009847) from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Denny%27s_Coffee_Shop_(3974).jpg) at 1280 × 823 px. The back of the card was not inspected.

styles.note: A 1950s–60s Southern California coffee shop with an upswept roof and stacked pole sign, the core Googie building type, in the bright printed color of roadside postcards.

context: Boston Public Library catalogs the card as “Denny’s Coffee Shop,” Monrovia, Los Angeles County, a linen-texture color postcard, 2 1/4 × 3 1/2 in., dated ca. 1930–1945, with “No known copyright restrictions.” [Digital Commonwealth](https://ark.digitalcommonwealth.org/ark:/50959/xs55n020g).

Wikipedia: Danny’s Donuts was founded in 1953 and renamed Denny’s Coffee Shops in 1959, open 24 hours. In the 1950s Armet & Davis designed a prototype Denny’s with a boomerang-shaped roof, and these designs helped spread Googie architecture across America. [Wikipedia: Denny’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny%27s). The card does not name the architect of this building.
observed: A long, low roof slab in white rises at the left end into a bright yellow prow that points up and out past the wall, like a tail fin.
The front is a band of tall plate-glass windows with thin mullions, broken by two panels of multicolored fieldstone.
A striped awning in yellow and white runs along the side wall.
A tall pole sign stacks three shapes: a red-and-white chevron with “24”, a green oval with “Denny’s” in white script, and a red rectangle with “COFFEE SHOP” in white outlined capitals.
Sky is saturated cyan with white clouds; the ground is pale gray; colors are flat and airbrushed, with the linen texture of the card visible.
Late-1950s cars are parked at left and right.
interpretation: The card shows the daytime version of the style: saturated yellow, red, and green on white walls under a cyan sky, not neon on a night ground.
Each sign shape is different (chevron, oval, rectangle), so the pole reads as a stack of badges, a common Googie sign structure.
borrow: Stack two or three badges of different shapes on one vertical line for a logo lockup.
Make one corner of a header panel rise into a point in the accent color.

images.alt: Linen postcard of a Denny’s coffee shop: a white roof rising into a yellow pointed prow at left over a glass front with stone panels, and a pole sign with a 24 chevron, a green Denny’s oval, and a red COFFEE SHOP panel, under a cyan sky with clouds.
images.caption: Tichnor Brothers, Denny’s Coffee Shop, Monrovia, linen postcard. Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers collection #3974, [Digital Commonwealth](https://ark.digitalcommonwealth.org/ark:/50959/xs55n020g); scan from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Denny%27s_Coffee_Shop_(3974).jpg).

rights.statement: Boston Public Library: “No known copyright restrictions. No known restrictions on use.” Commons license: PD-US-no notice (a United States work published before 1978 without a copyright notice). The back of the card was not checked for a notice. The building (United States, before 1990) is not protected as architecture. The Denny’s name and sign are trademarks, used here only for commentary.

references.title: Dieter Rams, RZ 62 armchair, 1962
references.lede: Dieter Rams’s lounge chair for Vitsœ: a dark glass-fibre shell of flat side panels, filled with loose upholstered cushions.
references.summary: Flat dark shell panels with visible fixing bolts, soft square cushions, and a set-back plinth. Rams for Vitsœ, about 1962.

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s image 2014HC8620 of object CIRC.430:1-1970 at 1600 × 1540 px, through the V&A IIIF service. The image is a black-and-white photograph, so it does not show color.

styles.note: Rams’s furniture follows his Braun method: flat panels, visible fixings, a modular frame, and no ornament.

context: The V&A dates the chair about 1962 and gives a black matt glass-fibre base, sides, and back, with suede-covered rubberised hair upholstery and a separate seat cushion. The record says it was manufactured by Vitsœ, Eschborn, and relaunched by Vitsœ in 2006. [V&A CIRC.430:1-1970](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O314704/).
The same record quotes R. Hollis (1970): Rams was head of the Product Design Division at Braun AG from 1955. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O314704/).
observed: Each side is one flat, dark panel with rounded corners. The armrest is a padded top edge that folds out over the panel.
Two small round bolt heads show on each side panel.
The seat and back are loose, square cushions with soft edges, set inside the shell.
The chair stands on a recessed plinth, so the body appears to float a little above the floor.
interpretation: The chair is the furniture branch of the style: a box of flat parts that is honest about its fixings. It is dark and upholstered, so it fits the structure and surface rules more than the white-and-grey palette.
borrow: Show the fixings as small, regular round details instead of hiding them.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The V&A allows non-commercial use of its images under its own terms, not an open license. The design is by living or recently deceased designers. No image is stored.

references.title: Drive (2011 film), US theatrical poster
references.lede: The US poster for Nicolas Winding Refn’s *Drive*: a sunlit photograph of Ryan Gosling and a huge hot-pink brush-script title on a white border.
references.summary: Hot-pink brush-script “Drive” over a sunlit portrait on white. US theatrical poster, 2011.

creator.name: FilmDistrict (distributor); designer not credited on the source

references.made: 2011; film released in the US on 16 September 2011 (Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Inspected the 1000 × 1500 poster image from [IMP Awards](http://www.impawards.com/2011/posters/drive_xlg.jpg) in a scratch folder. Not stored. This is the “Some heroes are real” one-sheet with the 09.16.11 date, not the steering-wheel poster in the Wikipedia infobox.

styles.note: Partial fit: the film is a named source of the synthwave revival and its hot-pink script title became a template, but this poster is light and photographic, with no neon, grid, or night sky.

context: Wikipedia: *Drive* was directed by Nicolas Winding Refn and released in the United States on 16 September 2011. “While *Drive* is set in the present day, it has a 1980s atmosphere, underlined by the vehicles, music, and clothes, and by the architecture.” Its hot-pink opening credits were inspired by *Risky Business* (1983), and the credits play over Kavinsky’s “Nightcall”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive_(2011_film)).

The [synthwave](style:synthwave) record lists *Drive* among the works that spread the look. Wikipedia says that *Hotline Miami* ([record](ref:hotline-miami-2012)) took inspiration from it, and that James White, who drew the *Blood Dragon* key art ([record](ref:far-cry-3-blood-dragon-2013)), had made artwork for the film.
observed: A white sheet frames a tall, warm photograph of a man in a dirty white T-shirt seen from below, against a hazy pale-yellow sky, with a concrete bridge at the lower right.
The title “Drive” is set very large in a hot-pink, rough-edged brush script. It overlaps the bottom of the photograph and runs out onto the white border.
“SOME HEROES ARE REAL” runs vertically up the left margin in small, widely spaced thin capitals.
“IN THEATRES 09.16.11” sits at the bottom in wide-spaced italic gray capitals.
interpretation: The poster shows where the hot-pink script came from: a daylight, film-poster gesture that later synthwave covers moved onto a black night ground and lit as neon. On its own it fails the rubric’s counter-sign of a light ground.
borrow: Set one short word very large in a hot-pink brush script, overlapping the edge of the image it names.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The poster is in copyright (FilmDistrict / Drive Film Holdings, 2011).

references.title: Dynamism of a Cyclist
references.lede: Umberto Boccioni breaks a racing cyclist into interlocking wedges and arcs of prismatic color, so that the rider, the machine, and the air around them read as one burst of speed.
references.summary: A cyclist dissolved into blue, ochre, and green wedges with red and violet arcs of force. Umberto Boccioni, 1913.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Dynamism of a Cyclist, credited to the Peggy Guggenheim Collection

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 3477 × 2520 px; a 1280 × 928 px rendering was inspected and stored, because the full file was rate-limited). The Commons credit is the Peggy Guggenheim Collection. The physical work is the oil on canvas, 70 × 95 cm, in the Gianni Mattioli Collection, on long-term loan to the Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, as the file description states.

styles.note: A canonical image of the plastic dynamism phase: a modern machine and its rider shown as interpenetrating planes and lines of force.

context: Oil on canvas, 70 × 95 cm, 1913. Gianni Mattioli Collection, which the Peggy Guggenheim Collection has hosted on long-term loan since 1997. [Peggy Guggenheim Collection press release](https://www.guggenheim-venice.it/en/press/press-releases/masterpieces-of-futurism-at-the-peggy-guggenheim-collection/).

The same press release names *Dynamism of a Cyclist* with *Materia* among the Boccioni masterpieces of the Mattioli Collection. [Peggy Guggenheim Collection](https://www.guggenheim-venice.it/en/press/press-releases/masterpieces-of-futurism-at-the-peggy-guggenheim-collection/).
observed: The figure, bent low, is built from overlapping wedges, cones, and curved planes in blue, ochre, brown, and green. No continuous outline separates rider from bicycle.
Two long arcs, one red and one violet, sweep down the left edge; a red and a green band cut across the top.
Thin straight black lines run diagonally through the forms, like spokes or lines of force.
The background is short, dabbed strokes of yellow, pink, lilac, and pale blue, with no horizon.
Pale chevrons and wedges at lower right appear to repeat the forms behind the moving figure.
interpretation: Compared with [The City Rises](ref:boccioni-the-city-rises-1910), the divisionist strokes remain but the forms are now cut into Cubist-like planes. The picture shows motion by fusing the object with its environment, not by drawing a trail.
The palette is prismatic rather than flat: many saturated hues side by side, which a printed Futurist page later reduces to a few inks.
borrow: Build a moving subject from overlapping wedges that point the same way, and let the background planes continue the same angles.
Use long sweeping arcs at one edge to give a composition a direction of travel.
Cross the forms with a few thin straight lines to suggest force and structure.

images.alt: Painting of a cyclist bent forward, broken into interlocking wedges of blue, ochre, brown, and green. Red and violet arcs sweep down the left edge, and thin black lines cross the forms against a speckled yellow and lilac ground.
images.caption: Umberto Boccioni, *Dynamism of a Cyclist*, 1913, oil on canvas, 70 × 95 cm. Gianni Mattioli Collection, on long-term loan to the Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Umberto_Boccioni,_1913,_Dynamism_of_a_Cyclist_(Dinamismo_di_un_ciclista),_oil_on_canvas,_70_x_95_cm,_Gianni_Mattioli_Collection,_on_long-term_loan_to_the_Peggy_Guggenheim_Collection,_Venice.jpg), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain. Boccioni was Italian and died in 1916, so the painting is public domain in Italy. It dates from 1913 and its author died more than 70 years ago, so it is also public domain in the United States. The image is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

identifiers.commons: File:Umberto Boccioni, 1913, Dynamism of a Cyclist (Dinamismo di un ciclista), oil on canvas, 70 x 95 cm, Gianni Mattioli Collection, on long-term loan to the Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice.jpg

references.title: eDEX-UI terminal emulator
references.lede: An open-source science-fiction terminal emulator that wraps a real shell in heads-up-display panels: a clock, system graphs, a wireframe globe, and an on-screen keyboard, all in hairline cyan on near-black.
references.summary: Pale cyan hairline panels, monospace shell text, and HUD readouts on a near-black ground. Gabriel Saillard (GitSquared), version 2.2, 2019.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected `media/screenshot_default.png` (1934 × 1094 px) from the repository’s master branch, the screenshot the README captions “neofetch on eDEX-UI 2.2 with the default "tron" theme & QWERTY keyboard”. Also inspected the “blade” theme screenshot (3840 × 2160 px), which uses orange instead of cyan.

styles.note: A working interface built as a movie HUD: a near-black ground, glowing pale cyan hairline frames, numbered panels, and monospace terminal text throughout.

context: The GitHub repository describes eDEX-UI as “a cross-platform, customizable science fiction terminal emulator with advanced monitoring & touchscreen support”. It was created in January 2017 and archived in October 2021. [GitHub](https://github.com/GitSquared/edex-ui).

The README says the project is “heavily inspired from the TRON Legacy movie effects (especially the Board Room sequence)” and began as a distributable version of Seena Burns’s [DEX-UI](https://github.com/seenaburns/dex-ui). [README](https://github.com/GitSquared/edex-ui/blob/master/README.md).
The repository is licensed GPL-3.0. It ships several themes, including “tron”, “blade”, “matrix”, and “tron-disrupted”, which adds glitch effects. [GitHub](https://github.com/GitSquared/edex-ui).
observed: The ground is near-black blue-gray. All text, lines, and icons are one pale cyan-gray, with a brighter white for active text.
The screen divides into labelled panels: “PANEL SYSTEM”, “TERMINAL MAIN SHELL”, “PANEL NETWORK”, and “FILESYSTEM”. Each label is small capitals with a thin rule under it.
A large clock reads “20 : 27 : 46” in a squared sans-serif. Below it sit uptime, CPU graphs with “#1-2 Avg. 55%”, temperature, memory as a dot matrix, and a process table.
The central terminal has tabs with diagonal cut edges (“MAIN SHELL”, “EMPTY”) and shows monospace shell output with ASCII art.
A dotted wireframe globe titled “WORLD VIEW / GLOBAL NETWORK MAP” and a network-traffic line chart fill the right column.
An on-screen keyboard of outlined keys fills the lower right. Frames are 1 px lines with square corners.
interpretation: The interface is the HUD branch of the style without the neon city: one cool hue, many small labelled readouts, and type that is all data. It shows that the look can work as a single-color system.
Its source is film interface design (TRON: Legacy), which ties it to the screen graphics of the genre more than to its street imagery.
borrow: Put a small capital label and a right-aligned category over a 1 px rule at the top of every panel.
Use one pale cyan for all lines and text, and show state with brightness, not with more colors.
Cut the corners of tabs on the diagonal to suggest a HUD without rounding anything.

images.alt: A dark screen divided into thin-outlined panels in pale cyan: a large digital clock and system graphs at left, a terminal with tabs and shell text in the center, a dotted wireframe globe and traffic chart at right, and a file browser and on-screen keyboard below.
images.caption: eDEX-UI 2.2 with the default “tron” theme, running neofetch, April 2019. Screenshot from the [eDEX-UI repository](https://github.com/GitSquared/edex-ui), GPL-3.0.

rights.statement: The screenshot is a file in the eDEX-UI repository, which is licensed GPL-3.0 as a whole. It shows the program’s own interface and the output of neofetch, which is free software. The interface is inspired by TRON: Legacy but does not reproduce its graphics. The lead curator may confirm that a repository license covers its media files.

references.title: Elasticity
references.lede: Umberto Boccioni fuses a galloping horse and rider with an industrial landscape of pylons and factories, so that the bodies, the ground, and the buildings share one set of curving planes.
references.summary: A red horse and rider burst through planes of green fields, pylons, and factories. Umberto Boccioni, 1912.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Umberto Boccioni, 1912, Elasticity, Museo del Novecento

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (1100 × 1089 px; credited to the blog artblart, not to the museum). The physical work is the painting in the Museo del Novecento, Milan, Jucker Collection, according to [Italian Wikipedia](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elasticit%C3%A0_(Boccioni)) as summarized by a web search; that page was not opened directly. The museum’s inventory number was not checked.

styles.note: Plastic dynamism at its most developed: horse, rider, and industrial landscape interpenetrate in one field of planes and lines of force.

context: Oil on canvas, 100 × 100 cm, 1912, Museo del Novecento, Milan, Jucker Collection. The painting shows a rider at speed in an industrial landscape. [Italian Wikipedia: Elasticità (Boccioni)](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elasticit%C3%A0_(Boccioni)).

The Museo del Novecento has digitized the painting in gigapixel resolution. [Finestre sull’Arte](https://www.finestresullarte.info/musei/museo-del-novecento-milano-digitalizzati-tecnologia-gigapixel-capolavori-boccioni-modigliani-klee).
observed: A red and crimson horse fills the lower half, its legs and body drawn as stacked curved planes; a rider in ochre and brown sits above it.
A dark blue-black form at the center, possibly the horse’s head or a harness, is the only near-black area.
Behind and through the figures are green fields, red-roofed factories, smoking chimneys, and a lattice electricity pylon at upper right.
Thin straight black lines cross the lower left like struts or rays.
Pale yellow spirals and arcs at the bottom suggest dust or the curve of the gallop.
The palette is saturated and prismatic: red, crimson, violet, ochre, green, and blue, with small white highlights.
interpretation: *Elasticity* sits between [The City Rises](ref:boccioni-the-city-rises-1910) and [Dynamism of a Cyclist](ref:boccioni-dynamism-of-a-cyclist-1913): the horse is still present, but the forms are now planes that also belong to the surrounding landscape, so the animal and the machine age merge.
The pylon and chimneys keep the Futurist subject of the electrified, industrial city in a picture of a horse.
borrow: Let a moving subject share its planes with the background so that the boundary disappears at the points of greatest speed.
Use a square format filled edge to edge, with no calm margin.
Put one dark accent at the center of a hot palette to anchor the composition.

images.alt: Square painting of a red horse and an ochre rider made of curved, overlapping planes, bursting through a background of green fields, red-roofed factories, chimneys, and an electricity pylon. Black struts cross the lower left and pale yellow spirals fill the bottom.
images.caption: Umberto Boccioni, *Elasticity*, 1912, oil on canvas, 100 × 100 cm. Museo del Novecento, Milan. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Umberto_Boccioni,_1912,_Elasticity_(Elasticit%C3%A0),_oil_on_canvas,_100_x_100_cm,_Museo_del_Novecento.jpg), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain. Boccioni was Italian and died in 1916, so the painting is public domain in Italy. It dates from 1912 and its author died more than 70 years ago, so it is also public domain in the United States. The image is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

identifiers.commons: File:Umberto Boccioni, 1912, Elasticity (Elasticità), oil on canvas, 100 x 100 cm, Museo del Novecento.jpg

references.title: Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon
references.lede: Ubisoft Montreal’s 2013 stand-alone game: a parody of 1980s action films set on a neon-lit island, with a synthwave score by Power Glove and key art by James White.
references.summary: Neon-lit 1980s action parody with VHS colour fringing and a Power Glove score. Ubisoft Montreal, 2013.
references.made: Released 30 April 2013 (PlayStation 3) and 1 May 2013 (Windows, Xbox 360), per Wikipedia

evidence.note: Inspected four 1920 × 1080 screenshots from the [Steam store page](https://store.steampowered.com/app/233270/) in a scratch folder. Not stored. The James White key art and logo were not inspected at a usable size: the Steam header is 460 px wide and [Signalnoise’s post](https://blog.signalnoise.com/far-cry-3-blood-dragon-art/) returned HTTP 404.

styles.note: Partial fit: the game made the neon-and-VHS 1980s look mainstream, and its key art is by a leading synthwave cover artist, but the screenshots show interiors, not the sunset-and-grid scene.

context: Wikipedia: “*Blood Dragon* is a retro-futuristic parody of 1980s action films, cartoons and video games.” It was released on 30 April 2013 for PlayStation 3 and on 1 May 2013 for Windows and Xbox 360. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_Cry_3:_Blood_Dragon).

Wikipedia: “Australian synthwave duo Power Glove composed the game’s music,” and “The virtual box art cover for the game was designed by James White, who had previously created artwork for the film *Drive*.”

Kotaku (Luke Plunkett, 16 April 2013) reports that James White made the logo and posters with Ubisoft’s art team. [Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/the-man-behind-blood-dragons-80s-drenched-box-art-472933157).
The Steam description reads: “Welcome to an 80’s vision of the future. The year is 2007 and you are Sargent Rex Colt, a Mark IV Cyber Commando.” [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/233270/).
observed: The screenshots show dark industrial interiors lit by magenta, cyan, green, and orange tube lights and glowing panels.
Every frame has a red and cyan colour offset at the edges of objects and a faint horizontal scan-line texture, like a played-back VHS tape.
The hero wears a black helmet with a red visor and a red armoured suit with a glowing red Ω emblem.
One frame shows a first-person laser gun firing a burst of white, orange, and cyan sparks.
interpretation: The game shows how synthwave colour and VHS surface carry into a 3D world without the horizon composition. Its parody tone is louder than the sincere music covers, but the palette is the same.
borrow: Use a slight red-and-cyan offset on edges as a period accent, not as heavy glitch.
Light dark scenes with coloured tube lights instead of white light.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The game and its artwork are in copyright (Ubisoft, 2013).

references.title: FM-84, Atlas (album cover)
references.lede: James White’s cover for FM-84’s 2016 album: one huge striped sun, yellow at the top and magenta at the bottom, above a band of neon horizon lines on a starry night.
references.summary: A striped yellow-to-magenta sun on a starry navy sky, neon horizon lines below. James White, 2016.

source.label: Dribbble: FM-84: Atlas by James White

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px front-cover image from the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release-group/77f48f84-3d95-4e57-aae0-2d0d80dc7626) in a scratch folder. Not stored. The artwork credit is from the [Discogs record of the 2016 self-released digital edition](https://www.discogs.com/release/11581585-FM-84-Atlas).

styles.note: The retrosun alone: a striped yellow-to-magenta disc on a navy starry sky, which is the motif in its most reduced, iconic form.

context: Discogs records *Atlas* as a self-released digital album of 25 April 2016, produced by Col Bennett, with artwork by James White. [Discogs](https://www.discogs.com/release/11581585-FM-84-Atlas).
James White, who works as Signalnoise, also made the key art for *Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon* ([record](ref:far-cry-3-blood-dragon-2013)) and the GUNSHIP cover ([record](ref:gunship-album-cover-2015)).
observed: A sky of dark navy-violet with fine white and cyan stars and a soft grain fills the square.
A sun disc fills most of the frame. It shades from yellow at the top through orange and coral to hot magenta at the bottom, with a pink outer glow.
The upper half of the sun is solid. The lower half is cut by about ten horizontal dark bars, and the bars get thicker toward the bottom.
Under the sun, thin horizontal lines in pink, violet, and blue form a horizon band, like a reflection on water. There is no perspective grid.
“FM-84” sits small at the top left in a thin, wide white sans-serif.
interpretation: The cover is the motif as a logo: one sun, one gradient, and one set of cuts. The bars that widen toward the bottom give the sun a sense of sinking into the horizon.
borrow: Grade a sun from yellow to magenta from top to bottom, and cut only its lower half with bars that widen as they descend.
Keep the band name small and thin in a corner when the image is the logo.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The cover art is in copyright (James White / FM-84, 2016).

references.title: Ford’s Theatre playbill for *Our American Cousin*, 14 April 1865
references.lede: The narrow playbill for the evening of Lincoln’s assassination stacks a dozen display faces, an arched line, and pointing hands down one centred column.
references.summary: Tall theatre playbill with Tuscan, shaded, condensed, and slab lines on one axis. Washington, 1865.

source.label: Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection: Ford’s Theatre … Friday evening, April 14th, 1865

evidence.note: Inspected the Library of Congress scan (rbpe 2040580c, Portfolio 204, Folder 58c; 1992 × 5165 px). LoC holds other copies of this playbill under other numbers, and some are later facsimiles, so details may differ between copies.

styles.note: A canonical playbill: centred lines, a new face for almost every line, pointing hands, rules, and a dotted cast list, in black on paper.

context: LoC catalogues the bill as 1 p., 48 × 15 cm, Washington, 1865, in the Printed Ephemera Collection. [LoC rbpe.2040580c](https://www.loc.gov/item/rbpe.2040580c/).

The bill announces a benefit and the last night of Laura Keene in Tom Taylor’s *Our American Cousin* on Friday, 14 April 1865, the night Abraham Lincoln was shot at the theatre. The imprint reads “H. Polkinhorn & Son, Printers, D street, near 7th, Washington, D. C.”
observed: The bill is about three times as tall as it is wide, and every display line is centred.

“FORD’S THEATRE” is in a condensed slab capital; “BENEFIT!” in a shaded Tuscan with split serifs; “LAST NIGHT” in a wide sans-serif; “LAURA KEENE” and “COUSIN” in very tall condensed Tuscan-style letters.
“ONE THOUSAND NIGHTS,” is set on an arch, with a pointing hand on each side.
Short centred dashes frame “AND” and “OF MISS” as small connecting lines between big ones.
Thin and thick rules separate the sections. The cast list uses dotted leaders between role and actor.
“THE OCTOROON” at the foot uses a decorated outline face, and “EDWIN ADAMS” a wide shaded roman.
Black ink on white paper, with handwritten notes in the margin of this copy.
interpretation: The playbill is the theatre form of the style: the star’s name and the play title get the largest and most unusual letters, and the small lines read as connectives between them.
The arched line shows that printers bent the strict horizontal grammar only for one short line, as an ornament.
borrow: Give names and titles the largest lines, and set the joining words (“and”, “of”, “entitled”) small between them.
Use dotted leaders for a list of roles, prices, or times.

images.alt: Long narrow black-and-white playbill. Centred lines in many typefaces read Ford's Theatre, Benefit!, Last Night of Miss Laura Keene, One Thousand Nights on an arch between two pointing hands, Our American Cousin, a cast list with dotted leaders, The Octoroon, and Edwin Adams.
images.caption: Ford’s Theatre playbill, Friday 14 April 1865. Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection, [rbpe.2040580c](https://www.loc.gov/item/rbpe.2040580c/).

rights.statement: The Library of Congress says that, with a few exceptions, it “is not aware of any U.S. copyright protection … or any other restrictions in the materials in the Printed Ephemera Collection.” The bill was published in the United States in 1865, so it is in the public domain.

references.title: French Clarendon wood type at the Hamilton Wood Type & Printing Museum
references.titleBreak: French Clarendon wood type|at the Hamilton museum
references.lede: A tray of condensed French Clarendon wood letters, the reverse-contrast poster face with heavy slab serifs and thin stems that the Victorian bill used for names and slogans.
references.summary: Tray of condensed reverse-contrast wood type, stained with years of coloured ink. Two Rivers, Wisconsin.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: French Clarendon wood type (photograph by Jessica Fiess-Hill)

creator.name: Unknown wood type maker; photograph by Jessica Fiess-Hill

evidence.note: Inspected a 1280 × 850 px Commons thumbnail of the photograph (original 4288 × 2848 px), used instead of the original because Wikimedia returned HTTP 429. Commons says the type is at the Hamilton Wood Type Museum; no maker, date, or object number is given, so the font is unidentified.

styles.note: French Clarendon is one of the wood type genres named for the style, and the tray shows the physical letters behind the condensed theatre lines.

context: Commons describes the photograph as “French Clarendon wood type at the Hamilton Wood Type Museum, Wisconsin,” taken 8 November 2009 by Jessica Fiess-Hill.

Wikipedia lists the reverse-contrast or “French Clarendon” among the common wood type styles, with slab serif, fat face, sans-serif, Tuscan, and Grecian, and says Hamilton’s surviving materials are kept at the Hamilton Wood Type and Printing Museum in Two Rivers. [Wikipedia: Wood type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_type).
observed: A shallow wooden tray holds three rows of wood letters standing on end, with their faces mirrored as type is.
The letters are condensed, with thin vertical stems and very heavy horizontal serifs and bars: the reverse-contrast pattern.
Exclamation marks, figures, and an ampersand sit among the capitals.
The faces carry old ink in yellow, red, brown, and black, and the wood grain shows through the worn surfaces.
Loose letters and spacing material lie in the tray below.
interpretation: The tray explains a visual trait of the posters: the thick-and-thin was cut into wood, and the worn faces and grain are the reason big poster letters print unevenly.
Reverse contrast is one of the most recognisable Victorian letters, and it is almost absent from later design until Western and circus revivals.
borrow: Use a reverse-contrast condensed face for names and dates on an event page.
Let large letters carry a little unevenness of ink, rather than a smooth vector fill.

images.alt: A wooden tray of condensed wood type letters standing in rows, seen from above. The letters have thin vertical stems and heavy slab serifs, and their faces are stained yellow, red, brown, and black from old ink.
images.caption: French Clarendon wood type at the Hamilton Wood Type & Printing Museum, Two Rivers, Wisconsin. Photograph by Jessica Fiess-Hill, 2009, [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/), through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:French_Clarendon_wood_type.jpg) (1280 px thumbnail).

rights.statement: Commons licenses the photograph CC BY 2.0 (Flickr review passed), credit Jessica Fiess-Hill. The subject is utilitarian wood type; typeface designs are not protected by copyright in the United States.

references.title: Frontend Mentor “Bento grid” challenge design
references.lede: A free coding exercise of 2024 that asks learners to build a marketing section as a bento grid from a supplied desktop and mobile design.
references.summary: Eight tiles in purple, yellow, cream, and white with large tight headlines and a “>56%” figure, on light grey. Frontend Mentor, 2024.

source.label: Frontend Mentor: Build a Bento Grid Layout

evidence.note: Inspected `design/desktop-design.jpg` (1440 × 1029) in the starter repository [frontendmentorio/bento-grid](https://github.com/frontendmentorio/bento-grid), and read its `style-guide.md` and README. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: tiles of mixed sizes on one grid with even gutters and one message each, but most tiles are saturated purple or yellow and the radius is small.

context: The repository describes the exercise as “perfect for testing your CSS Grid and responsive skills with this bento grid layout”. The README tells learners that the two components in the left column on desktop move to the bottom on mobile.

The style guide gives the palette as Purple 100 hsl(254, 88%, 90%), Purple 500 hsl(256, 67%, 59%), Yellow 100 hsl(31, 66%, 93%), Yellow 500 hsl(39, 100%, 71%), white, and black hsl(0, 0%, 7%), with DM Sans at weights 400 and 500.
The repository has no license file. Search results list many learners’ solutions on GitHub and on frontendmentor.io.
observed: Eight tiles sit on a light grey ground in four columns with even gutters of about 32 px. The tiles span one or two columns and one or two rows: a wide purple hero tile at the top center, tall tiles at the left and right edges, and a wide purple tile at the bottom right.
Corners are rounded with a small radius, about 10 px. There are no outlines and no shadows on the tiles.
Tile fills are saturated purple, warm yellow, pale lavender, cream, and white.
Headlines are large, in a geometric sans-serif with very tight letter spacing and tight leading, for example “Create and schedule content quicker.” with “quicker.” in purple italic.
One white tile carries a very large black figure, “>56%”, over the small line “faster audience growth” and three cartoon avatars.
Several tiles hold small interface fragments: a bar chart, a calendar strip, chat bubbles, and a follower-growth card.
interpretation: By 2024 the bento grid was a standard exercise in CSS Grid placement, separate from Apple’s look. This design keeps the layout and the large figure but trades the neutral tonal tiles for brand color, which is the most common way the pattern is adapted on SaaS pages.
borrow: Use `grid-template-areas` to move tiles to a new order on small screens, and keep the source order logical.
Put a small interface fragment at the bottom of a tile and let the tile edge crop it.

rights.statement: Frontend Mentor challenge design; the repository has no license file. No image is stored here.

references.title: Garden Party, riso-printed micro-edition
references.lede: A close view of a riso-printed micro-edition laid out with web-to-print tools: red-pink and black ink broken into coarse pixel dither and grain.
references.summary: Close-up of a riso micro-edition in red-pink and black with coarse dither and grain.

creator.name: Cetrl (Commons user), as uploader and author of the photograph

evidence.note: Viewed the 959 × 959 px original on Commons, a close photograph of part of one page. A closer crop exists ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Garden_Party,_closeclose.jpg)).

styles.note: Partial fit: grain and two inks are clear, but the close crop shows little of the page layout.

context: The Commons description says: “Vue de près de l'impression de la micro édition Garden Party, imprimée en risographie et mise en page en web-to-print.” (Close view of the printing of the micro-edition Garden Party, printed by risograph and laid out with web-to-print.) The file is in Category:Fanzines and Category:Duplicator art.
observed: Two inks, a red-pink and black, cover the frame.
The image is broken into blocky dither, like enlarged pixels, with soft grain inside each block.
Black lies over the pink in places and leaves paper showing in others.
interpretation: Web-to-print layouts often reach riso through digital dithering, which links the print grain to screen pixels.
borrow: Threshold an image with an ordered or error-diffusion dither before you print it in one ink.

images.alt: A close-up of a printed page in red-pink and black, made of coarse pixel-like dither and grain.
images.caption: *Garden Party* micro-edition, close view, 2022, by Cetrl. CC0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Garden_Party,_close.jpg).

rights.statement: Commons: “own work” by Cetrl, released under CC0 ({{self|cc-zero}}). The description does not say explicitly that Cetrl made the edition. Credit: Cetrl, via Wikimedia Commons.

references.title: Ghost in the Shell
references.lede: Mamoru Oshii’s 1995 animated film of Masamune Shirow’s manga, set in a city modelled on Hong Kong, whose opening credits of computer code inspired the digital rain of The Matrix.
references.summary: Cyborg bodies, a Hong Kong-like city, and opening credits built from computer code. Mamoru Oshii, Production I.G, 1995.

source.label: Wikipedia: Ghost in the Shell (1995 film)

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia articles on the film and on cyberpunk, read as wikitext on 2026-10-02. No image of the film was inspected for this record.

styles.note: A canonical work of Japanese cyberpunk: the cyborg body, a Hong Kong-based city, and screen code as imagery. Wikipedia names it among the most notable cyberpunk anime.

context: Wikipedia: the city of the film was based on Hong Kong. Oshii felt that its streets, where “old and new exist in confusing relationships”, fit the theme of the film. [Cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk).

The opening credits were produced by CG director Seichi Tanaka, who converted code in a computer language displayed in romanized Japanese letters. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_(1995_film)).

The Wachowskis showed the film to producer Joel Silver, saying “We wanna do that for real.” The digital rain of *The Matrix* was inspired by its opening credits. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_(1995_film)).
interpretation: The film turns code itself into imagery. That is the source of the style’s terminal text used as decoration, which [The Matrix website](ref:whatisthematrix-website-2000) later made a web look.
Its city follows [Blade Runner](ref:blade-runner-1982) in taking Hong Kong as the model, which makes Hong Kong streets the most common real reference for the style.
borrow: Use real-looking code or data as a texture behind a title, in one color, and keep it legible.
Show the cyborg theme through interface overlays on a body or face, not through ornament.
next: Find an inspectable image and upgrade the evidence level. Check the color of the opening-credit code, which this record does not state.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The film, its posters, and its stills are in copyright. This record does not name the rights holders.

references.title: GUNSHIP, GUNSHIP (album cover)
references.lede: James White’s cover for GUNSHIP’s debut album: a cyan wireframe mountain under a striped sun on a magenta and orange laser grid, with a brushed orange logotype.
references.summary: Striped sun, cyan wireframe mountain, magenta-orange laser grid, brush logotype. James White, 2015.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px front-cover image from the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release-group/85778172-d037-4718-b028-950de54620cf) in a scratch folder. Not stored. The artwork credit is from the [Discogs record of the UK and Europe CD](https://www.discogs.com/release/7272688-GUNSHIP-GUNSHIP) (INgrooves, HITH002CD).

styles.note: Every Outrun motif in one frame: a striped sun, a receding laser grid, a glowing wireframe mountain, a star field, and a brushed logotype.

context: Discogs records the CD as released on 24 July 2015 in the UK and Europe by INgrooves (HITH002CD), written and produced by Alex Westaway and Dan Haigh, with artwork by James White. [Discogs](https://www.discogs.com/release/7272688-GUNSHIP-GUNSHIP).
observed: A starry night sky shades from violet-black at the top to near-black at the horizon. Thin red and blue lines cross it at the sun’s upper third.
A large striped sun shades from yellow at the top to coral and pink at the bottom. Horizontal bars cut its lower half, and the sun has a magenta halo.
A low-polygon mountain drawn in glowing cyan lines rises in the centre. A cyan dodecahedron floats above its peak in a beam of light.
A perspective grid in orange lines at the back and magenta lines at the front recedes to the horizon.
“GUNSHIP” is set in heavy, brushed, slightly italic capitals that shade from yellow to orange, at the bottom centre over the grid.
A fine scan-line texture and grain cover the whole image.
interpretation: This is the canonical complete Outrun scene, with strict central symmetry about the vanishing point. The grid changes colour from orange to magenta with depth, which reads as the sunset light falling on it.
borrow: Change the grid colour with depth, warm at the horizon and magenta in the foreground.
Put one glowing wireframe object on the central axis between the sun and the grid.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The cover art is in copyright (James White / GUNSHIP, 2015).

references.title: Hachi Maru Pop typeface
references.lede: Nonty’s open-source Japanese font, based on the round handwriting (marumoji) that girls made popular in the 1970s and 1980s.
references.summary: Rounded handwriting-style Japanese and Latin font with circular dots and loops. Nonty (Norio Kanisawa), 2020, OFL.

evidence.note: Inspected the repository’s sample image `HachiMaruPop_sample.png` (2000 × 1000 px). Read the README, `DESCRIPTION.en_us.html`, and `OFL.txt` in the repository.

styles.note: A digital revival of marumoji, the round handwriting that the style record names as the source of kawaii lettering.

context: The README says the font was made for Google Fonts and takes its idea from the round letters (丸文字) popular in Japan around the 1980s. The English text calls it “a cute font” based on the round handwriting popular among young Japanese girls in the 1970s and 1980s, and notes that some schools prohibited the round letters. [GitHub README](https://github.com/noriokanisawa/HachiMaruPop).

The name refers to “80” for the 1980s. The designer writes that it is eye-catching but “lacks a little on readability”, and recommends it for large sizes. It covers hiragana, katakana, Latin, numerals, symbols, and about 6,700 kanji (JIS levels 1 and 2 and IBM extensions), and it works in vertical text. [DESCRIPTION.en_us.html](https://github.com/noriokanisawa/HachiMaruPop/blob/master/DESCRIPTION.en_us.html).

`OFL.txt` reads “Copyright 2020 The Hachi Maru Pop Project Authors” and licenses the font under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. [OFL.txt](https://github.com/noriokanisawa/HachiMaruPop/blob/master/OFL.txt).
observed: The sample shows “はちまるポップ” and “HachiMaruPop” in black on white.
Strokes are a single even weight with fully round ends, like a felt-tip pen.
Kana are wide and bulbous: the loops of は, ま, and る are large closed circles, and the handakuten on ポ and プ are open rings.
In the Latin line, the “i” has a ring for its dot, the bowls of a, o, and p are near-perfect circles, and the capitals H and M are narrow and soft-cornered.
Letters sit loosely spaced on a common baseline, with no contrast between thick and thin.
interpretation: The face shows the typographic side of kawaii: everything that can be a circle is a circle, and dots become rings. This matches the style record’s “Round letters.” rule.
The designer’s own warning about readability supports the style’s rule to use such faces for headings and keep body text in a plainer rounded sans.
borrow: Use a round handwriting face for short headings, names, and labels, and a plain rounded sans for body text.
Replace small dots in icons and decoration with open rings to echo the type.

images.alt: Type sample on white: the Japanese name はちまるポップ in large round black kana with circular loops, and below it HachiMaruPop in round Latin letters with a ring as the dot of the i.
images.caption: Hachi Maru Pop sample image from the [project repository](https://github.com/noriokanisawa/HachiMaruPop), © 2020 The Hachi Maru Pop Project Authors, SIL Open Font License 1.1.

rights.statement: The repository, including the sample image, is published under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 (GitHub license OFL-1.1). The image shows only glyphs of the font. Letterform designs are not copyrightable in the United States, and the Japanese Supreme Court (2000) gave typefaces copyright only in exceptional cases. Whether the OFL covers the sample PNG as part of the “Font Software” should be confirmed by the lead curator.

references.title: Hannah Höch, Cut with the Kitchen Knife, 1919
references.lede: Hannah Höch’s large Berlin photomontage cuts politicians, Dadaists, crowds, machines, and press headlines out of the illustrated papers and packs them into one sheet.
references.summary: Dense photomontage of press photographs, gears, crowds, and cut words such as “dada” and “Die anti dadaistische Bewegung”. Höch, Berlin, 1919.

source.label: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Neue Nationalgalerie: Schnitt mit dem Küchenmesser Dada …, NG 57/61

references.notice: No image is stored. Hannah Höch died in 1978, so the work is in copyright in Germany until the end of 2048. The SMB credits the image © VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn.

evidence.note: Read the [SMB collection record](https://recherche.smb.museum/detail/961048/schnitt-mit-dem-k%C3%BCchenmesser-dada-durch-die-letzte-weimarer-bierbauch-kulturepoche-deutschlands) and inspected, in a scratch folder only, a 1248 × 1584 px reproduction uploaded to the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/jpg-hannah-hoch-schnitt-mit-dem-kuchenmesser-dada-durch-die-letzte-weimarer-bier) without a stated source. The object is unique: SMB, Neue Nationalgalerie, NG 57/61.

styles.note: The canonical Berlin Dada photomontage: press photographs cut and joined at clashing scales, with cut-out words in many faces.

context: The SMB records the work as *Schnitt mit dem Küchenmesser Dada durch die letzte Weimarer Bierbauch-Kulturepoche Deutschlands* (Cut with the Kitchen Knife Dada through the Last Weimar Beer-Belly Cultural Epoch in Germany), 1919, collage, paper on card, 114 × 90 cm, NG 57/61, bought in 1961 from Galerie Meta Nierendorf with funds from BASF. [SMB](https://recherche.smb.museum/detail/961048/schnitt-mit-dem-k%C3%BCchenmesser-dada-durch-die-letzte-weimarer-bierbauch-kulturepoche-deutschlands).

The SMB text says that Höch and Raoul Hausmann made their first Dada photomontages after a summer stay on the island of Wollin in 1918. It says the upper half joins technical progress and war politics, with Albert Einstein and Wilhelm II, and that Höch often stages ironic gender swaps, for example Hindenburg as a belly dancer and George Grosz as a ballerina. [SMB](https://recherche.smb.museum/detail/961048/schnitt-mit-dem-k%C3%BCchenmesser-dada-durch-die-letzte-weimarer-bierbauch-kulturepoche-deutschlands).
Compare the sparse Cologne montage [by Baargeld](ref:baargeld-typische-vertikalklitterung-1920).
observed: Hundreds of cut photographs from the illustrated press fill the whole sheet with almost no empty ground: heads, crowds, soldiers, dancers, an elephant, ball bearings, gears, a car, and a large wheel.
The scale of the pieces does not agree. Huge heads sit next to tiny full figures, and a giant ball bearing curves through the middle.

Cut words and headlines are pasted among the images in many faces: lowercase “dada” in a heavy roman at upper left, “Die anti dadaistische Bewegung” at upper right, “Die große Welt dada” on a tilted slip, and “DADAiSten” in mixed condensed letters at lower right.
Small slips carry phrases such as “Legen Sie Ihr Geld in dada an!”, “He, he, Sie junger Mann Dada ist keine Kunstrichtung”, and “Tretet dada bei.”
Large single letters, such as a black “e” at lower left and a “V”, are cut from posters and used as shapes.

Most of the image is in sepia and grey halftone. A strip of blue at the left edge, a pale blue figure at the top, and a dark ground at upper right are the main other tones. The initials “HH” sit at lower left.
interpretation: This is the reference for the style’s photomontage facet: the cut edges, the mixed scales, and the press type all stay visible, and the density is itself the message.
The type here comes from cut printed matter, not from a printer’s case. This is the same move as in [Schwitters’s Mal Kah](ref:schwitters-mz-245-mal-kah-1921), but at the scale of a wall.
borrow: Mix photographs at very different scales, so that a head can be larger than a crowd.
Paste short slogans on small slips at slight angles among the images.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Hannah Höch, a German author, died in 1978, so the work is protected in Germany until the end of 2048. The SMB photograph is credited “Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Neue Nationalgalerie / Jörg P. Anders” and “© VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn, 2021”. The Internet Archive copy states no source or license.

references.title: Hans Gugelot, Kodak Carousel S slide projector, 1963
references.lede: Hans Gugelot’s redesign of the Kodak round-tray projector for Europe: a square grey box under a clear-lidded slide ring, with small black controls.
references.summary: A square grey housing, a black numbered slide ring under a clear lid, and black lens and knobs. Gugelot for Kodak AG, 1963.

creator.name: Hans Gugelot (form design); Kodak AG, Stuttgart

evidence.note: Inspected the HfG-Archiv image of object HfG-Ar MS 0156 at 960 × 669 px through museum-digital. The case of this copy reads “Kodak Carousel S-AV”, a variant of the S. A second photograph, of a “Carousel S” on the Die Neue Sammlung website (1800 × 1371 px), shows the same form. Its object number could not be read, because the page loads its text by script.

styles.note: An Ulm-made industrial design for a non-Braun client: a plain grey box, numbered ring, and controls reduced to a few black parts.

context: The HfG-Archiv record credits Kodak AG (Stuttgart) with the manufacture and Hans Gugelot (1920–1965) with the form design, both 1963, and gives metal and electronics, 26 × 26 cm, 15 cm high. [museum-digital 2088570](https://global.museum-digital.org/object/2088570).

The record says that in the early 1960s Kodak Germany commissioned Gugelot’s “institut für produktgestaltung und design e.V.” in Neu-Ulm to redesign the round-tray projector for Europe. Gugelot bevelled the tray edge so that slides were easier to take out, and added a Plexiglas lid against dust. [museum-digital](https://global.museum-digital.org/object/2088570).
observed: The body is a square, matte grey box with slightly rounded vertical edges and a thin seam around its middle.
A round black slide tray sits on top, edged with a ring of small white numerals, under a clear flat lid.
The lens, a slide slot, and a knurled knob are black. A small vent of vertical slots sits on one side.
The name “Kodak Carousel S-AV” is printed small in white on the grey side, with “Kodak” in bold.
There is no colored accent.
interpretation: The projector shows the Ulm method outside Braun: a technical object made calm by one grey volume, one radius, and small black controls.
borrow: Put a numbered scale around a circular control, in small white figures on black.

rights.statement: The museum-digital record marks the image “RR-P” (rights reserved). Photograph by Ernst Fesseler for Museum Ulm/HfG-Archiv. Gugelot died in 1965, so the design is protected in Germany until the end of 2035. No image is stored.

references.title: Harunobu, Evening Snow on a Floss Shaper
references.lede: Two women stretch silk floss in a quiet room, a visual pun on a snowy mountain, in Suzuki Harunobu’s Eight Views of the Parlor, one of the first sets of full-color prints.
references.summary: Pale pinks and grays, patterned robes, and an open diagonal floor. Suzuki Harunobu, about 1766.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Art Institute of Chicago image of impression 1928.903 (1686 × 2214 px).

styles.note: An early nishiki-e from the decade when full-color printing began: thin outlines, soft flat colors, patterned textiles, and a diagonal interior.

context: AIC catalogues the sheet as a color woodblock print, chūban, 28.7 × 21.6 cm, about 1766, from the series Eight Views of the Parlor. [AIC 1928.903](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/88977).

AIC says that the series appeared around the time full-color prints emerged, that the floss stands for snow and the floss shaper for the mountain, and that this sheet carries the handwritten signature of the patron Kyosen (Ōkubo Tadanobu), not Harunobu’s. [AIC](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/88977).
observed: A lattice window at upper left and the edges of the floor and wall run as long diagonals across a plain cream ground.
Two women in patterned robes sit to the right of center. One robe has a gray check, another a beige lattice, and an under-robe a red key pattern.
The lines are thin, even, and black. Faces and hands are unprinted paper.
Colors are soft and flat: pale pink floor, brown, gray, salmon red, and black.
White floss mounds at lower left are left almost unprinted, with only faint contour lines.
A two-character signature and a red square seal sit in the empty area at right.
interpretation: Harunobu’s prints show the style before Prussian blue: the same outlines, flat areas, and empty grounds, with a softer palette of pinks and grays.
Pattern is confined to garments, and the large empty wall is part of the composition.
borrow: Leave large areas plain and let thin diagonal lines divide the space.
Put small all-over patterns inside clothing-like shapes, and keep each pattern to one area.

images.alt: Color woodblock print. Two women in patterned kimonos sit in a room with a lattice window, beside mounds of white silk floss on a pale pink floor. A short vertical signature and a red seal are at right.
images.caption: Suzuki Harunobu, Evening Snow on a Floss Shaper, from Eight Views of the Parlor, c. 1766. [Art Institute of Chicago 1928.903](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/88977), Clarence Buckingham Collection. CC0.

rights.statement: The Art Institute of Chicago marks the object public domain (`is_public_domain: true`) and releases images of public-domain works under CC0. [AIC open access](https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). Harunobu died in 1770, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Hello Kitty
references.lede: Yuko Shimizu’s white cat for Sanrio, 1974: a big round head, dot eyes, a yellow nose, a red bow, and no mouth.
references.summary: White cat with dot eyes, a red bow, and no mouth, first sold on a vinyl coin purse in 1975. Yuko Shimizu for Sanrio, 1974.

creator.name: Yuko Shimizu for Sanrio; later lead designers Setsuko Yonekubo (1976) and Yuko Yamaguchi (from 1980)

evidence.note: Relies on Wikipedia and the V&A’s description of Hello Kitty goods. The 1975 coin purse was not inspected. The character as drawn on later goods was observed on the V&A’s [toaster](ref:hello-kitty-toaster-sanyo-1998), [kettle](ref:hello-kitty-kettle-t-fal-2013), and [rice cooker](ref:hello-kitty-rice-cooker-2014).

styles.note: The founding character of kawaii goods: a big round head, dot eyes, a bow, and a minimal face, applied to everyday products since 1975.

context: Wikipedia says Hello Kitty was designed by Yuko Shimizu and added to Sanrio’s lineup in 1974, and first appeared on an item in March 1975, a vinyl coin purse sold in Japan, sitting between a bottle of milk and a goldfish bowl. [Wikipedia: Hello Kitty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hello_Kitty).

Sanrio describes her as a British anthropomorphic white cat with a red bow and no visible mouth, five apples tall. Setsuko Yonekubo took over as lead designer in 1976; Yuko Yamaguchi has led the design since 1980. [Wikipedia: Hello Kitty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hello_Kitty).

The V&A calls Hello Kitty “the ultimate symbol of Japanese cute”, launched for pre-adolescent girls and now on kettles, toasters, and rice cookers. [V&A FE.21-2015](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1322385/toaster/).
observed: On the V&A appliances, the head is a wide rounded oval with two pointed ears, outlined in black.
The eyes are two black vertical ovals set wide and low; the nose is a small yellow oval; three whiskers sit on each side. No mouth is drawn.
A red or pink bow, or a flower, sits at one ear.
interpretation: Hello Kitty fixes the kawaii face in its most reduced form. The missing mouth makes the face neutral, so the viewer reads its mood into it.
Because the head works alone as a badge, the character can be put on any product, which is how kawaii spread from stationery to appliances.
borrow: Design a mascot whose head alone works as an icon at small sizes.
Give the character one signature accessory in one accent color.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Hello Kitty is © and a trademark of Sanrio Co., Ltd.

references.title: Hello Kitty electric kettle
references.lede: A small T-fal Aprecia kettle in white and pale pink, with a black line drawing of Kitty holding a name plate.
references.summary: White and pale-pink electric kettle with a line-drawn Hello Kitty holding a name sign. Japan, 2013.

source.label: V&A: Kettle, showing Hello Kitty, FE.20:1, 2-2015

creator.name: T-fal (brand marked on the kettle); Hello Kitty character by Sanrio

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph 2015HW1065 of object FE.20:1, 2-2015 (1200 × 1448 px, IIIF) in a scratchpad copy. The V&A record names no maker; the T-fal Aprecia+ mark is read from the photograph. Not stored.

styles.note: A rounded white-and-pink appliance whose only decoration is Kitty with dot eyes and a red bow, drawn as a sticker-like line figure.

context: The V&A describes the object as “Kettle, plastic and metal; electrical components, showing Hello Kitty, Japan, 2013”. It was acquired in 2015 with a Hello Kitty toaster and rice cooker. [V&A FE.20:1, 2-2015](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1322383/kettle/).
observed: The kettle has a bulbous white body, a wide rounded handle, and a pale-pink lid and base ring.
A gray, pill-shaped water window carries the marks “0.8 L MAX” and “0.5 L”.
Kitty is drawn in an even black outline with a red bow and a yellow nose; her paws hold the top of a rounded plate that reads “HELLO KITTY” in bold rounded capitals.
The T-fal logo in red and the word “APRECIA+” in gray sit to the right of the window.
interpretation: Compared with the [1998 toaster](ref:hello-kitty-toaster-sanyo-1998), the character here is a clean outline figure with one red accent, and the pink is reduced to the lid and the base. The style is quieter, but the face and the rounded plate still carry it.
borrow: Let a character peek over the top edge of a label or card, holding it with its paws.
Use white as the main surface and a pale pastel only for caps, bases, and borders.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The Hello Kitty character belongs to Sanrio; the T-fal mark to Groupe SEB.

references.title: Hello Kitty rice cooker
references.lede: A round rice cooker in two pinks with a large Hello Kitty face on its body and a pink oval control panel.
references.summary: Cylindrical rice cooker in hot and pale pink with a large Hello Kitty face. Japan, 2014.

source.label: V&A: Rice cooker, decorated with Hello Kitty, FE.19-2015

creator.name: Unknown manufacturer; Hello Kitty character by Sanrio

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph 2015HU1286 of object FE.19-2015 (1200 × 1600 px, IIIF, lid open) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: the round form, the big face, and the bow are core kawaii, but the main pink is saturated rather than pastel.

context: The V&A describes it as a “Rice cooker, plastic and metal; electrical components, pink and decorated with Hello Kitty, Japan, 2014”, part of a group of Hello Kitty appliances acquired in 2015. [V&A FE.19-2015](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1322382/rice-cooker/).
observed: The body is a short cylinder in saturated hot pink; the base ring, the latch, the lid rim, and the steam vent are pale pink.
A large white Kitty head with black outline, dot eyes, whiskers, a yellow nose, and a pink bow fills much of the front.
The control panel is a rounded oval with “HELLO KITTY” in small capitals and two indicator lights.
Inside the open lid, the steel plate is pierced with rings of small round holes.
interpretation: Here the character is the main graphic, not a small badge. The cylinder, the oval panel, and the ring of round holes show how the round geometry extends from the character to the object.
The hot pink pushes this toward the bolder end of character goods; pastel is kept for the trim.
borrow: Scale a simple face large enough to fill a panel, and keep everything around it plain.
Repeat circles at different scales: the body, the panel, and small dotted details.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The Hello Kitty character belongs to Sanrio.

references.title: Hello Kitty toaster
references.lede: A two-slice Sanyo toaster in pale pink, with Hello Kitty’s face and a script logo on its side: a kitchen appliance turned into character goods.
references.summary: Pale-pink two-slice toaster with a Hello Kitty face and script logo on a stacked pink base. Sanyo, Japan, 1998.

source.label: V&A: Toaster, showing Hello Kitty, FE.21-2015

creator.name: Sanyo Denki (manufacturer); Hello Kitty character by Sanrio

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph 2015HW1063 of object FE.21-2015 (1200 × 900 px, IIIF) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: A household appliance in pale pink with a soft, rounded body and the face of Kitty with dot eyes, the core of Japanese character goods.

context: The V&A describes the toaster as “plastic and metal; electrical components, manufactured by Sanyo Denki, Japan, 1998”, and acquired it with a Hello Kitty kettle and rice cooker in 2015. [V&A FE.21-2015](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1322385/toaster/).

The museum calls Hello Kitty “the ultimate symbol of Japanese cute”, launched by Sanrio in 1974 for pre-adolescent girls and later used on domestic appliances such as kettles, toasters, and rice cookers. [V&A FE.21-2015](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1322385/toaster/).
observed: The body is a rounded box in pale, slightly glossy pink, with a chrome top around two bread slots.
On the side, a Kitty head in white with a hot-pink fuzzy outline, a pink flower at one ear, black dot eyes, whiskers, and a yellow nose, sits under the words “Hello Kitty” in a pink script.
The base is three stacked bands of a stronger pink with rounded ends; the lever and the browning knob are pink too.
The Sanyo name is printed small and pale below the face. There are no other markings.
interpretation: The toaster shows kawaii as a surface applied to an ordinary product: the form stays a standard toaster, and color plus one small character face carry the style.
Pink is used in two tones, pale for the body and stronger for the base and controls, so the object stays soft without becoming one flat color.
borrow: Put one small character face on a large plain pastel surface, with the name in a rounded script above it.
Use a pale tint for the main surface and a stronger tint of the same hue for controls and edges.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. The Hello Kitty character and marks belong to Sanrio.

references.title: Hiroshige, Mitsumata Wakarenofuchi
references.lede: Cargo boats cross the Sumida River below a distant Mount Fuji, under a sky that fades from Prussian blue at the top and a river that darkens at the bottom: bokashi at both ends of the sheet.
references.summary: Bokashi bands at the top and bottom, flat blue water, and a distant Fuji. Utagawa (Andō) Hiroshige, 1857.

source.label: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, FP 2 - JPD, no. 1300, p. 14

creator.name: Utagawa Hiroshige (catalogued by the Library of Congress as Andō Hiroshige)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Library of Congress reference JPEG (689 × 1024 px, the largest JPEG offered). This impression is mounted in the album Gajō icchō, p. 14 (Donald D. Walker collection). A brown stain is visible at lower right.

styles.note: A clear example of bokashi used as a band at the top of the sky and the bottom of the water, with flat color fields, cartouches, and an off-center Fuji.

context: The Library of Congress catalogues the print as a color woodcut, 36.3 × 24.1 cm, vertical ōban nishiki-e, [1857], from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei). [LoC 2009631870](https://www.loc.gov/item/2009631870/).
The record summary: barges on the waterways near Edo, with Mount Fuji in the distance. [LoC](https://www.loc.gov/item/2009631870/).
observed: The sky fades from a dark Prussian-blue band at the top into pale cream, then into a pink band at the horizon.
The river is flat pale blue in the middle and darkens to deep blue along the bottom edge.
Mount Fuji is a flat gray cone with a white cap, small, left of center, on a dark blue ridge.
A band of green reeds crosses the river as a flat shape with thin black blade lines.
A sailboat with a cream sail sits low and right of center. Other boats are cut by the left and right edges.
A red vertical series cartouche with a yellow title panel is at upper right. A red signature cartouche is at lower left.
A thin black frame line runs around the picture inside a cream paper margin.
interpretation: The print shows the two standard bokashi places, the top of the sky and the bottom of the water, in one image. The rest of the picture is flat.
The calm horizontal bands of sky, land, reeds, and water are typical of Hiroshige’s late landscapes.
borrow: Fade the top of a header from deep blue into the page color, and fade the bottom of a footer the same way.
Stack calm horizontal bands of flat color, and break them with one vertical element.

images.alt: Color woodblock print. Sailboats and cargo barges on a pale blue river with a band of green reeds. Mount Fuji rises small in the distance under a sky that is deep blue at the top and pink at the horizon. Red cartouches are at upper right and lower left.
images.caption: Utagawa Hiroshige, Mitsumata Wakarenofuchi, from One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1857. [Library of Congress 2009631870](https://www.loc.gov/item/2009631870/). No known restrictions on publication.

rights.statement: The Library of Congress gives the rights advisory “No known restrictions on publication.” Hiroshige died in 1858 and the print was published in 1857, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Hiroshige, Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
references.lede: Travellers hurry across a high wooden bridge under black rain lines and a hand-wiped storm cloud, in Hiroshige’s One Hundred Famous Views of Edo.
references.summary: Diagonal bridge, fine rain lines, and a dark bokashi cloud. Utagawa Hiroshige, 1857.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Art Institute of Chicago image of impression 1925.3742 (1686 × 2533 px).

styles.note: A canonical late landscape print: a bridge cut diagonally by the sheet edges, rain as fine key-block lines, and bokashi clouds and water.

context: AIC catalogues the sheet as a color woodblock print, ōban, 33.4 × 21.8 cm, from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. [AIC 1925.3742](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/26545).
AIC’s description says that the printer applied the gradation of the dark clouds by hand in a scalloped shape rather than the usual straight line. [AIC](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/26545).
observed: A wooden bridge enters at the lower left and leaves the sheet at the right edge. Its piers are cropped by the bottom edge.
Rain falls as hundreds of fine, straight black and gray lines over the whole picture.
The top of the sky is a black cloud that fades in uneven, scalloped edges into gray-blue.
The river is a flat gray-blue. It deepens to Prussian blue along the bottom edge and near the bridge.
The far bank is a band of dark green-gray trees without outlines.
A red vertical cartouche with the series title and a square title panel with colored cloud shapes sit at upper right. A red signature cartouche sits at lower left.
Small figures with straw hats and umbrellas, in yellow, green, and red, lean into the rain on the bridge.
interpretation: The print shows how far the style goes with asymmetry: the subject, the bridge, is pushed to one corner and cut by two edges.
Bokashi carries the weather. It is used at the top and bottom of the sheet, not to model the forms.
borrow: Use a strong diagonal that leaves the frame on two sides, and keep the open area flat.
Put a small saturated red label in a corner of a calm blue-gray field.

images.alt: Color woodblock print. Fine vertical rain lines fall over a gray-blue river and a dark storm cloud. A wooden bridge crosses diagonally from lower left to right, with small travellers under hats and umbrellas. Red title cartouches are at upper right and lower left.
images.caption: Utagawa Hiroshige, Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake, 1857. [Art Institute of Chicago 1925.3742](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/26545), Clarence Buckingham Collection. CC0.

rights.statement: The Art Institute of Chicago marks the object public domain (`is_public_domain: true`) and releases images of public-domain works under CC0. [AIC open access](https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). Hiroshige died in 1858, and the print was published in 1857, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Hochschule für Gestaltung building, Ulm
references.lede: Max Bill’s building for the Ulm School of Design (1953–1955): low volumes of bare concrete on a hillside, with ribbon windows in wooden frames.
references.summary: Bare grey concrete volumes on a slope, rows of wood-framed windows, and a thin flat entrance canopy. Max Bill, Ulm, 1953–1955.

evidence.note: Inspected two Wikimedia Commons photographs as 1280 px thumbnails: [HfGUlmbuilding 5.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HfGUlmbuilding_5.jpg) by Trop86 (30 May 2021, CC BY-SA 4.0) and [HfG Ulm Main Entrance](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HfG_Ulm_Main_Entrance_photo_by_Christian_G%C3%A4nshirt.JPG) by Christian Gänshirt (July 2014, CC BY-SA 4.0). These are recent views, so later repairs may differ from the 1955 state. No image is stored.

styles.note: The school’s own building: plain modular volumes and visible material, the architectural frame of the Ulm method.

context: Wikipedia: “In 1953 the new building was started, designed by Max Bill, and the inauguration took place on October 2, 1955.” The building “remains intact today” under the Foundation Ulm. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulm_School_of_Design).
A Commons description by Martin3d says that some rooms are now used by the HfG-Archiv Ulm. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hochschule_f%C3%BCr_Gestaltung,_Ulm.jpg).
observed: The volumes are low, flat-roofed boxes of bare grey concrete. They step down a grassy slope.
Windows run in rows of equal, nearly square panes with orange-brown wooden frames, the only warm color on the facade.
The entrance is a thin flat concrete canopy on two slim square posts.
Low concrete retaining walls and plain metal rails edge the paths.
The 2021 photograph shows a tall twisted stainless-steel column in the lawn. It is not identified here.
interpretation: The building shows the school’s method in architecture: modular parts, raw material, and no ornament. Its palette is concrete and wood, not the white and grey of the Braun products, so it fits the structure of the style more than its surface.
borrow: Repeat one window module along a long wall, and let one warm material frame it.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photographs are CC BY-SA 4.0, but the building is by Max Bill, who died in 1994, so it is protected in Germany. German freedom of panorama (§ 59 UrhG) probably permits exterior photographs. The lead curator can decide on an upgrade.

references.title: Hokusai, South Wind, Clear Sky (Red Fuji)
references.lede: Mount Fuji fills the right of the sheet as one red-brown triangle under a sky that darkens to Prussian blue at the top, from Hokusai’s Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.
references.summary: One red triangle, a bokashi blue sky, and rows of cloud. Katsushika Hokusai, early 1830s.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art print image of 1930.189 (3400 × 2329 px, viewed at 1600 × 1096).

styles.note: A canonical landscape print: one large flat shape placed off center, bokashi at the top of the sky and across the slope, and a title cartouche.

context: Cleveland catalogues the sheet as a color woodblock print, 25.6 × 37.5 cm, early 1830s, from Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, sometimes known as “Red Fuji.” [CMA 1930.189](https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.189).
Cleveland notes that the grain of the cherry-wood block printed onto the paper with the red dye. [CMA](https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.189).
observed: Mount Fuji is one large red-brown triangle at right. Its right slope runs off the right edge of the sheet.
The peak darkens to brown, with white snow streaks left as paper.
The sky fades from a dark Prussian-blue band at the top into a lighter blue, crossed by rows of cream cloud shapes with blue edges.
The lower slope is a dark blue-green field of small tree marks that fades upward into the red.
Wood grain is visible in the red area.
A narrow vertical cartouche with the series title is at upper left, with the signature in a column beside it.
interpretation: The print reduces the landscape to three areas, sky, mountain, and forest, so the bokashi transitions carry most of the depth.
The visible wood grain is a trace of the medium that flat digital color does not have.
borrow: Make one large, simple shape the whole composition, and let it leave the frame on one side.
Use a narrow vertical label in the empty corner opposite the main shape.

images.alt: Color woodblock print. A huge red-brown Mount Fuji with white snow streaks rises at right against a blue sky with rows of white clouds. Dark blue-green forest covers the lower left slope. A vertical title cartouche is at upper left.
images.caption: Katsushika Hokusai, South Wind, Clear Sky (Red Fuji), from Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, early 1830s. [Cleveland Museum of Art 1930.189](https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.189). CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art open access API gives `share_license_status: CC0` for this object. Hokusai died in 1849, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
references.lede: A Prussian-blue wave curls over three boats and frames a small Mount Fuji, in the most famous print of Hokusai’s Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.
references.summary: Blue wave, cream sky, and a tiny Fuji in an off-center composition. Katsushika Hokusai, 1830–1833.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Art Institute of Chicago image of impression 1925.3245 (1686 × 1155 px).

styles.note: A canonical landscape print: key-block outlines, flat Prussian blue, a dark bokashi band at the horizon, a title cartouche, and an asymmetric, cropped composition.

context: AIC catalogues the sheet as a color woodblock print, ōban format, 25.4 × 37.6 cm, signed “Hokusai aratame Iitsu fude”, published by Nishimura-ya Yohachi. [AIC 1925.3245](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/24645).

AIC’s description says that the series, begun in 1830, used the newly affordable Berlin (Prussian) blue for sky and water, and that it established the popularity of landscape prints. [AIC](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/24645).
observed: A large wave rises from the left and curls toward the center. Its crest breaks into claw-like white foam outlined in thin dark lines.
The wave is printed in two flat blues, a dark Prussian blue and a pale blue, with cream paper left for the foam.
Mount Fuji is small, near the center of the lower half, framed by the trough of the wave.
The sky is a flat buff tone. A dark gray band fades upward from the horizon behind Fuji.
A narrow vertical cartouche with a thin border holds the title at upper left. The signature runs in a vertical column beside it.
Three long boats cross the lower half. A second wave at right is cut by the edge of the sheet.
The pink tones that some impressions show on the boats and sky are not visible in this copy.
interpretation: The print shows the style’s main graphic devices together: one even key line, few flat colors, a gradient used only as a band, and a cropped, asymmetric composition.
The small Fuji against the large wave is the near–far contrast that Western artists took from these prints.
borrow: Let one large shape enter from one edge and crop at another, and put the real subject small inside it.
Use two values of one blue, dark and pale, with the paper color as the third tone.
