images.alt: Color woodblock print. A huge blue wave with white claw-like foam curls over three long boats. Small snow-capped Mount Fuji sits low in the trough. A vertical title cartouche is at upper left.
images.caption: Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa, 1830/33. [Art Institute of Chicago 1925.3245](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/24645), Clarence Buckingham Collection. CC0.

rights.statement: The Art Institute of Chicago marks the object public domain (`is_public_domain: true`) and releases images of public-domain works under CC0. [AIC open access](https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). Hokusai died in 1849, and the print was published about 1831, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Holiday Bowl coffee shop, Los Angeles
references.lede: The coffee shop of a 1958 Crenshaw Boulevard bowling alley, by Armet & Davis: a zigzag folded-plate roof whose beams shoot up past the eaves like tail fins.
references.summary: A folded-plate zigzag roof with upswept outrigger beams over a street front. Armet & Davis, Los Angeles, 1957–58.

source.label: Library of Congress: HABS CA-2775, Holiday Bowl, 3730 Crenshaw Boulevard, Los Angeles

creator.name: Armet & Davis (Louis Armet and Eldon Davis)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected HABS photographs 1, 11, 12, 26, and 28 of survey HABS CA-2775 (2002, black and white, 1024 px versions). Photographs 11 and 26 are stored. The photographs show the building in 2002, shortly before demolition, not as new.

styles.note: HABS names the coffee shop “a good architectural representative of the Googie style”; its zigzag roof and upswept beams are the style’s angular, lifting structure.

context: HABS significance statement: the Holiday Bowl was built in 1958, run by Japanese American businessmen, open 24 hours for shift workers, and “the ‘attached’ coffee shop stands out as a good architectural representative of the Googie style.” The coffee shop became a City of Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument on 19 December 2000. HABS gives construction dates of 1957–1958 and demolition after 2003. [Library of Congress, HABS CA-2775](https://www.loc.gov/item/ca3275/).
Wikipedia names the Holiday Bowl among the Googie work of Armet & Davis and of designer Helen Liu Fong. [Wikipedia: Googie architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Googie_architecture).

The HABS survey also holds copies of the 1957 construction drawings and a 1956 perspective sketch of the coffee shop (photographs 29–36). They were not stored, because HABS warns that images copied from other sources may be restricted.
observed: The roof of the coffee shop is a row of folded plates: each bay rises to a ridge and drops to a valley, so the eave line is a continuous zigzag.
Above each ridge a pair of thin beams crosses and runs past the roof edge, ending in upswept points against the sky.
The undersides of the folded plates are smooth and carry round recessed lights.
Script lettering (“...lday” and “open”) is fixed to the fascia above the roof. In photograph 1 a tall pylon carries a “BOWL” panel in irregular capitals and a “COFFEE SHOP” panel.
Inside, the folded plates read as tall pitched bays over a long counter with low stools; pendant lamps hang on chains and a glass wall runs along one side.
The photographs are black and white, so they show no color.
interpretation: The zigzag roof and the beams that pierce it are the Googie habit of making the structure itself the sign: from a car the roofline reads as an energetic pattern, not as a shelter.
Wikipedia quotes a 1999 description of orange-and-green decor; the HABS photographs cannot confirm this.
borrow: Use a repeating zigzag or sawtooth edge on a header or card top to give a panel lift.
Let thin lines cross a panel and run past its edge, ending in points, like the outrigger beams.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a low street-front building with a zigzag roof edge; pairs of thin beams cross above each roof ridge and project up past the edge. The wall below is covered with pasted posters.
images.caption: Holiday Bowl coffee shop, west side, facing northeast. HABS CA-2775, photograph 11, 2002. [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/ca3275.photos.218525p/). The pasted posters on the wall (films and music, 2002) are incidental third-party works.

images.alt: Black-and-white interior: a long counter with low stools under a ceiling of tall pitched folded bays, with pendant lamps on chains and a glass wall at left.
images.caption: Holiday Bowl coffee shop interior, facing north. HABS CA-2775, photograph 26, 2002. [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/ca3275.photos.218540p/).

rights.statement: Library of Congress rights advisory: “No known restrictions on images made by the U.S. Government; images copied from other sources may be restricted.” The stored images are HABS field photographs, not copies. The building was finished in 1958 in the United States, before December 1990, so it is not protected as an architectural work.

references.title: Hotline Miami
references.lede: Dennaton Games’ 2012 top-down action game set in Miami in 1989: hot-pink and violet pixel art, wobbling magenta screens, and a soundtrack of synthwave artists.
references.summary: Top-down pixel art in hot pink, violet, and teal, set in 1989 Miami, with a synthwave soundtrack. 2012.

creator.name: Dennaton Games (Jonatan Söderström and Dennis Wedin)

evidence.note: Inspected a 1920 × 1080 gameplay screenshot and the 1920 × 620 library artwork from [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/219150/) in a scratch folder. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: one of the works that spread the synthwave sound and its pink-violet night palette, palms, and 1980s Miami setting, but in pixel art and without the grid and sun.
Clear: top-down pixel-art sprites and rooms on one coarse grid, in a neon palette.

context: Wikipedia: the game was released on Steam on 23 October 2012. Dennaton Games is “Swedish designer and programmer Jonatan Söderström and artist Dennis Wedin.” It is “Set in Miami in 1989.” Its graphics use “pixel art with a high-contrast colour palette.” [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotline_Miami).

Wikipedia: the film *Drive* (2011) inspired the creators, and the soundtrack “combines many music genres like electronic, techno, vaporwave, and synthwave”, with artists including M.O.O.N. and Perturbator.
The [synthwave](style:synthwave) record names *Hotline Miami* among the works that spread the look.
observed: The gameplay screenshot shows rooms from directly above in chunky pixel art: a pink rug, teal walls, cream sofas, and blood splatter.
The area outside the building is a flat hot-pink to magenta gradient, not black.
Scores such as “6501pts” and “+600PTS” are set in a wobbly, wide pixel script with a dark drop shadow, in cream, magenta, and teal.
The library artwork is a painted crowd of men in pale 1980s suits around a figure in a pig mask and a letterman jacket, under a dark violet night sky with lit windows and palm silhouettes.
interpretation: It belongs to the synthwave story more through sound, setting, and palette than through the Outrun scene. Its colours are the style’s magenta and teal, but they fill whole areas rather than glowing on black.
borrow: Set score numbers in a wide, wobbling display face in magenta and teal on a dark plate.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The game and its artwork are in copyright (Dennaton Games / Devolver Digital, 2012).

references.title: Hyper Scrypt typeface, Velvetyne
references.lede: An open-source stencil display face by Jérémy Landes that draws gothic letters as heavy, molten-looking black shapes cut by thin channels, after the lead lines of stained glass.
references.summary: Heavy gothic stencil letters with molten curves and thin cuts. Jérémy Landes, Velvetyne, 2018, SIL Open Font License.

evidence.note: Downloaded the web font `hyperscrypt-stencil.woff` from the Velvetyne page and rendered “HYPER SCRYPT”, “MY LORD BELZEBUTH”, and a pair alphabet at 90–170 px in a 1400 px scratch image with Pillow. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: a free gothic display face whose designer cites molten metal and heavy metal. It supplies the blackletter-metal letterforms of the style, but it is flat and needs a chrome treatment to read as the core.

context: Velvetyne: “The Hyper Scrypt typeface was designed for the Hyper Chapelle exhibition. It was commissioned by AAAAA Atelier to Studio Triple's designer Jérémy Landes.” It is “a modern stencil typeface inspired by the stained glass technique used in the Metz cathedral”. [Velvetyne](https://velvetyne.fr/fonts/hyper-scrypt/).

Velvetyne: Hyper Scrypt “is at the intersection between 3 metals : the sacred lead of stained glass, the lead of print characters and the heavy metal. Despite its organic look inherited for the molted metal, Hyper Scrypt is based upon a rigorous grid”.
The page gives the license as SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1, and one style, Stencil.
observed: Letters are heavy black slabs with rounded corners, split by thin horizontal and diagonal channels, so that each letter reads as several cast pieces.
The forms mix straight gothic verticals with swelling, liquid curves in letters such as S, O, and C.
Counters are small, and the letters sit close, so lines read as a dense black band.
All rendered letters share one cap height. Upper and lower case look much alike.
interpretation: The face gives a designer a free, legal blackletter-and-metal display type for the style. With a chrome gradient and a black ground it would come close to the core look. Alone it is a gothic stencil.
borrow: Use a gothic stencil for one display word and fill it with a chrome gradient.
Let thin channels cut through heavy letters to suggest cast metal.

rights.statement: The font software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 (Velvetyne). No specimen image is stored, because no openly licensed image of the typeface was found and the design itself is not public domain.

references.title: In the Evening, Lying on Her Bed, She Reread the Letter from Her Artilleryman at the Front
references.titleBreak: In the Evening, Lying on Her Bed,|She Reread the Letter from Her Artilleryman at the Front
references.lede: F. T. Marinetti’s best-known words-in-freedom plate: a woman reads a letter from the front, and the page explodes with the sounds of the battle it describes, in letters of every size, face, and angle.
references.summary: Onomatopoeia in huge mixed capitals, black hooks and wedges, and a small silhouette of a woman lying down. F. T. Marinetti, 1917, published 1919.

source.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Le Soir, couchée dans son lit, elle relisait la lettre de son artilleur au front (1995.511.1)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Met’s image as uploaded to [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:In_the_Evening,_Lying_on_Her_Bed,_She_Reread_the_Letter_from_Her_Artilleryman_at_the_Front_(Le_Soir,_Couch%C3%A9e_dans_son_lit,_elle_relisait_la_lettre_de_son_artilleur_au_front),_published_in_Les_Mots_en_libert%C3%A9_futuristes_MET_DP371749.jpg) (original 2690 × 3877 px; a 1110 × 1600 px rendering was inspected and stored). The physical copy is the Met’s sheet, accession number 1995.511.1, as stated in the Commons record. The Met API and website were not read directly.

styles.note: A canonical words-in-freedom page: many typefaces and sizes, words at all angles, huge onomatopoeia, and shapes of force, all in one ink.

context: Letterpress, 34.9 × 23.2 cm. Created 1917 and published 1919 in Marinetti’s book *Les mots en liberté futuristes*. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Drawings and Prints, 1995.511.1, gift of W. Michael Sheehe, 1995. [Commons record from the Met](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:In_the_Evening,_Lying_on_Her_Bed,_She_Reread_the_Letter_from_Her_Artilleryman_at_the_Front_(Le_Soir,_Couch%C3%A9e_dans_son_lit,_elle_relisait_la_lettre_de_son_artilleur_au_front),_published_in_Les_Mots_en_libert%C3%A9_futuristes_MET_DP371749.jpg).
The Art Institute of Chicago also holds *Les mots en liberté futuristes* (Milan: Edizioni futuriste di “Poesia”, 1919), object 238061, but marks it as not public domain.
observed: At the top, “SCRABrrrRrraaNNG” runs in mixed capitals and lower case of different faces and sizes.
Below, a huge black hook shape holds the small word “futurista”.
Across the middle, “GRAAAAG” and “TRAC” are set in very large letters that tilt in different directions, some serif and some sans serif.
Small lines such as “tumb tumb-tumb-tumb-tumb” and “FUUM PAMPAM” are set in tiny bold type between the giant letters.
Words “SIMULTANEITÀ” and “ESPLOSIONE” run at steep angles near the center; letters “A” and “SCHI” scatter outward like fragments.
Rows of small letters at upper right curve like a trajectory; handwritten lines are reproduced at upper right and lower left.
A second black hook points from the lower left into the center; a black silhouette of a reclining woman sits at lower right.
Printed in black only on brown-buff paper with a center fold.
interpretation: The page turns a letter into the battle it describes: the reading woman is small and quiet in the corner, and the war is the typography. Size and angle stand for loudness and direction.
The black hook shapes act as lines of force and organize the scattered words into two sweeping movements.
borrow: Use letter size as volume: one shouted word many times larger than the text around it.
Mix serif and sans serif capitals inside one word.
Set a small quiet figure or line against the noise to give scale.
Use one ink only and let angles and sizes do the work.

images.alt: Black letterpress on buff paper: the words SCRABrrrRrraaNNG, GRAAAAG, and TRAC in huge mixed letters at different angles, small lines of onomatopoeia between them, two large black hook shapes, scattered letters, and a black silhouette of a reclining woman at lower right.
images.caption: F. T. Marinetti, *Le Soir, couchée dans son lit, elle relisait la lettre de son artilleur au front*, created 1917, published 1919 in *Les mots en liberté futuristes*, letterpress. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1995.511.1. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:In_the_Evening,_Lying_on_Her_Bed,_She_Reread_the_Letter_from_Her_Artilleryman_at_the_Front_(Le_Soir,_Couch%C3%A9e_dans_son_lit,_elle_relisait_la_lettre_de_son_artilleur_au_front),_published_in_Les_Mots_en_libert%C3%A9_futuristes_MET_DP371749.jpg), CC0.

rights.statement: The Metropolitan Museum of Art released the image under CC0 through its Open Access programme. Marinetti was Italian and died in 1944, more than 70 years ago, so the work is public domain in Italy. It was published in 1919, before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States. The Art Institute of Chicago marks its copy of the book as not public domain; its image was not used.

identifiers.commons: File:In the Evening, Lying on Her Bed, She Reread the Letter from Her Artilleryman at the Front (Le Soir, Couchée dans son lit, elle relisait la lettre de son artilleur au front), published in Les Mots en liberté futuristes MET DP371749.jpg

references.title: Intonarumori (noise intoners)
references.lede: Luigi Russolo and Ugo Piatti stand among their intonarumori, wooden boxes with large metal horns built to play the music of Russolo’s manifesto The Art of Noises.
references.summary: Box-shaped noise machines with flaring horns, built by Luigi Russolo and Ugo Piatti in Milan, photographed c. 1913.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Luigi Russolo and assistant Ugo Piatti in their Milan studio with Intonarumori, 1913

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 2301 × 1821 px; a 1280 × 1013 px rendering was inspected and stored). The file is a photograph of a printed reproduction of the period photograph, by an unknown photographer. Commons says it was first published with Russolo’s *The Art of Noises*. The instruments themselves are lost: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intonarumori) says most were destroyed in Paris during the Second World War.

styles.note: The Futurist programme of noise and machines made into objects: musical instruments designed as plain industrial boxes and horns. Partial fit: the visual grammar of type and lines of force is absent.

context: Russolo invented and built the intonarumori from about 1910 to 1930, in 27 varieties. A wheel touched a string attached to a drum; a handle changed the string’s tension and pitch; a horn amplified the sound. [Wikipedia: Intonarumori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intonarumori).
They were built to perform the music described in Russolo’s 1913 manifesto *The Art of Noises*, published as a book in 1916. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intonarumori).

The Commons description names the men as Russolo and his assistant Ugo Piatti in their Milan studio. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Luigi_Russolo_and_assistant_Ugo_Piatti_in_their_Milan_studio_with_Intonarumori,_L%E2%80%99Arte_dei_rumori_(The_Art_of_Noises),_1913.jpg).
observed: About fifteen instruments are stacked across the room. Each is a plain dark rectangular box with a large flaring metal horn, aimed in different directions.
The horns are smooth cones with a bright rim; there is no ornament on the boxes, only small handles and fittings.
Two men in suits stand behind the instruments at the center.
A tall cabinet with pipes stands at right; the floor has a hexagonal tile pattern and a lamp hangs from the ceiling.
The print is sepia with a strong glare at upper left.
interpretation: The instruments look like machinery, not like orchestral instruments. The pile of horns pointing in many directions is itself an image of simultaneous noise.
The photograph has become an emblem of the movement’s aim to bring industrial sound into art.
borrow: Repeat one simple industrial form, such as a horn or cone, in many sizes and directions to suggest noise.
Show sound as direction: aim shapes outward from a cluster.

images.alt: Sepia photograph of a room filled with dark box-shaped instruments with large flaring metal horns pointing in different directions. Two men in suits stand behind them; a lamp hangs from the ceiling and the floor has hexagonal tiles.
images.caption: Luigi Russolo and Ugo Piatti with the intonarumori in their Milan studio, c. 1913, photographer unknown. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Luigi_Russolo_and_assistant_Ugo_Piatti_in_their_Milan_studio_with_Intonarumori,_L%E2%80%99Arte_dei_rumori_(The_Art_of_Noises),_1913.jpg), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain and says the photograph was first published with Russolo’s *The Art of Noises* (manifesto 1913, book 1916). Publication before 1931 makes it public domain in the United States. In Italy, a simple photograph is protected for 20 years from production, and Russolo (died 1947) and Piatti (died 1953) died more than 70 years ago, so the instruments shown are also public domain.

identifiers.commons: File:Luigi Russolo and assistant Ugo Piatti in their Milan studio with Intonarumori, L’Arte dei rumori (The Art of Noises), 1913.jpg

references.title: iOS 14 Home Screen widgets
references.lede: The 2020 iPhone Home Screen on which widgets of three sizes sit in the same grid as the app icons.
references.summary: Rounded widgets in small, medium, and large sizes share one grid with app icons on the iPhone Home Screen. iOS 14, 2020.

source.label: Apple Newsroom: Apple reimagines the iPhone experience with iOS 14 (2020-06-22)

evidence.note: Inspected the press image `Apple_ios14-widgets-redesigned_06222020_inline.jpg.large_2x.jpg` (1306 × 1770) from the Apple Newsroom release. It is an Apple marketing render of the Home Screen, not a device screenshot. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit, as a precursor: rounded tiles of three sizes share one grid with even gaps, but app icons and a wallpaper fill the rest of the screen.

context: Apple’s release says that the new widgets “present timely information at a glance and can be pinned in different sizes on any Home Screen page”.
The WWDC 2020 summary slide for iOS 14 shows the widgets in one of its tiles ([slide](ref:apple-wwdc-2020-ios-14-summary-slide)).
observed: An iPhone shows a Home Screen over an orange, red, blue, and grey wallpaper of large curved shapes.

Three widgets sit in the icon grid: a black Activity widget the size of four icons, a Photos widget of the same size with a portrait and the white condensed words “FRIENDS Sep 10, 2019”, and a white Music widget with an album cover.
The widgets have the same large corner radius as the app icons, scaled up, and they line up with the icon rows and columns.
The Activity widget sets its figures large in three colors on black: “375/500CAL” in red, “19/30MIN” in yellow-green, and “4/12HRS” in cyan.
interpretation: Widgets in fixed multiples of the icon cell are a bento grid in miniature, and Apple shipped them on every iPhone two years before the name spread. Interpretation: no source in this record says that the widgets inspired the web trend.
borrow: Size tiles as whole multiples of one base cell (1 × 1, 2 × 2, 4 × 2), so that any mix of tiles lines up.
Give a status tile a dark fill and set its figures large in a few signal colors.

rights.statement: Apple press image and software; copyrighted by Apple Inc. No image is stored here.

references.title: iOS 26 Home Screen
references.lede: The iPhone Home Screen of iOS 26, shown in Apple’s launch images with clear, dark, and default Liquid Glass looks.
references.summary: iPhone Home Screen in clear, dark, and default glass looks. Apple, 2025.

evidence.note: Inspected the Apple Newsroom image Apple-WWDC25-iOS-26-Home-Screen-customization-250609 (1960 × 1102, large_2x variant) in a scratchpad copy. It is a press render, not a device photo. Not stored.

styles.note: Apple’s own launch image of the Home Screen, with clear glass icons and widgets and a floating search capsule.

context: Apple: iOS 26 is “crafted with Liquid Glass — a new translucent material that reflects and refracts its surroundings”. It brings “new customization options to app icons and widgets, including a stunning clear look”. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/06/apple-elevates-the-iphone-experience-with-ios-26/).
The same release says that on the Lock Screen “the time fluidly adapts to the available space in an image”, and that in Safari web pages flow from the top edge to the bottom of the screen.
observed: Three iPhones on white show one blue-and-teal wave wallpaper with three icon looks: clear (left), dark (middle), and default color (right).
In the clear look, icons and widgets are colorless glass tiles. The wallpaper shows through, and each tile has a bright rim on its upper-left edge and a darker lower edge.
A small “Search” capsule floats above the Dock. The Dock is one wide glass platter inset from the screen edges, with corners that follow the rounded screen.
Widget text is white and thin-weighted on glass. The weather widget in the right phone takes a darker blue tint from the wallpaper.
interpretation: The clear look is the style at its purest and at its weakest: the glass becomes almost invisible, and labels depend on the wallpaper for contrast.
borrow: Light only one edge of a glass tile and let the opposite edge go darker. This reads as thickness without a drawn border.

rights.statement: Apple press image of copyrighted software. No image is stored here.

references.related: See also the overview record [Apple Liquid Glass](ref:apple-liquid-glass-2025).

references.title: Jack Smith and Jeremy Rieger, “Lotus” artwork
references.lede: A square artwork in gray and violet: a melted-chrome flower in an arched frame, a tall liquid display word, op-art spirals, and Japanese katakana.
references.summary: Liquid-chrome flower, melted display lettering, violet op-art rings and spirals on a scratched black ground. Jack Smith and Jeremy Rieger.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2019): “Acid Graphics” Are the New Psychedelia

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px image `Lotus-By-Jack-Smith-and-Jeremy-Rieger.jpg` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) published with the article, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image as the magazine published it, not a named physical copy. The caption reads “Lotus by Jack Smith and Jeremy Rieger, as featured on @acidgraphix”.

styles.note: Liquid-metal imagery, melted display letters, op-art rings, and horror vacui on black. The accent is violet, not green.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) shows the work in its 2019 article on acid graphics, with the caption “Lotus by Jack Smith and Jeremy Rieger, as featured on @acidgraphix”.
observed: The ground is black with scratches and dust, like a worn sleeve.
A flower in an arched frame is rendered as melted, reflective gray chrome with hard black contours.
A tall word runs down the left in melted, wavy pale-gray letters, with violet ivy growing over it. Katakana run down the right and across the lower left.
Violet concentric rings form a long capsule at the top. Black-and-white op-art spirals and violet dots run down the right edge.
Small pseudo-script text sits in violet at the lower right.
interpretation: The work has the liquid-chrome surface, the melted lettering, and the op-art patterns of the style in a dense layout. Its violet accent shows that acid green is common but not required.
borrow: Put a liquid-chrome image in an arched frame and surround it with op-art spirals.
Draw one display word as melted, wavy letters and let a plant motif grow over it.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright. The rights holder is the designer or the client.

references.title: Jan-Willem Doornenbal, Riso Fort Zuid Wilgen
references.lede: A scan of an A3 three-color riso print of willows reflected in water, in blue, yellow, and black.
references.summary: Scan of a three-color A3 riso photo print in blue, yellow, and black.

source.label: Flickr: Jan-Willem Doornenbal, “Riso Fort Zuid Wilgen”

evidence.note: Viewed the 1024 × 726 px Flickr “large” file, a flatbed scan of the whole sheet, so the color is closer to the print than in a photograph.

styles.note: Three spot inks separate a photograph, with banding and grain from the drum.

context: The Flickr description says: “Scan van een 3-kleuren risoprint op A3-formaat. Blauw, geel en zwart.” (Scan of a three-color riso print in A3 format. Blue, yellow, and black.)
observed: The photograph is split into three inks: a mid blue for water, a pale yellow for the far bank, and black for branches.
Blue and yellow overlap into green in the trees at the left.
Large blue areas show fine horizontal banding and grain near the lower edge.
The image is printed with a wide white paper margin.
interpretation: Riso separations do not reproduce full color. They turn a photograph into a few flat, translucent layers.
borrow: Split an image into two or three ink layers with hard thresholds instead of a smooth full-color photo.

images.alt: A scanned print of willow branches reflected in water, in blue, pale yellow, and black, with a white margin.
images.caption: Jan-Willem Doornenbal, *Riso Fort Zuid Wilgen*, 2025. CC BY 2.0. [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/mededeler/54312665558/), 1024 px “large” size.

rights.statement: Published by the author on Flickr under CC BY 2.0. The author licenses a scan of his own print. Credit: Jan-Willem Doornenbal.

references.title: Jan-Willem Doornenbal, Risoprint Meerpaaltjes
references.lede: A two-color riso print of mooring posts and reeds mirrored in water, in a warm pink and a blue that overprint into violet.
references.summary: Two-color riso photo print in pink and blue, overprinting into violet.

evidence.note: Viewed the 1024 × 577 px Flickr “large” file, a photograph of one sheet. The pink looks warmer and duller than fluorescent ink usually does, possibly because of the camera.

styles.note: Two inks overprint into a third color, with grain and uneven coverage.

context: The Flickr description says: “Vier foto's van paaltjes en riet, gespiegeld in het water.” (Four photos of posts and reeds, mirrored in the water.)
observed: Two inks: a salmon pink and a blue.
Where they overlap, the color is violet, especially in the reeds and reflections.
The ink is patchy, and paper shows through in streaks.
The image fills a long horizontal band with an off-white margin.
interpretation: The work depends on overprint: the violet is not an ink but the overlap of two translucent layers.
borrow: Print the same image in two inks, slightly different in threshold, so the overlap draws the shadows.

images.alt: A wide print of wooden posts and reeds reflected in water, in pink and blue that mix into violet.
images.caption: Jan-Willem Doornenbal, *Risoprint Meerpaaltjes*, 2024. CC BY 2.0. [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/mededeler/53561560559/), 1024 px “large” size.

rights.statement: Published by the author on Flickr under CC BY 2.0. The author licenses a photograph of his own print. Credit: Jan-Willem Doornenbal.

references.title: Joe Crawford (artlung), Cube Cat’s Drink
references.lede: A letter-size multi-color riso print of a punk cat in a spiked jacket, in a hand-numbered edition of 25, with heavy grain in every ink.
references.summary: Multi-color riso illustration with heavy grain, edition of 25.

source.label: Flickr: Joe Crawford, “Do You Want To Art Trade?!”

creator.name: Joe Crawford (artlung); printed by @burn_all_books, as the post states

evidence.note: Viewed the 1024 × 1024 px Flickr “large” file, a photograph of a stack of prints. The top sheet is signed in pencil “25/25 ‘Cube Cat’s Drink’ Sep 2020” and carries an “ARTLUNG” mark.

styles.note: Partial fit: several riso inks, strong grain, and overprinted mixes, but more inks and a fuller color image than the two-ink core.

context: The Flickr title says: “‘Cube Cat’s Drink’ is Riso printed by the amazing @burn_all_books at 8-1/2"x11".” The post offers the print for art trades. The “ARTLUNG” mark matches the uploader’s Flickr name.
observed: Blue, yellow, pink, and a dark ink build the image. Their overlaps give green, orange, and purple.
The blue night sky is a coarse grain with white speckles.
The drawing has fine dark line work, and the inks fill it in loose, grainy areas.
A wide white paper margin holds the pencil edition number and title.
interpretation: Grain is the image’s main texture: the fills are deliberately rough, and the paper shows through.
borrow: Use a coarse speckle in a dark ink for a sky or background instead of a gradient.

images.alt: A stack of prints; the top one shows a grinning cat in a spiked jacket in grainy blue, orange, pink, and green, signed in pencil.
images.caption: Joe Crawford (artlung), *Cube Cat’s Drink*, 2020. CC BY 2.0. [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/artlung/50665147228/), 1024 px “large” size.

rights.statement: Published on Flickr under CC BY 2.0 by Joe Crawford, whose “ARTLUNG” mark is on the print. Credit: Joe Crawford.

references.title: Jonathan Castro, lettering for a Skechers China project
references.lede: Four lines of spiky chrome lettering on black, each wrapped in a different neon glow, for a Skechers project in China.
references.summary: Spiky, bevelled chrome lettering with acid yellow-green, pink, and blue glows on black. Jonathan Castro, before 2019.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2019): “Acid Graphics” Are the New Psychedelia

references.made: Before September 2019 (the article does not give a year)

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px image `Jonathan-Castro-skechers-china-jonathan-castro-.jpg` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) published with the article, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image as the magazine published it, not a named physical copy. The caption reads “Jonathan Castro. Skechers China project”.

styles.note: A direct example of the chrome-type core: bevelled liquid-metal letters with thorny spurs, an acid accent, and glows on black.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) shows this image in its 2019 article on acid graphics, with the caption “Jonathan Castro. Skechers China project”. The article does not say what the project was or when it ran.
observed: Four lines of lettering are centred on a pure black ground: “2028” (or similar) with Chinese characters, “SKECHERS”, “MOVE”, and a long wide word that is hard to read.
The letters are rendered as polished, bevelled chrome with gray-to-white reflections and dark bands.
Thorny spurs and blade-like points grow from the letterforms. Some lines are drawn in hairline outlines, others as solid chrome.
Each line has a different glow or outline: acid yellow-green, hot pink, cyan, or electric blue. Acid yellow-green also fills streaks inside the chrome.
Lines overlap each other, and legibility is low.
interpretation: The work shows the style at its most concentrated: chrome as the material of the letters, spiky custom letterforms, and neon accents on black. It is close to Y2K in its chrome, but its sharp spurs and aggressive tone separate it.
borrow: Grow thorny spurs from a few stroke ends of a wide display face, and render the letters as chrome.
Give each display line its own single accent glow on a black ground.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright. The rights holder is the designer or the client.

references.title: Julia Ballmann, “Pppanik” liquid-chrome numerals
references.lede: The numerals “2009” drawn as melted, iridescent chrome blobs, alone on a black square.
references.summary: “2009” as melted, iridescent liquid chrome on black. Julia Ballmann, Pppanik.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2019): “Acid Graphics” Are the New Psychedelia

references.made: Not stated. The caption reads “Pppanik, 2009”, and “2009” is also the content of the image, so the year may be the title, not the date.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px image `Julia-Ballmann-Pppanik-2009.jpg` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) published with the article, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image as the magazine published it, not a named physical copy. The caption reads “Julia Ballmann, Pppanik, 2009”.

styles.note: Liquid-metal type, the trait that Eye on Design describes as “viscously dripping liquid metal”, here with no other element.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) shows the image in its 2019 article on acid graphics, with the caption “Julia Ballmann, Pppanik, 2009”.
observed: Four numerals, “2009”, sit in the middle of a square black ground with nothing else.
The numerals are tubes of glossy, melted metal. Their outlines wobble like poured liquid, and the counters are irregular.
The surface reflects white highlights and iridescent violet, blue, cyan, and green, like oil on chrome.
The first numeral keeps a flat, square-cut edge on one side, so it reads as a melted solid letter rather than a drawn outline.
interpretation: The image isolates the liquid-chrome lettering of the style. It has no acid green and no layout, so it shows that the metal effect alone can carry the look.
borrow: Render a short word or number as melted iridescent chrome and give it a whole black field.
Keep one straight cut edge on a melted letter so that it still reads as type.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright. The rights holder is the designer or the client.

references.title: Kabukichō in a rainstorm at night
references.lede: A narrow street in Tokyo’s Kabukichō entertainment district during heavy rain: stacked vertical signs in pink, green, and white, and their reflections on the wet asphalt.
references.summary: Pink-lit facades, vertical Japanese signs, and a rain-wet street at night. Photograph by Benlisquare, Shinjuku, Tokyo, 2024.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Kabukicho during rainstorm at night.jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons 1920 px rendition of the 4000 × 3000 px original. The file description reads “Kabukichō at night, during a heavy rainstorm.”

styles.note: Partial fit: a real street of the kind the genre took as its model, with rain, reflections, and vertical neon signs in Japanese. It has no HUD frames or terminal text.

context: Wikipedia’s [Cyberpunk article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk) quotes William Gibson: “Modern Japan simply was cyberpunk.” He describes Shibuya’s “towering, animated crawl of commercial information” and a journalist saying “It is Blade Runner”. See [Blade Runner](ref:blade-runner-1982) and [Akira](ref:akira-film-1988).

Kabukichō is an entertainment and red-light district in Shinjuku, Tokyo. The photograph is in the Commons category “Kabukichō Sakura Street at night”. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kabukicho_during_rainstorm_at_night.jpg).
observed: The left side is a wall of yellow, red, and blue illuminated panels edged with green and blue LED strips.
The buildings on the right are washed in pink light. Vertical signs read “ROBOT★RESTAURANT”, “NEO TOKIO”, and “Shisha Alchemist 3F” with Japanese text, and floor numbers such as “1F” and “B1”.
The asphalt is wet and reflects pink and yellow light in long streaks. Rain is visible against the black sky.
A black van stands in the center. Paper lanterns and a backlit menu board are at lower right.
The sky and the upper buildings are near-black. Almost all light comes from the signs.
interpretation: The photograph shows where the style’s palette comes from: no daylight, all light emitted by signs, and a wet ground that doubles it.
The colors here are warmer and more varied (pink, yellow, green) than the cyan-and-magenta palette of designed cyberpunk graphics. Designers reduce this to two or three hues.
borrow: Light a dark composition only from its signs and labels, and add a soft reflection below a bright element.
Stack short labels vertically, with floor or level codes such as “3F” and “B1”, as data.

images.alt: A narrow street at night in heavy rain. Bright yellow and red illuminated panels line the left; pink-lit buildings with vertical signs in Japanese and English line the right. A black van stands on the wet, reflecting road.
images.caption: Kabukichō, Shinjuku, Tokyo, during a rainstorm, 7 August 2024. Photograph by Benlisquare, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kabukicho_during_rainstorm_at_night.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0. Shop signs and advertising appear incidentally as part of the street.

rights.statement: Photograph by Benlisquare, “Own work”, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons. The main subject is a public street. Shop signs, logos, and a printed advertisement appear as incidental parts of the street scene, not as the subject.

references.title: Käpt’n Börgers Piratennest (PixelPlaza)
references.lede: A small isometric pirate harbor from the German pixel art community PixelPlaza, with a timber house, a fort wall, a ship, and figures a few pixels tall.
references.summary: Isometric pirate lair on a rock, with a timber house, a galleon, palms, and turquoise water. Boerger, PixelPlaza, 2008, CC BY-SA 3.0.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Pixel-Art Käpt'n Börgers Piratennest.gif

evidence.note: Downloaded the Commons file (216 × 146 px, one frame, about 250 colors) and inspected it enlarged 5× to 1080 × 730 px.

styles.note: Partial fit: hand-placed pixels at a fixed scale with tiny figures, but in the isometric branch that the style record lists as related, with many more colors than the 8-bit core.

context: Commons describes the file as “Artwork from the German pixel art community named PixelPlaza, depicting a pirates’ lair”, author Boerger (@pixelplaza.de), dated 11 April 2008, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pixel-Art_K%C3%A4pt%27n_B%C3%B6rgers_Piratennest.gif).
Wikipedia names isometric pixel art as a common form, with Habbo Hotel and eBoy as examples. [Wikipedia: Pixel art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel_art).
observed: A harbor seen from above at an isometric angle, on a white ground: a timber-framed house with a brown roof, a jetty on stilts, a gray stone fort wall, and a tower on a rock.
A brown galleon with two masts lies in turquoise water. A red parrot sits on the wall.
Figures are about 5 to 8 pixels tall.
Walls and roofs follow stepped two-to-one diagonals.
Rock and stone are shaded with many close tones and scattered single pixels, so the texture looks noisy rather than flat.
No smooth gradient appears. White spray pixels mark the waves at the rock.
interpretation: The piece shows the community form of pixel art in the 2000s: a self-contained scene for its own sake, not a game asset.
Its many tones and textured rock move away from the flat 8-bit palette. Use it for the isometric branch, not as a model for interfaces.
borrow: Draw isometric edges with a regular two-pixels-across, one-pixel-down step.
Give tiny figures one bright color each so that they read against a detailed ground.

images.alt: Isometric pixel-art pirate harbor on white: a brown timber house on a jetty, a gray stone fort wall and tower on a rock, palm trees, and a brown two-masted ship in turquoise water.
images.caption: Boerger (PixelPlaza), “Käpt’n Börgers Piratennest”, 2008, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pixel-Art_K%C3%A4pt%27n_B%C3%B6rgers_Piratennest.gif), CC BY-SA 3.0. Enlarged 4× with nearest-neighbor scaling and saved as PNG.

rights.statement: Commons license: CC BY-SA 3.0, author Boerger (@pixelplaza.de). The enlarged copy here is shared under the same license.

references.title: Kavinsky, OutRun (album cover)
references.lede: The cover of Kavinsky’s 2013 album: a red Ferrari Testarossa with its headlights on and a man in silhouette under lightning, with a red-and-blue brush-script name.
references.summary: Red Testarossa, palm silhouette, lightning, red-and-blue script “Kavinsky”. Album cover, 2013.

creator.name: Charlotte Delarue (art direction); The Directors Bureau Special Projects (design concept, photography)

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px front-cover image from the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release/e07d3a7a-e3e4-4786-b758-27715e830652/cover-art) in a scratch folder. Not stored. Credits are from the [Discogs record of the US CD](https://www.discogs.com/release/4384034-Kavinsky-OutRun) (Record Makers, Casablanca, Republic, B0018156-02).

styles.note: The album that named the Outrun look after the 1986 Sega game: a Testarossa, palms, a night sky, and a neon brush-script logotype.

context: Wikipedia: the album was “released on 22 February 2013 by Record Makers, Vertigo Records and Mercury Records” and is “named after Sega’s 1986 arcade game of the same name, which featured the Ferrari Testarossa.” The cover shows “a red Ferrari Testarossa with its headlights on, and a silhouette of a man with clouds behind them.” [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OutRun_(album)).

Wikipedia: Kavinsky’s backstory is of a young man who crashed his Testarossa in 1986 and came back in 2006 as a zombie who makes electronic music, and the visual style draws on 1980s video games, *Miami Vice*, and the films of Dario Argento.

Discogs credits art direction to Charlotte Delarue, the design concept and photography to The Directors Bureau Special Projects, image manipulation to Adrien Blanchat, and the film stills to director Marcus Herring. [Discogs](https://www.discogs.com/release/4384034-Kavinsky-OutRun).
The [synthwave](style:synthwave) record cites PC Gamer: the Testarossa and palm trees on this cover reference the game.
observed: Black bands fill the top and bottom quarters, so the picture reads as a wide letterboxed film frame across the middle.
The frame is a misty blue night: a palm tree and dark foliage at the left, white forked lightning at the upper right.
A red Ferrari Testarossa sits low across the centre with one headlight on and a beam of light to the right. A man in a jacket stands in silhouette at the right.
“Kavinsky” runs across the upper left in a red, dry-brush script with a blue offset shadow. “OUTRUN” sits under it in small, widely spaced pale capitals.
There is no grid, no sun, and no chrome type.
interpretation: This is the photographic, cinematic branch of the style: the car, the palm, and the night carry the period, and a neon-like script carries the logo. It shows that the grid and the sun are not required when the car and the script are present.
borrow: Letterbox a hero image between black bands to make it read as a film still.
Pair a fast brush-script name with a small, widely tracked capital subtitle.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The cover art is in copyright (Record Makers and Republic Records, 2013).

references.title: Kenney 1-Bit Pack
references.lede: Kenney’s public-domain sheet of more than 1,000 game tiles draws every tree, wall, monster, weapon, icon, and letter on a 16-pixel grid with a few flat colors.
references.summary: A tilesheet of one-color 16 × 16 icons, tiles, and letters on dark plum, with a few accent colors. Kenney, 2019–2020, CC0.
references.made: Posted on OpenGameArt 6 May 2019; version 1.1 dated 6 May 2020 in its License.txt

evidence.note: Downloaded `1bitpack_kenney_1.1.zip` from the OpenGameArt page and inspected `Tilesheet/colored_packed.png` (768 × 352 px) enlarged 2× to 1536 × 704 px. The file has exactly 8 colors. The sample map on the page was not used, because it is resampled (254 colors) and carries a license banner.

styles.note: A complete low-resolution sprite and tile vocabulary: whole-pixel shapes on a 16-pixel grid, an 8-color palette, a bitmap alphabet, and game items such as hearts, keys, coins, and cards.

context: OpenGameArt describes the pack as more than 1,000 tiles, characters, objects, and items for roguelike and RPG games, with tiles for UI, platformers, and puzzle games, a monochrome version, and transparent versions. [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/1-bit-pack).

The License.txt in the download says “Created/distributed by Kenney (www.kenney.nl)”, “Creation date: 06-05-2020”, and “License: (Creative Commons Zero, CC0)”. The OpenGameArt page shows the submission date 6 May 2019, so the 2020 date is probably version 1.1. [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/1-bit-pack).
observed: A dense grid of 16 × 16 tiles on a dark plum ground (#472d3c).
Most tiles are one flat light color (#cfc6b8): characters, skulls, swords, bows, walls, fences, furniture, and frames.
A few groups use one accent each: green trees and plants, blue water, brown furniture, red bricks and playing cards, yellow coins and crowns.
The sheet has a full bitmap alphabet and digits, arrows, hearts, crosses, dice, and warning signs at the lower right.
Shading is absent. Each sprite is a silhouette with interior lines cut out of it.
All diagonals, such as the swords and the diamond frame, step one pixel at a time.
interpretation: The pack shows the most reduced form of the style: one color per object and one pixel unit for everything. It reads as game art without any shading.
The sheet is also a ready inventory of the game furniture that the rubric names: hearts, coins, keys, cursors, frames, and a pixel alphabet.
borrow: Draw icons as one-color silhouettes on a 16-pixel grid, and color each family of icons with one accent.
Use a dark, slightly warm ground instead of pure black, so the light pixels read softly.

images.alt: A large grid of small one-color pixel tiles on dark plum: trees, buildings, furniture, characters, monsters, weapons, potions, playing cards, arrows, hearts, and a pixel alphabet, mostly in off-white with green, blue, brown, red, and yellow accents.
images.caption: Kenney, 1-Bit Pack, `colored_packed.png` from the download on [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/1-bit-pack), CC0. Enlarged 2× with nearest-neighbor scaling and saved as PNG.

rights.statement: License.txt: “License: (Creative Commons Zero, CC0) … This content is free to use in personal, educational and commercial projects. Support us by crediting Kenney or www.kenney.nl (this is not mandatory).”

references.title: Kleine Dada Soirée poster and program, 1922
references.lede: Theo van Doesburg and Kurt Schwitters print the program of their Dutch Dada evenings in black over giant red letters, with every line in a different face, size, and angle.
references.summary: Black type in many faces and angles over huge red DADA letters, with a pointing hand. Van Doesburg and Schwitters, 1922.

source.label: National Gallery of Art: Kleine Dada Soirée (Small Dada Evening), 2010.124.1

creator.name: Theo van Doesburg and Kurt Schwitters

evidence.note: Inspected the National Gallery of Art scan on Wikimedia Commons ([file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_and_Kurt_Schwitters,_Kleine_Dada_Soir%C3%A9e_(Small_Dada_Evening),_1922,_NGA_154076.jpg), 3975 × 4000 px original, viewed at 1200 px). The copy is NGA 2010.124.1. The NGA site refused scripted access (HTTP 403), so the object data comes from the Commons record that the NGA uploaded.

styles.note: A canonical Dada typographic collage: many unrelated faces, lines at all angles, red behind black, and printer’s ornaments such as the pointing hand.

context: The NGA records the sheet as a lithographic poster and program, printed in red and black on wove paper, 30.16 × 30.16 cm, gift of the Collectors Committee, accession number 2010.124.1. [Commons record of the NGA upload](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_and_Kurt_Schwitters,_Kleine_Dada_Soir%C3%A9e_(Small_Dada_Evening),_1922,_NGA_154076.jpg).

Commons places the sheet in its category for the Dutch Dada tour (Dada-tournee). Another Commons copy is dated between 1 December 1922 and 10 January 1923 and attributed to van Doesburg alone. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_kleine_Dada_soir%C3%A9e.jpg).

The program names van Doesburg, Schwitters, and Vilmos Huszár as performers and quotes Tristan Tzara and Francis Picabia. Van Doesburg also wrote Dada poetry as I.K. Bonset. [Wikipedia: Theo van Doesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_van_Doesburg).
observed: The sheet is square, on warm cream paper. Large red letters, rotated about 45° and partly hidden, spell DADA across the whole sheet behind the black text.

The black text mixes at least five kinds of letter: tall condensed sans-serif capitals, heavy wide roman capitals, small lowercase, slab letters, and a boxed sans-serif “BANALITÄTEN”. Letters change size and case inside single words, as in “ReVoLUTIon” and “SCHWitteRS”.
Text runs horizontally, vertically, and upside down. “J’ENFILE MES BOTTINES TOUS LES MATINS — PICABIA” is printed upside down at the top.
Small printed cuts appear as images: a pointing hand at the lower right, a leaping deer with an arrow, a bird, a wreath, a heart shape, and a black square.
Diagonal black bars at the top left and vertical black rules at the right act as visual marks, not dividers.
Only two inks are used: black and an orange-red. The paper shows the folds of the sheet.
interpretation: The sheet is the style’s rubric in one image: the red DADA letters set the scale, and the program lines collide over them with no grid.
Although van Doesburg also led De Stijl, nothing here is orthogonal. The two movements share only the red and black and the heavy bars.
borrow: Set one huge word in the accent color behind the content, rotated and cropped by the edges.
Change face, size, and case letter by letter inside a heading, but keep each letter clean.
Use one stock cut, such as a pointing hand, as the only image in a corner.

images.alt: Square cream sheet: huge red DADA letters run diagonally behind lines of black type in many faces, sizes, and directions announcing a Dada evening with van Doesburg and Kurt Schwitters, with small cuts of a pointing hand, a deer, and a bird.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg and Kurt Schwitters, *Kleine Dada Soirée*, 1922. National Gallery of Art, Washington, 2010.124.1, CC0 image via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theo_van_Doesburg_and_Kurt_Schwitters,_Kleine_Dada_Soir%C3%A9e_(Small_Dada_Evening),_1922,_NGA_154076.jpg).

rights.statement: The National Gallery of Art released the image under CC0 through its Open Access policy. Van Doesburg (Dutch) died in 1931 and Schwitters (German) died in 1948, so the work is public domain in the Netherlands and Germany. It was published in 1922 or 1923, so it is public domain in the United States. The other names on the program are performers, not authors of the design.

identifiers.commons: File:Theo van Doesburg and Kurt Schwitters, Kleine Dada Soirée (Small Dada Evening), 1922, NGA 154076.jpg

references.title: Kowloon Walled City from the air, 1989
references.lede: Ian Lambot’s aerial photograph of Kowloon Walled City in 1989: one solid block of self-built towers, without streets, between new public housing estates.
references.summary: A single dense block of weathered concrete towers between clean new housing blocks. Photograph by Ian Lambot, Hong Kong, 1989.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Kowloon Walled City - 1989 Aerial.jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons rendition at 1920 × 1449 px of the 1942 × 1466 px file. Commons credits the photograph to Ian Lambot and names its source as [City of Darkness](http://cityofdarkness.co.uk/order-print/01-aerial-view/) and the book *City of Darkness: Life in Kowloon Walled City* (ISBN 1-873200-13-7).

styles.note: Partial fit: the real place that Wikipedia names as an inspiration for cyberpunk landscapes. The photograph is a daylight view, so it shows the megastructure and density but not the neon.

context: Wikipedia: “Hong Kong’s Kowloon Walled City is particularly notable for its disorganized hyper-urbanization and breakdown in traditional urban planning to be an inspiration to cyberpunk landscapes.” [Cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk).

By 1987 the walled city had an estimated 33,000 residents. Demolition began on 23 March 1993 and finished in April 1994, and Kowloon Walled City Park replaced it. [Wikipedia: Kowloon Walled City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_Walled_City).

The Commons description notes that the new park on the site of the former Sai Tau Tsuen squatter settlement is visible at the south edge of the city. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kowloon_Walled_City_-_1989_Aerial.jpg).
observed: The walled city is one continuous mass of towers of about ten to fourteen storeys, with no visible streets between them, only a few narrow light wells.
Its surfaces are weathered gray, brown, and stained white concrete, crowded with small windows, rooftop structures, washing, and aerials.
Its outer walls rise sheer at the edges, like a single building.
Clean, regular, pale pink housing towers stand above and to the right. A long slab block runs along the left side.
The foreground is open park land under construction, with curved paths, small white pavilions, and a round paved structure.
The view is in daylight, in soft, warm light.
interpretation: The contrast between the organic, self-built block and the planned towers around it is the cyberpunk city in miniature: an ungoverned megastructure inside a regulated city.
For graphics, the lesson is density and accretion, not neon: many small units packed into one mass with no empty space.
borrow: Pack many small, slightly irregular panels into one solid block, with thin gaps as the only breathing room.
Set a dense, worn element against a clean, regular grid to show the conflict that the style is about.

images.alt: Aerial photograph of a single dense block of weathered concrete towers with no streets between them. Clean pale housing towers stand behind it, and new park land with curved paths lies in front.
images.caption: Kowloon Walled City, Hong Kong, from the air in 1989. Photograph by Ian Lambot, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kowloon_Walled_City_-_1989_Aerial.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Photograph by Ian Lambot, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. The Commons file is in the category “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”, which records that the photographer’s permission was verified. The subject is an informal, self-built settlement with no identified architect, demolished in 1993–1994.

references.title: Kumamon
references.lede: Kumamoto Prefecture’s black bear mascot, made by art director Manabu Mizuno in 2010 for the Kyushu Shinkansen opening: round eyes, red cheek circles, and an open smile.
references.summary: Black round-headed bear with white eyes, red cheek circles, and a wide smile. Manabu Mizuno for Kumamoto Prefecture, 2010.

creator.name: Manabu Mizuno (Good Design Company) for Kumamoto Prefecture

evidence.note: Inspected the photograph [Kumamon on the wall](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kumamon_on_the_wall_(14987894668).jpg) by foooomio (2014, CC BY 2.0, 1280 px scratchpad copy), which shows a large Kumamon face on the glass facade of an office building in central Kumamoto. Not stored, because the character is its main subject.

styles.note: Partial fit: a yuru-chara with the kawaii face (round eyes, blush circles, big head), but drawn in black, white, and red instead of pastels.

context: Wikipedia says Kumamon was established in 2010 by the Kumamoto Prefecture government, in a campaign to draw tourists after the Kyushu Shinkansen line opened, and ranked first in the 2011 nationwide mascot competition with more than 280,000 votes. [Wikipedia: Kumamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumamon).
Kumamoto Prefecture grants usage rights for free when products promote goods and services from the prefecture. [Wikipedia: Kumamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumamon).

UWC ISAK Japan names Manabu Mizuno, creative director of Good Design Company, as the creator of Kumamon. [UWC ISAK Japan](https://uwcisak.jp/blog/news-events/guest-speaker-manabu-mizuno-creator-of-kumamon/).
observed: On the building, the face covers several storeys of glass: a black round head with two small round ears.
The eyes are white circles with black pupils, set high and wide; two solid red circles mark the cheeks.
A white muzzle with a wide open mouth sits low in the face.
The surrounding city street, signs, and tram tracks are ordinary; the face is the only character in view.
interpretation: Kumamon shows how the yuru-chara branch carries the kawaii face into public promotion and signage. The strong black and red make it readable at building scale, which pastels would not.
Compared with Sanrio characters, the face is more graphic and less sweet, close to a logo.
borrow: Reduce a mascot to a few flat shapes (head, two eyes, two cheek circles, a muzzle) so it reads at any size.
Keep cheek blush as two solid circles of one color.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Kumamon is © Kumamoto Prefecture and used under its licensing scheme. The Commons photograph is CC BY 2.0, but its main subject is the character.

references.title: Kung Fury (2015 film), Cannes poster
references.lede: The painted poster for David Sandberg’s crowd-funded short film: a 1980s-style montage of heroes, dinosaurs, lightning, a sun, and a red Countach under a red brush-script title.
references.summary: Painted 1980s action-film montage: sun, lightning, palms, dinosaurs, red Countach, red brush title. 2015.

creator.name: David Sandberg (film); poster signed by the painter, listed as “A. Bennwik” by Auctionet

references.made: 2015; premiered at Cannes on 22 May 2015 and online on 28 May 2015 (Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Inspected two copies from [The Movie Database](https://www.themoviedb.org/movie/251516-kung-fury/images/posters) in a scratch folder: a 1000 × 1500 artwork-only version and an 851 × 1211 Cannes Directors’ Fortnight poster with credits. Not stored. The painter’s name is from an [Auctionet listing](https://auctionet.com/en/2285231-kung-fury-2015-a-bennwik-original-poster); the signature on the image is too small to read with certainty.

styles.note: Partial fit: the film is a named landmark of the style and the poster has the sun, lightning, palms, Countach, and a red-and-blue offset brush title, but it is a warm painted montage, not a neon-on-black scene.

context: Wikipedia: *Kung Fury*, written and directed by David Sandberg, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival on 22 May 2015 and then “on YouTube, Steam, SVT2 in Sweden, and the El Rey Network in the United States, on 28 May 2015.” Its Kickstarter ended on 25 January 2014 with $630,019 from 17,713 backers. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung_Fury).

Wikipedia: “visual effects artists softened the film clarity and added videotape wear effects to give the illusion of it being a worn VHS copy,” and the score is by “Swedish synthwave musicians Mitch Murder and Lost Years”. David Hasselhoff sings the song “True Survivor”.
The Cannes copy of the poster carries the Quinzaine des Réalisateurs (Directors’ Fortnight) 2015 laurel and the tagline “IT TAKES A COP FROM THE FUTURE TO FIGHT AN ENEMY FROM THE PAST”.
observed: The painting is split in light: orange and yellow at the left with a large pale sun, blue and violet at the right with white forked lightning.
A large face of a man with a red headband dominates the top. A tyrannosaur, a triceratops, a Viking, a man in a Hitler costume, a woman with a minigun, and soldiers crowd below.
A red Lamborghini Countach with lit headlights sits at the lower right. Palm silhouettes and city towers appear at the left.
“KUNG FURY” is set in red, ragged, italic brush capitals with a dark blue offset shadow and a red underline swash.
interpretation: This is the parody, airbrushed-VHS-box branch of the style. The car, the sun, the lightning, and the brush title link it to [the Kavinsky cover](ref:kavinsky-outrun-cover-2013), but the painted warmth and crowd belong to 1980s action-film posters.
borrow: Split a hero image into a warm half and a cold half, with the sun on one side and electric light on the other.
Give a brush-script title a dark offset shadow and an underline swash.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The poster and film are in copyright (Laser Unicorns, 2015).

references.title: Kuniyoshi, Splendid View at Futamigaura Bay (triptych)
references.lede: Three sheets form one beach scene: pilgrims and travellers at the Wedded Rocks near Ise, with the sun rising between the rocks, by Utagawa Kuniyoshi.
references.summary: Three-sheet panorama with indigo robes, a bokashi sky, and a red sun. Utagawa Kuniyoshi, 1854.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art print image of the joined triptych 1943.10 (3400 × 1707 px, viewed at 1600 × 803).

styles.note: A late Edo triptych: dense patterned robes, flat blue sea and sky with bokashi bands, a red sun, and red signature cartouches, across three sheets.

context: Cleveland catalogues the work as a triptych of color woodblock prints, each sheet 36.9 × 25.4 cm, 1854. [CMA 1943.10](https://clevelandart.org/art/1943.10).

Cleveland describes a continuous scene of visitors at Futamigaura Bay near Ise Grand Shrine, with the sun rising between the Wedded Rocks joined by a shimenawa rope. [CMA](https://clevelandart.org/art/1943.10).
observed: Three vertical sheets join edge to edge. The figures continue across the joins.
The sky is pale blue with a dark Prussian-blue band at the top and a pink-red glow at the horizon. A flat red sun sits between two dark rocks at left.
The sea is pale blue-green with white wave crests outlined in blue. The beach in the foreground is flat dark gray-black.
Robes carry dense patterns in indigo, gray, red, and white: flowers, checks, and wave shapes.
Red and yellow signature cartouches with seals stand on the dark beach under each sheet’s figures. A red title cartouche is at upper right.
A dark brown cliff at right is cut by the top and right edges.
interpretation: By 1854 the palette is denser and more saturated than in Harunobu’s or Utamaro’s prints, but the devices are the same: outline, flat ground, bokashi sky, and cartouches.
The triptych shows that the style composes across panels without a gutter break.
borrow: Run one scene across three equal panels and let figures cross the joins.
Use a dark flat foreground band under busy patterned figures to make them read.

images.alt: Color woodblock triptych. Women in indigo and gray patterned kimonos and children on a dark beach in front of a blue sea. At left a red sun rises between two rocks joined by a rope. A palanquin and a brown cliff are at right.
images.caption: Utagawa Kuniyoshi, Splendid View at Futamigaura Bay, 1854, triptych. [Cleveland Museum of Art 1943.10](https://clevelandart.org/art/1943.10). CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art open access API gives `share_license_status: CC0` for this object. Kuniyoshi died in 1861, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Kurt Schwitters, Anna Blume. Dichtungen, 1919 (cover)
references.lede: Schwitters’s first book of poems has a cover he drew himself: script, letter-spaced capitals, a scattered drawing, and four large red letters that spell dada.
references.summary: Pen drawing of a face, wheel, and windmill, script and capitals in black, and big red lowercase d a d a. Kurt Schwitters, Hannover, 1919.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Kurt Schwitters, Anna Blume. Dichtungen, 1919, first edition

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons photograph of a first-edition copy offered on ZVAB ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kurt_Schwitters_-_Anna_Blume._Dichtungen,_1919.jpg), 843 × 1302 px original; the stored 960 px Commons thumbnail is slightly upscaled). The copy is a dealer’s copy; its owner is not known.

styles.note: A Dada book cover: red letters spelling dada break through a scattered black drawing, and script, capitals, and roman letters mix. Partial fit: it is drawn by hand, not set from type or photographs.

context: Commons records the image as *Anna Blume. Dichtungen*, Paul Steegemann Verlag, Hannover, 1919, first edition, in the series Die Silbergäule, volumes 39–40, tagged PD-Art (PD-old-auto-1923, death year 1948). [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kurt_Schwitters_-_Anna_Blume._Dichtungen,_1919.jpg).

Wikipedia says that the publication of the poem “An Anna Blume” in August 1919, with his first one-man show at Der Sturm, made Schwitters a well-known artist by the end of that year. [Wikipedia: Kurt Schwitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Schwitters). He later printed it again in [Merz 1](ref:schwitters-merz-1-holland-dada-1923).
observed: The cover is printed in black and red on grey-green paper.
The series title “Die Silbergäule.” is in a large German script at the top, underlined.
“A-N-N-A” is letter-spaced in thin capitals with hyphens. “ANNA BLUME.” is in thin roman capitals in the lower third, and “Kurt Schwitters.” and “Dichtungen.” are in script, each underlined.
Four large red lowercase serif letters, “d a d a”, climb diagonally across the middle from lower left to upper right.
A loose pen drawing fills the middle: a face in profile, a large wheel, a windmill, a small figure, a heart, a cart, arrows, and small crosses, signed “Schwitters 1919”.
The publisher’s line “Paul Steegemann, Verlag, Hannover.” is in script at the bottom.
interpretation: The red “dada” letters do the same job as the giant red letters on [the 1922 soirée program](ref:van-doesburg-schwitters-kleine-dada-soiree-1922): one word in the accent color cuts across everything else. The rest of the cover is closer to expressionist drawing.
borrow: Run one word in large red letters diagonally across a black drawing, so the accent sets the direction.
Mix script, letter-spaced capitals, and roman capitals for title, author, and series.

images.alt: Grey-green book cover with a black pen drawing of a face, a wheel, a windmill, and arrows, the words Die Silbergäule and Kurt Schwitters in script, ANNA BLUME in thin capitals, and four large red letters d a d a climbing diagonally across the middle.
images.caption: Kurt Schwitters, cover of *Anna Blume. Dichtungen*, Paul Steegemann Verlag, Hannover, 1919. Dealer’s copy, image via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kurt_Schwitters_-_Anna_Blume._Dichtungen,_1919.jpg), PD-Art.

rights.statement: Commons tags the image PD-Art (PD-old-auto-1923, death year 1948). Schwitters, a German author, signed the cover drawing and died in 1948, so the cover is public domain in Germany. It was published in 1919, so it is public domain in the United States. The photograph is a plain record of a flat cover.

references.title: Kurt Schwitters, Mz 245. Mal Kah, 1921
references.lede: A small Merz collage built from cigarette packaging, a Bayer label, a ticket, and painted paper, with the brand names left as type.
references.summary: Cut cigarette labels with “MAL-KAH” and “BLUME”, a Bayer mark, and blue and brown papers. Kurt Schwitters, Hannover, 1921.

source.label: Lempertz, sale 877, lot 1062: Kurt Schwitters, Mz 245. Mal Kah. Merzzeichnung

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image taken from the Lempertz auction catalogue ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kurt_Schwitters_Mz_245_Mal_Kah_Merzzeichnung.jpg), 3353 × 4250 px original, viewed at 1200 px). The Lempertz page itself was not opened. The current owner is not known.

styles.note: A Merz collage: found printed matter with its own type, cut edges, and paper tones. Partial fit: the commercial labels, not set type, carry the lettering, and there is no photograph.

context: Commons, after the Lempertz catalogue, describes the work as “Mz 245. Mal Kah. Merzzeichnung”: collage of colored and printed papers, card, and colored chalk on paper, 12.6 × 10 cm, mounted on card 23.4/23.8 × 18 cm, signed and dated K. Schwitters 1921, catalogue raisonné Orchard 83. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kurt_Schwitters_Mz_245_Mal_Kah_Merzzeichnung.jpg).

Schwitters called his collages Merz, after a fragment of found text from the phrase “Commerz und Privatbank”. [Wikipedia: Kurt Schwitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Schwitters). Compare his magazine [Merz 1](ref:schwitters-merz-1-holland-dada-1923) and the cover of [Anna Blume](ref:schwitters-anna-blume-dichtungen-1919).
observed: A cigarette label with “„MAL-KAH“” in black bold slab-serif capitals, framed by thin ornamental rules, fills the upper middle. A second “„MAL-KAH“” appears below it.
A strip with a circled monogram “J D Z” and “BLUME” in a plain heavy grotesque lies across the first label.
At the top a fragment reads “…urreine Zigarette” upside down.
At the left are a round “BAYER” cross mark on a label reading “SCHUTZ-MARKE”, a piece of checked paper, a black-grey wedge, and a strip of blue paper.
A patch of deep blue chalk covers part of a printed ticket or form with Fraktur text. Small cut pieces at the right show a black and pink letter and an ornamental print.

The pieces are mostly rectangles and triangles with straight cut edges. The colors are brown card, cream, black, and blue. The signature “Mz 245. Mal Kah” and “K. Schwitters 1921.” are in pencil on the mount.
interpretation: The collage shows how Dada makes type from printed waste: brand names, a trademark, and a ticket keep their own faces and are cut and layered at angles. The upside-down fragment and the clash of slab, grotesque, and Fraktur letters echo the typographic sheets.
borrow: Build a heading area from fragments of real labels, each keeping its own face, and overlap them at slight angles.
Use one strong blue patch as the only saturated color in a brown and cream field.

images.alt: Small collage of brown card, cigarette labels reading MAL-KAH and BLUME, a round Bayer trademark, checked paper, a black wedge, blue paper, and a patch of blue chalk, signed Mz 245 Mal Kah, K. Schwitters 1921 on the mount.
images.caption: Kurt Schwitters, *Mz 245. Mal Kah*, 1921, collage. Image from the Lempertz catalogue via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kurt_Schwitters_Mz_245_Mal_Kah_Merzzeichnung.jpg), PD-Art. The cigarette labels and the Bayer mark are anonymous commercial printing from before 1921.

rights.statement: Commons tags the image PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired, death year 1948). Schwitters, a German author, died in 1948, so the collage is public domain in Germany. In the United States the collage is public domain whether or not it was published before 1931, because the life-plus-70 term for unpublished works ended in 2018. The pasted labels are anonymous commercial printing of about 1921 or earlier. The Bayer cross is still a trademark, which does not restrict this documentary use.

identifiers.commons: File:Kurt Schwitters Mz 245 Mal Kah Merzzeichnung.jpg

references.title: Liberated Pixel Cup base assets
references.lede: The shared sprites and tiles of the 2012 Liberated Pixel Cup: one style guide, a 32-pixel grid, and openly licensed characters that hundreds of later free games reuse.
references.summary: A four-direction, nine-frame walk cycle of a base character in flat skin tones with dark outlines. Liberated Pixel Cup, 2012, CC BY-SA 3.0.

source.label: OpenGameArt: Liberated Pixel Cup (LPC) Base Assets (sprites & map tiles)

creator.name: Lanea Zimmerman (Sharm), Stephen Challener (Redshrike), Charles Sanchez (CharlesGabriel), Daniel Armstrong (HughSpectrum), and others listed in CREDITS.TXT

evidence.note: Downloaded `lpc_base_assets.zip` from the OpenGameArt page and inspected `sprites/people/male_walkcycle.png` (576 × 256 px, 12 colors) on white, enlarged 2× to 1152 × 512 px. Also inspected the page preview `house_7.png` (288 × 224 px) enlarged 4×. CREDITS.TXT gives the walk cycle to Stephen Challener.

styles.note: Partial fit: hand-drawn sprites and tiles with hard dark outlines and flat palette-step shading, but drawn at a finer 32-pixel scale with more colors than the 8-bit core, closer to 16-bit console art.

context: OpenGameArt describes these as “the base assets from the 2012 Liberated Pixel Cup competition” and lists the license as CC-BY-SA 3.0. [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/liberated-pixel-cup-lpc-base-assets-sprites-map-tiles).

The attribution instructions say that the images are copyright their authors as listed in CREDITS.TXT, and that the assets by Lanea Zimmerman and Stephen Challener are also available under OGA-BY 3.0. [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/liberated-pixel-cup-lpc-base-assets-sprites-map-tiles).

CREDITS.TXT gives the base tileset (including `house.png`) and much style-guide work to Lanea Zimmerman, the character templates (walk, hurt, slash, and spellcast sheets) to Stephen Challener, and the monsters to Charles Sanchez.
observed: Four rows of nine frames: the figure walks away, to the left, toward the viewer, and to the right.
Each figure is about 32 pixels tall with a one-pixel dark brown outline, not black.
Skin is shaded in three or four flat steps of peach and brown, with one pale highlight on the head. There is no gradient or anti-aliasing to the background.
The side views swing the legs and arms between frames. The front and back views change only a few pixels per frame.
The house tiles in the page preview use red brick, gray stone, and wood in the same flat-step shading, seen from a high three-quarter view.
interpretation: The base assets show the 16-bit end of the style: more colors per sprite and colored outlines, but still whole square pixels, hand placement, and a frame-by-frame walk.
A shared style guide let many artists produce compatible sprites, which shows how a fixed grid and palette make pixel art a system.
borrow: Outline sprites with a dark shade of their own color, not pure black.
Animate a character with a short cycle of frames on a fixed cell, with no tweening.

images.alt: Sprite sheet of a bald base character walking in four directions, four rows of nine frames, in peach skin tones with dark brown outlines on white.
images.caption: Stephen Challener (Redshrike), male walk cycle from the Liberated Pixel Cup base assets, [OpenGameArt](https://opengameart.org/content/liberated-pixel-cup-lpc-base-assets-sprites-map-tiles), CC BY-SA 3.0. Transparent ground filled with white, enlarged 2× with nearest-neighbor scaling, saved as PNG.

rights.statement: OpenGameArt lists CC-BY-SA 3.0. “Images are copyright their respective authors, as listed in CREDITS.TXT.” The walk cycle by Stephen Challener is also available under OGA-BY 3.0. The modified copy here (white ground, enlargement) is shared under the same license.

references.title: Liquid Glass 3D effect for icons, 2025 and 2026 versions
references.lede: A Wikimedia Commons diagram that renders the same simple icon in Icon Composer with the 2025 and the 2026 Liquid Glass edge effect.
references.summary: One icon, two years of the glass edge: wide bevels in 2025, thin edges in 2026.
references.made: 2026-06-10 (made with Apple Icon Composer, per the file description)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons original (3000 × 2000 PNG). The stored copy is resized to 1600 px.

styles.note: Documents the style’s icon edge treatment and how Apple reduced it in the 2026 revision.

context: The file description: in the iOS/macOS 27 version “there are for each form or layout narrower 3D borders, a black tiny border and an optional light shadow”. Source given as Apple Icon Composer. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Liquid_Glass_-_3D_effect_for_icons_2025-2026.png).

Wikipedia reports that at WWDC 2026 Apple reduced default transparency, changed the effect of the glass, and revamped app icons to make them more recognizable. [Wikipedia: Liquid Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Glass).
observed: A light grey canvas with a bold black title, “Liquid Glass 3D effect for icons 2025 and 2026 version”.

Left, labeled iOS/iPadOS/macOS/watchOS 26 (2025): a cyan rectangle with an orange disc. Both have wide bevels: a bright upper-left edge, a dark lower-right edge, and a soft specular highlight on the disc.
Right, labeled 27 (2026): the same shapes with flat fills, a thin black outline, and a soft drop shadow. The bevel is almost gone.
interpretation: The 2025 icon edge is the specular rim of the style applied to opaque shapes. The 2026 version moves toward flat design with outlines, which shows how quickly Apple softened the look after criticism.
borrow: For a dimensional edge, light one corner and shade the opposite corner of the same shape, instead of adding a separate gloss layer.

images.alt: Two cyan rectangles with an orange disc. The left one has wide light and dark bevels; the right one is flat with a thin black outline and a shadow.
images.caption: “Liquid Glass - 3D effect for icons 2025-2026” by LucaLindholm, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Liquid_Glass_-_3D_effect_for_icons_2025-2026.png), CC BY 4.0. Resized to 1600 px.
