rights.statement: Commons: own work by LucaLindholm, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0, marked “trademarked”. The image shows simple shapes drawn by the uploader and rendered with Apple’s tool. It contains no Apple icon or artwork.

references.title: Liquid Glass revision in iOS 27 and macOS 27
references.lede: Apple’s 2026 revision of Liquid Glass: a user slider from ultra-clear to fully tinted, sharper icons, and on the Mac a return to edge-to-edge sidebars and a uniform toolbar.
references.summary: The 2026 revision: less transparency, a clear-to-tinted slider, and sharper icons. Apple.
references.made: 2026 (announced at WWDC in June 2026; released September 2026)

evidence.note: Inspected the Apple Newsroom image Apple-OS-27-updates-260608 (1960 × 1102, large_2x variant) in a scratchpad copy. The screens are small, so glass detail is not visible at this size, and the description relies mostly on Apple’s text. Not stored.

styles.note: The second version of the style. It keeps the floating control layer but makes the glass more opaque and the edges more defined.

context: Apple: “A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalize Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultra-clear to fully tinted”, and “app icons have been updated to be sharper and more defined. On Mac, updates reincorporate cornerstones of the macOS design … including a more uniform toolbar across the top of apps, edge-to-edge sidebars, colored sidebar icons, and more.” [Apple Newsroom, June 2026](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/06/apple-unveils-next-generation-of-apple-intelligence-siri-ai-and-more/).

Apple’s developer release: “the design continues to evolve, with improvements to legibility, customizability, and consistency”. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/06/apple-aids-app-development-with-new-intelligence-frameworks-and-advanced-tools/). The software shipped in September 2026. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/09/major-updates-for-apples-software-platforms-are-now-available/).

Wikipedia reports that the revision addressed criticism, reduced default transparency, and changed sidebar corners on iPadOS and macOS. [Wikipedia: Liquid Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Glass).
observed: A product group on white: Vision Pro, a MacBook, an iPad, an iPhone, and an Apple Watch.
On the Mac, the Image Playground window is dark. Its sidebar runs to the window edge instead of floating as an inset panel, and the toolbar buttons are small separate capsules.
On the iPad, an “Allowed Apps” sheet is an opaque white rounded panel over a beige wave wallpaper, with a blue check button in a circle.
The Mac Dock is a dark strip with a faint rim.
interpretation: The revision moves the style back toward opaque, structured surfaces. The capsule controls and concentric corners remain, so these are what define the style after 2026, more than strong transparency.
borrow: Offer a user setting from clear to tinted glass instead of one fixed transparency.

rights.statement: Apple press image of copyrighted software and hardware. No image is stored here.

references.related: See also [the 2025 and 2026 icon edge](ref:liquid-glass-icon-effect-2025-2026-comparison) and [macOS Tahoe 26 Control Center](ref:macos-tahoe-26-control-center-2025).

references.title: liquid_glass_renderer: glass shapes demo
references.lede: A demo image from an open-source Flutter renderer for Liquid Glass: three clear glass shapes that bend a drawing grid at their rims.
references.summary: Three clear glass shapes refracting a grid. Open-source Flutter renderer, 2025.
references.made: 2025 (first pub.dev release June 13, 2025; image committed June 19, 2025)

evidence.note: Inspected the repository file packages/liquid_glass_renderer/doc/shapes.png (1844 × 1262) at commit c3209ea323. The stored copy is resized to 1600 px.

styles.note: An independent reimplementation that isolates the material: refraction at the rim and a specular edge, with no blur and no border.

context: pub.dev describes the package as “the raw renderer for a liquid glass effect in Flutter”. Its first version, 0.1.1-dev.0, was published on June 13, 2025, four days after WWDC. [pub.dev](https://pub.dev/packages/liquid_glass_renderer).

Wikipedia describes a wave of unofficial libraries after the announcement that approximate refraction and lensing with shaders, because platforms outside Apple have no native material. [Wikipedia: Liquid Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Glass).
observed: A beige-to-white gradient with a fine and a coarse grid of grey lines fills the frame.
Three glass shapes sit in a row: a rounded square, a circle, and a squircle with slightly flatter sides.
Inside each shape the grid lines stay straight in the middle but curve and compress in a band along the rim, as through a thick lens edge.
A thin bright highlight runs along the upper-left and lower-right rims. There is no fill color, no blur, no border, and no shadow.
interpretation: The image shows the one trait that separates the style from glassmorphism: the content under the glass is displaced, not blurred.
borrow: Test a glass effect over a regular grid. A grid shows at once whether the edge refracts or only blurs.

images.alt: Three clear glass shapes, a rounded square, a circle, and a squircle, on a beige grid. The grid lines curve near the edges of each shape.
images.caption: Demo image shapes.png from [whynotmake-it/flutter_liquid_glass](https://github.com/whynotmake-it/flutter_liquid_glass/tree/main/packages/liquid_glass_renderer), © 2025 Tim Lehmann for whynotmake.it, MIT License. Resized to 1600 px.

rights.statement: The package directory’s LICENSE grants MIT permissions, “Copyright 2025 Tim Lehmann for whynotmake.it”. The image is a file in that directory and shows only output of the software (a generated grid and shapes), with no third-party content. Keep the copyright and permission notice with copies.

references.title: liquid-glass-react
references.lede: A React component library by Max Rovensky, published on npm on June 10, 2025, one day after Apple announced Liquid Glass.
references.summary: The first popular web reimplementation of Liquid Glass, as React components. 2025.
references.made: 2025 (npm 0.0.1 published June 10, 2025; repository last pushed June 13, 2025)

evidence.note: Inspected the repository file assets/card.png (1296 × 736) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit. It carries the lensing glass to the web, but it puts content in a glass card, which Apple’s guidelines reserve for controls.

context: The repository describes itself as “Apple’s Liquid Glass effect for React”, under the MIT license, with about 6,300 GitHub stars when checked. [GitHub](https://github.com/rdev/liquid-glass-react).

Wikipedia calls it the earliest web implementation and the most downloaded Liquid Glass package on npm, and says that its development stopped shortly after release. [Wikipedia: Liquid Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Glass).
observed: A warm, sepia photo of a ruined pier over the sea with gulls fills the frame.
A rounded glass card in the middle holds a “User Info” profile: initials in a circle, a name, and three label-value rows in white sans-serif.
Through the card the pier is heavily blurred and warmed to amber, and the dark pier struts smear sideways near the left edge of the card.
The card has a thin light rim, slightly brighter on its upper edge, and a soft shadow.
interpretation: The demo blends the two styles: Liquid Glass edge distortion, but glassmorphism’s content card with strong blur.
borrow: Raise the blur under text-bearing glass and keep the refraction for the rim.

rights.statement: The code is MIT (© 2025 Max Rovensky). Kept as link only because the demo image shows a third-party photograph whose license is not stated.

references.title: liquidGL
references.lede: A framework-free JavaScript library by NaughtyDuk that renders refracting glass panes over live web content with WebGPU or WebGL.
references.summary: WebGPU and WebGL glass panes with refraction, bevels, and specular light for the web. 2025–2026.
references.made: 2025 (repository created June 21, 2025; still maintained in October 2026)

evidence.note: Inspected the repository file assets/images/_0006_multiple-lenses.jpg (2400 × 1260) in a scratchpad copy. The repository also holds frost-and-specular and menu-bar images, which were downloaded but not reviewed. Not stored.

styles.note: The most complete web version of the material: refraction, bevel, specular light, and tint. Its demos use glass for content tiles, which goes beyond Apple’s rules.

context: The README: liquidGL “turns any fixed or sticky-positioned element into a perfectly refracted, glossy ‘glass pane’ rendered in WebGPU (with automatic fallback to WebGL)”, and “recreates Apple’s ‘Liquid Glass’ aesthetic in the browser”. It falls back to CSS backdrop-filter and offers tint, chromatic aberration, and stacked lenses. [GitHub](https://github.com/naughtyduk/liquidGL).

The LICENSE file is MIT, “Copyright (c) NaughtyDuk”. Wikipedia calls it the most actively maintained of the widely used web implementations as of September 2026. [Wikipedia: Liquid Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Glass).
observed: A photo of a red running track with the legs of runners and their shadows.

Six rounded glass tiles form a fitness dashboard: distance, heart rate (a large “137 BPM”), speed, power, resistance, and an interval delta. Labels are small uppercase white sans-serif with green accents.
Each tile has a bevelled rim where the track texture and the white lane line bend and magnify. The line through the heart-rate tile kinks at the tile edge.
Rims catch thin highlights, and the tiles keep the red-brown color of the track. A large white “liquidGL” wordmark sits at the lower right.
interpretation: The library shows that the refraction can be reproduced on the web, but only with a shader and an offscreen copy of the page, not with CSS alone.
borrow: Concentrate the distortion in a narrow bevel and keep the center of the pane flat, so text inside stays readable.

rights.statement: The code is MIT (© NaughtyDuk). Kept as link only because the demo image shows a third-party photograph whose license is not stated.

references.title: macOS Tahoe 26 Control Center
references.lede: Control Center on macOS Tahoe 26: clear glass circles and capsules that sit straight on the desktop wallpaper.
references.summary: Clear glass controls on the Mac desktop, with no panel behind them. Apple, 2025.

evidence.note: Inspected the Apple Newsroom image Apple-WWDC25-macOS-Tahoe-26-Control-Center-250609 (1960 × 1306, large_2x variant) in a scratchpad copy. A press render. Not stored.

styles.note: Shows the control layer alone: separate glass shapes with lit rims over the wallpaper, and no shared panel.

context: Apple: macOS Tahoe 26 “is crafted with Liquid Glass, a translucent new material that reflects and refracts its surroundings”. “The menu bar is now completely transparent”, and users can choose which controls appear in the menu bar and Control Center. [Apple Newsroom](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2025/06/macos-tahoe-26-makes-the-mac-more-capable-productive-and-intelligent-than-ever/).
observed: The upper-right corner of a MacBook screen with a blue, teal, and sand wave wallpaper. The menu bar has no background. Only the active Control Center icon sits in a light blue capsule.

Control Center has no window. Each control is its own glass shape: capsules for Wi-Fi and Focus, circles for Bluetooth and AirDrop, rounded rectangles for Now Playing, Display, and Sound, and a row of four circles.
Each shape is nearly clear, takes the blue of the wallpaper, and has a bright rim that is strongest on the upper-left edge.
Active toggles (Bluetooth, AirDrop) are opaque white circles with blue glyphs. The Display and Sound sliders are deeper blue glass with white tracks.
Gaps between shapes are equal, and inner corners follow the outer corners.
interpretation: Removing the panel and keeping only separate glass controls is the clearest sign of the style’s two-layer idea: the controls float, and nothing else is glass.
borrow: Show an active state as an opaque fill inside the glass set, and keep inactive controls clear.

rights.statement: Apple press image of copyrighted software. No image is stored here.

references.related: See also [the iOS 26 Home Screen](ref:ios-26-home-screen-2025) and the overview record [Apple Liquid Glass](ref:apple-liquid-glass-2025).

references.title: Magic UI Bento Grid component
references.lede: An open-source React component that lays out feature cards as a bento grid, published by Magic UI in November 2023.
references.summary: MIT-licensed React and Tailwind bento grid: white cards with a 12 px radius in one- and two-column spans. Magic UI, 2023.

evidence.note: Captured the live documentation page at 1440 × 900 on 2026-10-02 with `tools/capture.mjs` and inspected it. Read the component source `apps/www/registry/magicui/bento-grid.tsx` and the demo `apps/www/registry/example/bento-demo.tsx` in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/magicuidesign/magicui). The stored image is a 728 × 382 crop of the first row of the demo.

styles.note: Partial fit: tiles of different spans with one gap, but the radius is small (12 px) and the light cards carry a faint shadow instead of a tonal step.

context: The documentation page, dated 2023-11-09 in its source file, describes the component as “a layout used to showcase the features of a product in a simple and elegant way”.

The source sets the grid to three columns with `gap-4` (16 px) and rows of 22 rem. Each card is `rounded-xl` (12 px) and spans one or two columns; on small screens every card spans all three columns. Light cards use a 1 px shadow ring at 3 % black plus two soft shadows at 5 %. Dark cards use a 1 px border at 10 % white and an inset glow.

The repository is under the MIT License (“Copyright (c) Magic UI”). It was created on 2023-06-26 and the component file was first committed on 2025-09-15 at its current path; the docs date shows that the component is older than that path.
observed: Two white cards sit side by side on a white panel: a narrow card on the left and a card about twice as wide on the right, separated by a narrow gap.
Both cards have rounded corners of the same small radius and a very faint shadow; there is no visible outline.
Each card carries one feature: a thin line icon, a semibold dark grey heading (“Save your files”, “Notifications”), and one light grey sentence.
The upper half of each card holds a faded, masked illustration of the feature: blurred file cards in the left card and notification rows in the right card.
interpretation: The component reduces the bento grid to a reusable pattern for SaaS feature sections. It keeps the unequal spans and the one-feature-per-tile rule, but uses the small radius and soft shadow of shadcn/ui cards, so it sits between the core look and [Material Design](style:material-design) cards.
borrow: Put a faded, masked illustration of the feature in the top half of the tile and the heading and one sentence in the bottom half.
Define spans per card (`col-span-1` or `col-span-2` on a three-column grid) and let every card span the full width on small screens.

images.alt: Two white rounded cards side by side: a narrow card with blurred file previews, a document icon, and the heading Save your files; a wide card with faded notification rows, a bell icon, and the heading Notifications.
images.caption: First row of the demo on the [Magic UI Bento Grid documentation page](https://magicui.design/docs/components/bento-grid), captured 2026-10-02. The second row, which shows a third-party logo, is not stored.

rights.statement: The component, the demo, and the documentation site are in the [magicuidesign/magicui repository](https://github.com/magicuidesign/magicui) under the MIT License: “Copyright (c) Magic UI. Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software …”. The stored crop shows only MIT-licensed demo content and Radix and Lucide icons (MIT and ISC). Credit: Magic UI.

references.title: Mario Felipe, Mano V/S Regla
references.lede: A 36-page riso-printed artist’s book in an edition of 50, printed in one blue ink on cream and turquoise paper.
references.summary: Riso artist’s book in blue ink on colored paper stocks, edition of 50.

source.label: Flickr: Mario Felipe, “Mano Vs Regla | Book”

creator.name: Mario Felipe; published by Gran Negro Ediciones

evidence.note: Viewed the 1024 × 728 px Flickr “large” file of an open spread. A second photo shows the cover ([Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/cuandoelsolexplote/23060245766/)).

styles.note: Partial fit: one spot ink on colored stocks, with grainy screened photography. There is no overprint.

context: The Flickr description says: “Editado por Gran Negro Ediciones … Impreso en Risografía. Edición de 50. 20,5 x 13,5 cm. 36 páginas. Primavera 2015.” It links to the author’s own online store.
observed: A single bright blue ink prints on two paper colors: cream on the left page and turquoise on the right.
The left page has a hand-drawn line figure with dots at the corners.
The right page has a photograph of a hand, screened into fine grain, in the same blue.
The paper color changes the apparent color of the ink.
interpretation: The book uses colored stock as a second “color” at no extra drum, a common riso economy.
borrow: Change the page ground between sections and keep one ink, so the palette shifts without new colors.

images.alt: Two hands hold an open booklet. The left page is cream with a blue line drawing; the right page is turquoise with a grainy blue photograph of a hand.
images.caption: Mario Felipe, *Mano V/S Regla*, 2015. CC BY 2.0. [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/cuandoelsolexplote/22667887428/), 1024 px “large” size.

rights.statement: Published by the author on Flickr under CC BY 2.0. The author licenses a photograph of his own book, so the depicted work is openly licensed. Credit: Mario Felipe.

references.title: Mario Felipe, two-color riso print of chairs
references.lede: An A3 riso art print in a numbered edition of 30: six stylized chairs in fluorescent red and black, each on a grainy pink screen.
references.summary: A3 two-color riso print of six chairs in fluorescent red and black on pink screens.

evidence.note: Viewed the 1280 × 853 px Commons thumbnail of the photograph (the full-size original returned HTTP 429). It shows one copy of the edition held by hand.

styles.note: Two spot inks, with a pink screen of the red ink as the ground, and visible grain in the flat areas.

context: The Flickr description says: “Print en risografia a dos colores en formato A3. Edición de 30 copias numeradas. Impresión: A3press.” ([Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/cuandoelsolexplote/15680565058/))

The photograph is on Commons as [Impressão em risografia em dua cores, 2014](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Impress%C3%A3o_em_risografia_em_dua_cores,_2014.jpg), with a FlickreviewR license check passed on 2023-01-06.
observed: Two inks only: a fluorescent red-pink and black, on white paper.
Each chair sits on a square of the pink ink printed as a screen, so the square reads as a light, mottled pink.
The flat pink squares are grainy and uneven, with a faint grid texture.
Chairs are drawn as flat, isometric planes with no outlines.
interpretation: The print makes a third tone from a screen of one ink, a typical way to widen a two-drum palette.
borrow: Use a 30 to 40 % screen of the main ink as a panel ground, and full ink for the subject.

images.alt: A person holds an A3 print with six squares of grainy pink, each with a stylized chair in red and black.
images.caption: Mario Felipe’s two-color riso print, 2014. CC BY 2.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Impress%C3%A3o_em_risografia_em_dua_cores,_2014.jpg), from [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/cuandoelsolexplote/15680565058/). 1280 px thumbnail.

rights.statement: Published by the author on Flickr under CC BY 2.0; FlickreviewR passed on Commons. The author licenses a photograph of his own print, so the depicted work is openly licensed. Credit: Mario Felipe.

references.title: Max Bill, Junghans kitchen clock with timer, 1956
references.lede: A kitchen wall clock designed by Max Bill, with Ernst Moeckl, while he directed the Ulm School: a pale blue ceramic body, a white dial with thin grotesque numerals, and a timer below.
references.summary: Pale blue drop-shaped body, white dial with thin numerals and fine ticks, and a round timer. Max Bill for Junghans, 1956.

creator.name: Max Bill and Ernst Moeckl, designers; Junghans, maker

references.made: Designed 1956; the V&A also gives 1960–1970 for this example

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A’s primary image 2007BP8871 of object M.224-2007 at 1067 × 1600 px, through the V&A IIIF service.

styles.note: Made by the school’s first rector during his Ulm years. The dial follows Ulm discipline, but the curved, colored body does not.

context: The V&A says the clock “was designed by Max Bill whilst Director of the Hochschule für Gestaltung (HfG Ulm)”. It gives glazed earthenware, glass, chrome, painted metal, plastic, and a quartz mechanism, a design date of 1956 with Ernst Moeckl, and Junghans, Schramberg, as maker. [V&A M.224-2007](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O164396/).
The record describes the body as “coloured a pale blue” outside and white inside, moulded in an inverted “V” shape. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O164396/).
observed: The body is a glossy pale blue shape like a rounded drop, wide at the top.
The white dial carries thin, light grotesque numerals 1 to 12, fine minute ticks, and small “JUNGHANS” capitals with wide spacing.
The hands are plain black strips with pointed ends, around a small white disc.
A round white timer dial below has small numerals every five minutes and a pale cream pointed knob.
interpretation: The dial is the Ulm part: thin type, an exact scale, and no decoration. The color and the curved body belong more to general 1950s domestic design, so the clock is a bridge object and not a core example.
borrow: Set a scale with thin numerals and fine, even ticks, and let the scale be the decoration.

rights.statement: Image © Victoria and Albert Museum, London, under the V&A’s own terms, not an open license. Max Bill died in 1994, so the design is protected in Switzerland and Germany. No image is stored.

references.title: McDonald’s, Downey, California
references.lede: The oldest surviving McDonald’s, opened in 1953 to Stanley Clark Meston’s standard design: two yellow arches pierce a roof slab that slopes down toward the street.
references.summary: Two yellow sheet-metal arches through a sloped roof slab over a glass walk-up stand. Stanley Clark Meston, Downey, 1953.

source.label: Library of Congress: John Margolies, McDonald’s, Downey, California, 1985

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected John Margolies’s 1985 color slide, Library of Congress LC-MA05-6987, 1024 × 703 px. Also inspected his 1985 detail of the roadside sign (LC-MA05-1501) in a scratchpad; it is not stored.

styles.note: Wikipedia names this stand as a preserved Googie example; the arches are pure sign, and the roof slab slopes at an angle.

context: The stand at 10207 Lakewood Boulevard opened on 18 August 1953. It is the third McDonald’s outlet and keeps the original Golden Arches facade. Franchisees of the McDonald brothers had to use Stanley Clark Meston’s design. With its sign it was found eligible for the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. [Wikipedia: Oldest McDonald’s restaurant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldest_McDonald%27s_restaurant).
The Googie article names the Downey stand as a preserved example of the style. [Wikipedia: Googie architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Googie_architecture).
observed: A tall parabolic arch of yellow sheet metal, outlined with several parallel tubes along its length, rises from one end of the roof and lands at the other.
A second arch shows behind it, at the far side of the roof.
A band of yellow tubes runs along the roof edge, and a thick white roof slab slopes down from right to left over a glass front.
Yellow wedge-shaped panels end the roof at both corners; a wall at left has red and white horizontal stripes.
The ground is clear blue sky with white cloud; the palette is yellow, white, red, and blue.
interpretation: The arches carry no load: they are a sign built into the building, which Googie made into a rule. The parallel tubes along them look like lighting tubes, but this daytime photograph does not show them lit.
borrow: Put one bold parabolic arc across a header, outlined with two or three parallel lines.
Slope the main panel down at an angle and end it with a wedge in the accent color.

images.alt: Color photograph of a yellow arch outlined with parallel tubes rising over a sloped white roof slab, with a second arch behind it, blue sky, and a glass storefront below.
images.caption: John Margolies, McDonald’s, Downey, California, 1985. John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2017709079/). A small neighboring shop sign at lower right is incidental.

rights.statement: Library of Congress rights advisory: “No known restrictions on publication.” The Library acquired the rights to the Margolies photographs with the archive. The building was finished in 1953 in the United States, before December 1990, so it is not protected as an architectural work. The arches are a McDonald’s trademark; this record uses them only for commentary.

references.title: Mécano no. 3 (Red): “Chroniek-Mécano”, 1922
references.lede: In his Dada magazine Mécano, Theo van Doesburg reports the 1922 Weimar congress of Constructivists and Dadaists as a mock telegram, under a title that mixes capitals and lowercase letter by letter.
references.summary: A mixed-case sans title, telegram-style text cut by heavy black dashes, and thick rules on pink-red paper. Van Doesburg, 1922.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Mécano no. 3, “Chroniek-Mécano” (scan from RKD)

creator.name: Theo van Doesburg (attributed by Commons and RKD; the page is unsigned)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons scan credited to RKD (1500 × 1922 px original, viewed at 1200 px). Commons does not name the physical copy or its owner. The page is one page of the magazine, not its cover.

styles.note: A page from a Dada magazine: a letter-by-letter mixed-case title, heavy black dashes as ornaments, and one strong color. Partial fit: the body is one plain roman in a justified block.

context: Commons describes the page as “Chroniek-Mécano”, *Mécano* no. 3 Rouge, Rood, Rot, Red, about October 1922, by [Theo van Doesburg], source RKD. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:M%C3%A9cano_no_003_rouge,_rood,_rot,_red_Chroniek-M%C3%A9cano.jpg).

*Mécano* was the Dutch Dada magazine that van Doesburg published in 1922–1923 under his Dada name I.K. Bonset. [Wikipedia: Theo van Doesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_van_Doesburg). Each issue was named for a color: Commons also holds the [yellow](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:M%C3%A9cano_yellow_001.jpg) and [blue](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wrapper_M%C3%A9cano_Blue_1922.jpg) wrappers.

The text reports the International Congress of Constructivists and Dadaists in Weimar in September 1922, with Tzara, Arp, Schwitters, Lissitzky, and Moholy-Nagy. The [style record](style:dada) treats the overlap of late Dada and Constructivism.
observed: The page is printed in black on a strong pink-red paper.
The title “ChRoNiEk-MÉCaNo” is a geometric sans-serif in which capitals and small letters alternate inside the word, and some letters drop below the baseline.
Under it, “Cablogramme” and a line of cities, “Weimar—Paris—Zürich—Budapest—Moskau”, are set in a lighter grotesque.
The body is one justified block of a plain roman. It switches between French, Dutch, and German, and short heavy black dashes separate the items, as in a telegram.
Two words, “constatation” and “Bauchgehirn”, are set in a bold grotesque inside the roman text.
Thick black rules frame the page at top and bottom. One rule ends the last line of text.
interpretation: The disorder here is verbal and in the title, not in the layout. The page shows the Dutch side of Dada, where van Doesburg kept the strong rules of De Stijl and put the chaos into the letters and the languages.
borrow: Alternate capitals and small letters inside one heading word, and keep the body in a plain roman.
Use short heavy black dashes as item separators in running text.
Print a whole page on one strong colored ground with black only.

images.alt: Pink-red magazine page with the title ChRoNiEk-MÉCaNo in alternating capitals and small letters, the subtitle Cablogramme, and a justified block of black text about the 1922 Weimar congress of Constructivists and Dada, cut by short heavy dashes and framed by thick black rules.
images.caption: Theo van Doesburg, “Chroniek-Mécano”, *Mécano* no. 3 (Red), about October 1922. Scan from RKD via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:M%C3%A9cano_no_003_rouge,_rood,_rot,_red_Chroniek-M%C3%A9cano.jpg), PD-old-70-expired.

rights.statement: Commons tags the scan PD-old-70-expired. Van Doesburg, a Dutch author, died in 1931, so the work is public domain in the Netherlands. It was published in 1922, so it is public domain in the United States. The page is unsigned; if another editor wrote it, the attribution would need review, but the only other names on the page are subjects of the report.

identifiers.commons: File:Mécano no 003 rouge, rood, rot, red Chroniek-Mécano.jpg

references.title: Merz 1: Holland Dada, January 1923
references.lede: The first issue of Kurt Schwitters’s magazine Merz puts a condensed MERZ, a heavy roman HOLLAND DADA, a crossed DA sign, and a pointing hand on one plain cover.
references.summary: Condensed sans MERZ, heavy roman HOLLAND DADA, a crossed DA sign, and a pointing hand on buff paper. Kurt Schwitters, 1923.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Merz no. 1 (Holland Dada), Rijksmuseum RP-P-BR-2013-2-3

evidence.note: Inspected JoJan’s photograph of the Rijksmuseum copy, RP-P-BR-2013-2-3, on loan from the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Merz_jan_1923_001.JPG), 1551 × 2259 px original, viewed at 1200 px). The photograph is taken at a slight angle and has a glare spot on the last letter A. The Rijksmuseum object URL in the old format returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-02, so the object data comes from the Commons record.

styles.note: A Dada magazine cover that mixes a condensed sans, a heavy roman, small grotesque labels, and a printer’s pointing hand. Partial fit: the layout is calmer and more aligned than a Dada broadside.

context: Commons records the object as the first number of the journal *Merz*, January 1923, letterpress, in the Rijksmuseum (RP-P-BR-2013-2-3), on loan from the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam since 2013. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Merz_jan_1923_001.JPG).

The table of contents on the cover lists “Dada in Holland”, poems by Kok and Bonset, “An Anna Blume”, and drawings by Picabia and Hannah Höch. [Commons inscription field](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Merz_jan_1923_001.JPG).

Schwitters published *Merz* from Hannover from 1923 to 1932. [Wikipedia: Kurt Schwitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Schwitters). The first issue followed the Dutch Dada tour with Theo van Doesburg; see [the soirée program](ref:van-doesburg-schwitters-kleine-dada-soiree-1922).
observed: “MERZ” fills the top half in very tall, condensed sans-serif capitals, set wide apart.
Below it, a large numeral “1” and “HOLLAND DADA” in a heavy roman with bracketed serifs, a different face from the title.
At the right, a black X with “DA” in each of its four angles, and below it a small dark blue square pasted or printed on the page.
A large black pointing hand, a stock printer’s cut, points up at the lower left.
The contents at the top and the imprint at the bottom are small heavy grotesque capitals between thin rules.
The ink is black on buff-brown paper. The blue square is the only other color.
interpretation: The cover shows Hannover Dada at its most typographic: three unrelated faces and a stock cut on one page, but held in a mostly left-aligned column. It points ahead to Schwitters’s later constructive typography.
borrow: Pair a very condensed sans title with a heavy roman subtitle, so the contrast of faces does the work.
Use a large pointing hand as the only image, and point it at the title.

images.alt: Buff magazine cover with MERZ in tall condensed black capitals, a large 1, HOLLAND DADA in a heavy serif face, a black X with DA in each angle, a small blue square, and a black pointing hand at the lower left above the imprint January 1923, Kurt Schwitters, Hannover.
images.caption: Kurt Schwitters, *Merz* no. 1, January 1923. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, RP-P-BR-2013-2-3. Photograph by JoJan, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Merz_jan_1923_001.JPG).

rights.statement: The photograph is by JoJan, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0; credit “JoJan, Wikimedia Commons”. Commons also tags the work PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired, death year 1948). Schwitters, the cover’s designer, died in 1948, so the cover is public domain in Germany. It was published in 1923, so it is public domain in the United States. The cover shows no work by Höch or other living-term contributors; only their names appear in the contents.

references.title: Merz 8/9: Nasci, 1924
references.lede: El Lissitzky and Kurt Schwitters edit the double issue of Merz on nature and form. Lissitzky’s title page sets a Brockhaus definition in red sans-serif capitals between blue bars.
references.summary: Blue MERZ with serif numerals, red sans-serif capitals between blue bars, vertical imprints, and a pointing hand. Lissitzky and Schwitters, 1924.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: 8 Merz 9 / Nasci (Ketterer Kunst copy)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image of a copy sold by Ketterer Kunst (3850 × 5003 px original, viewed at 1200 px). Commons gives the size as 30.8 × 23.5 cm. A second Commons copy from charnelhouse.org exists ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1924._Merz_Magazine_Layout_by_El_Lissitzky.jpg)) and was not compared.

styles.note: A late issue of Schwitters’s Dada magazine, with mixed serif and sans faces, vertical text, and a pointing hand. Partial fit: the bars and the aligned red block are Constructivist order, as the style’s confusion notes say.

context: Commons describes the image as the title page of *Merz* double issue 8/9, 1924, title design by El Lissitzky, 30.8 × 23.5 cm, from Ketterer Kunst, tagged PD-scan (PD-old-auto-expired, death year 1941). [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:8_Merz_9_Doppelheft.jpg).
The page itself states that the double issue appeared under the editorship of El Lissitzky and Kurt Schwitters, with typography by Lissitzky.

Wikipedia says Lissitzky edited and typeset *Merz 8/9*. The [Dada style record](style:dada) cites it as a work between Dada and [Constructivism](style:constructivism). Compare [Merz 1](ref:schwitters-merz-1-holland-dada-1923).
observed: “MERZ” is set in tall blue condensed sans-serif capitals, between a blue serif “8” and “9” of a different face.

Below it, the definition “NATUR von lat. NASCI d. i. werden oder entstehen heisst alles, was sich aus sich selbst durch eigene Kraft entwickelt gestaltet und bewegt” runs in red sans-serif capitals, with “NASCI” in a heavy bold.
Each red line sits between thick blue horizontal bars that start at one long blue vertical bar at the left.
Two imprints run vertically at the left: “REDAKTION DES MERZVERLAGES …” and “TYPOGRAPHIE ANGEGEBEN VON EL LISSITZKY”.
A small blue pointing hand points up at the left margin. The date “APRIL JULI 1924” is letter-spaced in blue capitals at lower left.
A French version of the definition, with a red “NASCI”, is set in small type at the bottom. The paper is off-white, and only red and blue inks are used.
interpretation: The page shows where Dada typography ends: the mixed faces, the pointing hand, and the vertical imprints survive, but the bars and the aligned text block give a clear order. It is a good contrast record for the Dada rubric.
borrow: Run thick bars between lines of a text block, all starting from one vertical bar.
Set a running imprint vertically in small capitals along the left edge.

images.alt: Magazine title page: 8 MERZ 9 in blue at the top, a definition of the word Nasci in red sans-serif capitals between blue horizontal bars, vertical blue imprints at the left, a small blue pointing hand, and April Juli 1924 at lower left.
images.caption: El Lissitzky and Kurt Schwitters, *Merz* 8/9 (*Nasci*), 1924, title page. Copy sold by Ketterer Kunst, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:8_Merz_9_Doppelheft.jpg), PD-scan.

rights.statement: Commons tags the scan PD-scan (PD-old-auto-expired, death year 1941). Lissitzky died in 1941 and Schwitters in 1948, and the issue was published in Germany in 1924, so it is public domain in Germany. It was published before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States.

references.title: Mindustry
references.lede: Anuken’s open-source factory and tower-defense game builds conveyors, turrets, ore fields, and its menus from crisp pixel tiles and a bitmap interface face.
references.summary: A top-down pixel factory on sand and rock with conveyor lines, a wave counter, and pixel icon menus. Anuken, version 3.5, 2019, GPL 3.
references.made: Repository created 2017; screenshot of version 3.5, January 2019

evidence.note: Inspected [Mindustry 3.5.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mindustry_3.5.png) on Wikimedia Commons, 1189 × 748 px, a screenshot taken by the uploader on 26 January 2019.

styles.note: Partial fit: tiles, sprites, menus, and type are all whole-pixel art with flat colors, but translucent smooth circles for turret ranges and thin laser lines lie over the map.

context: Wikipedia describes Mindustry as a free and open-source real-time strategy, factory management, and tower defense game developed and published by Anuken under the GNU GPL v3. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindustry).
The repository describes “The automation tower defense RTS” and carries the GPL 3.0 license. [GitHub](https://github.com/Anuken/Mindustry).
observed: A top-down map of beige sand, a dark gray rock field, and red-orange ore, each a field of square tiles with stepped edges.
Blocks in teal, blue, and purple are linked by conveyor lines with small item pixels on them.
At top left, square icon buttons and a dark panel read “WAVE 62” in orange and “12 ENEMIES” in white, in a bitmap face.
At right, a dark panel lists resource counts (“42K”, “3.5K”) and a grid of ship sprites in square frames, with one selected frame outlined in orange.
Translucent blue circles, a dashed green circle, and green beam lines are drawn over the tiles.
interpretation: Mindustry shows that the style scales to dense strategy screens: a strict tile grid and a bitmap face keep many small parts legible.
The smooth range circles are game information, not decoration, but they break the one-grid rule.
borrow: Set counters and labels in a bitmap face inside dark square panels, with one orange highlight for the selected item.
Give each material one flat color family so that a dense map stays readable.

images.alt: Game screenshot: a top-down pixel factory of teal and blue blocks and conveyor lines on beige sand and dark rock, with translucent blue range circles. A dark panel at top left reads wave 62, 12 enemies. A panel at right shows resource counts and ship icons.
images.caption: Anuken, Mindustry version 3.5, screenshot by a Commons user, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mindustry_3.5.png), GPL.

rights.statement: Commons lists the file as GPL, credit “Anuken and Mindustry contributors”: “This is a screenshot of a free and open-source game Mindustry version 3.5, taken by me. The game is licensed under the GPL as a whole.” The repository is licensed GPL 3.0.

references.title: NCSA Mosaic (web browser)
references.lede: The 1993 browser that brought pages with inline images, blue underlined links, and a gray page ground to a wide audience.
references.summary: NCSA Mosaic: the default rendering of early web pages, with serif headings and blue underlined links.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: NCSA Mosaic Browser Screenshot

creator.name: National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA), University of Illinois

evidence.note: The Commons screenshot (772 × 668 px, CC0, by Charles Severance, 2013) is below the 800 px threshold for an observed record, so no traits are recorded as observed. The release year comes from general histories and was not checked against an NCSA source.

styles.note: Lineage: an early browser whose default rendering became the look that later brutalist sites copy on purpose.

references.notice: This is a lineage reference. Mosaic’s default page ground was gray, not white.
context: The Commons description reads “NCSA Mosaic for X Screenshot”. The license is CC0 for the screenshot, but the browser interface belongs to the University of Illinois, so the image is not stored.
[NN/g (2017)](ref:nngroup-brutalism-antidesign-article-2017) ties the style to early 1990s websites, which were shaped by browsers of this generation.
interpretation: A source for the defaults that [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design) restates: link blue, underlines, bold serif headings, and native gray controls. A larger image is needed to record the traits as observed.

rights.statement: Screenshot CC0 (Charles Severance); the depicted software interface is © University of Illinois. Not stored.

references.title: Neko Atsume: Kitty Collector
references.lede: Hit-Point’s mobile game in which round, simply drawn cats visit a yard; its interface uses thick outlines, rounded panels, and paw-print motifs.
references.summary: Cat-collecting mobile game with outlined cats, rounded cream panels, and a paw-print menu button. Hit-Point, 2014.

source.label: App Store: Neko Atsume: Kitty Collector

evidence.note: Inspected three App Store screenshots of the current English iOS version (1000 px wide, scratchpad copies): the yard view and the shop. The screenshots may differ from the 2014 release. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: dot-eyed cats, rounded outlined panels, and paw motifs are kawaii interface grammar, but the palette is muted earth and green rather than pastel.

context: Wikipedia describes Neko Atsume as a cat-collecting game for iOS and Android by Hit-Point, released on 20 October 2014; players set out food, toys, and furniture to attract cats, then take photos and receive gifts of dried sardines. It won the CEDEC Award for game design in August 2015. [Wikipedia: Neko Atsume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neko_Atsume).
observed: The yard is drawn in flat fills with an even dark-brown outline: a green hedge, a red-roofed house, a tree stump, a tatami mat, and a cardboard box.
Cats are short, round bodies with small round heads, two dot eyes, and a tiny “ω” mouth; one hugs a ball, one lies on a stump.
The menu button is a rounded square in orange with a white paw print and the word “Menu” in a rounded hand-drawn face.
In the shop, items sit in cream cards with thick dark outlines and very round corners, on a mint-green ground patterned with faint paw prints.
A pill-shaped speech bubble reads “Gifts Await”; prices use bold rounded numerals next to small fish icons.
interpretation: The game applies kawaii to a whole interface: the characters set the mood, and the controls are drawn in the same outlined, rounded hand. The cats are decorative and never carry information, which matches the style’s rules.
The muted, domestic palette is a quieter branch of the style; it relies on line and shape more than on pastel color.
borrow: Draw interface cards and buttons with the same thick outline as the characters, so the whole screen feels like one sticker sheet.
Use a faint repeated motif (paw prints) as a low-contrast background pattern.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The game and its artwork are © Hit-Point Co., Ltd.

references.title: Neon and LED signs on Portland Street, Mong Kok
references.lede: Hand-bent neon and LED-dot signs in Chinese characters glow red, yellow, and green against black building facades in Mong Kok, Hong Kong.
references.summary: Red and green neon tubes and LED-dot characters on a black night ground. Photograph by Benlisquare, Mong Kok, Hong Kong, 2025.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: LED and neon signs on Portland Street at night.jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons 1920 px rendition of the 6000 × 4000 px original. The description reads “An assortment of LED and neon shop signs on Portland Street in Mong Kok at night.”

styles.note: Partial fit: the neon-on-black source of the style’s palette and glow, from the Hong Kong streets that Wikipedia names as a model for the cyberpunk city. It has no HUD or terminal elements.

context: Wikipedia: Ridley Scott envisioned the Los Angeles of [Blade Runner](ref:blade-runner-1982) as “Hong Kong on a very bad day”, and the city of [Ghost in the Shell](ref:ghost-in-the-shell-film-1995) was based on Hong Kong. [Cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk).

The photograph is in the Commons categories “Neon signs in Portland Street, Hong Kong” and “Shop signs in Mong Kok”. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LED_and_neon_signs_on_Portland_Street_at_night.jpg).
observed: The ground is black or deep red: unlit facades with air conditioners, pipes, and window frames, lit only by the signs.
A tall vertical neon sign at upper left has orange-yellow characters inside a green neon outline.
Two horizontal signs in the center have characters drawn in orange LED dots on dark blue panels, edged with rows of blue and white dots.
A red neon sign at right, with large characters inside a red tube frame, casts red light over the building above it.
A smaller sign at left has pink-white neon characters over green neon text, including “卡拉OK”.
The halos around the tubes are soft and centered, with no offset.
interpretation: Here the grammar’s “glow, not shadow” is literal: each line is a light source, and its halo spreads evenly on all sides.
The green outline around the yellow vertical sign is the same device as a glowing hairline frame around a panel.
borrow: Draw a frame as a single glowing line in a second color around text of a first color.
Build large characters from dots, as on LED signs, for a display face that reads as light.

images.alt: Shop signs at night in Chinese characters: a tall yellow neon sign with a green outline, two dark panels with orange dot-matrix characters, and a large red neon sign that lights the building red. The facades behind are almost black.
images.caption: LED and neon shop signs on Portland Street, Mong Kok, Hong Kong, 31 July 2025. Photograph by Benlisquare, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LED_and_neon_signs_on_Portland_Street_at_night.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Photograph by Benlisquare, “Own work”, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons. The subject is a group of commercial shop signs on a public street. Hong Kong’s Copyright Ordinance (s. 71) permits photographs of works of artistic craftsmanship permanently in public places; the lead curator may confirm that this covers neon signs.

identifiers.commons: File:LED and neon signs on Portland Street at night.jpg

references.title: Neon signs on Shantung Street, Mong Kok
references.lede: A crowded pedestrian street in Mong Kok, Hong Kong, under a canopy of illuminated Chinese and English signs for pharmacies, hotels, and shops.
references.summary: Layers of red, green, and magenta signs over a night street crowd. Photograph by Benh Lieu Song, Mong Kok, Hong Kong, 2019.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Mong Kok Neon Signs Night (48127904386).jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons 1920 px rendition of the 6000 × 4000 px original, uploaded from Flickr (photo 48127904386) and reviewed by FlickreviewR 2. The description reads “Night busy life and neon signs on Shantung Street, near the Ladies Market in Mong Kok, Hong Kong.”

styles.note: Partial fit: the dense Hong Kong sign canopy that the genre took as a model for its night city. It is a real street, without HUD or terminal elements.

context: Wikipedia names Hong Kong and Kowloon Walled City as models for the cyberpunk city, and Ridley Scott described the look of Blade Runner as “Hong Kong on a very bad day”. See [Blade Runner](ref:blade-runner-1982) and [Kowloon Walled City](ref:kowloon-walled-city-aerial-1989).

Mong Kok is a district of Kowloon known for street markets and dense shop signage. The photograph is in the Commons categories “Luminous shop signs in Hong Kong” and “Street photography in Hong Kong”. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mong_Kok_Neon_Signs_Night_(48127904386).jpg).
observed: Signs fill the upper half of the frame in several overlapping layers, each projecting over the street.

The largest are a red-on-blue LED sign with Chinese characters and a red-and-white checkered “Rx” mark at left, a green sign reading “REGENG HOTEL” at top center, and a magenta-edged sign reading “GOLDEN DISPENSARY” at right.
Many signs are framed by rows of small LED dots. Text is mostly heavy Chinese characters, with smaller English capitals below.
Two red no-entry road signs and metal barriers stand in the street. The crowd below is blurred by a slow shutter.
A dark tower block with lit windows closes the far end of the street. The sky is not visible.
interpretation: The density is the point: sign over sign with no empty sky, which is the visual model for the style’s many small labelled panels.
Each sign is a framed panel with an outline of lights. That is the street origin of the glowing hairline frame.
borrow: Overlap many small framed panels in depth, each with its own outline of light, rather than one large hero image.
Pair a large heavy heading with a small line of capitals below it, as on bilingual signs.

images.alt: A crowded night street lined with many projecting illuminated signs in Chinese and English, in red, green, blue, and magenta. People walk, blurred by motion, between barriers and two red no-entry signs.
images.caption: Shantung Street, Mong Kok, Hong Kong, 13 June 2019. Photograph by Benh Lieu Song, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mong_Kok_Neon_Signs_Night_(48127904386).jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0. Shop signs appear incidentally as part of the street.

rights.statement: Photograph by Benh Lieu Song from Torcy, France, published on Flickr under CC BY-SA 2.0 and transferred to Wikimedia Commons. The main subject is a public street. The many shop signs are commercial signage seen as part of the street scene, not a single copyrighted work.

references.title: Neuromancer, first edition
references.lede: William Gibson’s 1984 novel, published by Ace Books with a cover by James Warhola, which set the terms of cyberpunk: cyberspace, the matrix, and jacking in.
references.summary: The novel that defined cyberpunk and named cyberspace. William Gibson, Ace Books, 1984; cover by James Warhola.

creator.name: William Gibson (author); James Warhola (cover artist, first edition)

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article, read as wikitext on 2026-10-02, whose infobox names James Warhola as the cover artist of the first edition. The cover image was not inspected, so this record makes no claim about its appearance.

styles.note: The genre’s defining novel. The style record dates the look from Blade Runner and Akira in 1982 and Neuromancer in 1984. It supplies the vocabulary of the terminal and HUD side of the style.

context: Wikipedia: *Neuromancer* was published by Ace Books on 1 July 1984, with a first-edition cover by James Warhola. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer).
It “remains the first and only novel to win all three of the Hugo Award, the Nebula Award for Best Novel, and the Philip K. Dick Award”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer).
Wikipedia’s Cyberpunk article notes that the novel is set in Chiba, Japan, and that its influence “dominated the early cyberpunk movement”. [Cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk).
interpretation: The book gives the style its ideas rather than its pictures: a city of data, terminals, and bodies wired into machines. Designers turn these into terminal type, data panels, and HUD frames.
Its Japanese setting links it to the same Tokyo and Hong Kong imagery as [Blade Runner](ref:blade-runner-1982) and [Akira](ref:akira-film-1988).
borrow: Name panels and controls with short technical terms and codes, as the novel names its systems.
next: Inspect the 1984 Ace first-edition cover from a reliable copy (for example a library or ISFDB scan) and add observations.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The text and the cover art are in copyright.

references.title: NN/g, “Brutalism and Antidesign”
references.lede: A usability firm separates raw, stripped-down web brutalism from deliberately chaotic antidesign.
references.summary: Kate Moran’s 2017 NN/g article: brutalism echoes bare 1990s HTML; antidesign is a separate, chaotic branch.

evidence.note: Article text read on 2026-10-02. The byline and the date (5 November 2017, modified 30 April 2020) are in the page’s structured data. The example screenshots in the article were not inspected.

styles.note: The main design-authority source for the name, and the source of the split between the raw core and antidesign.

context: Definition: “Brutalism in digital design is a style that intentionally attempts to look raw, haphazard, or unadorned. It echoes early 1990s-style websites (think Craigslist and the Drudge Report).”
On form: “Sometimes this aspect of brutalism is expressed as bare-bones, almost naked HTML site with blue links and monochromatic Monospace text.”

It notes that Craigslist was plain from the late 1990s because of HTML and CSS limits, not by artistic choice, and that NN/g’s own site in 2000 used “an unadorned, protobrutalist style”. Justin Jackson’s blog is cited for “black and blue Monospace typography”.
Antidesign, “often also referred to as brutalism”, is described separately: no visual hierarchy, harsh colors, disorienting patterns, odd cursors, and distracting animation.
interpretation: This article sets the scope of [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design): the raw, readable core. The chaotic branch is antidesign and is not part of the style.
borrow: Use the article’s test: does the page feel raw because it shows its HTML, or because it is hard to use? Only the first is this style.

rights.statement: © Nielsen Norman Group. Link and quotation only.

references.title: no style, please! (Jekyll theme)
references.lede: An open-source blog theme with about 1 kB of CSS that leaves almost everything at browser defaults.
references.summary: riggraz’s 2020 Jekyll theme: black monospace text on white, default blue and purple underlined links, nested bullets.

evidence.note: Opened the repository’s README screenshot `_screenshots/featured-image.png` (2678 × 1500 px) with the Read tool on 2026-10-02, and read `_sass/no-style-please.scss`. Repository created 10 July 2020 (GitHub API). The live demo was not captured.

styles.note: Nearly unstyled HTML on purpose: default links, default lists, black on white, one monospace face.

context: The README describes it as “A (nearly) no-CSS, fast, minimalist Jekyll theme”, “Inspired by [elly’s site](http://tilde.town/~elly/)”, with “1kb of CSS”.
The stylesheet sets `color: black; font-family: monospace; font-size: 16px` on a white body, a 640 px column, and a dark mode made with `filter: invert(1)`. It does not set link colors.
MIT license. A Hugo port exists: [hanwenguo/hugo-theme-nostyleplease](https://github.com/hanwenguo/hugo-theme-nostyleplease) (2022).
observed: The light screenshot shows a bold monospace title, “no style, please!”, above a nested bulleted list with disc, circle, and square markers.
Links are underlined; unvisited links are bright blue and visited links purple, as in browser defaults.
Post dates in ISO form (2020-07-09) sit before each link. No images, rules, boxes, or shadows.
The dark screenshot is the same page inverted: white monospace on black, with a yellow footnote link.
interpretation: A clear current example of [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design) in the monospace variant that [NN/g (2017)](ref:nngroup-brutalism-antidesign-article-2017) describes: “blue links and monochromatic Monospace text”.
borrow: Use nested lists as navigation and let the default bullet shapes show the hierarchy.
Make a dark mode by inverting the page instead of designing a second palette.

rights.statement: The code is MIT-licensed. The screenshot was viewed at its source and is not stored.

references.title: Otl Aicher, Ulm Volkshochschule poster “Realistische Weltliteratur der Gegenwart”, 1956
references.lede: A square poster by Otl Aicher for the Ulm adult education centre: alternating red and black bars on pale paper, with the course text set inside them.
references.summary: Red and black horizontal and vertical bars on pale paper, with text in a bold sans set inside the bars. Aicher, Ulm, 1956.

evidence.note: Inspected the HfG-Archiv image of poster HfG-Ar Ai G 591 at 960 × 958 px through museum-digital. The lower left corner of the sheet is torn.

styles.note: Aicher’s Ulm graphic work from the school’s founding years. It belongs to the graphic branch, not the grey product core.

context: The HfG-Archiv record gives Otl Aicher (1922–1991) as author, 1956, print on paper, 40.5 × 40.5 cm, and calls it a poster of the Ulm Volkshochschule for a course by Hans Werner Richter. [museum-digital 2047820](https://global.museum-digital.org/object/2047820).

The record says that Richter, Inge Scholl, the founder of the Volkshochschule, and Otl Aicher met in November 1947 at a meeting of the “Gruppe 47”, and planned a “new school” from which the Hochschule für Gestaltung grew. [museum-digital](https://global.museum-digital.org/object/2047820).
observed: The square sheet is pale grey-beige paper, filled with flat bars of red and black that alternate.
On the left, eight horizontal bars of different lengths stack with even gaps. On the right, four vertical bars stand above five horizontal bars.
The title “Realistische Weltliteratur der Gegenwart” runs vertically up two red bars, in a bold sans-serif.
“Kurs Hans Werner Richter” and the lowercase word “dienstags” sit inside red bars in black type.
There is no image and no ornament.
interpretation: The poster shows the graphic side of Ulm before the product program: a modular system of bars, text placed inside the system, and two colors. It is louder than the Braun products and closer to the Swiss style, so it marks the edge of this record.
borrow: Build a layout from bars of one width and set the text inside them.

rights.statement: The museum-digital record marks the image “RR-P” (rights reserved) and names Museum Ulm/HfG-Archiv and Florian Aicher. Otl Aicher died in 1991, so the work is protected until the end of 2061. No image is stored.

references.title: P. T. Barnum’s American Museum handbill, January 1845
references.lede: A narrow New York handbill for Barnum’s museum that stacks shaded, fat, and Egyptian lines around a stock woodcut of an orangutan.
references.summary: Museum handbill with a shaded headline, wavy rules, pointing hands, and a woodcut. New York, 1845.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Houghton TCS 65 – Playbill, Barnum American Museum, 1845

creator.name: Designer unidentified (Houghton Library); P. T. Barnum, proprietor

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image of the Houghton Library copy (Harvard Theatre Collection, TCS 65, Playbills and Programs from New York City Theaters). The original file is 573 × 1805 px; it was viewed through a Commons thumbnail because the original returned HTTP 429, and the stored copy is 508 × 1600 px.

styles.note: A show bill with centred lines in many faces, wavy and straight rules, pointing hands, and a stock cut. Partial fit: two lines run vertically beside the cut.

context: Commons describes the file as a handbill advertisement for P. T. Barnum’s American Museum, c. 6 January 1845, in Playbills and Programs from New York City Theaters (TCS 65), Harvard Theatre Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University, designer unidentified.
The bill names the museum at the corner of Broadway and Ann Street, P. T. Barnum as proprietor, and F. Hitchcock as manager.
observed: “MUSEUM!” is set in a shaded open letter with a drop shadow; “AMERICAN” above it in small spaced capitals.
Below, centred lines alternate between fat face, letterspaced Egyptian (“LECTURE ROOM”), bold roman, and italic, with wavy rules between them.
A woodcut of an orangutan seated on a chair fills the middle, with “ORANG” and “Outang!” set vertically on each side.
Pointing hands lead into “MAD’LE FANNY,” and “Petrologist!”.
“Mad. Rockwell,” is in a fat face with ball terminals.
Black ink on buff paper, foxed at the edges, with “TURN OVER” at the foot.
interpretation: Barnum’s bill shows the showman’s use of the style: each attraction gets a new face, and the sensational words get the heaviest letters.
The vertical lines next to the cut are an exception to the horizontal rule, used to fit a big name beside a picture on a narrow sheet.
borrow: Put a wavy rule between light announcements and a straight rule between sections.
Wrap a single picture with the name of the thing it shows.

images.alt: Narrow buff handbill. Centred lines in many typefaces read American Museum!, Every Day and Evening this Week, Grand Performances!, Lecture Room, and Splendid Company of Performers. A woodcut of a seated orangutan has the words Orang and Outang! set vertically on each side, and lower lines with pointing hands read Mad'le Fanny and Petrologist!
images.caption: Handbill for P. T. Barnum’s American Museum, New York, January 1845. Houghton Library, Harvard University, TCS 65, through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Houghton_TCS_65_-_Playbill,_Barnum_American_Museum,_1845.jpg). Public domain.

rights.statement: Commons tags the file {{PD-old}} and links the [Harvard catalogue record](http://id.lib.harvard.edu/aleph/012690355/catalog) for TCS 65 as source. The handbill was published in New York in 1845 by an unidentified designer.

identifiers.commons: File:Houghton TCS 65 - Playbill, Barnum American Museum, 1845.jpg

references.title: Parole in libertà (premier record)
references.lede: A words-in-freedom sheet by F. T. Marinetti that mixes hand lettering, cut-out printed type, maps, cars, aeroplanes, and an airship to celebrate the first record of speed and distance.
references.summary: A huge “1er RÉCORD” among arrows, cars, aeroplanes, and lettering at every angle. F. T. Marinetti, 1916.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, parole in libertà (premier record), 1916 (coll. priv.)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 1652 × 2136 px; stored at 1237 × 1600 px). It is a photograph by the Commons user Sailko, taken on 26 June 2017 at the exhibition *Intuition* at the Palazzo Fortuny, Venice. The file title says the work is in a private collection. The photo is taken through glazing; the frame and slight reflections are visible.

styles.note: A full words-in-freedom page: type in many sizes and at many angles, very large numbers, arrows of force, and the machines of speed.

context: The Commons file names the work *parole in libertà (premier record)*, 1916, in a private collection, and records that it was photographed in the exhibition *Intuition* at the Palazzo Fortuny, Venice, in 2017. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Filippo_tommaso_marinetti,_parole_in_libert%C3%A0_(premier_record),_1916_(coll._priv.).jpg).
observed: A tall black “1” cut from paper and a hand-lettered “er” and “RÉCORD” in brown ink dominate the upper half.
At the top, “PREMIER” and “MOI” are written many times in different sizes and in both capitals and lower case, running off at slight angles.
Arrows and dashed lines point upward to the right toward the word “PÔLE”; along them run stretched words such as “COURAAAAAAGE” and “ENCOOOOORE”.
Cut-out printed pictures of cars, an airship, a biplane, a locomotive, and a map of Labrador and Newfoundland are pasted at different angles.
Brown ink drawings of racing cars, a horse and rider, and a running figure fill the lower half.
A black jagged line runs diagonally down the right side; the words “5000 Km” and “ATLANTIQUE” follow another diagonal.
The palette is brown ink and black on aged buff paper.
interpretation: The sheet treats a page as a map of effort and speed: records, distances, and machines are joined by arrows. The repeated “MOI” and “PREMIER” make the egotism of the record into typography.
Hand lettering, printed fragments, and pictures sit together without a grid, which is the core of the words-in-freedom method.
borrow: Make one number or word much larger than everything else and let the rest orbit it.
Repeat a short word at many sizes to build a chant.
Join words with arrows and dashed paths so the reading order becomes a route.

images.alt: Framed sheet of aged buff paper with a huge black 1 and the brown hand-lettered words er RÉCORD and PÔLE. Repeated words PREMIER and MOI fill the top; arrows, dashed lines, cut-out pictures of cars, an airship, a biplane, a map, and a locomotive, and ink drawings of racing cars cover the rest at many angles.
images.caption: F. T. Marinetti, *Parole in libertà (premier record)*, 1916, private collection, in the exhibition *Intuition*, Palazzo Fortuny, Venice, 2017. Photograph by Sailko, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Filippo_tommaso_marinetti,_parole_in_libert%C3%A0_(premier_record),_1916_(coll._priv.).jpg), CC BY 3.0.

rights.statement: Photograph by Sailko, licensed CC BY 3.0 on Wikimedia Commons. Marinetti was Italian and died in 1944, more than 70 years ago, so the work is public domain in Italy. It dates from 1916; published or not, it is public domain in the United States because it predates 1931 or its author died more than 70 years ago. Cut-out printed pictures in the collage are by unknown makers and date from before 1916.

identifiers.commons: File:Filippo tommaso marinetti, parole in libertà (premier record), 1916 (coll. priv.).jpg

references.title: Paul van Ostaijen, manuscript of Bezette Stad, 1920–1921
references.lede: In the handwritten draft of his “rhythmic typography” poem cycle, Paul van Ostaijen already lays out words as sound: isolated words, letter-spaced words, and capitals scattered across the sheet.
references.summary: Handwritten poem page with scattered words, capitals, letter-spaced words, and sound words such as BOM BAM and PLOEMP. Van Ostaijen, Berlin, 1920–21.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Bezette Stad manuscript, sheet 102r (Letterenhuis EHC 859433)

references.made: Between 1920 and 1921 (Commons). Written in Berlin between July 1920 and April 1921 (Literaire Canon).

evidence.note: Inspected manuscript sheet 102r on Commons (viewed at 1200 px from the 1280 px thumbnail), and sheet 58r for comparison ([Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bezette_Stad,_0103_EHC_859433_58r.jpg)). Commons gives the source as “DAS Antwerp”; the file names carry the collection number EHC 859433. The printed 1921 book was not inspected.

styles.note: A draft of Flemish Dada-era rhythmic typography: words scattered across the page at many sizes and cases. Partial fit: it is handwritten, has no photographs, and the poet is usually called an expressionist influenced by Dada.

context: Van Ostaijen wrote *Bezette Stad* (Occupied City) in Berlin between July 1920 and April 1921. The first edition appeared in 1921 from his own Antwerp publishing house Sienjaal. [Literaire Canon: Bezette Stad](https://literairecanon.be/canon-2025/bezette-stad).

A bookseller’s description of the first edition credits its typography to O. Jespers and R. Victor and gives an edition of 540 copies. [Arine van der Steur](https://arinevandersteur.nl/product/literature-1921-vlaams-dada-paul-van-ostaijen-bezette-stad-antwerpen-sienjaal-1921-first-edition-151-pp-typography-o-jespers-and-r-victor-printed-in-540-copies/).

Flanders bought the complete manuscript and placed it on the Flemish heritage list. It is kept at the Letterenhuis in Antwerp from 27 March 2021. [VRT NWS](https://www.vrt.be/vrtnws/nl/2021/02/18/bezette-stad-van-paul-van-ostaijen-wordt-vlaams-topstuk/).
Wikipedia names Dadaism among the influences on his poetry. [Wikipedia: Paul van Ostaijen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_van_Ostaijen).
observed: The sheet is greyish paper with black ink, a red folio number “102” at the top, and a central fold.
Words sit at many positions on the page, not in lines from one margin: “BOM”, a struck-through “B”, and “BAM” spread across one row, “O-” alone below them, and “PLOEMP” at the right.
Some words are capitals in a print-like hand; most are in a cursive script. Size changes from small script to large capitals.
Two words are letter-spaced with dots: “r-a-n-j-e” and “a-k-r-o-k-a-t-e-n”.
Some lines step to the right in a staircase: “golft mee de zaal / rolt mee de zaal / klotst mee de zaal”.
On sheet 58r the poet also draws a small box labelled “Obus” and a large bracket-shaped letter H.
interpretation: The manuscript shows that the scattered layout was part of the writing, not only a printer’s idea. It belongs to the same freeing of type from the line as Dada and Futurist poetry, but without printer’s cuts or photographs.
borrow: Place sound words as separate units across the width, and let white space set the rhythm.
Letter-space a word with dots or hyphens to slow its reading.
Step a repeated phrase down and to the right.

images.alt: Handwritten manuscript page in black ink with words scattered across the sheet: BOM and BAM in capitals, letter-spaced words, PLOEMP at the right, and three stepped lines, with a red page number 102 at the top.
images.caption: Paul van Ostaijen, manuscript of *Bezette Stad*, sheet 102r, 1920–1921. Letterenhuis, Antwerp, EHC 859433, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bezette_Stad,_0181_EHC_859433_102r.jpg), PD-old-70.

rights.statement: Commons tags the scan PD-old-70. Van Ostaijen, a Belgian author, died in 1928, so the manuscript is public domain in Belgium. In the United States an unpublished work is protected for life plus 70 years, which ended in 1998. The printed 1921 book is not stored, because its typography is also credited to Oscar Jespers, who died in 1970.

references.title: Pikachu soft toy
references.lede: A yellow plush Pikachu from the late-1990s Pokémon boom: a round body, stubby limbs, dot eyes with highlights, and red cheek discs.
references.summary: Seated yellow plush Pikachu with black-tipped ears and round red cheeks. Made in Germany, 1995–1999.

creator.name: Deutshe Toy GMBH (manufacturer, as the V&A spells it); Pokémon created by Satoshi Tajiri

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph 2006AE8391 of object B.89-2004 (1200 × 1600 px, IIIF) in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: the big round head, short limbs, highlighted dot eyes, and blush circles are the kawaii face, but the yellow is strong rather than pastel.

context: The V&A says Pokémon was created by Satoshi Tajiri as games for Nintendo’s Game Boy in 1995, then moved to television, trading cards, and merchandise including soft toys; it calls Pikachu “probably the best known of the Pokémon creatures”. [V&A B.89-2004](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O107469/pikachu-soft-toy/).

The museum records a yellow nylon plush toy, 275 mm high, with black plastic eyes with white dots, cheeks of plastic discs covered in red material, and a stitched nose and mouth, manufactured in Munich. [V&A B.89-2004](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O107469/pikachu-soft-toy/).
observed: The toy sits upright; the head is almost as wide as the body, and the arms and feet are short rounded stubs.
The eyes are black domes with a white highlight, set wide and low; the mouth is a small stitched wavy line under a dot nose.
Two bright red circles mark the cheeks.
The long ears end in black tips; the plush is an even lemon yellow.
interpretation: The face follows the kawaii formula almost exactly: wide-set highlighted dot eyes, a tiny mouth, and cheek blush. The proportions are those of the chibi baby schema.
The saturated yellow shows that the kawaii face and proportions can work without the pastel palette, in the toy and game branch of the style.
borrow: Place dot eyes wide apart and low on the face, each with one small white highlight.
Make cheek blush a clean circle in a single warm color.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Pikachu and Pokémon belong to Nintendo, Creatures, and Game Freak.

references.title: Pilowlava typeface, Velvetyne
references.lede: An open-source display face by Anton Moglia and Jérémy Landes with viscous, lava-like letters built from compass curves and teardrop terminals.
references.summary: Viscous, blobby display letters with teardrop terminals. Anton Moglia and Jérémy Landes, Velvetyne, 2019, SIL Open Font License.

creator.name: Anton Moglia and Jérémy Landes, with Maksym Kobuzan (Cyrillic)

references.made: First published on 26 April 2019, updated on 28 May 2024 (Velvetyne)

evidence.note: Downloaded the web font `pilowlava-regular.woff` from the Velvetyne page and rendered “Pilowlava”, “Quantum leaps”, and a pair alphabet at 90–170 px in a 1400 px scratch image with Pillow. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: free liquid letterforms of the kind the style renders as dripping metal. The face itself is flat and closer to 1970s psychedelic lettering.

context: Velvetyne: the typeface “recalls cooled lava flows drawn with a compass” and “seeks a balance between viscous energy and controlled geometry”. Its geometric approach draws on Armin Hofmann’s *Graphic Design Manual* (1965), and its glyphs draw on “both calligraphic and graffiti references”. [Velvetyne](https://velvetyne.fr/fonts/pilowlava/).
The page gives the license as SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1, two styles (Atome and Regular), and Latin and Cyrillic support.
Fonts In Use lists a 2019 use of Pilowlava in a user-made set called “Acid”. [Fonts In Use](https://fontsinuse.com/sets/14955/acid).
observed: Letters are heavy black blobs with smooth, swelling curves and round teardrop terminals.
Counters are narrow, pointed slits or triangles.
Upper and lower case look alike, and letter widths vary a lot.
Strokes do not follow a constant angle. Some letters lean, and some look upside down.
interpretation: The face provides the liquid letter shapes of the trend under a free license. It needs a chrome or iridescent fill and a dark ground to read as acid graphics rather than psychedelic or 1970s lettering.
borrow: Use a viscous display face for one word and fill it with a chrome gradient.
Keep running text in a plain sans-serif when the display face is this irregular.

rights.statement: The font software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 (Velvetyne). No specimen image is stored, because no openly licensed image of the typeface was found and the design itself is not public domain.

references.title: Pixel Dungeon
references.lede: Oleg Dolya’s open-source roguelike draws its dungeon, its hero, and its whole interface, from health bar to message log, in coarse enlarged pixels.
references.summary: A dark stone dungeon with small sprites, a bitmap message log in green and white, and square pixel buttons. Watabou (Oleg Dolya), 2012, GPL 3.

evidence.note: Inspected the developer’s screenshot `level_up.png` as copied to Wikimedia Commons, [Screenshot of Pixel Dungeon.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Screenshot_of_Pixel_Dungeon.png), 540 × 888 px. Android version, floor 7.

styles.note: Partial fit: sprites, tiles, bitmap type, and stepped interface frames are all pixel art, but a smooth dark vignette of light and shadow covers the map.

context: Wikipedia calls Pixel Dungeon a 2012 roguelike indie game by Oleg Dolya, first for Android, and says that it is open source and that many games build on its code, most notably Shattered Pixel Dungeon. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixel_Dungeon).

The GitHub repository, created in July 2014, describes a “Traditional roguelike game with pixel-art graphics and simple interface” and carries the GPL 3.0 license. [GitHub](https://github.com/watabou/pixel-dungeon).
observed: A top-down dungeon of gray stone tiles and dark water on black, with wooden doors and a staircase sign on the walls.
The hero is a small sprite with red hair and a gray tunic. A skeleton, a green bag, and a scroll lie near him.
Text is set in a bitmap face: “+5EXP level up!” in green over the map and a message log in white and green at the bottom.
The top bar has the hero portrait in a square frame, a red health bar with a stepped end, and white pixel counters at the right.
Square gray buttons at the bottom hold pixel icons: a clock, a magnifier, a question mark, a backpack, and a quick slot reading “1/2”.
A smooth, unstepped shadow darkens the map away from the hero and at the edges, and a soft glow surrounds a wall lamp.
interpretation: The game applies one pixel scale to the world and the interface, so the buttons, bars, and text belong to the same grid as the sprites.
The smooth lighting is a later technique laid over the pixel art. It is a branch from the strict 8-bit core, so the fit is partial.
borrow: Draw interface buttons as square tiles with one pixel icon each, on the same pixel scale as the content.
Use two text colors in a log, one for events and one for system messages.

images.alt: Portrait game screenshot: a dark stone dungeon with a red-haired hero sprite, a skeleton, and green text reading plus 5 EXP, level up. A health bar and portrait sit at the top, a green and white message log and square icon buttons at the bottom.
images.caption: Watabou, Pixel Dungeon on Android, level-up screen. Developer screenshot via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Screenshot_of_Pixel_Dungeon.png), GPL 3.

rights.statement: Commons lists the file as GPLv3, author Watabou, 2013, from `https://pixeldungeon.watabou.ru/screens/level_up.png`. The game repository is licensed GPL 3.0.

references.title: Plusea, PIFpack riso poster
references.lede: An instruction poster for a wearable tool bag, riso-printed in fluorescent pink and a dark blue-gray, with technical drawings and dot-matrix lettering.
references.summary: Instruction poster in fluorescent pink and dark blue riso ink with technical drawings.

evidence.note: Viewed the 727 × 1023 px Flickr “large” file of one poster, photographed flat. Other photos in the same set show other copies and color variants.

styles.note: Fluorescent pink with one dark ink, screened tints, and grain in the solid areas.
