context: The Flickr title is “PIFpack RISO printed posters”, posted under CC BY 2.0 by Plusea. The poster’s footer reads “www.wsp.plusea.at”, the uploader’s own Wearable Studio Practice site, which supports that the uploader made it.
observed: Two inks: fluorescent pink for the tools and labels, and a dark blue-gray for drawings, dimensions, and text.
The blue-gray bands that mark the bag’s seams are screened and grainy.
Pink squares hold dot-and-line monograms, and the title “PIFPACK” is drawn from dots and lines.
Text is a clean sans-serif and stays sharp.
interpretation: The poster shows that riso suits diagrams as well as art: the fluorescent ink highlights, the dark ink explains.
borrow: Use fluorescent pink only for the objects to notice, and a dark spot ink for all structure and text.

images.alt: A poster with technical drawings of a bag; tools and labels are fluorescent pink, and lines and text are dark blue-gray.
images.caption: PIFpack riso poster by Plusea, 2016. CC BY 2.0. [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/plusea/29434481574/), 1024 px “large” size.

rights.statement: Published on Flickr under CC BY 2.0 by Plusea, whose site is printed on the poster. Credit: Plusea.

references.title: Poster for a Risograph demo
references.lede: A two-color poster that announces a Risograph demonstration, printed in red and blue with hand-drawn lettering and a drawing of the machine.
references.summary: Two-color red and blue riso poster for a Risograph demo, with hand lettering.

creator.name: Unknown. The Flickr uploader, lee leblanc, does not say who designed it.

evidence.note: Viewed the 1024 × 765 px Flickr “large” file, a photograph of two copies taped to a wall. The poster names the event (“Monday Nov 30, 6–7 pm”) but not the venue or designer.

styles.note: Partial fit: two spot inks and hand lettering, but little overprint or grain is visible at this size.

context: Posted on Flickr under CC BY 2.0 with the description “see what it can do!”. The designer is not named.
observed: Only two inks appear: a warm red for the title, the machine drawing, and one line, and a blue for the date and script words.
“Magic! Mystery Delight!” is written in blue script over the red drawing of the duplicator.
The paper is white, and both copies look the same, as in a short duplicator run.
interpretation: The poster advertises the machine with its own look: two drums, hand-drawn type, and a drawing of the duplicator.
borrow: Let a script word in the second ink cross a drawing in the first ink.

rights.statement: Photo posted CC BY 2.0 by lee leblanc. The designer is not named, so the poster is treated as in copyright. Link only.

references.title: Press Start 2P typeface
references.lede: CodeMan38’s open bitmap font revives the 8 × 8 character set of 1980s Namco arcade games, with heavy two-pixel strokes and a full lowercase.
references.summary: A heavy 8 × 8 arcade bitmap face with capitals, lowercase, and digits. CodeMan38, 2011, SIL Open Font License.

source.label: Font Stuff from codeman38: Press Start

references.made: First version about 2001; revised as Press Start 2P in June 2011; on Google Fonts from April 2012

evidence.note: Downloaded `PressStart2P-Regular.ttf` from the [Google Fonts repository](https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/ofl/pressstart2p), rendered a specimen at its 8 px design size without anti-aliasing, enlarged it 5× to 1000 × 500 px, and inspected it.

styles.note: A canonical bitmap face for the style: every glyph is drawn on an 8 × 8 pixel cell with square steps, after arcade game fonts.

context: CodeMan38 writes that the font “is based on the fonts from a number of classic Namco arcade games”, specifically the character set of *Return of Ishtar*, one of the first Namco games with a full lowercase. The June 2011 revision added Latin Extended-A, Cyrillic, and Greek. [zone38.net](https://www.zone38.net/font/).

The Google Fonts metadata names the designer CodeMan38, the license OFL, the category Display, and the date added 4 April 2012. The copyright line reads “Copyright 2012 The Press Start 2P Project Authors … with Reserved Font Name ‘Press Start 2P’”. [Google Fonts repository](https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/ofl/pressstart2p).
observed: Each letter fills an 8 × 8 pixel cell. Vertical strokes are two pixels wide and horizontal strokes one pixel high, so the face looks heavy and square.
Curves of C, G, O, and S are cut by single-pixel notches at the corners.
The lowercase has short ascenders and descenders that stay inside the cell.
The face is monospaced: “1UP” and “HI-SCORE” line up on a fixed column grid.
The specimen has two colors only, black on white, with no intermediate gray.
interpretation: The font gives web pages the arcade score-counter look with one family. It suits headings and labels; its heavy strokes and fixed width make long text slow to read.
borrow: Set headings and counters at whole multiples of 8 px, and turn off font smoothing so the strokes stay sharp.
Use capitals for labels such as “1UP” and “HI-SCORE”, and keep body text in a more readable face.

images.alt: Black on white specimen of a heavy square pixel font: Press Start 2P, the alphabet in capitals and lowercase, the digits, and the words Player 1, 1UP, and Hi-Score.
images.caption: Specimen of Press Start 2P by CodeMan38, rendered for this catalogue from the OFL font file at 8 px and enlarged 5× with nearest-neighbor scaling.

rights.statement: “This Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1.” The specimen is new work rendered from the font file. The letterforms follow Namco arcade character sets, as the designer states.

references.title: Riso zine page, “stuck indoors 2”
references.lede: A zine page about VHS films, printed in fluorescent pink and blue: collage, text, and drawing on separate layers that overprint into violet and do not quite align.
references.summary: Zine page in pink and blue riso ink, with collage layers that overprint and misregister.

creator.name: Unknown. The Flickr uploader, themostinept, does not say who made the zine.

evidence.note: Viewed the 704 × 1024 px Flickr “large” file, a phone photograph of one page. The Flickr description is “stuck indoors 2”. The zine’s title and maker are not stated.

styles.note: Two inks, pink and blue, overprint into violet, and the layers are visibly misregistered.

context: Posted on Flickr under CC BY-SA 2.0 by themostinept. It is not clear that the uploader made the zine, so the rights of the printed work are unknown.
observed: The page uses fluorescent pink and a mid blue on off-white paper, and no black.
A pink rectangle with the word “VHS” sits under a blue drawing of a VHS case and a deer. Where they cross, the color is violet.
Blue text bars at the top are knocked out of the ink, and the pink layer sits a few millimeters off from the blue.
Blue areas are grainy and uneven, with streaks in the large photographic areas.
interpretation: The page shows nearly every riso trait at once: two inks, overprint mixing, grain, and misregistration, used for a personal, collaged zine.
borrow: Put text in knocked-out bars of a single ink, and let a second ink block run under it slightly off register.

rights.statement: Photo posted CC BY-SA 2.0 by themostinept. The zine’s author is not named, so the printed work is treated as in copyright. Link only.

references.title: Risograph RZ670 duplicator
references.lede: A Riso Kagaku RZ670 stencil duplicator in a public learning center in Nagoya: the office machine whose drums and stencils give the style its look.
references.summary: An RZ670 Risograph duplicator in a community learning center in Nagoya.
references.made: Photographed 17 October 2021. The model date was not checked.

evidence.note: Viewed the 1280 × 1920 px Commons thumbnail. The file is in Category:Interiors of Nagoya City Kita Lifelong Learning Center.

styles.note: Not an example of the look itself: the duplicator whose one-color-per-drum process produces it.

context: Wikipedia describes the Risograph as a brand of digital duplicators by Riso Kagaku, introduced in Japan in 1980, which became popular among artists in the 2010s for zines and comics ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risograph)).
observed: A beige office machine on a stand, labeled “RISOGRAPH RZ670” and “RISO”.
The front cover is closed, so no ink drum is visible. A side paper tray is open.
A sign behind it, in Japanese, reminds users not to forget their originals.
interpretation: The machine is a plain office duplicator. The style comes from its limits: one ink per drum, stencil masters, and imperfect registration between passes.
borrow: Treat each color as a separate pass that may shift, not as a channel of one image.

images.alt: A beige Risograph RZ670 duplicator on a wheeled stand beside a window in a public building.
images.caption: Risograph RZ670 at the Kita Lifelong Learning Center, Nagoya, 2021, by 円周率３パーセント. CC BY-SA 4.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Kita_20211017-117.jpg). 1280 px thumbnail.

rights.statement: Commons: own work by 円周率３パーセント, CC BY-SA 4.0. The duplicator is a utilitarian office machine. “RISO” and “RISOGRAPH” are trademarks of Riso Kagaku Corporation. Credit: 円周率３パーセント, via Wikimedia Commons.

references.title: Rivers & Derious’ Combination Circus handbill
references.lede: A small Washington circus bill of 1864 in which every act gets its own line, face, and rule, inside a border of cast ornaments.
references.summary: Circus handbill with a Tuscan headline, slab and condensed lines, rules, and an ornament border. Washington, 1864.

source.label: Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection: Rivers & Derious’ combination circus!

creator.name: H. Polkinhorn & Son’s Steam Job Press, Washington (imprint)

evidence.note: Inspected the Library of Congress scan (Printed Ephemera Collection, Portfolio 204, Folder 51b, copy scanned: 2; 1995 × 3589 px). LoC records six duplicate copies.

styles.note: A jobbing circus bill: centred lines, a different face for each act, full-width rules between acts, and a border of type ornaments.

context: LoC catalogues the bill as 1 p., 30 × 17 cm, Washington, 1864. [LoC 2020776481](https://www.loc.gov/item/2020776481/).

The bill advertises the circus and a “Bedouin Arab Troupe” on the lot at New York Avenue and 6th Street from Thursday, 29 September 1864. The imprint reads “H. Polkinhorn & Son’s Steam Job Press, 375 and 377 D street.”
observed: A border of cast scroll ornaments with corner pieces frames the whole bill.
“CIRCUS!” is the largest line, in a black Tuscan-style letter with forked serifs and swelling stems.

Other lines use a shaded slab (“RIVERS & DERIOUS’”), a wide sans-serif (“COMBINATION”, “WONDERFUL ACTS!”), condensed slabs (“MASTER EDDIE RIVERS!”, “THE DELAVANTE BROTHERS!”), a wide Clarendon (“JOHN FOSTER!”), and a very condensed roman (“EVERY AFTERNOON & EVEN’G”).
Full-width thick-and-thin rules divide the acts. Small capitals under each name describe the act.
Admission prices use dotted leaders. Every line except the price rows is centred.
Black ink on white paper, with some broken and over-inked letters.
interpretation: The bill shows the style at small scale: the hierarchy comes only from face, width, and size, and the ornament border gives the sheet a frame without any picture.
Each act behaves like a card: a big name, a small description, and a rule.
borrow: Treat each item as a block of a big name, a small description line, and a rule.
Frame a whole page with a border of small repeated ornaments and corner pieces.

images.alt: Black-and-white circus handbill inside a border of scroll ornaments. Centred lines in different typefaces read Rivers and Derious' Combination Circus!, Bedouin Arab Troupe, Thursday September 29 1864, Master Eddie Rivers!, Wonderful Acts!, The Delavante Brothers!, John Foster!, and Every Afternoon and Evening, with rules between them.
images.caption: Rivers & Derious’ Combination Circus handbill, Washington, 1864. Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection, [2020776481](https://www.loc.gov/item/2020776481/).

rights.statement: The Library of Congress says that, with a few exceptions, it “is not aware of any U.S. copyright protection … or any other restrictions in the materials in the Printed Ephemera Collection.” The bill was published in the United States in 1864, so it is in the public domain.

references.title: Rob Roy Kelly, *American Wood Type, 1828–1900*
references.lede: The 1969 survey that catalogued nineteenth-century American wood type styles from printers’ stock and specimen books, and the main source for later digital revivals.
references.summary: Rob Roy Kelly’s 1969 history and catalogue of American wood type. Reference work, not a period object.

evidence.note: Documented from the Wikipedia articles “Rob Roy Kelly” and “Wood type”. I did not open a copy or an image of the book, so this record states nothing about its appearance.

styles.note: The standard reference on the wood type faces of the style. It documents the style; it is not an example of it.

context: Wikipedia says Kelly was a design educator and a collector and scholar of wood type, that he wrote *American Wood Type, 1828–1900* (1969), and that his wood type collection is now at the University of Texas. [Wikipedia: Rob Roy Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Roy_Kelly).

Wikipedia (Wood type) says Kelly built his collection from old print shops and printers’ families in the 1950s, judged that the aesthetic quality of wood type declined in the twentieth century, and that Adobe drew a series of wood type revivals in the early 1990s from proofs he supplied. [Wikipedia: Wood type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_type).
interpretation: The dates in the title, 1828 to 1900, match the core of this style. Kelly’s judgement that the craft declined after 1900 supports ending the core era before the twentieth century.
borrow: Use Kelly’s genre names (Antique, French Clarendon, Tuscan, Gothic, Grecian) as the vocabulary when choosing display faces for this style.
next: Open a library copy and record its plates, or link the University of Texas collection record.

rights.statement: The book is in copyright. No image is stored.

references.title: Roto-Sphere sign, Joe’s Liquors, Memphis
references.lede: A spinning “Sputnik” sign from Warren Milks’s Roto-Sphere series of 1960–71: a red ball with sixteen colored spikes over a zigzag arrow and a “JOE’S” box.
references.summary: A red ball with sixteen colored neon-edged spikes over a zigzag arrow, the “Sputnik” of Joe’s Liquors. Warren Milks, about 1962, photographed 2021.

source.label: Library of Congress: Carol M. Highsmith, Colorful space satellite-like sign for Joe’s Restaurant in Memphis, Tennessee, 2021

references.made: Roto-Spheres made 1960–1971; this one shown in a 1962 grand-opening advertisement (Roadside Architecture); restored 1999; photographed 14 October 2021

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Carol M. Highsmith’s 2021 photograph, Library of Congress LC-DIG-highsm-68164, 683 × 1024 px, in a scratchpad. Not stored. The Library of Congress title says “Joe’s Restaurant”; the sign and the Roadside Architecture account identify the business as Joe’s Liquors (now Joe’s Wines & Liquor).

styles.note: A spiked sphere over a zigzag arrow, the satellite-and-starburst symbol of the style as a roadside sign.

context: Roadside Architecture: Warren Milks made about 234 Roto-Spheres at his sign shop in Bossier City, Louisiana, from 1960 to 1971. Each has sixteen eight-foot aluminum spikes outlined in neon, and a motor turns the ball and its counter-rotating halves. The Memphis store’s grand-opening advertisement called it “the Sign of the Sputnik”; the owners raised $12,000 to restore it in 1999. [Roadside Architecture: Roto-Spheres](https://www.roadarch.com/sca/roto.html).

The Daily Memphian reports that Roto-Spheres were not, according to historians, inspired by Sputnik, although locals call the sign “the Sputnik.” [Daily Memphian](https://dailymemphian.com/article/22246/sputnik-returns-to-its-midtown-post).
observed: A glossy red ball sits on a white pole; long tapering spikes radiate from it in all directions, each a different color: yellow, red, blue, green, teal, white, and orange.
Each spike is edged with a thin line of tube along its length.
Below the ball, a yellow-orange arrow bent into a zigzag points down to the box sign.
The box sign reads “JOE’S” in white capitals on a black panel with a red corner block.
The ground is a cloudy gray-blue sky; the neon is not lit.
interpretation: Whatever its maker intended, the sign reads as the style’s starburst-satellite: a central sphere with radiating rays in many saturated colors.
The zigzag arrow is a second Googie motif, the lightning bolt or boomerang that directs the driver’s eye.
borrow: Use a central dot with radiating spikes of different colors as a badge or a loading mark.
Use a bent zigzag arrow to point from a heading to an action.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Highsmith photograph has “No known restrictions on publication” (Library of Congress), but the sign is the main subject. Roto-Spheres were sold commercially from 1960, which may have published the design; whether they carried a copyright notice was not checked.

references.title: Sanrio Puroland
references.lede: Sanrio’s indoor theme park in Tama New Town, opened in 1990: a pastel castle front under a rainbow arch, built to house its characters.
references.summary: Indoor character theme park with a lavender and pink facade, rainbow arch, and white spire. Tama, Tokyo, 1990.

creator.name: Sanrio; Landmark Entertainment Group (conceptual design, per Wikipedia)

evidence.note: Inspected two exterior photographs by Kakidai on Wikimedia Commons in scratchpad copies at 1280 px: [2014](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sanrio_Puroland.jpg) and [November 2024](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2024_Sanrio_Puroland_(1).jpg), both CC BY-SA 4.0. The interior was not inspected. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: the facade translates the palette into architecture (lavender, pink, rainbow, rounded domes), but the exterior shows no character faces.

context: Wikipedia gives the opening date as 7 December 1990, describes an indoor theme park in Tama, Tokyo, with attractions for Hello Kitty, My Melody, Cinnamoroll, Gudetama, and Aggretsuko, and says Landmark Entertainment Group was commissioned to design facilities in the conceptual phase. Construction began on 16 November 1988. [Wikipedia: Sanrio Puroland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanrio_Puroland).

Wikipedia reports more than 1.5 million visitors per year and calls the park “a bold attempt to challenge Disney and its theme parks”. [Wikipedia: Sanrio Puroland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanrio_Puroland).
observed: A large semicircular arch frames the entrance. Its outer band is a rainbow of pastel stripes divided by thin gold ribs.
Inside the arch, stylized trees in pale green and blue spread over a stained-glass-like screen; a white, scalloped sign reads “Sanrio Puroland” in red rounded letters.
A white spire with small turrets rises above the arch; small domes in pale yellow and blue, with round windows, stand on the wings.
The flanking walls are pale lavender with wavy lines of pink, mint, and yellow; the railings are pink with wavy lavender panels.
Four ticket kiosks have white pointed roofs; the 2024 photograph shows a pale pink dome to the left.
interpretation: The park front applies the kawaii palette and the wavy, rounded line to a fairy-tale castle, a form borrowed from Western theme parks. The faces are kept for the interior and the characters.
It shows that the palette alone (pale lavender, pink, mint, rainbow) is enough to signal the style at the scale of a building.
borrow: Run thin wavy lines in three pastels along a pale wall or a long horizontal band.
Frame an entrance or a hero with a large rainbow arch in pastel stripes.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Commons photographs are CC BY-SA 4.0 by Kakidai, but the 1990 building and its decoration are protected works. Japanese copyright law (Article 46) allows photographs of buildings; the lead curator can decide whether to upgrade.

references.title: Sharaku, The Actor Ōtani Oniji III as Edobei
references.lede: A half-length kabuki actor grimaces with spread, claw-like hands against a dark ground, in one of Tōshūsai Sharaku’s actor portraits of 1794.
references.summary: Black outlines, flat striped robe, and a dark plain ground. Tōshūsai Sharaku, 1794.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Art Institute of Chicago image of impression 1934.207 (1686 × 2516 px).

styles.note: A canonical actor print (yakusha-e): key-block outlines, flat color areas with a striped textile, and a figure cropped by the sheet edges.

context: AIC catalogues the sheet as a color woodblock print, ōban, 37.9 × 25 cm, dated 1794, signed “Tōshūsai Sharaku ga”. AIC gives the artist as active 1794–1795. [AIC 1934.207](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/18765).
observed: The actor fills the sheet and is cut by the left and bottom edges. He faces right, and the right third is empty ground.
The ground is a dark, mottled gray, printed flat, with no horizon or setting.
The face and hands are unprinted paper, drawn with thin black lines. Eyebrows, hair, and robe are solid black areas.
The robe is a brown-red with fine cream stripes, a repeating textile pattern inside an outlined area.
Small areas of pale green and pink-red sit between the black robe and the hands.
The signature runs in one vertical column at the right, with a small seal under it.
interpretation: The portrait reduces the figure to a few flat shapes, so the outline and the black areas carry the expression.
The striped robe shows how the style keeps pattern inside a bounded shape rather than over the whole surface.
borrow: Crop a figure hard at two edges and leave the opposite side as flat ground for one column of text.
Put a fine stripe pattern inside one outlined shape only.

images.alt: Color woodblock print. Half-length kabuki actor with black topknot, fierce frowning face, and two spread hands, wearing a black robe with a brown-red striped outer garment, on a dark gray ground. A vertical signature is at right.
images.caption: Tōshūsai Sharaku, The Actor Ōtani Oniji III as Edobei, 1794. [Art Institute of Chicago 1934.207](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/18765), Clarence Buckingham Collection. CC0.

rights.statement: The Art Institute of Chicago marks the object public domain (`is_public_domain: true`) and releases images of public-domain works under CC0. [AIC open access](https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). Sharaku worked in 1794–1795 and the print was published in 1794, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Shinjuku Ōgādo in the rain at night
references.lede: A panning long exposure of a Yamanote Line train crossing the Shinjuku Ōgādo railway bridge in the rain: blue-cyan streaks of light under a red illuminated billboard.
references.summary: Cyan and blue motion streaks, a blurred train, and a red sign over a wet night street. Photograph by Kznrhsd, Shinjuku, Tokyo, 2020.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: 雨の新宿大ガード.jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons rendition at 1920 × 1371 px of the 4426 × 3161 px original. The Japanese description, “雨の新宿大ガードで山手線を流し撮り”, says it is a panning shot of the Yamanote Line at Shinjuku Ōgādo in the rain. The Commons categories include “Rain in Tokyo”, “Neon signs in Tokyo”, and “JR East E235-0”.

styles.note: Partial fit: a real rain-wet Tokyo night reduced to cold cyan light and horizontal streaks, close to the style’s scan-line and glitch motion. It has no HUD or terminal elements.

context: Wikipedia’s [Cyberpunk article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk) quotes William Gibson: “Modern Japan simply was cyberpunk.” See also [Kabukichō in a rainstorm](ref:kabukicho-rainstorm-night-2024) in the same district.

The Ōgādo is the railway bridge that carries the JR lines over Ōme Kaidō at Shinjuku. The Commons category for this view is “Views of Omekaido Overbridge from the Shinjukuogado-W. Intersection at night”. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%E9%9B%A8%E3%81%AE%E6%96%B0%E5%AE%BF%E5%A4%A7%E3%82%AC%E3%83%BC%E3%83%89.jpg).
observed: Almost the whole frame is a cold cyan to steel blue. Only a red illuminated billboard at top center and small orange and pink lights break it.
A silver-and-green commuter train crosses the bridge in the middle third. It is sharper than everything else because the camera followed it.
Buildings, cars, a cyclist, and pedestrians are smeared into horizontal streaks.
Bright horizontal bars of white light repeat across the frame, like scan lines.
The wet road in the lower half reflects pink and white lights as soft vertical smears.
interpretation: The motion blur makes the city look like an unstable display: horizontal streaks and doubled edges, as in the style’s glitch and scan-line effects.
The near-monochrome cyan with one red accent is a working two-color version of the style’s palette.
borrow: Use one cold cyan field with a single red accent for the most important element.
Suggest motion or interference with horizontal light streaks, in small areas only.

images.alt: A blurred night scene in cyan and blue: a train crosses a railway bridge, buildings and cars smear into horizontal streaks, a red billboard glows at top, and a wet road reflects pink light.
images.caption: Yamanote Line train at Shinjuku Ōgādo in the rain, 25 September 2020. Photograph by Kznrhsd, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%E9%9B%A8%E3%81%AE%E6%96%B0%E5%AE%BF%E5%A4%A7%E3%82%AC%E3%83%BC%E3%83%89.jpg), CC0. The billboard text is blurred and incidental.

rights.statement: Photograph by Kznrhsd, “Own work”, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0 on Wikimedia Commons. The subject is a street, a railway bridge, and a train. Billboards appear blurred and incidental.

references.title: Shunshō, Three Beauties Chatting by a Veranda
references.lede: A hanging-scroll painting of three women at a veranda on a summer evening, by Katsukawa Shunshō, a print designer who also painted ukiyo-e on silk.
references.summary: Ink and color on silk: outlined figures, patterned robes, and gold mist bands. Katsukawa Shunshō, about 1792.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Art Institute of Chicago image of 1960.65 (843 × 1715 px, the largest size the IIIF server returned for this narrow scroll). The image includes the brocade mounting.

styles.note: A painted ukiyo-e (nikuhitsu-ga): the same outlined figures, flat patterned robes, and off-center composition as the prints, in ink and color on silk. Partial fit: the painting has soft tonal washes that prints do not have.

context: AIC catalogues the work as a hanging scroll, ink and colors on silk, 89.4 × 34.6 cm, about 1792. [AIC 1960.65](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/11613).

Wikipedia’s Ukiyo-e article says that ukiyo-e artists produced paintings as well as prints, and names hanging scrolls (kakemono) among the most common painted formats. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukiyo-e).
observed: The painting sits in a tall, narrow mount of green and gold brocade with a gold-flecked band above and below.
A post of the veranda divides the picture vertically to the right of center. Two women lean out at right, a third stands on the ground at lower left.
Figures have thin black outlines. Faces are flat white with no modelling.
The standing woman’s robe is black with large cream hexagons. Her sash and under-robe are bright red. The other robes have fine gray stripes and small flower patterns.
Bands of gold mist with soft edges cross the upper third and fade into the silk.
A short vertical signature with a red seal sits high at the right.
interpretation: The scroll shows that the style is a pictorial language, not only a print technique: the painter keeps the print’s outlines and flat pattern.
The mist bands do in paint what bokashi does in print.
borrow: Divide a tall layout with one vertical line placed off center, and let figures overlap it.
Use soft-edged horizontal bands to separate the top of a tall panel from the content.

images.alt: Hanging scroll in a green and gold brocade mount. Three women in patterned kimonos at a wooden veranda: two lean over the rail at right, one stands below at left holding a round fan. Gold mist bands cross the upper part.
images.caption: Katsukawa Shunshō, Three Beauties Chatting by a Veranda, about 1792. [Art Institute of Chicago 1960.65](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/11613). CC0.

rights.statement: The Art Institute of Chicago marks the object public domain (`is_public_domain: true`) and releases images of public-domain works under CC0. [AIC open access](https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). Shunshō died in 1793, so the painting is public domain in Japan and the United States. The brocade mounting is an old textile with no known author.

references.title: Silkscreen typeface
references.lede: Jason Kottke’s tiny bitmap face for web graphics draws most capitals in 4 × 5 pixels and became a common pixel label face on websites of the 2000s.
references.summary: A small, wide-spaced 5-pixel bitmap face in capitals only. Jason Kottke, about 1999–2001, SIL Open Font License.
references.made: Copyright 2001 per the OFL release; Commons calls the drawn version 1.1 “(2000)”

evidence.note: Downloaded `Silkscreen-Regular.ttf` from the [Google Fonts repository](https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/ofl/silkscreen), rendered a specimen at its 8 pt design size without anti-aliasing, enlarged it 7× to 868 × 616 px, and inspected it.

styles.note: A bitmap face built on a 5-pixel cap height for screen labels: square steps, one weight, and capitals only.

context: Kottke calls Silkscreen “a typeface for your Web graphics” and says he drew the letters with the pencil tool in Photoshop 5.02, then built the font in Fontographer 3.52. Most characters are 4 × 5 pixels and the largest 5 × 5. It should be used at 8 pt or multiples of 8 pt. [kottke.org](https://kottke.org/plus/type/silkscreen/).
Kottke lists Flickr, Sephora.com, Volvo Cars, and *The Bourne Legacy* among its uses. [kottke.org](https://kottke.org/plus/type/silkscreen/).

The Google Fonts release names Jason Kottke as designer, the license OFL, and the copyright “2001 The Silkscreen Project Authors”, with source at [googlefonts/silkscreen](https://github.com/googlefonts/silkscreen). [Google Fonts repository](https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/ofl/silkscreen).
observed: Capitals are 5 pixels high and mostly 4 pixels wide, with one-pixel strokes and two pixels of space between letters.
The lowercase row renders as capitals: the face has no separate lowercase.
The small letters read as a wide-spaced line of dots and bars, and they keep their shape only at whole-number enlargements.
Digits and punctuation follow the same 5-pixel grid.
interpretation: Silkscreen is the label face of early-2000s pixel web graphics. Its tiny cell makes it a navigation and caption face rather than a heading face like [Press Start 2P](ref:press-start-2p-typeface).
borrow: Use a 5-pixel bitmap face in capitals for small navigation labels, and space the letters widely.
Set it at 8 px or a whole multiple, never at an in-between size.

images.alt: Black on white specimen of a small square pixel font in capitals: Silkscreen, the alphabet twice, the digits, and the words Home, About, Archive.
images.caption: Specimen of Silkscreen by Jason Kottke, rendered for this catalogue from the OFL font file at 8 px and enlarged 7× with nearest-neighbor scaling.

rights.statement: “Copyright 2001 The Silkscreen Project Authors … This Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1.” The specimen is new work rendered from the font file.

references.title: Smashing Magazine, “The Split Personality of Brutalist Web Development”
references.lede: An essay that splits web brutalism into l’Internet brut, built from raw HTML, and l’Internet fou, built for shock.
references.summary: Frederick O’Brien’s 2020 essay: raw HTML brutalism (light ground, black text, blue links) versus audacious brutalism.

evidence.note: Article text read on 2026-10-02. The publication time (8 January 2020) is in the page’s metadata, and the author link is on the page. The article’s screenshots were not inspected.

styles.note: Names and describes the raw core of the style and separates it from the audacious branch.

context: “Type One: l’Internet Brut … where the raw materials are HTML and, to a lesser extent, CSS. The backgrounds are light, the text is black, and the hyperlinks are blue.”

Examples it names for the raw type: the first website, David Bryant Copeland’s [Brutalist Web Design](ref:copeland-brutalist-web-design-guidelines), Craigslist, Wikipedia, the old A List Apart, old Reddit, Bloomberg, and Freecycle.
“Type Two: l’Internet Fou” covers the many “brutalist” sites built to provoke. It quotes Vitaly Friedman: brutalism in architecture is “unconcerned aesthetics, not intentionally broken aesthetics”.
interpretation: Its Type One is the scope of [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design). Some of its examples, such as Bloomberg, are bolder than default HTML and need a capture before they count as evidence.
borrow: Treat HTML as the material: let the structure of the document set the look, and shape each page around its content.

rights.statement: © Smashing Magazine and the author. Link and quotation only.

references.title: Solarpunk community center
references.lede: A miners’ memorial statue holds a wind turbine in front of a community centre that retrains miners as turbine technicians.
references.summary: Bronze miners with a wind turbine before a solar-fitted community centre, in clear daylight. The.lemonaut.ukr, 2024.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 2284 × 2823 px PNG, viewed at 1295 × 1600 px).

styles.note: A solarpunk scene about a just transition: a turbine, solar panels, a public building, and a blue sky. Partial fit: the palette is warm orange and bronze more than leaf green.

context: The uploader describes it as a digital illustration of a solarpunk community centre that provides re-specialization for miners so that they can become wind turbine technicians. It is dated 5 July 2024. [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_community_center.png).
observed: In the foreground, a bronze statue of a miner in a helmet and harness pulls a second miner out of a manhole. The standing figure holds a small three-bladed wind turbine like a staff, and a pickaxe lies on the ground.
A girl in an orange coat with a yellow helmet and a paper in her hand looks at the statue.
Behind, a building with orange, cream, and glass blocks carries the sign “COMMUNITY CE…”, small solar panels on brackets, and a hedge of flowering shrubs.
At left, an older brick hall has round-arched windows, and a tree has pale violet blossom.
The sky is light blue with soft white clouds. Thin dark outlines, flat colour, and a visible grain texture.
interpretation: The scene puts the politics of solarpunk (a fair transition for workers) into a civic square. Old labour and new energy share one monument.
The palette leans orange and bronze, so the image is a partial fit to the green, blue, and gold grammar. The blue sky and the visible renewables keep it in the style.
borrow: Combine a familiar civic form (a monument, a town square) with renewable technology, so the change reads as continuity.

images.alt: Illustration of a town square: a bronze statue of one miner pulling another from a manhole while holding a wind turbine, a girl in an orange coat looking up at it, and a colourful community centre with solar panels behind.
images.caption: The.lemonaut.ukr, “Solarpunk community center”, 2024. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_community_center.png), CC BY 4.0.

rights.statement: Commons: self-published work by The.lemonaut.ukr, licensed CC BY 4.0. The statue is part of the illustration, not a real sculpture. Credit: The.lemonaut.ukr, via Wikimedia Commons.

references.title: Solarpunk flag
references.lede: A green and yellow flag split on the diagonal, with a sun whose lower half is a gear: the most widely shared emblem of the solarpunk movement on Wikimedia Commons.
references.summary: Diagonal green and yellow field with a counterchanged sun and half-gear. @Starwall@radical.town, 2019.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 5000 × 3000 px, viewed at 1600 × 960 px). The flag exists only as this digital file and its vector redraw, [File:Solarpunk Flag Vectorized Version.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_Flag_Vectorized_Version.svg).

styles.note: The movement’s own emblem: sun gold and leaf green, a sun with plant-like rays, and a gear for repaired, reclaimed technology.

context: The uploader’s description says the yellow stands for solar power, the green for sustainability, the half-gear for reclaiming technology for sustainable projects and infrastructure, and the sunbeams for hopefulness and futurism. [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_Flag.jpg).

Commons lists the file in [Category:Solarpunk unofficial flags](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Solarpunk_unofficial_flags), with a blue-diagonal variant by the same author and several other community logos. No body has adopted an official flag.
observed: A diagonal line runs from the lower left to the upper right. The upper left is a strong leaf green and the lower right is a warm sun yellow.
A circular sun sits at the centre. Its disc is counterchanged across the diagonal, yellow on the green half and green on the yellow half.
Seven curling, flame- or sprout-like rays rise from the upper half of the sun. The lower half has a ring of square gear teeth.
The colours are flat, with no outline, gradient, or shadow.
interpretation: The flag compresses the style’s argument into one sign: half sun, half machine, with rays drawn like shoots. The curling rays are the only organic, Art Nouveau-like line in an otherwise geometric design.
Its two-colour palette is narrower than solarpunk illustration, which adds sky blue. The blue-diagonal variant on Commons adds that third family.
borrow: Split a field on the diagonal and counterchange one central motif across it.
Draw the rays of a sun as curling shoots so that one shape reads as both energy and growth.

images.alt: Flag divided diagonally, green at upper left and yellow at lower right. In the centre a sun with curling rays on top and gear teeth on the bottom, its colours swapped across the diagonal.
images.caption: Solarpunk flag by @Starwall@radical.town, 2019. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_Flag.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Commons: “Own work” by @Starwall@radical.town, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. The author licenses the design itself, so the depicted work is openly licensed. Credit: @Starwall@radical.town, via Wikimedia Commons.

references.title: Solarpunk Technology and Nature together
references.lede: A woman in a green dress pulls a small robot cart past a canal and a tram line, under buildings overgrown with vines and a pale, gridded wind tower.
references.summary: Tall, sun-washed street scene of vines over buildings, a tram, and a cart robot. Loop-chan, 2024.

source.label: Story Seed Library: Solarpunk Technology and Nature together

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_Technology_and_Nature_together.jpg) (original 2000 × 3421 px, viewed at 935 × 1600 px).

styles.note: Plants overgrow a dense, lived-in city with public transport and friendly machines, in bright greens, sky blue, and sun-washed cream.

context: Story Seed Library, a solarpunk archive of openly licensed art and stories, lists the work as an illustration dated 25 March 2024, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, and tags it Vertical, People, City, Transport, and Tram. [Story Seed Library](https://storyseedlibrary.org/art/loop-chan/solarpunk-technology-nature/).
The Commons upload uses the same title and license. [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_Technology_and_Nature_together.jpg).
observed: The format is tall and narrow. In the foreground, a red-haired woman in a straw hat and green dress pulls a wooden two-wheeled cart that carries a small robot with rabbit-like ears.
Behind her, a pale tram runs on tracks beside a canal with lily pads, and a yellow and black level-crossing sign stands at right.
Above, buildings with ribbon windows and balconies are covered in vines and bright green trees. Lanterns and bunting hang over a café terrace.
On the skyline, a water tower and a windmill-like tower are drawn as pale, gridded silhouettes against a light blue sky. A vertical sign reads “LOOP”.
The light is strong and hazy, washing the upper half toward white and cream. Flat shapes are combined with photo-like textures and screen patterns.
interpretation: The image shows the gentle, everyday side of solarpunk: technology as a helper (the cart robot, the tram) inside a garden city, not as spectacle.
The bleached, high-key light matches the style’s daylit ground and its high lightness. Its anime-influenced figure and collage textures are a common variant in online solarpunk art.
borrow: Use a tall format with plants hanging from the top edge, so the viewer looks up through foliage.
Let strong light wash the background toward cream, and keep saturated green for the foreground leaves.

images.alt: Tall illustration: a woman in a green dress and straw hat pulls a cart with a small robot past a tram and a canal, under vine-covered buildings, with a pale windmill tower against a hazy blue sky.
images.caption: Loop-chan, “Solarpunk Technology and Nature together”, 2024. [Story Seed Library](https://storyseedlibrary.org/art/loop-chan/solarpunk-technology-nature/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk_Technology_and_Nature_together.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Story Seed Library labels the illustration “CC BY-SA 4.0”, and Commons uses the same license. Credit: Loop-chan, Story Seed Library.

references.title: Solarpunk village on a former oil platform
references.lede: An offshore oil platform rebuilt as a terraced garden village with geodesic greenhouses, kite turbines, and sailing boats at its jetty.
references.summary: Repurposed oil platform with greenhouses, gardens, and airborne turbines on a blue sea. Commando Jugendstil, before 2022.
references.made: Before November 2022 (Commons upload 2022-11-19; alxd.org says it was made “a few years earlier”)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons copy](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Commando_Jugendstil_Solarpunk_Platform.jpg) (709 × 1000 px). It carries the Commando Jugendstil signature at lower right.

styles.note: Repurposed fossil infrastructure becomes a garden village with greenhouses, wind power, and sail boats: solarpunk’s core idea of reuse, in sky blue, leaf green, and yellow.

context: The Commons description reads: “An image of a former oil platform at sea, repurposed as a greenhouse and powered by wind turbines. It’s a representation of solarpunk values, repurposing infrastructure and getting rid of fossil fuels.” [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Commando_Jugendstil_Solarpunk_Platform.jpg).

The Polish blog post captions it “Solarpunkowa wioska na porzuconej platformie wiertniczej - CC-BY-SA 3.0 Commando Jugendstil” (a solarpunk village on an abandoned drilling platform). It says the collective made it to illustrate an unpublished article in the Swedish magazine LiberalDebatt, and that Gazeta Wyborcza later printed it with an interview about solarpunk. [alxd.org](https://alxd.org/nudne-science-fiction-uratuje-swiat-pl.html).
The same post calls Commando Jugendstil one of the most active solarpunk art collectives in Europe, with murals, city-programme illustrations, and magazine covers.
observed: A yellow steel platform stands on legs in a deep blue sea, with a yellow lattice crane bridge running off to the right.
Its decks hold rows of trees behind glass, a stepped green terrace with a stair, and three glazed geodesic domes on the top deck.
Four tethered, ducted turbines fly above the platform like kites. Two more turbine shells, decorated with a red scale pattern, hang from the crane.
A white tower at right is topped by a bowl of trees and red pennants. Red flags fly across the decks.
Sailing boats and a trimaran are moored at a wooden jetty. Small figures work on stairs and walkways.
Soft white cumulus clouds fill a clear blue sky. The rendering is a painted digital illustration with fine dark linework.
interpretation: The image is a direct answer to the style’s critics: it shows the fossil economy turned to gardens rather than a clean new city from nothing.
The domes and terraces supply the style’s greenhouse and arched-structure motif. The yellow steel and red pennants give the scheme a festive, maritime accent.
borrow: Show an old industrial structure kept and reused, with new planting and energy added on top.
Use one strong structural colour (yellow steel) against sky blue and leaf green.

images.alt: Illustration of a yellow offshore oil platform turned into a garden village, with glass domes, planted terraces, kite turbines in the sky, a crane bridge, and sailing boats at a jetty on a blue sea.
images.caption: Commando Jugendstil, solarpunk village on a former oil platform. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Commando_Jugendstil_Solarpunk_Platform.jpg), CC BY-SA 3.0, from [alxd.org](https://alxd.org/nudne-science-fiction-uratuje-swiat-pl.html).

rights.statement: Commons lists the file as CC BY-SA 3.0 by Commando Jugendstil, from alxd.org. The alxd.org post (whose own content is CC BY-SA 4.0) credits it “CC-BY-SA 3.0 Commando Jugendstil”. No Commons license review and no statement on the collective’s own site were found.

references.title: Solarpunk, realism, and dystopia (comic, page 1)
references.lede: The first page of a six-page explainer comic that argues for “realistic solarpunk”, lettered by hand in green, coral, and yellow washes on white.
references.summary: Hand-lettered explainer comic in watercolour-like green, coral, and yellow on white. The.lemonaut.ukr, 2025.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: File:Solarpunk, realism, and dystopia - page 1.jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected page 1 on Commons (original 2400 × 2663 px, viewed at 1442 × 1600 px). Pages 2 to 6 were not inspected.

styles.note: Solarpunk as graphic layout: light ground, rounded hand-drawn panels in green and yellow, friendly mixed lettering, and scenes of a tool library and shared food.

context: Commons describes the six pages as “a comic discussing realistic Solarpunk”, dated 14 May 2025, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. [Commons file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk,_realism,_and_dystopia_-_page_1.jpg).
observed: The page has a white ground. Text sits in soft, irregular washes of pale green, coral, and pale yellow, like watercolour blobs.
The lettering is hand-drawn capitals in dark plum, with some words bolder and highlighted in green: “I LIKE REALISTIC SOLARPUNK.”
A strip of small line drawings shows a “TOOL LIBRARY” with a planted entrance, a person mending a sock, a reading group with tablets, and a free soup pot.
A coral panel lists “NO MAGIC, NO SUPERNATURAL ELEMENTS*, NO CURE-ALL TECH” beside a fire-wielding figure, a talking cat, and a man saying “THIS WILL SOLVE EVERYTHING!”.
A yellow rounded box asks “What is SOLARPUNK for?”, with “SOLAR” in ochre and “PUNK” in green, beside a yellow-washed self-portrait in a “LEMONAUT” shirt.
interpretation: This is the style in an editorial format, not a scene. It shows the rounded, framed panels on a light ground that the style’s grammar describes for layouts, and a mixed-case friendly hand.
Colour carries meaning: green for the hopeful position, coral for what the author rejects.
borrow: Set short statements in soft rounded colour washes on white, and use a second hue for counter-arguments.
Pair each idea with a small line drawing of a shared practice (tool library, repair, free food).

images.alt: Comic page on white with hand-lettered text in green, coral, and yellow washes. Small drawings show a tool library, people mending and reading, and a free soup pot. A box at the bottom asks “What is solarpunk for?”.
images.caption: The.lemonaut.ukr, “Solarpunk, realism, and dystopia”, page 1, 2025. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Solarpunk,_realism,_and_dystopia_-_page_1.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Commons: self-published work by The.lemonaut.ukr, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Credit: The.lemonaut.ukr, via Wikimedia Commons.

references.title: Space Age Lodge sign, Gila Bend
references.lede: The roadside sign of a 1960s desert motel: a tilted flying-saucer disc with the lodge’s name in blue capitals around its rim, under a later chain-hotel panel.
references.summary: A tilted flying-saucer disc sign with red portholes and blue capitals, beside a space-age motel lobby. Gila Bend, Arizona, photographed 2003.

source.label: Library of Congress: John Margolies, Space Age Lodge sign, Gila Bend, Arizona, 2003

creator.name: Al Stovall (owner and developer, per Roadside America)

references.made: Motel opened 1963 or 1965, sources differ; photographed 2003

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected John Margolies’s 2003 color slide, Library of Congress LC-MA05-1423, 704 × 1024 px, in a scratchpad. Not stored.

styles.note: A flying saucer as a roadside sign, one of the space-age symbols the style uses as ornament.

context: Roadside America reports that Al Stovall built the lodge and that his plastics factory made its space-age decorations. It gives the opening as 1963 in one account and 1965 in another (from the restaurant menu), and says three satellite replicas on the roof were replaced by a flying saucer in a 1969 renovation. [Roadside America](https://www.roadsideamerica.com/story/15079).
The Library of Congress record gives only the title and the date of the photograph. [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2017703537/).
observed: A large disc, tilted up to the right, shows a flying saucer from below: a pale dome ringed with red portholes, gray radiating panels, and a rim of small bulbs.
“SPACE AGE LODGE” runs around the lower rim of the disc in heavy blue capitals that follow the curve.
Above it, a separate shield-shaped Best Western panel in navy and gold carries “SPACE AGE LODGE” in white serif capitals; this is later chain branding.
Below, rectangular reader boards list rooms, cable TV, a coffee shop, and a salad bar in black and red capitals.
At left, the lobby has a domed cylinder on top and a blue steel space frame with slanted struts.
The ground is an even, deep blue desert sky.
interpretation: The tilted disc is a Googie habit: the sign is not a rectangle but a symbol of the future, set at an angle so it seems to fly.
The serif chain panel above shows how later branding sits on top of the original sign without its energy.
borrow: Set a name around the curve of a disc or ellipse, and tilt the whole badge a few degrees.
Edge a badge with a row of small dots, like sign bulbs.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Margolies photograph has “No known restrictions on publication” (Library of Congress), but the sign is the main subject, its designer and date are not documented, and the photograph also shows the Best Western trademark.

references.title: Space Invaders
references.lede: Tomohiro Nishikado’s arcade game for Taito made rows of two-frame bitmap aliens the first icons of video game pixel art.
references.summary: Rows of two-frame bitmap aliens over bunkers and a laser cannon, in black and white with colored cellophane strips. Taito, 1978.

creator.name: Tomohiro Nishikado for Taito; distributed outside Japan by Midway

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article and its cited sources. No image was inspected for this record: the game graphics are in copyright, and no open, verified image was found.

styles.note: A founding work of the style: hand-drawn bitmap sprites with two-frame animation, which the style record names as the start of its era.

context: Wikipedia calls Space Invaders a 1978 fixed shooter developed and published by Taito for arcades, released in Japan in July 1978 and abroad through Midway later that year. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Invaders).

Nishikado created bitmap images of octopus-like aliens after *The War of the Worlds*, with other aliens after squids and crabs. After he drew the pixel art, he made a tool to animate two frames of movement for each character and adjusted the designs on screen with a light pen. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Invaders).

The game runs on an Intel 8080 and draws raster graphics through a bitmapped framebuffer. The hardware could not show color, so the first releases have black-and-white graphics with strips of orange and green cellophane over parts of the screen. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Invaders).
Wikipedia says the pixelated aliens “have become pop culture icons, sometimes representing video games as a whole”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Invaders).
interpretation: The two-frame aliens are the model for the style’s motion rule: animation steps between a few frames, with no easing.
The cellophane strips show that the first color in the style came from hardware limits, as bands of flat color, not shading.
borrow: Animate small sprites with two frames that alternate in step with movement.
Color whole horizontal bands of a monochrome screen instead of shading single objects.
next: Find an openly licensed image of the original arcade screen or of the alien bitmaps, and check its rights.

rights.statement: Commercial game graphics by Taito, in copyright. Link and metadata only.

references.title: Stardust roadside sign, Las Vegas
references.lede: The Stardust casino’s roadside sign at night: the name in bulb-filled capitals inside a cloud of lit four-point stars that rises to a point, on black sky.
references.summary: Bulb-filled capitals in a cloud of lit four-point stars, some outlined in blue neon, on black night sky. Las Vegas, 1968 sign, photographed 1980–2006.

source.label: Library of Congress: Carol M. Highsmith, Historic Stardust sign, Las Vegas, Nevada

creator.name: Paul Miller, Ad Art Company (roadside sign, per Wikipedia); the Library of Congress note credits Kermit Wayne for Young Electric Sign Company

references.made: Roadside sign installed February 1968, lettering replaced 1991 (Wikipedia); the Library of Congress note says 1958. Photographed between 1980 and 2006.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Carol M. Highsmith’s photograph, Library of Congress LC-HS503-1563, 1750 × 1280 px (50 % IIIF size), in a scratchpad. Not stored.

styles.note: Starbursts as pure ornament, lit on a night sky: the style’s neon-on-dark color and star imagery in one sign.

context: Highsmith’s note: built in 1958, fabricated by Young Electric Sign Company, with Kermit Wayne’s design chosen for both the facade and the roadside signs. [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2011631018/).

Wikipedia gives a different account: Kermit Wayne designed the 1958 facade sign (216 feet long, 7,100 feet of neon, 11,000 bulbs); a roadside sign by Paul Miller of the Ad Art Company was installed in February 1968; its lettering was replaced with Helvetica in 1991; it was dismantled in 2007 and given to the Neon Museum. *Learning from Las Vegas* studied the 1968 roadside sign. [Wikipedia: Stardust Resort and Casino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stardust_Resort_and_Casino).
observed: “STARDUST” runs across the middle in heavy sans-serif capitals filled with white bulbs and edged in red.
Around the word, dozens of four-point stars of different sizes, filled with gold, orange, red, and white bulbs, form a broad cloud.
A few large stars are outlined in light-blue neon tube instead of bulbs.
Above the word the stars thin into a single column that rises to a point, like a rocket trail or a flame.
Rows of single dots of light fill the gaps; the ground is fully black night sky.
The letters have straight-cut terminals and a plain grotesque form; they may be the 1991 replacement lettering, not the original.
interpretation: The sign is closest to the style’s night version: points of warm light and one cool neon accent on black, with the star repeated until it becomes a texture.
The tower of stars turns a horizontal name panel into an upswept, pointed silhouette.
borrow: Repeat a four-point star at several sizes as a field around a heading, on a black ground.
Outline a few of the stars in a cool color while most are warm, so a second hue punctuates the field.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The Highsmith photograph has “No known restrictions on publication” (Library of Congress), but the sign is the main subject and its own copyright status was not checked. Sources disagree on its designer and date.

references.title: Station for aeroplanes and trains, La Città Nuova
references.titleBreak: Station for aeroplanes and trains,|La Città Nuova
references.lede: Antonio Sant’Elia’s drawing for the Città Nuova shows a station where trains run under a landing strip, between towers of lifts and stepped buildings, on several street levels at once.
references.summary: A symmetrical station of tracks, ramps, and lift towers in one-point perspective. Antonio Sant’Elia, 1914.

source.label: Lombardia Beni Culturali: Stazione d'aeroplani e treni ferroviari, con funicolari e ascensori su tre piani stradali

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a [Commons file](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Stazione_d%27aeroplani_e_treni_(La_Citt%C3%A0_Nuova)_1914_ART_Antonio_Sant%27Elia_2023_RET_WjArendshorst.png) (original 2210 × 2733 px; a 1280 × 1583 px rendering was inspected and stored). The uploader, WjArendshorst, says the image was edited “for a cleaner look” and does not name the scan it started from, so tone and paper texture are not reliable. The physical work is most likely the definitive drawing in the Musei Civici di Como, inventory A 342; a preliminary version, A 343, also exists, and this image was not compared with either.

styles.note: The canonical image of Futurist architecture: a city of transport, lifts, and multiple traffic levels, shown in a dramatic perspective. Partial fit: it is symmetrical and monochrome, without the mixed type and loud inks of Futurist print.

context: Black pencil, blue pencil, and black ink on tracing paper, 500 × 390 mm, 1914. Musei Civici di Como, Pinacoteca Civica, Palazzo Volpi, inventory A 342. The catalogue attributes it to Sant’Elia (1888–1916). [Lombardia Beni Culturali, SIRBeC 1m030-00142](https://www.lombardiabeniculturali.it/opere-arte/schede-complete/1m030-00142/).

The catalogue says this is the final version of a rougher preliminary sheet (A 343). It was shown at the first exhibition of the Nuove Tendenze group at the Famiglia Artistica, Milan, 20 May to 10 June 1914, and reproduced with the same caption on the leaflet of the *Manifesto of Futurist Architecture* of 11 July 1914. [Lombardia Beni Culturali](https://www.lombardiabeniculturali.it/opere-arte/schede-complete/1m030-00142/).
observed: One-point perspective seen from high above: all lines run to a vanishing point at the top center, marked by two converging construction lines.
Seven parallel ribbed vaults or tracks fall from a raised platform toward the viewer and pass under a horizontal bridge.
Four tall towers of stacked cages, with paired masts on top, flank the central tracks; between each pair is a column of stacked arched bays.
Sunken courtyards and long stepped blocks fill the foreground on both sides; large plain blocks frame the far edges.
Small vehicles appear on the tracks and on the road in front.
The drawing is fine black linework with flat gray shading; it is symmetrical about the vertical axis.
interpretation: Here the Futurist subject of speed becomes infrastructure: transport lines, lifts, and bridges are the building, not services hidden inside it. The overhead perspective makes the plan itself look like motion converging on a point.
The symmetry is unusual for Futurism and is a reminder that the movement’s architecture is monumental rather than scattered.
borrow: Use a steep one-point perspective so that parallel lines converge hard and pull the eye into the page.
Express circulation (tracks, ramps, lift shafts) as the main forms of a composition.
Stack levels visibly, with bridges crossing over lower paths.

images.alt: Ink drawing in steep one-point perspective of a symmetrical station: seven ribbed tracks descend from a raised platform under a bridge, flanked by four tall lattice towers with masts and columns of arched bays, with stepped blocks and sunken courts in the foreground.
images.caption: Antonio Sant’Elia, station for aeroplanes and trains with funiculars and lifts on three street levels, from La Città Nuova, 1914. Musei Civici di Como. Image edited by WjArendshorst, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Stazione_d%27aeroplani_e_treni_(La_Citt%C3%A0_Nuova)_1914_ART_Antonio_Sant%27Elia_2023_RET_WjArendshorst.png), CC0.

rights.statement: The edited image is released under CC0 by its uploader on Wikimedia Commons. Sant’Elia was Italian and died in 1916, so the drawing is public domain in Italy. It was exhibited and reproduced in 1914, before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States.

identifiers.commons: File:Stazione d'aeroplani e treni (La Città Nuova) 1914 ART Antonio Sant'Elia 2023 RET WjArendshorst.png

references.title: Strawberry Newspaper (Ichigo Shimbun)
references.lede: Sanrio’s own magazine, published since April 1975: character news, manga, recipes, and cut-out crafts for readers called “Strawberry Mates”.
references.summary: Sanrio’s full-color tabloid magazine of character news and crafts, published since 1975.

evidence.note: Relies on the Wikipedia article. No issue was inspected; covers seen only as small shop thumbnails were not used.

styles.note: The house magazine that has spread Sanrio’s character culture to readers since 1975; its look is not yet verified here.

context: Wikipedia says the first issue was published in April 1975 with Snoopy on the cover and cost 100 yen. It appeared twice a month and became monthly in 1982. By 2019, 600 issues had been published, each printed in 100,000 copies according to Sanrio. [Wikipedia: Strawberry Newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawberry_Newspaper).

The magazine carries news about Sanrio characters and products, drawing lessons, origami, manga serials, character recipes, paper crafts, and cut-out games. It uses a large tabloid format printed in full color, with a poster and a bonus item in each issue. Readers have helped name new characters, starting with the Little Twin Stars in 1975. [Wikipedia: Strawberry Newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawberry_Newspaper).
interpretation: The magazine is the editorial side of the style: it made Sanrio’s characters a serial world that readers took part in, not just decorations on goods.
next: Find an open or museum image of an early issue (1975–1985) and record its layout, color, and type.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The magazine is © Sanrio Co., Ltd.

references.title: Studio Cryo, Drumstation vs. Eternia poster, Cross Club 2018
references.lede: A dark event poster with a red line-up band at the top and a rendered collage of clear plastic, smoke, rock, and dripping flowers.
references.summary: Black ground, red type band, rendered clear-plastic shapes, orange smoke, and dripping flowers. Studio Cryo (Mindaugas Gavrilovas), 2018.

source.label: AIGA Eye on Design (5 September 2019): “Acid Graphics” Are the New Psychedelia

references.made: 2018 (Eye on Design file name and caption). The poster gives the date “07.12”.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px image `Studio-Cryo-Drumstation-VS-Eternia-event-Cross-Club-2018.jpg` that [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) published with the article, in a scratch folder. Not stored. The object is a digital image as the magazine published it, not a named physical copy. Eye on Design names Mindaugas Gavrilovas and Studio Cryo in the article text.

styles.note: Partial fit: a black ground, rendered clear and metallic forms, and flyer-style line-up type, but in red and orange, with no chrome lettering.

context: [Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/acid-graphics-are-the-new-psychedelia-with-a-heady-dose-of-cynicism/) names Studio Cryo and Mindaugas Gavrilovas in its 2019 article and shows this poster, captioned as the Drumstation vs. Eternia event at Cross Club, 2018.
observed: A red band at the top holds “DRUMSTATION VS. ETERNIA” in heavy grotesque capitals, “CROSS CLUB 07.12” in a thin, flared display face, and two blocks of small capitals with the line-up.
A red rule separates the band from a near-black image field.
The field holds rendered, transparent plastic shapes with engraved circles, a brown rock surface, a plume of orange smoke, and a bunch of red and white flowers that drip blue and white paint.
A perforated mesh surface crosses the lower right.
There is no green and no chrome type.
interpretation: The poster shows the rendered-object side of the trend: glossy clear materials, smoke, and drips on black, with a dense club line-up. It shares the mood and the rendering, not the chrome lettering.
borrow: Confine all type to one dense band, and give the rest of the sheet to a single rendered scene on black.
Pair a heavy grotesque with a thin flared display face in the same band.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is recent and in copyright. The rights holder is the designer or the client.

references.title: Supertree Grove, Gardens by the Bay
references.lede: Eighteen steel “trees”, 25 to 50 metres tall, carry vertical gardens, photovoltaic cells, and cooling exhausts in Singapore’s Bay South Garden.
references.summary: Planted steel tree structures with solar cells and a skyway, by Grant Associates. Singapore, opened 2012.

creator.name: Grant Associates, with engineering by Atelier One and Atelier Ten

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons photograph [Singapore Gardens by the Bay Supertree Grove 22.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Singapore_Gardens_by_the_Bay_Supertree_Grove_22.jpg) by Zairon, 4 November 2015 (original 4566 × 3003 px, viewed at 1600 × 1053 px), in a scratch folder. It is the image on the Wikidata item. The photo shows the grove by day; the night light show was not inspected.

styles.note: Built technology shaped like trees, wrapped in living plants and fitted with solar cells: one of the buildings most often cited as solarpunk. Partial fit: it is a state-funded spectacle, not a handmade, community-scale work.

context: Wikipedia: the Supertrees are 18 tree-like structures between 25 and 50 metres tall, conceived and designed by Grant Associates with the engineering of Atelier One and Atelier Ten. They are vertical gardens planted with ferns, vines, orchids, and bromeliads. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardens_by_the_Bay).

Wikipedia: they carry photovoltaic cells that power some functions such as lighting, collect rainwater for irrigation and fountains, and act as air intakes and exhausts for the cooling systems of the conservatories. The OCBC Skyway joins two of the larger Supertrees. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardens_by_the_Bay).
Wikimedia Commons files the park under [Category:Solarpunk](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Solarpunk) as an example.
observed: A large Supertree has a trunk covered in climbing plants and a flared crown of dark purple steel members, branching in short angled segments.
Inside the crown, a white funnel-shaped core has thin green vertical ribs. Cables tie the crown to a neighbouring tree.
A yellow-railed elevated walkway passes the trunk at mid-height, with visitors on it.
Smaller Supertrees at right have planted crowns. At left, the curved glass shell of a conservatory with white arched ribs rises behind the trees.
Below, a dense tropical garden in bright greens. The sky is overcast white.
The solar cells are not legible at this scale and angle.
interpretation: The grove is the built version of solarpunk’s plant-and-technology hybrid: the structure takes the form of a tree, and living plants clothe it. The arched glass conservatory beside it supplies the greenhouse motif.
Its scale, purple steel, and night light show also make it a tourist spectacle. That aligns it partly with the glossy, corporate Frutiger Eco branch, so treat it as a partial fit.
borrow: Shape a technical structure like a plant, and let real planting cover its lower part.
Combine a branching steel lattice with a smooth arched glass shell for contrast.

rights.statement: No image stored. The Supertrees are a recent design (2012) and protected as works. The Commons photograph by Zairon is CC BY-SA 4.0, but the structures it shows are not in the public domain, so the catalogue links to it only.

references.title: Susan Kare’s icons and bitmap fonts for the Macintosh
references.lede: Susan Kare’s one-bit icons, cursors, and bitmap fonts gave the first Macintosh its visual language, drawn pixel by pixel on small grids such as 32 × 32.
references.summary: Black-and-white 32 × 32 icons (the Happy Mac, the bomb, the trash can) and the Chicago bitmap font. Susan Kare, Apple, 1983–1984.

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article and its cited sources, including the Musée de l’Imprimerie et de la Communication Graphique exhibition page. No image was inspected for this record: the icons are in copyright.

styles.note: The canonical pixel interface: one-bit icons and bitmap type drawn by hand on small square grids. The style record cites Kare as a pioneer of pixel art.

context: Wikipedia says Kare contributed interface elements and typefaces for the first Apple Macintosh from 1983 to 1986 and calls her “a pioneer of pixel art and of the graphical computer interface”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Kare).

In one year she designed the core visual language of the original Macintosh, launched in January 1984, including typefaces such as Chicago (1984), the system error bomb, the Happy Mac, and the Sad Mac. She made pixel portraits of staff as 32 × 32 one-bit icons. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Kare).
The Musée de l’Imprimerie et de la Communication Graphique in Lyon held an exhibition “Icônes by Susan Kare”. [MICG](https://www.imprimerie.lyon.fr/en/susan-kare).
interpretation: Kare’s work shows the style in interfaces rather than games: a fixed grid, one bit of color, and pictograms that stay legible at their real size.
The Chicago font shows the bitmap-type trait at the scale of a whole system.
borrow: Draw icons on a 32 × 32 or 16 × 16 grid in one color, and check them at their real size as well as enlarged.
Give system states a small character, as the Happy Mac and the bomb do.
next: Check whether the MICG or another museum publishes images of Kare’s sketches with an open license.

rights.statement: Apple interface graphics by Susan Kare, in copyright. Link and metadata only.

references.title: Synthwave banner (j4p4n, Openclipart)
references.lede: A public-domain vector banner: a striped orange sun, a glowing magenta wireframe landscape, and the word “Synthwave” in green brush script on a flat dark violet ground.
references.summary: Striped sun, magenta wireframe grid, green script “Synthwave” on dark violet. CC0 vector, 2018.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1920 × 1255 PNG rendering of the SVG through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave.svg) and stored a reduced copy. A later CC0 edit by another user, [Synthwave Edit creative commons test.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave_Edit_creative_commons_test.jpg) (2024), reuses this sun and grid and adds laser beams. It has no separate record.

styles.note: The author made it as a banner for the genre’s aesthetic: a striped sun, a glowing magenta grid, and a neon script word on a dark ground.

context: The Commons description reads: “Synthwave is a kind of 1980s inspired dance retrofuturistic pop synth music. It appeals to a sort of nostalgia for music of the past. This ‘banner’ was inspired by that and the aesthetic of the genre.” [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave.svg).

The file came from Openclipart, which publishes all its clip art in the public domain. Commons marks it with the PD-OpenClipart template. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave.svg).
observed: The ground is a flat, dark grayish violet with no gradient and no stars.
A large sun disc in the centre shades from orange at the left to yellow at the right. Eight horizontal violet gaps cut it into bands from top to bottom.
The word “Synthwave” crosses the sun in a bright green brush script with a thin orange outline.
A magenta wireframe mesh fills the lower half. It rises like a wave from the left, dips behind the sun, and tightens into small cells at the right. The lines have a soft magenta glow.
interpretation: A plain, flat statement of the motif set: sun, grid, and script. The muted violet ground is lighter than the black night of the rubric, and there is no chrome lettering, so it shows the minimum that still reads as synthwave.
borrow: Cut evenly spaced horizontal bars through the whole sun disc and run a one-word script logotype across its middle.
Add a soft outer glow to thin magenta grid lines so that a flat vector reads as neon.

images.alt: Flat vector banner: a striped orange-to-yellow sun with the green script word Synthwave across it, above a glowing magenta wireframe landscape, on a dark violet ground.
images.caption: Synthwave banner by j4p4n, 2018. CC0, from [Openclipart](https://openclipart.org/detail/301642/synthwave) through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave.svg).

rights.statement: Released to the public domain through Openclipart (CC0); Commons license template PD-OpenClipart. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Synthwave.svg). Credit: j4p4n.

references.title: Takeshita Street gate, Harajuku
references.lede: The entrance arch of Harajuku’s Takeshita Street in 2024, crowned with a balloon rabbit, stars, and sparkles above daisy-patterned posts.
references.summary: Street gate with a pink-and-white balloon rabbit, stars, and sparkles over a busy shopping street. Harajuku, Tokyo, photographed 2024.

creator.name: Jakub Hałun (photograph); gate and decoration by unrecorded makers

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons photograph by Jakub Hałun at 1280 × 1930 px. Also compared a [CC0 photograph by Syced from November 2024](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Takeshita_Street.jpg), in which the balloon rabbit is gone and the arch carries a pink banner reading “かわいいがすぎる〜” with two dot-eyed characters.

styles.note: Partial fit: the gate decoration is kawaii (a dot-eyed rabbit, stars, sparkles, daisies, pink and white), but the surrounding street is a mixed commercial scene.

context: Takeshita Street is a street in Harajuku, Tokyo (Wikidata Q3179287). The photographer describes the image as “Takeshita street, Harajuku, Tokyo” and dates it 22 August 2024. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Takeshita_street,_Tokyo,_20240822_1032_5383.jpg).

The gate decoration changes over time: the November 2024 photograph by Syced shows a printed banner in place of the balloon figure. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Takeshita_Street.jpg).
observed: A steel arch spans the street on two posts decorated with small white daisy shapes; the words “Takeshita Street” sit above a light box.
On top, a rabbit built from white and pink balloons has dot eyes and a small smiling mouth; it rises out of a burst of pink and red balloons.
Yellow and blue stars made of balloons and red four-pointed sparkle shapes surround the rabbit.
Under the light box hangs an anime banner with six large-eyed characters.
Beyond the gate, a narrow pedestrian street is crowded with umbrellas, shop signs, and a McDonald’s sign.
interpretation: The gate is kawaii at street scale: one friendly face, scattered stars and sparkles, and a pink-and-white palette, used to mark the entrance to a youth shopping street.
The temporary balloon figure shows how the style is used for seasonal, changeable decoration rather than permanent architecture.
borrow: Mark an entrance or a page header with one character and a scatter of stars and four-pointed sparkles.
Use a small repeated flower shape as a pattern on a plain structural element.

images.alt: A shopping street seen through a steel arch. On top of the arch, a rabbit made of white and pink balloons, with dot eyes and a small smile, is surrounded by balloon stars in yellow and blue and red sparkle shapes. The words Takeshita Street sit above a light box and an anime banner. People with umbrellas walk down the narrow street between shop signs.
images.caption: Takeshita Street gate, Harajuku, 22 August 2024. Photograph by Jakub Hałun, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Takeshita_street,_Tokyo,_20240822_1032_5383.jpg). Incidental: an anime banner with six characters, shop signs, and a McDonald’s sign. Stored from the 1280 px Commons thumbnail.

rights.statement: Photograph © Jakub Hałun, CC BY 4.0, own work per Wikimedia Commons. The main subject is a public street and its gate. The balloon rabbit is a street decoration, not a licensed character; the anime banner and shop signs are incidental third-party works. Japanese copyright law (Article 46) allows photographs of works permanently installed outdoors, but the balloon figure was temporary, so the lead curator should confirm the tier.

references.title: The City Rises
references.lede: Umberto Boccioni’s first fully Futurist painting: a red horse and its handlers surge diagonally across a suburban building site, dissolved into streaks of divided color.
references.summary: A giant red horse and straining workers sweep across a building site in streaked, divided color. Umberto Boccioni, Milan, 1910.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: The City Rises by Umberto Boccioni 1910.jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (2583 × 1715 px, stored at 1600 × 1062 px). The Commons credit is moma.org. The physical work is the painting in the Museum of Modern Art, New York, accession number 507.1951 according to [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_City_Rises). The MoMA collection page refused scripted access (HTTP 403), so the accession number is not checked against MoMA.

styles.note: A canonical painting of the first Futurist phase: modern labor and the growing city shown as one surge of force, with divisionist brushwork and sweeping diagonals.
