context: Oil on canvas, 199 × 301 cm, 1910. It was first shown at the Mostra d’arte libera in Milan in 1911 under the title *Il lavoro* (Work). The composer Ferruccio Busoni bought it in 1912 during the travelling Futurist exhibition. It is now in the Museum of Modern Art, New York. [Wikipedia: The City Rises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_City_Rises).

Wikipedia describes it as Boccioni’s first true Futurist work, with “men and horses, merged in a dynamic effort” in a suburb where buildings are under construction. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_City_Rises).
observed: A huge red horse with a blue-black collar fills the center and plunges from upper left toward lower right.
Small figures lean hard against the horse on ropes; their bodies are drawn as long streaks in the direction of the pull.
The paint is laid in long separate strokes of red, orange, blue, green, and white, so that every surface appears to vibrate.
At the top, scaffolding, red brick buildings, chimneys, and a tram stand in an upright band of thin vertical lines.
There is no single light source and almost no still area: diagonals and arcs run across the whole canvas.
The signature “U. Boccioni” is at lower right.
interpretation: The painting is still divisionist in technique, but its subject and composition are Futurist: the force of work and the expanding industrial city are shown as one motion. It shows the style before the Cubist planes of 1912.
The horse is not a machine, but it plays the role of one: a symbol of energy that the figures must strain to control.
borrow: Point every stroke, line, and shape along one dominant diagonal so the whole surface reads as a single motion.
Set a calm vertical band (here the scaffolding) against the diagonal mass to make the motion read stronger.
Use a warm red as the dominant field with cool blue accents at the points of greatest force.

images.alt: Painting dominated by a giant red horse plunging diagonally across the canvas while small workers strain on ropes around it. All forms are made of long streaks of red, orange, blue, and white. Scaffolding and brick buildings with chimneys line the top edge.
images.caption: Umberto Boccioni, *The City Rises*, 1910, oil on canvas. Museum of Modern Art, New York. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_City_Rises_by_Umberto_Boccioni_1910.jpg), credited to moma.org, marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain. Boccioni was Italian and died in 1916, more than 70 years ago, so the painting is public domain in Italy. It was exhibited in 1911, before 1931, and its author died more than 70 years ago, so it is also public domain in the United States. The photograph is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

identifiers.commons: File:The City Rises by Umberto Boccioni 1910.jpg

references.title: The Midnight live at Brixton Academy, 2022
references.lede: A concert photograph of the synthwave band The Midnight at Brixton Academy, London: performers in violet and magenta haze in front of white horizontal light bars.
references.summary: Synthwave band on stage in violet, magenta, and blue haze with horizontal light bars. London, 7 May 2022.

evidence.note: Inspected a 1920 px rendering of the 5977 × 3378 original through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:MidnightBrixton070522_(14_of_30)_(52061571120).jpg) and stored a reduced copy. Previews of eight other photos from the same set were compared; this one shows the clearest magenta and blue light.

styles.note: Partial fit: it documents how a leading synthwave band stages itself, in magenta, violet, and blue light with neon-like horizontal bars, but it is a concert photograph, not designed graphics.

context: The photographer published a set of 30 photographs of The Midnight at Brixton Academy on 7 May 2022 under CC BY 2.0. A Commons review bot confirmed the license on 10 May 2022. Commons files it under Category:The Midnight and Concerts at Brixton Academy. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:MidnightBrixton070522_(14_of_30)_(52061571120).jpg).

The Midnight released its first album, *Endless Summer*, in 2016 ([record](ref:the-midnight-endless-summer-cover-2016)). The set’s photo 30 shows the venue marquee reading “THE MIDNIGHT 7TH MAY SOLD OUT”.
observed: A singer in a black top sings into a hand-held microphone at the centre. A guitarist in a pink and red patterned shirt with a red guitar sings at a stand on the right. A drummer sits behind them.
The stage is filled with haze lit violet and magenta from above and blue from the left.
Thin white light bars run horizontally across the back of the stage, stacked at intervals. Vertical pink light tubes stand at the right.
Round LED fixtures glow as white rings at the lower left. Raised hands and a phone screen in silhouette fill the bottom edge.
interpretation: The stacked horizontal light bars echo the cut bands of the striped sun, and the magenta, violet, and blue haze is the style’s palette in real light. It shows the style as a live, physical experience rather than a flat graphic.
borrow: Stack thin, evenly spaced horizontal light lines behind a central subject, as a stage-scale version of the striped sun.
Light a dark scene from two sides, magenta from above and blue from the side.

images.alt: Concert stage in violet and magenta haze: a singer at the centre, a guitarist with a red guitar on the right, a drummer behind, white horizontal light bars at the back, and raised hands in silhouette in front.
images.caption: The Midnight at Brixton Academy, London, 7 May 2022. Photograph by Raph_PH, CC BY 2.0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:MidnightBrixton070522_(14_of_30)_(52061571120).jpg), from [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/raph_ph/52061571120/). Stage lighting and instruments are incidental.

rights.statement: Published by the photographer under CC BY 2.0 on Flickr; license reviewed on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:MidnightBrixton070522_(14_of_30)_(52061571120).jpg) on 10 May 2022. Credit: Raph_PH. The main subject is a live performance, not a copyrighted artwork. Identifiable performers are shown, so personality rights may apply to reuse.

references.title: The Midnight, Endless Summer (album cover)
references.lede: The cover of The Midnight’s first album: a glowing pink neon script over a star-speckled figure, with VHS tracking noise and an on-screen play label.
references.summary: Pink neon script “The Midnight”, cosmic figure, VHS noise, “▶ ENDLESS SUMMER ©1984”. 2016.

evidence.note: Inspected the 1200 px front-cover image from the [Cover Art Archive](https://musicbrainz.org/release-group/764fe9af-fff9-478a-bda3-b697e99d9047) in a scratch folder. Not stored. The artist credit comes from The Midnight Wiki; the [Discogs record of the 2016 digital release](https://www.discogs.com/release/8888236) lists no artwork credit.

styles.note: A neon-tube script logotype, a black ground, and VHS tracking lines used as a nostalgic accent: the type and surface side of the style.

context: The Midnight Wiki: *Endless Summer* is the band’s first album, released independently on 5 August 2016. “A small snip of the album artwork (done by Taylor Allen) was revealed in July,” and the full artwork was revealed with the announcement on 25 July. [The Midnight Wiki](https://themidnight.wiki/wiki/Endless_Summer).
Discogs records the original release as a self-released digital file of 5 August 2016, written by Tim McEwan and Tyler Lyle. [Discogs](https://www.discogs.com/release/8888236).
observed: The ground is near-black, crossed by faint horizontal lines of video noise. Two bands of heavier static run across the lower third.
A tilted female figure, filled with a star field in cyan, blue, violet, and magenta, rises through the centre.
“The Midnight” crosses the figure in a monoline script drawn as a pink neon tube: a white-hot core, a magenta glow, and a thin cyan and yellow colour offset.
Below, “▶ ENDLESS SUMMER” and “©1984” are set in small, light, pixel-like capitals, like a VCR on-screen display, with a red and cyan colour fringe.
interpretation: The cover shows that VHS artefacts in synthwave are an accent of memory, not decay: the image stays sharp and saturated, and the noise sits on top of it. The false “©1984” date sets the scene in an imagined past.
borrow: Draw a script logotype as a neon tube: a white core line, a wide magenta glow, and a one-pixel cyan offset.
Label a section like a VCR display: a play triangle and small pixel capitals.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The cover art is in copyright (The Midnight / Taylor Allen, 2016).

references.title: The Revolt
references.lede: Luigi Russolo paints a crowd in revolt as a red mass driving a row of repeated chevrons into a blue street, the clearest painted diagram of a Futurist line of force.
references.summary: Repeated red chevrons drive a red mass into tilted blue buildings. Luigi Russolo, Milan, c. 1911.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the [Commons file](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Luigi_Russolo_La_Rivolta_1911.jpg) (original 1677 × 1075 px; a 1280 × 821 px rendering was inspected and stored). The physical work is the painting in the Kunstmuseum Den Haag, object number 0333154. The Commons file is credited to secondary websites, not to the museum, so its color may differ from the canvas.

styles.note: A canonical early Futurist painting: the crowd and the city shown through repeated wedge shapes that act as lines of force.

context: Oil on canvas, 150.8 × 230.7 cm, c. 1911, made in Milan. Kunstmuseum Den Haag, object number 0333154, acquired from the Estate of Myrtil Frank and Flory Frank-Marburger. [Kunstmuseum Den Haag](https://www.kunstmuseum.nl/en/collection/revolt).
observed: Five or more red chevrons, each the same angle, repeat from the lower left toward the upper right, growing smaller and closer together.
The right half is a dense red-orange field with small scratched figures, the crowd, pushing into the angle of the chevrons.
Blue and violet buildings with dark square windows tilt away from the force, as if bent by it.
A yellow-green band runs between the red field and the buildings along the same diagonal.
Color is flat and nearly unmixed: red, orange, blue, yellow, green, and black.
interpretation: The repeated chevron is the Futurist idea of motion by repetition in its most graphic form. It works like a printed arrow and predicts the wedges of later poster design, including [Lissitzky’s red wedge](ref:lissitzky-beat-the-whites-red-wedge-poster), although no direct link is documented here.
The painting is political: the force is a crowd, and the city bends before it.
borrow: Repeat one wedge or chevron several times along a diagonal, closer together toward the target, to show direction and acceleration.
Let the shapes that receive the force tilt away from it.
Use one hot dominant field (red-orange) against a cool one (blue) with a narrow yellow band at the boundary.

images.alt: Painting in which a row of repeated red chevrons, getting smaller toward the upper right, drives a red-orange mass of small figures into blue buildings with dark windows that tilt away. A yellow-green band runs along the diagonal.
images.caption: Luigi Russolo, *The Revolt*, c. 1911, oil on canvas. Kunstmuseum Den Haag, 0333154. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Luigi_Russolo_La_Rivolta_1911.jpg), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain. Russolo was Italian and died in 1947, more than 70 years ago, so the painting is public domain in Italy. The Commons file states that it is public domain in the United States because it was first published before 1931. The image is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.

references.title: Theatre Royal, Birmingham, playbill for *The Dragon of Wantley* pantomime
references.lede: An English Christmas pantomime playbill for New Year’s Day 1845, with condensed and fat display lines above a dense cast list braced and dotted in many small faces.
references.summary: British theatre playbill with very condensed display lines, fat slabs, braces, and dotted leaders. Birmingham, 1845.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Theatre Royal Birmingham – playbill – 1844

references.made: 1845 (dated on the bill: Wednesday, January 1, 1845; Commons gives 1844)

evidence.note: Inspected a 1280 × 2157 px Commons thumbnail, because the full-size original (1216 × 2049 px according to Commons) returned HTTP 429. The thumbnail is slightly upscaled from that original. Commons gives a blog post as source; the holding collection of the physical bill is not named, so the copy is unidentified.

styles.note: A British playbill in full Victorian form: centred display lines in condensed and fat faces, many sizes, rules, braces, and dotted leaders.

context: Commons describes the file as a playbill from the [Theatre Royal, Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_Royal,_Birmingham), dated 1844, author anonymous, source [The Iron Room](https://theironroom.wordpress.com/2017/01/01/its-behind-you/), and tags it {{PD-anon-70-EU}}.

The bill itself announces the play *Foundling of the Forest* and the Christmas pantomime *The Dragon of Wantley! or, Harlequin Knight and the Fire King of the Burning Isle!* for Wednesday, 1 January 1845, “produced under the immediate direction” of Mr. J. Ridgway.
observed: “CONTINUED SUCCESS!” uses two faces in one line: a very condensed roman for “CONTINUED” and a fat condensed slab for “SUCCESS!”.
“DRAGON OF WANTLEY!” is the largest line, in a very condensed heavy roman, with “OF” stacked small between the two words. “FOUNDLING OF THE FOREST!” repeats the trick with “OF THE”.
“WEDNESDAY, JANUARY 1, 1845,” is set in a wide, letterspaced fat face.
“THE VAULTED CHAMBER OF GIGANTIC CYCLOPS!” runs full width in a condensed sans-serif capital.
The cast list fills most of the sheet: dotted leaders join roles to actors, and curly braces group several roles to one description.
Wide sans-serif, bold roman, italic, small capitals, and an outline letter (“GRAND AUDIENCE CHAMBER”) appear in the small lines.
Thin rules divide the sections. Black ink on off-white paper, with show-through and creases.
interpretation: The British playbill packs more text than the American poster. The display lines act as signposts in a dense page of small type, which is the pattern Meggs’s phrase about every inch of space describes.
Stacking a small “OF” between two big words is a typical device of the condensed theatre line.
borrow: Stack small joining words between two large words in one line.
Use braces and dotted leaders to organise a dense list without a table.

images.alt: Long black-and-white playbill with centred lines: Theatre Royal, Birmingham, Continued Success!, Wednesday January 1 1845, Foundling of the Forest!, and very large condensed letters reading Dragon of Wantley!, above a dense cast list with dotted leaders and braces.
images.caption: Theatre Royal, Birmingham, playbill for 1 January 1845. Anonymous, through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theatre_Royal_Birmingham_-_playbill_-_1844.jpg) (1280 px thumbnail). Public domain.

rights.statement: Commons tags the file {{PD-anon-70-EU}}: an anonymous work published more than 70 years ago. The bill was published in England in 1845, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.

references.title: Theme Building, Los Angeles International Airport
references.lede: The 1961 landmark at LAX: a saucer-shaped restaurant floating on a blue core under two crossed parabolic arches, like a flying saucer that has landed on four legs.
references.summary: A white saucer on a blue core under two crossed parabolic arches, with a perforated screen wall. Pereira & Luckman with Paul Williams and Welton Becket, 1961.

creator.name: James Langenheim of Pereira & Luckman (initial design); William Pereira, Charles Luckman, Paul Williams, and Welton Becket

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Benoît Prieur’s CC0 photograph of July 2023 on Wikimedia Commons, 1920 × 1440 px. Also inspected his second July 2023 view, in which a new people-mover guideway crosses the foreground; it is not stored.

styles.note: A flying saucer on parabolic legs, the Space Age symbol built at full scale; Wikipedia calls it an example of the style later known as Googie.

context: Wikipedia: the building is an example of Space Age design, influenced by Populuxe and later known as Googie. It resembles a flying saucer that has landed on four legs. James Langenheim of Pereira & Luckman made the first design, and a team led by William Pereira and Charles Luckman, with Paul Williams and Welton Becket, completed it. [Wikipedia: Theme Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theme_Building).

The crossed arches look homogeneous but are four concrete legs topped by hollow stucco-covered steel trusses. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson dedicated the building on 25 June 1961. It became Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument no. 570 in 1993. Walt Disney Imagineering designed a retro-futurist interior and lighting for the Encounter Restaurant in 1997. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theme_Building).
observed: Two white parabolic arches cross high above the building; each arch splits near the top into a loop and lands on splayed feet at the corners.
A wide white saucer with a thin upturned rim hangs from the arches; under it, a ring of slanted glass windows wraps a lower disc.
A ribbed, saturated cobalt-blue cylinder carries the saucer and rises through it to a smaller blue drum on top.
Thin cables run from the arches to the top drum.
Around the base, a curved white screen wall is pierced by rows of rounded openings.
The ground is a deep blue sky with thin cloud; the palette is white, cobalt, and pale concrete. A 1990s control tower and a parking structure stand behind it.
interpretation: The building is the style’s space-age imagery taken literally: the saucer, the parabola, and the impression of lift-off.
Its color is more restrained than the roadside signs: white form and one strong blue, so the silhouette does the work.
borrow: Frame a heading with two crossing parabolic arcs, and hang the content panel from them.
Use a field of small rounded openings, like the screen wall, as a quiet pattern under a loud silhouette.

images.alt: Color photograph of the Theme Building at LAX: two white crossed parabolic arches over a white saucer-shaped restaurant on a ribbed cobalt-blue core, with a perforated white screen wall at the base and a control tower behind, under a blue sky.
images.caption: Benoît Prieur, Theme Building (Los Angeles International Airport) in July 2023 (2), CC0. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Theme_Building_(Los_Angeles_International_Airport)_in_July_2023_(2).jpg). The control tower (1990s) and other airport buildings behind it are incidental.

rights.statement: Photograph: Benoît Prieur, own work, CC0 1.0 (Commons). Building: finished in 1961 in the United States, before December 1990, so it is not protected as an architectural work. Buildings in the background are incidental, and 17 U.S.C. § 120(a) permits pictures of buildings visible from public places.

identifiers.commons: File:Theme Building (Los Angeles International Airport) in July 2023 (2).jpg

references.title: Thorowgood specimen of Egyptian types, 1825
references.lede: A fold-out page from a London typefounder’s specimen of about 1825, showing 12- and 14-line pica Egyptians, the heavy slab serifs of the early poster.
references.summary: Huge black slab-serif capitals, roman and italic, from a London type specimen. Thorowgood, 1825.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Thorowgood 1825 Slab Type Specimen (photograph by James Puckett)

creator.name: William Thorowgood, Fann Street Foundry, London (as attributed by the photographer)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons copy of James Puckett’s photograph (1024 × 683 px), uploaded from Flickr and credited to dailytypespecimen.com. The photograph does not name the library or shelfmark of the volume, so the physical copy is unidentified.

styles.note: The fat Egyptian slab is one of the founding display faces of the poster style, shown here at poster size in roman and italic.

context: Wikipedia says the printed poster spurred demand for bold new types like the fat face and later the slab serif, and that Robert Thorne’s Fann Street Foundry popularised fat faces in London. [Wikipedia: Fat face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_face).
Wikipedia dates the slab serif to the early nineteenth century. [Wikipedia: Slab serif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slab_serif).
observed: An open specimen book with a large fold-out page held flat by a hand at the upper right.
“TERM” in roman capitals with heavy rectangular slab serifs and very little contrast between strokes, labelled “14 Line Pica Egyptian.”
“MINER” in an italic of the same slab design, labelled “12 Line Pica Egyptian.”
Black ink on aged cream paper, with ink show-through from the other side of the leaf.
The labels are set small and centred above each specimen in a bold roman.
interpretation: The page shows the raw material of the poster style: one word per line, set as large as the page allows, with only a small label to name it.
Slab capitals at this weight read from across a street, which is why they took over posting bills.
borrow: Set one short word per line at the largest size the measure allows.
Pair a heavy slab roman with its italic for contrast inside one family.

images.alt: Open old specimen book on a table. A large fold-out page shows the word TERM in huge black slab-serif capitals and below it MINER in a slab-serif italic, each with a small label naming the size of Egyptian type.
images.caption: Thorowgood specimen of 14- and 12-line pica Egyptian, about 1825. Photograph by James Puckett, [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/), through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Thorowgood_1825_Slab_Type_Specimen_(7609775334).jpg).

rights.statement: Commons licenses the photograph CC BY 2.0, credit James Puckett. The specimen was printed in London about 1825; its letterforms and pages are in the public domain in the United Kingdom and the United States.

references.title: Toyokuni I, Ichikawa Danjūrō VII as Fujiwara no Shihei (fan print)
references.lede: An actor portrait printed to be pasted on a flat round fan (uchiwa-e): Utagawa Toyokuni I sets the actor against a pink fan-shaped ground with falling cherry petals.
references.summary: Black outlines, a lattice-patterned robe, and a pink fan-shaped ground. Utagawa Toyokuni I, about 1816.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Art Institute of Chicago image of 2000.70 (1686 × 1418 px).

styles.note: A fan print: the style applied to an everyday object, with flat pattern, key-block outlines, and a figure cropped by the fan shape.

context: AIC catalogues the sheet as a color woodblock print, uchiwa-e (fan print), 22.9 × 26.8 cm, about 1816, depicting Ichikawa Danjūrō VII in the play Ume Sakura Aioi-zōshi. [AIC 2000.70](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/154248).
observed: A rounded fan shape fills the sheet in flat pale pink. The corners outside it are cream paper.
The actor’s head and shoulders fill the right two thirds. His robe is cut by the lower edge and by the fan outline.
The robe is purple with an orange and cream lattice and round green flower crests, a dense pattern inside outlined areas.
The hair and cap are solid black. A ribbon from the cap carries a black diamond pattern.
Cherry petals are drawn only as red outlines on the pink ground at left.
The actor’s name, the artist’s signature, and a seal run in vertical columns at right. A date column sits outside the fan at lower right.
interpretation: The fan print shows the style on a commercial object: the format is the frame, and the figure is cut by it.
Pattern density changes on purpose: a dense robe, an open pink ground, and a few scattered petals.
borrow: Use the shape of the object as the frame, and crop the main figure against it.
Set a dense pattern against an open ground with a few scattered outlined motifs.

images.alt: Color woodblock fan print. Head and shoulders of a kabuki actor with a black cap and a patterned ribbon, in a purple robe with an orange lattice and round flower crests, on a pink fan-shaped ground with outlined cherry petals.
images.caption: Utagawa Toyokuni I, Ichikawa Danjūrō VII as Fujiwara no Shihei, uchiwa-e, c. 1816. [Art Institute of Chicago 2000.70](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/154248), Margaret Gentles Fund. CC0.

rights.statement: The Art Institute of Chicago marks the object public domain (`is_public_domain: true`) and releases images of public-domain works under CC0. [AIC open access](https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). Toyokuni I died in 1825, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Typische Vertikalklitterung als Darstellung des Dada Baargeld, 1920
references.lede: Cologne Dadaist Johannes Theodor Baargeld pastes a photograph of his own capped head on a reproduction of the Venus de Milo’s torso, and leaves the cut edges in view.
references.summary: A cut photograph of a young man’s head on a classical marble torso, alone on yellowed paper. Baargeld, Cologne, 1920.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Baargeld, Typische Vertikalklitterung als Darstellung des Dada Baargeld (Kunsthaus Zürich)

creator.name: Johannes Theodor Baargeld (Alfred Emanuel Ferdinand Gruenwald, 1892–1927)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons image (1438 × 1800 px original, viewed at 1200 px). Commons describes it as the Kunsthaus Zürich, Graphische Sammlung, sheet, cropped, and takes it from a Cologne cemetery-society website, not from the museum. No Kunsthaus inventory number was checked.

styles.note: A Dada photomontage: press and studio photographs cut and joined so that the scale and the cut edges show. Partial fit: it has no type.

context: Commons records the work as *Typical Vertical Mess as Depiction of the Dada Baargeld*, 1920, Kunsthaus Zürich, Graphische Sammlung, with the license PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired, death year 1927). [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Johannes_Theodor_Baargeld_%E2%80%93_Typische_Vertikalklitterung_als_Darstellung_des_Dada_Baargeld_-_1920.jpg).

An exhibition caption gives the medium as photomontage, 37.1 × 31 cm, Kunsthaus Zürich, Grafische Sammlung. [Art Blart](https://artblart.com/tag/typical-vertical-mess-as-depiction-of-the-dada-baargeld/). MoMA used the work in the audio guide of its Dada exhibition. [MoMA audio](https://www.moma.org/audio/playlist/198/2636).
Baargeld founded Cologne Dada with Max Ernst in 1919–1920. [Wikipedia: Johannes Theodor Baargeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Theodor_Baargeld).
observed: A black-and-white photograph of a young man’s face under a peaked cap is cut along the jaw and neck and laid on a photograph of a classical marble torso with broken arms.
The face is warmer and smoother in tone than the grey, pitted marble, so the join is plain.
The torso stands on a cut photograph of a cloth-draped plinth, whose trapezoid edge is clearly cut.
The montage sits in the middle of a large sheet of yellowed paper with stains and creases. A small signature, “zobaargeld”, is written at lower right.
There is no type and no second color.
interpretation: The work shows the photomontage branch of Dada at its plainest: two photographs, one cut, and a joke about the classical ideal. The empty sheet makes the cut more visible than in the crowded Berlin montages.
borrow: Join two black-and-white photographs at one clean cut, and let the difference in tone show the join.
Place one small montage in a large empty field of warm paper.

images.alt: Photomontage on yellowed paper: the head of a young man in a peaked cap is pasted on the photographed marble torso of the Venus de Milo, which stands on a cut photograph of a draped plinth.
images.caption: Johannes Theodor Baargeld, *Typische Vertikalklitterung als Darstellung des Dada Baargeld*, 1920. Kunsthaus Zürich, Graphische Sammlung. Cropped image via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Johannes_Theodor_Baargeld_%E2%80%93_Typische_Vertikalklitterung_als_Darstellung_des_Dada_Baargeld_-_1920.jpg), PD-Art.

rights.statement: Commons tags the image PD-Art (PD-old-auto-expired). Baargeld, a German author, died in 1927, so the montage is public domain in Germany. It was made in 1920. The photographs in it are a portrait of Baargeld and a reproduction of an ancient statue; their photographers are not named, and any term for a pre-1927 anonymous photograph has expired. In the United States the work is public domain in both cases: if published before 1931 the term has expired, and if unpublished the term of life plus 70 years ended in 1997.

identifiers.commons: File:Johannes Theodor Baargeld – Typische Vertikalklitterung als Darstellung des Dada Baargeld - 1920.jpg

references.title: Ulm stool (Ulmer Hocker), 1954
references.lede: The school’s multipurpose stool by Max Bill, Hans Gugelot, and Paul Hildinger: three spruce boards joined at the corners, with a beech rod between the sides.
references.summary: Three plain spruce boards with finger joints and one round beech rod. A seat, side table, or shelf. HfG Ulm, 1954.

creator.name: Max Bill, Hans Gugelot, Paul Hildinger, and Hochschule für Gestaltung Ulm

evidence.note: Inspected the Museum Angewandte Kunst image of inventory 17619 at 1600 × 1067 px, through the museum’s online collection.

styles.note: A key Ulm object: minimal parts, visible joints, and several uses for one form. Its material is plain wood, not the grey housing of the product core.

context: The museum credits Max Bill, Hans Gugelot, Paul Hildinger, and the Hochschule für Gestaltung Ulm with the design, dates it 1954, places production in Ulm, and gives spruce seat and side panels with a beech dowel and beech trim on the bottom edges. [Museum Angewandte Kunst 17619](https://sammlung-digital.museumangewandtekunst.de/detailpage/collection/7146c7d2-0625-4f3b-bfa7-7876aa5f724e).

The museum says that a small building budget led Gugelot and Bill to keep the furniture simple. The stool “consists of three spruce boards, which are joined together by a finger joint”, and the dowel can be used as a handle. It served as a seat, a book carrier, a low table, a pedestal, or, in a row, a shelf. In 1960 it cost 11 Deutschmarks. [Museum Angewandte Kunst](https://sammlung-digital.museumangewandtekunst.de/detailpage/collection/7146c7d2-0625-4f3b-bfa7-7876aa5f724e).
observed: The stool is an upside-down U of three flat, light spruce boards with straight grain and knots.
Finger joints show as a row of small rectangles at both top corners.
A round beech rod joins the two sides near the bottom.
Thin strips of a slightly different wood edge the bottoms of the sides.
There is no finish color, hardware, or ornament.
interpretation: The stool is the Ulm method in its most basic form: the fewest parts, visible joints, and a form open to several uses. It shares the structure of the style, not its grey palette.
borrow: Make the joint the only detail, and repeat it evenly.

rights.statement: The museum states “Rechte am Objekt: © VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn 2024”. Max Bill died in 1994. No image is stored.

references.title: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space
references.lede: Umberto Boccioni’s striding figure, whose muscles stream backward in flame-like planes, as if the body were shaped by the air it moves through.
references.summary: A bronze striding figure with flaring, wind-swept planes, on two blocks. Umberto Boccioni, 1913, bronze cast in the Museo del Novecento, Milan.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Umberto Boccioni Forme uniche nella continuità dello spazio 1913.jpg, photograph by Paolobon140

references.made: 1913 (plaster); the Milan bronze cast 1949 according to Wikipedia

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a photograph by the Commons user Paolobon140, 8 December 2015 (original 2912 × 4368 px; a 1067 × 1600 px rendering was inspected and stored). The file description says it shows the cast exhibited at the Museo del Novecento, Milan. Several casts exist; this record describes that cast. The photo has warm lighting, so the bronze color is not reliable.

styles.note: The movement’s best-known sculpture: a body in motion merged with the space around it, the three-dimensional form of lines of force.

context: The original plaster of 1913 is in the Museu de Arte Contemporânea da Universidade de São Paulo. Bronze casts were made in 1931 (one at MoMA), in 1949 (one at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and one at the Museo del Novecento, Milan), and in 1972 (Tate, and eight more cast from a 1949 bronze). The height is about 111 cm. [Wikipedia: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_Forms_of_Continuity_in_Space).
The sculpture is on the obverse of the Italian 20-cent euro coin. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_Forms_of_Continuity_in_Space).
observed: A headless or helmeted figure strides forward to the right, its rear leg stretched far back; each foot stands on its own rectangular block.
The calves and thighs flare backward into curved, blade-like fins, like flames or the wake of the motion.
The torso is made of hollow, overlapping curved planes; a short flat projection juts from the chest.
The surfaces are smooth and polished, with sharp edges where planes meet.
The photograph shows the sculpture on a white plinth against a plain warm wall.
interpretation: The figure does not show a body and then its trail; the trail is part of the body. This is the sculptural equivalent of Boccioni’s painted interpenetration of object and space in [Dynamism of a Cyclist](ref:boccioni-dynamism-of-a-cyclist-1913).
Its smooth, aerodynamic planes link it with the streamlined forms of later machine design.
borrow: Show speed by stretching the back edge of a form into trailing fins.
Let a form open into hollow planes so space passes through it.
Set a dynamic silhouette on two plain rectangular bases for contrast.

images.alt: Bronze sculpture of a striding figure on two rectangular blocks, against a plain warm wall. Its legs flare backward into curved fins like flames, and its torso is made of hollow overlapping planes.
images.caption: Umberto Boccioni, *Unique Forms of Continuity in Space*, 1913, bronze cast, Museo del Novecento, Milan. Photograph by Paolobon140, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Umberto_Boccioni_Forme_uniche_nella_continuit%C3%A0_dello_spazio_1913.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0.

rights.statement: Photograph by Paolobon140, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons. Boccioni was Italian and died in 1916, so the sculpture is public domain in Italy. The plaster was exhibited in 1913. Because the work was already public domain in Italy on 1 January 1996, its US copyright was not restored under the URAA, so it is public domain in the United States even if the first casts of 1931 count as publication.

identifiers.commons: File:Umberto Boccioni Forme uniche nella continuità dello spazio 1913.jpg

references.title: Utamaro, Picture Book of Selected Insects (Ehon mushi erabi)
references.lede: A two-volume color-printed book in which Kitagawa Utamaro’s insects and plants face comic poems on the opposite page, inside thin printed frames.
references.summary: Insects and plants in soft flat color beside vertical poems, inside a ruled frame. Kitagawa Utamaro, 1788.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Art Institute of Chicago image of 2022.633 (1686 × 1331 px). The image shows one open spread; other spreads were not inspected.

styles.note: A color-printed picture book (ehon): the same key-block line and flat block colors as single-sheet prints, with text and picture sharing a framed page.

context: AIC catalogues the work as color woodblock printed books, two volumes, 27 × 18.3 cm, 1788. [AIC 2022.633](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/220320).
Wikipedia’s Ukiyo-e article names illustrated books among the formats of ukiyo-e production. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukiyo-e).
observed: The open spread has two pages, each with a thin double-ruled frame printed in black.
On the left page a katydid sits on a large dark purple eggplant among olive-green leaves and pale pink flowers. The plant sits on the lower edge of the frame and leaves the upper half empty.
The plant continues across the gutter to the right page, where a snail climbs a stem.
On the right page, poems in cursive script run in vertical columns from the upper right.
Colors are flat and muted: dark purple, olive green, pale pink, and buff. Fine black lines draw the veins, the legs, and the antennae.
The paper is cream with a visible laid texture.
interpretation: The book shows how the style handles text and image together: one frame for both, text in a column, picture in the lower half.
The picture that crosses the gutter treats the spread as one composition.
borrow: Put the image low in a ruled frame and run the text in a column above or beside it.
Let one element cross the boundary between two panels to join them.

images.alt: Open book spread with thin black-ruled frames. Left: a katydid on a large dark purple eggplant with leaves and pale flowers. Right: a snail on a flowering stem and vertical columns of cursive poems.
images.caption: Kitagawa Utamaro, Picture Book of Selected Insects (Ehon mushi erabi), 1788. [Art Institute of Chicago 2022.633](https://www.artic.edu/artworks/220320), Frederick W. Gookin Collection. CC0.

rights.statement: The Art Institute of Chicago marks the object public domain (`is_public_domain: true`) and releases images of public-domain works under CC0. [AIC open access](https://www.artic.edu/open-access/open-access-images). Utamaro died in 1806, and the book was published in 1788, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: Utamaro, The Flirtatious Type, from Ten Types in the Physiognomy of Women
references.lede: A half-length woman glances back over a bare shoulder against a plain pink ground, in one of Kitagawa Utamaro’s close-up portraits of beauties.
references.summary: One figure on a flat pink ground, thin outlines, and a title cartouche. Kitagawa Utamaro, about 1793.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Cleveland Museum of Art print image of 1930.218 (2274 × 3400 px, viewed at 1070 × 1600).

styles.note: A canonical bijinga close-up: one figure cut by the sheet edges on a flat ground, thin key lines, patterned robes, and a title cartouche.

context: Cleveland catalogues the sheet as a color woodblock print, 36.9 × 25.4 cm, about 1793, from the series Ten Types in the Physiognomy of Women. [CMA 1930.218](https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.218).
Cleveland says that Utamaro was known for close-up portraits in the bijinga genre, and that only two impressions from this series have pink mica. [CMA](https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.218).
observed: The ground is one flat dusty pink over the whole sheet, with no setting.
The woman is cut by the bottom edge. She stands right of center and looks back to the right.
Her face, neck, and hands are unprinted paper with thin dark outlines. The hair is solid black with fine hair lines at the edges.
The outer robe is translucent pale green with a wave-line pattern and round crests. The under-robe shows black leaf shapes on yellow.
A cartouche of three joined vertical panels at upper left holds the series title, the signature, and a seal.
interpretation: The plain colored ground removes setting and leaves outline, pattern, and pose to carry the image.
The cartouche is part of the composition: it balances the figure on the left side of the sheet.
borrow: Use one flat colored ground behind a single subject, and balance the subject with a narrow text panel on the other side.
Show one pattern through another, like the translucent robe over the under-robe.

images.alt: Color woodblock print. Half-length woman with a black upswept hairdo looking back over her bare shoulder, wearing a pale green patterned robe over a yellow robe with black leaves, on a flat pink ground. A three-panel title cartouche is at upper left.
images.caption: Kitagawa Utamaro, The Flirtatious Type, from Ten Types in the Physiognomy of Women, c. 1793. [Cleveland Museum of Art 1930.218](https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.218). CC0.

rights.statement: The Cleveland Museum of Art open access API gives `share_license_status: CC0` for this object. Utamaro died in 1806, so the work is public domain in Japan and the United States.

references.title: VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action
references.lede: Sukeban Games’s bartending visual novel: pixel-art characters in a neon-lit bar in Glitch City, framed by a screen of dark, outlined interface panels.
references.summary: Pixel art in magenta, violet, and cyan, with monospace dialogue in framed dark panels. Sukeban Games, Venezuela, 2016.

source.label: Steam: VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action

references.made: 2016 (released 21 June 2016 for Windows, macOS, and Linux)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected eight 1920 × 1080 px screenshots from the Steam store listing (app 447530) in a scratch folder. The observations come from the two bar screenshots with the drink-mixing panel.

styles.note: Partial fit: a cyberpunk interface in pixel art. It has the dark ground, magenta and cyan neon, framed panels, and monospace text, but its tone is warmer and more comic than dystopian.
Clear: the whole game is drawn in coarse pixel art, with framed dialogue panels and bitmap-style type.

context: Wikipedia: “VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action … is a 2016 visual novel developed by Venezuelan studio Sukeban Games and published by Ysbryd Games.” It was first released for Windows, OS X, and Linux on 21 June 2016. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VA-11_Hall-A).

Wikipedia: “The game features a retro-futuristic look based on cyberpunk media, PC-98 games, and anime-inspired visuals.” Corruption and food shortages “run rampant” in Glitch City, where the bar is. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VA-11_Hall-A).
observed: The screen is a frame of near-black and dark violet panels with thin outlines and small notches along the top edge.
The left panel shows the bar in pixel art: magenta and violet walls, a blue neon logo reading “KIRIRIN Light”, a pink neon bottle, and two round cyan-and-red gauges.
At top right, “Cyberpunk Bartender Action” in thin pink type sits above “VA-11 HALL-A” in heavy italic pink capitals.

The mixing panel is a grid of outlined cells labelled “Adelhyde”, “Bronson Ext”, “Pwd Delta”, “Flanergide”, and “Karmotrine” in a monospace pixel font, with gray beveled buttons “Reset”, “Mix”, “Slot 1”, and “Slot 2”.
Dialogue appears in a black box at the bottom, with the speaker’s name in magenta or blue (“Dorothy:”, “Jill:”) and the text in white monospace.
interpretation: The game reduces the style to a few interface rules (dark panels, outlined cells, monospace labels, neon accents) and shows that they work at a low resolution.
Its beveled gray buttons and anime characters pull it toward [pixel art](style:pixel-art) and away from the strict HUD look.
borrow: Color the speaker’s name, not the message, when you put dialogue or log lines in neon on black.
Lay out controls as a grid of outlined cells, each with a short monospace label.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The game and its screenshots belong to Sukeban Games and its publishers. The screenshots were viewed on the Steam store page only.

references.title: Viktor Hachmang, poster for Trailer/Min Expo
references.lede: A riso-printed exhibition poster by the Dutch illustrator Viktor Hachmang: fluorescent pink and dark blue, with coarse halftone dots and overprinted violet.
references.summary: Riso poster in fluorescent pink and blue with coarse halftone and violet overprint.

source.label: Flickr: Marcel van Schooten, “Poster Trailer/Min Expo”

creator.name: Viktor Hachmang (design), as the Flickr description states

evidence.note: Viewed the 1024 × 576 px Flickr “large” file of a close photograph of one printed copy, owned and photographed by Marcel van Schooten. The image shows a detail, not the whole sheet.

styles.note: Two spot inks, fluorescent pink and blue, with halftone screens and a third color where they overprint.

context: The Flickr description says: “Printed on RISO printer with an awesome design by Viktor Hachmang.” The photo is licensed CC BY 2.0 by the photographer, who is not the designer.
observed: Fluorescent pink and a dark blue are the only inks on cream paper.
A regular pink halftone dot field fills the background. A finer blue screen gives a light gray-blue tint.
Where blue lines and fills cross the pink, the overlap prints a dark violet.
Line drawing and lettering are clean and of even weight. There are no black key lines.
interpretation: A clear example of the two-ink riso poster: the third color is made by overprint, and halftone screens stand in for extra inks.
borrow: Use a pink halftone as a background tint and let a second ink overprint it, instead of adding a third color.

rights.statement: The photograph is CC BY 2.0 by Marcel van Schooten, but the poster design is a third-party work in copyright. Link only.

references.title: W3C CSS 2, Appendix D: “Default style sheet for HTML 4”
references.lede: The W3C’s informative sample style sheet that writes down how browsers render unstyled HTML.
references.summary: W3C CSS 2 Appendix D: body margin 8px, h1 2em, h2 1.5em, 40px indents, underlined links.

evidence.note: Read the appendix on 2026-10-02. The dates are the publication years of the CSS 2 and CSS 2.1 Recommendations as generally cited; the page itself was not checked for its date line.

styles.note: Documentation of the default rendering that the style keeps or restates.

context: The appendix lists `body { margin: 8px }`, `h1 { font-size: 2em; margin: .67em 0 }`, `h2 { font-size: 1.5em; margin: .75em 0 }`, `blockquote { margin-left: 40px; margin-right: 40px }`, and `:link, :visited { text-decoration: underline }`.
The current equivalent is the [Rendering section of the HTML Living Standard](ref:whatwg-html-rendering-defaults).
interpretation: The sizes here explain the narrow type scale in the [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design) fingerprint: the largest default heading is twice the body size.
borrow: Start from these values instead of a reset. Change only what the content needs.

references.title: Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign
references.lede: Betty Willis’s 1959 roadside sign: a stretched diamond ringed with bulbs, “Welcome” in neon silver dollars, “Fabulous” in cursive, and an eight-point star on top.
references.summary: A bulb-ringed diamond with silver-dollar letters, cursive “Fabulous,” red capitals, and an eight-point neon star. Betty Willis for Western Neon, Las Vegas, 1959.

source.label: Library of Congress: Carol M. Highsmith, Sign in daytime, Las Vegas, Nevada

references.made: Funded May 1959 and erected soon after (Wikipedia); photographed 2007

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected Carol M. Highsmith’s photograph (Library of Congress LCCN 2010630140; Commons file [Sign in daytime, Las Vegas, Nevada LCCN2010630140.tif](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sign_in_daytime,_Las_Vegas,_Nevada_LCCN2010630140.tif), Exif date 6 September 2007) at 1920 × 1165 px. Also compared the CC0 2009 view by Ypsilon from Finland on Commons. The south face of the original sign at 5100 Las Vegas Boulevard South is shown; replicas exist elsewhere.

styles.note: The style record names this sign’s starburst as pure ornament; Wikipedia calls the design characteristic of Googie.

context: The sign was funded in May 1959 and built by Western Neon under contract with Clark County. Betty Willis, a Western Neon employee, designed it at the request of the salesman Ted Rogich. It cost $4,000. [Wikipedia: Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_to_Fabulous_Las_Vegas_sign).

Wikipedia describes it as 25 feet tall, a horizontally stretched diamond with pointed top and bottom and rounded sides, internally lit, with chasing yellow incandescent bulbs around the edge. The white neon circles represent silver dollars for “the Silver State.” The eight-point star is red-painted metal outlined in yellow neon. The back reads “Drive Carefully / Come Back Soon.” Wikipedia calls the design characteristic of Googie architecture. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_to_Fabulous_Las_Vegas_sign).

Willis never claimed copyright. Wikipedia quotes her: “If I had copyrighted the sign, it probably wouldn’t have been used as much and wouldn’t be as famous.” YESCO has owned the physical sign since it bought Western Neon in the early 1960s. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_to_Fabulous_Las_Vegas_sign); [Time, 2015](https://time.com/3829207/welcome-to-fabulous-las-vegas-sign-betty-willis/).
observed: The cabinet is a wide white diamond with a yellow frame; dozens of round yellow bulbs stand out from its edge on short stalks.
Seven silver-white discs, edged with ridges like coins and showing faint coin relief, run across the top and each holds one red letter of “WELCOME” outlined in neon tube.
“TO” in small blue capitals sits beside “Fabulous” in a slanted, connected blue script with a long underline swash.
“LAS VEGAS” fills the width in heavy red sans-serif capitals; “NEVADA” sits below in small, widely spaced blue capitals.
An eight-point star, a long four-point star in yellow neon over a shorter red one, bursts out of a blue rectangular frame formed by the two poles and their cross piece.
Colors are red, blue, yellow, and white, flat and saturated, against clear blue sky.
interpretation: The sign is a compact grammar of the style: an angular non-rectangular panel, a starburst that breaks its frame, one word in neon-style script next to bold capitals, and a chasing-bulb border.
The diamond with rounded sides points up and down at once, so the static sign reads as energetic.
borrow: Put the name on a stretched diamond panel with pointed ends, and ring it with evenly spaced dots.
Set one word in a slanted script between lines of capitals, and let a star overlap the panel’s frame.

images.alt: The Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign against blue sky: a white diamond ringed with yellow bulbs, WELCOME in red letters on seven silver discs, Fabulous in blue script, LAS VEGAS in large red capitals, NEVADA in blue, and a red and yellow eight-point star on a blue frame above.
images.caption: Carol M. Highsmith, Sign in daytime, Las Vegas, Nevada, 2007. Carol M. Highsmith’s America, [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/item/2010630140/); copy from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sign_in_daytime,_Las_Vegas,_Nevada_LCCN2010630140.tif).

rights.statement: Photograph: Carol M. Highsmith placed her archive in the public domain; Library of Congress advisory “No known restrictions on publication,” Commons license “Public domain.” Sign: designed in 1959 and displayed publicly with no copyright claim; Betty Willis never copyrighted it, and a United States work published before 1978 without notice entered the public domain. Wikipedia calls the public-domain account a legend, so the lead curator may want to confirm. The design may carry trademark uses by Clark County or YESCO; this record uses it only for commentary.

identifiers.commons: File:Sign in daytime, Las Vegas, Nevada LCCN2010630140.tif

references.summary: WHATWG Rendering section: the default link colors #0000EE and #551A8B, and h1 at 2em.

evidence.note: Read the Rendering section on 2026-10-02. A living standard changes, so the values are as of that date.

styles.note: Defines the exact default colors and sizes that the style’s tokens copy.

context: The expected style sheet contains `:link { color: #0000EE; }` and `:visited { color: #551A8B; }`.
It sets `:heading(1) { margin-block: 0.67em; font-size: 2.00em; }`, the same h1 size as [CSS 2 Appendix D](ref:css2-default-style-sheet-for-html).
interpretation: The source for the primary and secondary colors in the [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design) tokens.

references.title: Wikipedia iOS app 8.0 on iOS 26
references.lede: The Wikimedia Foundation’s iPhone app, version 8.0.0, whose floating glass tab bar and search button bend the photo that scrolls under them.
references.summary: A third-party app with a floating glass tab bar that visibly refracts the content. 2026.
references.made: 2026 (release tag releases/8.0.0 dated April 13, 2026; screenshot April 19, 2026)

evidence.note: Inspected the Commons screenshot IOS App 8.0.0 Explore.png (1179 × 2556) by EvanTech10, with a 1:1 crop of the tab bar. Also looked at the companion IOS App 8.0.0 Article.png. Not stored.

styles.note: A non-Apple app that adopts the system material: content-first pages under a floating glass tab bar that refracts at its rim.

context: The app is open source under the MIT license. Its code calls Apple’s glassEffect API, for example in WMFHomeView.swift and WMFFindInPageView.swift. [GitHub: wikimedia/wikipedia-ios](https://github.com/wikimedia/wikipedia-ios).

Apple Developer: standard SwiftUI, UIKit, and AppKit controls and navigation elements “pick up the appearance and behavior of this material automatically”. [Apple Developer: Liquid Glass](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technologyoverviews/liquid-glass).
observed: Dark mode. A “Today” feed with a serif featured-article card and a “Picture of the day” photo of a green and violet faceted glass dome.
At the top, the Wikipedia “W” sits in a separate dark glass circle on the left, and two icons share a dark glass capsule on the right. Neither is pinned to the screen edge.
At the bottom, a glass capsule holds four tabs (Explore, Places, Saved, Activity), and a separate glass circle holds the search icon. Both float over the photo.

In the 1:1 crop the straight frame lines of the dome curve into loops just inside the rims of the capsule and the circle, while the middle stays nearly undistorted. A thin bright line marks the rim. The selected tab sits in a lighter inner capsule.
The Article screenshot shows the same pattern: a back button, a “W” circle, and a three-icon capsule float over the lead image, and a toolbar capsule floats over the article text.
interpretation: Because the app uses system components, it shows the default behavior of the material that any developer gets, not an Apple marketing render.
borrow: Split navigation into a tab capsule and a separate search circle, so the most used action has its own target.

rights.statement: The Commons file is CC BY-SA 4.0 by EvanTech10, and the app code is MIT. It is kept as link only because the frame also shows Apple’s system interface and a picture of the day whose own license was not checked.

references.title: Wm. H. Page & Co., *Specimens of Chromatic Wood Type, Borders, &c.*
references.titleBreak: Wm. H. Page & Co.,|*Specimens of Chromatic Wood Type*
references.lede: The 1874 colour specimen book of the largest American wood type maker of its day, showing Tuscan, pointed, and shaded letters cut as separate blocks for each ink.
references.summary: Wood type specimen sheets with chromatic Tuscan and paneled gothic letters in ornament borders. Greeneville, Connecticut, 1874.

source.label: Internet Archive (Columbia University Libraries): Specimens of chromatic wood type, borders, etc.

evidence.note: Inspected two plates through Commons copies of photographs by Flickr user CircaSassy (818 × 1100 px each): [Tuscan plate](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pointed_and_Tuscan_wood_type,_Wm._H._Page_%26_Co.,_1874_specimen.jpg) and [paneled gothic plate](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Specimens_of_chromatic_wood_type,_borders,_etc._manufactured_by_Wm._H._Page_%26_Co._by_Wm._H._Page_%26_Co._Published_1874.jpg). The uploader names the Columbia scan as the source. I read the Internet Archive metadata, not the scan itself.

styles.note: The supply side of the style: the Tuscan, pointed, and shaded display letters that printers bought for posters. Partial fit: the chromatic colours are richer than most bills, which print in black and one ink.

context: The Internet Archive record gives the title, Greeneville, Connecticut, 1874, [98] leaves of colour illustrations, 47 cm, contributed by Columbia University Libraries, with the rights note “Digital version available with no restrictions.” [archive.org](https://archive.org/details/ldpd_10147342_000).

Wikipedia says William H. Page was one of the larger wood type makers until the 1880s, and that wood type came in widths from condensed to ultra-wide. [Wikipedia: Wood type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wood_type).
Each plate gives the type’s size in “lines” (picas) and its price per letter “each color”, and is “Printed with Wade’s Inks, from H. D. Wade & Co., 50 Ann St., New York.”
observed: Tuscan plate: the words MATCH, ROSE, and SIGN in light blue letters with white outlines on ochre panels with notched ends. The letters have pointed spurs and, in SIGN, forked Tuscan serifs.
Tuscan plate: a pink and black chain border with interlaced corner pieces frames the page.
Paneled plate: RIND and USE in green capitals with a white inline, a black outline, and a deep red three-dimensional shade, in two sizes.
Paneled plate: a red border of repeated heart-shaped ornaments inside a gold scroll border.
Small centred lines of roman text name each face, its size in lines, its class, and its price.
The maker’s name at the top is set in a shaded slab with a drop shadow.
interpretation: The book shows how printers got colour and depth from letterpress: separate wood blocks for the face, the outline, and the shade, printed one ink at a time.
Its letters are the vocabulary of the late wood type poster. The chromatic sets were the expensive end of a range that most country printers used in black.
borrow: Build a display letter from layers: a fill, a contrasting inline, and an offset shade in a third colour.
Frame a page with a repeating border and separate corner pieces.

images.alt: Specimen plate with a pink chain border. The words Match, Rose, and Sign in light blue Tuscan and pointed letters with white outlines sit on ochre panels with notched ends, with small captions naming each typeface.
images.caption: Wm. H. Page & Co., plate of chromatic streamer gothic pointed and antique Tuscan types, 1874. Photograph by CircaSassy, [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/), through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pointed_and_Tuscan_wood_type,_Wm._H._Page_%26_Co.,_1874_specimen.jpg).

images.alt: Specimen plate with a red and gold ornament border. The words Rind and Use in large green capitals with white inline, black outline, and a deep red three-dimensional shade.
images.caption: Wm. H. Page & Co., plate of chromatic gothic paneled No. 2, 1874. Photograph by CircaSassy, [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/), through [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Specimens_of_chromatic_wood_type,_borders,_etc._manufactured_by_Wm._H._Page_%26_Co._by_Wm._H._Page_%26_Co._Published_1874.jpg).

rights.statement: Commons licenses both photographs CC BY 2.0, credit CircaSassy (Flickr). The book was published in the United States in 1874 and is in the public domain; the Columbia scan is marked “Digital version available with no restrictions.”

references.title: WorldWideWeb browser and the first website (CERN)
references.lede: Tim Berners-Lee’s first browser and the CERN project page it displayed: the unstyled hypertext that web brutalism looks back to.
references.summary: CERN, 1990–1991: black text on white, underlined links, a plain heading, and a two-column link list.
references.made: 1990–1991 (browser and first pages); 2019 (CERN rebuild in a modern browser)

evidence.note: Opened Wikimedia Commons “[W3 First Website.png](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:W3_First_Website.png)” (1366 × 655 px, uploaded 8 November 2021) with the Read tool on 2026-10-02. It shows the first project page, info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html, in CERN’s 2019 browser rebuild, not on original NeXT hardware. Also viewed “WorldWideWeb.1.png” (834 × 642 px), a screenshot of the original NeXTSTEP application’s panels.

styles.note: Lineage: the unintended original of the look. Smashing Magazine (2020) calls the first website an “inadvertent disciple”.

references.notice: This is a lineage reference. The page was plain because early HTML had no styling, not by choice. Its sans-serif rendering comes from NeXTSTEP, not from later browser defaults.
context: [Smashing Magazine (2020)](ref:smashing-split-personality-brutalist-web-2020) names the first website as the first example of raw-HTML brutalism.

Commons tags both screenshots as public domain because “the whole project was released into the public domain in 1993”, citing CERN document record 1164399. That record was behind a bot check on 2026-10-02 and was not read. The NeXTSTEP screenshot itself shows “Copyright 1990,91,93,94, TBL, CERN. Distribution restricted: ask for terms.”
observed: In the rebuild, a white document window with a black title bar sits on a dark gray desktop beside a gray menu column (Info, Navigate, Document, Edit, Links, Style, Print).
The page has a bold, centered sans-serif heading, “World Wide Web”, and two indented paragraphs of black text.
Below them, a two-column list pairs underlined link titles (What’s out there?, Help, Software Products, Technical, Bibliography) with plain descriptions.
Links are black and underlined. There is no color, image, rule, or box on the page.
interpretation: The first page already shows the core of [Brutalist web design](style:brutalist-web-design): structure carried only by headings, paragraphs, lists, and underlines. Blue links came later, with browsers such as [NCSA Mosaic](ref:ncsa-mosaic-browser-1993).
borrow: Write link text that says where the link goes, and put a one-line plain description next to it.

rights.statement: Commons tags the screenshots public domain, but the status of the depicted interface is unclear (see context). Viewed at the source; not stored.

references.title: Zang Tumb Tumb
references.lede: F. T. Marinetti’s first book of words in freedom, about the siege of Adrianople: on its orange cover the sound “TUUUMB” fans out in three directions like a shell burst.
references.summary: Orange cover with heavy black grotesque type; TUUUMB, TUUUM, and PAROLE IN LIBERTÀ radiate from one point. F. T. Marinetti, Milan, 1914.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, Zang Tumb Tuum, 1914 (coll. priv.), photograph by Sailko

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected a photograph by the Commons user Sailko, 15 December 2019 (original 3978 × 3072 px; a 1280 × 988 px rendering was inspected and stored). It shows an open copy of the book in a display case; the file title says the copy is in a private collection, and the exhibition is not named. The copy has a later red binding with marbled boards, and a strip of tape or paper covers the right edge of the cover. Only the cover was seen; the inner pages were not inspected.

styles.note: The founding book of words in freedom. Its cover sets onomatopoeia in heavy grotesques that radiate from a point, on a loud colored paper.

context: *Zang Tumb Tumb* was Marinetti’s first published collection of parole in libertà. Begun in 1912 and published in 1914, it recounts his experience of the siege of Adrianople in the First Balkan War, which he covered as a war correspondent. [Wikipedia: Zang Tumb Tumb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zang_Tumb_Tumb).
The cover names the publisher as Edizioni futuriste di “Poesia”, Corso Venezia 61, Milan, 1914.

Wikipedia says the Vorticist magazine BLAST was directly influenced by the book. [Wikipedia: Futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism). The Museum of Modern Art holds a copy ([MoMA 31450](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/31450)); its page refused scripted access.
observed: The cover is a saturated orange paper printed in black only.
“F. T. MARINETTI FUTURISTA” is a small line of capitals at the top.
“ZANG” is set in a condensed capital, tilted upward; “TUMB TUMB” below it is a very heavy, wide grotesque, horizontal and the largest type on the page.
“ADRIANOPOLI OTTOBRE 1912” is a line of spaced bold capitals.

From one point, three lines radiate: “TUUUMB” in large capitals up to the left, “PAROLE IN LIBERTÀ” up to the right in smaller capitals, and a run of “TUUUM” words stepping down to the right, each smaller than the one before.
“PAROLE” runs vertically downward from the same point; the publisher’s imprint below is a small serif set on a slight curve.
interpretation: The cover is a compact lesson in the style: four or more type styles, words at several angles, one dominant word much larger than the rest, and a radiating composition that reads as an explosion.
The stepped, shrinking “TUUUM” words show sound fading with distance, a typographic version of motion by repetition.
borrow: Radiate three lines of type from one point at different angles to suggest a burst.
Repeat a word and make each repetition smaller to show it fading away.
Print black on a single loud colored paper, such as orange.

images.alt: Open book in a display case. The orange cover reads F. T. Marinetti futurista, ZANG, and TUMB TUMB in very heavy black type, then Adrianopoli ottobre 1912. Below, the words TUUUMB, PAROLE IN LIBERTÀ, and a series of shrinking TUUUM words radiate from one point.
images.caption: F. T. Marinetti, *Zang Tumb Tumb*, Edizioni futuriste di “Poesia”, Milan, 1914, copy in a private collection. Photograph by Sailko, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Filippo_tommaso_marinetti,_zang_tumb_tuum._adrianpoli_1912._parole_in_libert%C3%A0,_1914_(coll._priv.).jpg), CC BY 3.0.

rights.statement: Photograph by Sailko, licensed CC BY 3.0 on Wikimedia Commons. Marinetti was Italian and died in 1944, more than 70 years ago, so the book is public domain in Italy. It was published in 1914, before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States.

identifiers.commons: File:Filippo tommaso marinetti, zang tumb tuum. adrianpoli 1912. parole in libertà, 1914 (coll. priv.).jpg

references.title: Zang Tumb Tuuum, collage
references.lede: F. T. Marinetti cut words and black hairpin shapes out of printed matter from his book Zang Tumb Tumb and pasted them into a fanning bombardment of sound.
references.summary: Pasted strips read BUM BUM BUM and ZANG TUMB TUUUM inside fanned black hairpin shapes. F. T. Marinetti, 1915.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti - ZANG TUMB TUUUM 1915.jpg

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (original 2048 × 1408 px; a 1280 × 880 px rendering was inspected and stored). Commons gives the source as the Sotheby’s sale “Zang Tumb Tuuum: la révolution futuriste” (Paris, 2021). The physical work is the single original collage offered there; its present owner is not known. The Sotheby’s lot page loads only with JavaScript, so its details come from a search summary and are not verified.

styles.note: Words in freedom made physical: onomatopoeia in heavy type, set at angles inside repeated shapes that fan out like a burst of shells.

context: The Commons description gives the full title of the poem as “BOOOOOMBOOOOOMBAAAAARDAAAMENTO. BUM BUM BUM. ZANG TUMB TUUUM” and describes the work as an original collage of typographical letters and shapes on paper. [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Filippo_Tommaso_Marinetti_-_ZANG_TUMB_TUUUM_1915.jpg).

According to a search summary of the [Sotheby’s lot](https://www.sothebys.com/en/buy/auction/2021/zang-tumb-tuuum-la-revolution-futuriste/marinetti-zang-tumb-tuuum-1915-historic-collage-2) (not opened), the sheet measures about 21 × 31 cm, Marinetti numbered it in blue pencil, and he cut the fragments from the book *Zang Tumb Tumb* published in 1914.
*Zang Tumb Tumb* (1914) recounts the siege of Adrianople in the First Balkan War, which Marinetti reported on in 1912. [Wikipedia: Zang Tumb Tumb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zang_Tumb_Tumb).
observed: Three black hairpin or U shapes, cut from paper, fan out from the lower left, each larger than the one before; a fourth thin one sits at the top.
Inside the largest, three pasted labels read “ZANG”, “TUMB”, and “TUUUM” in a heavy condensed grotesque, rising along the shape.
Inside the middle one, “BUM BUM BUM” is set in a condensed serif at an angle.
A narrow strip at upper right reads “BOOOOOMBOOOOOMBAAAAARDAAAMENTO” in small condensed capitals, horizontal.
A black pointed shape like a shell or a tower stands at the lower left edge.
Blue pencil scribble and the number “72” are at the upper left. The sheet is off-white, creased, and stained around the pasted parts.
interpretation: The work shows the grammar of words in freedom in its plainest form: shapes repeat and grow along a path, and the sound words ride along them like projectiles. Only black and the paper tone are used, so the motion comes entirely from the angles and the repetition.
The mix of a heavy grotesque, a condensed serif, and small capitals is typical of Marinetti’s pages.
borrow: Put the loudest words inside a repeated shape that grows along a diagonal, so the shape carries the words.
Set each word of an onomatopoeic phrase in its own block, stepped upward.
Contrast one very long, very small line of type with a few huge words.

images.alt: Collage on creased off-white paper: three black hairpin shapes fan out from the lower left, growing larger. Pasted labels inside them read BUM BUM BUM and ZANG, TUMB, TUUUM in heavy type. A small strip at top right reads BOOOOOMBOOOOOMBAAAAARDAAAMENTO, and blue pencil marks a number 72 at top left.
images.caption: F. T. Marinetti, *Zang Tumb Tuuum*, 1915, collage of printed paper on paper. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Filippo_Tommaso_Marinetti_-_ZANG_TUMB_TUUUM_1915.jpg), sourced from Sotheby’s (2021), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain. Marinetti was Italian and died in 1944, more than 70 years ago, so the work is public domain in Italy. It dates from 1915; if it was published, that was before 1931, and if unpublished, its author died more than 70 years ago, so it is public domain in the United States either way. The image is a faithful reproduction of a flat work.
